documents.title: Humanitarian Coalition’s Venezuela Earthquake Response appeal raises more than $7.5 million for life-saving aid
documents.body_text:
*With support from generous Canadians and the Government of Canada, our members are reaching more than 40,000 people with critical assistance*

After back-to-back earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, Canadians rallied to support people affected through the Humanitarian Coalition’s Venezuela Earthquake Response. With the Government of Canada’s matching fund, the appeal raised more than **$7.5 million** from June 25 to July 14, 2026.

"We’re very moved by the generosity of Canadians," said Tiffany Baggetta, Executive Director of the Humanitarian Coalition. “Every dollar given and every dollar matched will help our members deliver life-saving relief to families affected by the Venezuela earthquakes. We’re extremely grateful to our donors, our community and media partners, and the Government of Canada for standing with communities as they continue to face the devastating impacts of displacement and destruction.”

In temporary camps and affected communities, the Humanitarian Coalition’s 12 member organizations are working tirelessly to provide essential support, such as:

- **Emergency food assistance** for families living in temporary shelters and other affected communities.
- **Safe water, sanitation and hygiene services**, including water trucking, handwashing stations, water treatment supplies and hygiene promotion activities.
- **Shelter and essential household items**, such as shelter kits, mattresses and kitchen supplies for families who have lost their homes and belongings.
- **Health services**, including mental health and psychosocial support, community health activities and rehabilitation services for people injured by the earthquakes.
- **Protection services** for families, including child-friendly spaces and psychosocial support.
- **Nutrition programs**, such as malnutrition screening for children, treatment and referral for acute malnutrition cases, and nutrition counselling.
- **Support for people with disabilities** and those recovering from serious injuries.

As humanitarian needs in Venezuela remain high, the Humanitarian Coalition is continuing to accept donations for the[ **Venezuela Emergency Response**](https://donate.humanitariancoalition.ca/ui/RS262E/donations/start).

**Notes:**

The Humanitarian Coalition is immensely grateful to the following supporters and charitable partners for their contributions to the Venezuela Emergency Response: Bell Media, CanadaHelps, Canadaland, Canadian Affairs, CanadianSME, CHOQFM, Cogeco Média, Corus, Fairchild Radio, Golden West Media, Jazz 91.1 FM, Métro, Rabble, Rogers tv, SJC, The Free Press, The Globe and Mail, The Walrus, TLN Media Group and Venezuelan Canadian Society of British Columbia.

documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #19 (31 de julio al 3 de agosto 2026)
documents.body_text:
El Reporte de Situación No. 19 presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, cubriendo el período comprendido entre el 31 de julio y el 3 de agosto de 2026.

## Aspectos destacados

Entre el 31 de julio y el 3 de agosto, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación y gestión de campamentos, salud, protección, Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene (WASH), gestión de información y Prevención de la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS).

Durante el período, la OIM distribuyó **245 lonas plásticas, 234 lámparas solares, 234 bidones plegables, 235 sets de cocina, 227 kits de higiene y 74 mosquiteros** para atender necesidades prioritarias de alojamiento y enseres domésticos de familias afectadas por los terremotos.

A la fecha, los equipos apoyados por la OIM han realizado **7.615 consultas médicas a 6.733 personas afectadas** mediante servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas.

La OIM inició la caracterización de asentamientos comunitarios afectados por los terremotos, alcanzando **20 asentamientos en La Guaira, uno en Miranda y uno en Carabobo**, ampliando el monitoreo de necesidades y desplazamiento fuera de los campamentos transitorios.

## Actividades de la OIM

La OIM continuó la cogestión de cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Polideportivo José María Vargas, Playa Grande y César Nieves, apoyando la prestación de servicios, el registro de población, los mecanismos de información comunitaria y la coordinación operativa.

En Campo de Golf continuó la asignación de nuevas carpas familiares, la ampliación de iluminación solar y la adecuación de espacios comunitarios y de atención. En Mare Abajo II inició el abordaje comunitario para promover los servicios disponibles, identificar necesidades y fortalecer los canales de comunicación con la población alojada, mientras continuaron las actividades de registro y verificación de grupos familiares. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se mantuvieron servicios esenciales para **796 personas pertenecientes a 221 grupos familiares**, incluyendo registro, orientación comunitaria, conectividad y restablecimiento de contacto familiar.

Durante el período, la OIM distribuyó **245 lonas plásticas, 234 lámparas solares, 234 bidones plegables, 235 sets de cocina, 227 kits de higiene y 74 mosquiteros**. A la fecha, la OIM ha entregado **4.987 sets de cocina, 4.580 lonas plásticas, 3.441 lámparas solares, 3.313 bidones plegables, 2.527 kits de higiene, 2.384 baldes, 1.066 mosquiteros y 822 kits de refugio para emergencias** a familias afectadas por los terremotos.

En WASH, la OIM continuó ampliando el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento mediante la activación de un sistema de agua potable en Campo de Golf, actividades de monitoreo de calidad del agua, cloración, mejoras de infraestructura sanitaria y apoyo a la gestión de residuos. A la fecha, la OIM ha distribuido **3.313 bidones plegables de 10 litros, 285 bidones semiplegables de 10 litros y 2.527 kits de higiene**.

La OIM y su socio implementador Ven Da Tu Mano continuaron prestando servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico mediante equipos móviles. Durante el período se realizaron **90 consultas** en César Nieves, mientras que las jornadas móviles en el Polideportivo José María Vargas alcanzaron un acumulado de **2.509 consultas**. A la fecha, las intervenciones apoyadas por la OIM han permitido realizar **7.615 consultas médicas a 6.733 personas afectadas**.

La OIM continuó las actividades de registro y gestión de información mediante el Sistema Unificado de Gestión de Información (IMS) en los cinco campamentos transitorios. Durante el período, inició el levantamiento de información en asentamientos comunitarios afectados por los terremotos, logrando caracterizar **20 asentamientos en La Guaira, uno en Miranda y uno en Carabobo**, mientras equipos de la Matriz de Seguimiento de Desplazamiento (DTM) realizaron evaluaciones adicionales en Carabobo.

En protección, la OIM continuó brindando asistencia legal, gestión de casos, actividades de protección infantil, prevención de la trata de personas, prevención de la violencia contra mujeres y niñas y mecanismos de información comunitaria. Asimismo, inició actividades de abordaje comunitario en Mare Abajo II y apoyó la coordinación de una jornada de documentación que permitió a **182 personas** acceder a servicios de cedulación.

Como colíder del Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales junto con ACNUR, la OIM continuó apoyando la coordinación operativa, el mapeo de servicios, la gestión de información y la planificación conjunta en los campamentos transitorios.

En PEAS, la OIM realizó sesiones de refrescamiento con **24 trabajadores humanitarios**, distribuyó **1.000 volantes informativos y mensajes clave** al equipo de NFI y llevó a cabo actividades de sensibilización con **15 lideresas comunitarias** y **17 trabajadores humanitarios** en Playa Grande.

## Respuesta Prevista de la OIM

La OIM continuará fortaleciendo la infraestructura, la prestación de servicios, las intervenciones WASH, el apoyo en alojamiento y las actividades de Coordinación y Gestión de Campamentos (CCCM) en los campamentos transitorios.

La OIM también continuará prestando servicios de salud, salud mental, apoyo psicológico y protección, al tiempo que fortalecerá los mecanismos de derivación para asistencia especializada.

Asimismo, mantendrá el monitoreo de movilidad, las actividades de registro, la gestión de información, las evaluaciones en asentamientos comunitarios y la coordinación con autoridades y organizaciones implementadoras para apoyar la planificación de una respuesta basada en evidencia.

documents.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #19 (31 July to 3 August 2026)
documents.body_text:
The nineteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 31 July to 3 August 2026.

## Highlights

Between 31 July and 3 August, IOM continued its multisectoral response in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities through interventions in shelter and camp coordination and management, health, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA).

During the reporting period, IOM distributed **245 plastic tarpaulins, 234 solar lamps, 234 collapsible water containers, 235 kitchen sets, 227 hygiene kits and 74 mosquito nets** to address priority shelter and household needs of earthquake-affected families.

To date, IOM-supported teams have delivered **7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people** through health, mental health and psychological support services in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities.

IOM initiated the characterization of earthquake-affected community settlements, reaching **20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo**, expanding needs and displacement monitoring beyond temporary accommodation sites.

## IOM Activities

IOM continued co-managing five temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, Playa Grande and Cesar Nieves, supporting service delivery, population registration, community information services and operational coordination.

At Campo de Golf, the allocation of new family tents, expansion of solar lighting and improvement of community and service spaces continued. At Mare Abajo II, community outreach activities began to promote available services, identify needs and strengthen communication channels with site residents, while household registration and verification activities continued. At Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for **796 people from 221 households**, including registration, community orientation, connectivity and restoring family links.

During the reporting period, IOM distributed **245 plastic tarpaulins, 234 solar lamps, 234 collapsible water containers, 235 kitchen sets, 227 hygiene kits and 74 mosquito nets** to earthquake-affected families. To date, IOM has delivered **4,987 kitchen sets, 4,580 plastic tarpaulins, 3,441 solar lamps, 3,313 collapsible water containers, 2,527 hygiene kits, 2,384 buckets, 1,066 mosquito nets and 822 emergency shelter kits**.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water and sanitation services through the activation of a potable water system at Campo de Golf, water quality monitoring, chlorination activities, sanitation infrastructure improvements and waste management support. To date, IOM has provided **3,313 collapsible 10-liter water containers, 285 semi-collapsible 10-liter water containers and 2,527 hygiene kits**.

IOM and its implementing partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued delivering health, mental health and psychological support services through mobile teams. During the reporting period, **90 consultations** were conducted in Cesar Nieves, while mobile health services at Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex reached a cumulative total of **2,509 consultations**. To date, IOM-supported interventions have provided **7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people**.

IOM continued registration and information management activities through the unified Information Management System (IMS) across the five temporary accommodation sites. During the reporting period, IOM initiated data collection in earthquake-affected community settlements, characterizing **20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo**, while Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) teams conducted additional assessments in Carabobo.

In protection, IOM continued providing legal assistance, case management, child protection activities, trafficking in persons prevention, violence against women and girls prevention and community information services. Community outreach activities were launched in Mare Abajo II, and IOM supported the coordination of a documentation campaign that enabled **182 people** to access national identification services.

As co-lead of the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group together with UNHCR, IOM continued supporting operational coordination, service mapping, information management and joint planning across temporary accommodation sites.

In PSEA, IOM conducted refresher sessions with **24 humanitarian workers**, distributed **1,000 informational leaflets and key messages** to NFI teams, and carried out awareness activities with **15 community leaders** and **17 humanitarian workers** in Playa Grande.

## IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue strengthening infrastructure, service delivery, WASH interventions, shelter support and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) activities in temporary accommodation sites.

IOM will also continue delivering health, mental health, psychological support and protection services while strengthening referral pathways for specialized assistance.

In addition, IOM will maintain mobility monitoring, registration activities, information management, community settlement assessments and coordination with authorities and implementing organizations to support evidence-based response planning.

documents.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #05 (Reporting period: 24 – 31 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
*This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.*

**Summary Points**

• Since 05 July, an inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator has been deployed in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination and lead efforts to identify connectivity gaps and operational requirements for targeted humanitarian response support. A new inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator will assume the role on 03 August and continue supporting the response.

• The inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator is working with UN OCHA, Comisión Nacional de Telecomunicaciones (CONATEL), Compañía Anónima Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar, Digitel, G-Network, emergency.lu, Grupo Telefónica, and other partners to deploy connectivity solutions in the most affected areas.

• Through the Internet for Communities solution, GNetwork’s fibre internet connection will remain free for all users at Polideportivo, César Nieves, and a third site until the end of the year or until the emergency ends. This helps address immediate concerns related to service contracts and recurring connectivity costs.

Venezuela: Earthquakes
LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #05
Reporting period: 24 – 31 July 2026
This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026
(magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for
the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.
Summary Points
• Since 05 July, an inter-agency LTC Telecoms
Coordinator has been deployed in Caracas to
strengthen in-country coordination and lead efforts
to identify connectivity gaps and operational
requirements for targeted humanitarian response
support. A new inter-agency LTC Telecoms
Coordinator will assume the role on 03 August and
continue supporting the response.
• The inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator is
working with UN OCHA, Comisión Nacional de
Telecomunicaciones (CONATEL), Compañía Anónima
Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV),
Movistar, Digitel, G-Network, emergency.lu, Grupo
Telefónica, and other partners to deploy connectivity
solutions in the most affected areas. A solar powered charging kiosk is established
in César Nieves to support affected
• Through the Internet for Communities solution, G- communities and humanitarian responders to
recharge their ICT devices.
Network’s fibre internet connection will remain free Photo: WFP/Francisco Garrido.
for all users at Polideportivo, César Nieves, and a
third site until the end of the year or until the
emergency ends. This helps address immediate concerns related to service contracts and
recurring connectivity costs.
Situation Overview
The humanitarian situation in Venezuela remained severe during 24 – 31 July, driven primarily by the
aftermath of the devastating 24 June earthquakes, which compounded pre-existing vulnerabilities
linked to food insecurity, weakened public services, and chronic humanitarian needs. One month after
the disaster, humanitarian actors continued to scale up life-saving assistance while recovery and
reconstruction efforts of civil infrastructure advanced in heavily affected areas, particularly La Guaira,
Caracas Metropolitan Area, Petare, and Catia.
1 The ETC and Logistics Cluster have been merged into the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), following the humanitarian reset in 2025.
Bringing logistics and emergency telecommunications under one coordination structure, the WFP-led LTC is the backbone of the entire humanitarian
response, enabling humanitarian action to move, communicate, coordinate, and deliver lifesaving assistance.
Page 1 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

Food security remained a major concern. Many households reported reducing meal portions and
skipping meals, while disrupted livelihoods and constrained market access continued to affect
recovery. In response, WFP had provided food assistance to more than 120,000 people through hot
meals, food baskets, ready-to-eat rations, and electronic vouchers, while planning to reach up to
500,000 people during the initial response phase
Despite extensive relief efforts, humanitarian organizations warned that substantial funding gaps and
growing recovery needs could hamper the response. International partners continued to appeal for
additional resources to support emergency assistance, early recovery, livelihood restoration, and
reconstruction efforts. Humanitarian actors emphasized that the earthquake had intensified an already
fragile humanitarian context, where millions of Venezuelans required assistance even before the
disaster struck.
Telecommunications Overview
Telecommunications and electricity remained among the most severely impacted sectors following the
earthquakes. Although targeted emergency interventions and repair works have restored partial
telecommunications services in key population centres, damaged network infrastructure, power
instability, and intermittent connectivity disruptions persist across La Guaira, Petare, Catia, and other
affected communities.
Reliable communications remain essential for humanitarian coordination, information management, and
access to assistance. While mobile network operators (MNOs), including CANTV, Movistar, and Digitel,
maintained operations across most of the country, localized outages and reduced network
performance continued in earthquake-affected areas. Service providers and authorities are actively
restoring damaged infrastructure; however, sustained operational support is required to stabilize
connectivity and close remaining coverage gaps.
At the same time, damage to electricity transmission and distribution networks continues to disrupt
households, health facilities, water systems, telecommunications equipment, and temporary
displacement sites. These power constraints are slowing the restoration of essential services and
complicating broader recovery efforts. Accelerated investment in telecommunications and energy
infrastructure repairs, complemented by emergency connectivity solutions, remains critical to restoring
reliable communications, strengthening humanitarian response capabilities, and supporting the long-
term recovery of affected communities.
LTC Telecoms Activities
Coordination
Since 05 July, an inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator has been deployed in Caracas to strengthen
in-country coordination and lead efforts to identify connectivity gaps and operational requirements for
targeted humanitarian response support. A new inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator will assume
the role on 03 August and continue supporting the response. The Coordinator is working with OCHA,
CONATEL, CANTV, Movistar, Digitel, G-Network, emergency.lu, Grupo Telefónica, and other partners
to deploy connectivity solutions in the most affected areas.
Coordination and planning are channelled through the country-level ICT Working Group and inter-
agency focal points to avoid duplication, reduce Starlink congestion, improve network design, share
local contacts and engage mobile network operators on recovery plans. This mechanism enables WFP,
Page 2 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

UN agencies, NGOs, technical partners, local providers and government counterparts to share
information and align deployments.
Government authorities have supported humanitarian response efforts, with field teams generally able
to access sites, pass checkpoints using UN identification and secure installation permissions.
CONATEL has been key in facilitating telecoms authorizations and site access, while responders
remain prepared for a timeline dependent on government approval.
Internet connectivity
A combination of Starlink kits and the Internet Service for Communities solution continue to provide
connectivity for humanitarian responders and affected population across the response priority
locations.
Starlink kits continues to provide essential connectivity for inter-agency services at Polideportivo,
César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande. Playa Grande remains highly uncertain after authorities
initially indicated the camp would close on 17 July. Although it remains operational to date, the risk of
sudden closure continues to constrain planning and limits the team’s ability to commit to longer-term
infrastructure investments. The community internet solution originally planned for Playa Grande may be
redirected to the new camp location if relocation proceeds. If deployment at the relocated site is not
feasible, Playa Verde remains the alternative option for the pending community connectivity package.
Polideportivo has reliable Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) services while local ISPs are also offering
free internet connectivity to the affected population at the site. For this reason, the team is not
currently planning to deploy a separate community internet service at Polideportivo, as affected
populations already have access to multiple free connectivity options. Despite occasional congestion,
inter-agency Starlink connectivity at Polideportivo is available for the WFP, United Nations High
Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), United Nations
Population Fund (UNFPA) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) personnel.
Power supply
LTC Telecoms is improving power continuity at Polideportivo and César Nieves sites by monitoring
battery systems supporting solar-powered internet. This provides timely visibility on power gaps,
enabling teams to adjust configurations, add batteries and keep critical connectivity operational for
responders and affected communities. Each camp has 800 watts of solar capacity with energy
batteries, enough to power internet equipment and related connectivity infrastructure. This efficient
model may be replicated at future sites to reduce reliance on La Guaira’s unstable public grid.
Grupo Telefónica provided charging kiosks at Polideportivo and César Nieves, each with 48 power-
strip connections for affected people to charge phones and other ICT devices. The kiosks will be
returned to Grupo Telefónica once the emergency fully transitions to recovery.
Services for communities
The Internet Service for Communities initiative was developed through coordination among
emergency.lu, CONATEL, WFP, and local Internet Service Provider (ISP) G-Network. Its technical
design enables connectivity across multiple sites, and since 13 July the service has been operational at
Polideportivo and César Nieves Stadium. Users can move between sites without additional approvals
or login credentials. Connectivity, delivered through G-Network’s fibre connection, is free for all users
until the end of the year or until the emergency concludes. G-Network confirmed that it will provide
free internet service for all three Internet for Communities sites through this period, removing
immediate concerns over service contracts and recurrent connectivity costs.
Page 3 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

Polideportivo, and Cesar Nieves Stadium sites are registering 99 percent service availability,
demonstrating that the current mix of solar power, Eco Flow batteries, Starlink kits, and partner
connectivity is supporting reliable service delivery. Cesar Nieves is consuming 877 GB of data, while
Polideportivo is consuming 1.2 TB. Registered clients exceed 3,000 at each site, although active user
numbers are declining. The inter-agency LTC Telecoms coordinator views this trend as an important
operational signal and are planning field assessments to understand whether the decline is linked to
population movement between camps, changing community needs, or other access-related factors.
Information Management
A dedicated LTC Telecoms emergency operations page was established to provide operational
updates and response information.
Visit the LTC Telecoms Dashboard for an overview of planned and active services.
LTC Telecoms and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) activated the Disaster
Connectivity Map (DCM) on 25 June to monitor connectivity impacts across affected areas. The DCM
is integrated into LogIE for Venezuela to support operational planning.
Funding
Donor engagement remains ongoing as humanitarian funding requirements are consolidated under the
forthcoming Flash Appeal.
The US Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA) has committed USD 9 million, with a further USD 6
million under processing, bringing the expected total contribution to USD 15 million. Funding is
primarily focused on humanitarian supply chain operations and the delivery of emergency assistance.
The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) has allocated USD 15 million for the earthquake
response, of which approximately USD 2 million is expected to be allocated to WFP.
Meetings
A Global LTC Telecoms Partner Teleconference was held on 27 July at 14:00 UTC to support
information exchange and coordination. Minutes of the meeting are available here.
LTC Logistics Area
For more information on the logistics component of the LTC response, a dedicated Venezuela logistics
webpage is available here with the latest updates on working group meetings, key documents, maps,
and available support.
The latest LTC Logistics Situation Report is available here.
Page 4 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

Challenges
Equipment security: Connectivity equipment remains exposed in several locations. In the absence of
secure storage, equipment must be dismantled each evening and reinstalled each morning, increasing
the risk of damage, loss, delayed start-up, and service interruptions.
Fuel movement restrictions: Generator operations are constrained by challenges associated with
transporting fuel between sites.
Evolving site requirements: Population growth at existing sites and the emergence of new locations,
such as Playa Verde, require continuous reassessment of connectivity and power needs.
Contacts

Global LTC Telecoms
Phyza Jameel Remote Phyza.Jameel@wfp.org
Deputy Coordinator
Global LTC Telecoms
Mufaro Masuka Information Management Remote Mufaro.Masuka@wfp.org
Officer
More information: www.etcluster.org/emergency/venezuela-earthquakes

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Country Appeal (July - December 2026)
documents.body_text:
Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck on 24 June 2026. The states most affected include La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and neighbouring areas.

The loss of livelihoods, disruption of health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of gender-based violence and harmful coping mechanisms, especially among women, girls and adolescents.

The health system is under severe strain. Many health facilities have sustained structural damage and are facing critical shortages of medicines, medical equipment and personnel, while disruptions to electricity, water supply and supply chains continue to hamper service delivery.

To respond to the crisis, UNFPA is seeking US$10 million to scale up life-saving sexual and reproductive health services and strengthen gender-based violence prevention and response across the affected areas.

UNFPA is targeting 64,000 people with life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, including emergency obstetric care, antenatal and postnatal care, neonatal care, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, family planning services, clinical management of rape, and essential reproductive health information.

In addition, UNFPA is aiming to reach 57,780 people through gender-based violence prevention and response programmes, providing case management, psychosocial support, psychological first aid, the distribution of dignity kits, and awareness sessions on risk mitigation and available support services for survivors.

As humanitarian needs continue to grow, these interventions are critical to protecting the health, rights and dignity of those most at risk, preventing further loss of life, and ensuring continued access to essential care as affected communities recover and rebuild.

Venezuela Earthquakes
Country Appeal
July - December 2026
Snapshot
On 24 June, two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 on the Richter scale
struck the northern area of Venezuela, causing widespread devastation.
The most urgent needs for affected populations are healthcare, including
sexual and reproductive health (SRH); safe water; food; shelter; mental
health and psychosocial support; sanitation and hygiene; and specialized
protection services, particularly for gender-based violence (GBV).
The loss of livelihoods, disruptions to health and protection services, and
precarious living conditions—especially for those residing in temporary
shelters—is increasing the risk of GBV and harmful coping strategies,
particularly for women, girls and adolescents. Older persons and people
with disabilities also face heightened vulnerabilities and additional
barriers to accessing information and protection services.
The health system is under immense strain. Many facilities have
sustained structural damage; face shortages of medicines, equipment
and staff; as well as disruptions to electricity, water supply, and supply
chains. This is impacting the continuity of SRH services, including
prenatal care and emergency obstetric care.
UNFPA has been responding to the crisis to scale up life-saving SRH
services and strengthen GBV prevention and response. It requires
US$10 million to reach 121,780 people with prenatal care, family
planning, psychosocial support, clinical management of rape, provision
of reproductive health supplies, and other critical health and protection
services.

UNFPA Venezuela Earthquakes Appeal / Venezuela / July - December 2026
Situation Overview
Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes and
almost 1,500 aftershocks. The states most affected include La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda,
Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and neighbouring areas. To date, 5,398 people are reported to have died
and 16,740 injured.1
Authorities indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes. Currently, 23,350 people are residing in
107 transitional shelters, where conditions such as overcrowding, limited privacy in sleeping
arrangements and bathroom facilities, and insufficient lighting are increasing the risk of GBV.
The high number of injuries, coupled with damage to health facilities, has impacted both routine and
emergency care. The disruption of health services and diversion of resources to trauma care has
particularly serious consequences for SRH.
Infants, pregnant women, and breastfeeding mothers face an increased risk of malnutrition due to
rising food insecurity, disruptions to health services, and acute stress.
The earthquakes have not only caused widespread destruction but have also exposed and
exacerbated gaps in access to healthcare, protection, and essential services, leaving the most
vulnerable populations at even greater risk.
Target Population
1.3 million 368,420 19,290 64,000 57,780
Total people Women of Estimated pregnant People targeted w/ People targeted w/
affected2 reproductive age3 women3 SRH services GBV programmes
UNFPA Response Strategy
Existing national response capacities are stretched, leaving critical gaps in SRH services, GBV
prevention and response, and mental health and psychosocial support. UNFPA’s interventions are
essential to addressing these gaps by ensuring the availability of life-saving SRH and protection
services, as well as psychosocial support for women, girls, adolescents, older persons, and other
vulnerable populations.
With a strong operational presence, longstanding partnerships, and leadership in SRH and GBV,
UNFPA is uniquely positioned to respond rapidly, including in hard-to-reach and underserved
communities. Fully aligned with national priorities and the Humanitarian Response Plan for
Venezuela, UNFPA’s response strengthens national capacities while ensuring that the most
vulnerable populations receive timely, integrated, and quality services.
1 OCHA. Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #30 (22 July 2026). Figure updated from 2.3 million in earlier reports.
2 Venezuela Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum. June 2026 Earthquakes.

UNFPA Venezuela Earthquakes Appeal / Venezuela / July - December 2026
Sexual and reproductive health priorities
UNFPA is supporting national and provincial authorities to ensure the continuity of life-saving
maternal, newborn and obstetric care. In maternity wards of hospitals across La Guaira, Caracas,
and Miranda, UNFPA is:
● Delivering critical medical equipment and reproductive health supplies.
● Providing on-the-job training for health personnel.
At displacement shelters, UNFPA and implementing partners are delivering critical sexual and
reproductive health services, including:
● Antenatal care for pregnant women.
● Referrals for emergency obstetric care.
● Family planning services, including providing contraceptives and distributing condoms.
● Testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
● Clinical management of rape.
● Conducting SRH awareness and information sessions on prenatal care, family planning
services and STI prevention.
Gender-based violence priorities
UNFPA is delivering GBV services for women and adolescent girls through both mobile and static
facilities in transitional shelters in La Guaira, providing safe spaces to deliver:
● Psychosocial support and psychological first aid.
● GBV case management.
● Legal counselling.
● Dignity kits containing essential items for health and menstrual hygiene management,
along with key messages on the prevention of GBV and information on available services.
● GBV awareness-raising and information sessions on GBV risk mitigation and available
support services.
● Conducting safety audits and risk and needs assessments in displacement shelters and
providing technical recommendations on improvements to site planning and
strengthening risk mitigation interventions.
● Training frontline responders in temporary shelters on protection from sexual
exploitation and abuse (PSEA), covering safeguarding, safe camp management,
psychological first aid, and referral pathways.
As the lead agency for the GBV Area of Responsibility (AoR) in Venezuela, UNFPA coordinates
inter-agency GBV prevention and response efforts among 72 partners, including UN agencies,
international NGOs, national organizations, and women-led and women’s rights organizations.
Through this coordination role, UNFPA strengthens collaboration, improves service delivery,
enhances operational coordination, and reduces duplication of interventions.
