documents.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #04 (Reporting period: 15 - 23 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
*This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.*

**Summary Points**

• LTC Telecoms in Venezuela is working with government authorities, mobile network operators, internet service providers (ISPs), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), and other partners to restore critical communications, and prioritize support in the most affected areas.

• LTC Telecoms is strengthening power continuity across response sites through real-time monitoring of battery systems linked to solar-powered internet connectivity. This provides timely visibility on energy gaps, allowing teams to monitor and take corrective action to keep critical internet connectivity services operational for over 1,400 humanitarian responders and affected communities.

• Grupo Telefónica has provided a charging kiosk at each of Polideportivo and César Nieves, supporting 48 power-strip connections, enabling affected people to charge mobile phones and other Information Communication Technology (ICT) devices to maintain access to communication, information and basic services. The kiosks will be returned to Grupo Telefónica once the emergency transitions fully into recovery.

Venezuela: Earthquakes
LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #04
Reporting period: 15 – 23 July 2026
This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026
(magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for
the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.
Summary Points
• LTC Telecoms in Venezuela is working with
government authorities, mobile network operators,
internet service providers (ISPs), the UN Office for
the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA),
and other partners to restore critical
communications, and prioritize support in the most
affected areas.
• LTC Telecoms is strengthening power continuity
across response sites through real-time monitoring
of battery systems linked to solar-powered internet
connectivity. This provides timely visibility on energy
gaps, allowing teams to monitor and take corrective
action to keep critical internet connectivity services
operational for over 1,400 humanitarian responders
and affected communities. Internet connectivity and solar power is
established in César Nieves to support
• Grupo Telefónica has provided a charging kiosk at
affected communities and humanitarian
responders. Photo: WFP/Francisco Garrido.
each of Polideportivo and César Nieves, supporting
48 power-strip connections, enabling affected
people to charge mobile phones and other
Information Communication Technology (ICT) devices to maintain access to communication,
information and basic services. The kiosks will be returned to Grupo Telefónica once the
emergency transitions fully into recovery.
Situation Overview
The humanitarian response remains active and is shifting from immediate lifesaving operations to
sustained recovery support. Between 15 and 23 July, the response to Venezuela's 24 June magnitude
7.2 and 7.5 twin earthquakes entered a transition phase from large-scale search and rescue toward
displacement management, restoration of critical services, and sustained humanitarian support.
Humanitarian partners continued scaling assistance while telecommunications actors focused on
1 The ETC and Logistics Cluster have been merged into the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), following the humanitarian reset in 2025.
Bringing logistics and emergency telecommunications under one coordination structure, the WFP-led LTC is the backbone of the entire humanitarian
response, enabling humanitarian action to move, communicate, coordinate, and deliver lifesaving assistance.
Page 1 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

restoring connectivity in heavily affected areas, particularly La Guaira, Caracas Metropolitan Area,
Petare, and Catia.
As of 23 July, authorities reported more than 1,200 aftershocks, approximately 4,829 fatalities, 16,740
injuries, and nearly 17,907 people displaced from their homes. The Government, UN agencies, NGOs,
and Red Cross partners continued operating transitional camps, delivering relief assistance, and
expanding support to affected populations. A USD 299 million addendum to the 2026 Humanitarian
Response Plan was launched to address the needs of approximately 1.3 million earthquake-affected
people over the next six months.
Telecommunications Overview
Telecommunications and electricity remained among the most severely impacted sectors following the
earthquakes, continuing to impede recovery efforts and humanitarian operations. Although targeted
emergency interventions and repair works have restored partial telecommunications services in key
population centres, damaged network infrastructure, power instability, and intermittent connectivity
disruptions persist across La Guaira, Petare, Catia, and other affected communities.
Reliable communications remain essential for humanitarian coordination, information management, and
access to assistance. While mobile network operators, including Compañía Anónima Nacional
Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar, and Digitel, maintained operations across most of the
country, localized outages and reduced network performance continued in earthquake-affected areas.
Service providers and authorities are actively restoring damaged infrastructure; however, sustained
operational support is required to stabilize connectivity and close remaining coverage gaps.
At the same time, damage to electricity transmission and distribution networks continues to disrupt
households, health facilities, water systems, telecommunications equipment, and temporary
displacement sites. These power constraints are slowing the restoration of essential services and
complicating broader recovery efforts. Accelerated investment in telecommunications and energy
infrastructure repairs, complemented by emergency connectivity solutions, remains critical to restoring
reliable communications, strengthening humanitarian response capabilities, and supporting the long-
term recovery of affected communities.
LTC Telecoms Activities
Coordination
Since 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator has been deployed to Caracas to support inter-agency
coordination, telecommunications assessments, and the delivering critical communications services. In
coordination with OCHA, Comisión Nacional de Telecomunicaciones (CONATEL), CANTV, Movistar,
Digitel, G-Network, emergency.lu, Grupo Telefónica, and other partners, LTC Telecoms is leading
telecommunications coordination mechanism, identify connectivity gaps, and prioritize support in the
most affected areas.
As of 22 July, efforts remain focused on high-impact locations such as La Guaira, where power
outages, network disruptions, and infrastructure damage continue to affect connectivity. Planned and
ongoing interventions include shared internet services, public Wi-Fi, satellite communications, and
solar-powered charging facilities to support humanitarian coordination, information-sharing, and
access to services. LTC’s broader response is scaling, telecommunications support to affected
communities, including temporary service points and common operational support.
Page 2 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid telecommunications and connectivity
survey across affected areas. The assessment is mapping available connectivity services, including
mobile, fibre, VSAT, BGAN, and Starlink connectivity, to identify service gaps and prioritize locations
for shared connectivity solutions.
ICT assessments
On 09 July, LTC Telecoms conducted an ICT assessment at Playa Verde, a displacement site in La
Guaira, to identify connectivity and power requirements. The assessment found limited access to
reliable electricity and internet connectivity. The team is reassessing the most appropriate setup for
the site before installing solar panels, power generators and batteries to support reliable
communication for multiple inter-agency service delivery. Playa Verde also remains a priority option for
the pending community internet service and power charging kiosk deployment.
Internet connectivity
A combination of Starlink kits and the Internet Service for Communities solution developed through
coordination among National Telecommunications Commission (CONATEL), WFP, Emergency.lu, and
local ISP, G-Network, continue to provide connectivity across the response priority locations. The
connectivity solution continues to provide approximately 1,400 humanitarian responders and affected
population with reliable internet services and power supply at Caraballeda and César Nieves Stadium
Transitional Camp. Solar- and battery-backed power solutions were installed at César Nieves to
sustain emergency connectivity services amid repeated national grid electricity interruptions.
Starlink kits continues to provide essential connectivity for inter-agency services at Polideportivo and
Playa Grande. The community internet solution originally planned for Playa Grande may be redirected
to the new camp location if relocation proceeds. If deployment at the relocated site is not feasible,
Playa Verde remains the alternative option for the pending community connectivity package.
Polideportivo has reliable Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) services while local ISPs are also offering
free internet connectivity to the affected population at the site. For this reason, the team is not
currently planning to deploy a separate community internet service at Polideportivo, as affected
populations already have access to multiple free connectivity options. Despite occasional congestion,
Starlink internet connectivity at Polideportivo is available for the World Food Programme (WFP), United
Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), United
Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) personnel.
Power supply
LTC Telecoms is strengthening power continuity across response sites through real-time monitoring of
battery systems linked to solar-powered internet connectivity. This provides timely visibility on power
gaps, allowing teams to adjust configurations, add battery support and take corrective action to keep
critical connectivity services operational for humanitarian responders and affected communities.
During the reporting period, the LTC Telecoms team installed solar panels and EcoFlow Uninterrupted
Power Supply (UPS) batteries at Polideportivo and César Nieves to meet the site’s power. The current
configuration at each camp includes 800 watts of solar capacity supported by EcoFlow batteries,
providing sufficient power for the site’s internet equipment and related connectivity infrastructure. This
approach is expected to be replicated at future sites where needed, as it offers a more efficient power
solution and reduces reliance on the unstable public grid amid frequent blackouts in La Guaira.
Grupo Telefónica has provided a charging kiosk at each of Polideportivo and César Nieves, supporting
48 power-strip connections, enabling affected people to charge mobile phones and other ICT devices
Page 3 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

to maintain access to communication, information and basic services. The kiosk will be returned to
Grupo Telefónica once the emergency transitions fully into recovery.
Services for communities
Since 13 July, the solution has been operational at two locations: Caraballeda, and Cesar Nieves
Stadium. The Internet Service for Communities initiative was developed through coordination among
emergency.lu, National Telecommunications Commission (CONATEL), WFP, and the local ISP, G-
Network. The technical design of the internet connectivity solution ensures provision of service at
multiple sites. Users can move between sites without requiring additional approval nor login
credentials. Internet access, supplied through local ISP G-Network fibre connection, is currently free
for all users with an anticipated cost starting sometime in August. The potential cost has been included
in the response budget for the coming months until the emergency ends. On 13 July, emergency.lu
transferred the community connectivity solution to WFP. Discussions are ongoing with service
providers to maintain services throughout the response and recovery period.
Following the completion of its mission, emergency.lu departed Venezuela on 14 July. The deployment
was carried out through the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) system as
part of the European Civil Protection Mechanism and is co-funded by the European Union (EU).
Information Management
A dedicated LTC Telecoms emergency operations page was established to provide operational
updates and response information.
Visit the LTC Telecoms Dashboard for an overview of planned and active services.
LTC Telecoms and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) activated the Disaster
Connectivity Map (DCM) on 25 June to monitor connectivity impacts across affected areas. The DCM
is integrated into LogIE for Venezuela to support operational planning.
The DCM showed national connectivity dropping from more than 90 percent to approximately 59–65
percent immediately following the earthquakes before partially recovering to around 77 percent within
24–48 hours. As of 22 July, La Guaira remained the most affected area, while connectivity in Caracas
had largely recovered. Service disruptions continued to affect parts of Yaracuy and Carabobo States.
Additional IM support is being provided by MapAction and Kobo Toolbox for mapping, data collection,
analysis, and information-sharing activities.
Funding
Donor engagement remains ongoing as humanitarian funding requirements are consolidated under the
forthcoming Flash Appeal.
The US Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA) has committed USD 9 million, with a further USD 6
million under processing, bringing the expected total contribution to USD 15 million. Funding is
primarily focused on humanitarian supply chain operations and the delivery of emergency assistance.
The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) has allocated USD 15 million for the earthquake
response, of which approximately USD 2 million is expected to be allocated to WFP.

Meetings
A Global LTC Telecoms Partner Teleconference was held on 13 July at 14:00 UTC to support
information exchange and coordination. Minutes of the meeting are available here.
LTC Logistics Area
For more information on the logistics component of the LTC response, a dedicated Venezuela logistics
webpage is available here with the latest updates on working group meetings, key documents, maps,
and available support.
The latest LTC Logistics Situation Report is available here.
Challenges
Equipment security: Connectivity equipment remains exposed in several locations. In the absence of
secure storage, equipment must be dismantled each evening and reinstalled each morning, increasing
the risk of damage, loss, delayed start-up, and service interruptions.
Connectivity congestion: High numbers of Starlink units and unmanaged routers may reduce service
quality and affect community access.
Fuel movement restrictions: Generator operations are constrained by challenges associated with
transporting fuel between sites.
Evolving site requirements: Population growth at existing sites and the emergence of new locations,
such as Playa Verde, require continuous reassessment of connectivity and power needs.

documents.body_text:
El decimosexto Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, con información correspondiente al período del 22 al 23 de julio.

## **Aspectos destacados**

Entre el 22 y el 23 de julio, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, salud, protección, WASH y gestión de información.

A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado a **8.676 personas únicas mediante 16.265 asistencias y servicios**, principalmente en alojamiento y coordinación de campamentos transitorios, salud, WASH y protección.

La OIM y su socio Fundación Vivienda Popular han distribuido **3.175 sets de cocina, 3.617 lonas, 2.115 baldes, 1.759 lámparas solares y 819 kits de refugio** a hogares afectados.

## **Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM continuó gestionando y coordinando cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira y avanzó la transición operativa de tres de ellos al Consejo Noruego para los Refugiados (NRC).

En el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena continuó la organización de espacios para alojamiento y prestación de servicios, mientras que en Mare Abajo II se actualizó la capacidad de alojamiento y continuó el seguimiento a la posible reubicación de familias desde Playa Grande.

En WASH, continuó ampliando el acceso a artículos para almacenamiento seguro de agua e higiene. A la fecha, se han distribuido **1.552 bidones plegables, 1.091 kits de higiene y 93 bidones**.

La OIM y su socio Ven Da Tu Mano han realizado **6.194 asistencias y servicios de salud**, incluyendo atención primaria, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial. Los servicios móviles de salud y SMAPS continuaron operativos en el Polideportivo José María Vargas y el Estadio César Nieves.

La OIM finalizó la Encuesta de Hogares en Campamentos Transitorios y el análisis de flujos de movilidad durante los primeros 15 días de julio, al tiempo que avanzó la preparación de una evaluación de los 107 campamentos transitorios.

En protección, continuó brindando orientación, asistencia legal, apoyo en documentación y derivaciones a servicios especializados, con **218 asistencias y servicios de protección registrados a la fecha**, mientras que 130 personas han recibido atención y acompañamiento especializado.

## **Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La OIM continuará la transición operativa de tres campamentos a NRC, las mejoras de infraestructura y prestación de servicios, y reforzará los servicios de WASH, salud, salud mental y protección.

Asimismo, fortalecerá el monitoreo de los campamentos y de la movilidad, avanzará las evaluaciones de campamentos transitorios y poblaciones afectadas, y continuará la coordinación con autoridades y socios humanitarios.

ALOJAMIENTO, TIERRA Y ASENTAMIENTOS
Acciones realizadas
• OIM continuó gestionando y coordinando 5 campamentos transitorios en La Guaira y avanzó la transición de tres de ellos al
Consejo Noruego para los Refugiados (NRC) como socio implementador.
• A la fecha, OIM y Fundación Vivienda Popular han distribuido 3.175 sets de cocina, 3.617 lonas, 2.115 baldes, 1.759 lámparas
solares, 819 kits de refugio, 672 mosquiteros y 208 linternas solares recargables.
• En Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena, OIM avanzó la organización de espacios para alojamiento y prestación de servicios e

stalación de conectividad para facilitar el registro y la prestación de servicios. En Mare Abajo II, continuaron las mejoras de
infraestructura, incluidas divisiones familiares, drenaje y nuevas instalaciones sanitarias.
• En Playa Grande continuó el seguimiento a la eventual reubicación de familias hacia otro punto cercano.

• Continuar la transición operativa de 3 campamentos a NRC y las mejoras de infraestructura, drenaje, organización y

• Dar seguimiento a las necesidades de alojamiento en Campo de Golf y al proceso de traslado desde Playa Grande.

Acciones realizadas
• OIM continuó ampliando el acceso a artículos para almacenamiento y manejo seguro del agua e higiene. A la fecha, se han
distribuido 1.552 bidones plegables de 10 litros, 1.091 kits de higiene y 93 bidones de 10 litros.
• En Campo de Golf avanzó la planificación para instalar una planta potabilizadora de 10.000 litros y la coordinación técnica
para mejorar almacenamiento de agua, saneamiento, drenajes y gestión de residuos. Se identificaron necesidades relacionadas
con higiene, vectores y calidad del agua.
Acciones planificadas para cubrir necesidades urgentes
• Avanzar la instalación de la planta potabilizadora en Campo de Golf y reforzar el suministro y almacenamiento seguro de
agua.
• Continuar las mejoras de saneamiento, drenaje, gestión de residuos, promoción de higiene y control de vectores en los cam-
pamentos.

Acciones realizadas
• OIM continuó prestando atención primaria y servicios de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS) mediante equipos pro-

• En el Polideportivo José María Vargas y Estadio César Nieves se mantuvieron operativos los equipos móviles, con servicios
de medicina general, medicina interna, pediatría, ginecología y obstetricia, enfermería, y apoyo psicológico.
• Durante el período se identificaron necesidades de continuidad de tratamiento para enfermedades no transmisibles, así co-
mo atención especializada y apoyo psicológico entre población alojada y comunidades aledañas.
Acciones planificadas para cubrir necesidades urgentes
• Mantener los equipos móviles de salud y SMAPS, y fortalecer las rutas de derivación para atención especializada, en coordi-

• Reforzar el seguimiento de enfermedades transmisibles y crónicas, salud materna y necesidades de apoyo psicológico.

documents.body_text:
The sixteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 22 to 23 July.

## **Highlights**

Between 22 and 23 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, WASH and information management.

To date, IOM has reached **8,676 unique individuals through 16,265 instances of assistance and services**, mainly in shelter and transitory camp coordination, health, WASH and protection.

IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed **3,175 kitchen sets, 3,617 tarpaulins, 2,115 buckets, 1,759 solar lamps and 819 shelter kits** to affected households.

## **IOM activities**

IOM continued managing and coordinating five transitory camps in La Guaira and advanced the operational transition of three of them to the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).

At Tanaguarena Golf Course, IOM continued preparations to expand accommodation and service provision capacity, while in Mare Abajo II accommodation capacity was updated with 206 bunk beds and 635 mattresses recorded.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water storage and hygiene items. To date, **1,552 collapsible water containers, 1,091 hygiene kits and 93 water containers** have been distributed.

IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano have provided **6,194 health assistance and services**, including primary healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support. Mobile health and MHPSS teams remained operational at José María Vargas Sports Complex and César Nieves Stadium.

IOM finalized the Household Survey in Transitory Camps and the analysis of mobility flows during the first 15 days of July, while advancing preparations for the assessment of 107 transitory camps.

In protection, IOM continued providing guidance, legal assistance, documentation support and referrals to specialized services, with **218 protection assistance and services recorded to date**.

## **IOM planned response**

IOM will continue the operational transition of three camps to NRC, infrastructure improvements and service delivery activities, while strengthening WASH, health, mental health and protection services.

It will also strengthen camp and mobility monitoring, advance assessments of transitory camps and affected populations, and continue coordination with authorities and humanitarian partners.

VENEZUELA (BOLIVARIAN REPUBLIC OF) EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
Situation Report #16 | From 22 to 23 July 2026
SHELTER, LAND AND SITE COORDINATION
Actions undertaken
• IOM continued managing and coordinating five transitory camps in La Guaira and advanced the transition of three of them to
the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) as an implementing partner.
• To date, IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed 3,175 kitchen sets, 3,617 tarpaulins, 2,115 buckets, 1,759 solar
lamps, 819 shelter kits, 672 mosquito nets and 208 rechargeable solar flashlights.
• At the Tanaguarena Golf Course, the organization of spaces for accommodation and service provision progressed, and an
estimated need for 117 additional tents was identified. At Mare Abajo II, accommodation capacity was updated, with 206
bunk beds and 635 mattresses recorded.
• At Playa Grande, follow-up continued on the possible relocation of families to another nearby site.
Planned / ongoing actions
• Continue the operational transition of three camps to NRC and advance improvements to infrastructure, drainage, site
organization and service provision.
• Follow up on accommodation needs at the Golf Course and the relocation process from Playa Grande.
WATER, SANITATION AND HYGIENE — WASH
Actions undertaken
• IOM continued expanding access to items for the safe storage and handling of water and hygiene. To date, 1,552 collapsible
10-litre jerrycans, 1,091 hygiene kits and 93 10-litre jerrycans have been distributed.
• At the Golf Course, planning progressed for the installation of a 10,000-litre water treatment plant, alongside technical
coordination to improve water storage, sanitation, drainage and waste management. Needs related to hygiene, vectors and
water quality were identified.
Planned / ongoing actions
• Advance installation of the water treatment plant at the Golf Course and strengthen safe water supply and storage.
• Continue improvements to sanitation, drainage, waste management, hygiene promotion and vector control across the camps.
HEALTH AND MHPSS
Actions undertaken
• IOM continued providing primary health care and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) through its own teams
and partner Ven Da Tu Mano. To date, 6,194 health assistance and services have been recorded.
• At the Polideportivo José María Vargas and César Nieves Stadium, mobile teams remained operational, with general medicine,
internal medicine, pediatrics, gynecology and obstetrics, nursing, and psychological support services.
• During the period, needs for continuity of treatment for non-communicable diseases were identified, as well as specialized
care and psychological support among the population in temporary camps and surrounding communities.
Planned / ongoing actions
• Maintain mobile health and MHPSS teams and strengthen referral pathways for specialized care, in coordination with
authorities.
• Strengthen monitoring of communicable and chronic diseases, maternal health and psychological support needs.
DATA, DTM AND NEEDS ASSESSMENTS
Actions undertaken
• The Household Survey in Transitory Camps and the analysis of mobility flows during the first 15 days of July were finalized.
• IOM advanced preparations for an assessment of the 107 transitory camps, including methodology and operational planning.
Formal authorization to implement the exercise is currently being sought.
• IOM supports the registration of people in the 5 transitional camps managed by the United Nations through a unified system.
Coordination is being made with partner organizations to use this tool to consolidate information on a single platform,
strengthening the quality, consistency, and availability of data.
Planned/ongoing actions
• Advance the assessment of the 107 camps once operational coordination arrangements are completed.
• Continue mobility tracking in affected and unaffected states and assessments inside and outside transitory camps.
• IOM is planning a mapping exercise of transitory camps to improve their identification and strengthen understanding of the
presence of affected populations. This activity will improve the available information and provide additional evidence for
humanitarian planning and response.

Situation Report #16 | From 22 to 23 July 2026
PROTECTION
Actions undertaken
• IOM continued providing information and orientation, legal assistance, documentation support, referrals, and activities to
prevent violence against women, trafficking in persons and sexual exploitation and abuse through prevention of sexual
exploitation and abuse (PSEA) measures. To date, 218 protection assistance and services have been recorded, while 130
people have received specialized protection assistance and follow-up.
• At José María Vargas Sports Complex, awareness-raising activities on violence against women, PSEA and trafficking in persons
were conducted, protection cases were assisted and referrals to specialized services facilitated. At the Golf Course,
information requests were addressed and referrals made to health, psychosocial support and legal orientation services.
• At Mare Abajo II, two sessions on protection risks and trafficking in persons were conducted with 10 officials and orientation
on documentation and family reunification. At César Nieves, accountability mechanisms with women community leaders were
strengthened, and security and Governor’s Office personnel were sensitized on PSEA.
Planned/ongoing actions
• Strengthen referral mechanisms, community feedback, legal orientation, and prevention of gender-based violence (GBV),
trafficking in persons and PSEA.
• Advance the analysis of sexual exploitation and abuse risks across the five transitory camps and strengthen awareness-raising
with authorities, humanitarian actors and community leaders.

operational and information management planning for the monitoring and assessment of the 107 transitory camps.
• At Playa Grande, IOM coordinated planning around the possible relocation of families, while at Mare Abajo II it continued
strengthening joint coordination and community feedback mechanisms.

• Follow up on the operational transition of the three camps and decisions regarding the relocation of families from Playa

**CIFRAS CLAVE**

- 5,3K personas fallecidas tras dos poderosos terremotos que sacudieron Venezuela el 24 de junio
- 43,5K casos confirmados de sarampión en América Latina y el Caribe en 2026, 3,8 veces más que en 2025
- 61K personas quedaron aisladas debido a fuertes tormentas en Chile

**VENEZUELA: TERREMOTO**

Un mes después de los terremotos del 24 de junio que sacudieron el centro-norte de Venezuela, los socios humanitarios continúan ampliando la asistencia en las zonas más afectadas, mientras las autoridades avanzan en los esfuerzos de recuperación y reconstrucción para las comunidades afectadas. Al 22 de julio, el número de personas fallecidas ha aumentado a 5.398 y las autoridades han registrado más de 1.460 réplicas. Unas 23.843 personas permanecen en 107 campamentos transitorios. Los socios humanitarios están brindando asistencia en materia de salud, alimentación, protección, alojamiento y WASH en los estados más afectados. Más de 117.000 personas han tenido acceso a servicios esenciales y apoyo humanitario a través de la respuesta coordinada. La planificación de recuperación y reconstrucción también avanza, incluyendo esfuerzos para identificar soluciones de vivienda para las familias afectadas. Persisten necesidades significativas en materia de alojamiento, servicios básicos, seguridad alimentaria y apoyo psicosocial.

[Apoya aquí al Fondo Humanitario Venezolano](https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis)

Para más información, visita: [ReliefWeb Response](https://response.reliefweb.int/es/venezuela/terremoto-junio-2026)

**CHILE: FUERTES LLUVIAS**

Las autoridades han declarado estado de catástrofe en la región chilena de Coquimbo, la provincia de Huasco y en la comuna de Tierra Amarilla, provincia de Copiapó, debido a un sistema de tormentas que comenzó el 13 de julio en 11 de las 16 regiones del país. Al 22 de julio, el Servicio Nacional de Prevención y Respuesta ante Desastres (SENAPRED) informa que el clima severo ha afectado a 3.532 personas, dejando 13 personas fallecidas y 4 personas aún desaparecidas. Las precipitaciones han alcanzado niveles históricos de hasta 200 mm en algunas zonas. Más de 1.500 personas permanecen en albergues, concentrados en las regiones de Valparaíso, La Araucanía, Biobío y Coquimbo. Aunque el acceso se ha restablecido en algunas zonas, al menos 61.000 personas siguen aisladas. La Cruz Roja Chilena ha activado una alerta amarilla y está coordinando con SENAPRED.

**PERU: TERREMOTO**

Un terremoto de magnitud 5,1, de unos 10 km de profundidad, sacudió la región de Junín, en el centro de Perú, el 18 de julio, causando la muerte de al menos seis personas y dejando a más de 30 heridas, según el Instituto Nacional de Defensa Civil de Perú (INDECI). El sismo, cuyo epicentro se ubicó cerca de la provincia de Chupaca, a unos 300 km al este de Lima, provocó una réplica de magnitud 3,7 y derrumbó decenas de viviendas en un distrito rural poco poblado, con menos de 5.000 habitantes, dejando a cientos de personas desplazadas. Dos hospitales y varias estructuras históricas sufrieron daños y se reportaron cortes de electricidad en las comunidades afectadas. El Gobierno ha desplegado alrededor de 100 profesionales de la salud y un hospital móvil, mientras que los bomberos y el personal de las fuerzas armadas continúan limpiando escombros y buscando a quienes aún puedan estar atrapados. Las autoridades advirtieron que las cifras de víctimas podrían aumentar a medida que continúen las evaluaciones en comunidades más remotas.

**REGIONAL: SARAMPIÓN**

El sarampión sigue siendo una preocupación de salud pública en las América, aunque las tendencias de transmisión se han ralentizado en las últimas semanas. Entre las semanas epidemiológicas 1 y 27 de 2026, las autoridades informan de 43.559 casos confirmados y 44 muertes en 17 países y territorios, lo que representa un aumento de 3,8 veces respecto al mismo periodo de 2025. Durante las dos últimas semanas de reporte, se notificaron 1.818 nuevos casos, lo que representa una disminución del 38% respecto al periodo anterior. Guatemala, México, Estados Unidos y Canadá representan el 98% de todos los casos notificados en la región. Tras los recientes terremotos en Venezuela, los socios de salud continúan priorizando las actividades de vigilancia y vacunación para reducir el riesgo de transmisión del sarampión entre las poblaciones desplazadas que viven en alojamientos temporales.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**KEY FIGURES**

- 5.3K people dead after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela on 24 June
- 43.5K confirmed cases of measles in LAC in 2026, 3.8 times higher than 2025
- 61K people isolated due to severe storms in Chile

**VENEZUELA: EARTHQUAKE**

One month after the 24 June earthquakes that struck north-central Venezuela, humanitarian partners continue to scale up assistance across the most affected areas, while authorities advance recovery and reconstruction efforts for impacted communities. As of 22 July, the death toll has risen to 5,398 and authorities have recorded more than 1,460 aftershocks. Some 23,843 people remain in 107 transitional camps. Humanitarian partners are providing health, food, protection, shelter and WASH assistance across the most affected states. More than 117,000 people have now accessed essential services and humanitarian support through the coordinated response. Recovery and reconstruction planning is also advancing, including efforts to identify housing solutions for affected families. Significant needs persist in shelter, basic services, food security and psychosocial support.

[Support the Venezuelan Humanitarian Fund here](https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis)

For more information, visit: [ReliefWeb Response](https://response.reliefweb.int/es/venezuela/terremoto-junio-2026)

**CHILE: HEAVY RAINFALL**

Authorities have declared a state of catastrophe in Chile’s Coquimbo region, Huasco province and in the Tierra Amarilla commune, Copiapó province, due to a storm system that began on 13 July across 11 of the country’s 16 regions. As of 22 July, the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (SENAPRED) report that the severe weather has affected 3,532 people, left 13 dead and 4 still missing. Rainfall has reached historic levels of up to 200mm in some areas. More than 1,500 people remain in shelters, concentrated in the Valparaíso, La Araucanía, Biobío, and Coquimbo regions. Although access has been restored in some areas, at least 61,000 people remain cut off. The Chilean Red Cross has activated a yellow alert and is coordinating with SENAPRED.

**PERU: EARTHQUAKE**

A magnitude 5.1 earthquake about 10 km deep struck the Junín region of central Peru on 18 July, killing at least six people and injuring more than 30, according to Peru’s National Institute of Civil Defense (INDECI). The quake, centered near Chupaca province roughly 300 km east of Lima, triggered a magnitude 3.7 aftershock and collapsed dozens of homes in a sparsely populated rural district of fewer than 5,000 people, leaving hundreds displaced. Two hospitals and several historic structures sustained damage, and power outages were reported in affected communities. The Government has deployed around 100 health professionals and a mobile hospital, while firefighters and armed forces personnel continue clearing debris and searching for anyone still trapped. Authorities cautioned that casualty figures could rise as assessments in more remote communities continue.

**REGIONAL: MEASLES**

Measles remains a public health concern across the Americas, although transmission trends have slowed in recent weeks. Between epidemiological weeks 1 and 27 of 2026, authorities report 43,559 confirmed cases and 44 deaths across 17 countries and territories, representing a 3.8-fold increase compared with the same period in 2025. During the last two reporting weeks, 1,818 new cases were reported, representing a 38 per cent decrease compared with the previous reporting period. Guatemala, Mexico, the United States and Canada account for 98 per cent of all reported cases in the region. Following the recent earthquakes in Venezuela, health partners continue to prioritize surveillance and vaccination activities to reduce the risk of measles transmission among displaced populations living in temporary shelters.

**HIGHLIGHTS**

• More than three weeks after the two earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, affecting at least seven states, the emergency response remains active. While the most acute phase of rescue, trauma care and immediate postdisaster surgery has eased, priorities are now focused on sustaining essential health services, strengthening referral pathways, supporting temporary camps and preventing public health risks.

• The health response continues transitioning from emergency care to early recovery, prioritizing restoration of integrated health service networks, continuity of specialized care, and implementation of the Ministry of Health’s National Mental Health Response Plan.

• Integrated epidemiological surveillance continues to reinforce early detection, laboratory verification and environmental risk monitoring. PAHO/WHO supported the roll-out of a real-time surveillance dashboard and the delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen national preparedness.

• PAHO/WHO continues supporting the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) through the deployment of its Regional Response Team, covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, laboratory, WASH, immunization, risk communication and community engagement, and EMT coordination. In coordination with the MPPS, PAHO/WHO is also supporting the virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization, with fourteen EMTs now operational across La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda, and Aragua, increasing clinical capacity in the affected areas.

• PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response through the delivery of computers to strengthen on-site epidemiological surveillance and body bags for the dignified management of the deceased, and through the coordination of in-kind donations from seven partners, most recently from Direct Relief: water purification tablets covering 20 days of chlorinated supply, medicines, and hygiene kits. A second distribution of TESK and IEHK kits to 18 health facilities and 36 transitional camps is planned.

Situation Report N.7
SAFE AND SCALABLE CARE

KEY TAKEAWAYS
• The response is progressively transitioning from emergency trauma care towards restoration
and strengthening of essential health services and health system functionality.
• EMTs continue expanding clinical care while progressively integrating with national referral
networks and routine health services.
• Health facility characterization, service mapping and hospital network assessments are
supporting prioritization of recovery interventions and continuity of specialized care.
• Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) has entered an implementation phase
following formal approval of the national response plan.
SITUATION ANALYSIS
Continuity of essential health services
Health sector activities continue transitioning from immediate emergency response towards early
recovery and restoration of essential health services. Current priorities focus on strengthening integrated
health service networks, maintaining referral pathways, restoring hospital functionality and supporting
continuity of specialized clinical services.
Field assessments increasingly emphasize functional characterization of health facilities and integrated
health service networks rather than structural damage alone. During the reporting period, PAHO/WHO
supported health facility characterization and georeferencing of Community Integrated Health Areas
(ASICs) in La Guaira, providing operational information to prioritize recovery actions and strengthen
continuity of care.
Hospital functionality
Hospital assessments continue identifying operational constraints affecting service delivery, including
infrastructure damage, reduced inpatient capacity, and gaps in specialized health services affecting
selected facilities. Recent assessments also highlighted the need to optimize patient distribution across
the health network to improve access to specialized services and reduce pressure on referral hospitals.

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.7
Health service delivery
Health service delivery continues to transition from acute trauma care towards the provision of
comprehensive essential health services. The most frequently reported conditions included minor
injuries, upper respiratory tract infections, acute mental health conditions, skin diseases and acute watery
diarrhea, reflecting evolving health needs among affected populations and increasing demand for primary
health care, mental health services and management of common communicable diseases.
Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs)
Emergency Medical Teams continue providing essential clinical care while progressively integrating into
national health services. During the reporting period, deployed EMTs submitted 234 daily operational
reports documenting 23,779 consultations, 544 admissions, 200 major surgical procedures, 238
minor surgical procedures, and 1,507 occupied bed-days. Women accounted for 57% of
consultations and men for 43%, demonstrating the continued contribution of EMTs to maintaining service
availability in earthquake-affected areas.
Rehabilitation and recovery
Recovery activities increasingly prioritize restoration of specialized services, continuity of care for chronic
diseases, and rehabilitation planning. During the reporting period, PAHO/WHO supported assessment of
oncology services in La Guaira, confirming continuity of oncology services, including chemotherapy,
despite structural damage.
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS)
The Ministry of Health has formally approved the National Mental Health Response Plan, marking the
transition from planning to implementation. The plan establishes Mental Health Points within each
transitional camp to coordinate psychosocial support and referral pathways between Community
Integrated Health Areas (ASICs) and displaced populations.

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.7
During the reporting period, operational protocols for Mental Health Points were finalized; daily
implementation meetings continued; seven psychological support hotlines remained operational.
Additional specialized mental health personnel were deployed to support implementation in Distrito
Capital, Miranda and La Guaira, while collaboration with national and international partners continued to
strengthen technical guidance, referral pathways and specialized mental health services.
Health Cluster Partner Assessments of Health Facilities
Health Cluster partners continue conducting rapid assessments to monitor health facility functionality and
identify priority recovery needs across affected areas. To date, 73 health facilities have been assessed,
with 27 reporting earthquake-related damage (13 in Distrito Capital, 9 in La Guaira and 5 in Miranda).
Three facilities in La Guaira remain non-operational or are functioning with severe limitations. Findings
continue to support coordinated recovery planning and prioritization of partner assistance, while
assessment gaps persist in Carabobo and Yaracuy.
PRIORITY NEEDS
• Continuity of Health Services – Strengthen service delivery networks, referral coordination and
restoration of damaged facilities.
• Hospital Recovery and Infrastructure – Address infrastructure rehabilitation, water supply,
hygiene, cleaning and essential hospital support services.
• Specialized Clinical Services – Sustain oncology, rehabilitation and chronic disease services while
strengthening diagnostic and specialized care capacity.
• Health Information and Service Management – Strengthen health facility characterization, digital
information systems and operational analysis to support recovery planning.
• Mental Health and Psychosocial Support – Expand implementation of the national MHPSS plan,
deploy Mental Health Points across transitional camps, strengthen referral pathways and continue
workforce capacity building.
PAHO/WHO RESPONSE
• PAHO/WHO continued supporting Emergency Medical Team (EMT) coordination and progressive
integration with national health services to sustain continuity of essential health care in affected
areas.
• Contributed to assessment and recovery planning for specialized health services, including oncology
networks and continuity of care for people living with chronic diseases.
• Facilitated implementation of the Ministry of Health National Mental Health Response Plan, including
development of operational guidance for Mental Health Points in transitional camps and intersectoral
coordination.
• Delivered Psychological First Aid (PFA) training for 63 health and social service professionals in
Miranda and facilitated deployment of additional technical personnel to strengthen camp-based
mental health services.
• Continued to assist in health facility assessments, hospital recovery planning and prioritization of
recovery interventions in coordination with the Ministry of Health and Health Cluster partners.
• Conducted infection prevention and control (IPC) training for 50 nursing professionals from the
Greater Caracas area to strengthen safe clinical care.
• Facilitated high-level technical coordination between the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Education

KEY TAKEAWAYS
• Digital surveillance tools are strengthening real-time analysis and reporting from transitional
camps, improving operational decision-making.
• No major outbreaks have been detected despite continued verification of priority public health
events.
• Brazil donated 1.15 million vaccine doses through PAHO/WHO, strengthening national

SITUATION ANALYSIS
Strengthening epidemiological surveillance
Integrated epidemiological surveillance continues to support early detection and rapid investigation of
priority public health events following the earthquakes. Surveillance activities are implemented jointly by
the MPPS and PAHO/WHO through indicator-based surveillance, event-based surveillance,
environmental surveillance, laboratory surveillance and vaccination monitoring.
Field operations remain focused on restoring and strengthening surveillance capacity across La Guaira.
Activities include epidemiological and environmental assessments in transitional camps, verification of
mandatory disease reporting in health facilities, investigation of priority public health events, and
continued strengthening of the State Epidemiological Situation Room.
Integrated surveillance has been further strengthened through joint field operations involving
epidemiology, environmental health and immunization teams, enabling coordinated investigation of
priority public health events and rapid implementation of outbreak prevention and control measures.
The MPPS continues strengthening its Health Information Command Centre to support post-disaster
information management. During the reporting period, PAHO/WHO supported the deployment of an
automated surveillance dashboard that enables real-time visualization of epidemiological information
from transitional camps, facilitates trend analysis, and automatically generates operational reports in
PowerPoint and PDF formats for decision-making by health authorities.
The MPPS has also strengthened epidemiological intelligence through a national surveillance dashboard
that monitors 18 priority diseases and events using historical baselines and weekly trend analysis. The

Early warning, alert verification and laboratory surveillance
Early warning and laboratory-supported surveillance continue to strengthen timely detection and
verification of priority public health events. Laboratory confirmation remains coordinated through the
National Reference Laboratory (National Institute of Hygiene), supported by daily specimen referral from
affected areas and close coordination between epidemiology, laboratory and environmental health
teams.
During the reporting period, investigations confirmed four imported Plasmodium vivax malaria cases
among military personnel deployed from Bolívar State and identified one case of pulmonary tuberculosis,
allowing prompt public health follow-up according to national protocols.
Despite continued progress, laboratory surveillance remains constrained by infrastructure damage,
limited operational capacity at state and ASIC laboratories, and logistical challenges affecting specimen
collection, preservation and diagnostic capacity.
Arrival of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by the Government of Brazil to
support immunization activities in earthquake-affected areas of Venezuela.
Event-based surveillance
Event-based surveillance implemented through deployed Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) continues
to complement routine indicator-based surveillance by supporting early detection, verification and
assessment of public health signals reported from health facilities and transitional camps. Current
surveillance focuses on syndromic trends requiring epidemiological assessment, including acute
respiratory infections, acute diarrheal syndromes, acute febrile illnesses and other priority conditions,
with verification conducted jointly by Ministry of Health epidemiologists and PAHO/WHO field teams.
Trend analysis indicates that the observed increase in acute respiratory infections is primarily associated
with the progressive expansion of surveillance coverage rather than increased transmission, while
localized monitoring of acute diarrheal diseases continues in affected areas. Information generated
through this system continues to support rapid risk assessment and operational decision-making without
indicating confirmed outbreaks.
Environmental surveillance and public health risks
Environmental surveillance continues to identify public health risks in transitional camps, particularly
those associated with inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), poor solid waste management,
and vector proliferation. Joint investigations conducted by environmental health and epidemiology teams
continue to support rapid implementation of vector control, environmental sanitation, and outbreak
prevention measures.

Situation Report N.7
Field assessments identified deficiencies in drinking water, solid waste management, and sanitation in
two of the six transitional camps visited, reinforcing the need for integrated WASH interventions to reduce
the risk of communicable disease transmission.
Handwashing facilities installed in a transitional camp in La Guaira support infection
prevention and reduce the risk of communicable diseases among displaced populations.
Vaccination activities
Vaccination remains a central component of the public health response in affected areas. During the
reporting period, PAHO/WHO supported the delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by the
Government of Brazil to strengthen the National Immunization Programme and sustain protection
against vaccine-preventable diseases. Vaccination activities continue in affected communities and
transitional camps according to national priorities and epidemiological risk.
Other public health events
The Ministry of Health reported three confirmed fatal cases of hantavirus infection in Anzoátegui State.
According to national authorities, this event is unrelated to the earthquake response. Two additional
deaths under investigation in Barinas State are considered a separate event with no epidemiological link
to the hantavirus cases. Investigations remain ongoing.
PRIORITY NEEDS
• Early warning and outbreak investigation – Strengthen early warning, alert verification and rapid
outbreak investigation capacity across transitional camps, health facilities and EMTs, including timely
reporting, laboratory confirmation and feedback to operational teams.
• Laboratory surveillance – Restore and strengthen laboratory diagnostic capacity at the National
Reference Laboratory, state laboratories and ASIC surveillance networks, including specimen
collection, preservation and transport.
• Health information systems – Expand digital health information systems, real-time reporting and
epidemiological data management capacities to improve integration, visualization and automated
analysis of surveillance information across reporting units.
• Operational logistics – Sustain logistics, transportation and field mobility required for integrated
epidemiological surveillance, environmental investigations and rapid response activities.
• Environmental surveillance and WASH – Strengthen environmental surveillance, integrated
vector management and WASH interventions in camps presenting the highest public health risks.
• Vaccination – Continue targeted vaccination and catch-up immunization activities in affected

SITUATION ANALYSIS
National authorities report 107 transitional camps with an installed capacity of 27,950 places, of which
23,122 are occupied, representing an overall occupancy rate of 83%. Camps are located in Distrito
Capital (41), La Guaira (28), Miranda (28), and Aragua (10). The expanding camp network has
progressively reduced the number of displaced people sheltering in informal locations such as sidewalks,
roads, and areas around buildings undergoing structural assessment, but the high occupancy rate
continues to strain essential services and local authorities' capacity to ensure adequate health and
protection conditions.
Field visits indicate gradual improvements in the internal organization of several transitional camps.
Significant challenges remain, however, in establishing a standardized health response model that
effectively coordinates interventions among camp management, NGOs, ASICs, and health authorities.
The continued presence of security forces within temporary accommodation sites also underlines the
need to strengthen intersectoral coordination mechanisms that ensure a protection-centered approach
while safeguarding equitable and timely access to health services.
Environmental assessments continue to identify conditions that increase public health risks within camp
settings. Key findings include stagnant water, the accumulation of containers that may serve as mosquito
breeding sites, and limited capacity for adequate solid waste management. These conditions increase
the risk of vector- and rodent-borne diseases, as well as other illnesses associated with inadequate
WASH conditions. Strengthened integrated environmental surveillance, vector control, and solid waste
management interventions remain essential, particularly in camps presenting the highest levels of
vulnerability.
Transitional camps in La Guaira. Source:

Health access
The organization of health service delivery across shelters continues to vary considerably across affected
states. In Miranda, a structured coordination model has been established, including the designation of a
Health Director for each territorial axis and a Health Focal Point in every camp, strengthening coordination
between health services and camp management. However, this governance model has not yet been
replicated in the other affected states, resulting in coordination gaps and uneven implementation of health
interventions. In this context, PAHO/WHO provides direct technical support to the health authorities in La
Guaira to strengthen the health sector’s presence, coordination mechanisms, and service delivery across
transitional camps.
Immunizations / Vaccination Activities:
Active surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs) continues in transitional camps and the wider
community. Following the reorganization of vaccination brigades in La Guaira, training on camp
vaccination protocols in emergency settings was delivered across three Community Integral Health Areas
(ASIC), reaching 51 vaccinators. Efforts continue to secure vaccine supply through procurement via the

Epidemiological surveillance
The epidemiological situation continues to require intensified surveillance. Although no large-scale
outbreaks have been confirmed in transitional camps to date, overcrowding and persistent WASH
deficiencies continue to pose a high risk for the transmission of communicable diseases. These events
reinforce the need to strengthen event-based surveillance, rapid epidemiological investigation, laboratory
diagnostic capacity, and early warning systems to ensure the timely detection and response to emerging
public health threats within and beyond the earthquake-affected areas.
PRIORITY NEEDS
• Continuity of essential health services – Assess and characterize priority needs for essential
medicines, medical supplies, and health commodities at health service delivery points within
prioritized camps, in coordination with the Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental Health
programme, to ensure continuity of care for people with chronic conditions, mental health needs,
disabilities, older persons, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups.
• Integrated surveillance and outbreak prevention – Strengthen public health surveillance,
environmental health monitoring, vector control, and rapid response capacity in high-risk camps to
reduce the risk of communicable disease outbreaks associated with overcrowding, inadequate WASH
conditions, and emerging public health threats.
• Camp-based health governance – Promote standardized health coordination mechanisms across
all affected states by strengthening the integration of ASICs, camp health focal points, and state
health authorities, building on the coordination model implemented in Miranda to improve service
delivery, referral pathways, and operational oversight in transitional camp.
• Health coordination in transitional camps – Strengthen coordination among the MPPS, ASICs,
camp management, local health authorities, and humanitarian partners by prioritizing the transitional
camps where PAHO/WHO will implement direct CERF-supported interventions, ensuring an
integrated operational approach and evidence-based allocation of resources according to health risks
and population needs.
• Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) in La Guaira – Secure portable field laboratory kits for
microbiological water monitoring, along with vehicle support for technical staff; provide sanitation
equipment (motorized backpack sprayers, uniforms, personal protective equipment (PPE), and color-
coded medical and biohazard waste bags); arrange waste transport to decongest health facilities;
and recruit a WASH engineer to provide technical coordination and support.
• Immunization: transport and vaccine supply – Secure dedicated transport to enable faster access
to transitional camps, prioritizing those hosting over 1,000 people; and maintain a stable, sufficient
and timely supply of vaccines across the life course.
PAHO/WHO RESPONSE
• PAHO/WHO continued strengthening of risk communication capacities and institutional
coordination through the development of a joint communication strategy with the MPPS, the
formulation of tailored communication materials, training of 60 people on risk communication, and
enhanced visibility of emergency health interventions.
• Conducted a comprehensive needs assessment with the coordinators of the nine ASICs to identify
operational gaps and strengthen the health sector’s presence and response capacity across
transitional camps.
• Coordinated a strategic planning meeting with the Social Vice Presidency to define priority
interventions for MHPSS, strengthening intersectoral coordination to address the emerging
psychosocial needs of displaced populations living in transitional camps.
• Supported the identification of people living with NCDs through the implementation of a standardized
assessment tool, led by the Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental Health programme, informing
follow-up actions and continuity of care for vulnerable populations.

SITUATION ANALYSIS
Health Cluster
As of 17 July, the Health Cluster’s 3W (Who, What, Where) reporting system had registered 587 response
activities implemented by 42 organizations – UN agencies, national and international NGOs, the Red
Cross Movement, and national foundations – across 22 municipalities in eight states. Operational
presence remains highly concentrated in three areas: La Guaira with 316 reported activities (54%),
Distrito Capital with 144 (24%) and Miranda with 105 (18%), together accounting for more than 96% of
all reported interventions. This reflects the prioritization of response efforts in areas with the highest levels
of damage, population displacement, and concentration of transitional camps.
Primary health care remains the cornerstone of the partner response at nearly 58% of reported activities,
delivered through mobile medical brigades, community outreach, transitional camps, field hospitals and
existing health establishments, with MHPSS expanding across affected communities and camps and

Partners continue reinforcing the national health system with essential medicines, emergency medical
kits, IPC supplies, hospital and IT equipment, surveillance materials and logistical support for health
facilities, vaccination brigades and mobile medical teams.
Sexual and reproductive health services are also sustained, including antenatal care, contraceptive
distribution, HIV and syphilis rapid testing, STI prevention and community awareness, and deliver
targeted interventions for populations with specific needs, such as physical and functional rehabilitation
and assistive devices for persons with disabilities.
The Health Cluster coordination mechanism has transitioned toward a more operational coordination
model supported by dynamic information management, enabling continuous monitoring of partner
interventions, operational capacities, geographical coverage, and response gaps, including those of
newly deployed health actors following the 24 June earthquakes.

PAHO Regional Response Team/GOARN
PAHO/WHO has mobilized 14 specialists who are deployed, scheduled, or in the deployment process
through the PAHO Regional Response Team/GOARN roster. A second group of experts is arriving this
week, expanding support in epidemiology, humanitarian coordination, public health laboratory
coordination, infection prevention and control, and surveillance in shelters and affected communities.
The team is supporting health emergency and Health Cluster coordination, logistics, information
management and communications, risk communication and community engagement, WASH,
immunization, Emergency Medical Team coordination, and health facility assessments. The newly arriving
specialists will strengthen the early detection, investigation and analysis of public health events;
epidemiological surveillance in shelters; laboratory diagnostics and sample management; infection
prevention and control; partner coordination; gap analysis; and evidence-based operational decision-
making. This support is helping to align national and international assistance with identified needs and
priorities of the ongoing emergency response.
EMTs
Virtual CICOM (Coordination Cell) was established in La Guaira under the leadership of the MPPS, with
technical support from PAHO, to process international EMT offers and to coordinate their acceptance
and deployment. As of 23 July 2026, fourteen EMTs are providing services across La Guaira, Caracas,
Miranda; one team is mobilizing to their assigned locations and expected to become operational over
the coming hours and days; and seven have demobilized or are demobilizing after completing their
mission. See Annex 1 for further details.

documents.title: Un mes después de los terremotos en Venezuela, las comunidades comienzan a recuperarse
documents.body_text:
CARACAS – Un mes después de que devastadores terremotos sacudieran Venezuela, las comunidades afectadas están demostrando una notable resiliencia mientras las familias comienzan a recuperarse del desastre, reconstruyendo sus rutinas diarias y apoyándose mutuamente en un camino aún incierto hacia la recuperación.

En los sitios temporales de acogida y los barrios afectados, lideresas y líderes comunitarios, voluntarios, autoridades y trabajadores humanitarios están ayudando a las familias a acceder a asistencia, reconectarse con servicios esenciales y dar los primeros pasos para reconstruir sus vidas. Aunque las necesidades siguen siendo significativas, los esfuerzos conjuntos están contribuyendo a restablecer la estabilidad y la esperanza para miles de personas afectadas por el desastre.

Aprovechando su larga trayectoria de presencia en Venezuela, ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, ha apoyado a las familias a acceder a apoyo psicosocial, recibir asistencia legal, reemplazar documentos de identidad perdidos y conectarse con servicios especializados. Asimismo, ha proporcionado artículos esenciales y asistencia en los sitios temporales de acogida, en el marco de la respuesta más amplia del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y en estrecha coordinación con las autoridades nacionales y locales.

“Un mes después, seguimos inspirados por la fortaleza, la solidaridad y la determinación de las comunidades afectadas”, afirmó Kristin Halvorsen, Representante a cargo de ACNUR en Venezuela. “Las personas que han perdido sus hogares, seres queridos y medios de vida ya están ayudándose mutuamente a reconstruir. Nuestra prioridad es acompañarlas durante todo el proceso de recuperación, garantizando que las personas más vulnerables reciban la protección, asistencia y apoyo que necesitan para seguir adelante con dignidad y esperanza”.

Como organización líder del Clúster de Protección, ACNUR está contribuyendo a identificar y apoyar a las personas que enfrentan mayores riesgos tras el desastre, entre ellas mujeres, niñas y niños, personas mayores, personas con discapacidad, refugiadas, solicitantes de asilo, retornadas y miembros vulnerables de las comunidades de acogida. Las evaluaciones rápidas realizadas junto con socios permitieron identificar preocupaciones clave relacionadas con el impacto psicológico, la pérdida de documentación, el desplazamiento, la separación familiar y la limitada privacidad en los albergues colectivos.

Hasta la fecha, ACNUR y sus socios han brindado más de 4.000 servicios de protección en sitios temporales de acogida en La Guaira, incluyendo información y orientación, asistencia legal, primeros auxilios psicológicos, apoyo relacionado con documentación y derivaciones a servicios especializados. Más de 2.500 mujeres y niñas han recibido asistencia en materia de protección, mientras que se han realizado más de 400 derivaciones para atención médica, protección infantil, apoyo psicosocial y otros servicios especializados.

La pérdida de documentos de identidad sigue siendo un desafío importante para muchas familias afectadas. Sin documentación, las personas pueden enfrentar obstáculos para acceder a servicios de salud, educación, apoyo de vivienda y otros servicios esenciales. Desde los terremotos, ACNUR ha proporcionado más de 320 servicios de orientación y asistencia relacionados con documentación y está apoyando a las autoridades en los esfuerzos de registro y gestión de datos para ayudar a identificar necesidades y facilitar la asistencia.

ACNUR también ha movilizado artículos de emergencia provenientes de suministros preposicionados y puentes aéreos humanitarios, aportando más de 55 toneladas métricas de artículos, incluidos sistemas de iluminación solar, carpas para la provisión de servicios de protección, mosquiteros y otros artículos esenciales para apoyar a las familias que viven en sitios temporales de acogida y comunidades afectadas. La organización también está proporcionando apoyo técnico para mejorar la seguridad, la accesibilidad y la privacidad de las personas más vulnerables.

“Estamos profundamente agradecidos por la solidaridad demostrada por gobiernos, donantes, socios humanitarios y personas de todo el mundo en apoyo a las personas de Venezuela”, señaló Halvorsen. “Su apoyo ha permitido una respuesta rápida en un momento crítico, ayudando a las familias afectadas a acceder a servicios de protección, información, asistencia de emergencia y apoyo especializado. A medida que avanza la recuperación, el apoyo continuo será fundamental para garantizar que las personas permanezcan conectadas con los servicios que necesitan, que los riesgos emergentes de protección sean identificados de manera temprana y que nadie quede atrás”.

Para las personas sobrevivientes de los terremotos, la recuperación no consiste únicamente en reconstruir viviendas, sino también en fortalecer los vínculos que permiten a las comunidades sanar. En conversaciones con varias familias afectadas, todas expresaron su deseo de reconstruirse y recuperarse, con la esperanza de volver a encontrar la estabilidad necesaria para construir un futuro.

Un mes después del desastre, el impacto humanitario sigue siendo grave. Las autoridades informan de más de 5.000 personas fallecidas, más de 16.000 heridas y casi 18.000 que han perdido sus hogares. Más de 850 edificios han resultado afectados, incluidos 190 que colapsaron, mientras miles de familias continúan viviendo en sitios temporales de acogida o con familiares y comunidades de acogida mientras avanzan los esfuerzos de recuperación.

Las Naciones Unidas y sus socios humanitarios han lanzado una adenda de 298 millones de dólares estadounidenses al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026 para atender las necesidades derivadas de los terremotos de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses. El plan complementa las actividades humanitarias en curso y busca apoyar a las comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en protección, alojamiento, salud, educación, agua y saneamiento, seguridad alimentaria y recuperación temprana.

documents.title: Miles de niños y niñas siguen enfrentando múltiples riesgos un mes después de los devastadores terremotos en Venezuela
documents.body_text:
El desplazamiento, la interrupción de los servicios y las múltiples réplicas afectan a los más vulnerables mientras las comunidades intentan recuperarse de los efectos del desastre

**CARACAS/CIUDAD DE PANAMÁ/NUEVA YORK, 24 de julio de 2026 –** Un mes después de que dos poderosos terremotos azotaran la costa centro-norte de Venezuela, niños, niñas y familias continúan enfrentando los impactos causados por los sismos, entre ellos el desplazamiento, los daños a la infraestructura y las interrupciones de los servicios básicos.

Actualmente, casi 23.100 personas permanecen en los campamentos transitorios habilitados en La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda y Aragua. UNICEF está trabajando para llegar a aproximadamente 470.000 personas, incluyendo 169.000 niños y niñas, con asistencia para salvar vidas, lo que incluye servicios en salud, nutrición, agua, saneamiento e higiene, protección infantil, educación y protección social.

"Un mes después de los terremotos, niños, niñas y familias aún enfrentan las consecuencias de esta devastadora catástrofe. Más allá del daño visible, el miedo, la incertidumbre y las alteraciones causadas por el desplazamiento pueden tener impactos duraderos en el bienestar de la niñez", dijo **el representante de UNICEF en Venezuela, Manuel Rodríguez Pumarol**. "El apoyo continuo es esencial para asegurar que los niños, niñas y adolescentes tengan acceso a agua segura, atención médica, protección y los servicios que necesitan para recuperarse".

Los terremotos, que alcanzaron magnitudes de 7,2 y 7,5, causaron más de 5.390 muertes, dejaron más de 16.700 personas heridas y registraron más de 1.400 réplicas.

Las evaluaciones de daños continúan revelando la magnitud del impacto, con al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 que colapsaron por completo. Los daños a las instalaciones de salud y a cientos de escuelas están interrumpiendo servicios esenciales para miles de niños, mientras que las continuas réplicas siguen generando riesgos para las familias que viven en los refugios temporales.

Los niños y niñas afectados por la emergencia enfrentan mayores probabilidades de experimentar angustia psicológica, violencia, negligencia, explotación y separación familiar, lo que agrava los riesgos para su seguridad y bienestar. Las condiciones de hacinamiento, la interrupción de la rutina y la incertidumbre prolongada pueden aumentar aún más estas amenazas, especialmente para los niños y niñas más vulnerables.

UNICEF está trabajando con el Gobierno, el sistema de las Naciones Unidas y socios humanitarios para ofrecer servicios que salvan vidas y garantizan el acceso a salud, nutrición, agua, saneamiento e higiene, y protección infantil. Hasta la fecha, UNICEF ha distribuido más de 82 toneladas métricas de suministros de emergencia, incluyendo kits de salud, equipo de purificación y almacenamiento de agua, y materiales para el desarrollo infantil temprano y recreativo.

A medida que los esfuerzos de recuperación entran en una nueva fase, UNICEF hace un llamado a donantes y socios para que mantengan el apoyo a los niños, niñas y familias afectados por los terremotos, pero se estima que se requieren 65,7 millones de dólares estadounidenses para responder al impacto humanitario de los terremotos en los próximos meses.

En los campamentos temporales y en comunidades afectadas, UNICEF, junto con sus socios:

- Ha proporcionado agua segura a más de 8.900 personas mediante la distribución diaria de 80.000 litros de agua en tres campamentos de transición en La Guaira, y ha distribuido suministros esenciales de higiene para apoyar hasta 29.000 personas.
- En coordinación con el Ministerio de Salud, UNICEF apoyó a equipos móviles de salud en la provisión de servicios de atención primaria, incluyendo vacunaciones, a más de 21.000 personas, entre ellas niños, niñas y mujeres embarazadas. UNICEF también suministró medicamentos esenciales a 198 centros de salud, con la capacidad de brindar servicios de atención primaria a unas 49.000 personas.
- Más de 5.000 personas han recibido servicios de nutrición, incluyendo detección aguda de desnutrición, suplementación con micronutrientes, asesoría nutricional y apoyo en la lactancia materna para mujeres embarazadas y lactantes.
- UNICEF estableció espacios amigables para la infancia en campamentos transitorios en La Guaira, con los que ha llegado a más de 4.000 niños, niñas, adolescentes y cuidadores con apoyo psicosocial, actividades recreativas, manejo de casos y servicios especializados de protección infantil.
- UNICEF también apoya las Evaluaciones de Necesidades Post-Desastre en sectores clave, incluyendo WASH, salud, nutrición y educación, para ayudar a acelerar la restauración de servicios sociales esenciales para niños, niñas y sus familias en las áreas afectadas.

"A medida que las familias comienzan a recuperarse, los niños y niñas deben permanecer en el centro de la respuesta", dijo **Rodríguez Pumarol**. "Las próximas semanas serán críticas y un apoyo sostenido puede ayudar a evitar que la emergencia de hoy se convierta en una crisis a largo plazo para la niñez".

documents.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

One month after the earthquakes in Venezuela, access to food remains one of the top concerns for families across the affected areas.

WFP has reached more than 120,000 people with food assistance through four modalities, since no two families are living through this period the same way. Assistance include hot meals in shelters, ready-to-eat rations for those still on the move, food baskets for households that can still cook and in communities who lost their sources of income, and prepaid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning, giving families the power to prioritize their own needs.

The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response, moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies with the transport and storage of supplies spanning shelter, health, protection, and WASH.

To date, WFP has secured one third of the USD 80 million required to sustain and scale the response. Efforts continue to close the gap and safeguard the support for 500,000 people in 3 months.
