documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake: One month update – 24 July 2026
documents.body_text:
One month following the devastating earthquakes of June 24, Venezuela continues to grapple with the aftermath, facing profound grief as thousands mourn the loss of family, friends, and everything they owned. ​

This sudden natural disaster that affected particularly the coastal state of La Guaira, near Caracas, has transitioned into a complex, protracted crisis characterized by massive population displacement, severe infrastructural damage, and deep psychological trauma. In La Guaira and Caracas, the urgent needs include access to clean water, adequate shelter, mental health care, and protection. ​

The official death toll has reached 5,398, with 16,740 individuals injured, 17,907 displaced, and 6,462 rescued from the rubble. The structural devastation is staggering; 190 buildings have officially collapsed, while over 895 structures, including schools, vital public infrastructure, and hospitals, have suffered severe damage and are at risk of collapse. ​

Thousands are currently residing in makeshift Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) sites or sleeping in tents adjacent to their damaged homes. In Maiquetía (La Guaira), approximately 3,000 individuals are camping on the pavement directly in front of 20 severely damaged and unstable buildings. Similarly, in Avenida Bolívar (Caracas), another 3,000 individuals are living on the streets, stripped of proper shelter and basic services. ​

In response to the crisis, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) currently operates four mobile clinics providing Primary Health Care, Mental Health support, Health Promotion, and WASH activities across the most affected areas: three in La Guaira (Maiquetía, Catia La Mar, and Tamaguarena) and one in Caracas (Avenida Bolívar). These clinics offer primary healthcare, clean water, and emergency mental health interventions to families who have lost everything. In the past month, MSF medical teams have conducted 2,217 medical consultations.

The injuries sustained extend beyond physical; families still searching for loved ones beneath the rubble, along with the shock of sudden homelessness and displacement, have given rise to a psychological crisis. To address these mental health challenges, MSF has integrated mental health support into its mobile response, providing: 113 individual mental health, 323 group therapy sessions, 1,402 psycho-education sessions. With local infrastructure severely compromised, MSF teams are implementing water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) intervention: ​

- Installed a 5,000-liter water bladder in Playa Verde to serve as a reliable clean water source.
- Initiated the ongoing chlorination of four primary water distribution sites alongside continuous water purification monitoring.
- Distributed 5,000 bottles of emergency drinking water to families living on the streets.

Over the past month, MSF has donated approximately 8.5 tons of emergency medical supplies. This extensive logistical effort has supported immediate, life-saving operations and addressed the healthcare needs of an estimated 10,000 patients. MSF teams continue to provide disinfectants and Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) materials not only to active hospitals but also to overwhelmed local morgues, ensuring safety, hygiene, and dignity amid unprecedented loss.

documents.title: Venezuela earthquakes 1 month: protect girls from a second crisis
documents.body_text:
Following the twin earthquakes that killed more than [5,300](https://reliefweb.int/OCHA:%20https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-28-21-july-2026-time-0900-pm) people in Venezuela, children, especially girls, are now facing a rising risk of gender-based violence, disruption to essential services including menstrual health care, and increasingly uncertain access to education.

More than [23,000 ](https://reliefweb.int/OCHA:%20https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-28-21-july-2026-time-0900-pm)people still live in transitional camps across Venezuela.

Among them, girls and adolescents face risks that go beyond the immediate emergency.

## Overcrowded shelters increase violence risk

In some camps, overcrowded shelters without separate toilets or private spaces for women and girls increase exposure to violence and abuse.

Thousands of families are not in official camps at all, having set up makeshift shelters in public squares and open spaces near their damaged homes, with little access to clean water, food or protection services.

Fear of overcrowding and lack of privacy is pushing some families to stay in informal settlements rather than move to organised sites.

“I’d rather be in a plaza where I know the people around me than go somewhere huge where you don’t know who comes in and who goes out,” said Andreina, a 26-year-old mother who has been living in a public square with her husband and young daughter since 25 June.

“During emergencies, the protective environment for children weakens. Caregivers are under immense stress, and it is in these moments that trafficking networks and other perpetrators take advantage,” said Yesica Serrano, Plan International’s Regional Child Protection Advisor for Humanitarian Action, speaking from Caracas.

“The emergencies do not affect all children in the same way. Girls, especially adolescent girls face greater exposure to sexual exploitation, violence and domestic work, while adolescent boys face risks of recruitment by criminal groups,” Serrano added.

Adolescent girls who have been separated from their families, or whose caregivers have died or been hospitalised, face the sharpest exposure of all.

## Significant challenges accessing menstrual health supplies

Another major concern is the access to menstrual health supplies. Without adequate materials and private facilities, adolescent girls face barriers to accessing other forms of support available in the camps, compounding their isolation at exactly the moment they are most vulnerable.

“People are focused on finding food, water, torches and basic resources. But no one is thinking about what women need: sanitary towels, toilet paper, the basics,” said Andrea, a 17-year-old volunteer with a Plan International partner organisation.

## Disrupted education

Although Venezuelan schools are currently in their summer break, the earthquake cut the last school year short for thousands of children.

With several school buildings now being used to house displaced families, there is no certainty that classes will resume when the new school year is due to begin in September, putting at uncertainty the availability of one of the few safe spaces that help them recover.

## Hidden toll on children’s health

The physical and mental health of children and adolescents is increasingly affected by conditions in the areas hardest hit by the disaster.

Plan’s local partners in Venezuela report that physical complaints with no clear cause are appearing more and more, alongside signs of post-traumatic stress and a constant sense of insecurity, and on closer listening, they reveal weeks of disrupted sleep, jumpiness and accumulated fear.

“When it gets windy, I run into my room and hide, and I get scared,” says nine-year-old Victoria in La Guaira. Naomi, who is only 5, describes how recurring nightmares are disrupting her sleep: “I was on the beach, and a tsunami was chasing me.”

Michele, a 25-year-old mother of three girls, sums up what she sees every day: “They’re scared, they’re frightened. Right now, the children need psychological support to help them.”

“At this stage of the emergency, children’s mental health can no longer be treated as a secondary response. If we don’t address both the physical and emotional wellbeing together recovery will be impossible,” explains Yesica Serrano.

## Recovery funding must address all these risks from the outset

One month on, the challenge is no longer only humanitarian relief. Communities now face a longer recovery process that will determine whether girls return safely to school, regain access to protection services, manage their menstrual health with dignity and remain protected from exploitation and abuse in the months ahead.

The risk is that once global attention shifts elsewhere, girls will be left facing the consequences of this disaster alone. Plan International warns that recovery funding must go beyond rebuilding infrastructure.

Protecting girls, restoring education and strengthening community support systems are essential investments from the outset if we are to prevent a long-term crisis and ensure a more resilient recovery for Venezuela’s children and communities.

Plan International has been providing emergency assistance to communities since the first days after the earthquakes, working with local partner organisations across affected states.

The response includes protection services for children, with a focus on adolescent girls, psychosocial support, safe spaces in schools and communities, hygiene kits and essential household items, emergency education activities and primary health care.

documents.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #30 (23 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 30**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**23 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
- Official toll: **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks.**

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

**Note**

> ###### Starting with this edition, the report will be published on a weekly basis. The next edition will be released on 30 July. We thank partner organizations, United Nations entities and donors for their valuable contributions, and encourage them to continue reporting their earthquake response activities through the 345W platform. For more information on reporting and the use of the tool, please refer to the presentation: [345W Preparedness and Response](https://drive.google.com/file/d/12Tdck_8iHPTcj6BRDeYMwkp1lwS_-rYq/view?usp=sharing).

Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan
to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six
months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target
population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632
million to US$931 million.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira
state, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects
intended for affected populations.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
National response
 The Government response remains focused on assistance to affected people, as well as the
establishment and management of transitional camps.
 According to authorities, the response continues through 107 transitional camps for affected
populations, with a total capacity of 28,171 people and a current occupancy of 23,843 people. As of
22 July, 41 camps are located in Caracas, 28 in La Guaira, 28 in Miranda and 10 in Aragua. Of the
total camp population, 12,500 people are accommodated in La Guaira, 8,835 in Caracas, 1,833
in Miranda and 675 in Aragua.
 On 20 July, authorities announced the allocation of fully equipped housing units to an initial 240
families affected by the earthquakes. The housing units are located in Fuerte Tiuna, Caracas, and
form part of the Venezuela Renace plan.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com).
 School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto
Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital
District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión,
Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda (updated as of 21 July)
 In Miranda state, the humanitarian response has been primarily concentrated in the municipalities of
Plaza (Guarenas), Zamora (Guatire), Chacao, Sucre and Baruta, which have been identified among
the areas most affected by the earthquakes. In these locations, humanitarian organizations including
IOM, UNICEF, WFP, World Vision and the Venezuelan Red Cross have supported search and
rescue operations, structural assessments, medical and psychosocial care, distribution of food, safe
drinking water and hygiene items, as well as assistance for displaced people. Child protection
mechanisms have also been strengthened, support services have been established in transitional
camps, and early recovery interventions have been promoted.
La Guaira (updated as of 22 July)
 On 21 July, the President of the Presidential Commission for the Assessment of Infrastructure
Habitability reported that 6,907 buildings had been inspected in La Guaira using the traffic light
assessment methodology to determine the condition of structures. Of the total inspected, most
(3,237) received a green tag, indicating that the infrastructure poses no risk. Some 1,785 structures
received a yellow tag, indicating restricted use, while 1,885 were classified with a red tag. Structures
assigned either yellow or red classifications will undergo a second assessment.
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone) (updated as of 21 July)
 IOM, UNICEF, PAHO/WHO, Action Against Hunger, Cáritas Venezuela, CRS, CAMPO, Laboratorio
de Paz, the Yaracuy Human Rights Network and the Human Rights Committee of Bolívar
Municipality continue to implement response activities in areas affected by the earthquakes.
Reported interventions include the distribution of basic assistance and support across the nutrition,
water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and protection sectors, with a particular focus on
accompanying and supporting affected communities.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Falcón (Silva municipality)
 CEPOREJUN and ODISEF continue to strengthen capacities in Psychological First Aid (PFA)
through a training programme targeting 300 Civil Protection, Fire Department and VEN 911
personnel. As part of this initiative, the Bolivarian Militia requested a similar training, which is being
coordinated for next week with ODISEF’s support. In addition, OCHA and Civil Protection agreed to
extend this training to officials in Silva municipality, an initiative currently being coordinated with
Centroccidente. As a follow-up to previous efforts, Civil Protection also expressed interest in
continuing training to improve data collection on affected structures.
 The Local Coordination Forum (LCF) led an analysis and planning exercise for post-earthquake early
recovery in Silva municipality, consolidating inputs from six (6) organizations. The process identified
more than 30 activities and helped define priorities to strengthen essential services and support
people in vulnerable situations. The proposal incorporates sustainability, inter-institutional
coordination and community resilience approaches, and will be presented to state authorities to help
guide medium- and long-term recovery efforts, in line with the objectives of the Humanitarian
Response Plan (HRP) Addendum.
 In Falcón, UNICEF supported the interagency RNA and is deploying a team to deliver humanitarian
assistance through the delivery of critical WASH services and supplies.
Other states
 Trujillo: Authorities reported the relocation of 102 families across 14 municipalities, primarily from
La Guaira and Distrito Capital, who are being hosted by family and community networks. Local
organizations and academic institutions continue to provide assistance in health, nutrition,
protection, psychosocial support and food assistance. In Boconó, the State Government and
Municipal Mayor’s Office established a Situation Room under the Emergency Operations Centre
(EOC), with the participation of Civil Protection and the Great Mission Barrio Nuevo Barrio Tricolor.
Sediment removal and preventive tree-felling activities are also underway. The State Secretariat for
Infrastructure reported more than 40 road failures in the municipality. Identified priorities include the
rehabilitation of Trunk Road 007, the restoration of agricultural roads and critical areas of Boconó
Hospital, as well as strengthening support to host families.
 Work continues with municipal governments and Protection Councils to implement standardized
mechanisms for the registration and monitoring of needs at the municipal level.
Humanitarian coordination
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
continues to coordinate the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner
organizations, prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, water, sanitation and hygiene,
logistics and protection.
 As of 21 July, more than 117,000 people affected by the earthquakes had accessed essential
services and humanitarian support through the coordinated response of authorities,
communities, humanitarian partners and donors. More than 90 per cent of the people reached
are concentrated in the seven affected states, particularly in La Guaira, Miranda, Distrito
Capital and Aragua. The response was made possible through the efforts of at least 49
organizations implementing activities in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); food
security; health; shelter; nutrition; protection, including child protection and gender-based
violence (GBV) response; and education.
 UNESCO activated an institutional technical contingency plan focused on heritage protection and
continuity of education. In the area of cultural heritage, UNESCO assessed the Foro Libertador and
endorsed the preventive transfer of 287 historical volumes registered under the Memory of the World
Programme to the vaults of the Central Bank of Venezuela.
 UNICEF continues to scale up its multi-sectoral humanitarian response with a focus on health,
nutrition, WASH, child protection and early childhood development services in transitional camps,
communities and institutions reaching more than 21,176 people with life-saving assistance in the
most affected areas. In addition, supplies were distributed to cover the needs of up to 150,000 people
(health, nutrition and WASH supplies).
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
through the United Nations system, with support from UNDP. In line with the internationally
recognized PDNA methodology, coordination with relevant institutions and counterparts will continue
in the coming period.
 In addition, UNDP provided technical assistance to national institutions on the use of drones, artificial
intelligence and geospatial technologies for post-earthquake recovery and reconstruction planning,
with the aim of strengthening debris management and supporting evidence-based decision-making.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 Today, WFP's efforts focused on several parishes of Catia La Mar, La Guaira, where a total of 1,165
food baskets were distributed to families severely affected by the earthquakes who still retained the
capacity to cook. In the Playa Grande transitional camp, WFP distributed 650 ready-to-eat meals to
displaced people residing there. Additionally, across 24 community kitchens and 3 U.N. led
transitional camps, WFP and its partners served a total of 23,512 hot meals. Since the onset of the
emergency, WFP has reached 121,544 people with food assistance.
Education and Early Childhood Development
 UNICEF initiated early childhood development (ECD) activities in transitional camps, closely
integrated with child protection interventions. These activities reached an initial group of 82 children
under five years of age, including 42 girls, as well as seven pregnant and breastfeeding women.
 UNICEF provided guidance to families on nurturing care and child development practices, reaching
a total of 66 caregivers. These interventions aim to support the well-being, development and
resilience of young children affected by the earthquake and living in displacement settings.
Health
 PAHO/WHO continues coordinating the Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) response. As of 23 July,
14 EMTs remain deployed and operational, one is in the process of mobilization and seven have
been demobilized, with a cumulative total of 22,427 patients treated since the onset of the
emergency.
 PAHO/WHO participated in the Health Committee alongside the Military Single Authority and the
Health Single Authority in La Guaira. In addition, it strengthened inter-agency coordination through
bilateral engagement with UNICEF, UNFPA and IOM to clarify geographical and sectoral coverage
and avoid duplication of efforts in the health response.
 In coordination with the Ministry of People’s Power for Health (MPPH), PAHO/WHO supported the
designation and training of mental health focal points within the ASICs linked to the 107 camps
established for affected populations.
 PAHO/WHO distributed WHO Interagency Emergency Health Kits (IEHKs) to four camps—César
Nieves, Ciudad Los Caracas, Polideportivo ONU and Universidad Marítima—with sufficient supplies
to cover the primary health-care needs of approximately 1,000 people in each site.
 PAHO/WHO and the MPPH continued epidemiological surveillance of diarrhoeal diseases and other
notifiable diseases in camps and affected communities, following up on health alerts identified during
the emergency.
 Through the deployment of medical teams and joint efforts with its partner Ven Da Tu Mano, IOM is
expanding access to health services for people affected by the earthquake. To date, 5,900 people
have benefited from 7,025 medical consultations, including general medicine, internal medicine,
paediatrics, gynaecology and obstetrics services, as well as the provision of medicines and individual
psychological support.
 Since the onset of the emergency, UNFPA-led Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) activities
have reached 2,255 people through awareness-raising initiatives. Condoms were distributed to
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
1,365 people, 832 information and educational materials were provided, and 12 hygiene kits were
distributed. In addition, 154 pregnant women received antenatal care, 1,055 women received
contraceptive methods, and 86 HIV tests and 85 syphilis tests were conducted.
 UNICEF has significantly expanded access to essential health services in earthquake-affected
communities through the provision of medical supplies, deployment of mobile health teams and
support to national health authorities.
 UNICEF reached 5,135 people with essential primary healthcare services.
 Vaccination campaigns have reached 21,176 children, pregnant women and adults in transitional
camps, healthcare facilities and communities affected by the earthquake.
 UNICEF distributed essential health supplies and medicines sufficient to support the provision of
healthcare services for approximately 49,000 people in affected areas.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 Today, an Airlink flight carrying 34.4 metric tons (MT) of humanitarian assistance for eight (8)
organizations responding to the emergency in the country arrived at Simón Bolívar International
Airport in Maiquetía. Of this cargo, the Logistics Working Group supported the transportation of 9.42
MT, including 3.37 MT of temperature-controlled cargo, as well as the storage of 7.5 MT.
 Under the Emergency Telecommunications response, the internet system established for
communities settled in Caraballeda, La Guaira, was verified to be functioning properly. Remote
monitoring of the system is planned to continue.
 Authorities from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs report that information for humanitarian organizations
and cooperation actors is available through the platform www.venezuelanoestasola.com regarding
procedures for the arrival of aircraft and vessels carrying humanitarian assistance, as well as
guidance on the registration of routes, means of transport, crew members and cargo.
. Nutrition
 UNICEF continued to support the nutritional needs of vulnerable children and women affected by
the earthquakes. A total of 2,964 children under five years of age and 655 pregnant and lactating
women among displaced populations received a package of essential nutrition services, including
nutritional screening, micronutrient supplementation, counselling and referral to specialized services
when required.
 Approximately 1,492 caregivers of children under two years of age received counselling on
recommended infant and young child feeding practices, including breastfeeding support and age-
appropriate complementary feeding. Micronutrient supplementation was provided to reach up to
72,000 children and pregnant women.
 UNICEF also supported community outreach activities implemented by the National Institute of
Nutrition (INN), the Ministry of Health and NGO partners in affected communities. In coordination
with WFP, UNICEF promoted age-appropriate feeding practices for young children within the food
assistance response and facilitated a technical exchange between national authorities and the
Brazilian Human Milk Bank Network on quality assurance and safe management of human milk in
emergency settings.
Protection (including Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence)
 Protection activities implemented by UNHCR and its partners in the Polideportivo José María
Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande and Mare Abajo transitional camps included legal
assistance, case management, psychosocial support, counselling and referrals, reaching 1,399
people. In addition, 111 children and their families received legal guidance on birth registration,
identity documentation and legal representation, while 93 children participated in psychosocial,
recreational and socio-emotional support activities aimed at strengthening coping mechanisms in
the aftermath of the earthquakes. Overall, UNHCR and its implementing partners have provided
4,721 instances of assistance, including 119 instances of support to returnees.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
 A total of 685 instances of assistance were provided through information desks and community
sessions on access to rights, services available in the camps, protection mechanisms, referral
pathways, Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and
Abuse (PSEA).
 At the José María Vargas Sports Complex transitional camp, IOM is facilitating access to protection
services through guidance, legal assistance and documentation support. To date, 130 people have
received specialized assistance and case management.
 Under the Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Response component led by UNFPA,
awareness-raising activities reached 1,097 people. A total of 77 dignity kits were distributed, 100
people received psychosocial support and psychological first aid, 25 cases were managed, and two
(2) people received legal counselling.
 UNICEF continues to strengthen child protection services through psychosocial support,
identification of vulnerable children, case management and referral services delivered through Child-
Friendly Spaces and mobile child protection teams in affected areas.
 Across four transitional camps in La Guaira, four Child-Friendly Spaces remained operational,
reaching 3,099 children, adolescents and caregivers with psychosocial support, structured
recreational activities and protective services.
 To further strengthen the child protection response following the earthquake emergency, UNICEF
supplied key equipment and resources to local child protection teams in La Guaira, enhancing their
capacity to provide timely and quality services to affected children and families.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 In coordination with local authorities, IOM continues to manage the five transitional camps (José
María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium, Playa Grande, Golf Course and Mare Abajo),
supporting site improvements, strengthening coordination with humanitarian and cooperation
partners, and supporting registration processes.
 To date, IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed 3,175 cooking sets, 3,617
plastic tarpaulins, 2,115 buckets, 1,758 solar lamps, 819 shelter kits, 672 mosquito nets and 208
rechargeable solar flashlights.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 UNICEF continued to support access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services in displacement
settings and affected communities. UNICEF maintains the operation of emergency latrines, laundry
points, and handwashing stations, supported through regular water trucking operations providing
approximately 80,000 litres of water per day. Solid waste management, routine cleaning of sanitation
facilities, and replenishment of hygiene and cleaning supplies continue to be sustained.
 More than 465 people received hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available
life-saving services. In addition, family hygiene kits were distributed, reaching 8,906 people,
contributing to safer practices and improved living conditions among displaced populations.
 In parallel, UNICEF strengthened coordination with the Ministry of Water (MINAGUAS), HIDROVEN
and local water utilities, conducting technical assessments of critical water treatment, transmission
and distribution infrastructure affected by the earthquake.
 As part of its humanitarian response, IOM is strengthening access to essential supplies for the safe
storage and handling of water and hygiene needs. To date, it has distributed 1,552 collapsible 10-
litre water containers, 1,091 hygiene kits and 93 semi-collapsible 10-litre water containers.
Humanitarian financing and contributions
 The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced an additional appeal under the
Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela. The appeal outlines the multisectoral needs of 1.3
million people over the next six months. To reach those in need, US$299 million is required, in
addition to the US$632 million requested at the beginning of the year.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
 Several United Nations agencies, funds and programmes have issued emergency appeals to scale
up humanitarian assistance and support the response and recovery efforts following the
earthquakes, in line with the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Addendum.
 UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to fund its earthquake emergency response. The aim is to assist
470,000 people, including 160,000 children and adolescents, through water, sanitation and hygiene
(WASH), health, nutrition, child protection and education interventions in the most affected areas
over the coming months. IOM requires US$98 million to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities over
the next six months. PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support
the health response and early recovery efforts over the next six months and allocated US$1.5 million
from its Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP issued an initial appeal for US$80 million to
provide food assistance to 500,000 people over a six-month period. UNHCR, for its part, indicated
that it requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 Canada increased its matching contribution for donations supporting the earthquake response in
Venezuela from CAD 4 million to CAD 7 million, bringing its total support for the emergency to CAD
12 million. The funding, channelled through the Canadian Red Cross and the Humanitarian Coalition,
will support the provision of health, shelter and WASH services for affected populations.
 The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria approved an emergency funding package
of US$1.77 million to support HIV and tuberculosis services in Venezuela following the earthquakes.
The resources, to be managed through UNDP, will enable 7,000 people to continue HIV treatment,
ensure tuberculosis treatment for 500 people, and support prevention, testing and outreach services
for 1,500 members of key populations in the most affected areas.
 The European Union announced an additional contribution of €20 million to support humanitarian
action in the country. Of this amount, €10 million will support search and rescue operations, medical
assistance, the deployment of additional experts, and material assistance in the country. This
contribution comes in addition to the €5 million previously announced for the earthquake response
and the €52 million already allocated to humanitarian operations in Venezuela this year.
 In addition, under the European Union Humanitarian Air Bridge launched in June, three EU-funded
flights have already arrived in the country. The latest flight landed on 17 July carrying 48 metric
tonnes of medical supplies and shelter items.
 The Government of Italy allocated US$5.7 million to support the humanitarian response to the
earthquakes, helping deliver life-saving assistance, protection and access to essential services for
affected populations through AICS, WFP and IFRC.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country.
 The Republic of Korea announced an additional contribution of US$3.5 million in humanitarian
assistance. Of this amount, US$3 million will be channelled through UNDP to support debris removal
activities, while the remainder will be provided in-kind, specifically through 30 metric tons of
temporary shelters (family tents). The Republic of Korea had previously allocated US$1.25 million to
WFP and US$2.5 million to UNICEF in support of the humanitarian response in Venezuela.
 Japan allocated US$3.5 million to support the earthquake response. The funding will provide
humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and non-food
items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
and IOM.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden contributed SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.

OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.
NOTE
Starting with this edition, the report will be published on a weekly basis. The next edition will
be released on 30 July. We thank partner organizations, United Nations entities and donors
for their valuable contributions, and encourage them to continue reporting their earthquake
response activities through the 345W platform. For more information on reporting and the
use of the tool, please refer to the presentation: 345W Preparedness and Response.
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
Contact information
For more information, please contact the OCHA Venezuela Office:
Vanessa May – Head of Office a.i. – mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Humanitarian Affairs Officer – alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Public Information Officer – moreno7@un.org

**Reporte de situación N.º 30**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**23 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio.
- Balance oficial: **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para  
     atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas.**

A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.**

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.** Esta adenda complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.

**Nota**

> ###### A partir de esta edición, el informe se publicará de manera semanal. La próxima edición será publicada el jueves 30 de julio. Agradecemos a las organizaciones socias, entidades de las Naciones Unidas y donantes por sus valiosos aportes, y les invitamos a continuar reportando sus actividades de respuesta a la emergencia ocasionada por los terremotos a través de la plataforma 345W. Para más detalles sobre cómo reportar y la herramienta, puede consultar la presentación: [345W Preparación y respuesta](https://drive.google.com/file/d/12Tdck_8iHPTcj6BRDeYMwkp1lwS_-rYq/view?usp=sharing).

autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la
respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y
Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta
Humanitaria 2026 por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3
millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses. Esta adenda
complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones
a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.
Impacto en infraestructura
 Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.
 Como parte de la planificación para la recuperación y reconstrucción, las autoridades identificaron
40 terrenos en el estado La Guaira, equivalentes a aproximadamente 584.000 metros cuadrados,
para el desarrollo de proyectos habitacionales destinados a la población afectada.
 Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de
Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil
millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas,
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
comercios, escuelas, hospitales e instalaciones públicas. Entre tanto, estimaciones preliminares de
PNUD indican daños físicos directos por 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 6 % del PIB.
Respuesta nacional
 La respuesta gubernamental se mantiene centrada en la atención de las personas afectadas, así
como la instalación y manejo de los campamentos transitorios.
 De acuerdo con las autoridades, la respuesta continúa con 107 campamentos transitorios
habilitados para la atención de personas afectadas, con una capacidad instalada de 28.171
personas y una ocupación de 23.843 personas. Hasta el 22 de julio, 41 campamentos se encuentran
instalados en Caracas, 28 en La Guaira, 28 en Miranda y 10 en Aragua. Del total de población
alojada, 12.500 personas se encuentran en La Guaira, 8.835 en Caracas, 1.833 en Miranda y
675 en Aragua.
 Este 20 de julio, las autoridades anunciaron la entrega de viviendas equipadas a unas primeras 240
familias afectadas por los terremotos. Las viviendas se encuentran en Fuerte Tiuna, Caracas, y son
parte del plan Venezuela Renace.
 Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad
(Conapdis) para coordinar una respuesta oportuna e inclusiva en las zonas afectadas.
 Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas
(www.localizapacientes.com).
 Las actividades escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados
Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José
Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas);
Distrito Capital (Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo,
Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).
Situación por estado
Distrito Capital (Caracas) y Miranda (actualizado al 21 de julio)
 En el estado Miranda, la respuesta humanitaria se ha concentrado principalmente en los municipios
Plaza (Guarenas), Zamora (Guatire), Chacao, Sucre y Baruta, identificados entre las zonas con
mayores afectaciones. En estas localidades, organizaciones humanitarias como la OIM, UNICEF,
el PMA, World Vision, la Cruz Roja Venezolana, han apoyado labores de búsqueda y rescate,
evaluaciones estructurales, atención médica y psicosocial, distribución de alimentos, agua potable
y artículos de higiene, además de asistencia para personas desplazadas. Asimismo, se han
fortalecido los mecanismos de protección de la niñez, se han habilitado apoyos en campamentos
transitorios y se han impulsado acciones de recuperación temprana.
La Guaira (actualizado al 22 de julio)
 El presidente de la Comisión Presidencial de Evaluación de Habitabilidad de Infraestructuras
informó el 21 de julio que se han inspeccionado 6.907 edificaciones en La Guaira, bajo el método
del semáforo, para indicar el estado de las estructuras. Del total, la mayoría (3.237) obtuvieron
etiqueta verde, es decir, que la infraestructura no representa riesgos. Unas 1.785 estructuras
recibieron etiqueta amarilla, indicando un uso restringido, y 1.885 fueron clasificadas con la etiqueta
roja. Ambas calificaciones pasarían a una segunda revisión.
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro) (actualizado al 21 de julio)
 OIM, UNICEF, OPS/OMS, Acción Contra el Hambre, Cáritas Venezuela, CRS, CAMPO, Laboratorio
de Paz, la Red de Derechos Humanos de Yaracuy y el Comité de Derechos Humanos del municipio
Bolívar, mantienen acciones de respuesta en las áreas afectadas por los sismos. Las intervenciones
reportadas incluyen distribución de asistencia básica y apoyo en los sectores de nutrición, agua,
saneamiento e higiene (ASH) y protección, con énfasis en el acompañamiento a las comunidades
afectadas.
Falcón (Municipio Silva)
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
 CEPOREJUN y ODISEF continúan fortaleciendo las capacidades en Primeros Auxilios
Psicológicos (PAP) mediante un proceso formativo dirigido a 300 funcionarios de Protección Civil,
Bomberos y VEN 911. En el marco de esta iniciativa, la Milicia Bolivariana solicitó una capacitación

condiciones de vida de las poblaciones desplazadas.

documents.title: Thousands of children continue to face multiple risks one month after devastating earthquakes in Venezuela
documents.body_text:
**CARACAS/PANAMA CITY/NEW YORK, 24 July 2026 –** One month after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela’s north-central coast, children and families continue to face the lasting impacts of displacement, damaged infrastructure and disruption to essential services.

Nearly 23,100 people are currently in temporary camps across La Guaira, the Capital District, Miranda and Aragua. UNICEF is working to reach approximately 470,000 people, including 169,000 children, with life-saving assistance across health, nutrition, water and sanitation, child protection, education and social protection.

“One month after the earthquakes, children and families are still dealing with the consequences of this devastating disaster. Beyond the visible damage, the fear, uncertainty and disruption caused by displacement can have lasting impacts on children’s well-being,” said UNICEF Representative in Venezuela, Manuel Rodriguez Pumarol. “Continued support is essential to ensure children have access to safe water, health care, protection and the services they need to recover.”

The earthquakes, measuring 7.2 and 7.5 in magnitude, killed more than 5,390 people, injured over 16,700 and triggered more than 1,400 aftershocks.

Damage assessments continue to reveal the scale of the impact, with at least 856 buildings affected, including 190 that collapsed entirely. Damage to health facilities and hundreds of schools is disrupting essential services for thousands of children, while continued aftershocks are sustaining risks for families living in temporary shelters.

Children affected by emergencies face heightened risks of psychological distress, violence, neglect, exploitation and family separation which compounds risk to their safety and wellbeing. Overcrowded conditions, disruption to routine and prolonged uncertainty can further increase these risks, particularly for the most vulnerable children.

UNICEF is working with the Government, the United Nations system and humanitarian partners to deliver life-saving and protective services across health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene, and child protection. To date, UNICEF has distributed more than 82 metric tons of emergency supplies, including health kits, water purification and storage equipment, and early childhood development and recreational materials.

As recovery efforts enter a new phase, UNICEF is calling on donors and partners to sustain support for children and families affected by the earthquakes, but an estimated US$65.7 million is required to respond to the humanitarian impact of the earthquakes in the months ahead.

In temporary camps and affected communities, UNICEF and partners have:

- Provided safe water to more than 8,900 people through the daily distribution of 80,000 litres of water across three transitional camps in La Guaira, and distributed essential hygiene supplies to support up to 29,000 people.
- In coordination with the Ministry of Health, UNICEF supported mobile health teams in providing primary healthcare services, including vaccinations, to more than 21,000 people, including children and pregnant women. UNICEF also supplied 198 health facilities with essential medicines, with the capacity to provide primary healthcare services to up to 49,000 people.
- Reached more than 5,000 people with nutrition services, including acute malnutrition screening, micronutrient supplementation, nutrition counselling, and breastfeeding support for pregnant and lactating women.
- Established child-friendly spaces in transitional camps in La Guaira, reaching more than 4,000 children, adolescents, and caregivers with psychosocial support, recreational activities, case management, and specialized child protection services.
- UNICEF is also supporting Post-Disaster Needs Assessments (PDNAs) across key sectors, including WASH, health, nutrition, and education, to help accelerate the restoration of essential social services for children and their families in affected areas.

“As families begin recovering, children must remain at the centre of the response,” said Pumarol. “The weeks ahead will be critical and sustained support can help prevent today's emergency from becoming a longer-term crisis for children.”

documents.title: Envíos aéreos de ayuda humanitaria a Venezuela (24 julio 2026)
El Programa Mundial de Alimentos alcanza a más de 100.000 personas con asistencia tras los terremotos en Venezuela
documents.body_text:
CARACAS – Un mes después de que dos poderosos terremotos sacudieran el centro-norte de Venezuela, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) continúa brindando asistencia alimentaria a las comunidades afectadas por la devastación. Esta respuesta sin precedentes, adaptada a las diferentes necesidades de cada zona afectada, ya ha alcanzado a más de 100.000 personas y, con la financiación adecuada, espera llegar a medio millón en los próximos dos meses.

En las primeras 72 horas de la emergencia, WFP puso en marcha una serie de diagnósticos que ya han sido completados en más de 80 comunidades de siete estados afectados. Estos han permitido orientar la respuesta con base en información sobre acceso a alimentos, funcionamiento de los mercados, cadenas de suministro y riesgos de protección. Este trabajo se ha realizado en estrecha coordinación con el Gobierno de Venezuela y los socios humanitarios.

"Ninguna familia afectada está viviendo esta catástrofe de la misma manera, y la asistencia debe moverse tan rápido como cambian las condiciones sobre el terreno", afirmó Stephanie Hochstetter, Representante de WFP en Venezuela. "Estábamos aquí antes de los terremotos, y nos quedamos con las y los venezolanos, junto a las autoridades locales y nuestros socios, el tiempo que sea necesario para que las familias afectadas puedan volver a ponerse en pie".

**Una respuesta adaptada a las condiciones y necesidades de cada comunidad**

WFP está ajustando su asistencia a las circunstancias específicas de cada comunidad:

- Comidas calientes para personas en albergues y comedores comunitarios: comidas completas con proteínas, vegetales y agua, preparadas en el lugar como parte de un esfuerzo coordinado entre múltiples socios.
- Raciones listas para consumir para personas sin medios para cocinar: dirigidas a quienes aún están en movimiento o refugiándose donde se sienten seguros. Estas raciones no requieren preparación y cubren tres días de necesidades alimentarias por persona.
- Canastas de alimentos para hogares cuyas viviendas siguen siendo habitables, pero cuyos medios de vida y acceso a los mercados se han visto afectados: consisten en alimentos básicos secos que cubren el 75 por ciento de las necesidades alimentarias mensuales de una familia.
- Cupones electrónicos prepagados en zonas donde los mercados están funcionando: permiten a las familias priorizar sus necesidades más urgentes y, al mismo tiempo, apoyan la recuperación de la economía local.

**Ampliando la respuesta de emergencia mientras se atienden las necesidades existentes en todo el país**

WFP busca alcanzar hasta 500.000 personas durante los primeros tres meses de la respuesta. La organización también actúa como columna vertebral logística de la respuesta humanitaria, movilizando suministros de socorro hacia comunidades de difícil acceso en apoyo a toda la comunidad humanitaria.

Los servicios logísticos de WFP han apoyado a organizaciones no gubernamentales y agencias de las Naciones Unidas, con el transporte de 261 toneladas métricas de asistencia y el almacenamiento de más de 1.300 metros cúbicos de suministros, incluidos artículos relacionados con albergue, salud, protección, recuperación temprana y agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH).

La asistencia se entrega en coordinación con la respuesta del Gobierno de Venezuela y como complemento a ella, junto a socios humanitarios y organizaciones de la sociedad civil presentes sobre el terreno.

**Brecha de financiación**

WFP solicita 80 millones de dólares para sostener y ampliar su respuesta. Sin contribuciones oportunas de los donantes, la expansión de las operaciones y la capacidad de seguir adaptando la asistencia a las necesidades cambiantes de las comunidades se verán limitadas.

\# # #

**Nota para los editores:**

[Aquí](https://multimedia.wfp.org/Share/rdy64s56nee55g23godbc2u614dtqgc5?FR_=1&W=1526&H=948) se puede acceder a material de vídeo con calidad de emisión.

Se puede acceder a fotografías en alta resolución [aquí](https://multimedia.wfp.org/Share/asobbfj2wcg85w2l17554o44ff4c4045).

El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas es la mayor organización humanitaria del mundo dedicada a salvar vidas en emergencias y a utilizar la asistencia alimentaria para allanar el camino hacia la paz, la estabilidad y la prosperidad de las personas que se recuperan de conflictos, desastres y los efectos del cambio climático.

documents.title: WFP reaches more than 100,000 people with assistance since Venezuela earthquakes
documents.body_text:
CARACAS – A month after two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela, the World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide food assistance to communities impacted by the devastation. This unprecedented response, tailored to different needs in each affected area, has already reached more than 100,000 people and, with proper funding, hopes to reach a total of half a million over the next two months.

Within 72 hours of the emergency, WFP launched a series of assessments that have now been completed across more than 80 communities in seven affected states. These have helped shape WFP’s response based on indicators involving access to food, market functionality, and supply chains and protection risks., These efforts have been undertaken in close coordination with the Government of Venezuela and humanitarian partners.

“No two affected families are living through this catastrophe the same way, and assistance must move as fast as conditions on the ground change,” said Stephanie Hochstetter, WFP Representative in Venezuela. “We were here before the earthquakes, and we will stay with Venezuelans, and alongside the local authorities and partners, for as long as it takes for families to get back on their feet”.

**A response built around real, changing conditions**

WFP is tailoring its support to each community’s specific circumstances and needs:

- Hot meals for people in shelters and community kitchens: Full meals with protein, vegetables, and water, prepared on site as part of a coordinated multi-partner effort.
- Ready-to-eat rations for people without the means to cook: For those still on the move or sheltering wherever they feel safe. These rations require no preparation and cover three days of food needs per person.
- Family food baskets for households whose homes remain habitable, but whose livelihoods and access to markets have been disrupted: this takes the form of dry staples covering 75 percent of a family's monthly food needs.
- Pre-paid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning: this enables families to prioritize their most urgent needs while supporting local economic recovery.

**Scaling the emergency response while continuing to address pre-existing needs across the country**

WFP aims to reach up to 500,000 people over the response's first three months. The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response; moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities in support of the wider humanitarian community. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies, with 261 metric tons transported and over 1,300 m³ stored — spanning shelter, health, protection, early recovery, and WASH supplies.

Assistance is being delivered in coordination with, and as a complement to, the Government of Venezuela's response and alongside humanitarian and civil-society partners on the ground.

**Funding gap**

WFP is appealing for USD 80 million to sustain and scale its response. Without timely donor contributions, the pace of expansion and the ability to continue tailoring assistance to evolving needs will be constrained.

\# # #

documents.title: IFRC: Un mes después de los terremotos de Venezuela, la atención en salud, el apoyo psicosocial y el acceso a agua potable son prioridad urgente
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas, Ciudad de Panama, Ginebra, 23 de julio de 2026** — Un mes después de los dos terremotos que sacudieron el centro-norte de Venezuela, la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC) y la Cruz Roja Venezolana (CRV) han identificado tres áreas críticas para la asistencia humanitaria en el corto y mediano plazo: la atención primaria en salud, el cuidado de la salud mental y el acceso a agua potable.

La IFRC y la CRV concentran ahora sus esfuerzos en la distribución de ayuda humanitaria, la prestación de servicios de salud y la realización de nuevas evaluaciones de necesidades. Sus hallazgos señalan que muchas familias todavía dependen del agua embotellada para beber, asearse y cocinar. El acceso al saneamiento también sigue siendo limitado, lo que eleva el riesgo de brotes de enfermedades en las zonas donde se aloja la población desplazada. Miles de personas con enfermedades crónicas no han recuperado del todo la continuidad de su tratamiento, una interrupción que amenaza su bienestar y puede añadir presión al sistema de salud. Los sobrevivientes conviven también con ansiedad, miedo, tristeza e insomnio mientras atraviesan el duelo por la pérdida de sus seres queridos, sus trabajos y sus medios de vida.

*“A un mes de los devastadores terremotos que sacudieron nuestro país, reafirmamos nuestro compromiso con los venezolanos. Hemos activado todos los mecanismos de cooperación del Movimiento Internacional de la Cruz Roja y la Media Luna Roja para fortalecer y complementar nuestra respuesta, y seguiremos aquí para quienes más lo necesitan”.* Dijo el presidente de la Cruz Roja Venezolana, Luis Manuel Farías Villanueva. “*Apuntamos a una operación de 24 meses para seguir acompañando a la población; las necesidades han ido cambiando y nuestra respuesta se ha ajustado para servir más y mejor.”*

Desde el minuto uno, los equipos locales de la Cruz Roja han estado al lado de las personas afectadas: primero instalando un hospital de campaña, acompañando el rescate de sobrevivientes y reconectando a familias que habían perdido el rastro de sus seres queridos; y ahora, con la distribución de ayuda humanitaria y el refuerzo de la atención primaria en salud a través de una clínica de emergencia en La Guaira.

Esta clínica, instalada por la IFRC y gestionada por la Cruz Roja Española, refuerza el hospital de campaña de la Cruz Roja Venezolana. Operará durante cuatro meses y ya presta servicios de salud y apoyo psicosocial que beneficiarán a cerca de 30.000 personas. Una de ellas es Gabriel Cipriani, quien perdió a familiares cercanos cuando su edificio colapsó y vive con una condición neurológica que requiere medicación constante. Para él, que la Cruz Roja siga ahí es la diferencia entre continuar su tratamiento o interrumpirlo: *"Saber que puedo contar con una doctora de la Cruz Roja me hizo sentir que no estoy solo, que hay una mano que está conmigo. Eso te da seguridad, te da confianza".*

En las próximas semanas y meses, la prioridad de la IFRC y la CRV será sostener esa atención de salud y ampliar el acceso a agua segura mientras se sientan las bases de la recuperación: reforzar la vigilancia epidemiológica para prevenir brotes, mantener el apoyo psicosocial y el tratamiento de enfermedades crónicas, y empezar a acompañar a las familias en la recuperación de sus medios de vida. La asistencia se ajustará a medida que las necesidades cambien, con especial atención a quienes corren mayor riesgo: la niñez, las personas mayores, las mujeres embarazadas y lactantes, y las personas con enfermedades crónicas o discapacidad.

*"El desastre está lejos de terminar. Continuar con las distribuciones de artículos esenciales y cuidar del bienestar de la población y de la salud pública es y seguirá siendo una prioridad en el mediano plazo; pero más adelante también lo será garantizar que las personas recuperen sus medios de vida y sus actividades de generación de ingresos",* dijo la directora regional de la IFRC para las Américas, Loyce Pace. *"Un desastre como este exige una asistencia multisectorial, integral y de largo aliento. La IFRC está comprometida con la Cruz Roja Venezolana y con la población venezolana para hacerlo posible, y por eso abogamos por un financiamiento sostenido y flexible, capaz de acompañar a las familias durante todo su proceso de recuperación".*

El financiamiento tiene una cifra concreta. La IFRC lanzó un llamamiento de emergencia para recaudar 50 millones de francos suizos para asistir a 300.000 personas durante dos años. A un mes del desastre, cuenta con un 25,19 por ciento de cobertura. A medida que las necesidades de la población incrementan y se hacen más complejas, los recursos deberían crecer al mismo ritmo.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #3 (23 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
**1. Context**   
  
Three weeks after the 24 June earthquakes, the death toll and affected population continue increasing. OCHA has formalized the national response into a six-month Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July–Dec. 2026).   
  
**Toll:** 5,278 dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued alive. Of the confirmed dead, 7% remain unidentified, mainly due to missing fingerprint records and identity system gaps.   
  
**Displacement:** As of July 21, 107 transitional camps for affected populations have a total capacity of 27,822 people and current occupancy of 23,587 people. As of July 20, 41 camps are in Caracas, 28 in La Guaira, 28 in Miranda, and 10 in Aragua. Of the total camp population, 12,474 people are in La Guaira, 8,554 in Caracas, 1,877 in Miranda, and 682 in Aragua. These numbers are a snapshot, as the population in shelters changes constantly.   
  
**Debris:** An estimated 1 million tons of debris has resulted from the earthquake. Of this, only 6,700 tons has been cleared in La Guaira so far, representing just 1% of the total.   
  
**Humanitarian funding request**: OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum requests USD 298 million to reach 1.3 million people over six months (JulyDecember 2026). This is in addition to the USD 930 million humanitarian funding appeal required for 6.2 million people in Venezuela prior to the earthquake Limited humanitarian operational presence: OCHA's own access assessment finds that Aragua, Carabobo, and Yaracuy have a relatively limited humanitarian operational presence. These states are accessible; the gap is a lack of resources. Priority needs as per the OCHA Rapid Needs Assessment: health (53%), safe water (52%), food security (50%), psychosocial support (27%), sanitation/hygiene (22%), protection/safety/dignity (18%), shelter (17%).   
**Economic constraints**: June inflation hit 13.8%, more than double May's rate. National reconstruction cost estimates now range from USD 12–15 billion (internal field sourcing).

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Situation Report #8 (July 22, 2026)
documents.body_text:
**Project HOPE continues to expand its humanitarian response across northern Venezuela. The team is significantly increasing access to healthcare for displaced and affected communities by operating eight mobile medical units (MMU), which are providing primary and maternal healthcare services in shelters and underserved communities. Project HOPE also continues to provide additional clinical support at health facilities in Distrito Capital and Miranda, with expansion underway to facilities in La Guaira. To reduce the risk of secondary public health emergencies, Project HOPE is also connecting families to mental health support, providing essential medicines, distributed additional hygiene kits through complementary funding, and recently launched a water trucking initiative.**

**Situation Overview**

**Humanitarian needs remain high as communities transition from the immediate aftermath of the earthquakes into a prolonged recovery phase.** While debris removal and damage assessments continue, thousands of displaced people remain in temporary shelters with persistent needs for healthcare, safe water, sanitation, and protection services. Overcrowded living conditions, intermittent rainfall, and disruptions to essential services continue to increase the risk of infectious disease transmission. At the same time, health facilities face the pressure of a continued increase in demand for services, including for acute injuries and routine health needs that were interrupted by the disaster. As operations evolve, humanitarian partners are increasingly focused on restoring access to primary healthcare and strengthening local health services to support communities through recovery.

Project HOPE’s Response and Local Insights
Project HOPE continues to scale its integrated health, WASH, and protection response to
meet evolving humanitarian needs. The team’s capacity to provide medical care has
expanded, with eight MMU teams operational and six of these teams rotating among
the three largest displacement sites in La Guaira — Caraballeda, Playa Grande, and
Mare Abajo. Project HOPE’s two other MMU teams are being mobilized to communities
based on identified gaps and emerging humanitarian needs. All units are helping ensure
consistent access to primary healthcare, maternal healthcare, and referral services.
Alongside MMU services, Project HOPE is currently supporting operations at five
health centers in Distrito Capital and Miranda, with plans to expand this support to an
additional five health centers in La Guaira in the coming weeks. This will help strengthen
the weakened health system and ensure access to essential healthcare as communities
transition from emergency response toward early recovery.
Project HOPE continues to coordinate closely with national authorities, PAHO, UN
agencies, and humanitarian partners to identify priority health needs, avoid duplication
of services, and ensure resources reach the communities with the greatest needs.
Health
• Project HOPE is operating eight MMU teams, providing integrated primary
healthcare, maternal health services, obstetric ultrasounds, and referrals
across earthquake-affected communities.
• One of the MMU teams is responding while traveling between shelters for
people affected by the earthquake in Miranda.
In the last week, Project HOPE has conducted nearly 2,000 additional
primary healthcare consultations.
• The most common conditions being treated include dehydration,
respiratory infections, skin infections, diarrheal disease, urinary tract
infections, diabetes, hypertension, and other acute and chronic conditions.
Mental Health & Psychosocial Support

• Project HOPE provided 46 additional psychological first aid sessions across
the three supported states during the reporting period, continuing critical
mental health support for displaced families and frontline responders.
Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Support
• Project HOPE launched a water trucking initiative in coordination with the
Ministry of Water, delivering 10,000 liters of water twice weekly to the
Pedro Emilio Coll shelter in Distrito Capital, directly benefiting
approximately 600 displaced people during the initial delivery.
• Through complementary funding, Project HOPE distributed 360 personal
hygiene kits during MMU operations. Hygiene kit distributions were
accompanied by hygiene promotion sessions, guidance on proper kit use,
and Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) messaging.
Project HOPE has worked in Venezuela since 2019, strengthening access to health
services, medicines, and health education, while supporting local health workers and
community-based responses to humanitarian needs. Project HOPE has a team of
over 100 in the country, and additional Project HOPE emergency response team
members have mobilized to support the most urgent needs.
Project HOPE has responded to multiple earthquakes in recent years, including the
2025 Myanmar earthquake, the 2023 Türkiye-Syria earthquakes, the 2023 Morocco
earthquake, the 2022 West Java earthquake, and the 2021 Haiti earthquake.

documents.title: IFRC: Un mois après les séismes au Venezuela, les soins de santé, le soutien psychosocial et l'accès à l'eau potable demeurent des priorités urgentes
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas, Panama, Genève, 23 juillet 2026** — Un mois après les deux séismes qui ont frappé le centre-nord du Venezuela, la Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) et la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne (CRV) ont identifié trois domaines critiques nécessitant une assistance humanitaire à court et à moyen terme : les soins de santé primaires, la santé mentale et l'accès à l'eau potable.

L'IFRC et la CRV concentrent désormais leurs efforts sur la distribution de l'aide humanitaire, la fourniture de services de santé et la réalisation d'évaluations complémentaires des besoins. Leurs constatations montrent que de nombreuses familles dépendent encore de l'eau en bouteille pour boire, cuisiner et assurer leur hygiène. L'accès aux services d'assainissement reste également limité, ce qui accroît le risque de flambées de maladies dans les zones où vivent les personnes déplacées. Des milliers de personnes atteintes de maladies chroniques n'ont pas encore retrouvé un accès régulier à leurs traitements, une interruption qui menace leur santé et exerce une pression supplémentaire sur le système de santé. Les survivants vivent également avec l'anxiété, la peur, la tristesse et les troubles du sommeil, tout en faisant le deuil de leurs proches, de leur emploi et de leurs moyens de subsistance

*« Un mois après les séismes dévastateurs qui ont secoué notre pays, nous réaffirmons notre engagement envers le peuple vénézuélien. Nous avons activé tous les mécanismes de coopération du Mouvement international de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge afin de renforcer et de compléter notre réponse, et nous resterons aux côtés de celles et ceux qui en ont le plus besoin »*, a déclaré Luis Manuel Farías Villanueva, président de la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne. *« Nous préparons une opération de 24 mois afin de continuer à accompagner les populations. Les besoins ont évolué et notre réponse s'est adaptée pour venir en aide à un plus grand nombre de personnes et répondre plus efficacement à leurs besoins. »*

Dès les premières minutes, les équipes locales de la Croix-Rouge se sont tenues aux côtés des personnes touchées : elles ont d'abord mis en place un hôpital de campagne, participé au sauvetage des survivants et aidé à rétablir les liens entre les familles séparées, avant de distribuer une aide humanitaire et de renforcer les soins de santé primaires grâce à une clinique d'urgence à La Guaira.

Cette clinique, mise en place par l'IFRC et gérée par la Croix-Rouge espagnole, vient renforcer l'hôpital de campagne de la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne. Elle fonctionnera pendant quatre mois et fournit déjà des services de santé et de soutien psychosocial qui bénéficieront à près de 30 000 personnes. Parmi elles figure Gabriel Cipriani, qui a perdu plusieurs proches lors de l'effondrement de son immeuble et vit avec une maladie neurologique nécessitant un traitement permanent. Pour lui, la présence continue de la Croix-Rouge fait toute la différence entre poursuivre son traitement ou le voir interrompu : « Savoir que je peux compter sur un médecin de la Croix-Rouge m'a fait sentir que je n'étais pas seul, qu'il y avait une main tendue vers moi. Cela vous donne un sentiment de sécurité et de confiance. »

Au cours des prochaines semaines et des prochains mois, la priorité de l'IFRC et de la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne sera de maintenir cette prise en charge sanitaire, d'élargir l'accès à l'eau potable et de poser les bases du relèvement : renforcer la surveillance épidémiologique afin de prévenir les flambées de maladies, poursuivre le soutien psychosocial et les traitements des maladies chroniques, et accompagner les familles dans la reconstruction de leurs moyens de subsistance. L'assistance sera adaptée à l'évolution des besoins, avec une attention particulière portée aux personnes les plus vulnérables : les enfants, les personnes âgées, les femmes enceintes et allaitantes, ainsi que les personnes vivant avec une maladie chronique ou un handicap.

*« Cette catastrophe est loin d'être terminée. Continuer à distribuer des articles essentiels et à préserver le bien-être des populations ainsi que la santé publique est, et restera, une priorité à moyen terme. Mais, à plus long terme, il faudra également veiller à ce que les personnes puissent reconstruire leurs moyens de subsistance et reprendre leurs activités génératrices de revenus »*, a déclaré Loyce Pace, directrice régionale de l'IFRC pour les Amériques. *« Une catastrophe comme celle-ci exige une assistance multisectorielle, globale et durable. L'IFRC est pleinement engagée aux côtés de la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne et du peuple vénézuélien pour rendre cela possible. C'est pourquoi nous lançons un appel en faveur d'un financement durable et flexible, capable d'accompagner les familles tout au long de leur relèvement. »*

Ce financement correspond à un besoin concret. L'IFRC a lancé un appel d'urgence de 50 millions de francs suisses afin de venir en aide à 300 000 personnes pendant deux ans. Un mois après la catastrophe, cet appel est financé à hauteur de 25,19 %. À mesure que les besoins des populations évoluent et deviennent plus complexes, les ressources nécessaires pour y répondre doivent augmenter au même rythme.
