documents.title: IFRC: One month after Venezuela's earthquakes, health care, psychosocial support and safe water remain urgent priorities
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas, Panama City, Geneva 23 July 2026** — One month after the two earthquakes that struck north-central Venezuela, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and the Venezuelan Red Cross (VRC) have identified three critical areas for humanitarian assistance in the short and medium term: primary health care, mental health care and access to safe drinking water.

The IFRC and the VRC are now focusing their efforts on distributing humanitarian aid, delivering health services and carrying out further needs assessments. Their findings show that many families still depend on bottled water to drink, wash and cook. Access to sanitation also remains limited, raising the risk of disease outbreaks in the areas where displaced people are staying. Thousands of people with chronic conditions have yet to fully regain continuity of treatment — an interruption that threatens their wellbeing and can add further strain to the health system. Survivors are also living with anxiety, fear, sadness and sleeplessness as they grieve the loss of loved ones, of their jobs and of their livelihoods.

*"One month on from the devastating earthquakes that shook our country, we reaffirm our commitment to the Venezuelan people. We have activated every cooperation mechanism of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement to strengthen and complement our response, and we will remain here for those who need it most,"* said Luis Manuel Farías Villanueva, President of the Venezuelan Red Cross. *"We are planning a 24-month operation to keep standing with people; needs have been changing, and our response has adjusted to serve more people and to serve them better."*

From the very first minute, local Red Cross teams have been alongside the people affected: first setting up a field hospital, supporting the rescue of survivors and reconnecting families who had lost track of their loved ones; and now, distributing humanitarian aid and strengthening primary health care through an emergency clinic in La Guaira.

The clinic, set up by the IFRC and managed by the Spanish Red Cross, reinforces the Venezuelan Red Cross field hospital. It will operate for four months and is already delivering health and psychosocial services that will benefit close to 30,000 people. One of them is Gabriel Cipriani, who lost close relatives when his building collapsed and lives with a neurological condition that requires constant medication. For him, the Red Cross remaining there is the difference between continuing his treatment and having it interrupted: *"Knowing I can count on a Red Cross doctor made me feel that I am not alone, that there is a hand with me. That gives you security, it gives you confidence."*

In the coming weeks and months, the priority for the IFRC and the VRC will be to sustain that health care and expand access to safe water while laying the foundations for recovery: strengthening epidemiological surveillance to prevent outbreaks, maintaining psychosocial support and treatment for chronic conditions, and beginning to accompany families as they rebuild their livelihoods. Assistance will be adjusted as needs change, with particular attention to those at greatest risk: children, older people, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and people with chronic illnesses or disabilities.

*"This disaster is far from over. Continuing to distribute essential items and safeguarding people's wellbeing and public health is, and will remain, a priority in the medium term — but further ahead it will also mean making sure people recover their livelihoods and their income-generating activities,"* said Loyce Pace, IFRC Regional Director for the Americas\*. "A disaster like this one calls for assistance that is multisectoral, comprehensive and sustained over time. The IFRC is committed to the Venezuelan Red Cross and to the people of Venezuela in making that possible — and that is why we are calling for sustained, flexible funding, able to accompany families throughout their recovery."\*

That funding has a concrete figure. The IFRC launched an Emergency Appeal to raise 50 million Swiss francs to assist 300,000 people over two years. One month on from the disaster, it is 25.19 per cent funded. As people's needs evolve and grow more complex, the resources to meet them should grow at the same pace.

documents.title: Venezuela: One month after the earthquakes, humanitarian funding falls far short
documents.body_text:
*One month after the devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela, thousands of people are still living in temporary shelters while trying to rebuild their lives. International attention and financial support must be stepped up, without forgetting those who already needed humanitarian assistance, said the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)*.


[Venezuela](https://reliefweb.int/themes?categoryId=118) Published 23. Jul 2026

Up to 1.3 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance in the areas affected by the earthquakes, over 700,000 more people than before the earthquakes struck. The Humanitarian Response Plan has been revised to include the earthquake response, increasing requirements by nearly 50 per cent. The amended plan aims to support 6.2 million people over an initial six-month response period. Yet the plan is currently only 39 per cent funded.

"The first month after a disaster often brings global solidarity and attention. The real test now is whether that support continues after the headlines start to fade," said Elena Vicario, NRC’s country director in Venezuela. "Families who lost homes, livelihoods and access to essential services cannot rebuild their lives on short-lived commitments."

Prior to the earthquakes, over one quarter of the population was in need of humanitarian assistance and humanitarian organisations were already responding to significant needs, including protection, education, health, water and sanitation, and livelihoods across the country. The revised response plan integrates these existing priorities with emergency earthquake assistance within a single framework.

"We welcome the rapid mobilisation of resources following the earthquakes, but this funding must complement, not replace, support for existing humanitarian needs. Donors should ensure funding is sustained, reaches all sectors, and strengthens the capacities that already exist in Venezuela. Local communities, organisations, and long-standing humanitarian actors have the knowledge and access needed to reach affected populations, and new support should reinforce their work,” said Vicario.

After the earthquakes, nearly 24,000 children have had their education disrupted, further increasing the number of children in need of education support. So far, the education sector is only under 5 per cent funded, after years of underfunding from the international community, which has left education needs consistently unmet.

“For children living in temporary shelters, the emergency is far from over,” said Liliana Largo, NRC’s education programme development manager. “The routines that once provided stability and protection have been disrupted, and emotions such as fear emerge, affecting their ability to concentrate and learn. Temporary learning spaces and psychosocial support are critical in helping children rebuild a sense of normality and wellbeing, and must be treated as a core part of the emergency response."

NRC’s emergency response has evolved significantly over the past month. The organisation began by assessing needs in 16 temporary shelters. During the first month, NRC assisted more than 2,400 displaced people, distributing hygiene kits and other essential items to affected families, while also providing psychosocial support sessions for children, and legal counselling for people who have lost civil documentation and property ownership records.

"One month on, people affected by the earthquakes are still living with uncertainty every day. The humanitarian community now faces a choice: sustain the response and help communities recover or allow funding shortfalls to turn this disaster into a longer-term crisis. The world must not look away," said Vicario.

**Notes to editors**

- Photos and videos from Venezuela are available for use [here](https://visuals.nrc.no/?c=15116&k=5b02ed739f).
- Within two weeks of the earthquakes, the [2026 Humanitarian Response Plan](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/terremotos-venezuela-adenda-al-plan-de-respuesta-humanitaria-2026-enes) (HRP) was amended to incorporate earthquake-related needs.
- The revised HRP seeks to reach 6.2 million people, including 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/terremotos-venezuela-adenda-al-plan-de-respuesta-humanitaria-2026-enes)).
- Before the earthquakes, 596,000 people living in the municipalities affected by the earthquakes were included in the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan. 751,000 additional people were included in the plan to address humanitarian needs caused by the earthquakes ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/terremotos-venezuela-adenda-al-plan-de-respuesta-humanitaria-2026-enes)).
- Total funding requirements increased from 632 million US Dollars to 931.3 million US dollars, including 298 million US Dollars for earthquake response activities ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/countries/242/summary/2026), Financial Tracking Service).
- As of 22 July, the Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela is 39.2 per cent funded, with 365.1 million US dollars received against requirements of 931.3 million US dollars ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/countries/242/summary/2026), Financial Tracking Service).
- The education sector accounts for approximately 10.2 per cent of the total humanitarian appeal (94.5 million US dollars), yet as of 22 July it has received only 1.1 per cent of total funding reported, leaving the sector just 4.7 per cent funded and facing a funding gap of more than 90 million US dollars ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/countries/242/summary/2026), [Financial Tracking Service](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/1517/summary)).
- In 2025 the education sector was 20.3 per cent funded, while in 2024 it was 7.7 per cent funded ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/1277/summary)).
- The school year in Venezuela ends in July. Educational authorities have begun working on reorganising the academic calendar, and we welcome these efforts.
- NRC will continue to support the efforts of the authorities and the wider humanitarian response, in line with the principles of neutrality and impartiality.
- In the Capital District alone, 432 schools – around a third of all schools – have been affected by the earthquakes ([UNICEF](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/unicef-venezuela-humanitarian-situation-report-no3-earthquake-02-july-2026)).
- According to [Education Cannot Wait](https://www.educationcannotwait.org/news-stories/press-releases/education-cannot-wait-launches-emergency-response-help-children-return), 34 schools are currently serving as temporary shelters.
- According to [Education Cannot Wait](https://www.educationcannotwait.org/news-stories/press-releases/education-cannot-wait-launches-emergency-response-help-children-return), learning has been disrupted for nearly 24,000 students.
- Since 8 July, NRC has reached more than 200 children aged 5 to 16 with educational activities. The response is ongoing, and NRC hopes to set up 10 temporary learning spaces where 600 children can receive educational kits and psychosocial support.
- NRC has been working in Venezuela since 2005, providing education, protection, legal guidance, and water and sanitation support. In 2025 we reached more than 71,000 people across four border states (Bolívar, Zulia, Apure and Táchira). NRC has 70 colleagues in Venezuela and seven local partners. NRC’s teams are working across areas affected by the earthquakes to provide vital supplies, with a plan to provide water and sanitation support, emergency education and trauma support for children among other services.

**For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:**

- NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329

**Situation Report No. 29**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**22 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
- Official toll: **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks.**

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom

multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.
The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population
from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931
million.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira
state, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects
intended for affected populations.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
National response
 The Government response remains focused on assistance to affected people, as well as the
establishment and management of transitional camps.
 According to authorities, the response continues through 107 transitional camps for affected
populations, with a total capacity of 27,898 people and a current occupancy of 23,350 people. As of
22 July, 41 camps are located in Caracas, 28 in La Guaira, 28 in Miranda and 10 in Aragua. Of the
total camp population, 12,123 people are accommodated in La Guaira, 8,704 in Caracas, 1,833
in Miranda and 675 in Aragua.
 Health authorities announced the launch of fumigation and sanitary control measures in La Guaira
state, particularly in the parishes of Caraballeda, La Guaira and Macuto.
 On 20 July, authorities announced the allocation of fully equipped housing units to an initial 240
families affected by the earthquakes. The housing units are located in Fuerte Tiuna, Caracas, and
form part of the Venezuela Renace plan.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com).
 School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto
Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital
District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión,
Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda (updated as of 21 July)
 In Miranda state, the humanitarian response has been primarily concentrated in the municipalities of
Plaza (Guarenas), Zamora (Guatire), Chacao, Sucre and Baruta, which have been identified among
the areas most affected by the earthquakes. In these locations, humanitarian organizations including
IOM, UNICEF, WFP, World Vision and the Venezuelan Red Cross have supported search and
rescue operations, structural assessments, medical and psychosocial care, distribution of food, safe
drinking water and hygiene items, as well as assistance for displaced people. Child protection
mechanisms have also been strengthened, support services have been established in transitional
camps, and early recovery interventions have been promoted.
La Guaira
 On 21 July, the President of the Presidential Commission for the Assessment of Infrastructure
Habitability reported that 6,907 buildings had been inspected in La Guaira using the traffic light
assessment methodology to determine the condition of structures. Of the total inspected, most
(3,237) received a green tag, indicating that the infrastructure poses no risk. Some 1,785 structures
received a yellow tag, indicating restricted use, while 1,885 were classified with a red tag. Structures
assigned either yellow or red classifications will undergo a second assessment.
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone) (updated as of 21 July)
 IOM, UNICEF, PAHO/WHO, ACH, Cáritas Venezuela, CRS, CAMPO, Laboratorio de Paz, the
Yaracuy Human Rights Network and the Human Rights Committee of Bolívar Municipality continue
to implement response activities in areas affected by the earthquakes. Reported interventions
include the distribution of basic assistance and support across the nutrition, water, sanitation and
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
hygiene (WASH), and protection sectors, with a particular focus on accompanying and supporting
affected communities.
Falcón (Silva municipality)
 CEPOREJUN and ODISEF continue to strengthen capacities in Psychological First Aid (PFA)
through a training process targeting 300 personnel from Civil Protection, Fire Services and VEN 911.
As part of this initiative, the Bolivarian Militia requested similar training, which is being coordinated
for next week. In addition, OCHA and Civil Protection agreed to extend this training to personnel in
Silva municipality. As a follow-up to previous actions, Civil Protection expressed interest in continuing
the training to improve data collection on affected structures.
 OCHA initiated an exercise with the Local Coordination Forum (LCF) to identify potential early
recovery actions in Silva municipality, based on needs and priorities defined with local authorities, in
line with the objectives of the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Addendum.
Other states
 Amazonas: Authorities report that 75 earthquake-affected families have arrived in the state. As part
of the humanitarian response, the Local Coordination Forum (LCF), through Première Urgence
Internationale (PUI), is coordinating a health outreach campaign that will include the distribution of
hygiene kits and water filters for affected families.
 Sucre: A total of 651 people affected by the earthquakes have arrived in the state (470 transported
with institutional support and 181 through their own means). They are currently being accommodated
by host families and communities in the municipalities of Sucre, Bermúdez, Bolívar and Andrés Eloy
Blanco. The Local Coordination Forum (LCF) has distributed food and hygiene kits and strengthened
the capacities of more than 150 government officials in case management, mental health and
psychosocial support (MHPSS), safeguarding, and prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse
(PSEA). This week, Cáritas Cumaná assisted 36 families through the distribution of hygiene, food,
dignity and WASH kits. In the health sector, specialized care was provided to 15 families.
Additionally, 10 families with documentation issues were identified and are currently being supported
through case management. Institutional capacity-strengthening efforts also continue with the
Autonomous Institute of the National Council for the Rights of Children and Adolescents (IDENNA)
and Municipal Councils for the Rights of Children and Adolescents (CMDNNA) on protection and
emergency response.
 Zulia: The arrival of 87 families staying with relatives has been reported, with significant population
movements from La Guaira and Caracas towards municipalities in the Lake Maracaibo basin. The
predominant displacement pattern appears to be driven by psychological trauma. Organizations
within the Local Coordination Forum (LCF), including ASONACOP, the Venezuelan Red Cross,
HIAS, CESVI, ASOREZ, Cáritas and Aliadas en Cadena, continue to provide psychosocial support,
primary healthcare, protection services, and the distribution of water, food and hygiene kits. The
Citizen Assistance Office, Protection Councils and risk management authorities continue response,
monitoring and preventive inspection activities in Maracaibo. Inter-agency coordination is ongoing
through the LCF and OCHA’s sub-office in Maracaibo.
Humanitarian coordination
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
continues to coordinate the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner
organizations, prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, water, sanitation and hygiene,
logistics and protection.
 UNESCO activated an institutional technical contingency plan focused on heritage protection and
continuity of education. In the area of cultural heritage, UNESCO assessed the Foro Libertador and
endorsed the preventive transfer of 287 historical volumes registered under the Memory of the World
Programme to the vaults of the Central Bank of Venezuela.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
through the United Nations system, with support from UNDP. In line with the internationally
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
recognized PDNA methodology, coordination with relevant institutions and counterparts will continue
in the coming period.
 In addition, UNDP provided technical assistance to national institutions on the use of drones, artificial
intelligence and geospatial technologies for post-earthquake recovery and reconstruction planning,
with the aim of strengthening debris management and supporting evidence-based decision-making.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 Since the onset of the emergency, WFP has reached 115,459 people with food assistance. Today,
WFP's efforts focused on Catia La Mar, one of the most populated and heavily impacted areas of La
Guaira state. In Catia La Mar, WFP reached 3,808 people through the distribution of 952 family food
baskets, covering household food needs for one month. Additionally, 2,150 people living in
precarious conditions without access to cooking facilities received ready-to-eat food kits.
 WFP also began supporting one additional temporary shelter providing hot meals to affected
populations, expanding its coverage to 24 transitional camps, while continuing to cover the 3 UN-
coordinated transitional camps. Across these sites, WFP and its partners served a total of 23,448
hot meals.
 CONVITE, in partnership with Help-Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe and IRC, provided food assistance to 250
families (688 people), including 219 families (548 people) from the Pericoco community in Carayaca
parish (La Guaira) and 31 families (140 people) at kilometre 23 of the El Junquito road in Libertador
municipality (Capital District).
 FUNVAPE distributed 1,364 food and hydration baskets to affected people.
Education and Early Childhood Development
 UNICEF initiated early childhood development (ECD) activities in transitional camps, closely
integrated with child protection interventions. These activities reached an initial group of 82 children
under five years of age, including 42 girls, as well as seven pregnant and breastfeeding women.
 UNICEF provided guidance to families on nurturing care and child development practices, reaching
a total of 66 caregivers. These interventions aim to support the well-being, development and
resilience of young children affected by the earthquake and living in displacement settings.
Health
 IOM is expanding access to health services for populations affected by the earthquake through the
deployment of medical teams and the provision of primary healthcare services, both directly and
through its partner Ven Da Tu Mano. To date, 5,731 people have benefited from 6,856 medical
consultations, including general practice, internal medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology and obstetrics,
as well as the provision of medicines and individual psychological support.
 UNICEF has significantly expanded access to essential health services in earthquake-affected
communities through the provision of medical supplies, deployment of mobile health teams and
support to national health authorities. UNICEF reached 5,135 people with essential primary
healthcare services.
 Vaccination campaigns have reached 21,141 children, pregnant women and adults in transitional
camps, healthcare facilities and communities affected by the earthquake.
 UNICEF distributed essential health supplies and medicines sufficient to support the provision of
healthcare services for approximately 49,000 people in affected areas.
 As of 22 July, UNFPA, through its implementing partner Ven Da Tu Mano, reached 2,089 people
through sexual and reproductive health awareness-raising activities in the José María Vargas Sports
Complex, César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps. In addition, condoms were
distributed to 1,227 people, 782 information, education and communication (IEC) materials and 12
hygiene kits were provided; 132 pregnant women received antenatal care; 979 women accessed
modern contraceptive methods; and 85 HIV tests and 84 syphilis tests were conducted,
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
strengthening access to essential sexual and reproductive health services for the affected
population.
 Project HOPE provided medical care to 37 people in the Mare Abajo II transitional camp,
complementing available health services for the affected population.
 CONVITE provided primary healthcare, medicines for the management of non-communicable
diseases and assistive devices to older persons and other affected people living in transitional camps
in La Guaira (Santa Eduvigis National School, Maiquetía) and in the municipalities of Chacao and
Baruta, Miranda state.
 Humane World for Animals conducted a veterinary outreach campaign at the José María Vargas
Sports Complex transitional camp, providing care for pets belonging to camp residents and nearby
communities.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 Through the Logistics Working Group, the WFP continues to provide free transport and warehousing
services to humanitarian organizations supporting the earthquake response. Information on these
services is available on the dedicated webpage, and inquiries can be directed to
venezuela.clustercargo@wfp.org.
 To date, eight organizations and United Nations agencies have accessed these services. A total of
261 metric tonnes of humanitarian cargo have been transported, and more than 1,300 m³ of relief
items have been stored. Most of these supplies relate to shelter and housing assistance, although
health, protection, early recovery, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) items have also been
received.
 In the area of telecommunications, charging kiosks arrived on 21 July and will be installed in the
José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps to
provide mobile phone charging services for affected people. Installation is scheduled to begin
tomorrow, and each kiosk has the capacity to charge up to 24 mobile phones simultaneously.
 The Venezuelan Red Cross and the ICRC continued to provide Restoring Family Links (RFL)
services and connectivity support at the César Nieves transitional camp, reaching 24 people through
access to telephone calls, internet connectivity and device charging services.
 Authorities from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs report that information for humanitarian organizations
and cooperation actors is available through the platform www.venezuelanoestasola.com regarding
procedures for the arrival of aircraft and vessels carrying humanitarian assistance, as well as
guidance on the registration of routes, means of transport, crew members and cargo.
. Nutrition
 UNICEF continued to support the nutritional needs of vulnerable children and women affected by
the earthquakes. A total of 2,917 children under five years of age and 634 pregnant and lactating
women among displaced populations received a package of essential nutrition services, including
nutritional screening, micronutrient supplementation, counselling and referral to specialized services
when required.
 Approximately 1,427 caregivers of children under two years of age received counselling on
recommended infant and young child feeding practices, including breastfeeding support and age-
appropriate complementary feeding. Micronutrient supplementation was provided to reach up to
72,000 children and pregnant women
 UNICEF also supported community outreach activities implemented by the National Institute of
Nutrition (INN), the Ministry of Health and NGO partners in affected communities. In coordination
with WFP, UNICEF promoted age-appropriate feeding practices for young children within the food
assistance response and facilitated a technical exchange between national authorities and the
Brazilian Human Milk Bank Network on quality assurance and safe management of human milk in
emergency settings.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Protection (including Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence)
 To date, UNHCR and its implementing partners have provided 4,569 protection services in the José
María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium, Playa Grande and Mare Abajo transitional
camps, including 98 services delivered to returnees. Protection activities, legal assistance, case
management, psychosocial support, counselling and referrals reached 1,318 people. In addition,
111 children and adolescents and their families received legal counselling on birth registration,
identity documentation and legal representation, while 84 children and adolescents participated in
psychosocial support, recreational and socio-emotional activities aimed at strengthening coping
mechanisms in the aftermath of the earthquakes.
 Information and counselling desks on access to rights, available services, protection mechanisms,
referral pathways, Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) and prevention of sexual exploitation
and abuse (PSEA) provided 684 services across the four transitional camps. In addition, two
individuals received specialized support through gender-based violence (GBV) case management.
 IOM is facilitating access to protection services at the José María Vargas Sports Complex through
counselling, legal assistance and documentation support. To date, 130 people have received
specialized assistance and follow-up support.
 UNICEF continues to strengthen child protection services through psychosocial support,
identification of vulnerable children, case management and referral services delivered through Child-
Friendly Spaces and mobile child protection teams in affected areas.
 Across four transitional camps in La Guaira, four Child-Friendly Spaces remained operational,
reaching 3,076 children, adolescents and caregivers with psychosocial support, structured
recreational activities and protective services.
 To further strengthen the child protection response following the earthquake emergency, UNICEF
supplied key equipment and resources to local child protection teams in La Guaira, enhancing their
capacity to provide timely and quality services to affected children and families.
 As of 22 July, gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response activities led by UNFPA and
its implementing partners AVESA and Tinta Violeta reached 1,085 people through awareness-
raising activities in the José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium, Playa Grande
and Mare Abajo transitional camps. In addition, 77 dignity kits were distributed to women at risk of
or surviving GBV.
 Specialized GBV response services provided psychosocial support and psychological first aid to 85
people, managed 23 cases and delivered two legal counselling sessions, strengthening access to
protection and assistance mechanisms for affected populations.
 FUNVAPE provided psychosocial support to 125 people and case management/material assistance
to 425 people. In addition, it delivered Venezuelan Sign Language (LSV) interpretation services and
technical accessibility support to promote inclusive humanitarian assistance.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 IOM continues to support the management of five transitional camps co-managed with local
authorities (José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium, Playa Grande, Golf Course
and Mare Abajo), promoting site improvements, strengthening coordination with authorities,
humanitarian partners and cooperation actors, and supporting registration processes. To date, IOM
and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed 3,092 kitchen sets, 3,534 plastic
tarpaulins, 2,039 buckets, 1,675 solar lamps, 819 shelter kits, 672 mosquito nets and 208
rechargeable solar flashlights.
 UNHCR and its implementing partners continued to strengthen protection and shelter conditions in
transitional camps through the distribution of 547 solar lamp and mosquito net kits, 200 solar
flashlights, and the installation of 120 solar floodlights and lamps to mitigate protection risks in
communal areas, sanitation facilities and sleeping areas. In addition, 12 temporary modular shelter
units remain installed in the César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps.
 The Wayuu Taya Foundation distributed relief items to affected families in the César Nieves
transitional camp, including hygiene kits, family tents, food, nutritional supplements and mosquito
nets, helping address the basic needs of the displaced population
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 IOM is strengthening access to essential water storage, handling and hygiene items for affected
communities. To date, 1,552 collapsible 10-litre jerry cans, 1,009 hygiene kits and 92 semi-
collapsible 10-litre jerry cans have been distributed.
 UNICEF continued to support access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services in displacement
settings and affected communities. UNICEF maintains the operation of emergency latrines, laundry
points, and handwashing stations, supported through regular water trucking operations providing
approximately 20,000 litres of water per day. Solid waste management, routine cleaning of sanitation
facilities, and replenishment of hygiene and cleaning supplies continue to be sustained.
 More than 465 people received hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available
life-saving services. In addition, family hygiene kits were distributed to 8,906 people, contributing to
safer practices and improved living conditions among displaced populations.
 In parallel, UNICEF strengthened coordination with the Ministry of Water (MINAGUAS), HIDROVEN
and local water utilities, conducting technical assessments of critical water treatment, transmission
and distribution infrastructure affected by the earthquake.
 Action Against Hunger reported the cumulative distribution of 2,065 family hygiene kits, 2,002
menstrual hygiene kits, more than 2,000 units of bottled water, and 370,000 litres of water delivered
through water trucking operations in Mare Abajo II. The organization also carried out solid waste
management activities and supported the maintenance of sanitation services.
 CONVITE, in partnership with Help-Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe and IRC, distributed hygiene kits and
TANDAS kits to 250 families (688 people) in La Guaira and the Capital District, and continued the
distribution of these items in transitional camps in Baruta municipality, Miranda state.
 FUNVAPE distributed 162 hygiene kits to affected people.
Humanitarian financing and contributions
 The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced an additional appeal under the
Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela. The appeal outlines the multisectoral needs of 1.3
million people over the next six months. To reach those in need, US$299 million is required, in
addition to the US$632 million requested at the beginning of the year.
 Several United Nations agencies, funds and programmes have issued emergency appeals to scale
up humanitarian assistance and support the response and recovery efforts following the
earthquakes, in line with the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Addendum.
 UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to fund its earthquake emergency response. The aim is to assist
470,000 people, including 160,000 children and adolescents, through water, sanitation and hygiene
(WASH), health, nutrition, child protection and education interventions in the most affected areas
over the coming months. IOM requires US$98 million to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities over
the next six months. PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support
the health response and early recovery efforts over the next six months and allocated US$1.5 million
from its Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP issued an initial appeal for US$80 million to
provide food assistance to 500,000 people over a six-month period. UNHCR, for its part, indicated
that it requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 Canada increased its matching contribution for donations supporting the earthquake response in
Venezuela from CAD 4 million to CAD 7 million, bringing its total support for the emergency to CAD
12 million. The funding, channelled through the Canadian Red Cross and the Humanitarian Coalition,
will support the provision of health, shelter and WASH services for affected populations.
 The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria approved an emergency funding package
of US$1.77 million to support HIV and tuberculosis services in Venezuela following the earthquakes.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
The resources, to be managed through UNDP, will enable 7,000 people to continue HIV treatment,
ensure tuberculosis treatment for 500 people, and support prevention, testing and outreach services
for 1,500 members of key populations in the most affected areas.
 The European Union announced an additional contribution of €20 million to support humanitarian
action in the country. Of this amount, €10 million will support search and rescue operations, medical
assistance, the deployment of additional experts, and material assistance in the country. This
contribution comes in addition to the €5 million previously announced for the earthquake response
and the €52 million already allocated to humanitarian operations in Venezuela this year.
 In addition, under the European Union Humanitarian Air Bridge launched in June, three EU-funded
flights have already arrived in the country. The latest flight landed on 17 July carrying 48 metric
tonnes of medical supplies and shelter items.
 The Government of Italy allocated US$5.7 million to support the humanitarian response to the
earthquakes, helping deliver life-saving assistance, protection and access to essential services for
affected populations through AICS, WFP and IFRC.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country.
 The Republic of Korea announced an additional contribution of US$3.5 million in humanitarian
assistance. Of this amount, US$3 million will be channelled through UNDP to support debris removal
activities, while the remainder will be provided in-kind, specifically through 30 metric tons of
temporary shelters (family tents). The Republic of Korea had previously allocated US$1.25 million to
WFP and US$2.5 million to UNICEF in support of the humanitarian response in Venezuela.
 Japan allocated US$3.5 million to support the earthquake response. The funding will provide
humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and non-food
items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
and IOM.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden contributed SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.

OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
United Na tions Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 9
Contact information
For more information, please contact the OCHA Venezuela Office:
Vanessa May – Head of Office a.i. – mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Humanitarian Affairs Officer – alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Public Information Officer – moreno7@un.org
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

**Reporte de situación N.º 29**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**22 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio.
- Balance oficial: **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para  
     atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas.**

A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.**

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.** Esta adenda complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.
