La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención
de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las
autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la
respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y
Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta
Humanitaria 2026 por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3
millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses. Esta adenda
complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones
a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.
Impacto en infraestructura
 Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.
 Como parte de la planificación para la recuperación y reconstrucción, las autoridades identificaron
40 terrenos en el estado La Guaira, equivalentes a aproximadamente 584.000 metros cuadrados,
para el desarrollo de proyectos habitacionales destinados a la población afectada.
 Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de
Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil
millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas,
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
comercios, escuelas, hospitales e instalaciones públicas. Entre tanto, estimaciones preliminares de
PNUD indican daños físicos directos por 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 6 % del PIB.
Respuesta nacional
 La respuesta gubernamental se mantiene centrada en la atención de las personas afectadas, así
como la instalación y manejo de los campamentos transitorios.
 De acuerdo con las autoridades, la respuesta continúa con 107 campamentos transitorios
habilitados para la atención de personas afectadas, con una capacidad instalada de 27.898
personas y una ocupación de 23.350 personas. Hasta el 22 de julio, 41 campamentos se encuentran
instalados en Caracas, 28 en La Guaira, 28 en Miranda y 10 en Aragua. Del total de población
alojada, 12.123 personas se encuentran en La Guaira, 8.704 en Caracas, 1.833 en Miranda y
675 en Aragua.
 Las autoridades de salud anunciaron el inicio de un proceso de fumigación y control sanitario en el
estado La Guaira, especialmente en las parroquias Caraballeda, La Guaira y Macuto.
 Este lunes 20 de julio, las autoridades anunciaron la entrega de viviendas equipadas a unas
primeras 240 familias afectadas por los terremotos. Las viviendas se encuentran en Fuerte Tiuna,
Caracas, y son parte del plan Venezuela Renace.
 Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad
(Conapdis) para coordinar una respuesta oportuna e inclusiva en las zonas afectadas.
 Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas
(www.localizapacientes.com).
 Las actividades escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados
Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José
Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas);
Distrito Capital (Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo,
Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).
Situación por estado
Distrito Capital (Caracas) y Miranda (actualizado al 21 de julio)
 En el estado Miranda, la respuesta humanitaria se ha concentrado principalmente en los municipios
Plaza (Guarenas), Zamora (Guatire), Chacao, Sucre y Baruta, identificados entre las zonas con
mayores afectaciones. En estas localidades, organizaciones humanitarias como la OIM, UNICEF,
el PMA, World Vision, la Cruz Roja Venezolana, han apoyado labores de búsqueda y rescate,
evaluaciones estructurales, atención médica y psicosocial, distribución de alimentos, agua potable
y artículos de higiene, además de asistencia para personas desplazadas. Asimismo, se han
fortalecido los mecanismos de protección de la niñez, se han habilitado apoyos en campamentos
transitorios y se han impulsado acciones de recuperación temprana.
La Guaira
 El presidente de la Comisión Presidencial de Evaluación de Habitabilidad de Infraestructuras
informó el 21 de julio que se han inspeccionado 6.907 edificaciones en La Guaira, bajo el método
del semáforo, para indicar el estado de las estructuras. Del total, la mayoría (3.237) obtuvieron
etiqueta verde, es decir, que la infraestructura no representa riesgos. Unas 1.785 estructuras
recibieron etiqueta amarilla, indicando un uso restringido, y 1.885 fueron clasificadas con la etiqueta
roja. Ambas calificaciones pasarían a una segunda revisión.
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro) (actualizado al 21 de julio)
 OIM, UNICEF, OPS/OMS, ACH, Cáritas Venezuela, CRS, CAMPO, Laboratorio de Paz, la Red de
Derechos Humanos de Yaracuy y el Comité de Derechos Humanos del municipio Bolívar, mantienen
acciones de respuesta en las áreas afectadas por los sismos. Las intervenciones reportadas
incluyen distribución de asistencia básica y apoyo en los sectores de nutrición, agua, saneamiento
e higiene (ASH) y protección, con énfasis en el acompañamiento a las comunidades afectadas.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Falcón (Municipio Silva)
 La CEPOREJUN y ODISEF continúan fortaleciendo las capacidades en Primeros Auxilios
Psicológicos (PAP) mediante un proceso formativo dirigido a 300 funcionarios de Protección Civil,
Bomberos y VEN 911. En el marco de esta iniciativa, la Milicia Bolivariana solicitó una capacitación
similar, cuya realización se coordina para la próxima semana. Asimismo, OCHA y Protección Civil
acordaron extender esta formación a funcionarios del municipio Silva. Como seguimiento a
acciones previas, Protección Civil manifestó interés en continuar la capacitación para mejorar el
levantamiento de información sobre estructuras afectadas.
 OCHA inició un ejercicio con el Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC) para identificar posibles acciones
de recuperación temprana en el municipio Silva, basadas en las necesidades y prioridades
definidas con las autoridades, en línea con los objetivos de la adenda del Plan de Respuesta
Humanitaria (PRH).
Otros estados
 Amazonas: Las autoridades reportan 75 familias damnificadas por el terremoto que han llegado al
estado. Como parte de la respuesta humanitaria, el Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC), a través de
Première Urgence Internationale (PUI) coordina la realización de una jornada de salud que incluirá
la distribución de kits de higiene y filtros de agua para las familias afectadas.
 Sucre: Se reporta la llegada de 651 personas afectadas por los terremotos (470 movilizadas con
apoyo institucional y 181 por medios propios), actualmente acogidas en viviendas familiares y
comunitarias de los municipios Sucre, Bermúdez, Bolívar y Andrés Eloy Blanco. El Foro Local de
Coordinación (FLC) ha distribuido kits de higiene y alimentos y ha fortalecido capacidades de más
de 150 funcionarios en gestión de casos, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS), salvaguarda
y Prevención de la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS). Esta semana, Cáritas Cumaná atendió
36 familias con entrega de kits de higiene, alimentos, dignidad y ASH. En salud, se brindó atención
especializada a 15 familias. Asimismo, se identificaron 10 familias con problemas de
documentación, actualmente en gestión de casos, mientras continúan las acciones de
fortalecimiento institucional con el Instituto Autónomo Consejo Nacional de Derechos de Niños,
Niñas y Adolescentes (IDENNA) y los Consejos Municipales de Derechos del Niño, Niña y del
Adolescente (CMDNNA) en materia de protección y respuesta a emergencias.
 Zulia: Se reporta la llegada de 87 familias a viviendas de familiares, registrándose movimientos
significativos de población provenientes de La Guaira y Caracas hacia municipios de la cuenca del
Lago de Maracaibo, con un patrón predominante de desplazamiento inducido por trauma
psicológico. Las organizaciones del Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC), incluyendo ASONACOP,
Cruz Roja Venezolana, HIAS, CESVI, ASOREZ, Cáritas y Aliadas en Cadena continúan brindando
apoyo psicosocial, atención médica primaria, servicios de protección, distribución de agua,
alimentos y kits de higiene. La Gerencia de Atención al Ciudadano, los Consejos de Protección y
las autoridades de gestión de riesgos mantienen acciones de atención, monitoreo e inspección
preventiva en Maracaibo. Se mantiene la coordinación interinstitucional a través del FLC y la
suboficina de OCHA en Maracaibo.
Coordinación humanitaria
 OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales,
continúa coordinando la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y las organizaciones
socias, priorizando acciones en salud, alojamiento, alimentación, agua, saneamiento e higiene,
logística y protección.
 La UNESCO activó un plan técnico de contingencia institucional enfocado en la protección del
patrimonio y la continuidad educativa. En patrimonio, evaluó el Foro Libertador y avaló el traslado
preventivo de 287 tomos históricos del programa Memoria del Mundo a las bóvedas del Banco
Central de Venezuela.
 Las autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades
Posteriores al Desastre (PDNA, por sus siglas en inglés) a través del Sistema de las Naciones
Unidas y con el acompañamiento del Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo (PNUD).
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
De conformidad con la metodología internacional de la PDNA, se avanzará en las coordinaciones
correspondientes con las instituciones y contrapartes relevantes.
 Adicionalmente, el PNUD brindó asistencia técnica a instituciones nacionales para la incorporación
de drones, inteligencia artificial y tecnologías geoespaciales en la planificación de la recuperación y
reconstrucción posterior a los terremotos, con el fin de fortalecer la gestión de residuos y apoyar la
toma de decisiones basada en evidencia.
Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria
Seguridad Alimentaria
 Desde el inicio de la emergencia, el PMA ha alcanzado a 115.459 personas con asistencia
alimentaria. Durante la jornada del 22 de julio, concentró sus esfuerzos en Catia La Mar, una de las
zonas más pobladas y afectadas del estado La Guaira, brindando asistencia adaptada a las
necesidades de la población afectada. En este marco, alcanzó a 3.808 personas mediante la
distribución de 952 canastas alimentarias familiares, con capacidad para cubrir las necesidades
alimentarias de los hogares durante un mes. Asimismo, 2.150 personas que viven en condiciones
precarias y sin acceso a instalaciones para cocinar recibieron kits de alimentos listos para el
consumo.
 Adicionalmente, el PMA amplió su cobertura de alimentación caliente a un campamento transitorio
adicional, alcanzando un total de 24 campamentos temporales, además de los tres campamentos
transitorios coordinados por Naciones Unidas. En conjunto con sus socios, distribuyó 23.448
comidas calientes para la población afectada.
 CONVITE, en alianza con Help-Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe e IRC, distribuyó asistencia alimentaria a 250
familias (688 personas), incluyendo 219 familias (548 personas) de la comunidad Pericoco,
parroquia Carayaca (La Guaira), y 31 familias (140 personas) ubicadas en el km 23 de la carretera
El Junquito, municipio Libertador (Distrito Capital).
 FUNVAPE distribuyó 1.364 canastas de alimentos e hidratación a personas afectadas.
Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene
 La OIM refuerza el acceso de las comunidades afectadas a artículos esenciales para el
almacenamiento y manejo seguro de agua e higiene. A la fecha, se han distribuido 1.552 bidones
plegables de 10 litros, 1.009 kits de higiene y 92 bidones semiplegables de 10 litros.
 UNICEF continuó apoyando el acceso a servicios seguros de agua, saneamiento e higiene en
entornos de desplazamiento y comunidades afectadas. UNICEF mantiene la operación de letrinas
de emergencia, puntos de lavado de ropa y estaciones de lavado de manos, respaldadas por
operaciones regulares de distribución de agua mediante camiones cisterna que suministran
aproximadamente 20.000 litros de agua por día. Asimismo, se continúa garantizando la gestión de
desechos sólidos, la limpieza rutinaria de las instalaciones sanitarias y la reposición de insumos de
higiene y limpieza.
 Más de 465 personas recibieron mensajes de promoción de higiene e información clave sobre los
servicios vitales disponibles. Además, se distribuyeron kits de higiene familiar que alcanzaron a
8.906 personas, contribuyendo a prácticas más seguras y mejores condiciones de vida entre las
poblaciones desplazadas.
 Paralelamente, UNICEF fortaleció la coordinación con el Ministerio del Poder Popular de Atención
de las Aguas (MINAGUAS), HIDROVEN y las empresas prestadoras de servicios de agua a nivel
local, realizando evaluaciones técnicas de infraestructuras críticas de tratamiento, transmisión y
distribución de agua afectadas por el terremoto.
 Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) reportó la distribución acumulada de 2.065 kits de higiene familiar,
2.002 kits de higiene menstrual, más de 2.000 unidades de agua embotellada y 370.000 litros de
agua mediante camiones cisterna en Mare Abajo II, además de actividades de gestión de residuos
y mantenimiento de servicios sanitarios.
 CONVITE, en alianza con Help-Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe e IRC, distribuyó kits de higiene y kits TANDAS
a 250 familias (688 personas) en La Guaira y Distrito Capital, y avanzó en la entrega de estos
insumos en campamentos transitorios del municipio Baruta (Miranda).
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
 FUNVAPE entregó 162 kits de higiene a personas afectadas.
Alojamiento, Energía y Enseres
 La OIM mantiene su apoyo a la gestión de los cinco campamentos transitorios cogestionados con
las autoridades locales (Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande,
Campo de Golf y Mare Abajo), impulsando mejoras en los sitios, fortaleciendo la coordinación con
autoridades, socios humanitarios y actores de cooperación, y respaldando los procesos de registro.
A la fecha, la OIM y su socio Fundación Vivienda Popular han distribuido 3.092 sets de cocina,
3.534 lonas plásticas, 2.039 tobos, 1.675 lámparas solares, 819 kits de refugio, 672 mosquiteros y
208 linternas solares recargables.
 ACNUR y sus socios implementadores continuaron fortaleciendo las condiciones de protección y
alojamiento en los campamentos transitorios mediante la distribución de 547 kits de lámparas
solares y mosquiteros, 200 linternas solares y la instalación de 120 reflectores y lámparas solares
para mitigar riesgos de protección en áreas comunitarias, espacios sanitarios y zonas de pernocta.
Asimismo, permanecen instaladas 12 unidades modulares de alojamiento temporal en los
campamentos transitorios Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande.
 La Fundación Wayuu Taya entregó insumos de asistencia a familias afectadas en el campamento
transitorio César Nieves, incluyendo kits de higiene, carpas familiares, alimentos, suplementos
nutricionales y mosquiteros, fortaleciendo la respuesta a las necesidades básicas de la población
alojada.
Educación y desarrollo infantil temprano
 UNICEF inició actividades de desarrollo de la primera infancia (DPI) en campamentos transitorios,
estrechamente articuladas con las intervenciones de protección de la niñez. Estas actividades
alcanzaron a un grupo inicial de 82 niños y niñas menores de cinco años, incluidos 42 niñas, así
como a siete mujeres embarazadas y lactantes.
 UNICEF brindó orientación a las familias sobre prácticas de cuidado cariñoso y sensible y
desarrollo infantil, llegando a un total de 66 cuidadores. Estas intervenciones tienen como objetivo
apoyar el bienestar, el desarrollo y la resiliencia de niños y niñas pequeños afectados por el
terremoto y que viven en situaciones de desplazamiento.
Logística y Telecomunicaciones
 El PMA, a través del Grupo de Trabajo de Logística, continúa proporcionando servicios de
transporte y almacenamiento sin costo para las organizaciones humanitarias apoyando la
respuesta a los terremotos. Toda la información sobre estos servicios puede encontrarse en la
página web y pueden contactar a venezuela.clustercargo@wfp.org
 A la fecha, 8 organizaciones y agencias de Naciones Unidas han accedido a estos servicios. Un
total de 261 toneladas métricas han sido transportadas, y más de 1.300 m3 han sido almacenados.
La mayor parte de estos insumos son de refugio y alojamiento, pero también se han recibido ítems
da salud, protección, recuperación temprana y agua, saneamiento e higiene.
 En telecomunicaciones, el 21 de julio se recibieron los quioscos de carga, que serán instalados en
los campamentos transitorios del Polideportivo José María Vargas, César Nieves y Playa Grande,
con el fin de proporcionar una solución para la carga de celulares de las personas afectadas. Las
estructuras se empezarán a instalar el día de mañana y cada quioscos tiene capacidad para
conectar hasta 24 teléfonos.
 La Cruz Roja Venezolana y el CICR continuaron brindando servicios de restablecimiento del
contacto entre familiares y apoyo a la conectividad en el campamento transitorio César Nieves,
alcanzando a 24 personas mediante acceso a llamadas telefónicas, conexión a internet y recarga
de dispositivos.
 Las autoridades del Ministerio del Poder Popular para Relaciones Exteriores (MPPRE) informan
que, a través de la plataforma www.venezuelanoestasola.com, se encuentra disponible información
para organizaciones humanitarias y actores de cooperación sobre los procedimientos para la
llegada de aeronaves y embarcaciones con asistencia humanitaria, así como orientaciones para el
registro de rutas, medios de transporte, tripulación y carga.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Nutrición
 UNICEF continuó apoyando las necesidades nutricionales de niños, niñas y mujeres en situación
de vulnerabilidad afectados por los terremotos. Un total de 2.917 niños y niñas menores de cinco
años y 634 mujeres embarazadas y lactantes de poblaciones desplazadas recibieron un paquete
de servicios esenciales de nutrición, que incluyó tamizaje nutricional, suplementación con
micronutrientes, consejería y referencia a servicios especializados cuando fue necesario.
 Aproximadamente 1.427 cuidadores de niños y niñas menores de dos años recibieron consejería
sobre prácticas recomendadas de alimentación del lactante y de niños y niñas pequeños, incluidos
el apoyo a la lactancia materna y la alimentación complementaria adecuada para la edad.
Asimismo, se distribuyeron suplementos de micronutrientes para alcanzar hasta 72.000 niños,
niñas y mujeres embarazadas.
 UNICEF también apoyó actividades de alcance comunitario implementadas por el Instituto Nacional
de Nutrición (INN), el Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud y organizaciones no
gubernamentales en comunidades afectadas. En coordinación con el PMA, UNICEF promovió
prácticas de alimentación apropiadas para la edad de los niños y niñas pequeños en el marco de
la respuesta de asistencia alimentaria y facilitó un intercambio técnico entre las autoridades
nacionales y la Red Brasileña de Bancos de Leche Humana sobre aseguramiento de la calidad y
gestión segura de la leche humana en contextos de emergencia.
Protección (incluidos Áreas de Responsabilidad de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes y Violencia
Basada en Género)
 Hasta la fecha, ACNUR y sus socios implementadores han brindado 4.569 asistencias en los
campamentos transitorios Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande
y Mare Abajo, incluyendo 98 asistencias a personas retornadas. Las actividades de protección,
asistencia legal, gestión de casos, apoyo psicosocial, orientación y derivaciones alcanzaron a 1.318
personas. Asimismo, 111 niñas, niños y adolescentes (NNA) y sus familias recibieron orientación
legal sobre registro de nacimiento, documentación de identidad y representación legal, mientras
que 84 NNA participaron en actividades de apoyo psicosocial, acompañamiento lúdico y
socioemocional para fortalecer estrategias de afrontamiento frente a los efectos de los terremotos.
 Las mesas de información y orientación sobre acceso a derechos, servicios disponibles,
mecanismos de protección, rutas de atención, rendición de cuentas a las poblaciones afectadas
(AAP) y prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual (PSEA) brindaron 684 asistencias en los
cuatro campamentos transitorios. Asimismo, dos personas recibieron apoyo especializado
mediante la gestión de casos de violencia basada en género (VBG).
 La OIM facilita el acceso a servicios de protección en el Polideportivo José María Vargas mediante
orientación, asistencia legal y apoyo en materia de documentación. A la fecha, 130 personas han
recibido atención y acompañamiento especializado.
 UNICEF continúa fortaleciendo los servicios de protección de la niñez mediante apoyo psicosocial,
identificación de niños, niñas y adolescentes en situación de vulnerabilidad, gestión de casos y
servicios de referencia, proporcionados a través de Espacios Amigables para la Infancia y equipos
móviles de protección de la niñez en las zonas afectadas.
 En cuatro campamentos transitorios de La Guaira, cuatro Espacios Amigables para la Infancia
permanecieron operativos, alcanzando a 3.076 niños, niñas, adolescentes y cuidadores con apoyo
psicosocial, actividades recreativas estructuradas y servicios de protección.
 Con el fin de fortalecer la respuesta de protección de la niñez tras la emergencia por el terremoto,
UNICEF suministró equipos y recursos clave a los equipos locales de protección de la niñez en La
Guaira, mejorando su capacidad para brindar servicios oportunos y de calidad a los niños, niñas y
familias afectadas.
 Hasta el 22 de julio, las acciones de prevención y respuesta a la VBG lideradas por UNFPA y sus
socios implementadores AVESA y Tinta Violeta alcanzaron a 1.085 personas mediante actividades
de sensibilización en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César
Nieves, Playa Grande y Mare Abajo. Adicionalmente, se distribuyeron 77 kits de dignidad a mujeres
en situación de riesgo o sobrevivientes de VBG.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
 Los servicios especializados de respuesta a la VBG brindaron apoyo psicosocial y primeros auxilios
psicológicos a 85 personas, gestionaron 23 casos y proporcionaron dos asesorías legales,
fortaleciendo el acceso a mecanismos de protección y atención para las personas afectadas.
 FUNVAPE brindó apoyo psicosocial a 125 personas y gestión de casos/asistencia material a 425
personas. Además, proporcionó servicios de interpretación en Lengua de Señas Venezolana
(ILSV) y apoyo técnico en accesibilidad para garantizar una asistencia humanitaria inclusiva.
Salud
 La OIM amplía el acceso a servicios de salud para las poblaciones afectadas por el terremoto
mediante el despliegue de equipos médicos y la prestación de atención primaria, tanto de manera
directa como a través de su socio Ven Da Tu Mano. A la fecha, 5.731 personas se han beneficiado
de 6.856 atenciones médicas, incluyendo consultas de medicina general, medicina interna,
pediatría, ginecología y obstetricia, así como la entrega de medicamentos y apoyo psicológico
individual.
 UNICEF amplió significativamente el acceso a servicios esenciales de salud en las comunidades
afectadas por el terremoto mediante la provisión de insumos médicos, el despliegue de equipos
móviles de salud y el apoyo a las autoridades nacionales de salud. En este marco, 5.135 personas
recibieron servicios esenciales de atención primaria de salud.
 Las campañas de vacunación alcanzaron a 21.141 niños, niñas, mujeres embarazadas y adultos
en campamentos transitorios, establecimientos de salud y comunidades afectadas por el terremoto.
 UNICEF distribuyó insumos y medicamentos esenciales de salud suficientes para apoyar la
prestación de servicios de atención sanitaria para aproximadamente 49.000 personas en las zonas
afectadas.
 Hasta el 22 de julio, UNFPA, a través de su socio implementador Ven Da Tu Mano (VDTM), alcanzó
a 2.089 personas mediante actividades de sensibilización en salud sexual y reproductiva en los
campamentos transitorios Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande.
Asimismo, se distribuyeron condones a 1.227 personas, 782 materiales educomunicativos y 12 kits
de higiene; 132 mujeres embarazadas recibieron atención prenatal; 979 mujeres accedieron a
métodos anticonceptivos modernos, y se realizaron 85 pruebas de VIH y 84 pruebas de sífilis,
fortaleciendo el acceso a servicios esenciales de salud sexual y reproductiva para la población
afectada.
 Project HOPE brindó atención médica a 37 personas en el campamento transitorio Mare Abajo II,
complementando los servicios de salud disponibles para la población afectada.
 CONVITE brindó atención médica primaria, medicamentos para el control de enfermedades no
transmisibles y dispositivos de asistencia a personas mayores y personas afectadas alojadas en
campamentos transitorios de La Guaira (U.E.N. Santa Eduvigis, Maiquetía) y de los municipios
Chacao y Baruta, estado Miranda.
 Humane World for Animals realizó una jornada veterinaria en el campamento transitorio
Polideportivo José María Vargas, brindando atención a mascotas de familias alojadas en el
campamento y de comunidades cercanas.
Financiamiento humanitario y contribuciones
 El jefe humanitario de Naciones Unidas, Tom Fletcher, anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta
Humanitaria (PRH) para Venezuela. Este llamado contempla las necesidades multisectoriales de
1,3 millones de personas por los próximos seis meses. Para alcanzar a estas personas, se necesitan
299 millones de dólares, que se suman a los 632 millones de dólares solicitados al inicio del año.
 Varias agencias, fondos y programas de las Naciones Unidas han emitido llamamientos de
emergencia para ampliar la asistencia humanitaria y apoyar la respuesta y recuperación tras los
terremotos, en línea con la adenda del PRH presentada.
 UNICEF requiere 65.7 millones de dólares para financiar su respuesta de emergencia ante el
terremoto. La meta es atender a 470.000 personas (incluidos 160.000 niños, niñas y adolescentes)
mediante intervenciones de agua, saneamiento e higiene, salud, nutrición, protección infantil y
educación en las zonas más afectadas durante los próximos meses. OIM requirió 98 millones de
dólares para asistir a 850.000 personas y 140 entidades durante los próximos seis meses.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
OPS/OMS lanzó un llamamiento de emergencia por casi 24 millones de dólares para apoyar la
respuesta en salud y la recuperación temprana durante los próximos seis meses, además de asignar
1,5 millones de dólares del Fondo de Contingencia para Emergencias. El PMA presentó una
solicitud inicial de 80 millones de dólares para brindar asistencia alimentaria a 500.000 personas
durante seis meses. Por su parte, ACNUR indicó que requiere 14,8 millones de dólares para apoyar
a hasta 30.000 personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses.
 Parte del apoyo brindado por UNDAC incluye una especialista en coordinación con el sector privado
para fortalecer la participación empresarial en la respuesta y recuperación. Se encuentra disponible
un rastreador de contribuciones del sector privado para la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela
(https://ven-eq.connectingbusiness.org) y una nota informativa dirigida al sector privado sobre
oportunidades de apoyo. Punto focal: sanchez21@un.org.
 Canadá aumentó de 4 millones a 7 millones de dólares canadienses su contribución de
contrapartida para donaciones destinadas a la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela, elevando
su apoyo para la emergencia a 12 millones de dólares canadienses. Los fondos, canalizados a
través de la Cruz Roja Canadiense y la Humanitarian Coalition, apoyarán la provisión de servicios
de salud, alojamiento y agua, saneamiento e higiene para las poblaciones afectadas.
 El Fondo Mundial de lucha contra el sida, la tuberculosis y la malaria aprobó un paquete de
financiamiento de emergencia por 1.77 millones de dólares para apoyar los servicios de VIH y
tuberculosis en Venezuela luego de los terremotos. Los recursos, que se gestionarán a través del
PNUD, permitirán que 7.000 personas continúen el tratamiento del VIH, se garantice el tratamiento
de la tuberculosis para 500 personas y se respalde los servicios de prevención, pruebas de
detección y divulgación para 1.500 miembros de poblaciones clave en las zonas más afectadas.
 La Unión Europea realizó una contribución adicional de 20 millones de euros para apoyar la acción
humanitaria en el país. De este total, 10 millones de euros estarán destinados a apoyar operaciones
de búsqueda y rescate, asistencia médica y el despliegue de otros expertos, así como asistencia
material, en el país. Estos recursos se suman a los 5 millones de euros previamente anunciados
para la respuesta a la emergencia y a los 52 millones de euros ya destinados a las operaciones
humanitarias en Venezuela este año.
 Además, como parte del puente aéreo humanitario de la Unión Europea, puesto en marcha en junio,
ya han llegado al país tres vuelos financiados por la UE. El más reciente aterrizó el 17 de julio con
48 toneladas de suministros médicos y artículos de alojamiento.
 El Gobierno de Italia asignó 5,7 millones de dólares para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria a los
terremotos y proporcionar asistencia vital, protección y acceso a servicios básicos para las
poblaciones afectadas, a través de la Agencia Italiana de Cooperación para el Desarrollo (AICS), el
Programa Mundial de Alimentos (PMA) y la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja
y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC).
 El Fondo Central de Respuesta a Emergencias (CERF, por sus siglas en inglés) realizó una
asignación de 15 millones de dólares para una respuesta multisectorial, junto con la activación del
Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV). Noruega realizó una contribución para apoyar la respuesta
a través del CERF.
 Estados Unidos anunció una contribución de 100 millones de dólares al FHV, y una asignación
adicional de 100 millones de dólares en contribuciones bilaterales para operaciones de respuesta
de OIM, PMA, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse,
Proyecto Esperanza y la Cruz Roja.
 Alemania y Corea realizaron contribuciones al FHV por 5 millones y 1,25 millones de dólares,
respectivamente, para apoyar la acción humanitaria en el país.
 Corea realizó una contribución adicional para brindar asistencia por un monto de 3,5 millones de
dólares. 3 millones de dólares serán canalizados a través del PNUD para apoyar las labores de
remoción de escombros y el resto se proporcionará en insumos, específicamente, 30 toneladas de
alojamientos temporales (tiendas de campaña familiares). Corea ya había asignado 1,25 millones
de dólares al PMA y 2,5 millones de dólares a UNICEF para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en
Venezuela.
 Japón asignó 3,5 millones de dólares para apoyar la respuesta a los terremotos. Los fondos
permitirán brindar asistencia humanitaria en sectores clave, incluidos seguridad alimentaria, salud
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 9
y atención médica, alojamiento y artículos no alimentarios, a través del PMA, la Federación
Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (FICR) y la OIM.
 Australia informó de una contribución de 2 millones de dólares para la provisión de alimentos,
alojamiento, atención de salud y acceso a agua segura a través de IFRC y el PMA.
 Suiza anunció una contribución de 2,5 millones de francos suizos para apoyar la respuesta.
 Suecia asignó 25 millones de coronas suecas para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en el país,
mediante programas de asistencia alimentaria, agua, alojamiento temporal, protección y
reunificación familiar implementados por el PMA, ACNUR y Save the Children.
 Dinamarca anunció una contribución adicional de 11 millones de coronas danesas para apoyar la
respuesta humanitaria, incluyendo 10 millones de coronas danesas a través de ACNUR y 1 millón
de coronas danesas a través de DanChurchAid y la Cruz Roja Danesa.
 El Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) anunció una asignación inicial de 7,5 millones de libras
esterlinas para la respuesta al terremoto en Venezuela, incluyendo 2 millones de libras esterlinas
aportados por el Gobierno del Reino Unido mediante UK Aid Match. Los recursos serán
implementados por organizaciones miembros del DEC y sus socios locales para apoyar la respuesta
humanitaria.
 OCHA continúa coordinando con donantes y socios para asegurar una asignación rápida,
estratégica y basada en necesidades.
Apoya la respuesta humanitaria para atender el terremoto en Venezuela
Haz tu donación de forma segura y rápida ahora:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
Información de Contacto
Para mayor información, por favor contactar a la Oficina de OCHA Venezuela:
Vanessa May – Jefa de Oficina a.i. - mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Oficial de Asuntos Humanitarios - alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Oficial de Información Pública – moreno7@un.org

www.unocha.org

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Pregnant Women and New Mothers Face Growing Health Risks as about 130 Babies Born Every Day
documents.body_text:
**CARACAS, 23 July 2026 –** Thousands of pregnant women and new mothers require access to healthcare, nutritious food and safe shelter one month after two devastating earthquakes damaged health facilities and displaced [about 21,000 people ](https://news.un.org/es/story/2026/07/1541700https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/latin-america-caribbean-weekly-situation-update-17-july-2026)in Venezuela, Save the Children said.

 T[he UN estimates ](https://www.unfpa.org/resources/flash-update-earthquakes-venezuela-26-june-6-july-2026)there are 36,700 pregnant women who have been affected by the earthquakes, 4,000 of whom are expected to give birth in the next month, equivalent to about 130 babies born every day.\[1\]

 The twin earthquakes, of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, struck on 24 June, destroying and damaging dozens of health facilities and disrupting essential maternal and child healthcare services. Women have told Save the Children staff that some obstetricians and paediatricians were among the over 5,000 people killed in the disaster, leaving families uncertain where to seek care for themselves and their children.

 In La Guaira, which was hardest hit, the main maternity hospital remains closed and, while basic care is available, complicated cases must be referred to Caracas.

 Many pregnant women, caregivers, and their children who lost their homes are now living in temporary shelters where access to antenatal care, nutritious food, and clean water and sanitation is limited. At the same time, many are coping with the traumatic loss of loved ones.

 Research shows that high levels of stress and anxiety during pregnancy may affect a baby's brain development and immune system, increasing the risk of preterm birth or even miscarriage. Babies [exposed to elevated maternal stress](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/infa.12499) during pregnancy may also show more fear, sadness and distress at three months of age than those born to mothers who experienced less stress. Limited access to nutritious food, uncontrolled infant formula donations, and reduced antenatal care during pregnancy also heightens the risk of malnutrition in infants and increases the risk of preterm birth and low birth weight.

 **Yohana, \* 23,** who is pregnant with her first child and relies on glasses to see, was alone at home in one of the hardest-hit parts of La Guaira when the earthquake hit, causing her building to collapse. She managed to escape by breaking a window, although she could not get her glasses until later, adding to her panic.

 *“I went out barefoot, just wearing my house clothes,”* said Yohana\*. *“I lost my glasses...I couldn't see, or at least I could see less.”*

 *“When the whole house collapsed, I was scared. At that moment, I didn’t feel that I had hurt \[my stomach\], but with all the chaos, I wasn’t sure if I’d gotten hurt or not. But honestly, all I was thinking about was getting out alive.”*

 **Yohana\*** received a healthcare checkup at a mobile clinic run by Save the Children partner, Paluz in La Guaira.

 Meanwhile, newborn babies and infants living in sodden tents are falling sick from damp conditions or are at risk of mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue during the country’s rainy season. Some mothers living in temporary shelters say that along with feeling stressed and anxious, being able to buy nappies and other essential supplies for their babies is challenging.

 **Yennifer\*, 23,** who is breastfeeding her four-month-old baby, **Carmen\*,** struggled to take care of her own health after the earthquake. Carmen’s\* paediatrician was also killed in the earthquake.

 *“I couldn’t eat and I had a lot of headaches. I couldn't sleep because it felt like I was shaking. It was difficult for me, and any movement put me on alert and I felt very uneasy.”*

 *“Since \[Carmen’s\*\] paediatrician passed away, that's a big worry, because now how am I going to find someone to treat her because there's no money either,”* Yennifer\* said.

 *“Everything feels overwhelming and I can’t rest”.*

 **Fatima Andraca, Save the Children’s Country Director in Venezuela said:**

 *“Every day about 130 babies are born to mothers in Venezuela whose lives have been turned upside down by the earthquake and who are dealing with huge amounts of stress. Many are bringing their newborns into a world of uncertainty, displacement and disrupted healthcare services.*

 *“We’re hearing worrying reports of young babies becoming sick in camps where families are sleeping on damp mattresses exposed to rain and poor sanitation. At the same time, women are grieving loved ones, coping with trauma and worrying about where they can access healthcare after losing trusted obstetricians and paediatricians.*

 *"Pregnancy and caring for a newborn can be challenging under any circumstances. No mother should have to navigate those challenges while living in a tent, mourning losses and worrying about whether her child can access the healthcare they need.”*

 Save the Children said it is imperative that pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding women, and their children, are prioritised in the humanitarian response and recovery in Venezuela through urgent coordination, adequate funding, and targeted actions.

Save the Children is calling on international governments, donors and humanitarian partners to ensure that pregnant and breastfeeding women affected by the earthquake have continuous access to quality antenatal, delivery and postnatal care, skilled infant and young child feeding support, nutritious food, safe shelter, clean water and sanitation, and essential newborn supplies, both now and in the months ahead.

 Save the Children is on the ground in Venezuela, working with authorities and local partners providing primary healthcare through mobile clinics, distributing hygiene kits, clean water and essential supplies. Save the Children is also supporting parents and caregivers to access services for small and nutritionally at-risk babies under six months to help them survive and thrive, including nutrition assessments for babies, and breastfeeding counselling and mental health support for caregivers. The organisation is also exploring potential support to maternal and paediatric services in coordination with national health authorities.

 Save the Children has been working in Venezuela since 2019. Since the humanitarian crisis started to rapidly deteriorate a few years ago, Save the Children has been scaling up its response through local partners to support the increasing number of children in need. Save the Children is delivering health, nutrition, education, child protection, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene and food security and livelihoods support.

*Ends*

 \*Names changed for anonymity

 We have multimedia content available here:

 Interviews - [www.contenthubsavethechildren.org/Package/2O4C2SPNE94A](https://www.contenthubsavethechildren.org/Package/2O4C2SPNE94A)

 Photos & B-ROLL -www.contenthubsavethechildren.org/Package/2O4C2SPAIDCE

 **Notes to editors**

 \[1\] UNFPA estimated that 4,000 women will give birth in the next month, as of its 8 July 2026 update. [ https://www.unfpa.org/resources/flash-update-earthquakes-venezuela-24-26-june-2026](https://www.unfpa.org/resources/flash-update-earthquakes-venezuela-24-26-june-2026) . This is just over 130 births a day.

**For more information**

Aisha Majid, Data Media Manager (in Madrid), Aisha.majid@savethechildren.org

Out of hours (BST) contact, media@savethechildren.org.uk

documents.title: Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #1 (MDRVE015)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**A. SITUATION ANALYSIS**  
**Description of the crisis**

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 1,000 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.

The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira, a popular destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes.

As of 15 July, 4,829 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing1. It is expected for these figures to continue to rise in coming days as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors moves towards a focus on recovery, identification and return to family members of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG)2. International search and rescue deployments are progressively concluding, with several Movement teams having completed their missions. A response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, shelter provision and efforts to bridge emergency relief to recovery and reconstruction efforts continues under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery.

According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.3 A comprehensive technical evaluation of structures is underway by respective authorities to identify homes that can be repaired and those that are too dangerous to return to. Evaluation of safe areas to build permanent housing for those affected is also taking place. Damage to residences, commercial buildings and critical infrastructure also disrupted the functioning of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems, as well as public transportation and airport operations. Damaged roads and bridges have also restricted access and affected movement to and within some affected areas. The healthcare capacity has been particularly affected, with limited supply of water systems. More than 400 schools were also reported as affected, while some have been repurposed as temporary shelters until the academic cycle resumes after the summer. Damage to water systems has further affected the availability of basic services.

Moreover, it is important to note that the main affected area, La Guaira, fulfils multiple critical functions for the country. Its proximity to the Capital, Caracas, the presence of the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, makes it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people and logistical capacity affected.

The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with thousands of injured, many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, and with families displaced after the destruction or severe damage of their homes. Beyond these physical impacts, the earthquakes have also had significant effects on the mental health and psychosocial well-being of affected people. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, uncertainty regarding housing and recovery, and exposure to damaged environments and recovery operations has contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected populations.

Notably, La Guaira’s geographical location is prone to various types of emergencies. In December 1999, torrential rainfall triggered catastrophic landslides, flash floods and debris flows across the then State of Vargas—now La Guaira—causing widespread destruction and displacement. The exact death toll remains uncertain; however, the United States Geological Survey estimated that between 15,000 and 30,000 people were killed. The current earthquake has therefore affected communities with lived and intergenerational memories of one of Venezuela’s most severe disasters.

most severe disasters.
Summary of response
Overview of the host National Society and ongoing response
The Venezuelan Red Cross (VRC) maintains its presence across the whole of the country’s territory with 41 branches
and 42 local units. They have been responding to the emergency since the onset of the earthquakes in its auxiliary
role to the public authorities and in close coordination with national and local disaster management structures. VRC
operates through its 3,899 staff and volunteers, including the 388 staff and volunteers mobilised in the directly
3 Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #22 (15 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm) - Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) | ReliefWeb

affected areas. Notably, the VRC received 20,000 applications for new volunteers immediately following the
earthquakes.
As of 17 July, a total of 1,176 families (4,704 people) has been reached with distributions of essential household items
(kitchen sets, blankets, sleeping kits), and relief items for health and hygiene promotion (cleaning kits, hygiene kits,
jerrycans, buckets, water treatment tablets, mosquito nets, and water filters).
The VRC’s response is coordinated with the Government-led emergency structure and relevant public institutions.
National response arrangements have included Civil Protection and national and international Search and Rescue
teams, activation of the public and private health network, establishment of temporary accommodation sites, delivery
of essential supplies, and mechanisms for reporting missing people and housing damage. Within these arrangements,
the VRC has coordinated directly with authorities on field operations, health services, temporary accommodation,
affected water systems and access to communities, while maintaining its distinct humanitarian role and operational
responsibilities.

assistance delivery.
In coordination with national authorities, and with the support of the IFRC, ICRC and other National Societies, the VRC
continues to serve affected communities through physical, mental health and health services, protection activities,
shelter monitoring, humanitarian assistance and recovery planning. As the response is now transitioning towards
humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery and reconstruction, VRC will continue to
address urgent needs related to health, mental health and psychosocial support, shelter, WASH and protection.
Membership coordination has focused on aligning bilateral, multilateral, technical, financial and in-kind support with
the priorities identified by the Venezuelan Red Cross. Coordination with authorities and other actors has also
supported visa processing, humanitarian access, and the entry and deployment of rapid-response personnel, ERUs,
specialized equipment and relief supplies.
The VRC and IFRC have engaged national authorities, UN agencies, humanitarian partners, donors and diplomatic
representatives to share operational priorities, identify gaps, mobilize support and align interventions. This has
included participation in OCHA-led and sectoral coordination mechanisms, and engagement with government
institutions on humanitarian access, health services, temporary accommodation, water systems and recovery planning.
4

These efforts have supported complementarity while reinforcing the National Society’s auxiliary role and principled
humanitarian action.
Movement-wide coordination has supported a nationally led response under VRC leadership. A Joint Statement signed
on 10 July under the Sevilla Agreement 2.0 clarified the roles of the VRC as convener, IFRC as co-convener and ICRC
in accordance with its mandate. Movement partners have coordinated personnel, ERUs, technical expertise, relief
supplies, funding and joint sectoral actions, while the contribution-tracking mechanism has supported alignment with
National Society priorities and reduced duplication. More information in detail can be found under the Coordination
and Partnership section.
Needs analysis
The humanitarian situation remains severe, with an estimated 9.73 million people affected, including approximately
530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity. Analysis conducted by the Venezuelan Red Cross estimates that
approximately 331,068 people in La Guaira are in need of assistance from at least one humanitarian sector4. Three
parishes—Catia La Mar, Caraballeda and Carayaca—were classified as having catastrophic levels of severity, while five
additional parishes were classified as extreme. The following analysis takes into account primary and secondary data
collection.
The Venezuelan Red Cross has conducted a sectoral analysis covering health and care, MHPSS, WASH, shelter, PGI,
CEA and volunteering to further define needs, gaps and response priorities. The analysis was developed through a
collaborative process involving technical specialists from the Venezuelan Red Cross, IFRC and German Red Cross.
Sector focal points consolidated information from operational activities, rapid and sector-specific assessments, field
observations and programme monitoring data, using a common analysis template to identify key needs,
vulnerabilities, response gaps and priority actions. The analysis was further complemented by secondary data review,
including official information, humanitarian reports and other relevant assessments, to support a comprehensive
understanding of the evolving humanitarian situation.
On 14 July, four VRC and IFRC teams visited prioritized temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira and the Capital
District to review response progress and site conditions and help identify locations where distributions could be
considered. The teams engaged with affected people, local authorities and other stakeholders and reviewed a broad
range of areas relevant to operational planning, including shelter conditions, essential household items, hygiene, safe
water access and storage, existing capacities and access to services. The visits also highlighted differences between
sites and population groups. In addition, on 16 July, the IFRC PGI focal point conducted a rapid multisectoral
assessment in Las Caracas and Escuela Crimeles.
Secondary data review includes information from relevant humanitarian actors on site such as IOM, PAHO, Save the
Children and OCHA. It also includes perception-based assessments, such as the GeoPoll rapid needs assessment5
conducted through WhatsApp with 846 affected households, which has provided additional insights into priority
needs, access to information and perceptions of the evolving humanitarian situation.
The sections below provide a sector-by-sector analysis of the main needs, vulnerabilities and identified gaps.
Health and care, including MHPSS. The Venezuelan Red Cross estimates that approximately 247,563 people in La
Guaira may require some kind of health-related assistance as a result of the earthquake and its consequences,
reflecting the scale of disruption to health services and humanitarian conditions across affected communities.
Damage to health infrastructure and the displacement of health personnel have reduced service availability in
4 This number is the People in Need (PIN) calculated by the Venezuelan Red Cross using the Mosaico methodology.
5 Venezuela Earthquake: Dispatches from Inside the Disaster Zone #2 - GeoPoll
5

affected areas. The VRC sectoral analysis reports three hospitals were evacuated, 24 temporarily were affected, 20
with minor damage and approximately 50 health centres operating partially. Identified needs include follow-up
trauma care and rehabilitation, continuity of medicines and consultations for people with chronic conditions,
maternal and emergency obstetric care, epidemiological surveillance, infection prevention, nutrition screening and
support for people with disabilities, older people, families with small children and those with reduced mobility.
Operational gaps include shortages of qualified personnel, medical supplies, medicines, vehicles, fuel and
ambulances; restrictions in referral routes; limited specialized mental-health capacity; and weaknesses in
epidemiological and pre-hospital information systems. Additional needs include community-based health promotion
and disease-prevention activities, particularly in areas affected by displacement and disruptions to basic services.
These include health education, vaccination support, disease-prevention messaging and community surveillance
activities linked to evolving public health risks.
Moreover, the VRC and IFRC temporary accommodation visits identified additional needs related to the continuity of
treatment for people living with chronic diseases and potential barriers to regular access to medicines and health
services in temporary accommodations. Some sites also reported the need to strengthen basic first-aid capacities.
The assessments further identified psychosocial support needs, vector-related health concerns, and the importance
of follow-up for pregnant women and people with specific health requirements.
In mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), the VRC preliminary analysis estimates that approximately
28,690 people may require support. MHPSS volunteers and staff of the Venezuelan Red Cross have reported
significant psychosocial distress among people reached through field clinics, temporary accommodation sites, mobile
outreach and rescue-related activities. Analysis of MHPSS service records have identified frequent presentations of
acute stress, anxiety, fear, sleep disturbance, crying, irritability, avoidance, somatic complaints and grief. These
reactions occur in the context of bereavement, injury, repeated aftershocks, displacement, uncertainty regarding
missing relatives and the loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks.
These findings are consistent with observations reported by other humanitarian actors. On 9 July, Save the Children
reported that affected children were experiencing heightened reactions to noise, sleep disturbances, anxiety,
irritability, aggression, anger and fear about the future. The assessment also noted that older children who had
protected or rescued younger family members during the earthquake continued to experience anxiety. These findings
reinforce the need for sustained mental health and psychosocial support services for children, adolescents and
caregivers affected by the earthquake.6
Furthermore, VRC volunteers and staff, and other frontline workers including search and rescue personnel and health
workers, are experiencing emotional strain. This is linked to prolonged shifts, repeated contact with distressed
families and exposure to highly distressing situations, including serious injuries, deaths and the recovery of human
remains. Teams on the ground have reported reactions such as sadness, anxiety, crying, sleep difficulties and
avoidance.
Shelter, housing and displacement. Official national reports have identified 107 transitional camps accommodating
approximately 21,210 people7 8. IOM reporting indicates that displaced households have been staying in collective
centres, including schools and sports facilities, as well as spontaneous settlements.9 WFP teams also found affected
people outside formal shelters in hillside communities, informal settlements and mountainous areas around La
Guaira. Some had fled with few or no possessions and had not previously been reached by the broader response10.
6 https://www.savethechildren.net/news/theyre-flinching-slightest-noise-childrens-mental-wellbeing-stake-two-weeks-devastating
7 OCHA Situation Report No. 16 (issued 9 July 2026 at 21:00)
8 Sectoral Vice Presidency of Social and Territorial Socialism of Venezuela
9 Venezuela-Earthquake-Response-Sit-Rep-12-13-14-Jul-2026-EN.pdf
10 https://www.wfp.org/stories/venezuela-earthquakes-food-brings-hope-families-crisis
6

The VRC monitors 107 accommodation centres across five states, including official camps, spontaneous shelters, host
households and civil-society-managed sites. The sectoral analysis conducted by VRC identified overcrowding,
insufficient registration and site organization, limited lighting and access control, accumulated waste, vector risks and
loss of essential household items. Some families lack cooking equipment, blankets and other basic household items
needed to reduce dependence on communal services. Sanitation facilities in assessed accommodation sites are not
consistently separated by sex, sometimes lack internal locks and can be located in poorly lit areas. The changing
number and location of displaced people, including movement towards reception states and host-family
arrangements, also complicates planning and requires continued monitoring and reconciliation of accommodation
data.
Findings from the VRC and IFRC temporary accommodation visits highlighted important differences in infrastructure
conditions, availability of showers, living space and accommodation capacity. The prolonged stay of families in
collective accommodation is creating additional needs for household items and support to maintain adequate living
conditions, requiring continued monitoring of occupancy levels and site conditions.
Furthermore, during the week of 11-18 July, humanitarian partners through the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group led
by OCHA, conducted a joint multisectoral assessment of temporary camps in coordination with national authorities.
The assessment provided a consolidated overview of current conditions, priority needs, and service gaps across the
sites established for the affected population.
Water, sanitation and hygiene. Preliminary WASH analyses indicate that needs remain widespread across all nine
affected parishes of La Guaira. VRC identified WASH as the sector with the highest level of need, affecting an estimated
331,068 people, reflecting the extensive disruption of water systems across the state. Damage has affected public
water infrastructure, including aqueducts, water-intake systems, pumping systems and internal networks serving
schools, health facilities and shelters. Water provision in some areas depends on bottled water and tanker trucks,
while the quality of tanker-supplied water is not always known. Although this is not part of the Red Cross response at
the moment, it was observed by the RCRC teams during field visits. This analysis also identifies the need for household
water-treatment items and safe water-storage capacity. Sanitation coverage is low or absent in some sites,
maintenance of existing facilities is limited, and accessible facilities and facilities separated by sex are required to
improve privacy and dignity. Gaps also include showers, handwashing stations, laundry areas, menstrual-hygiene
spaces, personal and family hygiene items, waste management and vector-control measures. Precise technical
information on damaged water infrastructure remains incomplete, and changes in shelter populations complicate
the design of sustainable interventions.
The VRC and IFRC temporary accommodation visits conducted also identified needs related to household water
containers and larger-capacity water-storage systems in collective accommodation sites, further strengthening the
need to address this area of work. Across several locations, affected people reported continued needs for personal
and family hygiene items, cleaning materials for communal areas and support for safe water storage and treatment.
The assessments also highlighted the need for further analysis of sanitation conditions in some sites and
strengthening of safe water-management practices.
More specifically, women and girls are facing additional challenges in managing menstruation with dignity and
privacy, with Save the Children reporting that they are managing menstruation without adequate privacy, clean water
or sanitary products. Damage to water pipelines and waste-management systems was also reported.11
Protection, Gender and Inclusion, including RFL. The Protection Cluster reported that the destruction of homes,
displacement and the weakening of family, community and institutional support networks were increasing exposure
to protection risks while reducing people’s ability to cope. Affected people were staying in both government-managed
11 Families displaced by Venezuela earthquakes at risk of infection amid water and sanitation shortages | Save the Children
International
7

accommodation and informal sites, where inadequate privacy and security were identified as concerns.12 Protection
concerns are concentrated on temporary accommodation sites and displacement routes. Identified risks include
inadequate lighting, uncontrolled access, insufficient or unsafe sanitation facilities, limited privacy, mixed
accommodation arrangements, separated or unsupervised children, family separation and barriers to accessing
health, protection and justice services. The sectoral analysis also identified risks of trafficking, exploitation and abuse
of children, gender-based violence, sexual exploitation and abuse, and reduced access to sexual and reproductive
health services. Institutional protection and referral services are reported as overstretched, while specialised post-
GBV care and internal formal complaints and safeguarding mechanisms require strengthening. Families also need
connectivity and Restoring Family Links services to maintain or re-establish contact. Staff and volunteers require
training in PGI, gender-based violence, safeguarding and prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse, together with
clear, confidential and consent-based referral pathways and case follow-up arrangements.
The VRC and IFRC temporary accommodation visits identified groups with specific needs, including pregnant women,
children and persons with disabilities or other specific vulnerabilities. The concentration of displaced people in
collective accommodation settings highlights the need to strengthen identification of differentiated needs and ensure
privacy, dignity, accessibility and equitable access to assistance and services.
Moreover, the rapid multisectoral assessment conducted by IFRC PGI focal point in Las Caracas and Escuela Crimeles
identified additional PGI-related concerns and operational priorities in temporary accommodation settings. In Las
Caracas, where 997 people were registered, key measures already in place included regulated family visits in a
designated common area, restricted access to residential cabins and preventive security presence. However, the
assessment recommended developing a formal protection protocol adapted to the site, with the administration
expressing openness to coordination once formal contact is established with the VRC. In Escuela Crimeles, hosting
480 people, the administration identified training on gender-based violence prevention and child protection as highly
relevant, although timing will need to be adapted to avoid disrupting critical shelter-management tasks.
Community Engagement and Accountability. Affected people require timely, consistent information on available
services, safety measures, assistance criteria and feedback channels. There is a need for safe and confidential
mechanisms through which communities can raise questions, complaints and safeguard concerns. Community
feedback also needs to be systematically collected, analysed and used to adjust services and distributions.
Standardized messages and coordination across health, WASH, PGI, shelter and distribution teams are required to
reduce inconsistent information, rumours, exclusion and false expectations. CEA capacity within the National Society
also requires strengthening through practical training and orientation for staff and volunteers and the incorporation
of community participation into assessment, planning, distribution and monitoring processes.
The VRC and IFRC temporary accommodation visits highlighted the need to strengthen direct consultation with
affected people and establish accessible information and feedback mechanisms. They also identified the importance
of maintaining updated population registries and continuously tracking changes in camp occupancy in order to adapt
assistance planning and clearly communicate eligibility criteria, assistance modalities and available services.
Furthermore, recent perception data collected through a GeoPoll rapid needs assessment13 found that 58 per cent of
respondents reported that the information they most needed but could not access was related to aftershock and
safety updates. The assessment also found that nearly four out of five respondents relied on social media or
WhatsApp as their primary source of earthquake-related information. These findings reinforce the importance of
providing timely, consistent and accessible information through trusted communication channels and establishing
mechanisms to address information gaps and community concerns.

response
13 Venezuela Earthquake: Dispathes from Inside the Disaster Zone #2 - GeoPoll

Livelihoods and basic needs. WFP reported that the loss of homes and livelihoods, together with disruption to
supply chains, was expected to worsen hunger and access to essential services. In La Guaira, homes, markets and
household food supplies had been heavily affected, leaving some families with little or nothing to eat.14 VRC analysis
estimates that approximately 144,721 working-age adults could require livelihoods support across the affected
parishes of La Guaira. This reinforces findings from rapid assessments indicating that many households have not yet
resumed their normal income-generating activities and continue facing difficulties meeting essential needs. These
rapid needs assessments also revealed significant impacts on household livelihoods. Most people consulted reported
that they had not yet resumed their normal economic activities or recovered their regular sources of income. This
has reduced household capacity to independently meet basic needs and is affecting the ability to cover expenditures
related to food, transport, medicines, hygiene items and other essential goods. These findings support the continued
analysis of market-based assistance options, including multipurpose cash assistance.
Food security and nutrition. Food access remains an urgent concern. WFP reported on 16 July that homes, markets
and food stocks had been damaged and that loss of livelihoods and disruption to supply chains were expected to
worsen hunger. Some families in affected areas had little or no food remaining.15 While food distributions are
available in several temporary accommodation sites, rapid assessments identified concerns regarding specific
nutritional requirements, particularly among children. Additional analysis is required to better understand the
adequacy, diversity and nutritional quality of available food assistance and identify any remaining gaps.
GeoPoll findings indicate that 51 per cent of households in the most affected areas reported limited or no access to
food, while 41 per cent reported limited or no access to drinking water. Food was identified as the most frequently
reported need in respondents’ open-ended responses.
Operational risk assessment
The IFRC is taking a proactive approach to risk management, implementing an optimal set of controls to maximise
the effectiveness and efficiency of the operation. The overall risk management structure and plan (in line with the
IFRC Risk Management Policy and Framework) include:
• The risk management and risk reporting procedure for the Emergency Appeal (EA)
• How to guide – risk management cycle in detail
• Roles and responsibilities in managing risk
The IFRC Venezuela Delegation and operational teams are responsible for identifying, managing, monitoring, and
reporting risks inherent to the operational environment. This is facilitated by the Head of Operations, Operations
Managers and members of the operations team. Risks are captured in the risk register, reviewed, and reported on,
following an established process flow. Each month, the regional risk coordinator will review the risk register and
prepare a consolidated summary of relevant IFRC actors and partners. A Surge Risk Management coordinator is
also considered for further strengthening of this area of the operation.

B. OPERATIONAL STRATEGY
Update on the strategy
Since publication of the Operational Strategy, the overall objectives, target population and geographic focus remain
unchanged. The strategy has, however, been refined to strengthen the recovery lens across the operation, including
greater emphasis on restoring safe housing and essential services, supporting livelihoods and self-sufficiency,
reducing future risks, and further reinforcing the VRC’s institutional, operational and preparedness capacities.
The indicators included below have been reviewed and updated for each strategic sector of intervention to better
reflect the key interventions and progress achieved.
• PGI: Indicators have been adjusted to better represent the services delivered by the protection team,
measuring the number of Restoring Family Links services provided to people affected by the earthquake
rather than the number of individual people reached.
• CEA: Indicators now provide a more comprehensive view of community engagement and accountability by
including CEA training for staff as well as volunteers.
• Health and MHPSS: Training indicators have been broadened from “volunteers trained in MHPSS” to
“volunteers and staff trained in MHPSS”, with the target revised from 150 to 300 to reinforce sustainable
MHPSS capacity within the National Society. The indicator “Number of people receiving psychosocial care
services” has also been revised to “Number of people receiving MHPSS services” to better reflect the full range
of psychosocial support and psychological interventions delivered through the operation. In addition, the
indicator “Number of people reached with key community health messages delivered by volunteers” has been
broadened to include MHPSS messages, recognizing the integration of mental health and psychosocial
support communication into community outreach.
• Multipurpose cash: The indicator “Number of volunteers trained in cash” has been revised to “Number of
volunteers trained in cash and voucher assistance” to better reflect the scope of planned CVA capacity
strengthening. The indicator “Percentage of people participating in post-distribution interviews” has been
revised to “Percentage of people participating in post-distribution monitoring interviews” to clarify the
monitoring purpose of these interviews. The indicator or “Number of MPCT activation protocols” has been
removed, as it is not relevant to this response.
These indicators will be further revised with the National Society for the Operational Update 2 to ensure they reflect
the changing reality of the earthquake’s response. Furthermore, the response environment has continued to
expand, with additional humanitarian actors operating in affected areas and increased interest from Participating
National Societies in providing technical, operational, in-kind and financial support. This requires continued
coordination, contribution tracking and alignment with priorities identified by the VRC through the Federation-wide
approach.

The Venezuelan Red Cross, supported by the ICRC, IFRC and Movement partners, continued Restoring Family Links
and connectivity activities through fixed and mobile modalities.
Two connectivity and Restoring Family Links (RFL) mobile points were established and are currently operating in
La Guaira. Through these connectivity points, people affected by the earthquake can access free phone calls, Wi‑Fi
services, phone charging and top-ups, and Restoring Family Links services. These services support families to
maintain or re-establish contact with relatives, help prevent family separation, and facilitate communication
among people displaced or otherwise affected by the emergency.
As of 20 July, the Venezuelan Red Cross has provided 3,479 Restoring Family Links (RFL) services to people affected
by the earthquake, all in La Guaira. The services provided include 109 phone-call services, 1,521 Wi-Fi connections
and 1,849 battery-charging services. Of the services recorded, 1,508 were accessed by people who had previously
used the service, while 1,308 were accessed by first-time users; previous-use information was unavailable for the
remaining 663 services. The largest volume was recorded at the Campo de Golf location, with 43 phone-call
services, 641 Wi-Fi connections and 1,134 battery-charging services. These services have remained essential for
helping affected people maintain or re-establish contact with relatives, particularly among displaced households
and families searching for missing or separated family members.
Protection activities focused on child protection, safeguarding, gender-based violence risk mitigation and
strengthening referral pathways. The National Society approved the IFRC’s Child Safeguarding Risk Analysis, while
work continued on service mapping, the pathway for activation of Post-Exposure Prophylaxis kits, an emergency
fund for safe referrals, dignity kits, safeguarding materials and planning for PGI training.
To ensure a decentralized and sustainable response, the Venezuelan Red Cross plans to deploy a national PGI
specialist to the principal reception states identified through displacement monitoring, including Sucre, Zulia,
Apure, Falcón, Miranda, Anzoátegui, Delta Amacuro, Monagas, Aragua, Trujillo, Bolívar, Táchira and Barinas.
Through this initiative, 300 volunteers and staff will receive training in basic and specialized PGI approaches. The
training will strengthen local branch capacities to conduct protection screening, provide protection information
and orientation, identify and support people with specific needs, facilitate safe and confidential referrals, and
contribute to connectivity and RFL case management in their respective territories. This approach aims to expand
protection coverage while promoting locally led and sustainable service delivery.
Finally, coordination and technical engagement have continued to strengthen throughout the response,
supporting the delivery of protection services, the development of referral pathways and the enhancement of
protection capacities. Coordination with the ICRC has focused on technical accompaniment for the provision of
RFL services, as well as the planning of training and capacity-building activities for staff and volunteers. In parallel,
coordination with UNHCR has supported the activation and referral of protection cases identified in the field.
Engagement with the Protection Cluster Areas of Responsibility, particularly Child Protection and Gender-Based
Violence, has also contributed to strengthening referral pathways, information sharing and access to specialized
protection services for people with specific needs.
