Coordination has been particularly strong in communications and resource mobilisation, as many National Societies
worldwide have launched fundraising campaigns at domestic level, among them; the American Red Cross, Argentine
Red Cross, Austrian Red Cross, Canadian Red Cross, Colombian Red Cross Society, Italian Red Cross, Japanese Red
Cross, Mexican Red Cross, The Netherlands Red Cross, Norwegian Red Cross, Paraguayan Red Cross, Spanish Red
Cross, Thai Red Cross Society, Qatari Red Crescent, Honduran Red Cross, and Guatemalan Red Cross. And the Danish
Red Cross is advocating for support from its government. Financial data from National Societies collaborating
bilaterally with the Emergency Appeal response will be collected through a Federation-wide Financial Overview form.
Finally, the operation is guided by the Statutes of the Movement, the Fundamental Principles, the Venezuelan Red
Cross Law (10 March 2026), its Strategic Plan 2026-2030, the National Response Plan, its Preparedness for Effective
Response plan, and the IFRC Legal Status Agreement. Together, these provide a robust legal framework that facilities
the operation, recognises the National Society’s auxiliary role to the public authorities, and enables principled
humanitarian action. Humanitarian access, and entry of specialized personnel and goods has been promptly and
widely facilitated by the National authorities for the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, and other crucial
humanitarian actors for the response.

documents.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #15 (20 to 21 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
The fifteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 20 to 21 July.

## Highlights

Between 20 and 21 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, WASH and information management.

To date, IOM has reached **8,542 unique individuals through 15,460 instances of assistance and services**, mainly in shelter and transitory camp coordination, protection, health and WASH.

IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed **3,055 kitchen sets, 2,590 tarpaulins, 2,039 buckets, 1,676 solar lamps and 819 shelter kits** to affected households.

## IOM activities

IOM continued managing and coordinating five transitory camps in La Guaira and advanced the operational transition of three of them to the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).

At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM maintained essential services for 316 families and supported registration activities. Coordination and registration continued at César Nieves and Playa Grande, while preparations were finalized at Tanaguarena Golf Course for the installation of additional infrastructure.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water storage and hygiene items. To date, **1,552 collapsible water containers, 1,009 hygiene kits and 92 semi-collapsible water containers** have been distributed.

IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano have provided **5,552 medical consultations**, including general and specialized care, medication distribution and psychological support. Mobile health and MHPSS services remained operational at José María Vargas and César Nieves.

IOM continued household registration and population data updates across five camps and conducted a mobility intentions survey in José María Vargas, César Nieves and Playa Grande to identify needs, displacement patterns and intentions to return or relocate.

In protection, IOM continued providing guidance, legal assistance, documentation support and referrals to specialized services, with **130 people assisted and supported to date**.

## IOM planned response

IOM will continue the operational transition of three camps to NRC, assistance distributions and infrastructure improvements, while strengthening WASH, health, mental health and protection services.

It will also strengthen camp and mobility monitoring, multisectoral assessments inside and outside the sites, and coordination with authorities and partners.

documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #15 (20 al 21 de julio 2026)
documents.body_text:
El decimoquinto Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, con información correspondiente al período del 20 al 21 de julio.

## Aspectos destacados

Entre el 20 y el 21 de julio, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, salud, protección, WASH y gestión de información.

A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado a 8.542 personas únicas mediante 15.460 asistencias y servicios, principalmente en alojamiento y coordinación de campamentos transitorios, protección, salud y WASH.

La OIM y su socio Fundación Vivienda Popular han distribuido 3.055 sets de cocina, 2.590 lonas, 2.039 baldes, 1.676 lámparas solares y 819 kits de refugio a hogares afectados.

## Actividades de la OIM

La OIM continuó gestionando y coordinando cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira y avanzó la transición operativa de tres de ellos al Consejo Noruego para los Refugiados (NRC).

En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, mantuvo servicios esenciales para 316 familias y apoyó actividades de registro. En César Nieves y Playa Grande continuaron la coordinación y los registros, mientras que en el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena finalizaron los preparativos para instalar infraestructura adicional.

En WASH, continuó ampliando el acceso a artículos para almacenamiento seguro de agua e higiene. A la fecha, se han distribuido 1.552 bidones plegables, 1.009 kits de higiene y 92 bidones semiplegables.

La OIM y su socio Ven Da Tu Mano han realizado 5.552 atenciones médicas, incluidas consultas generales y especializadas, entrega de medicamentos y apoyo psicológico. Los servicios móviles de salud y SMAPS continuaron operativos en José María Vargas y César Nieves.

La OIM mantuvo el registro y actualización de información poblacional en cinco campamentos y realizó una encuesta sobre intenciones de movilidad en José María Vargas, César Nieves y Playa Grande para identificar necesidades, patrones de desplazamiento e intenciones de retorno o reubicación.

En protección, continuó brindando orientación, asistencia legal, apoyo en documentación y derivaciones a servicios especializados, con 130 personas atendidas y acompañadas a la fecha.

## Respuesta planificada de la OIM

La OIM continuará la transición operativa de tres campamentos a NRC, las distribuciones y mejoras de infraestructura, y reforzará los servicios de WASH, salud y salud mental y protección.

Asimismo, fortalecerá el monitoreo de los campamentos y de la movilidad, las evaluaciones multisectoriales dentro y fuera de los sitios y la coordinación con autoridades y socios.

documents.title: Comité de Emergencia Español: un mes después de los terremotos en Venezuela la ayuda es más necesaria que nunca
documents.body_text:
El Comité de Emergencia Español reitera el llamamiento para mantener la ayuda a las decenas de miles de personas afectadas por los terremotos que sacudieron Venezuela hace un mes. El desafío sigue siendo incalculable tras los seísmos que dejaron más de 5.069 muertos y más de 16.740 personas heridas, además de miles de familias afectadas y comunidades con daños severos. Los esfuerzos se centran ahora en que la población pueda retomar la vida cotidiana con seguridad: volver a entornos habitables, recuperar servicios básicos, reabrir espacios comunitarios y educativos y reducir la exposición a riesgos que amenazan la salud de miles de familias.

**La situación es crítica ya que las necesidades humanitarias son enormes.**

El trabajo de las **8 ONG del Comité de Emergencia Español** que están respondiendo a esta emergencia, **Acción contra el Hambre, Aldeas Infantiles SOS, Educo, Entreculturas, Médicos del Mundo, Oxfam Intermón, Plan International y World Vision,** continúa y se centra en estos momentos en la atención a la población en situación más vulnerable, incluídos niños, y niñas, proporcionando alimentos, agua y asistencia económica, protección y refugio, atención médica y psicosocial, prevención de brotes epidémicos y apoyo educativo para la infancia, principalmente.

“Un mes después de los terremotos el reto al que se enfrentan las ONG internacionales especialistas en ayuda humanitaria del Comité de Emergencia es que las familias puedan volver a una rutina segura sin que la emergencia se transforme en una crisis sanitaria. Evitar enfermedades y acompañar la recuperación física y emocional es ahora determinante”, **señala la directora del Comité de Emergencia Español, Sara Barbeira.**

**Llamamiento a mantener la solidaridad**

El **Comité de Emergencia Español, activado el 25 de junio**, canaliza la solidaridad de la sociedad española para apoyar la respuesta de las organizaciones en coordinación con entidades locales y socios sobre el terreno, especialmente en las zonas más afectadas, con La Guaira entre los estados con mayor impacto, y con efectos directos e indirectos en varios territorios del país.

“Ahora empieza el trabajo más largo: evitar una crisis sanitaria, sostener la atención médica y ayudar a las familias a recuperar su vida. La solidaridad de ciudadanos y empresas españolas ha sido enorme, pero debe mantenerse para que el pueblo venezolano pueda poco a poco recuperar una cierta normalidad. También para sanar en la manera de lo posible el trauma social de la terrible pérdida de miles de personas”, **agrega Sara Barbeira.**

**Retomar la vida cotidiana: una prioridad humanitaria**

Un mes después de los terremotos, las necesidades evolucionan y se vuelve clave impulsar una recuperación temprana que permita unas condiciones de vida digna y reducir riesgos secundarios. Para ello una de las prioridades de las ONG es garantizar **agua limpia, saneamiento e higiene** para prevenir enfermedades asociadas a la falta de letrinas, la contaminación del agua y la gestión deficiente de residuos.

Las ONG que forman parte del Comité de Emergencia están centradas en apoyar soluciones de alojamiento temporal y mejoras en refugios, así como en reforzar la **atención sanitaria** y el acceso a medicamentos esenciales, priorizando la atención primaria. También la atención psicosocial, especialmente para niños, niñas y familias que han sufrido pérdidas, desplazamiento o exposición a situaciones traumáticas, es fundamental. La **salud mental** de las personas afectadas es una de las grandes prioridades en esta fase.

La protección de los **grupos poblaciones más vulnerables** es una de las claves de esta respuesta, protegiendo frente a violaciones de sus derechos y promoviendo entornos más seguros. El foco se mantiene en quienes corren mayor riesgo tras el desastre, especialmente las niñas, adolescentes y mujeres, que se encuentran más expuestas a la violencia, la explotación y la interrupción de sus servicios de salud.

La respuesta también incluye la puesta en marcha de **Espacios Seguros para la Infancia** para que los niños y niñas tengan un entorno seguro donde retomar rutinas que favorezcan su bienestar emocional, y de espacios temporales de aprendizaje para que puedan continuar con su educación y recuperar la normalidad.

La recuperación también requerirá ampliar la cobertura hacia **comunidades receptoras** y estados que están recibiendo población desplazada, donde las vulnerabilidades preexistentes y la presión sobre los servicios básicos podrían agravar las necesidades humanitarias.

documents.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #4: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 22 July 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
documents.body_text:
As of 22 July, AMDA’s relief team has been working to provide aid to those affected by the earthquakes that devastated Venezuela on 24 June.

AMDA has been based in Caraballeda, La Guaira, one of the hardest-hit locations since the start of the quake response efforts. The below is the summary of its activities between 14-19 July:

■14 July

AMDA’s second relief team (comprising a Venezuelan physician and a nurse based in Peru) arrived in Venezuela on 14 July to join the ongoing quake response in Caraballeda.

Since the following day, the team began providing medical care at a temporary clinic in cooperation with local healthcare professionals and volunteers. Because the clinic was run by volunteers, AMDA’s medical team played a vital role in maintaining the clinic's services, as staff allocation of volunteers changed from day to day.

The AMDA team worked from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. each day and provided medical consultations to approximately 50 to 100 patients daily.

■18 July

On 18 July, one Japanese nurse arrived at Valencia Airport in Venezuela to join the advance team. The nurse was dispatched to respond to the ongoing humanitarian needs even though more than three weeks had passed since the earthquake struck.

Upon arrival, the nurse traveled approximately two hours by car to Caracas, the capital, to meet local partners for further coordination of aid work scheduled to begin the following day.

Meanwhile, the AMDA team on the ground continued providing medical assistance at the temporary clinic in La Guaira.

■19 July

On 19 July, AMDA’s aid workers took part in events to celebrate Children's Day in Venezuela, all of which were held in La Guaira.

At an event organized by the Blue Cross of Santa María University, medical assistance was provided alongside a play area for children. AMDA’s Japanese nurse supported the event by providing basic medical services, including blood pressure checks.

AMDA also joined another community event, "Lluvia de Sonrisas" (Rain of Smiles), organized by local medical professionals. In addition to medical consultations in internal medicine, pediatrics and other specialties, the event featured the distribution of relief supplies, games for children, and street performances, which attracted many children and their families.

AMDA distributed snacks, drinks and toys, while the aforementioned nurse worked together with a local psychologist to hold a colouring activity for children. (The colouring books used in it were donated by the Ohara Art Foundation in Japan, with which AMDA has concluded a comprehensive partnership agreement.)

Through these events, AMDA was able to provide not only medical support but also moments of joy and comfort for children and families facing difficult circumstances.

All this while, on the same day, AMDA’s second medical team (comprising a Venezuelan doctor and a nurse based in Peru) continued providing medical care at the temporary clinic.

The relief work will continue for the time being.

documents.title: Los terremotos en Venezuela dejan una huella invisible en la salud de la niñez
documents.body_text:
A casi un mes de los terremotos que sacudieron a Venezuela el 24 de junio, la organización humanitaria y de desarrollo Plan International advierte que la salud física y mental de niñas, niños y adolescentes se ve cada vez más afectada por las condiciones en las zonas más golpeadas por el desastre. Las condiciones inadecuadas de vivienda, la acumulación de escombros y cambio en los arreglos de cuidado están profundizando el impacto emocional del desastre en la niñez y sus familias.

Según el reporte de la agencia de Naciones Unidas responsable de coordinar la respuesta humanitaria ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-26-19-july-2026-time-0900-pm)), 107 campamentos transitorios albergan actualmente a más de 23.800 personas, cerca del 86% de su capacidad total, mientras que más de 17.900 personas continúan sin vivienda. Al 19 de julio, las cifras oficiales reportaban 5.208 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.

Las organizaciones socias de Plan International que responden en el terreno reportan que las molestias físicas sin causa clara aparecen cada vez con más frecuencia, junto con señales de estrés postraumático y una sensación constante de inseguridad, y que, al escuchar con más atención, revelan semanas de sueño interrumpido, sobresaltos y miedo acumulado.

“Cuando hace brisa yo me meto para el cuarto y me escondo y me asusto”, cuenta Victoria, de nueve años, en La Guaira. Naomi, de solo cinco años, describe cómo las pesadillas recurrentes le interrumpen el sueño: “Yo estaba en la playa y un tsunami me estaba persiguiendo”.

Michelle, madre de tres niñas de 25 años, resume lo que ve cada día: “Están asustadas, tienen miedo. La niñez ahorita necesita apoyo psicológico que les ayude”.

Yesica Serrano, asesora regional de Protección de la Niñez en Acción Humanitaria de Plan International, se encuentra actualmente en Venezuela y advierte que esta fase de la emergencia exige tanta atención como la primera.

“Cuando pasa el impacto inmediato del terremoto, el efecto no desaparece: se queda con niñas, niños y adolescentes, tanto en el cuerpo como en la mente. Un dolor de cabeza, un dolor de estómago, dificultad para dormir o miedo a los ruidos fuertes pueden ser señales de angustia que la niñez no logra expresar con palabras. En esta etapa de la emergencia, la salud mental de la niñez ya no puede tratarse como una respuesta secundaria. Si no atendemos el bienestar físico y emocional en conjunto, la recuperación será imposible”, afirmó Serrano.

Ella agrega que este impacto no se ve igual en todas las edades.

“Niñas, niños y adolescentes de distintas edades y etapas de desarrollo no siempre tienen las palabras o los medios para explicar lo que sienten, y no siempre lo demuestran de la misma manera. Las niñas y los niños más pequeños pueden dejar de comer, tener dificultad para dormir, presentar episodios de llanto sin razón aparente o sobresaltarse con facilidad, mientras que las y los adolescentes son más propensos a aislarse, a estar más callados, a mostrarse más agresivos o a alejarse de quienes los rodean. Estar conscientes de estas señales y actuar sobre ellas, junto con la atención médica, es tan urgente como reconstruir un techo”.

Niñas, niños y adolescentes continúan siendo agrupados en una sola categoría en la recolección de datos y las evaluaciones de necesidades, aun cuando enfrentan las crisis de manera distinta y se exponen a riesgos y desafíos diferentes. Plan International advierte que esta distinción todavía necesita reflejarse mejor en la respuesta humanitaria.

Junto con sus socios en territorio, Plan International brinda apoyo psicosocial grupal e individual a niñas, niños y adolescentes, ayuda a las familias a cubrir necesidades urgentes que salvan vidas, y fortalece los servicios de protección de la niñez, con especial atención a las niñas. Esto incluye espacios seguros donde la niñez puede comenzar a procesar lo que ha vivido, así como rutas de derivación hacia servicios especializados de salud mental.

A medida que la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela entra en una nueva fase, Plan International reconoce que existe ahora una oportunidad para integrar de forma más cercana el apoyo en salud física y mental en los campamentos de personas desplazadas y las comunidades afectadas. La organización también insta a actores humanitarios y a donantes a recopilar y utilizar datos que distingan entre niñas, niños, adolescentes y personas adultas, para ayudar a que el apoyo se ajuste a sus diferentes necesidades y llegue a quienes están en mayor riesgo.

**FIN**

**Si desea más información o solicitar una entrevista, póngase en contacto con:**

Rodrigo Morales, Regional Communication Officer for Public Relations

Plan International Americas

Tel: +503 7885 9315

Email: rodrigo.morales@plan-international.org

**Acerca de Plan International**

*Plan International es una organización independiente humanitaria y de desarrollo que promueve los derechos de la niñez y la igualdad para las niñas. Creemos en el poder y el potencial de cada niña y niño, pero sabemos que a menudo se ven limitados por la pobreza, la violencia, la exclusión y la discriminación. Y son las niñas las más afectadas.*

*En colaboración con niñas, niños, jóvenes, seguidores y socios, luchamos por un mundo justo, abordando las causas profundas de los problemas a los que se enfrentan las niñas y los niños en situación más vulnerable. Apoyamos a la niñez desde su nacimiento hasta la edad adulta y los capacitamos para prepararse y responder a las crisis y a la adversidad. Impulsamos el cambio de prácticas y políticas a nivel local, nacional y global gracias a nuestro alcance, experiencia y conocimientos.*

*Durante más de 85 años, hemos reunido a otros optimistas determinados para transformar la vida de todas las niñas y niños en más de 80 países.*

*No nos detendremos, hasta lograr la igualdad.*

documents.title: Venezuela's earthquakes take a hidden toll on children's health
documents.body_text:
Almost one month after the earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June, the development and humanitarian organisation, Plan International, warns that the physical and mental health of children and adolescents is increasingly affected by conditions in the areas hardest hit by the disaster. Inadequate housing conditions, accumulation of debris, and insufficient care arrangements are deepening the emotional impact of the disaster on children and their families.

According to the report from the UN agency responsible for coordinating humanitarian response ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-26-19-july-2026-time-0900-pm)), 107 transitional camps are currently sheltering more than 23.800 people, close to 86% of their total capacity, while more than 17,900 people remain without housing. As of 19 July, official figures reported 5.208 deaths and 16,740 people injured.

Plan International local partners responding on the ground report that physical complaints with no clear cause are appearing more and more, alongside signs of post-traumatic stress and a constant sense of insecurity, and on closer listening, they reveal weeks of disrupted sleep, jumpiness and accumulated fear.

"When it gets windy I run into my room and hide, and I get scared," says nine year old Victoria in La Guaira. Naomi, who is only five, describes how recurring nightmares are disrupting her sleep: "I was on the beach and a tsunami was chasing me."

Michelle, a 25-year-old mother of three girls, sums up what she sees every day: "They're scared, they're frightened. Right now, the children need psychological support to help them."

Yesica Serrano, Regional Child Protection in Humanitarian Action Adviser at Plan International, is currently in Venezuela and warns that this phase of the emergency demands as much attention as the first.

"Once the immediate shock of the earthquake has passed, the impact does not disappear – it stays with the children and adolescents both in body and mind. A headache, a stomach ache, difficulty sleeping or fear of loud noises can be signs of distress that children are unable to put into words. At this stage of the emergency, children's mental health can no longer be treated as a secondary response. If we don't address both the physical and emotional wellbeing together recovery will be impossible," Serrano said.

She adds that this toll doesn't look the same across ages.

"Children across different ages and development stages don't always have the words or means to explain what they're feeling, and they don't always show it the same way. Younger children may stop eating, struggle to sleep, have occasional crying spells with no apparent reason or startle easily, while adolescents are more likely to withdraw, grow quiet, be more aggressive or pull away from those around them. Being consciously aware of those signals and acting on them, alongside medical care, is just as urgent as rebuilding a roof."

Children and adolescents continue to be grouped into a single category in data collection and needs assessments, even though they experience crises differently and face distinct risks and challenges. Plan International warns that this distinction still needs to be better reflected in the humanitarian response.

With partners on the ground, the organisation is providing group and individual psychosocial support to children and adolescents, helping families meet urgent and lifesaving needs, and strengthening child protection services, with particular attention to girls. This includes safe spaces where children can begin to process what they have experienced, as well as referral pathways to specialised mental health support.

As the earthquake response in Venezuela enters a new phase, Plan International recognises there is now an opportunity for physical and mental health support to be more closely integrated across the displacement camps and affected communities. It also urges humanitarian actors and donors to collect and use data that distinguishes between children, adolescents and adults, helping ensure support is tailored to their different needs and reaches those most at risk.

**ENDS**

**For further information please contact:**

Rodrigo Morales, Regional Communication Officer for Public Relations

Plan International Americas

Tel: +503 7885 9315

Email: rodrigo.morales@plan-international.org

**About Plan International**

Plan International is an independent development and humanitarian organisation that advances children’s rights and equality for girls. We believe in the power and potential of every child but know this is often suppressed by poverty, violence, exclusion, and discrimination. And it is girls who are most affected.

Working together with children, young people, supporters, and partners, we strive for a just world, tackling the root causes of the challenges girls and vulnerable children face. We support children’s rights from birth until they reach adulthood, and we enable children to prepare for and respond to crises and adversity. We drive changes in practice and policy at local, national, and global levels using our reach, experience, and knowledge.

For over 85 years, we have rallied other determined optimists to transform the lives of all children in more than 80 countries.

We won’t stop until we are all equal.

documents.body_text:
**OPERATIONAL CONTEXT**

Nearly one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response in Venezuela is rapidly transitioning from the immediate emergency phase to a more structured, large-scale operation. Indeed, humanitarian needs remain immense: over 23,000 people live in transitional camps, thousands more remain displaced in host communities or informal settlements, and damaged housing and basic infrastructure continue to limit access to safe shelter, water, sanitation, healthcare and livelihoods.ii

As aftershocks continue – over 1,300 registered up until now – the humanitarian response continues to expand in scale and complexity. Humanitarian actors are now planning assistance for 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the coming six months, yet significant humanitarian gaps remain, as many communities remain underserved. This requires humanitarian actors that can rapidly identify unmet needs, coordinate effectively with existing response structures and deliver assistance where it is needed most.

Against this backdrop, CESVI has paired rapid operational deployment with early engagement in humanitarian coordination mechanisms, ensuring that field evidence collected from the first days of the emergency directly informed operational planning, strengthened partnerships and supported the targeting of communities that remained outside the initial humanitarian response.

documents.title: One month after earthquakes, Venezuela risks spiraling into deeper crisis without urgent investment in economic recovery
documents.body_text:
Caracas, Venezuela, July 22, 2026 — Nearly one month after devastating twin earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, the window is closing to set the country on a sustainable path toward recovery. Without immediate investment in local economies and livelihood support, the disaster risks spiraling into a deeper humanitarian crisis, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) warns.

Venezuela was already experiencing protracted economic instability long before the ground began to shake, with [over half of the population living in extreme poverty](https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/where/latin-america-and-caribbean/venezuela_en). Years of economic hardship drove roughly 8 million people, mainly young adults, to leave the country. This has left a critical gap in the workforce that has impacted search and rescue efforts and will continue to constrain capacity as the vital early recovery phase begins.

Now, the economic situation threatens to unravel further. An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure to cost approximately $37 billion. Nearly 8 million people were in humanitarian need in Venezuela before the earthquakes. In just four weeks that number has grown by 1.4 million. As response efforts scale up, access remains complicated by the indefinite closure of the Simón Bolívar International Airport and continuous aftershocks, with over 1,400 since the initial quakes.

*"Beyond the destroyed buildings and people being pulled from the rubble, there is a quieter economic devastation that is becoming more visible by the day. For reconstruction efforts to have any hope of success, we must focus serious attention on restarting local economies, supporting small businesses, and getting schools back up and running,”* \*\*said IRC’s Emergency Response Lead for the Venezuela Earthquakes, Rafael Velasquez Garcia. “\*\**With millions of futures in the balance, the time to act is now. Absolutely nothing will stop local communities from lifting each other up if they're given the resources to do so."*

The IRC urges the international community to scale up humanitarian funding to support Venezuelans impacted by the earthquakes and the millions who were already in urgent need.

The IRC has been working in Venezuela since 2021 to deliver programs across health, nutrition, protection, education, food security, and livelihoods. As soon as the earthquakes hit, the IRC started scaling up its response to support affected communities, designing and launching ten new programs in tandem with eight local partners on the ground. The IRC will continue its support in the months ahead, providing life-saving assistance and essential protection and early recovery programming to help Venezuela rebuild. Over the past month, the IRC has distributed hundreds of hygiene and water purification kits, supported our partners providing first aid and primary care to 300-400 people every day, and helped reactivate the diagnostic laboratory at the Central University of Caracas to track potential disease outbreaks.

**Media contacts**

Sylvan Foley

**sylvan.foley@rescue.org**

documents.body_text:
**Highlights**

- More than three weeks after the earthquakes of 24 June, official figures report 5,208 deaths, 16,740 people injured, and 17,907 people left without housing.1 Humanitarian needs remain significant, particularly among displaced families residing in transitional camps and communities with disrupted access to essential services.
- UNICEF continues to scale up multi-sectoral assistance, focusing on health, nutrition, WASH and child protection services for children and families affected by the earthquakes, reaching over 7,519 people in the initial phase of the response. Health services through mobile health teams have reached around 2,108 people, while vaccination campaigns have reached 6,466 people. More than 2,452 children have been screened for acute malnutrition. WASH services are expanding at temporary shelters reaching 7,180 with critical hygiene supplies and 2,861 benefiting from access to safe drinking water. Psychosocial support and recreational activities have reached more than 2,726 children, adolescents and caregivers. Additionally, more than 4,400 people have been reached with hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available life-saving services.
- UNICEF will reach 150,000 people with critical emergency supplies within the coming weeks, including 49,000 with health supplies, 72,000 with micronutrients, and 29,000 with WASH items. An additional 49 tons of emergency supplies arrived on 14 July to replenish in-country emergency stockpiles.
- In addition to the US$137.6 million requested under the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal and aligned with the addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan 2026, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to respond to the humanitarian impact of the earthquakes.

documents.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #28 (21 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 28**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**21 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
- Official toll: **5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks.**

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local
time) in the north-central region, with
the epicentre located along the San
Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis
(Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities
report 1,405 aftershocks.
Twenty-seven days after the
earthquakes, authorities report a toll of
5,346 people dead and 16,740
injured since the onset of the
emergency. Authorities also indicated
that 17,907 people lost their homes.
The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to
affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities,
continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United
Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom
Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the
multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.
The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population
from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931
million.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira
state, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects
intended for affected populations.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
National response
 The Government response remains focused on assistance to affected people, as well as the
establishment and management of transitional camps.
 According to authorities, the response continues through 107 transitional camps for affected
populations, with a total capacity of 27,950 people and a current occupancy of 23,122 people. As of
21 July, 41 camps are located in Caracas, 28 in La Guaira, 28 in Miranda and 10 in Aragua. Of the
total camp population, 12,123 people are accommodated in La Guaira, 8,508 in Caracas, 1,816
in Miranda and 675 in Aragua.
 Health authorities announced the launch of fumigation and sanitary control measures in La Guaira
state, particularly in the parishes of Caraballeda, La Guaira and Macuto.
 On 20 July, authorities announced the allocation of fully equipped housing units to an initial 240
families affected by the earthquakes. The housing units are located in Fuerte Tiuna, Caracas, and
form part of the Venezuela Renace plan.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com).
 School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto
Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital
District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión,
Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 In Miranda state, the humanitarian response has been primarily concentrated in the municipalities of
Plaza (Guarenas), Zamora (Guatire), Chacao, Sucre and Baruta, which have been identified among
the areas most affected by the earthquakes. In these locations, humanitarian organizations including
IOM, UNICEF, WFP, World Vision and the Venezuelan Red Cross have supported search and
rescue operations, structural assessments, medical and psychosocial care, distribution of food, safe
drinking water and hygiene items, as well as assistance for displaced people. Child protection
mechanisms have also been strengthened, support services have been established in transitional
camps, and early recovery interventions have been promoted.
La Guaira
 In 12 transitional camps in La Guaira, mobile protection, child protection and gender-based violence
(GBV) teams were deployed to support the authorities’ response in specialized areas. Implementing
partners involved in these activities include FUNDAINIL, UNICEF, Tinta Violeta, NRC, DRC,
FUNDANA, AVESA, CECODAP, PUI, ASONACOP, Construyendo Futuros, Luz y Vida, IOM,
UNHCR, HI, the Venezuelan Red Cross, UNFPA, HIAS and ENCILUZ.
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 IOM, UNICEF, PAHO/WHO, ACH, Cáritas Venezuela, CRS, CAMPO, Laboratorio de Paz, the
Yaracuy Human Rights Network and the Human Rights Committee of Bolívar Municipality continue
to implement response activities in areas affected by the earthquakes. Reported interventions
include the distribution of basic assistance and support across the nutrition, water, sanitation and
hygiene (WASH), and protection sectors, with a particular focus on accompanying and supporting
affected communities.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Falcón (Silva municipality)
 The Miranda Municipality Mayor’s Office is leading an intersectoral coordination platform to collect
information on the needs of people who have relocated to the municipality to stay with relatives
following the earthquakes. As a result, it was agreed that the findings would be shared with OCHA
to identify potential areas for complementary support through the Local Coordination Forum (LCF),
based on the priority needs identified.
 CEPOREJUN and ODISEF, in coordination with OCHA, launched a Psychological First Aid training
for 300 Civil Protection, Fire Department and VEN 911 personnel, aimed at strengthening emergency
response capacities
Other states
 Lara: Authorities reported the arrival of at least 71 families, primarily from La Guaira. Most are being
accommodated in private homes and through family support networks. Priority needs identified
include maintaining the cold chain for medicines and vaccines, ensuring continuity of treatment for
chronic diseases, and preparing the education system to integrate displaced children and
adolescents without complete academic documentation. The need for power generators to support
health and water services was identified in Torres municipality. Humanitarian organizations continue
to provide medical care, psychosocial support, food assistance, and support to essential services.
 Trujillo: Authorities reported the relocation of 102 families across 14 municipalities, with the state
government prioritizing monitoring efforts in Carache, La Ceiba, Candelaria and Pampanito. Most
families have arrived from La Guaira and the Capital District and are being accommodated through
family and community support networks. ODISEF, NURR-ULA, the community network ‘Tejiendo
abrazos tras el sismo’, local volunteer networks, the General Directorate of Social Development,
Civil Protection and the Fire Department continue to provide health, nutrition, protection,
psychosocial and food assistance to affected populations. The importance of rehabilitating the
Troncal 007 highway and strengthening support for host families to sustain temporary
accommodation solutions was highlighted.
 Work continues with municipal governments and Child Protection Councils to implement
standardized mechanisms for the registration and monitoring of needs at the municipal level.
Humanitarian coordination
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
continues to coordinate the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner
organizations, prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, water, sanitation and hygiene,
logistics and protection.
 As of 18 July, Venezuelan authorities had received 104 international contributions from 40 countries
and organizations, amounting to approximately 3,672 metric tons of humanitarian assistance. The
assistance primarily includes medical and health supplies (340 mt), food (236 mt), water, sanitation
and hygiene (123 mt), shelter and equipment (138 mt), as well as mixed assistance (2,835 mt) to
support response and recovery efforts in affected communities.
 IOM continues to implement a multisectoral response in La Guaira, Falcón and Carabobo, with a
focus on shelter, health, protection, WASH and information management, reaching 8,210 people
through 14,959 service deliveries. The organization manages five transitional camps in La Guaira
and continues strengthening essential services for displaced populations. In coordination with
UNHCR, IOM co-leads the Infrastructure and Temporary Shelter Working Group, supporting
operational planning and information management. It also maintains protection mechanisms, legal
counselling and documentation support for affected people, alongside health services, psychosocial
support and infrastructure improvements at accommodation sites.
 UNHCR and its partner ODISEF continued strengthening coordination with authorities, camp
managers and humanitarian actors, including IOM and the Venezuela Renace programme. During
the reporting period, inter-agency coordination mechanisms, community outreach activities and
meetings with community leaders were promoted to disseminate information on protection services,
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
strengthen communication channels and facilitate affected populations’ access to available
assistance.
 UNESCO activated an institutional technical contingency plan focused on heritage protection and
continuity of education. In the area of cultural heritage, UNESCO assessed the Foro Libertador and
endorsed the preventive transfer of 287 historical volumes registered under the Memory of the World
Programme to the vaults of the Central Bank of Venezuela.
 Wayuu Taya Foundation, in coordination with CORE, Acceso, Direct Relief, Food For The Poor,
Good Neighbors International and World Central Kitchen, supported affected communities in
Caracas, La Guaira, Carabobo and Aragua through the distribution of food, safe drinking water,
hygiene kits, medicines and essential relief items for affected and displaced families. The foundation
also supported search and rescue efforts, debris removal, cleaning activities, and the rehabilitation
of community spaces in the areas most severely impacted by the earthquakes.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
through the United Nations system, with support from UNDP. In line with the internationally
recognized PDNA methodology, coordination with relevant institutions and counterparts will continue
in the coming period.
 In addition, UNDP provided technical assistance to national institutions on the use of drones, artificial
intelligence and geospatial technologies for post-earthquake recovery and reconstruction planning,
with the aim of strengthening debris management and supporting evidence-based decision-making.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 Since the onset of the emergency, WFP has reached 108,753 people with food assistance. On 21
July, WFP continued its emergency response, reaching 3,876 people through the distribution of 140
family food baskets in El Junquito (Distrito Capital) and 829 family food baskets in Caruao (La
Guaira), covering household food needs for one month. Families living in precarious conditions
without access to cooking facilities received 2,500 ready-to-eat food kits in Carlos Soublette (La
Guaira). In addition, WFP and its partners served 4,420 hot meals in temporary shelters across La
Guaira
 Catholic Relief Services (CRS), in coordination with Cáritas Venezuela, distributed more than 1,800
emergency food kits in the areas most affected by the earthquakes in La Guaira and Caracas. In
addition, Cáritas reached nearly 18,000 people through the distribution of 8,000 food kits as part of
the earthquake response.
Education and Early Childhood Development
 UNICEF initiated early childhood development (ECD) activities in transitional camps, closely
integrated with child protection interventions. These activities reached an initial group of 82 children
under five years of age, including 42 girls, as well as seven pregnant and breastfeeding women.
 UNICEF provided guidance to families on nurturing care and child development practices, reaching
a total of 66 caregivers. These interventions aim to support the well-being, development and
resilience of young children affected by the earthquake and living in displacement settings.
 Construyendo Futuros distributed school kits, toys and recreational materials, while strengthening
the capacities of teachers, volunteers and education personnel through training on safeguarding and
the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), contributing to safer environments for
children and adolescents.
Health
 PAHO/WHO continues coordinating the Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) response. As of 21 July,
14 EMTs are deployed and operational, seven have been demobilized and one is in the process of
deployment, with operations primarily concentrated in La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda and Aragua.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
Cumulative clinical activities reported by EMTs include 21,666 consultations, 402 surgeries, 475
hospital admissions and 1,363 inpatient bed-days, highlighting their critical role in maintaining health
services for affected populations.
 PAHO/WHO conducted a practical training on Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) for 50 nursing
professionals from La Guaira, the Capital District and Miranda, strengthening emergency response
capacities within the Ministry of People’s Power for Health (MPPH).
 PAHO/WHO, together with the National Mental Health Directorate of the Ministry of People’s Power
for Health (MPPH), developed operational protocols for mental health service points and mental
health specialists working in transitional camps.
 PAHO/WHO continues supporting the Ministry of People’s Power for Health (MPPH) in the active
surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases in camps and affected communities, as well as in the
reorganization of vaccination brigades in La Guaira. In addition, PAHO/WHO and the MPPH trained
81 vaccinators from ASICs 507, 508 and 509 to strengthen immunization and epidemiological
surveillance capacities.
 IOM continues expanding access to health services for earthquake-affected populations through the
deployment of medical teams and the provision of primary health care, both directly and through its
partner Ven Da Tu Mano. To date, 5,552 medical consultations have been provided, including
general medicine, internal medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology and obstetrics consultations,
medicine distribution and individual psychological support.
 In the César Nieves transitional camp, UNFPA’s partner Ven Da Tu Mano (VDTM) reached 590
people through sexual and reproductive health (SRH) awareness-raising activities. In addition, six
pregnant women received antenatal care, 77 contraceptive methods were distributed, along with 364
condoms, 225 information materials and five hygiene kits.
 UNICEF has significantly expanded access to essential health services in earthquake-affected
communities through the provision of medical supplies, deployment of mobile health teams and
support to national health authorities. In coordination with health partners, UNICEF supported the
deployment of medical and immunization teams to transitional camps and affected communities in
La Guaira.
 UNICEF supported mobile health teams reached 2,108 people with essential primary healthcare
services, while vaccination campaigns reached 6,466 people.
 UNICEF distributed essential health supplies and medicines sufficient to support the provision of
healthcare services for approximately 49,000 people in affected areas.
 International Medical Corps (IMC) maintains a comprehensive health response in La Guaira through
a Type 1 Emergency Medical Team (EMT) and three Mobile Medical Units operating in affected
camps and communities. Since the beginning of operations, IMC has provided 2,960 medical
consultations, including 971 through its EMT and 1,989 through mobile teams deployed in César
Nieves, La Lucha, Las Salinas, Mamo II, Playa Grande, Playa Verde, Puerto Viejo and Punta de
Mulatos. Services include treatment of acute and chronic conditions, maternal and child health care,
injury management and provision of essential medicines.
 IMC also continues providing Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services, including
psychological first aid, safe spaces and referrals for specialized care. Since 3 July, 133 MHPSS
consultations have been conducted, responding to growing psychosocial needs among affected
populations, particularly children and people with pre-existing mental health conditions.
 Project HOPE reported 45 medical consultations and 91 medicine dispensations in Mare Abajo II. In
addition, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) continued providing health services to earthquake-
affected populations.
 Following the activation of a registry to identify people living with HIV affected by the earthquakes
and requiring access to treatment, UNAIDS, in coordination with the National HIV/AIDS, STI and
Hepatitis Programme of the MPPH, the Venezuelan Network of Positive People (RVG+) and Acción
Solidaria, has supported continuity of care through the provision of antiretroviral treatment, referrals
to health services and linkage of newly diagnosed individuals to treatment.
 PALUZ provided primary and emergency health care to more than 5,000 people through mobile
medical teams deployed in shelters and affected communities, complemented by WASH
interventions, hygiene kit distributions and needs assessments. Planned activities include expanding
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
health, mental health and psychosocial support services, as well as WASH interventions for affected
and displaced populations.
 AVESSOC, in partnership with IRC and DKH, initiated activities to provide healthcare services to
earthquake-affected populations in La Guaira and Miranda states, reaching a total of 895
consultations. To support these efforts, mobile health outreach services were deployed to deliver
primary healthcare, essential medicines and mental health support to communities in Catia La Mar,
Tanaguarena, Los Corales, Caraballeda and Guarenas. Continuous field data collection and
coordination with local partners and community leaders are being carried out to facilitate these
deployments.
 In addition, in coordination with San José de Maiquetía Hospital and the Spanish Red Cross,
AVESSOC established a service point near Padre Machado Square in Maiquetía, providing primary
healthcare, follow-up care for non-communicable diseases, services for pregnant women and
infants, and mental health and psychosocial support. Through this initiative, more than 3,000
consultations have been delivered.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 Today, WFP, through the Logistics Working Group (LWG), facilitated the transportation of 15 metric
tons (MT) of relief supplies for the Shelter and Housing sectors, contributing to the strengthening of
humanitarian response efforts in affected areas.
 As part of international humanitarian cargo movements, a flight carrying 41 MT of humanitarian
assistance from Global Empowerment Mission (GEM) arrived at Simón Bolívar International Airport
in Maiquetía. The cargo included Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) supplies and food
assistance to support earthquake-affected populations.
 The LWG, in coordination with Hulo, convened a meeting with at least 15 humanitarian organizations
to identify operational needs and coordination mechanisms for the transport of humanitarian
assistance from Colombia to Venezuela. Participating organizations expressed interest in
establishing coordinated channels to facilitate the movement of relief supplies into the country.
 Authorities from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs report that information for humanitarian organizations
and cooperation actors is available through the platform www.venezuelanoestasola.com regarding
procedures for the arrival of aircraft and vessels carrying humanitarian assistance, as well as
guidance on the registration of routes, means of transport, crew members and cargo.
 For inquiries related to these procedures, interested organizations may contact the Logistics Working
Group directly at: ven.coordinacionlogistica@wfp.org.
. Nutrition
 UNICEF continued to support the nutritional needs of vulnerable children and women affected by
the earthquakes. A total of 2,452 children under five years of age and 616 pregnant and lactating
women among displaced populations received a package of essential nutrition services, including
nutritional screening, micronutrient supplementation, counselling and referral to specialized services
when required.
 Approximately 1,300 caregivers of children under two years of age received counselling on
recommended infant and young child feeding practices, including breastfeeding support and age-
appropriate complementary feeding. Overall, 72,000 children and women were reached with
micronutrient supplementation.
 UNICEF also supported community outreach activities implemented by the National Institute of
Nutrition (INN), the Ministry of Health and partner organizations in affected communities. In
coordination with WFP, UNICEF promoted age-appropriate feeding practices for young children
within the food assistance response and facilitated a technical exchange between national
authorities and the Brazilian Human Milk Bank Network on quality assurance and safe management
of human milk in emergency settings.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 As of 21 July, UNHCR and its implementing partners have provided 4,372 instances of assistance
in the Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande and Mare Abajo
transitional camps through protection activities, legal assistance, case management, counselling,
psychosocial support, information desks and referrals to specialized services. During the reporting
period, 1,207 people were reached through protection interventions, while 96 children and their
families received legal guidance on birth registration, identity documentation and legal
representation. In addition, 72 children participated in psychosocial, recreational and socio-
emotional support activities to strengthen coping mechanisms following the earthquakes.
 UNHCR and its implementing partners also strengthened access to rights and services through
information desks, counselling and community sessions that reached 1,226 people, promoting
awareness of referral pathways, protection mechanisms, Accountability to Affected Populations
(AAP) and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). In addition, two people received
specialized support through gender-based violence (GBV) case management services.
 In Playa Grande, UNHCR and its implementing partner ODISEF held a coordination meeting with
the Ombudsperson’s Office to present available protection services and strengthen institutional
coordination in support of affected populations.
 UNICEF continues to strengthen child protection services through psychosocial support,
identification of vulnerable children, case management and referral services delivered through Child-
Friendly Spaces and mobile child protection teams in affected areas.
 Across four transitional camps in La Guaira, four Child-Friendly Spaces remained operational,
reaching 2,726 children, adolescents and caregivers with psychosocial support, structured
recreational activities and protective services.
 To further strengthen the child protection response following the earthquake emergency, UNICEF
supplied key equipment and resources to local child protection teams in La Guaira, enhancing their
capacity to provide timely and quality services to affected children and families.
 As of 21 July, UNFPA-led gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response activities,
implemented through AVESA and Tinta Violeta, reached 1,076 people through awareness-raising
activities in the Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande and Mare
Abajo transitional camps. In addition, 77 dignity kits were distributed, 93 people received
psychosocial support and psychological first aid, 21 cases were managed and two people received
specialized legal assistance.
 IOM continues facilitating access to protection services in the Polideportivo José María Vargas
transitional camp through information, legal assistance and documentation support. To date, 130
people have received specialized assistance and accompaniment.
 Construyendo Futuros continues providing psychosocial support, protection services and Child-
Friendly Spaces in more than 11 transitional camps across La Guaira, the Capital District and
Miranda, supporting children, adolescents and their families through recreational activities and
emotional well-being initiatives.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 IOM continues to support the management of the five transitional camps co-managed with local
authorities (José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium, Playa Grande, Golf Course
and Mare Abajo), promoting site improvements, strengthening coordination with authorities,
humanitarian partners and cooperation actors, and supporting registration processes. To date, IOM
and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed 3,092 kitchen sets, 3,024 plastic
tarpaulins, 2,039 buckets, 1,675 solar lamps, 819 shelter kits, 672 mosquito nets and 208
rechargeable solar flashlights.
 UNHCR and its implementing partners continued to strengthen protection and shelter conditions
through the distribution of 547 solar lamp and mosquito net kits benefiting 1,495 people, the provision
of 200 solar flashlights, the installation of 120 floodlights and solar lamps in community areas,
sanitation facilities and overnight accommodation areas, as well as the deployment of 12 temporary
modular shelter units in the César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
 CRS supported the response through the distribution of more than 1,600 tarpaulins for temporary
shelter, helping address the shelter needs of families whose homes were damaged or destroyed.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 UNICEF continued to support access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services in displacement
settings and affected communities. The organization maintained the operation of 24 emergency
latrines, 13 laundry points and 27 handwashing stations, supported through regular water trucking
operations providing approximately 20,000 litres of water per day. Solid waste management, routine
cleaning of sanitation facilities and replenishment of hygiene and cleaning supplies continue to be
sustained.
 More than 4,400 people received hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available
life-saving services. UNICEF distributed family hygiene kits reaching 7,180 people and conducted
hygiene promotion and handwashing awareness activities that reached more than 500 people during
the reporting period, contributing to safer practices and improved living conditions among displaced
populations.
 In parallel, UNICEF strengthened coordination with the Ministry of Water (MINAGUAS), HIDROVEN
and local water utilities, conducting technical assessments of critical water treatment, transmission
and distribution infrastructure affected by the earthquake.
 IOM continues strengthening access to essential items for safe water storage and hygiene practices
among affected communities. To date, 1,552 collapsible 10-litre jerrycans, 1,009 hygiene kits and
92 semi-collapsible 10-litre jerrycans have been distributed.
 International Medical Corps (IMC) strengthened the WASH response through assessments in five
displacement sites and the provision of 30,000 litres of safe water, benefiting approximately 2,400
people. IMC also continues implementing hygiene promotion and infection prevention and control
measures in its health facilities, while preparing to expand WASH assistance to additional
displacement sites with critical needs for safe water, sanitation and hygiene services.
 Action Against Hunger (ACH) distributed 30,000 litres of water and maintained sanitation services in
Mare Abajo II, benefiting 125 households in the camp and surrounding communities. In addition,
humanitarian actors and authorities held a technical coordination meeting to address water supply,
sanitation, waste management and water quality actions.
 Catholic Relief Services (CRS) and Cáritas Venezuela distributed 850 family hygiene kits, 400 baby
hygiene kits and more than 120,000 litres of safe drinking water, strengthening access to basic
services for earthquake-affected families.
Humanitarian financing and contributions
 The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced an additional appeal under the
Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela. The appeal outlines the multisectoral needs of 1.3
million people over the next six months. To reach those in need, US$299 million is required, in
addition to the US$632 million requested at the beginning of the year.
 Several United Nations agencies, funds and programmes have issued emergency appeals to scale
up humanitarian assistance and support the response and recovery efforts following the
earthquakes, in line with the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Addendum.
 UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to fund its earthquake emergency response. The aim is to assist
470,000 people, including 160,000 children and adolescents, through water, sanitation and hygiene
(WASH), health, nutrition, child protection and education interventions in the most affected areas
over the coming months. IOM requires US$98 million to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities over
the next six months. PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support
the health response and early recovery efforts over the next six months and allocated US$1.5 million
from its Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP issued an initial appeal for US$80 million to
provide food assistance to 500,000 people over a six-month period. UNHCR, for its part, indicated
that it requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 9
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 Canada increased its matching contribution for donations supporting the earthquake response in
Venezuela from CAD 4 million to CAD 7 million, bringing its total support for the emergency to CAD
12 million. The funding, channelled through the Canadian Red Cross and the Humanitarian Coalition,
will support the provision of health, shelter and WASH services for affected populations.
 The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria approved an emergency funding package
of US$1.77 million to support HIV and tuberculosis services in Venezuela following the earthquakes.
The resources, to be managed through UNDP, will enable 7,000 people to continue HIV treatment,
ensure tuberculosis treatment for 500 people, and support prevention, testing and outreach services
for 1,500 members of key populations in the most affected areas.
 The European Union announced an additional contribution of €20 million to support humanitarian
action in the country. Of this amount, €10 million will support search and rescue operations, medical
assistance, the deployment of additional experts, and material assistance in the country. This
contribution comes in addition to the €5 million previously announced for the earthquake response
and the €52 million already allocated to humanitarian operations in Venezuela this year.
 In addition, under the European Union Humanitarian Air Bridge launched in June, three EU-funded
flights have already arrived in the country. The latest flight landed on 17 July carrying 48 metric
tonnes of medical supplies and shelter items.
 The Government of Italy allocated US$5.7 million to support the humanitarian response to the
earthquakes, helping deliver life-saving assistance, protection and access to essential services for
affected populations through AICS, WFP and IFRC.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country.
 The Republic of Korea announced an additional contribution of US$3.5 million in humanitarian
assistance. Of this amount, US$3 million will be channelled through UNDP to support debris removal
activities, while the remainder will be provided in-kind, specifically through 30 metric tons of
temporary shelters (family tents). The Republic of Korea had previously allocated US$1.25 million to
WFP and US$2.5 million to UNICEF in support of the humanitarian response in Venezuela.
 Japan allocated US$3.5 million to support the earthquake response. The funding will provide
humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and non-food
items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
and IOM.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden contributed SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.

documents.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 28**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**21 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Las autoridades reportan 1.405 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio.
- Balance oficial: **5.346 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para  
     atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.405 réplicas.**

A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.346 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.**

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.** Esta adenda complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.

Humanitaria 2026 por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3
millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses. Esta adenda
complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones
a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.
Impacto en infraestructura
 Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.
 Como parte de la planificación para la recuperación y reconstrucción, las autoridades identificaron
40 terrenos en el estado La Guaira, equivalentes a aproximadamente 584.000 metros cuadrados,
para el desarrollo de proyectos habitacionales destinados a la población afectada.
 Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de
Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil
millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas,

Respuesta nacional
 La respuesta gubernamental se mantiene centrada en la atención de las personas afectadas, así
como la instalación y manejo de los campamentos transitorios.
 De acuerdo con las autoridades, la respuesta continúa con 107 campamentos transitorios
habilitados para la atención de personas afectadas, con una capacidad instalada de 27.950
personas y una ocupación de 23.122 personas. Hasta el 21 de julio, 41 campamentos se encuentran
instalados en Caracas, 28 en La Guaira, 28 en Miranda y 10 en Aragua. Del total de población
alojada, 12.123 personas se encuentran en La Guaira, 8.508 en Caracas, 1.816 en Miranda y
675 en Aragua.
 Las autoridades de salud anunciaron el inicio de un proceso de fumigación y control sanitario en el
estado La Guaira, especialmente en las parroquias Caraballeda, La Guaira y Macuto.
 Este lunes 20 de julio, las autoridades anunciaron la entrega de viviendas equipadas a unas
primeras 240 familias afectadas por los terremotos. Las viviendas se encuentran en Fuerte Tiuna,
Caracas, y son parte del plan Venezuela Renace.
 Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad

 Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas
(www.localizapacientes.com).
 Las actividades escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados
Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José
Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas);
Distrito Capital (Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo,
Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).

sin acceso a instalaciones para cocinar recibieron kits de alimentos listos para consumir en Carlos

en campamentos transitorios de La Guaira.
