 Zulia: Se estima la atención de 45 familias que han llegado a hogares de familiares en el estado.
La población desplazada se ubica principalmente en Maracaibo y municipios fronterizos, mientras
que algunas continúan en tránsito hacia Táchira y Colombia desde el terminal de pasajeros. Entre
las prioridades identificadas, las organizaciones del Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC), incluyendo
ASONACOP, Cruz Roja Venezolana, HIAS, CESVI, ASOREZ, Cáritas y Aliadas en Cadena, han
brindado apoyo psicosocial, atención médica primaria, servicios de protección, distribución de
agua, alimentos y kits de higiene. La Gerencia de Atención al Ciudadano, los Consejos de
Protección y las autoridades de gestión de riesgos mantienen acciones de atención, monitoreo e
inspección preventiva en Maracaibo. Se mantiene la coordinación interinstitucional a través del FLC
y la suboficina de OCHA en Maracaibo.
Coordinación humanitaria
 OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales,
continúa coordinando la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y las organizaciones
socias, priorizando acciones en salud, alojamiento, alimentación, agua, saneamiento e higiene,
logística y protección.
 Hasta el 18 de julio, las autoridades venezolanas han recibido 104 aportes internacionales de 40
países y organizaciones, que suman aproximadamente 3.672 toneladas de ayuda humanitaria. La
asistencia incluye principalmente insumos médicos y de salud (340 t), alimentos (236 t), agua,
saneamiento e higiene (123 t), refugio y equipamiento (138 t), además de ayuda mixta (2.835 t) para
apoyar la respuesta y recuperación de las comunidades afectadas.
 OIM mantiene una respuesta multisectorial en La Guaira, Falcón y Carabobo, con énfasis en
alojamiento, salud, protección, WASH y gestión de información, alcanzando a 8.210 personas
mediante 14.959 asistencias. Gestiona cinco (5) campamentos transitorios en La Guaira y fortalece
los servicios esenciales para la población desplazada. En coordinación con el ACNUR, colidera el
Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales, apoyando la planificación operativa
y la gestión de información. Asimismo, mantiene mecanismos de protección, orientación legal y
apoyo para la documentación de personas afectadas, junto con acciones de salud, apoyo
psicosocial y mejora de infraestructura en los sitios de alojamiento.
 ACNUR y su socio ODISEF continuaron fortaleciendo la coordinación con autoridades, gestores de
campamentos y actores humanitarios, incluyendo OIM y el programa Venezuela Renace. Durante
el período se promovieron mecanismos de coordinación interagencial, actividades de alcance
comunitario y reuniones con líderes comunitarios para difundir servicios de protección, fortalecer
canales de comunicación y facilitar el acceso de la población afectada a la asistencia disponible.
 La UNESCO activó un plan técnico de contingencia institucional enfocado en la protección del
patrimonio y la continuidad educativa. En patrimonio, evaluó el Foro Libertador y avaló el traslado
preventivo de 287 tomos históricos del programa Memoria del Mundo a las bóvedas del Banco
Central de Venezuela.
 Las autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades
Posteriores al Desastre (PDNA, por sus siglas en inglés) a través del Sistema de las Naciones
Unidas y con el acompañamiento del Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo (PNUD).
De conformidad con la metodología internacional de la PDNA, se avanzará en las coordinaciones
correspondientes con las instituciones y contrapartes relevantes.
 Adicionalmente, el PNUD brindó asistencia técnica a instituciones nacionales para la incorporación
de drones, inteligencia artificial y tecnologías geoespaciales en la planificación de la recuperación y
reconstrucción posterior a los terremotos, con el fin de fortalecer la gestión de residuos y apoyar la
toma de decisiones basada en evidencia.
Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria
Seguridad Alimentaria
 Desde el inicio de la emergencia, el PMA ha alcanzado a 96.865 personas con asistencia
alimentaria. Durante la jornada, el PMA apoyó a 3.540 personas mediante una intervención basada
en mercados en Naiguatá, a través de vales electrónicos prepagados que permiten a las familias
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
cubrir necesidades prioritarias y contribuir a la reactivación de la economía local. Asimismo, el PMA
y sus socios distribuyeron 4.913 comidas calientes en campamentos transitorios de La Guaira.
Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene
 Desde el inicio de la respuesta, UNICEF y sus socios implementadores han fortalecido el acceso a
agua segura, saneamiento e higiene en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo José María
Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande. Las intervenciones incluyeron el suministro de
36.000 litros de agua potable, la operación y mantenimiento de tanques de almacenamiento,
duchas, baños, puntos de lavado de manos y estaciones de lavado de ropa, así como la limpieza y
desinfección de instalaciones sanitarias. Asimismo, se realizaron actividades de gestión de residuos
que permitieron la recolección de aproximadamente 68,5 m³ de desechos sólidos. Las acciones de
promoción de higiene alcanzaron al menos a 770 personas mediante actividades de sensibilización
sobre lavado de manos, uso adecuado del agua, higiene y manejo seguro de desechos.
 La OIM ha fortalecido el acceso a artículos esenciales para almacenamiento y manejo seguro de
agua e higiene. A la fecha, se han distribuido 1.471 bidones plegables de 10 litros, 928 kits de
higiene y 92 bidones semiplegables de 10 litros.
Alojamiento, Energía y Enseres
 La OIM continúa la gestión y coordinación de los cinco campamentos transitorios cogestionados
con las autoridades locales (Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande,
Campo de Golf y Mare Abajo), impulsando mejoras en los sitios y fortaleciendo la coordinación con
autoridades, socios humanitarios y actores de cooperación, así como registro en los campamentos.
Asimismo, avanza el proceso de transición hacia NRC como socio implementador de 3 de los
campamentos.
 A la fecha, OIM ha distribuido directamente y con el socio Fundación Vivienda Popular, 3.022 sets
de cocina, 3.024 lonas plásticas, 2.024 tobos, 1.622 lámparas solares, 819 kits de refugio, 592
mosquiteros y 193 linternas solares recargables.
 ACNUR y sus socios fortalecieron las condiciones de alojamiento y protección en los campamentos
mediante la distribución de 547 kits de lámparas solares y mosquiteros, beneficiando a 1.495
personas, así como la entrega de 200 linternas solares a familias afectadas. Adicionalmente, se
instalaron 12 unidades modulares temporales y se donaron equipos de iluminación para apoyar la
gestión de los sitios y mejorar las condiciones de vida de las personas afectadas.
 Para mejorar la seguridad y reducir riesgos de protección en los espacios de alojamiento temporal,
ACNUR y sus socios instalaron un total de 120 reflectores y lámparas solares en baños, áreas
comunes y zonas de pernocta de los cuatro campamentos. Estas acciones contribuyen a mejorar
la movilidad y la seguridad de las personas afectadas, especialmente mujeres, niñas, niños y otros
grupos con necesidades específicas de protección.
 Global Empowerment Mission (GEM) continúa apoyando la respuesta a los terremotos mediante
la distribución de más de 681 toneladas de asistencia humanitaria en las zonas afectadas. A la
fecha, ha entregado 37.675 kits familiares, 46.554 kits de higiene, 2.707 tiendas de campaña y
lonas para familias con viviendas dañadas o destruidas, así como 60 generadores eléctricos para
fortalecer la continuidad de servicios esenciales y las capacidades de respuesta en las
comunidades afectadas.
Logística y Telecomunicaciones
 Desde el Grupo de Trabajo de Logística, liderado por el PMA, se ha registrado, al 20 de julio, la
llegada de 806 TM de ayuda humanitaria recibidas a través de 27 vuelos, para 11 organizaciones
que están apoyando la respuesta al terremoto.
 Las autoridades del Ministerio del Poder Popular para Relaciones Exteriores (MPPRE) informan
que, a través de la plataforma www.venezuelanoestasola.com, se encuentra disponible información
para organizaciones humanitarias y actores de cooperación sobre los procedimientos para la
llegada de aeronaves y embarcaciones con asistencia humanitaria, así como orientaciones para el
registro de rutas, medios de transporte, tripulación y carga.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
 Igualmente, desde el Grupo de Trabajo de Logística, en coordinación con OCHA, se está tomando
el registro de la llegada aérea y marítima de carga humanitaria, con la finalidad de notificar a las
autoridades. Los detalles se encuentran disponibles en la web del GTL.
 Para consultas relacionadas con estos procedimientos, las organizaciones interesadas pueden
dirigirse directamente al Grupo de Trabajo de Logística a través del correo electrónico:
ven.coordinacionlogistica@wfp.org.
 Desde Telecomunicaciones se realizó la instalación de paneles solares en el campamento
transitorio estadio César Nieves, para mantener la infraestructura de comunicaciones funcional y
reducir los riesgos asociados con la inconsistencia del servicio eléctrico en la locación.
Nutrición
 Los socios humanitarios continúan apoyando intervenciones nutricionales dirigidas a grupos
prioritarios, incluyendo niñas, niños, mujeres embarazadas y mujeres lactantes, mediante
actividades de tamizaje nutricional, consejería y seguimiento nutricional en campamentos
transitorios y comunidades afectadas.
Protección (incluidos Áreas de Responsabilidad de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes y Violencia
Basada en Género)
 Desde el inicio de la respuesta, ACNUR y sus socios, incluido ODISEF, han alcanzado a 4.240
personas en los campamentos transitorios de José María Vargas, César Nieves, Playa Grande y
Mare Abajo, incluidas 84 personas retornadas, mediante actividades de protección, asistencia
legal, gestión de casos, apoyo psicosocial, orientación y derivaciones. Además, 688 personas
recibieron información sobre derechos y acceso a servicios, mientras que 562 participaron en
sesiones informativas sobre protección, rutas de atención, rendición de cuentas a las poblaciones
afectadas (AAP) y prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual (PSEA). Asimismo, 96 niños,
niñas y adolescentes (NNA) y sus familias recibieron orientación legal sobre registro civil y
documentación, y 65 NNA participaron en actividades de apoyo psicosocial y acompañamiento
socioemocional. Las acciones también incluyeron gestión de casos de protección y VBG, así como
el fortalecimiento de mecanismos de coordinación y participación comunitaria en los campamentos.
 UNFPA continuó fortaleciendo la prevención y respuesta a la violencia basada en género en las
zonas afectadas, alcanzando a 1.081 personas mediante actividades de sensibilización. Asimismo,
distribuyó 77 kits de dignidad, brindó apoyo psicosocial y primeros auxilios psicológicos a 87
personas, gestionó 20 casos de protección y proporcionó una asesoría legal para personas
afectadas por la emergencia.
 UNICEF y su socio FUNDAINIL brindaron apoyo psicosocial y espacios seguros para NNA
afectados por la emergencia en los campamentos transitorios. A través de Espacios Amigables y
sesiones grupales de contención emocional, recreación dirigida y acompañamiento
socioemocional, se alcanzó a 141 NNA, fortaleciendo sus capacidades de afrontamiento y
bienestar emocional tras el impacto de los terremotos.
 La OIM sigue fortaleciendo el acceso a servicios de protección en los cinco campamentos
transitorios mediante orientación, asistencia legal y apoyo en documentación. A la fecha, 130
personas han sido atendidas.
Salud
 OPS/OMS coordina la respuesta de Equipos Médicos de Emergencia (EMT). Al 19 de julio registra
16 EMT desplegados y operativos, 5 desmovilizados y 1 en proceso de movilización, con presencia
principalmente en La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda y Aragua. La actividad clínica acumulada reporta
17.357 consultas, 249 cirugías, 447 ingresos y 1.115 días cama ocupados, lo que evidencia el rol
crítico de los EMT en la continuidad de la atención sanitaria para la población afectada.
 OPS/OMS también continúa apoyando la respuesta en La Guaira. El 19 de julio entregó 470 kits
de higiene personal al personal de salud de la Autoridad Única de Salud. Este 20 de julio distribuyó
en los campamentos transitorios César Nieves, Los Caracas, Polideportivo José María Vargas y
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
Universidad Marítima un módulo IEHK REF 1.3 de medicamentos e insumos renovables y un
módulo IEHK REF 1.1 de equipamiento médico para fortalecer la atención de salud.
 La OIM continúa apoyando la respuesta al terremoto mediante el despliegue de equipos médicos
y la prestación de servicios de atención primaria, directamente y a través de su socio Ven Da Tu
Mano. A la fecha, se han realizado 5.451 atenciones médicas, incluyendo consultas de medicina
general, medicina interna, pediatría, ginecología y obstetricia, así como entrega de medicamentos
y apoyo psicológico individual.
 Desde el inicio de la respuesta, UNFPA ha alcanzado a 1.961 personas mediante actividades de
sensibilización en salud sexual y reproductiva. Se distribuyeron condones a 1.137 personas, 726
materiales educomunicativos y 12 kits de higiene. Asimismo, 115 mujeres embarazadas recibieron
atención prenatal, se proporcionaron 877 métodos anticonceptivos modernos y se realizaron 82
pruebas de VIH y 81 pruebas de sífilis.
 En coordinación con el Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud, UNICEF apoyó acciones de
vacunación dirigidas a la población afectada por los terremotos. Hasta la fecha, se han aplicado 27
vacunas en el campamento Polideportivo José María Vargas para contribuir a la prevención de
enfermedades y la protección de la salud de las comunidades afectadas.
Financiamiento humanitario y contribuciones
(actualizado al 17 de julio)
 El jefe humanitario de Naciones Unidas, Tom Fletcher, anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta
Humanitaria (PRH) para Venezuela. Este llamado contempla las necesidades multisectoriales de
1,3 millones de personas por los próximos seis meses. Para alcanzar a estas personas, se necesitan
299 millones de dólares, que se suman a los 632 millones de dólares solicitados al inicio del año.
 Varias agencias, fondos y programas de las Naciones Unidas han emitido llamamientos de
emergencia para ampliar la asistencia humanitaria y apoyar la respuesta y recuperación tras los
terremotos, en línea con la adenda del PRH presentada.
 UNICEF requiere 65.7 millones de dólares para financiar su respuesta de emergencia ante el
terremoto. La meta es atender a 470.000 personas (incluidos 160.000 niños, niñas y adolescentes)
mediante intervenciones de agua, saneamiento e higiene, salud, nutrición, protección infantil y
educación en las zonas más afectadas durante los próximos meses. OIM requirió 98 millones de
dólares para asistir a 850.000 personas y 140 entidades durante los próximos seis meses.
OPS/OMS lanzó un llamamiento de emergencia por casi 24 millones de dólares para apoyar la
respuesta en salud y la recuperación temprana durante los próximos seis meses, además de asignar
1,5 millones de dólares del Fondo de Contingencia para Emergencias. El PMA presentó una
solicitud inicial de 80 millones de dólares para brindar asistencia alimentaria a 500.000 personas
durante seis meses. Por su parte, ACNUR indicó que requiere 14,8 millones de dólares para apoyar
a hasta 30.000 personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses.
 Connecting Business Initiative (CBi) fue invitado por Empresas Polar a acompañar su operación de
donación y distribución de agua para las poblaciones afectadas por los terremotos, en el marco de
las contribuciones del sector privado a la respuesta en emergencia. Empresas Polar expuso sus
esfuerzos, que incluyen entregas y envíos regulares de agua a escuelas, centros de salud, refugios,
organizaciones y centros de recolección verificados. La operación implica un importante apoyo
logístico, que incluye almacenamiento, paletización, transporte en camiones de gran tonelaje,
operaciones con montacargas y la participación de voluntarios para la carga y la distribución. Las
contribuciones son monitoreadas para garantizar que la ayuda llegue a los actores humanitarios y
a las personas afectadas.
 Parte del apoyo brindado por UNDAC incluye una especialista en coordinación con el sector privado
para fortalecer la participación empresarial en la respuesta y recuperación. Se encuentra disponible
un rastreador de contribuciones del sector privado para la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela
(https://ven-eq.connectingbusiness.org) y una nota informativa dirigida al sector privado sobre
oportunidades de apoyo. Punto focal: sanchez21@un.org.
 Canadá aumentó de 4 millones a 7 millones de dólares canadienses su contribución de
contrapartida para donaciones destinadas a la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela, elevando
su apoyo para la emergencia a 12 millones de dólares canadienses. Los fondos, canalizados a
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
través de la Cruz Roja Canadiense y la Humanitarian Coalition, apoyarán la provisión de servicios
de salud, alojamiento y agua, saneamiento e higiene para las poblaciones afectadas.
 El Fondo Mundial de lucha contra el sida, la tuberculosis y la malaria aprobó un paquete de
financiamiento de emergencia por 1.77 millones de dólares para apoyar los servicios de VIH y
tuberculosis en Venezuela luego de los terremotos. Los recursos, que se gestionarán a través del
PNUD, permitirán que 7.000 personas continúen el tratamiento del VIH, se garantice el tratamiento
de la tuberculosis para 500 personas y se respalde los servicios de prevención, pruebas de
detección y divulgación para 1.500 miembros de poblaciones clave en las zonas más afectadas.
 La Unión Europea realizó una contribución adicional de 20 millones de euros para apoyar la acción
humanitaria en el país. De este total, 10 millones de euros estarán destinados a apoyar operaciones
de búsqueda y rescate, asistencia médica y el despliegue de otros expertos, así como asistencia
material, en el país. Estos recursos se suman a los 5 millones de euros previamente anunciados
para la respuesta a la emergencia y a los 52 millones de euros ya destinados a las operaciones
humanitarias en Venezuela este año.
 Además, como parte del puente aéreo humanitario de la Unión Europea, puesto en marcha en junio,
ya han llegado al país tres vuelos financiados por la UE. El más reciente aterrizó el 17 de julio con
48 toneladas de suministros médicos y artículos de alojamiento.
 El Gobierno de Italia asignó 5,7 millones de dólares para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria a los
terremotos y proporcionar asistencia vital, protección y acceso a servicios básicos para las
poblaciones afectadas, a través de la Agencia Italiana de Cooperación para el Desarrollo (AICS), el
Programa Mundial de Alimentos (PMA) y la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja
y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC).
 El Fondo Central de Respuesta a Emergencias (CERF, por sus siglas en inglés) realizó una
asignación de 15 millones de dólares para una respuesta multisectorial, junto con la activación del
Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV). Noruega realizó una contribución para apoyar la respuesta
a través del CERF.
 Estados Unidos anunció una contribución de 100 millones de dólares al FHV, y una asignación
adicional de 100 millones de dólares en contribuciones bilaterales para operaciones de respuesta
de OIM, PMA, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse,
Proyecto Esperanza y la Cruz Roja.
 Alemania y Corea realizaron contribuciones al FHV por 5 millones y 1,25 millones de dólares,
respectivamente, para apoyar la acción humanitaria en el país.
 Corea realizó una contribución adicional para brindar asistencia por un monto de 3,5 millones de
dólares. 3 millones de dólares serán canalizados a través del PNUD para apoyar las labores de
remoción de escombros y el resto se proporcionará en insumos, específicamente, 30 toneladas de
alojamientos temporales (tiendas de campaña familiares). Corea ya había asignado 1,25 millones
de dólares al PMA y 2,5 millones de dólares a UNICEF para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en
Venezuela.
 Japón asignó 3,5 millones de dólares para apoyar la respuesta a los terremotos. Los fondos
permitirán brindar asistencia humanitaria en sectores clave, incluidos seguridad alimentaria, salud
y atención médica, alojamiento y artículos no alimentarios, a través del PMA, la Federación
Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (FICR) y la OIM.
 Australia informó de una contribución de 2 millones de dólares para la provisión de alimentos,
alojamiento, atención de salud y acceso a agua segura a través de IFRC y el PMA.
 Suiza anunció una contribución de 2,5 millones de francos suizos para apoyar la respuesta.
 Suecia asignó 25 millones de coronas suecas para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en el país,
mediante programas de asistencia alimentaria, agua, alojamiento temporal, protección y
reunificación familiar implementados por el PMA, ACNUR y Save the Children.
 Dinamarca anunció una contribución adicional de 11 millones de coronas danesas para apoyar la
respuesta humanitaria, incluyendo 10 millones de coronas danesas a través de ACNUR y 1 millón
de coronas danesas a través de DanChurchAid y la Cruz Roja Danesa.
 El Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) anunció una asignación inicial de 7,5 millones de libras
esterlinas para la respuesta al terremoto en Venezuela, incluyendo 2 millones de libras esterlinas
aportados por el Gobierno del Reino Unido mediante UK Aid Match. Los recursos serán
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 9
implementados por organizaciones miembros del DEC y sus socios locales para apoyar la respuesta
humanitaria.
 OCHA continúa coordinando con donantes y socios para asegurar una asignación rápida,
estratégica y basada en necesidades.
Apoya la respuesta humanitaria para atender el terremoto en Venezuela
Haz tu donación de forma segura y rápida ahora:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
Información de Contacto
Para mayor información, por favor contactar a la Oficina de OCHA Venezuela:
Vanessa May – Jefa de Oficina a.i. - mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Oficial de Asuntos Humanitarios - alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Oficial de Información Pública – moreno7@un.org
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

documents.title: WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies - Mid-Year Update | July 2026
documents.body_text:
## **Overview**

In the first half of 2026, the CFE continued to enable WHO to respond rapidly to health emergencies worldwide. WHO released more than US$ 10 million from the CFE to address the health consequences of 12 emergencies, including five disease outbreaks, three complex crises, and four natural disasters.

As a key source of WHO’s flexible, early financing for emergencies, the CFE ensures that life-saving operations can begin immediately, often before other donor funding is mobilized. Twelve Member States and the UN Foundation have pledged or contributed more than US$ 17 million to the CFE so far this year.

The Fund’s balance, however, remains critically low. Continued support is needed to ensure WHO can act first and fast when new health emergencies strike.

Typhoon Sinlaku: Delivering emergency health services to remote communities
CFE funding has enabled WHO to sustain life-saving health operations
in the aftermath of Typhoon Sinlaku in Chuuk State, Federated States of
Micronesia, particularly in hard-to-reach outer islands. Typhoon Sinlaku
struck Chuuk State between 9 and 12 April 2026, severely disrupting
health services across geographically dispersed communities. As the
scale of damage and access constraints became clearer, WHO used
a mid-May CFE allocation of US$ 150 000 to deliver essential health
services where needs persisted. The funding has supported follow-up
care for patients with noncommunicable diseases, who face heightened
risks because services remain disrupted and access is limited. It has also
helped WHO maintain operational continuity in a resource-constrained
setting where alternative financing has been exhausted, enabling teams
© WHO / A. Johannes
to reach remote populations despite high logistical costs.
For more information:
https://www.who.int/cfe Follow us on: Facebook Twitter

CFE MID-YEAR UPDATE | JULY 2026 | 2
Democratic Republic of the Congo: Containing the Ebola outbreak
© WHO / Natalie Ridgard
When the WHO Director-General declared the Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic
Republic of the Congo and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 17 May
2026, the situation was evolving rapidly. The outbreak was growing and the disease had already crossed
borders, and there are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain causing the outbreak.
Within 48 hours, WHO released US$ 3.9 million from the CFE, providing the immediate financing needed to
launch and scale up response operations mainly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which continues to
account for the majority of cases and operational requirements.
In the first three weeks of the response, WHO activated its incident management system and deployed more
than 100 experts through its staff and global partner networks. Leveraging its global logistics hubs, WHO
delivered 75 metric tonnes of life-saving supplies, including personal protective equipment, diagnostics and
clinical equipment. Clinical management capacity expanded rapidly, with isolation and treatment centres
established for suspected and confirmed cases within days, reaching over 500 beds by the end of June.
At the same time, WHO strengthened other key response
pillars working with the Ministry of Health and partners,
including infection prevention and control, community
engagement, surveillance, and preparations for critical
therapeutic clinical trials. Readiness measures were
expanded in eight priority countries to help prevent
further spread.
The first few weeks showed why rapid, flexible financing
matters: by unlocking immediate action, the CFE helped
transform an emergency declaration into a full-scale
© WHO / Josua Mulala Raymond
response when every day counted.
For more information:
https://www.who.int/cfe Follow us on: Facebook Twitter

CFE MID-YEAR UPDATE | JULY 2026 | 3
Venezuela earthquakes: Early financing for a rapid health response
© PAHO / WHO
On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude struck north-central Venezuela
within seconds of each other, affecting millions of people and causing widespread damage to homes, hospitals
and critical infrastructure. Authorities declared a state of emergency as reports emerged of deaths, injuries
and disruptions to essential services across multiple affected states.
PAHO/WHO immediately began supporting national authorities through technical cooperation, health-sector
coordination and rapid assessments of health facilities and priority public health risks. Initial efforts focused on
understanding the impact on hospitals and health services, identifying urgent needs, supporting information
management and coordinating with health partners.
To sustain and expand these efforts, US$ 1.5 million was released from the CFE within 48 hours. The funding
is being used to support emergency coordination and surge capacity, strengthen logistics and the delivery
of essential medical supplies, assess and restore the functionality of health facilities, enhance surveillance
for potential disease threats, and support risk
communication, community engagement, water,
sanitation and hygiene activities in affected
communities.
Operating in a country already facing a
protracted humanitarian crisis, the response
aims to ensure continuity of essential health
services while preventing secondary health
emergencies in the aftermath of the disaster. The
CFE allocation demonstrates the value of rapid,
flexible financing: enabling PAHO/WHO to move
quickly from assessment and coordination to
sustained operational support when health needs
© PAHO / WHO
are greatest.
For more information:
https://www.who.int/cfe Follow us on: Facebook Twitter

documents.title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report #06, 19 July 2026
documents.body_text:
Situation Update  
 • Twenty-five days after the twin earthquakes of 24 June, authorities report 5,208 deaths and 16,740 injuries. Following search and rescue operations, national authorities have shifted the efforts toward relocating displaced populations to transitional camps.  
 • According to authorities, 107 transitional camps have been established, with 23,828 people currently accommodated. As part of the UN-coordinated response, WFP is supporting three camps with two hot meals daily.  
 • WFP Acting Executive Director Carl Skau spoke with Venezuela's Acting President, Delcy Rodríguez, and reaffirmed the organization's commitment to continuing its support to authorities and humanitarian partners in meeting immediate food needs and assisting affected families in their recovery.

Venezuela: Earthquakes
Global LTC (Telecoms) Teleconference #02
Date: 13 July 2026 Time: 14:00 UTC
More information: www.etcluster.org/emergency/venezuela-earthquakes
Contact: Venezuela.LTCTelecoms@wfp.org
Attendance
Chair (LTC Telecoms) Phyza Jameel
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) Francisco M.C. Garrido
Maria Y. Saleh

Karin Garcia Guillen
Rami Shakra
UNICEF Simon Zeweldi
World Food Programme (WFP) Martin Kristensson
World Vision International Viviana De Annuntiis
Agenda
1. Situation update
2. Global LTC Telecoms update
3. Global LTC Logistics update
4. Partner updates
5. AOB
Page 1 of 7
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

Minutes
1. Situation Update
Overview
• Between 08 and 13 July, Venezuela remained in a severe humanitarian emergency
following the twin magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes that struck the north-central
region on 24 June, just 40 seconds apart. The earthquakes affected at least seven
states, including La Guaira, Capital District, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, and
Yaracuy, causing widespread damage to homes, public infrastructure, schools,
hospitals, electricity and telecommunications networks, and other essential services.
• The response transitioned from large-scale search and rescue operations to
humanitarian relief, emergency shelter, protection services, restoring and
strengthening communications services, health support, and early recovery planning.
• Road access remains a key operational enabler across LTC Telecoms priority
locations. The Caracas–La Guaira route was not affected by the earthquakes,
allowing teams to reach the main coastal response area from the capital in
approximately 40 minutes. Road movement between priority sites is also feasible,
with travel between Polideportivo Jose Maria Vargas, Cesar Nieves Stadium and
Playa Grande taking around 15 to 20 minutes. This access has supported timely site
visits, coordination, needs assessments, personnel deployment and delivery of
humanitarian assistance.
Telecommunications status
• As of 13 July, connectivity and power conditions improved across the main response
locations. However, communication needs remain dynamic as affected populations
move between assistance sites. Humanitarian movement also remained volatile, as
new locations have been set up to expand aid distribution.
• Public infrastructure has been progressively restored across most active sites,
including access to public electricity, local internet service providers, government-
supported connectivity and mobile coverage. LTC and other response actors have
complemented these restored services by establishing Starlink connectivity,
Uninterrupted Power Supply (UPS) systems and solar backup solutions to strengthen
service continuity where gaps remain. Dependence on satellite phones appears to be
decreasing as mobile coverage continues to improve by the day.
• LTC Telecoms has completed set up of inter-agency shared connectivity and power
solution services focusing on four priority locations: Polideportivo Jose Maria Vargas,
Cesar Nieves Stadium, Playa Grande and Playa Verde.
Page 2 of 7
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

2. Global LTC Telecoms Update
Cluster status
• As of 13 July, the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) has not been
formally activated for the response. Telecommunications and logistics coordination
continues through existing national and humanitarian working groups, enabling
partners to share operational information, align response priorities and coordinate
support without formal cluster activation. These established mechanisms are helping
maintain response coherence, reduce duplication and support timely decision-
making as needs evolve across affected sites.
Coordination
• Coordination and planning is being channelled through the country-level ICT Working
Group and inter-agency focal points, to avoid duplication of efforts, reduce Starlink
congestion, improve managed network design, share local contacts, engage mobile
network operators on recovery plans. This mechanism has enabled WFP, UN
agencies, NGOs, technical partners, local providers and government counterparts to
share information and align deployments.
• Government authorities have been supportive of all humanitarian response efforts.
Field teams have generally been able to access sites, pass checkpoints by showing
UN identification and obtain the permissions needed for installations. Comisión
Nacional de Telecomunicaciones (CONATEL) has played a particularly important role
in facilitating telecommunications authorizations and site access. Humanitarian
responders are maintaining readiness for a response timeline that remains uncertain
and dependent on government authorization.
Services for communities
• Community connectivity services are being established in priority displacement sites
through collaboration between emergency.lu, CONATEL, G-Networks, WFP, and
other response partners. Using fibre connectivity and wireless distribution networks,
the solution enables affected communities to communicate with family members,
access information, and maintain essential digital services during the emergency.
• As of 13 July, community connectivity networks had been installed at Caraballeda
and César Nieves Stadium Transitional Camp, providing internet access for
approximately 1,850 affected populations and humanitarian responders, across the
two locations. Installation at Playa Grande is scheduled for 15 July.
• On 13 July, emergency.lu transferred the community connectivity solution to WFP.
Discussions are ongoing with service providers to maintain services throughout the
response and recovery period.
Page 3 of 7
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

Site-by-Site operational update
Polideportivo Jose Maria Vargas
• Polideportivo Jose Maria Vargas remains the largest assistance and shelter site and
the closest major response location to Caracas, located approximately 40 minutes by
road from the capital. Field observations indicate that around 1,000 people are
currently present, with growing demand for essential services underscoring the need
to sustain and scale support at the site.
• Power availability has improved significantly since the initial response phase, with
most organizations now connected to electricity. However, some shelter tents still
lack reliable access, requiring continued support to close remaining gaps. Backup
options, including UPS and solar solutions, are available to strengthen service
continuity and reduce the impact of any outages.
• Internet access is available through multiple local providers offering free community
connectivity, alongside organizational connectivity for WFP and other agencies.
Despite this progress, community internet capacity requires further strengthening to
meet rising demand as the site population grows. Mobile services are functioning
well, enabling some NGOs to rely on cellular networks and reducing the immediate
need for radios or satellite phones at this location.
• Priority next steps: Continue improving power access in tents with remaining gaps;
expand community internet services; and monitor mobile service reliability and
capacity.
Cesar Nieves Stadium
• Cesar Nieves Stadium is located approximately 20 minutes from Polideportivo Jose
Maria Vargas and sits within the town of La Guaira. The site is supporting people
inside and around the stadium and is becoming an increasingly important location for
food assistance and other services.
• When the assessment team arrived on 5 July, UN agencies had no access to
electricity at the site. By 7 July, power had been restored to both WFP and IOM tents
through different interim arrangements: IOM operated a generator, while WFP
identified a connection to the national public electricity grid. Other organizations are
relying on a mix of small generators, solar systems and temporary power solutions.
Although access to electricity has improved, power reliability remains a priority area
for further strengthening.
• Internet connectivity has improved since the initial deployment, when services were
unavailable. WFP, IOM and several partners now have access through a mix of
connectivity solutions, while strong mobile reception provides an additional
communication channel. The site has also been included in plans for community
internet deployment, which will further expand access for affected people and
responders.
Page 4 of 7
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

• Priority next steps: Improve power reliability; advance community internet
deployment; and continue monitoring local mobile providers, including Digitel and
Movistar.
Playa Grande
• Playa Grande, located about 15 minutes from Cesar Nieves Stadium, is among the
areas most severely affected by the earthquake. The site has sustained extensive
structural damage and reported casualties, with many affected people now seeking
assistance from UN agencies and partners.
• Power deployment was completed on 11 July through public electricity services,
enabling the WFP tent to operate with a more stable supply. The connection is also
being shared with partner agencies, including UNICEF, which is running a small clinic
at the site, helping strengthen basic service delivery for affected people.
• Internet access is currently available through WFP Starlink, IOM’s CANTV connection
and government-provided open networks. However, the government service remains
congested and is not yet able to meet user demand, limiting reliable access for
affected communities and responders.
• Mobile services are available through local providers, providing a stronger
communications environment than during the initial response phase. However,
network capacity remains a key concern, particularly for community access, where
congestion continues to limit reliable use.
• Priority next steps: Strengthen power backup options; improve community internet
capacity; and continue monitoring mobile services.
Playa Verde
• Playa Verde has been identified as an emerging response site following earthquake-
related impacts. WFP is deploying a Mobile Storage Unit to support operations, while
another partner is constructing an additional tent. As the site becomes operational, it
is expected to receive a growing number of affected people, requiring timely power,
connectivity and service readiness.
• As of 13 July, Playa Verde remained without electricity, as the WFP Mobile Storage
Unit was still under construction. The team is assessing a potential connection to the
public electricity network through a local provider, while UPS and solar systems
remain the main backup options if public power cannot be secured. A Starlink unit is
ready for installation once the MSU is completed. Mobile coverage is weaker than in
Playa Grande and Cesar Nieves, but local providers continue to support basic voice
calls.
• Priority next steps: Secure public power or deploy backup power; install Starlink
after MSU completion; monitor mobile coverage; and assess whether additional
connectivity support is required as the site becomes operational.
Page 5 of 7
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

3. Partners update
Government of Luxembourg
• Emergency.lu reported increasing congestion risks from the high concentration of
Starlink units at the La Guaira coordination base, where approximately 15 units were
observed alongside additional vehicle-mounted systems. The team cautioned that
uncoordinated deployments could reduce service quality and recommended
managed network equipment with bandwidth control to improve reliability, noting
that standard routers may congest after around 50 users while the managed solution
being configured at Cesar Nieves could support up to 1,000 clients.
4. Key Constraints
• Equipment security: Connectivity equipment remains exposed in several locations.
In the absence of secure storage, equipment must be dismantled each evening and
reinstalled each morning, increasing the risk of damage, loss, delayed start-up, and
service interruptions.
• Power reliability: Power supply remains fragile across operational sites. Backup
solutions, including UPS units, generators, EcoFlow batteries, and solar panels,
remain essential to maintain service continuity during outages.
• Connectivity congestion: High density of Starlink units and unmanaged routers may
reduce service quality and affect community access.
• Fuel movement restrictions: Generator operations are constrained by challenges
associated with transporting fuel between sites.
• Evolving site requirements: Population growth at existing sites and the emergence
of new locations, such as Playa Verde, require continuous reassessment of
connectivity and power needs.
5. AOB
• N/a
The teleconference meeting ended at 14:49 UTC
Next meeting
The next Global LTC Telecoms Teleconference will be held on Monday 27 July at 14:00
UTC.

documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 26**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**19 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Authorities report 1,388 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
- Official toll: **5,208 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,388 aftershocks.**

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,208 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.
The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population
from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931
million.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira
State, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects
intended for affected populations.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
National response
 The Government response remains focused on assistance to affected people, as well as the
establishment and management of transitional camps.
 According to authorities, the response continues through 107 transitional camps for affected
populations, with a total capacity of 27,820 people and a current occupancy of 23,820 people. As of
19 July, 41 camps are located in Caracas, 28 in La Guaira, 28 in Miranda and 10 in Aragua. Of the
total camp population, 12,474 people are accommodated in La Guaira, 8,528 in Caracas, 1,904
in Miranda and 682 in Aragua.
 This week, authorities announced that more than 500 engineers from across the country have been
deployed to Caracas and La Guaira to assess earthquake-affected homes and determine their
structural safety and habitability.
 Authorities are advancing a unified registration process for affected families in transitional camps
through the collection of biometric and contact information to support assistance management, social
support programmes and housing solutions.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com).
 School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto
Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital
District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión,
Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
 As of 14 July 2026, national authorities had reported the receipt of 82 international humanitarian
assistance contributions, equivalent to approximately 3,624 metric tons of aid from 36 donor
countries, organizations and entities. The largest contributors include Colombia, Trinidad and
Tobago, Mexico, Panama, China and Chinese companies, the United States, and Brazil.
 The assistance received includes food, safe drinking water, medicines, medical supplies, vaccines,
hospital equipment, hygiene items, sleeping mats, blankets, tents, furniture, water treatment plants,
tools, batteries, and temporary shelter supplies. These contributions are helping strengthen health
service delivery, food security, access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and assistance to
families affected by the earthquake.
Situation by state
(updated as of 18 July)
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 In Miranda state, 37 organizations implemented 337 activities across 10 humanitarian sectors, with
response efforts primarily focused on health, coordination, protection, food security, and water,
sanitation and hygiene (WASH). The response reached 15 municipalities and 25 parishes,
strengthening assistance to affected communities through broad coordination among national and
international actors and a strategy focused on addressing priority needs and supporting early
recovery.
La Guaira
 According to reported information, as of 17 July 2026, a total of 82 humanitarian organizations had
implemented response activities in La Guaira State. Overall, 1,586 activities have been reported
across two municipalities as part of the response to populations affected by the earthquakes.
 The sectors with the highest number of interventions are Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH),
Food Security, Health and Protection, accounting for the majority of reported activities. In addition,
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
response efforts have been implemented in the areas of coordination, temporary shelter, nutrition,
education, early recovery, and gender-based violence prevention and response, reflecting a
multisectoral approach to addressing the priority needs of affected communities
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In Yaracuy, particularly in Veroes municipality and other localities near the epicentral area, homes
have been reported as destroyed or at high risk. Recent assessments have identified priority needs
in protection, mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene
(WASH), and food security.
Falcón (Silva municipality)
 Authorities continue assisting affected communities in Silva Municipality, where 252 people (87
families) have been affected in Boca de Aroa. Of the 698 houses assessed, 305 were classified as
habitable, 265 sustained repairable damage and 128 were deemed uninhabitable. Damage to road
infrastructure, housing, basic services and livelihoods linked to tourism, fishing and coconut
production continues to be reported.
 Through the Falcón Local Coordination Forum (LCF), OCHA continues coordinating the response
with the State Government, Civil Protection and local authorities. Actions include humanitarian
capacity mapping, joint monitoring missions with WFP, ACH, IOM and UNICEF, as well as
monitoring displaced populations arriving from La Guaira and coordinating assistance activities in
affected communities.
 In coordination with regional authorities, national and international organizations, the Venezuelan
Red Cross and United Nations agencies supported the response in Palma Sola, Las Delicias,
Cayumar, Tucacas and Boca de Aroa through the distribution of 184 hygiene kits, 350 water filters
and other essential relief items. In addition, 46 people received psychosocial support, while activities
in protection, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), WASH, nutrition and livelihood
recovery were strengthened.
Other states
 Bolívar: Authorities report that 81 displaced families (246 people) have been assisted, all of whom
are currently staying with host families. The affected population includes 71 children, 31 adolescents
and 20 older persons. Affected families have been identified in the municipalities of Caroní,
Angostura del Orinoco, Angostura, Padre Pedro Chien, Cedeño and Piar. The response focuses on
psychosocial support, medical assistance, guidance on obtaining identity documents and access to
services.

Delta Amacuro: The arrival of displaced people from earthquake-affected areas continues to be
reported, with further population movements expected. At least 23 families are currently being hosted
by relatives, mainly in Tucupita and Casacoima. Response planning is being carried out proactively
based on information provided by authorities, enabling the timely delivery of food, kits and other
essential relief items.

Táchira: Seven affected individuals have received assistance at the San Cristóbal passenger
terminal. Support included psychoeducational sessions, legal counselling, health care, hydration,
food assistance and temporary accommodation, when required. Those assisted include men,
women, boys, girls and adolescents who subsequently continue their journey to other states across
the country. Humanitarian partners have also distributed hygiene kits and provided legal and medical
assistance.

Trujillo: Authorities report that 314 people (approximately 102 families) have been relocated across
14 municipalities. Field monitoring indicates that most families are staying with relatives. Monitoring
of potential logistical risks continues due to damage to agricultural roads and infrastructure at La
Ceiba port, which could affect the transportation of essential goods and humanitarian assistance.

Zulia: Humanitarian partners continue to provide protection services, initial health care,
psychological first aid, legal assistance, and the distribution of food, water and hygiene kits, as well
as guidance at transit points. Authorities continue to implement preventive measures and conduct
structural inspections amid ongoing low-magnitude seismic activity.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
Humanitarian coordination
(updated as of 18 July)
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
continues to coordinate the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner
organizations, prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, water, sanitation and hygiene,
logistics and protection.
 According to information consolidated by the Logistics Working Group, led by the World Food
Programme (WFP), since the onset of the earthquake response on 24 June 2026, a total of 24
humanitarian air shipments have arrived in Venezuela, managed by 18 organizations and carrying
an estimated cumulative volume of 712 metric tons of relief supplies. Most shipments have entered
the country through Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía.
 The earthquake response has significantly expanded the operational capacity of the humanitarian
community in Venezuela. In this context, a number of organizations with recognized expertise in
emergency and disaster response in other international settings have joined the effort. These
organizations, originating from different regions of the world, particularly the Americas, Europe and
Asia, have contributed specialized technical capacities and operational expertise.
 Many of these organizations have integrated into existing sector coordination mechanisms,
participating in humanitarian clusters and working groups to promote a complementary, coordinated
response aligned with priorities identified on the ground. Several have also established partnerships
with national and local organizations already present in the country, contributing to capacity
strengthening, knowledge sharing and a more efficient and context-specific response for affected
communities.
 At the same time, the emergency has demonstrated the mobilization capacity of national
humanitarian actors. Various local and national organizations, some of which previously had limited
or no permanent presence in the country’s central region, have significantly expanded their
operations or deployed to affected areas to support response efforts, working in coordination with
clusters, authorities and other humanitarian actors.
 This mobilization reflects an expansion of the response capacity of national and local actors, as well
as the progressive strengthening of humanitarian coordination mechanisms across the country.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
through the United Nations system, with support from UNDP. In line with the internationally
recognized PDNA methodology, coordination with relevant institutions and counterparts will continue
in the coming period.
 In addition, UNDP provided technical assistance to national institutions on the use of drones, artificial
intelligence and geospatial technologies for post-earthquake recovery and reconstruction planning,
with the aim of strengthening debris management and supporting evidence-based decision-making.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 Since the onset of the emergency, WFP has reached 94,575 people with food assistance. On 19
July, WFP provided support to 1,600 people through the distribution of family food baskets in Urimare
parish, La Guaira State. In addition, WFP and its partners distributed 4,014 hot meals across three
temporary shelters in La Guaira and provided 700 ready-to-eat (RTE) food kits in the Playa Grande
temporary shelter to address the immediate food needs of affected populations.
Health
 PAHO/WHO is advancing the distribution of 26.96 metric tons of medicines, medical supplies and
specialized equipment to strengthen the health response in affected areas. The shipment includes
10 Interagency Emergency Health Kits (IEHK), with the capacity to cover the health needs of
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
approximately 20,000 people for three months, and 10 Trauma Emergency Surgery Kits (TESK),
designed to support between 800 and 1,000 surgical procedures.
 Distribution is being prioritized to transitional camps, Comprehensive Diagnostic Centres (CDI) and
strategic health facilities in Caracas and La Guaira, including referral hospitals and centres with
surgical capacity. The supplies include medicines, medical equipment and specialized materials for
trauma care, orthopaedics and complex surgical procedures. PAHO/WHO continues to monitor and
track the use of these supplies to ensure their appropriate utilization and the continuity of care for
affected populations.
 IOM continues supporting the earthquake response through the deployment of medical teams and
the provision of primary health care directly and through its partner Ven Da Tu Mano. To date, 5,281
health consultations have been provided, including general medicine, internal medicine, paediatrics,
gynaecology and obstetrics, medicine distribution and individual psychological support
consultations.
 Project HOPE provided 25 medical consultations and distributed medicines to 33 people in the Playa
Grande transitional camp. The most frequently reported health conditions included upper respiratory
infections, hypertension and myalgia.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 Through the Logistics Working Group, in coordination with OCHA, the arrival of 48 metric tons (MT)
of humanitarian assistance by air through Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía for GEM,
as well as 18.5 MT by sea through Puerto Cabello for the Evangelical Council of Venezuela, was
reported. These supplies are intended to support the earthquake response in the sectors of Water,
Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), Food Security, Shelter and Housing.
 The authorities of the Ministry of People's Power for Foreign Affairs (MPPRE) reported that the
platform www.venezuelanoestasola.com provides information for humanitarian organizations and
cooperation actors on procedures for the arrival of aircraft and vessels carrying humanitarian
assistance, as well as guidance for the registration of routes, means of transport, crew members and
cargo.
 For inquiries related to these procedures, interested organizations may contact the Logistics Working
Group directly at: Venezuela.clustercargo@wfp.org.
. Nutrition
 Humanitarian partners continue supporting nutrition interventions targeting priority groups, including
children, pregnant women and breastfeeding women, through nutritional screening, counselling and
nutritional follow-up activities in transitional camps and affected communities.
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 IOM continues to provide protection services across the five transitional camps, including information
provision, legal assistance and support with documentation-related procedures. To date, 130 people
have received protection services, facilitating access to information, referrals and support
mechanisms to exercise their rights.
 As part of Children’s Day celebrations, humanitarian organizations, public institutions and private-
sector actors organized recreational, cultural and sports activities in the Playa Grande, Polideportivo
José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Campo de Golf and Mare Abajo II transitional camps.
Activities included games, cultural performances, sports events, toy distributions and safe
recreational spaces, benefiting hundreds of children and adolescents affected by the earthquakes.
 In the Polideportivo José María Vargas transitional camp, the Venezuelan Red Cross established
connectivity and Restoring Family Links (RFL) services, enabling affected people to communicate
with family members and support networks.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 IOM continues to manage and coordinate the five transitional camps co-managed with local
authorities (Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande, Campo de Golf
and Mare Abajo), while supporting site improvements and strengthening coordination with
authorities, humanitarian partners and cooperation actors to ensure a comprehensive response to
the needs of affected populations. In addition, a range of recreational activities were coordinated
across the camps as part of Children's Day celebrations for displaced families and children.
 To date, IOM, directly and through its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular, has distributed 2,995
kitchen sets, 2,514 plastic tarpaulins, 2,024 buckets, 1,595 solar lamps, 819 shelter kits, 592
mosquito nets and 193 rechargeable solar flashlights to support affected households and improve
living conditions in transitional sites.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 IOM has strengthened access to essential items for safe water storage and hygiene practices. To
date, 1,471 collapsible 10-litre jerrycans, 928 hygiene kits and 92 semi-collapsible 10-litre jerrycans
have been distributed.
 CISP maintained water, sanitation and hygiene services in the Playa Grande transitional camp
through the provision of 24,000 litres of water, the distribution of 200 waste bags, the collection of
approximately 1.1 metric tons of solid waste, and the maintenance of 12 latrines, 14 handwashing
stations, four laundry stations and 32 operational showers.
Humanitarian financing and contributions
(updated as of 17 July)
 The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced an additional appeal under the
Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela. The appeal outlines the multisectoral needs of 1.3
million people over the next six months. To reach those in need, US$299 million is required, in
addition to the US$632 million requested at the beginning of the year.
 Several United Nations agencies, funds and programmes have issued emergency appeals to scale
up humanitarian assistance and support the response and recovery efforts following the
earthquakes, in line with the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Addendum.
 UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to fund its earthquake emergency response. The aim is to assist
470,000 people, including 160,000 children and adolescents, through water, sanitation and hygiene
(WASH), health, nutrition, child protection and education interventions in the most affected areas
over the coming months. IOM requested US$98 million to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities
over the next six months. PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to
support the health response and early recovery efforts over the next six months and allocated
US$1.5 million from its Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP issued an initial appeal for US$80
million to provide food assistance to 500,000 people over a six-month period. UNHCR, for its part,
indicated that it requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six
months.
 Canada increased its matching contribution for donations supporting the earthquake response in
Venezuela from CAD 4 million to CAD 7 million, bringing its total support for the emergency to CAD
12 million. The funding, channelled through the Canadian Red Cross and the Humanitarian Coalition,
will support the provision of health, shelter and WASH services for affected populations.
 The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria approved an emergency funding package
of US$1.77 million to support HIV and tuberculosis services in Venezuela following the earthquakes.
The resources, to be managed through UNDP, will enable 7,000 people to continue HIV treatment,
ensure tuberculosis treatment for 500 people, and support prevention, testing and outreach services
for 1,500 members of key populations in the most affected areas.
 The European Union announced an additional contribution of €20 million to support humanitarian
action in the country. Of this amount, €10 million will support search and rescue operations, medical
assistance, the deployment of additional experts, and material assistance in the country. This
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
contribution comes in addition to the €5 million previously announced for the earthquake response
and the €52 million already allocated to humanitarian operations in Venezuela this year.
 In addition, under the European Union Humanitarian Air Bridge launched in June, three EU-funded
flights have already arrived in the country. The latest flight landed on 17 July carrying 48 metric
tonnes of medical supplies and shelter items.
 The Government of Italy allocated US$5.7 million to support the humanitarian response to the
earthquakes, helping deliver life-saving assistance, protection and access to essential services for
affected populations through AICS, WFP and IFRC.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country.
 The Republic of Korea announced an additional contribution of US$3.5 million in humanitarian
assistance. Of this amount, US$3 million will be channelled through UNDP to support debris removal
activities, while the remainder will be provided in-kind, specifically through 30 metric tons of
temporary shelters (family tents). The Republic of Korea had previously allocated US$1.25 million to
WFP and US$2.5 million to UNICEF in support of the humanitarian response in Venezuela.
 Japan allocated US$3.5 million to support the earthquake response. The funding will provide
humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and non-food
items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
and IOM.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden contributed SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
Contact information
For more information, please contact the OCHA Venezuela Office:
Vanessa May – Head of Office a.i. – mayv@un.org

documents.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 26**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**19 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Las autoridades reportan 1.388 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio.
- Balance oficial: **5.208 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para  
     atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.388 réplicas.**

A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.208 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.**

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.** Esta adenda complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.
