La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la gestión de los campamentos
transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en
articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y
continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos
Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, anunció una adenda al Plan de
Respuesta Humanitaria por 299 millones de dólares, destinada a atender las necesidades
multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses. Este llamado se
suma a la meta de 5,5 millones de personas que ya contemplaba atenderse con el Plan este 2026, para
lo que se requieren 632 millones de dólares. De misión en el país, la Comisaria Europea de Gestión de
Crisis, Hadja Lahbib, realizó una visita a La Guaira junto con el Coordinador Humanitario de las Naciones
Unidas y representantes de agencias humanitarias para conocer de primera mano las necesidades de la
población afectada y la respuesta que se está brindando.
Impacto en infraestructura
 Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.
 Como parte de la planificación para la recuperación y reconstrucción, las autoridades identificaron
40 terrenos en el estado La Guaira, equivalentes a aproximadamente 584.000 metros cuadrados,
para el desarrollo de proyectos habitacionales destinados a la población afectada.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
 Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de
Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil
millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas,
comercios, escuelas, hospitales e instalaciones públicas. Entre tanto, estimaciones preliminares de
PNUD indican daños físicos directos por 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 6 % del PIB.
Respuesta nacional
 La respuesta gubernamental se mantiene centrada en las labores de búsqueda y rescate, así como
en la atención de las personas afectadas.
 De acuerdo con las autoridades, la respuesta continúa con 107 campamentos transitorios para
la atención de personas afectadas, con capacidad para 25.282 personas y una ocupación de
21.210 personas. Hasta el 16 de julio, 41 campamentos se encuentran instalados en Caracas, 28
en Miranda, 28 en La Guaira, y 10 en Aragua.
 Las autoridades avanzan en un proceso de registro único de las familias afectadas en campamentos
transitorios, mediante la recopilación de datos biométricos y de contacto para apoyar la gestión de
la asistencia, los programas de apoyo social y las soluciones habitacionales.
 El Gobierno venezolano anunció la creación de un fondo inicial de reconstrucción equivalente a 200
millones de dólares.
 Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad
(Conapdis) para coordinar una respuesta oportuna e inclusiva en las zonas afectadas.
 Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas
(www.localizapacientes.com) y el reporte de personas afectadas (0-800-RESCATE).
 Las actividades escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados
Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José
Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas);
Distrito Capital (Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo,
Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).
 Al 14 de julio de 2026, las autoridades nacionales habían reportado la recepción de 82 aportes de
ayuda humanitaria internacional, equivalentes a aproximadamente 3.624 toneladas de asistencia
provenientes de 36 países, organizaciones y entidades donantes. Entre los mayores contribuyentes
se encuentran Colombia, Trinidad y Tobago, México, Panamá, China y empresas chinas, Estados
Unidos y Brasil.
 La ayuda recibida incluye alimentos, agua potable, medicamentos, insumos médicos, vacunas,
equipos hospitalarios, artículos de higiene, colchonetas, mantas, carpas, mobiliario, plantas
potabilizadoras, herramientas, baterías y suministros para alojamiento temporal, contribuyendo a
fortalecer la atención sanitaria, la seguridad alimentaria, el acceso a agua y saneamiento, y la
asistencia a las familias afectadas por el terremoto.
Situación por estado
Distrito Capital (Caracas) y Miranda
 En el estado Miranda, 37 organizaciones implementaron 337 actividades en 10 sectores
humanitarios, destacando las acciones en salud, coordinación, protección, seguridad alimentaria y
agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH). La respuesta cubrió 15 municipios y 25 parroquias,
fortaleciendo la asistencia a las comunidades afectadas mediante una amplia articulación entre
actores nacionales e internacionales y una estrategia enfocada en la atención de necesidades
prioritarias y la recuperación temprana.
La Guaira
 En el estado La Guaira, 77 organizaciones reportaron 1.128 actividades humanitarias en los 11
sectores de la respuesta, con especial énfasis en salud, agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH),
protección, apoyo a niñas, niños y adolescentes y seguridad alimentaria. Las intervenciones
alcanzaron 12 parroquias en dos municipios, reflejando una respuesta multisectorial y coordinada
para atender las necesidades más urgentes de la población afectada.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
 Las autoridades y organizaciones humanitarias continúan fortaleciendo la respuesta en los
campamentos transitorios de La Guaira mediante la ampliación de servicios multisectoriales, la
mejora de las condiciones de alojamiento y la gestión coordinada de la asistencia.
 El grupo interclúster presentó una propuesta de Plan Multisectorial a autoridades de 12
campamentos transitorios ubicados en La Guaira. Igualmente, socios del grupo de trabajo de
infraestructura sostuvieron un espacio técnico con autoridades para mapeo de capacidades en
actividades prioritarias como acondicionamiento de espacios, dotación de enseres, entre otros, en
campamentos donde se realizó el levantamiento multisectorial de necesidades.
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro)
 En Yaracuy, particularmente en el municipio Veroes y otras localidades cercanas a la zona
epicentral, se reportan viviendas destruidas o en condición de alto riesgo. Se identifican
necesidades prioritarias en protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua,
saneamiento e higiene (ASH) y seguridad alimentaria.
Falcón (Tucacas – Municipio Silva)
 Organizaciones locales estiman la presencia de alrededor de 37 familias reubicadas
voluntariamente, acogidas por redes familiares en los municipios Miranda, Colina y Silva. Las
principales necesidades identificadas incluyen apoyo psicosocial, agua, saneamiento e higiene
(ASH), salud sexual y reproductiva, nutrición y recuperación temprana. Se mantienen
requerimientos de acompañamiento psicosocial para personas afectadas por el terremoto.
Otros estados
 Apure: Se reportan 247 personas desplazadas acogidas en casas de familiares, principalmente en
los municipios San Fernando, Biruaca, Achaguas, Rómulo Gallegos y Pedro Camejo. Las
necesidades más relevantes corresponden a alimentación, kits de higiene, enseres básicos y apoyo
para recuperación temprana, en un contexto de capacidad limitada de respuesta local.
 Bolívar: Se registra la llegada de personas desplazadas a los municipios Caroní, Angostura del
Orinoco, Cedeño y Piar, alojadas principalmente con familiares. Las necesidades iniciales
identificadas se concentran en apoyo psicosocial, manteniéndose en evaluación otros
requerimientos multisectoriales. Se consolidaron mecanismos de coordinación entre la
Gobernación, alcaldías y actores humanitarios. Se acordó la designación de puntos focales para
facilitar el intercambio de información y fortalecer la complementariedad de esfuerzos en apoyo a la
población afectada. Ya se iniciaron atenciones psicosociales.
 Zulia: Según información recopilada por organizaciones del Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC), se
han caracterizado al menos 87 personas desplazadas procedentes principalmente de La Guaira y
Caracas. La mayoría se aloja con familiares, mientras que otras permanecen en tránsito hacia
Colombia o hacia estados fronterizos. Los municipios receptores incluyen Maracaibo, Mara,
Machiques, Jesús Enrique Lossada, Rosario de Perijá y Jesús María Semprún. La movilidad
presenta una tendencia a la disminución. Las organizaciones humanitarias continúan brindando
triaje médico, primeros auxilios psicológicos, asistencia jurídica, derivaciones médicas, distribución
de alimentos, agua y kits de higiene, así co mo protección.
 Los Foros Locales de Coordinación continúan fortaleciendo la coordinación con autoridades
regionales y municipales para complementar la respuesta gubernamental y mejorar el seguimiento
de necesidades.
Coordinación humanitaria
 La Comisaria Europea de Gestión de Crisis, Hadja Lahbib, realizó una visita a La Guaira junto con
el Coordinador Humanitario de las Naciones Unidas y representantes de agencias humanitarias,
recorriendo el campamento transitorio Polideportivo José María Vargas para conocer de primera
mano las necesidades de la población afectada y los servicios de respuesta en curso. Durante la
visita se destacaron las acciones de salud, alimentación, alojamiento y protección implementadas
en el sitio, así como la importancia de mantener el apoyo humanitario a las comunidades impactadas
por los terremotos.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
 OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales,
continúa coordinando la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias,
priorizando acciones en salud, alojamiento, alimentación, agua, saneamiento e higiene, logística y
protección.
 Al 14 de julio de 2026, 100 organizaciones nacionales, internacionales, agencias de Naciones
Unidas, organizaciones locales, instituciones públicas y actores del Movimiento de la Cruz Roja
reportaron 2.200 actividades de respuesta en 57 municipios de 14 estados, abarcando 11 sectores
humanitarios.
 La mayor concentración de la respuesta se registra en La Guaira, con 77 organizaciones y 1.128
actividades, seguida por el Distrito Capital con 62 organizaciones y 536 actividades, y Miranda con
37 organizaciones y 337 actividades. Los sectores con mayor volumen de intervenciones son salud
(550 actividades), agua, saneamiento e higiene (476), protección (281), protección de niñas, niños
y adolescentes (230) y seguridad alimentaria (204), reflejando una respuesta multisectorial
orientada a atender necesidades críticas, fortalecer la protección de las poblaciones afectadas y
apoyar la recuperación temprana en las zonas impactadas por el terremoto
 El equipo UNDAC/OCHA desplegado en Venezuela apoyó a la coordinación de los equipos USAR,
el establecimiento de mecanismos iniciales de coordinación en La Guaira a través del OSOCC y,
de manera más amplia, el fortalecimiento de la capacidad operativa de la oficina de OCHA en
Venezuela, incluyendo gestión de información, evaluaciones de necesidades y apoyo técnico
especializado. A través del OSOCC, facilitó la coordinación entre el gobierno, Naciones Unidas,
organizaciones y otros actores clave, promoviendo una respuesta humanitaria integrada, basada
en evidencia y alineada con las prioridades nacionales.
 Asimismo, los especialistas de iMMAP y MapAction continuarán brindando apoyo técnico a la
comunidad humanitaria nacional e internacional en Venezuela, fortaleciendo las capacidades de
gestión de información, análisis geoespacial, cartografía humanitaria y apoyo logístico. Este
acompañamiento también contribuirá al trabajo de OCHA en Venezuela, apoyando la coordinación
entre actores, el análisis de necesidades y la toma de decisiones basadas en evidencia para
fortalecer la preparación y respuesta ante futuras emergencias.
 OCHA continuó fortaleciendo la coordinación con el sector privado para apoyar las acciones de
respuesta y recuperación temprana, promoviendo la articulación con actores especializados en
áreas como logística, gestión de escombros, rehabilitación de infraestructura y planificación de la
reconstrucción, a través de los mecanismos de coordinación existentes entre las Naciones Unidas
y el sector privado.
 Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores
al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del
PNUD. Conforme a la metodología internacional de la PDNA, se avanzará en las coordinaciones
correspondientes con las contrapartes relevantes.
 Además, PNUD brindó asistencia técnica a instituciones nacionales para la incorporación de drones,
inteligencia artificial y tecnologías geoespaciales en la planificación de la recuperación posterior a
los terremotos, con el fin de fortalecer la gestión de residuos y apoyar la toma de decisiones basada
en evidencia.
 La Oficina de las Naciones Unidas de Servicios para Proyectos (UNOPS, por sus siglas en inglés)
realizó una misión en Venezuela, durante la cual sostuvo reuniones con autoridades, representantes
del sector privado y socios internacionales para identificar oportunidades de cooperación en
recuperación temprana y respuesta humanitaria, incluyendo el apoyo a la rehabilitación de
infraestructura y la restitución de servicios esenciales.
Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria
Seguridad Alimentaria
 Al 16 de julio, el PMA ha alcanzado a 73.868 personas. De este total, 1.860 personas recibieron
asistencia alimentaria en Chichiriviche de la Costa, donde el acceso a los alimentos continúa siendo
limitado debido a la interrupción de las principales fuentes de ingreso de la población,
particularmente el turismo y la venta de pescado. Asimismo, el PMA asistió a 3.640 personas en el
estado La Guaira mediante la distribución de canastas alimentarias, a 1.000 personas con kits de
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
alimentos listos para el consumo para cubrir necesidades inmediatas y distribuyó 6.388 comidas
calientes en albergues temporales coordinados por las Naciones Unidas.
Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene
 En el campamento transitorio Playa Grande, CISP, socio implementador de UNICEF, suministró
12.000 litros de agua y mantuvo operativos cinco puntos de lavado de manos, cuatro estaciones
de lavado de ropa y 10 baños portátiles. Asimismo, distribuyó 80 bolsas para desechos, realizó
jornadas de recolección de residuos que abarcaron 74 contenedores, ejecutó labores de limpieza
y mantenimiento de las instalaciones sanitarias, completó la instalación de las duchas para
hombres y desarrolló actividades de promoción de higiene que alcanzaron a 106 personas,
incluyendo a 23 niñas, niños y adolescentes mediante sesiones sobre lavado de manos e higiene
en contextos de emergencia.
Alojamiento, Energía y Enseres
 ACNUR reforzó las condiciones de seguridad y protección en los campamentos transitorios
Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande y Mare Abajo mediante la
distribución de 541 kits de lámparas solares y mosquiteros, 200 linternas solares y la instalación
de 132 reflectores solares y otras estructuras temporales para mejorar la iluminación de áreas
comunitarias, espacios de alojamiento y zonas de baños.
Logística y Telecomunicaciones
 Arribaron al Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar dos vuelos humanitarios, uno coordinado por
Airlink, el Departamento de Estado de EE.UU. y Amazon, y otro organizado por UNHRD y
financiado por ECHO, con 85.25 toneladas métrica (TM) de ayuda humanitaria para nueve
organizaciones, de las cuales el PMA, a través del Grupo de Trabajo de Logística (GTL), apoyó en
la movilización y almacenamiento de 42.66 TM de carga humanitaria correspondientes a cuatro de
estas organizaciones, agilizando los movimientos de carga en el aeropuerto.
 A la fecha, el GTL ha apoyado, junto con OCHA, la coordinación de la llegada de 525.36 TM de
ayuda humanitaria por vía aérea al Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar. Estos envíos,
correspondientes a trece organizaciones, incluyen insumos de alimentación, salud, agua,
saneamiento e higiene y artículos de refugio/alojamiento.
 Desde Telecomunicaciones se fortaleció la capacidad operativa de la respuesta mediante la
instalación de sistemas de respaldo energético para garantizar la conectividad a internet en el
campamento transitorio Estadio César Nieves. Asimismo, se realizó una evaluación de campo y
estimación de requerimientos para las futuras instalaciones del campamento de Playa Verde
asignado al PMA. Asímismo, se apoyó a OIM en la adquisición de 30 unidades adicionales de
Starlink Standard para proyectos vinculados a la emergencia en Venezuela.
Nutrición
 UNICEF instaló tres espacios de apoyo a la lactancia materna en tres campamentos transitorios,
donde se brinda orientación y asistencia a madres lactantes.
Protección (incluidos Áreas de Responsabilidad de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes y Violencia
Basada en Género)
 En el campamento transitorio César Nieves, se dio continuidad al triaje especializado para la
identificación y detección de vulnerabilidades realizado por OIM, gestionando de manera articulada
e interinstitucional 45 derivaciones prioritarias: 25 a servicios de salud general, tres a servicios de
SMAPS, uno a la Defensoría del Pueblo, uno a UNFPA y 15 al Ministerio de Hábitat y Vivienda.
 En el componente de respuesta y prevención de la Violencia Basada en Género (VBG), las
actividades de sensibilización alcanzaron a 938 personas, se entregaron 77 kits de dignidad, se
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
brindó apoyo psicosocial y primeros auxilios psicológicos a 82 personas, se gestionaron 16 casos
y 1 persona recibió asesoría legal.
 Hasta el 16 de julio, ACNUR ha alcanzado a 915 personas mediante actividades de protección en
los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa
Grande, incluyendo asistencia legal, gestión de casos, apoyo psicosocial, orientación y
derivaciones a servicios especializados. Asimismo, 136 niñas, niños y adolescentes y sus familias
recibieron orientación sobre registro de nacimiento, documentación de identidad y representación
legal, complementada con acompañamiento psicosocial y socioemocional para fortalecer
estrategias de afrontamiento frente a los efectos de los terremotos.
 ACNUR fortaleció además el acceso a información y mecanismos de protección en los
campamentos transitorios, alcanzando a 533 personas mediante mesas de información sobre
derechos, acceso a servicios y rutas de atención, así como a 90 personas mediante sesiones
informativas sobre protección, rendición de cuentas a las poblaciones afectadas (AAP) y
prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual (PEAS).
Salud
 En el campamento transitorio Campo de Golf (Tanaguarena) se mantuvieron las jornadas móviles
de salud y salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS) proporcionadas por OIM, alcanzando 16
jornadas realizadas hasta la fecha y un total de 1.377 atenciones. Los servicios brindados
incluyeron medicina general, pediatría, medicina interna, consultas psicológicas individuales,
referencias, entre otras.
 UNFPA realizó 105 actividades de sensibilización en salud sexual y reproductiva, prevención y
educación comunitaria en los puntos de atención de los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo
Vargas, César Nieves y Playa Grande, alcanzando a la población afectada mediante sesiones
informativas y la distribución de condones y materiales educomunicativos.
 UNFPA también brindó seis consultas a mujeres embarazadas, identificando tres casos de alto
riesgo obstétrico (ARO) que requieren seguimiento especializado. Además, distribuyó y administró
76 métodos anticonceptivos modernos, incluidos 72 implantes subdérmicos y cuatro bolsas de
anticonceptivos inyectables. En el punto de atención del campamento transitorio César Nieves
también realizó 54 pruebas rápidas de VIH y 54 pruebas de sífilis, fortaleciendo el acceso a
servicios esenciales de salud sexual y reproductiva para las comunidades afectadas.
 Desde el inicio, las actividades del componente de Salud Sexual y Reproductiva (SSR) alcanzaron
a 1.615 personas mediante acciones de sensibilización.
 La Fundación Proyecto Maniapure (FPM) continuó brindando servicios en el estado La Guaira
mediante consultorios móviles. Durante la jornada realizada el 16 de julio en CTP II Fernando
Rísquez (Catia La Mar), atendió a 66 personas, con 72 consultas de salud y aproximadamente 120
atenciones en optometría. Los servicios de salud incluyeron medicina interna, pediatría,
traumatología y ginecología y obstetricia. Además, en el componente de salud mental y apoyo
psicosocial (SMAPS) se realizaron 18 atenciones, incluyendo acompañamiento individual y familiar.
Se identificaron síntomas de ansiedad, depresión y procesos de duelo, con atención específica
para seis niños, niñas y adolescentes. Entre las principales necesidades identificadas destacan el
fortalecimiento del suministro de medicamentos para enfermedades no transmisibles (ENT), la
continuidad de los servicios de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, la incorporación de servicios de
fisioterapia y atención odontológica, la distribución de kits de higiene personal y familiar, y una
mayor difusión comunitaria de los servicios disponibles.
 International Medical Corps (IMC) mantiene desplegadas Unidades Médicas Móviles y un Equipo
Médico de Emergencia (EMT Tipo 1) en el estado La Guaira, brindando atención primaria de salud,
salud sexual y reproductiva y salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS), además de apoyar el
acceso a agua segura. Entre el 1 y el 15 de julio, IMC realizó 1.785 consultas en comunidades
afectadas. Las principales causas de atención fueron enfermedades no transmisibles (47,6%) y
enfermedades transmisibles (37,8%), seguidas por servicios de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial
(5,7%), salud sexual y reproductiva (5,6%) y atención de traumatismos y lesiones (3,3%),
evidenciando una demanda sostenida de servicios esenciales de salud en las zonas afectadas. Del
total de consultas realizadas por las unidades médicas móviles, el 58,3% correspondió a mujeres.
Además, la mayor proporción de atenciones se concentró en personas de 19 a 49 años (32,7%).
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
 Además, EMT Tipo 1 de IMC ha realizado 524 consultas. Estos resultados evidencian una
demanda sostenida de servicios, destacando la importancia de mantener la continuidad de
servicios esenciales y el seguimiento comunitario en los puntos con mayor carga asistencial.
Financiamiento humanitario y contribuciones
 El jefe humanitario de Naciones Unidas, Tom Fletcher, anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta
Humanitaria (PRH) para Venezuela. Este llamado contempla las necesidades multisectoriales de
1,3 millones de personas por los próximos seis meses. Para alcanzar a estas personas, se necesitan
299 millones de dólares, que se suman a los 632 millones de dólares solicitados al inicio del año.
 Varias agencias, fondos y programas de las Naciones Unidas han emitido llamamientos de
emergencia para ampliar la asistencia humanitaria y apoyar la respuesta y recuperación tras los
terremotos, en línea con la adenda del PRH presentada.
 UNICEF requiere 65.7 millones de dólares para financiar su respuesta de emergencia ante el
terremoto. La meta es atender a 470.000 personas (incluidos 160.000 niños, niñas y adolescentes)
mediante intervenciones de agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH), salud, nutrición, protección infantil
y educación en las zonas más afectadas durante los próximos meses. OIM requirió 98 millones de
dólares para asistir a 850.000 personas y 140 entidades durante los próximos seis meses.
OPS/OMS lanzó un llamamiento de emergencia por casi 24 millones de dólares para apoyar la
respuesta en salud y la recuperación temprana durante los próximos seis meses, además de asignar
1,5 millones de dólares del Fondo de Contingencia para Emergencias. El PMA presentó una
solicitud inicial de 80 millones de dólares para brindar asistencia alimentaria a 500.000 personas
durante seis meses. Por su parte, ACNUR indicó que requiere 14,8 millones de dólares para apoyar
a hasta 30.000 personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses.
 El Fondo Mundial de lucha contra el sida, la tuberculosis y la malaria aprobó un paquete de
financiamiento de emergencia por 1.77 millones de dólares para apoyar los servicios de VIH y
tuberculosis en Venezuela luego de los terremotos. Los recursos, que se gestionarán a través del
PNUD, permitirán que 7.000 personas continúen el tratamiento del VIH, se garantice el tratamiento
de la tuberculosis para 500 personas y se respalde los servicios de prevención, pruebas de
detección y divulgación para 1.500 miembros de poblaciones clave en las zonas más afectadas.
 La Unión Europea realizó una contribución adicional de 20 millones de euros para apoyar la acción
humanitaria en el país. De este total, 10 millones de euros estarán destinados a apoyar operaciones
de búsqueda y rescate, asistencia médica y el despliegue de otros expertos, así como asistencia
material, en el país. Estos recursos se suman a los 5 millones de euros previamente anunciados
para la respuesta a la emergencia y a los 52 millones de euros ya destinados a las operaciones
humanitarias en Venezuela este año.
 Además, como parte del puente aéreo humanitario de la Unión Europea, puesto en marcha en junio,
ya han llegado al país dos vuelos financiados por la UE con cerca de 80 toneladas de insumos
esenciales.
 El Gobierno de Italia asignó 5,7 millones de dólares para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria a los
terremotos y proporcionar asistencia vital, protección y acceso a servicios básicos para las
poblaciones afectadas, a través de la Agencia Italiana de Cooperación para el Desarrollo (AICS), el
Programa Mundial de Alimentos (PMA) y la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja
y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC).
 El Fondo Central de Respuesta a Emergencias (CERF, por sus siglas en inglés) realizó una
asignación de 15 millones de dólares para una respuesta multisectorial, junto con la activación del
Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV). Noruega realizó una contribución para apoyar la respuesta
a través del CERF.
 Estados Unidos anunció una contribución de 100 millones de dólares al FHV, y una asignación
adicional de 100 millones de dólares en contribuciones bilaterales para operaciones de respuesta
de OIM, PMA, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse,
Proyecto Esperanza y la Cruz Roja.
 Alemania y Corea realizaron contribuciones al FHV por 5 millones y 1,25 millones de dólares,
respectivamente, para apoyar la acción humanitaria en el país.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
 Corea realizó una contribución adicional para brindar asistencia por un monto de 3,5 millones de
dólares. 3 millones de dólares serán canalizados a través del PNUD para apoyar las labores de
remoción de escombros y el resto se proporcionará en insumos, específicamente, 30 toneladas de
alojamientos temporales (tiendas de campaña familiares). Corea ya había asignado 1,25 millones
de dólares al PMA y 2,5 millones de dólares a UNICEF para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en
Venezuela.
 Japón asignó 3,5 millones de dólares para apoyar la respuesta a los terremotos. Los fondos
permitirán brindar asistencia humanitaria en sectores clave, incluidos seguridad alimentaria, salud
y atención médica, alojamiento y artículos no alimentarios, a través del PMA, la Federación
Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (FICR) y la OIM.
 Australia informó de una contribución de 2 millones de dólares para la provisión de alimentos,
alojamiento, atención de salud y acceso a agua segura a través de IFRC y el PMA.
 Suiza anunció una contribución de 2,5 millones de francos suizos para apoyar la respuesta.
 Suecia asignó 25 millones de coronas suecas para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en el país,
mediante programas de asistencia alimentaria, agua, alojamiento temporal, protección y
reunificación familiar implementados por el PMA, ACNUR y Save the Children.
 Dinamarca anunció una contribución adicional de 11 millones de coronas danesas para apoyar la
respuesta humanitaria, incluyendo 10 millones de coronas danesas a través de ACNUR y 1 millón
de coronas danesas a través de DanChurchAid y la Cruz Roja Danesa.
 El Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) anunció una asignación inicial de 7,5 millones de libras
esterlinas para la respuesta al terremoto en Venezuela, incluyendo 2 millones de libras esterlinas
aportados por el Gobierno del Reino Unido mediante UK Aid Match. Los recursos serán
implementados por organizaciones miembros del DEC y sus socios locales para apoyar la respuesta
humanitaria.
 Parte del apoyo brindado por UNDAC incluye una especialista en coordinación con el sector privado
para fortalecer la participación empresarial en la respuesta y recuperación. Se encuentra disponible
un rastreador de contribuciones del sector privado para la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela
(https://ven-eq.connectingbusiness.org) y una nota informativa dirigida al sector privado sobre
oportunidades de apoyo. Punto focal: sanchez21@un.org.
 OCHA continúa coordinando con donantes y socios para asegurar una asignación rápida,
estratégica y basada en necesidades.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes - Emergency Update #3, 5 - 14 July 2026
documents.body_text:
## HIGHLIGHTS

- As of 14 July, authorities reported at least 4,734 fatalities, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people without shelter following the earthquakes. Authorities also reported 1,275 aftershocks, maintaining risks for affected communities and response personnel, particularly around damaged buildings.
- Government-led transitional camps and sites continue to expand. Authorities reported 107 operational sites across La Guaira, the Capital District and Miranda. More than 20,000 survivors are being accommodated in these camps.
- The response has shifted from the initial search-and-rescue phase towards a broader recovery and protection response. Urban Search and Rescue coordination was formally transferred to Venezuela's Civil Protection, while humanitarian actors continued to scale up multisectoral support in coordination with national and local authorities.
- UNHCR and partners expanded protection services across three transitional camps in La Guaira, reaching more than 1500 people during the reporting period with protection activities, information and counselling, legal support, psychological first aid, psychosocial support, child protection interventions and referrals to specialized services.
- Documentation remains one of the main protection needs identified across sites. With support from UNHCR, government-led documentation services have helped people replace identity documents lost during the earthquakes and access procedures to renew official documentation. Through mobile documentation activities, affected families have been able to restore proof of identity, helping them access assistance, public services and other essential support..
- The Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator visited Venezuela and met with national authorities, the Humanitarian Country Team, international and national nongovernmental organizations and the United Nations Country Team. During the visit, the need for US$ 298 million in additional funding was announced to support 1.3 million people over the next six months.

EMERGENCY UPDATE #3
VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES
5 July – 14 July
HIGHLIGHTS
As of 14 July, authorities reported at least 4,734 fatalities, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people without
shelter following the earthquakes. Authorities also reported 1,275 aftershocks, maintaining risks for affected
communities and response personnel, particularly around damaged buildings.
Government-led transitional camps and sites continue to expand. Authorities reported 107 operational sites
across La Guaira, the Capital District and Miranda. More than 20,000 survivors are being accommodated in
these camps.
The response has shifted from the initial search-and-rescue phase towards a broader recovery and
protection response. Urban Search and Rescue coordination was formally transferred to Venezuela's Civil
Protection, while humanitarian actors continued to scale up multisectoral support in coordination with
national and local authorities.
UNHCR and partners expanded protection services across three transitional camps in La Guaira, reaching
more than 1500 people during the reporting period with protection activities, information and counselling,
legal support, psychological first aid, psychosocial support, child protection interventions and referrals to
specialized services.
Documentation remains one of the main protection needs identified across sites. With support from
UNHCR, government-led documentation services have helped people replace identity documents lost
during the earthquakes and access procedures to renew official documentation. Through mobile
documentation activities, affected families have been able to restore proof of identity, helping them access
assistance, public services and other essential support..
The Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator visited Venezuela
and met with national authorities, the Humanitarian Country Team, international and national non-
governmental organizations and the United Nations Country Team. During the visit, the need for US$ 298
million in additional funding was announced to support 1.3 million people over the next six months.

EMERGENCY UPDATE #3: VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT
Two weeks after the earthquakes, the response is increasingly focused on sustaining temporary
accommodation, restoring essential services and expanding protection and referral support for people unable
to return safely to their homes. As efforts transition from emergency relief to early recovery and reconstruction,
priorities are expanding to include safe housing rehabilitation, earthquake-resistant rebuilding and the
restoration of damaged infrastructure. UNHCR will continue to provide protection services, support access to
documentation, psychosocial assistance, referrals and protection monitoring, as well as reestablishment of
services provided by the Ombudsman Office. Working closely with authorities and partners, UNHCR will also
help ensure that protection standards are integrated temporary accommodation and recovery efforts
Authorities are gradually restoring public services and administrative activities. Commercial flights and airports
have resumed operations or activated contingency measures to maintain connectivity, while classes have
restarted in 18 unaffected states. However, school activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across
Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, La Guaira, the Capital District and Miranda while infrastructure and recovery needs
continue to be assessed.
Population internal movements linked to the earthquakes continue to be reported. Earthquake-affected families
continue to move towards transitional camps, spontaneous shelters and host communities where family and
community support networks are available. In addition, community sources in Táchira have observed
temporary returns of families from Caracas and other affected areas following housing damage and livelihood
losses. Authorities in Apure reported the relocation of more than 177 affected people from the Capital District,
La Guaira and Miranda to San Fernando de Apure. Local authorities also reported arrivals of affected people in
Anzoátegui and Zulia. These movements underline the need for timely information, protection monitoring and
referral pathways beyond the most affected central areas.
The Government has also announced the “Venezuela Renace” recovery initiative, including measures related
to cash assistance for affected households, subsidized housing repair and reconstruction support and a
national fund for rehabilitation of affected areas and critical infrastructure.

5 July – 14 July 2

EMERGENCY UPDATE #3: VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES
PROTECTION
Protect people at risk
UNHCR and partners provided integrated protection services across three transitional camps in La Guaira,
reaching more than 1550 people during the reporting period. Support included information and
counselling, legal assistance, psychological first aid, psychosocial support, child protection interventions,
support to access identity documents and referrals to specialized protection, health and other essential
services.
Documentation remained a priority protection concern. A total of 288 people received counselling and
assistance related to civil documentation, identity recovery and legal procedures. In coordination with the
Identification Authority, UNHCR supported mobile documentation activities, including the renewal of
national identity documents for affected people who had lost documentation during the earthquakes.
Children and families with specific protection needs continued to receive targeted support. At Playa
Grande, 20 children at heightened risk, including children facing documentation challenges or lacking
formal care arrangements, received legal counselling and protection support. UNHCR and partners also
supported referrals to child protection authorities and legal services for children requiring birth registration
or legal representation.
UNHCR and partners continued to strengthen referral pathways for health, psychosocial support and
specialized protection services. More than 285 individuals were referred to specialized services during the
reporting period, including health care, child protection, psychosocial support and state institutions. At José
María Vargas Transitional Camp, UNHCR facilitated access to specialized health services through
coordination with the Central University of Venezuela community medical service.
UNHCR also supported community-based protection activities. These included group sessions with women
leaders on psychological first aid, dissemination of key protection messages, information on available
services and communication of feedback mechanisms for affected communities.
At Playa Grande, provincial authorities continued safe information-gathering activities using the system
developed with UNHCR technical support. This supports the identification of needs and helps authorities
and partners plan services and referrals.
UNHCR also provided technical and logistical support to state institutions operating within transitional sites,
including support to the La Guaira Women’s Institute for the operation of a Humane Childbirth and
Breastfeeding Unit, which benefited eight women during the reporting period.
CORE RELIEF ITEMS AND SHELTER
Meet immediate basic needs and promote safe and dignified temporary accommodation
Since the start of the response, UNHCR has supported shelter and relief efforts through additional
humanitarian airlifts and in-country stocks, contributing more than 55 metric tons of relief items, family
tents, service tents and solar lighting to support affected communities and safer service delivery in
transitional sites.
UNHCR continued to support safer and more functional service delivery spaces in transitional camps.
UNHCR and UNFPA installed six protection service tents at Playa Grande to expand the availability of
protection services. UNHCR also supported the installation of solar lamps in communal areas to improve
lighting and reduce protection risks, including 30 solar light reflectors at José María Vargas Transitional
Camp, while at Mare Abajo Transitional Camp, 30 solar lamps were installed to improve safety and reduce
protection risks.
UNHCR also began supporting protection risk mitigation in Mare Abajo Transitional Camp, a newly
established site where humanitarian actors are supporting camp set-up and service provision
EMERGENCY UPDATE #3: VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES
5 July – 14 July 3

EMERGENCY UPDATE #3: VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES
A solar flashlight may seem like a simple item. For families who lost everything in the earthquakes, it can
mean much more: safety, peace of mind and protection throughout the night. At the José María Vargas
Transitional Camp, Tania and Samuel are using some of the emergency items provided by UNHCR,
including solar flashlights and mosquito nets, designed to help families stay safe as they begin rebuilding
their lives. Thanks to the support of UPS and LATAM Cargo, these relief supplies reached Venezuela
quickly to support people affected by the earthquakes.
COORDINATION
UNHCR continued to support coordination through the Protection Cluster, the Infrastructure and
Temporary Shelter Working Group and other inter-agency mechanisms. The Protection Cluster and the
Infrastructure and Temporary Shelter Working Group, together with government counterparts, conducted
joint visits to seven collective accommodation sites in La Guaira to strengthen the protection response
and support safe and dignified management of collective accommodation facilities.
Protection actors continued coordination with government institutions, United Nations agencies and
humanitarian partners to harmonize the response, strengthen referral mechanisms, expand specialized
services and address emerging protection needs. At site level, partners coordinated the delivery of
services for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse, child protection, health referrals, community
feedback mechanisms and coexistence arrangements.
Coordination efforts also expanded to areas receiving earthquake-affected people, including Táchira,
Zulia, Anzoátegui and Apure. Continued monitoring in these areas will be important to identify protection
risks linked to documentation, access to services, displacement and family tracing needs.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
La Evaluación Rápida de Necesidades (RNA), un esfuerzo interagencial para generar evidencia oportuna e identificar necesidades en la fase inicial de la emergencia, se realizó entre el 1 y el 3 de julio, dentro de los siete días posteriores a los terremotos. Complementada con información secundaria, análisis especializados e imágenes satelitales, la evaluación confirma una crisis multisectorial en los siete estados afectados:**La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón y Yaracuy.**

Los resultados muestran un deterioro de las condiciones de vida y de los servicios básicos, la pérdida de medios de vida y capacidad de compra de los hogares, y un impacto significativo sobre la vivienda, con efectos en el alojamiento, movilidad y cohesión comunitaria. Las mayores afectaciones se concentran en La Guaira, Miranda y el Distrito Capital, evidenciando la necesidad de una respuesta humanitaria multisectorial y sostenida.

documents.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #3: Children’s distress profound after earthquakes | NRC
documents.body_text:
Media update from the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) three weeks after the earthquakes on the distress children continue to experience and the need for psychosocial support.

Press release

[Venezuela](https://reliefweb.int/themes?categoryId=118) Published 16. Jul 2026

**Elena Vicario, NRC Country Director for Venezuela said:**  
“Weeks on from the earthquakes, children’s distress remains profound. For thousands of children, this moment of fear will be etched in their memory forever. Many of the safe places where they learned, played and grew no longer exist. Children have lost not only their homes and schools, but also friends, neighbours, teachers and family members.

“The need for psychosocial support is urgent. Without it is harder for children to recover from the traumatic experience and they will continue to live with the sense of danger generated by the earthquakes. This can affect their capacity to learn, thrive and achieve their full potential. For many children every loud noise can feel as though the tragedy is happening all over again. A child who receives timely support can find the words to understand and express what they are feeling and gradually regain a sense of calm and hope.

“One mother told our team how, after spending five days outdoors, a heavy storm arrived. As thunder rolled overhead, children began hugging one another and crying, convinced that another earthquake was coming. The fear and anxiety were immediate and visible.

“Many schools are closed because of damage, or because they are being used as temporary shelters, and there is now a need for temporary learning spaces. NRC has started providing psychosocial support in temporary shelters. Within the first days of our education response, we reached over 100 children, creating spaces where they can express themselves, play, regain routines and begin to process what they have lived through. We hope to set up 10 temporary learning spaces where we can support 600 children as they gradually overcome the initial shock and reduce the constant sense of fear and alertness.

“The solidarity of the Venezuelan people has played an important part in the first weeks after the earthquakes. On weekends, volunteer groups come from other states to organise recreational activities for children. These initiatives are really appreciated by families and the community. However, I have noticed that adolescents are often left out. Many of them told us how much they miss school, and some even asked our colleagues if they could give them maths lessons. This shows how eager they are to keep learning and regain a sense of normality.”

**Marisela, a primary school teacher from La Guaira said:**  
“Children have not yet let go of the overwhelming emotions caused by the earthquake that changed all our lives. We need that impact to fade little by little, working together.

“It is important to recreate learning spaces within shelters and to create activities and safe spaces to help children process what happened. There are teachers in the shelters. Activities can take place, even if it’s just under a tent.

“Seeing children suffer is horrible. Children are part of a country’s future.”

**Notes to editors:**

- Photos and videos from Venezuela are available for use [here](https://visuals.nrc.no/?c=15116&k=5b02ed739f), including photos of Marisela.
- Marisela teaches at two schools in La Guaira, the hardest-hit area, where the courtyards are currently being used as temporary shelters. In one of them, NRC distributed family mobility kits containing blankets, mosquito repellent, sunscreen, flashlights, batteries, power banks, and other essential items to each family living there. The school has been damaged by the earthquakes and can no longer be used. At best, some chairs and desks could be recovered for the children if a temporary tent were installed in the school courtyard. 29 families are currently living in the school's courtyard. Marisela estimates that around 200 of the school’s 765 students were killed.
- The school year in Venezuela ends in July. Educational authorities have begun working on reorganising the academic calendar, and we welcome these efforts.
- We welcome the statement recently issued by [education authorities](https://www.instagram.com/p/DaWcx17Ec5B/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA%3D%3D&img_index=4) highlighting socioemotional support as a priority in the areas affected by the earthquakes. NRC will continue to support the efforts of the authorities and the wider humanitarian response, in line with the principles of neutrality and impartiality.
- In the Capital District alone, 432 schools – around a third of all schools - have been affected by the earthquakes ([UNICEF](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/unicef-venezuela-humanitarian-situation-report-no3-earthquake-02-july-2026)).
- According to [Education Cannot Wait](https://www.educationcannotwait.org/news-stories/press-releases/education-cannot-wait-launches-emergency-response-help-children-return), 34 schools are currently serving as temporary shelters.
- According to [Education Cannot Wait](https://www.educationcannotwait.org/news-stories/press-releases/education-cannot-wait-launches-emergency-response-help-children-return), learning has been disrupted for nearly 24,000 students.
- Between 8 and 10 July, NRC reached more than 100 children aged 5 to 16 with educational activities. The response is ongoing, and NRC hopes to set up 10 temporary learning spaces where 600 children can receive educational kits, as well as psychosocial support programmes.
- NRC has been working in Venezuela since 2005 providing education, protection, legal guidance, and water and sanitation support. In 2025 we reached more than 71,000 people across four bordering states. NRC has 70 colleagues in Venezuela, and seven local partners. Our teams are working across areas affected by the earthquakes to provide vital supplies, and will be providing water and sanitation support, emergency education and trauma support for children among other services.

**For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:**

- NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Situation Report #7 (July 15, 2026)
documents.body_text:
Project HOPE continues expanding its earthquake response across northern Venezuela, adapting operations to meet evolving health and humanitarian needs while reducing the risk of secondary public health emergencies. Over the past several days, Project HOPE expanded services into a new community in La Guaira, continued scaling mobile medical services, and provided more than 1,300 additional primary healthcare consultations, despite severe weather temporarily disrupting operations in some locations. Disease surveillance; water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) remain central priorities as displaced families continue to face difficult living conditions.

**Situation Overview**

Humanitarian needs remain significant as recovery efforts continue across northern Venezuela. The official death toll has risen to nearly 4,500 people while more than 17,000 remain displaced or without permanent housing. Humanitarian partners have continued debris removal, structural assessments, and restoration of essential services. Shelters — including both official and unofficial makeshift shelters — remain crowded and limited access to sanitation facilities persist. Coupled with intermittent rainfall and remaining debris, there continues to be a heightened risk of communicable disease transmission.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake Response, July–December 2026 – Addendum to the 2026 UNICEF HAC Appeal
documents.body_text:
On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela, adding a new layer of humanitarian needs to an already fragile context. Two weeks after the earthquakes, official figures reported 4,490 deaths, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people left without housing.

The earthquakes have created a major child-focused humanitarian emergency on top of already significant needs. Children and families have lost homes, schools, access to safe water, health services, and protection systems, while aftershocks continue to heighten risks and complicate recovery.

UNICEF requires **US$65.7 million to reach 470,000 people; of which 167,000 are children**.

UNICEF’s earthquake response and is fully aligned with the addendum to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) in Venezuela, which targets **1.3 million people affected by the earthquake** across 7 states. Before the earthquakes, UNICEF’s Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) Appeal targeted 2.3 million people, including 1.2 million children, with a focus on addressing critical needs in health care, nutrition, safe water, sanitation, education, and child protection services.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 22**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**15 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,200 aftershocks.**
- Official toll: **4,829 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- **An additional appeal for US$299 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,284 aftershocks.**

Twenty-one days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **4,829 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency**. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan aimed at addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.** This is in addition to the 5.5 million people already targeted under the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires US$632 million in funding.

Venezuela is facing a national

high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and
7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local
time) in the north-central region, with
the epicentre located along the San
Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis
(Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities
report 1,284 aftershocks.
Twenty-one days since the
earthquakes, authorities report a toll of
4,829 people dead and 16,740
injured since the onset of the
emergency. Authorities also indicated
that 17,907 people lost their homes.
The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps
and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination
with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance.
United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom
Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan aimed at
addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months. This is in addition
to the 5.5 million people already targeted under the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires
US$632 million in funding.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira
State, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects
intended for affected populations.
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
National response
 The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, as well as assistance
to affected people.
 According to authorities, the response continues with 106 transitional camps supporting affected
populations, with a capacity of 25,351 people and a current occupancy of 20,857 people. As of
15 July, 40 camps are located in Caracas, 28 in Miranda, 28 in La Guaira, and 10 in Aragua.
 Authorities are advancing a unified registration process for affected families in transitional camps
through the collection of biometric and contact information to support assistance management, social
support programmes and housing solutions.
 The Government of Venezuela announced the creation of an initial reconstruction fund equivalent to
US$200 million.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com) and to
report affected individuals (0-800-RESCATE).
 School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto
Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital
District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión,
Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 A coordination meeting was held with authorities from the Miranda State Government and Inter-
Cluster members to share the results of the multisectoral needs assessment conducted in seven
transitional camps. Response priorities were presented, and partners agreed to strengthen the
capacities of shelter coordinators and frontline personnel through cluster-led training and capacity-
building activities.
Response actions: Organizations such as Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA and World Vision are providing
protection support to affected families, particularly through psychosocial assistance.
La Guaira
 Authorities and humanitarian organizations continue strengthening the response in La Guaira’s
transitional camps through the expansion of multisectoral services, improvements in accommodation
conditions and coordinated assistance management. The distribution of essential items, food
assistance, protection activities, health and psychosocial support interventions, as well as actions to
improve access to safe water, sanitation, connectivity and community infrastructure, continue.
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In Yaracuy, particularly in Veroes municipality and other localities near the epicentral area, homes
have been reported as destroyed or at high risk. Recent assessments have identified priority needs
in protection, mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene
(WASH), and food security.
Response actions: Five organizations (Venezuelan Red Cross, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón
and Empodérame) are providing response in health, food, water and the distribution of humanitarian
assistance.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
 The Local Coordination Forum (LCF) continues to monitor potential complementary support needs
for families displaced from La Guaira and Caracas. In coordination with UNICEF, the situation in
Silva municipality was reviewed, highlighting the need for sustainable and complementary
interventions.
 OCHA and authorities facilitated an inter-institutional coordination meeting to identify priorities for
complementary action in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health, nutrition, family planning,
environmental sanitation, and livelihoods. As a result, UNICEF will assess potential areas for
intervention.
Response actions: Capacity-building activities led by the Protection Cluster, as well as WASH and
psychosocial support interventions in Boca de Aroa and Palmasola, are ongoing. These activities are being
implemented by ACH, Azul Positivo, IOM, Centroccidente, ODISEF and AVSI in coordination with regional
authorities.
Other states
 Apure: The number of people affected mobilized to the state remains approximately 250. The Local
Coordination Forum (LCF) continues to monitor the situation and provide multisectoral assistance,
including psychological first aid.
 Bolívar: Representatives of the humanitarian community and the State Government coordinated
actions to strengthen the response for people displaced from earthquake-affected areas. Key
priorities identified include strengthening the technical capacities of frontline personnel and providing
specialized psychosocial support. According to official figures, 63 families (198 people) have been
registered and profiled: 42 in Caroní, 15 in Angostura del Orinoco, three in Padre Pedro Chien, two
in Cedeño and one in Piar. Identified families have received initial assistance, including needs
assessments, psychological first aid, health services and support for the regularization of identity
documents.
 Delta Amacuro: Authorities and humanitarian partners reviewed preparedness and response
actions for families mobilized from earthquake-affected areas. WFP plans to provide immediate food
assistance during the first 72 hours, while Cáritas Delta Amacuro may support with hygiene kits and
World Vision with food baskets for households with children. Humanitarian actors will also coordinate
capacity-strengthening and information management activities to support the registration, tracking
and assistance of people arriving in the state.
 Zulia: The medical triage and information point for families on the move remains operational at the
Maracaibo passenger terminal, in coordination with the Venezuelan Red Cross and ASONACOP.
Reports from 14 July indicate a declining mobility trend, with family groups arriving from Catia La
Mar and La Guaira, either bound for Maracaibo or transiting onwards to Colombia (Cartagena).
 In Monagas, Anzoátegui, Nueva Esparta, Trujillo and Lara, previously reported coordination,
stockpiling and monitoring activities remain ongoing. Local Coordination Forums continue to monitor
assistance delivery and protection risks affecting populations on the move.
Humanitarian coordination
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
continues to coordinate the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner
organizations, prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, WASH, logistics and protection.
 UNDAC and OCHA continued supporting Civil Protection in strengthening emergency coordination
and information management capacities, including technical exchanges on USAR coordination
mechanisms and operational tracking tools.
 A total of 71 search and rescue teams from 31 countries, comprising 2,786 personnel and 216 search
dogs, were deployed to the worst-affected areas in support of rescue operations. The total includes
teams that are currently being demobilized.
 OCHA continued strengthening coordination with the private sector to support response and early
recovery efforts, promoting engagement with specialized actors in areas such as logistics, debris
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
management, infrastructure rehabilitation and reconstruction planning through existing coordination
mechanisms between the United Nations and the private sector.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
within the framework of the United Nations system and with the support of UNDP. In line with the
internationally recognized PDNA methodology, the corresponding coordination efforts with relevant
counterparts will be advanced.
 Authorities informed the activation of a special mechanism to expedite the processing of a “Work
Visa for Special Situations” through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The procedure will be carried out
online under the coordination of the Office of the Vice Minister for Multilateral Affairs and the Consular
Affairs Office. It is intended for foreign personnel of international organizations, as well as United
Nations staff, deploying to Venezuela in support of the response to the earthquake emergency.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 WFP is progressively expanding its operation, providing critical food assistance beyond La Guaira.
While La Guaira was the most severely impacted state, other states (including Miranda, Yaracuy,
Falcón, Carabobo, and Aragua) are also grappling with the aftermath of the earthquakes. In
response, on 15 July alone, WFP carried out its first distribution in Miranda state, reaching 1,160
people affected by the earthquakes in the Higuerote, Curiepe, and Tacarigua parishes.
 In parallel with this expansion, WFP continued to deliver assistance there through general food
distribution, providing food baskets to 4,348 people in affected communities and serving 7,358 hot
meals to people living across the UN-coordinated temporary shelters. WFP will continue to expand
its reach while sustaining assistance to those most impacted by the earthquakes. Since the
beginning of the emergency response, WFP has reached 73,228 people with food assistance.
Health
 UNICEF supported the administration of 76 vaccine doses in the transitional camp of Polideportivo
Vargas (44) and César Nieves (32). At the Playa Grande transitorial camps, UNICEF, through the
Ministry of Health, provided basic health care services to 32 people.
 On 15 July, UNFPA reported activities in César Nieves, Playa Grande and Polideportivo transitional
camps, including 143 awareness-raising sessions and 32 antenatal consultations, of which 31 were
conducted in Polideportivo and one in César Nieves. In addition, 100 modern contraceptive methods
(MCMs) were distributed, including 91 subdermal implants, seven injectables and two oral
contraceptives.
 At the Playa Grande transitional camp, 147 medical consultations were provided by Project HOPE
and Ven Da Tu Mano.
 International Medical Corps (IMC) continues to deploy Mobile Medical Units and an Emergency
Medical Team (Type 1 EMT) in La Guaira state, providing primary health care, sexual and
reproductive health services, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), while also
supporting access to safe water through the provision of drinking water. Between 1 and 14 July, IMC
conducted 1,586 consultations in affected communities. The main reasons for consultation were
non-communicable diseases (47 per cent) and communicable diseases (38 per cent), followed by
mental health and psychosocial support services (6 per cent), sexual and reproductive health
services (6 per cent), and trauma and injury care (3 per cent), highlighting sustained demand for
essential health services in affected areas.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 Through the Logistics Working Group (LWG), WFP supported the transportation of 37.93 metric
tonnes of WASH and shelter supplies belonging to the International Federation of Red Cross and
Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) from Maiquetía International Airport to the LWG warehouses in La
Guaira.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
. Nutrition
 UNICEF established three breastfeeding support spaces in three transitional camps, providing
guidance and assistance to breastfeeding mothers.
 At the César Nieves transitional camp, UNICEF conducted nutritional screening for children and
adolescents and provided support to pregnant women.
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 As of 15 July, UNHCR had reached 875 people in the José María Vargas, César Nieves and Playa
Grande transitional camps through legal assistance, case management, psychosocial support,
counselling and referrals to specialized services. In addition, 136 children and adolescents and their
families received guidance on birth registration, identity documentation and legal representation,
complemented by psychosocial and socio-emotional support to strengthen coping mechanisms in
the aftermath of the earthquakes.
 UNFPA continued conducting awareness-raising activities on gender-based violence (GBV) and
menstrual hygiene in the César Nieves transitional camp, complemented by the distribution of 16
dignity kits to adolescents.
 UNICEF and its partners provided psychosocial support to 132 children and adolescents and 55
parents and caregivers through Child-Friendly Spaces and group sessions in the J.M. Vargas, César
Nieves and Playa Grande transitional camps.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 UNHCR strengthened shelter and protection conditions in the José María Vargas, César Nieves,
Playa Grande and Mare Abajo transitional camps through the distribution of 539 solar lamp and
mosquito net kits, 200 solar flashlights, and the installation of 132 solar floodlights and other
temporary structures to improve lighting and safety in communal areas, sanitary facilities and
accommodation spaces.
 In the La Guaira transitional camps, coordination, shelter support and multisectoral service provision
continued. At the José María Vargas transitional camp, IOM continued assisting 347 families,
updated population records and coordinated relocation processes to shelters in Caracas.
Government officials, diplomatic representatives and United Nations personnel also conducted
monitoring visits to the José María Vargas and Playa Grande camps to review assistance conditions
and the needs of the affected population.
 At the Playa Grande transitional camp, planning advanced for the relocation of the site to the
República del Salvador Educational Unit, while health, protection, food assistance, and water,
sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services continued to be provided.
 In Campo de Golf (Tanaguarena) transitional camp, IOM distributed 50 non-food item (NFI) kits,
advanced coordination for the establishment of spaces for humanitarian service delivery, and
conducted awareness-raising activities on safe coexistence and the prevention of trafficking in
persons.
 In Mare Abajo II transitional camp, humanitarian organizations strengthened inter-agency
coordination to improve service complementarity. Infrastructure improvements for shelter and
sanitation continued, including the installation of bunk beds, upgrades to tents, and the construction
of showers and drainage systems, alongside the provision of health, food assistance and WASH
services for the affected population.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 UNICEF and its partners continue to provide 80,000 litres of safe water per day across the three
identified transitional camps in La Guaira, benefiting approximately 3,500 people.
 In the identified transitional camps in La Guaira, UNICEF continued to maintain and upgrade laundry
facilities and handwashing stations, ensured the cleaning of portable toilets, and strengthened
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
sanitation conditions through the provision of laundry points, handwashing facilities, sanitation
services and water storage capacity. In addition, hygiene promotion activities reached 772 people.
Humanitarian financing and contributions
 The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced an additional appeal under the
Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela. The appeal outlines the multisectoral needs of 1.3
million people over the next six months. To reach those in need, US$299 million is required, in
addition to the US$632 million requested at the beginning of the year.
 IOM launched a US$98 million appeal to assist 850,000 people and support 140 entities over the
next six months. PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support
health response and early recovery activities over the next six months and released US$1.5 million
from the Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP launched an initial appeal for US$80 million to
provide food assistance to 500,000 people over a six-month period. UNHCR requires US$14.8
million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 The European Union announced on 15 July an additional contribution of €20 million to
support humanitarian action in the country. Of this amount, €10 million will support search
and rescue operations, medical assistance, the deployment of additional experts, and
material assistance in the country. This contribution comes in addition to the €5 million previously
announced for the earthquake response and the €52 million already allocated to humanitarian
operations in Venezuela this year.
 Additionally, as part of the European Union Humanitarian Air Bridge launched in June, two EU-
funded flights have already arrived in the country carrying nearly 80 tonnes of essential supplies.
 Authorities announced the arrival of two aircraft carrying 41.3 tonnes of humanitarian assistance
from Colombia. The supplies included non-perishable food items, personal hygiene kits, infant
formula and other relief items.
 The Government of Italy allocated US$5.7 million to support the humanitarian response to the
earthquakes, helping deliver life-saving assistance, protection and access to essential services for
affected populations through AICS, WFP and IFRC.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country.
 The Republic of Korea announced an additional allocation of US$3.5 million in humanitarian
assistance. Of this amount, US$3 million will be channelled through UNDP to support debris
removal activities, while the remainder will be provided in-kind, specifically through 30 metric tons
of temporary shelters (family tents). The Republic of Korea had previously allocated US$1.25
million to WFP and US$2.5 million to UNICEF in support of the humanitarian response in
Venezuela.
 Japan allocated US$3.5 million to support the earthquake response. The funding will provide
humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and non-food
items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
and IOM.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden contributed SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis

Vanessa May – Head of Office a.i. – mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Humanitarian Affairs Officer – alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Public Information Officer – moreno7@un.org
