United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom
Fletcher announced a US$298 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan aimed at
addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months. This is in addition
to the 5.5 million people already targeted under the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires
US$632 million in funding.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira
State, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects
intended for affected populations.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
National response
 The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, as well as assistance
to affected people.
 According to authorities, the response continues with 107 transitional camps supporting affected
populations, with a capacity of 25,064 people and a current occupancy of 20,231 people. As of
13 July, 40 camps are located in Caracas, 29 in Miranda, 28 in La Guaira, and 10 in Aragua.
 Authorities are advancing a unified registration process for affected families in transitional camps
through the collection of biometric and contact information to support assistance management, social
support programmes and housing solutions.
 The Government of Venezuela announced the creation of an initial reconstruction fund equivalent to
US$200 million.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com) and to
report affected individuals (0-800-RESCATE).
 School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto
Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital
District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión,
Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 First-line responders working in transitional camps participated on 13 July in a Mental Health and
Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) training coordinated by the MHPSS, Child Protection and Gender-
Based Violence (GBV) Areas of Responsibility, with support from the Ministry of Health, Cecodap
and Cedesex.
Response actions: Organizations such as Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA and World Vision are providing
protection support to affected families, particularly through psychosocial assistance.
La Guaira
 Authorities and humanitarian organizations continue strengthening the response in La Guaira’s
transitional camps through the expansion of multisectoral services, improvements in accommodation
conditions and coordinated assistance management. During the reporting period, progress was
made in the distribution of essential items, food assistance, protection activities, health and
psychosocial support interventions, as well as actions to improve access to safe water, sanitation,
connectivity and community infrastructure.
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In Carabobo, the most significant impacts continue to be concentrated in Juan José Mora
municipality (Morón parish). In Yaracuy, particularly in Veroes municipality and other localities near
the epicentral area, homes have been reported as destroyed or at high risk. Recent assessments
have identified priority needs in protection, mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter,
water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Response actions: Five organizations (Venezuelan Red Cross, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón
and Empodérame) are providing response in health, food, water and the distribution of humanitarian
assistance.
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
 In Boca de Aroa parish, soil liquefaction caused ground settlement and slab displacement affecting
87 houses, compromising the habitability of homes for 252 people. Civil Protection authorities and
structural engineers continue conducting technical assessments. Authorities also continue
monitoring the overflow of the Aroa River and Los Ingleses stream within a multi-hazard context
involving both earthquake and flood risks.
 A technical inspection conducted on 11 July by the Presidential Commission for Habitability
Assessment determined that the Boca de Yaracuy Bridge is the transport infrastructure most
severely affected by the earthquakes in the area. Temporary diversion measures are being prepared
while reconstruction planning is underway. The La Pava, El Paují and Punta Brava bridges sustained
minor damage and remain subject to traffic safety measures, speed restrictions and repair works to
maintain connectivity between Falcón and Carabobo states.
Response actions: Civil Protection requested support to provide Psychological First Aid (PFA) training to
approximately 300 Civil Protection, Fire Department and VEN 911 personnel, in coordination with
organizations participating in the Local Coordination Forum. Protection Cluster capacity-building activities
continue, alongside WASH and psychosocial support interventions in Boca de Aroa and Palmasola
implemented by Action Against Hunger (ACF), Azul Positivo, IOM, Centroccidente, ODISEF and AVSI.
Other states
 Anzoátegui: Civil society organizations and humanitarian actors strengthened coordination for the
response to affected populations, agreeing on a matrix of responsibilities. Eleven Civil Protection
officers were deployed to humanitarian brigades in La Guaira, and 72 pre-hospital emergency
students received training on seismic risk management.
 Apure: More than 250 people have been displaced as a result of the earthquakes. The Local
Coordination Forum (LCF) continues to monitor household vulnerabilities and provide multisectoral
assistance, including psychological first aid.
 Bolívar: Authorities reported assistance to 41 displaced families (127 people, including 60 adults,
10 older people, 42 children and 15 adolescents), primarily hosted by relatives in the municipalities
of Caroní (27 families), Angostura del Orinoco (13) and Cedeño (1). The VEN 911 facility was
activated as a temporary shelter with capacity for 120 people, and the state government has
dispatched seven humanitarian aid shipments. Coordination with Tinta Violeta is planned to support
at least 10 vulnerable families.
 Delta Amacuro: Humanitarian actors distributed 20 food kits and 20 hygiene kits to 20 families, as
well as approximately 30 kits for children, with support from World Vision International, Médecins
Sans Frontières and the Lutheran World Federation. Assessment activities were conducted under
the coordination of the health authority, Kape-Kape and Tinta Violeta. An inter-institutional
coordination platform was also established, bringing together regional authorities, the health sector
and OCHA.
 Monagas: The Municipality of Maturín provided support to families from La Guaira hosted by
relatives, including a group of 12 people displaced from Ciudad Caribe who are expecting the arrival
of four additional family members. Assistance included household items, medicines and supplies to
improve hosting arrangements, including mattresses, fans and construction materials.
 Táchira: IOM and ODISEF assisted 11 people on the move at the San Cristóbal bus terminal (five
women, three men and three children), providing psychoeducational sessions, legal counselling,
health services, psychological first aid and hygiene kits. An older person and a lactating woman were
prioritized for assistance.
 Sucre: A technical team of engineers was deployed to support the assessment, inspection and
monitoring of earthquake-affected infrastructure in La Guaira and Caracas, contributing to damage
analysis and recovery planning efforts.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
 Zulia: Assistance to displaced populations continues at the Maracaibo passenger terminal and in
receiving municipalities. The response is being implemented by the Citizen Assistance Office
(Gerencia de Atención al Ciudadano) and ASONACOP, in coordination with the Red Cross, HIAS,
CESVI, ASOREZ and Caritas, as well as Child Protection and Rights Councils.
 Nueva Esparta, Trujillo and Lara reported that coordination, relief collection and monitoring activities
remain ongoing, while Local Coordination Forums continue to monitor assistance delivery and
protection risks.
Humanitarian coordination
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
continues to coordinate the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner
organizations, prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, WASH, logistics and protection.
 UNDAC and OCHA continued supporting Civil Protection in strengthening emergency coordination
and information management capacities, including technical exchanges on USAR coordination
mechanisms and operational tracking tools.
 OCHA continued strengthening coordination with the private sector to support response and early
recovery efforts, promoting engagement with specialized actors in areas such as logistics, debris
management, infrastructure rehabilitation and reconstruction planning through existing coordination
mechanisms between the United Nations and the private sector.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
within the framework of the United Nations system and with the support of UNDP. In line with the
internationally recognized PDNA methodology, the corresponding coordination efforts with relevant
counterparts will be advanced.
 Authorities informed the activation of a special mechanism to expedite the processing of a “Work
Visa for Special Situations” through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The procedure will be carried out
online under the coordination of the Office of the Vice Minister for Multilateral Affairs and the Consular
Affairs Office. It is intended for foreign personnel of international organizations, as well as United
Nations staff, deploying to Venezuela in support of the response to the earthquake emergency.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 Since the start of the response, WFP and its partners have reached over 64,000 people with
critical food assistance across La Guaira. On 13 July, WFP distributed 390 family food baskets in
the Urimare communities of Playa Grande, reaching 1,160 people, and an additional 35 family food
baskets to support meal preparation in temporary shelters located in Carayaca and Catia La Mar,
benefiting 140 people. The baskets contain essential dry food commodities, including maize meal,
rice, pasta, lentils, beans, vegetable oil, and salt, providing approximately 75 percent of household
food requirements for 30 days.
 In parallel, hot meal distributions continued across temporary shelters in La Guaira, with 7,233 meals
served, including 1,364 meals in the Playa Grande community, 2,883 meals at the César Nieves
Baseball Stadium, and 2,986 meals at the José María Vargas Sports Stadium, ensuring continued
access to food for displaced and affected families. In parallel, assessment teams continue to
evaluate market conditions and how to tailor support to the different realities on the ground —
including beyond La Guaira — as WFP moves toward modalities that allow families to choose how
to best meet their needs.
 During the initial phase of the response, Caritas Venezuela distributed 4,481 food assistance kits,
reaching an estimated 72,000 people.
Health
 As of 12 July, 22 international Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) had been deployed, were
mobilizing or were demobilizing in earthquake-affected areas, supporting the health response
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
through emergency medical care, field hospitals, mobile health services and specialized assistance,
and complementing national capacities.
 UNICEF provided primary health-care services to 76 people at the José María Vargas Sports
Complex and César Nieves Stadium camps and administered a total of 183 vaccine doses to
children and adults across the three transitional camps in La Guaira, including yellow fever and
tetanus toxoid vaccines.
 According to Caritas' 13 July report, Caritas Venezuela distributed 73,356 medical supplies and
medicines, reaching 17,924 people.
 International Medical Corps (IMC) continues to deploy three Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) in La
Guaira state, providing health services in Catia La Mar, Playa Verde, Playa Grande, Puerto Viejo,
Las Salinas, La Lucha, Punta de Mulatos and other prioritized locations. The teams comprise general
practitioners, nurses, pediatricians, an obstetrics and gynecology (OB/GYN) specialist, support staff,
and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) personnel. Between 1 and 8 July 2026, the
mobile medical units conducted a total of 944 consultations in earthquake-affected communities in
La Guaira. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) accounted for the largest proportion of
consultations (44.3 per cent), followed by communicable diseases (36.3 per cent). Mental health and
psychosocial support consultations represented 8.1 per cent of all consultations, while sexual and
reproductive health services accounted for 7.0 per cent and trauma/injury-related consultations for
4.3 per cent. In addition, IMC continues to support access to safe water through water trucking
activities and has initiated the deployment of a Type 1 Emergency Medical Team (EMT) in Catia La
Mar to further strengthen health response capacity.
 On 10 July 2026, Project Hope continued providing health services through health facilities and
community spaces in La Guaira, Miranda and the Capital District, delivering 184 medical
consultations, 172 treatment courses and seven Pap smear (PAP) tests. In La Guaira, activities
focused on the Catia La Mar Baseball Field and Caraballeda, where 81 medical consultations were
provided, 172 treatments were distributed and seven PAP tests were conducted, contributing to
timely access to primary health care and preventive services. In addition, the organization provided
medical consultations in health facilities in the municipalities of Chacao and Libertador, including
facilities within the public health network, supporting continuity of care for affected populations.
 Japan will deploy a second contingent of the Japan Disaster Relief (JDR) Medical Team to the
affected area, comprising personnel from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Japan International
Cooperation Agency (JICA), as well as registered doctors, nurses and other health professionals.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 Through the Logistics Working Group (LWG), WFP is expanding the no-cost logistics services
available to humanitarian organizations. In response to requests from partners interested in shipping
cargo by sea to Puerto Cabello, support will also be provided for onward transportation from the port
to La Guaira.
 A PAHO/WHO flight carrying 26 metric tonnes of health supplies to support the emergency response
landed at Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía.
 The Telecommunications sector advanced the installation of a community internet system
(implemented by Emergency.lu) at César Nieves Stadium, with capacity to serve up to 1,000 users
and coverage of up to 300 metres.
. Nutrition
 UNICEF conducted nutrition activities at the Playa Grande transitional camp, including nutritional
screening, infant and young child feeding counselling in emergencies, and micronutrient distribution,
prioritizing young children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers.
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 UNHCR continued providing legal counselling, psychosocial support, documentation assistance and
referrals to specialized services in transitional camps in La Guaira. On 13 July, 119 people, including
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
children and adolescents, participated in protection activities, legal assistance, case management,
psychosocial support, counselling and referral services at the Playa Grande, César Nieves Stadium
and José María Vargas Sports Complex transitional camps.
 UNFPA continued supporting the protection response in the José María Vargas, César Nieves and
Playa Grande transitional camps through gender-based violence (GBV) awareness-raising activities,
reaching 142 people during the reporting period, primarily women, including adolescent girls,
pregnant women and breastfeeding women. Dignity kits were also distributed at the César Nieves
camp.
 In addition, UNFPA provided specialized protection support across the three camps through 13
psychosocial support interventions, including psychological first aid (PFA), and followed up on one
GBV case under case management.
 IOM continued strengthening the management of the José María Vargas temporary camp, providing
assistance and protection services to 369 families and coordinating, together with UNHCR and the
state authorities, the relocation of five family groups to alternative accommodation sites in Caracas.
Planning also advanced for the installation of large-capacity tents at Campo de Golf (Tanaguarena)
to expand shelter capacity and service delivery.
 At the César Nieves temporary camp, IOM-led protection screening resulted in 20 referrals to general
health services and three referrals to Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services.
In addition, three referrals were made to the Ombudsperson's Office. At the Playa Grande temporary
camp, IOM also facilitated seven referrals to health services and two referrals to psychosocial
services. Additionally, a Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) session was
delivered to police officers.
 UNICEF and its partners provided psychosocial support to 129 children and adolescents and 47
caregivers across the José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande
temporary camps through activities aimed at strengthening emotional expression, social cohesion,
protection, positive parenting, prevention of violence and child sexual abuse, early childhood care
and life skills development.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 At the Campo de Golf (Tanaguarena) transitional camp, Fundación Vivienda Popular, with support
from IOM, distributed 120 non-food item (NFI) kits, including tarpaulins, water storage containers,
solar lamps, mosquito nets and hygiene kits, to strengthen shelter conditions for affected families.
 At the Mare Abajo temporary camp, UNHCR supported the installation of 30 solar lamps in
communal and priority areas of the site to mitigate protection risks and improve safety conditions.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 UNICEF and its partners maintained WASH interventions across the José María Vargas Sports
Complex, César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps, including the distribution of
80,000 litres of safe drinking water, monitoring of water and sanitation services, hygiene promotion
activities reaching 130 people, provision of sanitation supplies, delivery of four shower units
(including two adapted for persons with reduced mobility), and solid waste management and
sanitation facility maintenance activities.
 At the Campo de Golf (Tanaguarena) transitional camps, IOM coordinated assessments with Action
Against Hunger (ACF), Solidarités International and other partners to strengthen water, sanitation
and hygiene services, including needs related to toilets, showers, handwashing facilities, water
storage and water treatment.
 According to Caritas data as of 13 July, more than 120,000 litres of safe drinking water had been
distributed to earthquake-affected communities.
Humanitarian financing and contributions
 The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced an additional appeal under the
Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela. The appeal outlines the multisectoral needs of 1.3
million people over the next six months. To reach those in need, US$298 million is required, in
addition to the US$632 million requested at the beginning of the year.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
 IOM launched a US$98 million appeal to assist 850,000 people and support 140 entities over the
next six months. PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support
health response and early recovery activities over the next six months and released US$1.5 million
from the Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP launched an initial appeal for US$50 million to
scale up food assistance and support emergency logistics and communications activities. UNHCR
requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 The Government of Italy allocated US$5.7 million to support the humanitarian response to the
earthquakes, helping deliver life-saving assistance, protection and access to essential services for
affected populations through AICS, WFP and IFRC.
 Caritas Spain announced an increase in its contribution to €1 million to support the earthquake
response in Venezuela, including the €300,000 mobilized during the first days of the emergency.
This support is complemented by the deployment of representatives from Caritas Spain and other
Caritas network organizations in the country, providing technical and coordination support in WASH,
food security, livelihoods, risk management and shelter.
 A new European Union Humanitarian Air Bridge flight landed on 13 July carrying 29 metric tonnes
of shelter and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) supplies. The cargo included European Union-
funded assistance for IOM, Irish-funded support for GOAL Global, and UNICEF supplies.
 On 12 July, a shipment from Germany carrying 9.6 metric tonnes of medical supplies, hygiene kits
and household items was received. In addition, a shipment carrying 33.9 metric tonnes of
humanitarian assistance arrived from Türkiye.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country. Other Member States and donors have
expressed their intention to support the response through the Fund.
 The Republic of Korea has also provided US$1.25 million to WFP and US$2.5 million to UNICEF to
support the humanitarian response in Venezuela.
 Japan allocated US$3.5 million to support the earthquake response. The funding will provide
humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and non-food
items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
and IOM.
 The Royal Netherlands Navy delivered an additional shipment of humanitarian assistance and
emergency relief supplies to La Guaira as part of a sustained support mechanism from Curaçao that
has already facilitated five consecutive missions. A new vessel will be deployed to ensure the
continuity of these operations and support the delivery of assistance to affected areas.
 The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52
million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.

documents.title: Korean Government Provides Additional Humanitarian Assistance to Venezuela Following Earthquake
sources: Government of the Republic of Korea
documents.body_text:
Following its earlier provision of USD 5 million in humanitarian assistance in response to the humanitarian crisis caused by the recent devastating earthquake in Venezuela, the government of the Republic of Korea has decided to provide additional humanitarian assistance worth USD 3.5 million in view of the increasing scale of the damage.

Of this additional assistance, USD 3 million will be provided through the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) to support debris removal activities to facilitate the swift return of affected communities to normalcy.

In addition, at the request of the government of Venezuela, the government of the Republic of Korea has also decided to provide 30 tons of temporary shelters (family tents), worth approximately USD 500,000, as in-kind assistance to accommodate displaced persons.

The government of the Republic of Korea will continue to provide humanitarian assistance to countries and people affected by natural disasters.

documents.title: Direct Relief COO Craig Redmond on Venezuela’s Earthquake and the Power of Local Disaster Response
documents.body_text:
By [**Talya Meyers**](https://www.directrelief.org/author/tmeyers/)

When a magnitude 9.3 earthquake struck just off the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia in 2004, triggering a tsunami and killing more than 200,000 people within 20 minutes, Craig Redmond quickly joined the response, helping community members rebuild their livelihoods amid the wreckage.

It was an early, formative moment in a career spent responding to dozens of cataclysmic disasters.

Redmond is Direct Relief’s Chief Operating Officer and a humanitarian leader who’s spent more than 30 years working in Central and Southeast Asia, in the Caucasus, in the Horn of Africa, and elsewhere. He described earthquake survivors in Nepal staggering, grief-stricken, around a flattened village after the country’s deadly 2015 disaster, family members digging through rubble after earthquakes in Java, Indonesia, and Turkey, and anger turning to community activism and new safety measures after a 2009 earthquake near Padang, Indonesia, killed more than 1,100.

Experiences like these provide an essential road map to a disaster like [Venezuela’s devastating June earthquakes](https://www.directrelief.org/emergency/venezuela-earthquakes-2026/?c_src=https://reliefweb.int/200516462560&c_src2=p&utm_source=google&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=23998553263&utm_term=venezuela%20donation&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23998553263&gclid=Cj0KCQjwsMLSBhD9ARIsAIpUTDo7iQttaPpcgIXn4FyyZo8mBbeRYcLpxXLpCToVHMAMhcgLbJm_nRUaAsh7EALw_wcB), he said.

Venezuela’s death toll has risen to more than 3,600 and is expected to rise much higher as recovery efforts continue. In the coming months, indirect deaths from lack of access to healthcare and unmet medical needs will likely add significantly to that toll.

“These kinds of disasters are force multipliers” for a community’s existing stressors, Redmond explained. [Preventing those unnecessary deaths is key to Direct Relief’s strategy](https://www.directrelief.org/2026/07/direct-relief-venezuela-earthquake-medical-aid/?_gl=1*r63p03*_up*MQ..*_ga*MjU2NDUzMzE4LjE3ODM3MDI0MDA.*_ga_WYKLEGJW76*czE3ODM3MDIzOTkkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODM3MDI0MDUkajU0JGwwJGgxNDU2OTkxNjk3) in Venezuela over the coming weeks and months.

**Direct Relief: What are some of the earthquake responses that really stuck with you? What did you learn from them?**

**Craig Redmond:** To be there a few days after over 200,000 people lost their lives in 20 minutes during the Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami changed my perception. Not only on what humanitarian organizations should do \[during emergencies\], but how communities can respond and how the international community can respond. Then in Indonesia, there were two other massive earthquakes soon after that: one in 2006 in central Java, and one in 2009 in Padang, Sumatra.

I also was part of an on-the-ground response after the 2010 Haiti earthquake. \[Haiti’s cataclysmic 2010 earthquake is estimated to have killed over 200,000 people.\] And responded in Nepal, after another massive earthquake in 2015, and in Turkey and Syria after the 2023 quake.

One of the commonalities of all of these was that they had this sickening way of bringing to the surface deep, deep grievances at the community level: problems with corruption, problems with poor governance.

You have this first stage in which the earthquake happens and, of course, everyone bursts into action to try to save as many lives as possible. It’s an amazing thing to witness. You have people just running on adrenaline for weeks. Then the horror of what has happened begins to settle in, and then the anger comes right after that, understandably. Communities are trying to figure out, “Why couldn’t we get more immediate help? Why did these buildings collapse the way they did?”

**Direct Relief: In those situations, what interventions work?**

**Craig Redmond:** Nepal was one of those earthquakes that everyone kind of knew was coming. Nobody knew when exactly, but there had been organizations that had been talking about it for a while. At the time I was with a different NGO, and we had pre-positioned some equipment in the event that it happened. And then, sadly, it did happen.

The organization I worked with at the time was doing a distribution of basic materials: pans, blankets, that kind of stuff. We were also experimenting with cash distribution after an emergency. And I remember seeing the line of people; they’re really thankful about the pans – and then they’re going straight over to a shop and trying to sell some of them back.

And I realized, “Oh, OK. We need to help people in a way that gives them agency like cash does. It’s about finding some way to work with communities so that they can have agency and make decisions about their own future. When they’re at the worst moment of their lives, when they feel as powerless as they’ve ever felt in their lives, helping them get some sort of control over their lives is essential.”

**Direct Relief: You said that in Nepal, people knew a major earthquake would be devastating, but of course they didn’t know when one might strike. We don’t have many natural disasters that work like this. We know days in advance that a tropical storm system like a hurricane is forming. We usually know hours ahead of time that a wildfire is a serious threat, and we can evacuate people, if not always as quickly as we would like.**

**But we only know that an earthquake is happening because it’s literally already happening. How does that change the way people on the ground are impacted, the needs they have, and how we strategize a response?**

**Craig Redmond:** One thing I believe so strongly in, particularly at this point in my career and my life, is the importance of working with local organizations. That’s why Direct Relief partners with organizations on the ground. They know the situation better than anybody. Believe me, they know where the threats are going to come from. And \[because of those partnerships\], we are uniquely placed to have deep impact, particularly after rapid-onset emergencies like earthquakes. These local organizations are going to be the first responders.

In every one of the earthquakes I’ve seen, in the first 72 hours, it was mostly local organizations that were responding. In Venezuela, even the groups that could get there as fast as possible, it took 48 or 72 or sometimes more than that to even arrive. But the local organizations were there saving lives and pulling people out where they could. Building out their capacity and helping those groups is where Direct Relief is focused.

Then second, it’s about helping those groups to think through what resilience looks like for them. In the case of that area of Venezuela, there are hurricanes, and it’s an earthquake zone. So it’s helping those organizations to think through, “What will it take for us to stay operational in the event that something happens?”

That preparedness piece, and thinking through what resilience looks like, is a role that we can play.

**Direct Relief: In Venezuela, we’ve built a strategy based on reports from partners, from regional contacts, but we also know from some experience what to expect in the coming weeks, and we’re planning for that.**

**Craig Redmond:** We’re thinking about this emergency in terms of waves of needs. The first shipment we sent in had the lifesaving first aid supplies and critical medicines that are needed for trauma and other emergency issues.

The second wave of things was really more focused on waterborne illnesses and those kinds of secondary impacts. Those are going to be critical. Then the hard truth is that while everyone is focused on the earthquake and the corresponding emergencies that it triggered, all the other medical needs just go on. Moms still have babies. People still have accidents. Chronic diseases still need treatment.

These kinds of disasters are force multipliers for all the other stuff that was going to happen anyway. We need to make sure that healthcare providers not only have the trauma supplies and emergency medicines they need to respond to the earthquake, but also they’re stocked with the backup essentials that they’re going to need, so they can continue to respond to what is going to be a long recovery.

**Direct Relief: That touches on something that often gets overlooked in the media: Virtually every large-scale disaster has much broader impacts and causes much broader casualties than that official death toll suggests. What are some of the broader impacts that we’re preparing for? How will Direct Relief contain the scale of that larger spread?**

**Craig Redmond:** I’m concerned about either the collapse of systems or the further undermining of confidence in those systems. We all know that in Venezuela, it’s been a tough, tough several years. It’s going to be very difficult for people to have faith. If there’s a time when you need to be able to rely on your own \[existing\] structures, it’s now. And our work is all about trying to support, as much as we possibly can, the healthcare system. We’re putting all our effort into making sure that they have the medicines and the supplies that they need, so the system doesn’t collapse.

Sadly, what begins to happen in many of these emergencies is that, some weeks and months later, the international community largely goes away. And that tough recovery period, when the community and the local government are left to try to pick up and get to some kind of normalcy again, that can last for years.

**Direct Relief: That brings us back to that local focus. Many people do believe that it is big NGOs and international agencies who do all the most critical on-the-ground work. And those players are very important, but it is often the local communities themselves, the specialized regional responders, the local healthcare providers and leaders who have both the most immediate and the longest-term role. Let’s talk a little about that.**

**Craig Redmond:** There is nothing more important than clearly identifying the key partners that you want to work with \[before a disaster happens\], and how strategically placed they are to respond to some potential threat. You form that close partnership with them so that you know each other very well. You learn what their needs are and how we can support each other.

Over time, many international organizations will pivot away. Certainly, those that are focused on shorter-term response will.

But local organizations are there for the long haul. They’re the ones who are going to stay through the recovery phase. They are the ones who are invested in a way that an international organization just will never be. We care deeply, but it’s not our home. It’s their home, so we need to invest in them.

A lot of international organizations have known this, but haven’t quite got to the point where they’re all in on that, philosophically. Direct Relief has done only that for a long, long time. Obviously, we work with international organizations as well. But really our main focus is those local organizations in the roughly 100 countries we work with around the world.

When you do that, the necessary trust is already there, particularly when something as awful as a massive earthquake happens. They’re able to tell us what’s most needed on the ground. And we’re able to say, “It’s on its way.”

I was speaking to a colleague the other day who was saying his group was about to conduct an assessment in Venezuela before they launched a response strategy. And I thought, “We have two waves of material medical aid already there.”

That’s the speed at which you can respond when you have a network of local partners. Our strategy is to think of those partners as an extension of who we are, and we of them. And if we have that, we have a global team that can’t be matched in terms of its reach and scope.

*This interview has been edited for length.*

documents.body_text:
**Highlights**

- Two weeks after two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, official figures report more than 4,490 deaths, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people left without housing. More than 1,200 aftershocks have been recorded, while damage assessments continue.
- UNICEF is delivering life-saving and protective services in the initial phase of the response. This includes WASH services across three temporary camps in La Guaira reaching more than 3,500 people. Hygiene supplies have been distributed to more than 6,900 people across temporary camps. Mobile health teams have been deployed across affected areas providing medical services to over 3,100 people. Child-Friendly Spaces are operational in four temporary camps in La Guaira, providing regular psychosocial support and recreational activities to more than 890 children and adolescents.
- UNICEF continues to scale up its humanitarian response, having distributed at least 82 metric tons of emergency supplies. The supplies include emergency health kits, water purification and storage equipment, tents for child-friendly spaces and service delivery points, and early childhood development and recreational kits.
- In addition to the US$137.6 million requested under the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal and aligned with the addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan 2026, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to respond to the humanitarian impact of the earthquakes.

documents.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #11 (10 to 12 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
The eleventh Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 10 to 12 July.

**Highlights**

Between 10 and 12 July, IOM expanded its response in La Guaira through interventions in transitory camps and affected communities. Operations focused particularly on five priority sites: César Nieves Stadium, José María Vargas Sports Centre, Playa Grande, Tanaguarena Golf Course and Mare Abajo II.

To date, IOM has reached 5,312 unique individuals through 8,227 instances of assistance and services, mainly in health, shelter and site coordination, protection, and water, sanitation and hygiene.

IOM continued strengthening protection screening and referrals, the restoration of identity documentation and the updating of population records. In coordination with the authorities, 237 identity documents were renewed at César Nieves Stadium.

**IOM Activities**

IOM continues supporting transitory camps and affected communities in La Guaira through shelter, site coordination, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, information management and inter-agency coordination.

At César Nieves Stadium, IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular distributed 78 kitchen sets and buckets, provided guidance to 49 people and installed an internet network. Twenty-four community showers, seven washing stations and new water supply points were also established.

In the El Campito community, 141 kits containing tarpaulins, buckets and kitchen sets were distributed, along with 139 hygiene kits. At Tanaguarena Golf Course and Mare Abajo II, progress was made in installing tents for accommodation, storage and service provision, while bunk beds and mattresses were received to improve conditions for affected families.

At José María Vargas Sports Centre, 52 additional health services were provided. To date, IOM has delivered 4,304 health services as part of the response and continues strengthening medical referral pathways and coordination with Emergency Medical Teams.

Registration reached 522 families and 1,566 individuals at César Nieves Stadium; 129 families and 404 individuals at Playa Grande; and 369 families and 1,319 individuals at José María Vargas Sports Centre. IOM also introduced a tool for the weekly monitoring of needs in temporary camps.

**IOM Planned Response**

IOM will continue strengthening the management and improvement of transitory camps, the organization of distributions, WASH, health and MHPSS services, protection screening and referrals, access to documentation, and measures to prevent sexual exploitation and abuse.

IOM will also continue population registration and monitoring, multisectoral assessments, mobility tracking and support to the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group to consolidate information and coordinate interventions.

Situation Report #11 | From 10 to 12 July 2026
IOM’S APPEAL: FUNDING PRIORITIES
IOM is appealing to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities between July and December 2026. Additional funding will enable
IOM to scale up a multisectoral response across six priority áreas, key proposed actions per sector are:
SHELTER, LAND AND SITE COORDINATION
• Procure and distribute emergency shelter materials and core relief items, including tarpaulins, tents, solar lamps, kitchen sets,
jerrycans, blankets and other essential household items.
• Improve transitory camps and collective sites through covered spaces, lighting, drainage, fire safety measures, debris removal,
accessibility upgrades and basic site improvements.
• Strengthen site management teams, community committees, information points, complaint and feedback mechanisms, refe-
rral systems and inclusive participation.
• Integrate exit strategies to facilitate safe, voluntary and dignified returns, relocations or transition to early recovery.
EARLY RECOVERY AND SOLUTIONS
• Support affected households to restore livelihoods, access basic rights, recover documentation, address housing, land and
property issues, and strengthen social cohesion.
• Assist authorities and communities to co-create recovery plans that link needs with longer-term durable solutions.
• Support civil society and community-based actors through technical assistance, grants, training and planning.
• Rehabilitate critical infrastructure and essential services, including water systems, schools, health facilities and marketplaces.
HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH AND PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT (MHPSS)
• Deploy additional multidisciplinary health and MHPSS teams to provide primary healthcare, emergency care, referrals and

documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #11 (10 al 12 de julio de 2026)
documents.body_text:
El undécimo Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, con información correspondiente al período del 10 al 12 de julio.

**Aspectos destacados**

Entre el 10 y el 12 de julio, la OIM amplió su respuesta en La Guaira mediante intervenciones en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas. Las operaciones se concentraron especialmente en el Estadio César Nieves, el Polideportivo José María Vargas, Playa Grande, el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena y Mare Abajo II.

A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado a 5.312 personas únicas mediante 8.227 asistencias y servicios, principalmente en salud, alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, protección, y agua, saneamiento e higiene.

La OIM continuó fortaleciendo el triaje y las derivaciones de protección, la restitución de documentación y la actualización de registros. En coordinación con las autoridades, se renovaron 237 documentos de identidad en el Estadio César Nieves.

**Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM continúa apoyando campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas en La Guaira mediante alojamiento, coordinación de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, registro, gestión de información y coordinación interagencial.

En el Estadio César Nieves, la OIM y la Fundación Vivienda Popular distribuyeron 78 sets de cocina y baldes, brindaron orientación a 49 personas e instalaron una red de internet. También se habilitaron 24 duchas comunitarias, siete estaciones de lavado y nuevos puntos de abastecimiento de agua.

En la comunidad El Campito se distribuyeron 141 kits con lonas, baldes y sets de cocina, además de 139 kits de higiene. En el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena y Mare Abajo II se avanzó en la instalación de carpas para alojamiento, almacenamiento y prestación de servicios, y se recibieron literas y colchones para mejorar las condiciones de las familias.

En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se brindaron 52 nuevas asistencias de salud. A la fecha, la OIM ha prestado 4.304 asistencias de salud durante la respuesta y continúa fortaleciendo las rutas de referencia médica y la coordinación con equipos médicos de emergencia.

El registro alcanzó 522 familias y 1.566 personas en el Estadio César Nieves; 129 familias y 404 personas en Playa Grande; y 369 familias y 1.319 personas en el Polideportivo José María Vargas. La OIM también inició una herramienta para el monitoreo semanal de necesidades en campamentos transitorios.

**Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La OIM continuará fortaleciendo la gestión y adecuación de campamentos transitorios, la organización de distribuciones, los servicios de WASH, salud y SMAPS, el triaje y las derivaciones de protección, la documentación y las medidas de prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual.

También continuará el registro y seguimiento de la población, las evaluaciones multisectoriales, el monitoreo de la movilidad y el apoyo al Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales para consolidar información y coordinar las intervenciones.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #3 (July 13, 2026)
documents.body_text:
**FAST FACTS**

- On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela consecutively, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira. In response, the government declared a state of emergency.
- A reported 9.73 million people have been affected by the quakes, with more than 530,000 people having been exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.
- Official figures have confirmed more than 4,490 fatalities, 16,700 injuries, 6,400 people rescued and nearly 18,000 without housing.
- Affected populations have been left without access to basic necessities such as medicines, healthcare services, food and safe water.

**OUR RESPONSE**

- International Medical Corps’ rapid-response teams immediately deployed after the quakes, conducting a rapid needs assessment on June 25.
- Based on identified needs, International Medical Corps deployed an mobile medical unit (MMU) that has so far provided 1,273 consultations since beginning operations.
- On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility to provide free medical services to impacted communities.
- Our teams have so far provided 164 consultations through the EMT Type 1 Fixed facility.
- International Medical Corps has conducted a detailed assessment of shelters housing displaced persons, and is conducting water trucking to multiple affected camps.

Needs are continuing to increase given the compromised living conditions and increased risk of communicable disease, accumulation of waste in affected communities, and the upcoming rainy season and associated flooding. As the situation on the ground evolves, International Medical Corps is continuing to communicate with local and international organizations involved in the response, to ensure that we continue to provide critically needed services in an effective, coordinated manner.

Funding  
USD 80 Million required to support families affected by the earthquakes.  
USD 20 Million for regular programmes, including school feeding. Resources and stock from regular programmes have been redirected to the emergency, making donor support critical on both fronts. Situation

Update  
• After the twin earthquakes of 24 June, families in the most affected areas continue to face dire conditions, depending on humanitarian assistance as a critical lifeline. Official figures now report over 4,490 deaths, with the toll still expected to rise.  
• WFP data collection across the seven most affected states reveals damage to infrastructure, disruptions to basic services, and severe impacts on livelihoods. Households struggle to access food and essential items, consistently identifying food assistance, safe drinking water, healthcare, and medicines, and hygiene items as their most urgent needs.  
• Commercial activity is gradually recovering, though significant challenges remain, including rising prices, transport constraints, and shortages of essential goods. In specific communities, however, markets are now functioning well enough to reliably supply food to families with purchasing capacity.

documents.title: Cáritas Española aumenta a un millón los fondos para responder a la emergencia humanitaria causada por el doble terremoto en Venezuela
documents.body_text:
**• Se une al equipo que gestiona la atención a la urgencia bajo el liderazgo de Cáritas Venezuela**

**• En las primeras semanas, la campaña “Cáritas con Venezuela” alcanza los 5 millones de euros**

Cáritas.- 13 de julio de 2026. Ante la crisis humanitaria causada por el doble terremoto del pasado 24 de junio en el norte de Venezuela, Cáritas Española ha decidido aumentar a un millón de euros los fondos que se enviarán a Cáritas Venezuela para responder a las necesidades de las personas afectadas por esta catástrofe. Esta partida incluye los 300.000 euros que ya han sido movilizados durante los primeros días de la tragedia. Además, ha desplazado a un cooperante con base en Bogotá (Colombia), que ya se ha incorporado al equipo de Cáritas Venezuela para apoyar en la coordinación de la respuesta y su operativa.

NOTA DE PRENSA
Cáritas Española aumenta a un millón los fondos para responder a la
emergencia humanitaria causada por el doble terremoto en Venezuela
• Se une al equipo que gestiona la atención a la urgencia bajo el liderazgo de
Cáritas Venezuela
• En las primeras semanas, la campaña “Cáritas con Venezuela” alcanza los 5
millones de euros
Cáritas.- 13 de julio de 2026. Ante la crisis humanitaria causada por el doble terremoto
del pasado 24 de junio en el norte de Venezuela, Cáritas Española ha decidido
aumentar a un millón de euros los fondos que se enviarán a Cáritas Venezuela para
responder a las necesidades de las personas afectadas por esta catástrofe. Esta partida
incluye los 300.000 euros que ya han sido movilizados durante los primeros días de la
tragedia. Además, ha desplazado a un cooperante con base en Bogotá (Colombia), que
ya se ha incorporado al equipo de Cáritas Venezuela para apoyar en la coordinación de
la respuesta y su operativa.
Nuestro cooperante se suma a los representantes de diversas Cáritas aliadas (CRS -
Cáritas Estados Unidos-, Cáritas Alemania, Cáritas América Latina y Caribe, Cáritas
Puerto Rico) que se encuentran desplegados en el país, trabajando hombro a hombro
con los equipos locales. Este contingente internacional incluye a especialistas de
primer nivel en las áreas de WASH (Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene), gestión de riesgos,
seguridad alimentaria y medios de vida, y refugio.
La presencia de este equipo internacional no solo está ayudando a atender la urgencia,
sino que busca diseñar e implementar estrategias conjuntas que fortalezcan las
capacidades de Cáritas Venezuela a futuro, transformando el dolor de esta tragedia en
una base sólida de resiliencia y esperanza para las comunidades más afectadas.
El cooperante de Cáritas Española ha enfocado estos primeros días sus esfuerzos en
entender la magnitud de la catástrofe. Además, ha visitado La Guaira y escuchado de
primera mano las necesidades de las personas y la respuesta global de los actores
humanitarios. El objetivo es identificar vacíos en la respuesta a los que dirigir los
recursos y que la ayuda de Cáritas Española contribuya a que nadie se quede sin la
atención necesaria.
Prensa Cáritas Española
Laura Daniele (618 893 880) – Merche Fernández (606 53 51 56)

CÁRITAS ESPAÑOLA EQUIPO DE COMUNICACIÓN Y SENSIBILIZACIÓN
91 444 10 16  comunicacion.ssgg@caritas.es  Embajadores 162 - 28045 Madrid
“La realidad es completamente desoladora, no hay palabras para describirla, pero los
equipos de Cáritas, personas voluntarias y profesionales trabajan sin descanso para
mitigar el sufrimiento de tantísimos afectados”, asegura Manuel Gutiérrez,
cooperante de Cáritas Española.
El voluntariado, corazón de la respuesta
Tras los terremotos del 24 de junio de 2026, Cáritas Venezuela activó sus mecanismos
de respuesta de emergencia y movilizó personal, voluntarios y recursos en los estados
afectados. Cáritas estableció un centro nacional de coordinación y activó una red de
centros de acopio en las sedes diocesanas y parroquias de todo el país para canalizar
donaciones y apoyo humanitario.
Durante la primera fase de la respuesta, Cáritas Venezuela benefició a 4.481 familias a
través de la entrega de igual número de kits de seguridad alimentaria, lo que equivale
a un estimado de 72.000 personas atendidas. Ha distribuido también 1.000 kits para
equipos de búsqueda y rescate, más de 120.000 litros de agua potable y 73.356
insumos médicos y medicamentos, alcanzando a 17.924 personas. El 61,3 % de los
insumos médicos fue entregado directamente a hospitales y centros de salud.
El voluntariado está siendo el corazón de esta respuesta. Cada día, un promedio de
280 voluntarios trabaja en la operación, con una jornada media de 7,5 horas por
persona, lo que representa 2.100 horas de servicio diarias al servicio de las familias
afectadas.
Las actividades se priorizan en los estados más afectados por el desastre, como La
Guaira, donde se concentra los mayores niveles de destrucción de viviendas,
infraestructura y servicios básicos. También hay importantes daños en el Distrito
Capital (Caracas) y Miranda, Carabobo y Yaracuy -ubicados cerca de la zona del
epicentro-, y Aragua y Falcón, donde los daños son considerables.
Además de las intervenciones en los estados directamente afectados, Cáritas
Venezuela brinda asistencia a familias desplazadas que se han trasladado a otras zonas
del país en busca de refugio con familiares, comunidades de acogida o instalaciones de
la Iglesia.
Cáritas Venezuela se encuentra realizando evaluaciones rápidas y sectoriales en las
zonas afectadas por el terremoto, en coordinación con autoridades, comunidades y
otros actores humanitarios. Dado que la situación continúa evolucionando, las
necesidades identificadas siguen actualizándose lo que permite adaptar en tiempo real
las prioridades de la respuesta humanitaria.
Prensa Cáritas Española
Laura Daniele (618 893 880) – Merche Fernández (606 53 51 56)

CÁRITAS ESPAÑOLA EQUIPO DE COMUNICACIÓN Y SENSIBILIZACIÓN
91 444 10 16  comunicacion.ssgg@caritas.es  Embajadores 162 - 28045 Madrid
5 millones de euros alcanzados
Durante las primeras semanas, la campaña Cáritas con Venezuela ha alcanzado los
cinco millones de euros. “Desde el inicio de la emergencia, la sociedad española ha
confiado en la red de Cáritas para apoyar a las personas víctimas del terremoto.
Agradecemos una vez más la enorme solidaridad de donantes, instituciones y
empresas. En toda la Confederación somos muy conscientes de la gran responsabilidad
que supone estar a la altura de la confianza que la sociedad deposita en Cáritas”,
explica María Ángeles García, coordinadora del equipo de Donantes y Relación con las
Empresas de Cáritas Española.
La directora de Cáritas Venezuela, Janeth Márquez, señala, por su parte, que “los
recursos movilizados hasta ahora cubren la fase inicial de la emergencia. En las
próximas semanas, las necesidades se mantendrán y las etapas de recuperación y
reconstrucción exigirán sostener la solidaridad en el tiempo. Por ello, hacemos un
llamado a mantener las contribuciones económicas, y a seguir caminando juntos”.
30 años de compromiso firme
Desde hace más de tres décadas, Cáritas Española sostiene un compromiso sólido y
continuado con Cáritas Venezuela. Fue especialmente importante la colaboración a
raíz de la emergencia por inundaciones y corrimiento de tierras en 1999 (Tragedia de
Vargas), cuyo acompañamiento se concretó con la presencia de un cooperante en el
terreno hasta 2004.
Posteriormente la presencia fue vinculándose a apoyos puntuales en el desarrollo de
planes estratégicos, programas de fortalecimiento institucional y de capacidades y/o
proyectos de desarrollo.
En 2015 se retomó de nuevo una colaboración más intensa con Caritas Venezuela para
seguir y responder a la crisis migratoria y articular el apoyo de la red internacional.
En los últimos años, la colaboración entre Cáritas Española y Cáritas Venezuela se ha
centrado en dos líneas de acción: un programa de atención y monitoreo de la
desnutrición de niños/as menores de 5 años y de mujeres embarazadas y lactantes y
otro programa de reducción de riesgos de desastres, a través de la organización
comunitaria para la preparación ante las principales amenazas.
Prensa Cáritas Española
Laura Daniele (618 893 880) – Merche Fernández (606 53 51 56)

documents.title: Dispatch of the Second Japan Disaster Relief Medical Team in Response to the Earthquake Damage in Venezuela
documents.body_text:
In light of the high demand for medical support in the earthquake-affected areas of Venezuela, the Government of Japan decided to dispatch the second batch of the Japan Disaster Relief (JDR) Medical Team to the affected area. The second team consists of staff of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), as well as registered doctors, nurses, and other health professionals, and is scheduled to depart Japan for Venezuela next week.  
  
The Government of Japan will continue to stand by the people of Venezuela and provide necessary assistance based on local needs.

## (Reference) Overview of Damage

In Venezuela, a magnitude 7+ earthquake that occurred at approximately 7:00 a.m. Japan Standard Time on Thursday, June 25, caused numerous casualties, including deaths and injuries, and property damage. According to the Venezuelan government's announcement, the damage includes 3,889 deaths and over 16,740 injuries (as of July 10, 6:00a.m.). According to an assessment by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), approximately 58,870 buildings across the affected areas may have been destroyed or damaged. The full extent of the damage is still unknown.

documents.title: Emergency Grant and Other Humanitarian Assistance in Response to the Earthquake Disaster in Venezuela
documents.body_text:
On July 10, the Government of Japan decided to provide an Emergency Grant of USD 3.5 million in response to the earthquake disaster in Venezuela.

With this Emergency Grant, the Government of Japan will provide humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food, health and medical care, shelters and non-food items through the World Food Programme (WFP), the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

1. In response to the earthquake disaster in Venezuela, the Government of Japan had already decided on June 30 to provide emergency relief goods, such as plastic sheet (Tarpaulin), portable jerry can, and water purifier, through the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), and on July 1 to dispatch the Japan Disaster Relief Medical Team. In addition, Japan Platform (JPF), a mechanism for emergency humanitarian assistance by NGOs, the business community and the government, plans to implement approximately USD 1 million of humanitarian assistance funded by the Japanese government’s grant.
2. The Government of Japan intends to work closely with relevant agencies and organizations to provide the necessary assistance that benefits the people of Venezuela in a timely manner.

## (Reference1) Implementing agencies, areas of assistance, and the amount of disbursement:

- - WFP: Food \[USD 1.5 million\]
- - IFRC: Health and medical care \[USD 1 million\]
- - IOM: Shelter and non-food items \[USD 1 million\]

## (Reference2) Overview of Damage (as of July 10, 6 a.m.)

In Venezuela, an earthquake measuring more than magnitude 7.0 that occurred at approximately 7:00 a.m. Japan Standard Time on Thursday, June 25, caused numerous casualties, and extensive property damage. According to the Venezuelan government's announcement, the damage includes 3,889 deaths and over 16,740 injuries. According to an assessment by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), approximately 58,870 buildings across the affected areas may have been destroyed or damaged. The full extent of the damage is still unknown.

## (Reference3) Humanitarian assistance through JPF

The amount of contributions: JPY 150 million (Approximately USD 1 million) Based on the ongoing needs assessment in the field, JPF member NGOs will provide support to disaster victims, utilizing funds provided by the Japanese government to JPF.

documents.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #19 (12 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 19**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**12 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,200 aftershocks.**
- Official toll: **4,490 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.**
- **Tom Fletcher, the United Nations humanitarian chief, concluded his four-day visit to the country and called for sustained international support for the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP).**
- **An additional appeal for US$298 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,222 aftershocks.**

Eighteen days after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **4,490 people dead, 16,740 injured and 6,462 rescued since the onset of the emergency**. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people remain without housing**. According to official reports of 11 July, 315 of those who died have yet to be identified.

The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher concluded his visit to Venezuela this week and called on the international community to sustain support for the humanitarian response. In this context, he **announced a US$298 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan, aimed at addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months**.
