high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and
7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local
time) in the north-central region, with
the epicentre located along the San
Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis
(Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities
report 1,222 aftershocks.
Eighteen days after the earthquakes,
authorities report a toll of 4,490 people
dead, 16,740 injured and 6,462
rescued since the onset of the
emergency. Authorities also indicated
that 17,907 people remain without
housing. According to official reports
of 11 July, 315 of those who died have
yet to be identified.
The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps
and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination
with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance.
United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom
Fletcher concluded his visit to Venezuela this week and called on the international community to sustain
support for the humanitarian response. In this context, he announced a US$298 million addendum to
the Humanitarian Response Plan, aimed at addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people
over the next six months.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira
State, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects
intended for affected populations.
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
National response
 The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, as well as assistance
to affected people.
 According to authorities, the response continues with 108 transitional camps supporting affected
populations, with a capacity of 25,087 people and a current occupancy of 19,583 people. As of
12 July, 41 camps are located in Caracas, 29 in Miranda, 28 in La Guaira, and 10 in Aragua.
 Authorities are advancing a unified registration process for affected families in transitional camps
through the collection of biometric and contact information to support assistance management, social
support programmes and housing solutions.
 The Government of Venezuela announced the creation of an initial reconstruction fund equivalent to
US$200 million.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com) and to
report affected individuals (0-800-RESCATE).
 School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto
Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital
District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión,
Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 In Chacao Municipality, authorities reported that technical infrastructure assessments remain
ongoing, with 26 buildings currently undergoing specialized review.
Response actions: Three (3) VHF-funded organizations operating in municipalities across Miranda
State and the Capital District (Cedesex, Construyendo Futuros and FUNDANA) are supporting the initial
response through general protection, child protection and gender-based violence (GBV) services. In
addition, organizations such as Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA and World Vision are providing protection
support to affected families, particularly through psychosocial assistance.
La Guaira
 Authorities and humanitarian organizations continue strengthening the response in La Guaira’s
transitional camps through the expansion of multisectoral services, improvements in accommodation
conditions and coordinated assistance management. During the reporting period, progress was
made in the distribution of essential items, protection activities, health and psychosocial support
interventions, as well as actions to improve access to safe water, sanitation, connectivity and
community infrastructure.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Response actions: Five (5) partners of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF) are supporting the
response through primary health care and psychological support services (Fundación Proyecto
Maniapure, Paluz, Ven Da Tu Mano, Venezuelan Red Cross and Tinta Violeta).
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In Carabobo, the most significant impacts continue to be concentrated in Juan José Mora
municipality (Morón parish). In Yaracuy, particularly in Veroes municipality and other localities near
the epicentral area, homes have been reported as destroyed or at high risk. Recent assessments
have identified priority needs in protection, mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter,
water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security.
Response actions: Five organizations (Venezuelan Red Cross, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón
and Empodérame) are providing response in health, food, water and the distribution of humanitarian
assistance.
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
 In Silva Municipality, localized flooding was reported in parts of Boca de Aroa as a result of high surf
conditions, affecting communities previously impacted by the earthquakes and by soil liquefaction
phenomena. Local authorities continue to monitor the situation and implement preventive measures
to reduce risks to the population.
 The situation highlights a multi-hazard scenario in Silva Municipality, where earthquake-related
impacts are compounded by coastal events, increasing protection, WASH, psychosocial support and
early recovery needs.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with Civil Protection and Local Coordination Forum (LCF) partners to
monitor the situation, verify humanitarian needs and identify potential complementary support
actions.
Response actions: The capacity-building activities led by the Subnational Protection Cluster continue,
alongside the operational agenda in Boca de Aroa, which has been expanded at the request of regional
authorities to include Palmasola Municipality. Activities focus on WASH and psychosocial support and are
being implemented by Action Against Hunger, Azul Positivo, IOM, Centroccidente, ODISEF and AVSI, in
coordination with regional authorities.
Other states
 Apure: Authorities report the arrival of more than 250 affected people. The Local Coordination
Forum (LCF) continues to monitor the situation and provide multisectoral assistance, including
psychological first aid (PFA).
 Delta Amacuro: Assistance continues for 98 people relocated from Caracas and La Guaira,
primarily through family reunification processes. Identified needs are concentrated in mental health
and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and the monitoring of population movements. Authorities and
humanitarian organizations are advancing preparations for multiservice outreach activities that will
include food assistance, hygiene kits, health support and protection services for host families in the
state. As part of these efforts, WFP plans to distribute food baskets to 52 people, World Vision will
complement the response with 22 food rations, and Cáritas Delta Amacuro will distribute 52 hygiene
kits.
 Sucre: Authorities report the movement of 641 people, mainly from La Guaira and Caracas, of
whom 187 moved independently and 454 received institutional support for transportation. Response
activities include reception, registration, medical assistance, psychosocial support and protection
services, with particular attention to children, older people and other vulnerable groups. A technical
commission is assessing the habitability of receiving facilities.
 Táchira: ASONACOP and UNICEF reported that, on 12 July, two families in transit were assisted
(including two children and two adults) through the distribution of hygiene kits and food kits. The
families were travelling to Aragua and Anzoátegui states. A multidisciplinary team followed up on the
arrival of a separated child and provided guidance on documentation, birth registration, medical and
psychological care, and school enrolment.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
 Zulia: Assistance continues for affected people arriving from La Guaira and Caracas, primarily
through the Maracaibo passenger terminal. The Citizen Assistance Unit and ASONACOP, together
with the Venezuelan Red Cross, HIAS, CESVI, ASOREZ and Cáritas, continue operating a joint
service point providing food assistance, legal support and hygiene kits. More than 30 family groups
were assisted this week, including around 20 families in Jesús Enrique Lossada municipality (San
José and Concepción parishes) and at least eight family groups at the Maracaibo terminal, in addition
to assistance provided through other outreach activities. The majority of those assisted are women,
children and older people. While some remain in the state, others continue their journey to Colombia.
 In Bolívar, Trujillo, Nueva Esparta and Lara states, coordination, collection of aid and monitoring
activities remain ongoing.
Humanitarian coordination
 The United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief
Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, concluded his visit to Venezuela this week, during which he met with
affected people, humanitarian workers, national authorities, private sector leaders and
representatives of the diplomatic community. He called for continued support to the Humanitarian
Response Plan (HRP) to help address the most urgent humanitarian needs.
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
continues to coordinate the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner
organizations, prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, WASH, logistics and protection. In
this context, the United Nations system held a working meeting with the Single Authority for
Operation Rescue and Hope 2026 to review priority needs, strengthen inter-institutional coordination
and follow up on joint earthquake response efforts.
 UNDAC and OCHA continued supporting Civil Protection in strengthening emergency coordination
and information management capacities, including technical exchanges on USAR coordination
mechanisms and operational tracking tools.
 OCHA continued strengthening coordination with the private sector to support response and early
recovery efforts, promoting engagement with specialized actors in areas such as logistics, debris
management, infrastructure rehabilitation and reconstruction planning through existing coordination
mechanisms between the United Nations and the private sector.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
within the framework of the United Nations system and with the support of UNDP. In line with the
internationally recognized PDNA methodology, the corresponding coordination efforts with relevant
counterparts will be advanced.
 Authorities informed the activation of a special mechanism to expedite the processing of a “Work
Visa for Special Situations” through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The procedure will be carried out
online under the coordination of the Office of the Vice Minister for Multilateral Affairs and the Consular
Affairs Office. It is intended for foreign personnel of international organizations, as well as United
Nations staff, deploying to Venezuela in support of the response to the earthquake emergency.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 To date, WFP has reached 62,429 people with food assistance as part of the earthquake
emergency response. On the reporting day, WFP and its cooperating partners continued providing
immediate food support through a combination of ready-to-eat rations, family food baskets, and hot
meals. A total of 7,756 ready-to-eat food kits were distributed to affected populations in Distrito
Capital and La Guaira, including 3,978 kits in Sucre parish (Libertador Municipality, Distrito Capital)
and 3,778 kits in Catia La Mar (Vargas Municipality, La Guaira State). In addition, WFP distributed
364 family food baskets in the Urimare area of Playa Grande, reaching 1,456 people, and 200 family
food baskets in a temporary shelter in Santa Rosalía parish, Distrito Capital, supporting 800 people.
 Hot meal distributions also continued across temporary shelters in La Guaira, with 7,262 meals
served, including 1,225 meals in Playa Grande community, 2,795 meals at the César Nieves
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
baseball stadium, and 3,242 meals at the José María Vargas sports stadium. Through these
interventions, WFP and its partners continue to ensure uninterrupted access to food for displaced
and earthquake-affected populations while supporting their immediate food security needs.
Health
 At Polideportivo José María Vargas Transitional Camp, IOM has supported the implementation of
12 mobile health outreach activities, through which 969 consultations have been provided to date in
general medicine, paediatrics, internal medicine, mental health, psychological first aid (PFA) and
case referrals.
 UNICEF supported the provision of health services in the Polideportivo Vargas, César Nieves
Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps, where 177 vaccine doses were administered,
including yellow fever, tetanus toxoid, measles and other childhood vaccines. In addition, UNICEF
provided individual psychological support to 44 people and primary health care services to 29 people.
 UNFPA has provided sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services in the Polideportivo Vargas,
César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps, reaching 1,063 people through
awareness-raising activities to date. In addition, it has provided antenatal care to 53 pregnant women
and has facilitated access to contraceptive methods for 331 people.
 At César Nieves Stadium Transitional Camp, IOM continued protection screening and inter-agency
coordination activities, facilitating referrals for 20 people to general health services, one person to
mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, and two gender-based violence (GBV)
cases.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 Several humanitarian organizations continue to channel the delivery of assistance by sea through
Puerto Cabello Port, currently the nearest operational commercial port to La Guaira, while La Guaira
Port prioritizes the reception of bilateral donations.
 WFP’s telecommunications team, with the support of emergency.lu, G-Networks and CONATEL,
advanced the installation of community internet access solutions in Caraballeda and at César Nieves
Stadium, which are expected to become operational by the end of the day. Each site will provide
coverage of approximately 200 metres and connectivity for up to 100 devices, while installation in
Playa Grande is scheduled for 15 July.
Nutrition
 UNICEF maintained nutrition activities in the Polideportivo Vargas, César Nieves Stadium and Playa
Grande transitional camps through nutritional screening, supplementation and counselling for
children under five, pregnant women and breastfeeding women, including nutritional monitoring, the
promotion of breastfeeding and the distribution of micronutrient supplements.
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 UNFPA strengthened gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response activities in the
Polideportivo Vargas, César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps, reaching 908
people through awareness-raising activities to date. In addition, UNFPA has provided psychosocial
support to 52 people, managed 11 protection cases and delivered legal counselling.
 UNICEF provided psychosocial support to 122 children and adolescents and 37 parents and
caregivers in the Polideportivo Vargas, César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps
through Child-Friendly Spaces and recreational, educational and psychosocial activities.
 At Campo de Golf (Tanaguarena) Transitional Camp, IOM strengthened Prevention of Sexual
Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) activities through awareness-raising initiatives targeting
communities, authorities and organizations present on site, the dissemination of information
materials in common areas, and coordination with World Central Kitchen (WCK) to expand
prevention messaging among the camp population.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
 At Mare Abajo II Transitional Camp, people with specific protection needs were referred to DRC for
guidance and referral to specialized health services, as well as to community structures for support
and referral of cases of extreme vulnerability.
 UNHCR will continue providing protection and psychosocial support services in the Playa Grande,
Polideportivo José María Vargas and César Nieves Stadium transitional camps on 13 July.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 At Mare Abajo II Transitional Camp, UNHCR supported the strengthening of shelter conditions
through the installation of 15 solar lamps in communal areas, helping improve site lighting and
mitigate protection risks.
 At Mare Abajo II Transitional Camp, 105 bunk beds were received through the “Beds for Venezuela”
initiative, along with 50 mattresses donated by the Flor de la Esperanza Foundation.
 UNHCR plans to conduct a distribution of non-food items (NFIs) on 13 July for people
accommodated at Polideportivo José María Vargas transitional camp.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 UNICEF maintained water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services in the Polideportivo Vargas,
César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande transitional camps, providing 20,000 litres of safe drinking
water per camp for the resident population. UNICEF also advanced efforts to strengthen WASH
infrastructure through the expansion of water storage capacity and the planning and installation of
complementary sanitation facilities, including toilets, showers and washing stations. In parallel,
sanitation activities, solid waste management, facility monitoring and hygiene promotion continued.
Humanitarian financing and contributions
 The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced an additional appeal under the
Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela. The appeal outlines the multisectoral needs of 1.3
million people over the next six months. To reach those in need, US$298 million is required, in
addition to the US$632 million requested at the beginning of the year.
 The Government of Japan allocated US$3.5 million to support the earthquake response. The funding
will provide humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and
non-food items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
(IFRC) and IOM.
 The Royal Netherlands Navy delivered an additional shipment of humanitarian assistance and
emergency relief supplies to La Guaira as part of a sustained support mechanism from Curaçao that
has already facilitated five consecutive missions. A new vessel will be deployed to ensure the
continuity of these operations and support the delivery of assistance to affected areas.
 Authorities announced the arrival of a new shipment from the Russian Federation carrying 25 metric
tons of humanitarian assistance, including household items and high-priority medical and
pharmaceutical supplies.
 In addition, on 12 July, 88 containers of humanitarian aid were received from CARICOM, including
medicines, food and other relief supplies.
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country. Other Member States and donors have
expressed their intention to support the response through the Fund.
 IOM launched a US$98 million appeal to assist 850,000 people and support 140 entities over
the next six months. PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to
support health response and early recovery activities over the next six months and released US$1.5
million from the Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP launched an initial appeal for US$50
million to scale up food assistance and support emergency logistics and communications activities.
UNHCR requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52
million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
Contact information
For more information, please contact the OCHA Venezuela Office:
Vanessa May – Head of Office a.i. – mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Humanitarian Affairs Officer – alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Public Information Officer – moreno7@un.org
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

documents.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 19**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**12 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), l**as autoridades reportan más de 1.200 réplicas.**
- Balance oficial: **4.490 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.**
- **Tom Fletcher, jefe humanitario de las Naciones Unidas, concluyó su visita de cuatro días al país e hizo un llamado a mantener el compromiso internacional con el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria.**
- **Se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$298 millones para ampliar la respuesta a los terremotos y atender las necesidades de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.**
- El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas.

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos  
 el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.222 réplicas.**

A 18 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **4.490 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas desde el inicio de la emergencia.** Asimismo, indicaron que **17.907 personas permanecen sin vivienda.** Según las autoridades, hasta el sábado 11 de julio, 315 de las personas fallecidas continuaban sin ser identificadas.

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la gestión de los campamentos  
 transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, concluyó esta semana su visita a Venezuela e instó a la comunidad internacional a mantener el apoyo a la respuesta humanitaria. En ese contexto, anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por 298 millones de dólares, destinada a atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.

Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
Impacto en infraestructura
 Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.
 Como parte de la planificación para la recuperación y reconstrucción, las autoridades identificaron
40 terrenos en el estado La Guaira, equivalentes a aproximadamente 584.000 metros cuadrados,
para el desarrollo de proyectos habitacionales destinados a la población afectada.
 Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de
Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil
millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas,
comercios, escuelas, hospitales e instalaciones públicas. Entre tanto, estimaciones preliminares de
PNUD indican daños físicos directos por 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 6 % del PIB.
Respuesta nacional
 La respuesta gubernamental se mantiene centrada en las labores de búsqueda y rescate, así como
en la atención de las personas afectadas.
 De acuerdo con las autoridades, la respuesta continúa con 108 campamentos transitorios para
la atención de personas afectadas, con capacidad para 25.087 personas y una ocupación de
19.583 personas. Hasta el 12 de julio, 41 campamentos se encuentran instalados en Caracas, 29
en Miranda, 28 en La Guaira, y 10 en Aragua.
 Las autoridades avanzan en un proceso de registro único de las familias afectadas en campamentos
transitorios, mediante la recopilación de datos biométricos y de contacto para apoyar la gestión de
la asistencia, los programas de apoyo social y las soluciones habitacionales.
 El Gobierno venezolano anunció la creación de un fondo inicial de reconstrucción equivalente a 200
millones de dólares.
 Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad
(Conapdis) para coordinar una respuesta oportuna e inclusiva en las zonas afectadas.
 Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas
(www.localizapacientes.com) y el reporte de personas afectadas (0-800-RESCATE).
 Las actividades escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados
Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José
Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas);
Distrito Capital (Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo,
Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).
Situación por estado
Distrito Capital (Caracas) y Miranda
 En el municipio Chacao, las autoridades informaron que continúan las evaluaciones técnicas de
infraestructura, con 26 edificios actualmente en proceso de revisión especializada.
Acciones de respuesta: Tres (3) organizaciones del Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV) con
proyectos financiados en municipios del estado y en Distrito Capital (Cedesex, Construyendo Futuros y
FUNDANA) apoyan la respuesta inicial con servicios en protección general, de la niñez y de violencia
basada en género (VBG). Además, organizaciones como Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA y World Vision se
encuentran brindando apoyo en el área de protección a familias afectadas, especialmente a nivel
psicosocial.
La Guaira
 Las autoridades y organizaciones humanitarias continúan fortaleciendo la respuesta en los
campamentos transitorios de La Guaira mediante la ampliación de servicios multisectoriales, la
mejora de las condiciones de alojamiento y la gestión coordinada de la asistencia. Durante la
jornada avanzaron las distribuciones de artículos esenciales, las actividades de protección, las
intervenciones de salud y apoyo psicosocial, así como las acciones para mejorar el acceso a agua
segura, saneamiento, conectividad e infraestructura comunitaria.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Acciones de respuesta: Cinco (5) organizaciones socias de FHV apoyan la respuesta con servicios de
atención primaria en salud y atención psicológica (Fundación Proyecto Maniapure, Paluz, Ven Da Tu
Mano, Cruz Roja Venezolana y Tinta Violeta).
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro)
 En Carabobo, las principales afectaciones se centran en el municipio Juan José Mora (parroquia
Morón). En Yaracuy, particularmente en el municipio Veroes y otras localidades cercanas a la zona
epicentral, se reportan viviendas destruidas o en condición de alto riesgo. Se identifican
necesidades prioritarias en protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua,
saneamiento e higiene (ASH) y seguridad alimentaria.
Acciones de respuesta: Cinco (5) organizaciones (Cruz Roja Venezolana, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas
Morón y Empodérame) brindan respuesta en salud, alimentación, agua y distribución de ayuda
humanitaria.
Falcón (Tucacas – Municipio Silva)
 En el municipio Silva se registraron anegaciones puntuales en sectores de Boca de Aroa como
consecuencia de un evento de mar de leva, afectando comunidades previamente impactadas por
los terremotos y por fenómenos de licuación de suelos. Las autoridades mantienen el monitoreo de
la situación y las acciones preventivas para reducir riesgos a la población.
 La situación evidencia un escenario multirriesgo en el municipio Silva, donde a las afectaciones
derivadas de los terremotos se suman impactos asociados a eventos costeros, incrementando las
necesidades de protección, ASH, apoyo psicosocial y recuperación temprana.
 OCHA continúa articulando con Protección Civil y los socios del Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC)
el seguimiento de la situación, la verificación de necesidades humanitarias y la identificación de
posibles acciones de apoyo complementario.
Acciones de respuesta: Continúa el ciclo de capacitaciones impulsado por el Clúster de Protección y
la agenda de trabajo en Boca de Aroa, ampliada, por solicitud de las autoridades regionales, al municipio
Palmasola en las jornadas de ASH y apoyo psicosocial, con acciones implementadas por Acción Contra
el Hambre, Azul Positivo, OIM, Centroccidente, ODISEF y AVSI, en coordinación con las autoridades
regionales.
Otros estados
 Apure: las autoridades reportan la llegada de más de 250 personas afectadas. El Foro Local de
Coordinación (FLC) mantiene el monitoreo de la situación y provee atenciones multisectoriales,
incluidos primeros auxilios psicológicos (PAP)
 Delta Amacuro: Se mantiene la atención a 98 personas reubicadas desde Caracas y La Guaira,
principalmente mediante procesos de reunificación familiar. Las necesidades identificadas se
concentran en SMAPS y en el seguimiento de la movilidad de la población desplazada. Las
autoridades y organizaciones humanitarias avanzan en la organización de jornadas multiservicio
que incluirán asistencia alimentaria, kits de higiene, apoyo sanitario y acompañamiento de
protección para las familias acogidas en la entidad. Como parte de estas acciones, el PMA prevé
distribuir cestas alimentarias a 52 personas, World Vision complementará la asistencia con 22
raciones alimentarias y Cáritas Delta Amacuro entregará 52 kits de higiene.
 Sucre: Las autoridades reportan la movilización de 641 personas procedentes principalmente de
La Guaira y Caracas, de las cuales 187 se desplazaron por iniciativa propia y 454 recibieron apoyo
institucional para su traslado. Las acciones de respuesta incluyen recepción, registro, atención
médica, apoyo psicosocial y protección, con especial seguimiento a niñas, niños y adolescentes,
personas mayores y otros grupos en situación de vulnerabilidad. Una comisión técnica evalúa la
habitabilidad de las edificaciones receptoras.
 Táchira: ASONACOP y UNICEF reportaron que este 12 de julio fueron atendidos dos grupos
familiares en movilidad (2 niñas, niños y adolescentes y 2 personas adultas), con entrega de kits de
higiene y kits de alimentos. Las familias se movilizaban hacia los estados Aragua y Anzoátegui.
Hubo seguimiento del equipo multidisciplinario a la llegada de un niño separado, así como
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
orientaciones en documentación, nacionalización de NNA, atención médica y psicológica y
escolarización.
 Zulia: Continúa la atención a personas afectadas procedentes de La Guaira y Caracas,
principalmente a través del terminal de pasajeros de Maracaibo. La Gerencia de Atención al
Ciudadano y ASONACOP, junto con la Cruz Roja Venezolana, HIAS, CESVI, ASOREZ y Cáritas,
mantienen un módulo unificado de atención que brinda alimentación, asistencia jurídica y kits de
higiene. En total, esta semana fueron atendidos más de 30 grupos familiares: alrededor de 20
familias en el municipio Jesús Enrique Lossada (parroquias San José y Concepción) y, en el terminal
de Maracaibo, al menos ocho grupos familiares, además de la atención en otras jornadas. El perfil
predominante es de mujeres, niñas, niños y adolescentes y personas mayores. Parte de la población
permanece en el estado, mientras otras personas continúan en tránsito hacia Colombia.
 En los estados Bolívar, Trujillo, Nueva Esparta y Lara se mantienen las acciones de coordinación,
acopio y monitoreo.
Coordinación humanitaria
 El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del
Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, concluyó esta semana su visita a Venezuela, en la que tuvo
la oportunidad de conversar con personas afectadas, personal humanitario, autoridades nacionales,
líderes del sector privado y representantes de la comunidad diplomática. Hizo un llamado a
mantener su apoyo al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria (PRH) para contribuir a la atención de las
necesidades más urgentes.
 OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales,
continúa coordinando la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias,
priorizando acciones en salud, alojamiento, alimentación, ASH, logística y protección. En este
marco, el Sistema de las Naciones Unidas sostuvo una reunión de trabajo con la Autoridad Única
de la Operación Rescate y Esperanza 2026 para revisar necesidades prioritarias, fortalecer la
coordinación interinstitucional y dar seguimiento a las acciones conjuntas de respuesta a los
terremotos.
 UNDAC y OCHA continuaron apoyando a Protección Civil en el fortalecimiento de capacidades de
coordinación y gestión de información para emergencias, incluyendo intercambio técnico sobre
mecanismos de coordinación USAR y herramientas de seguimiento operativo.
 OCHA continuó fortaleciendo la coordinación con el sector privado para apoyar las acciones de
respuesta y recuperación temprana, promoviendo la articulación con actores especializados en
áreas como logística, gestión de escombros, rehabilitación de infraestructura y planificación de la
reconstrucción, a través de los mecanismos de coordinación existentes entre las Naciones Unidas
y el sector privado.
 Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores
al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del
PNUD. Conforme a la metodología internacional de la PDNA, se avanzará en las coordinaciones
correspondientes con las contrapartes relevantes.
 Se informó la activación de un mecanismo especial para la tramitación expedita de una “Visa de
Trabajo para Situaciones Especiales”, gestionada a través del Ministerio del Poder Popular para
Relaciones Exteriores. El procedimiento podrá realizarse en línea, bajo la coordinación del
Despacho del Viceministro para Temas Multilaterales y la Oficina de Relaciones Consulares, y
estará dirigido a trabajadores extranjeros de organizaciones internacionales, así como a
funcionarios de las Naciones Unidas, que se desplieguen en Venezuela en el marco de la respuesta
a la emergencia ocasionada por los terremotos.
Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria
Seguridad Alimentaria
 Hasta la fecha, el PMA ha brindado asistencia alimentaria a 62.429 personas como parte de la
respuesta de emergencia a los terremotos. Durante el período reportado, el PMA y sus socios
implementadores continuaron proporcionando asistencia alimentaria inmediata mediante una
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
combinación de raciones listas para el consumo, cestas alimentarias familiares y comidas calientes.
En total, se distribuyeron 7.756 kits alimentarios listos para el consumo a poblaciones afectadas en
el Distrito Capital y La Guaira, incluidos 3.978 kits en la parroquia Sucre (municipio Libertador,
Distrito Capital) y 3.778 kits en Catia La Mar (municipio Vargas, estado La Guaira). Asimismo, el
PMA distribuyó 364 cestas alimentarias familiares en el sector Urimare de Playa Grande,
alcanzando a 1.456 personas, y 200 cestas alimentarias familiares en un albergue temporal de la
parroquia Santa Rosalía, Distrito Capital, beneficiando a 800 personas.
 Las distribuciones de comidas calientes también continuaron en los albergues temporales de La
Guaira, donde se sirvieron 7.262 comidas, incluidas 1.225 comidas en la comunidad de Playa
Grande, 2.795 en el Estadio de Béisbol César Nieves y 3.242 en el Estadio Deportivo José María
Vargas. A través de estas intervenciones, el PMA y sus socios continúan garantizando el acceso
ininterrumpido a alimentos para las personas desplazadas y afectadas por los terremotos, al tiempo
que apoyan la cobertura de sus necesidades alimentarias inmediatas.
Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene
 UNICEF mantuvo los servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH) en los campamentos
transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande, proporcionando 20.000
litros de agua potable por campamento para la población albergada. Asimismo, avanzó en el
fortalecimiento de la infraestructura ASH mediante la habilitación de capacidades de
almacenamiento de agua y la planificación e instalación de infraestructura complementaria de
saneamiento, incluyendo baños, duchas y estaciones de lavado. Paralelamente, continuaron las
acciones de saneamiento, gestión de residuos sólidos, monitoreo de instalaciones y promoción de
prácticas de higiene.
Alojamiento, Energía y Enseres
 En el campamento transitorio Mare Abajo II, ACNUR apoyó el fortalecimiento de las condiciones
de alojamiento mediante la instalación de 15 lámparas solares en áreas comunes, contribuyendo
a mejorar la iluminación del sitio y a mitigar riesgos de protección.
 Asimismo, en el campamento transitorio Mare Abajo II, se recibieron 105 literas a través de la
iniciativa “Camas para Venezuela” y 50 colchones donados por la Fundación Flor de la Esperanza.
 ACNUR prevé realizar el 13 de julio una distribución de artículos no alimentarios (NFI) para las
personas alojadas en el campamento transitorio Polideportivo José María Vargas.
Logística y Telecomunicaciones
 Varias organizaciones humanitarias continúan canalizando el ingreso de asistencia por vía
marítima a través del Puerto de Puerto Cabello, actualmente el puerto comercial operativo más
cercano a La Guaira; mientras que el Puerto de La Guaira prioriza la recepción de donaciones
bilaterales.
 El equipo de telecomunicaciones del PMA, con el apoyo de emergency.lu, G-Networks y
CONATEL, avanzó en la instalación de soluciones comunitarias de acceso a internet en
Caraballeda y el Estadio César Nieves, las cuales quedarán operativas al cierre de la jornada. Cada
sitio proporcionará cobertura aproximada de 200 metros y conectividad para hasta 100 dispositivos,
mientras que la instalación en Playa Grande está prevista para el 15 de julio.
Nutrición
 UNICEF mantuvo acciones de nutrición en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas,
Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande, mediante tamizaje nutricional, suplementación y consejería
para niños y niñas menores de cinco años, mujeres embarazadas y mujeres lactantes, incluyendo
monitoreo nutricional, promoción de la lactancia materna y entrega de suplementos de
micronutrientes.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Protección (incluidos Áreas de Responsabilidad de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes y Violencia
Basada en Género)
 UNFPA ha fortalecido las acciones de prevención y respuesta a la violencia basada en género
(VBG) en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa
Grande, alcanzando a 908 personas mediante actividades de sensibilización hasta la fecha.
Asimismo, ha brindado apoyo psicosocial a 52 personas, realizado la gestión de 11 casos de
protección y proporcionado asesoría legal.
 UNICEF brindó apoyo psicosocial a 122 niños, niñas y adolescentes y a 37 madres, padres y
cuidadores en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa
Grande, mediante Espacios Amigables y actividades lúdicas, recreativas y pedagógicas
 En el campamento transitorio Campo de Golf (Tanaguarena), OIM fortaleció las acciones de
prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual (PEAS) mediante actividades de sensibilización
dirigidas a comunidades, autoridades y organizaciones presentes, la difusión de materiales
informativos en áreas comunes del sitio y la coordinación con World Central Kitchen (WCK) para
ampliar la difusión de mensajes de prevención entre la población albergada.
 En el campamento transitorio Mare Abajo II, se realizaron derivaciones de personas con
necesidades específicas de protección a DRC para orientación y canalización a servicios
especializados de salud y a la estructura comunitaria para orientación en remisión para casos de
extrema vulnerabilidad.
 ACNUR continuará brindando servicios de protección y apoyo psicosocial en los campamentos
transitorios Playa Grande, Polideportivo José María Vargas y Estadio César Nieves el lunes 13 de
julio.
Salud
 En el campamento transitorio Polideportivo José María Vargas, OIM ha apoyado la realización de
12 jornadas móviles de salud, a través de las cuales se han brindado 969 consultas en medicina
general, pediatría, medicina interna, salud mental, primeros auxilios psicológicos (PAP) y referencia
de casos.
 UNICEF apoyó la prestación de servicios de salud en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo
Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande, donde se aplicaron 177 dosis de vacunas, incluidas
vacunas contra la fiebre amarilla, toxoide tetánico, sarampión y otras vacunas infantiles. Asimismo,
brindó atención psicológica individual a 44 personas y atención primaria de salud a 29 personas.
 UNFPA ha brindado servicios de salud sexual y reproductiva (SSR) en los campamentos
transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande, alcanzando a 1.063
personas mediante actividades de sensibilización hasta la fecha. Asimismo, ha proporcionado
atención prenatal a 53 mujeres embarazadas y facilitó el acceso a métodos anticonceptivos para
331 personas.
 En el campamento transitorio Estadio César Nieves, OIM mantuvo las acciones de triaje de
protección y coordinación interagencial, facilitando la derivación de 20 personas a servicios de
salud general, una persona a servicios de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS) y dos casos
de violencia basada en género (VBG).
Financiamiento humanitario y contribuciones
 El jefe humanitario de Naciones Unidas, Tom Fletcher, anunció esta semana una adenda al Plan
de Respuesta Humanitaria para Venezuela. Este llamado contempla las necesidades
multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas por los próximos seis meses. Para alcanzar a estas
personas, se necesitan 298 millones de dólares, que se suman a los 632 millones de dólares
solicitados al inicio del año.
 El Gobierno del Japón asignó 3,5 millones de dólares para apoyar la respuesta a los terremotos.
Los fondos permitirán brindar asistencia humanitaria en sectores clave, incluidos seguridad
alimentaria, salud y atención médica, alojamiento y artículos no alimentarios, a través del PMA, la
Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (FICR) y la OIM.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
 La Marina Real de los Países Bajos realizó una nueva entrega de asistencia humanitaria y
suministros de emergencia en La Guaira, en el marco de un mecanismo de apoyo sostenido desde
Curazao que ya ha facilitado cinco misiones consecutivas. Anunciaron la continuidad de estas
operaciones mediante el despliegue de una nueva embarcación para apoyar el flujo de asistencia
hacia las zonas afectadas.
 Autoridades anunciaron la llegada de un nuevo cargamento proveniente de Rusia con 25
toneladas de ayuda humanitaria, que incluye artículos para el hogar, insumos médicos y
farmacéuticos de alta prioridad.
 También fueron recibidos este domingo 12 de julio 88 contenedores de ayuda humanitaria, como
medicamentos, alimentos y otros insumos, enviados por CARICOM.
 Parte del apoyo brindado por UNDAC incluye una especialista en coordinación con el sector privado
para fortalecer la participación empresarial en la respuesta y recuperación. Se encuentra disponible
un rastreador de contribuciones del sector privado para la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela
(https://ven-eq.connectingbusiness.org) y una nota informativa dirigida al sector privado sobre
oportunidades de apoyo. Punto focal: sanchez21@un.org.
 El Fondo Central de Respuesta a Emergencias (CERF, por sus siglas en inglés) realizó una
asignación de 15 millones de dólares para una respuesta multisectorial, junto con la activación del
Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV). Noruega realizó una contribución para apoyar la respuesta
a través del CERF.
 Estados Unidos anunció una contribución de 100 millones de dólares al FHV, y una asignación
adicional de 100 millones de dólares en contribuciones bilaterales para operaciones de respuesta
de OIM, PMA, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse,
Proyecto Esperanza y la Cruz Roja.
 Alemania y Corea realizaron contribuciones al FHV por 5 millones y 1,25 millones de dólares,
respectivamente, para apoyar la acción humanitaria en el país. Otros Estados Miembros y donantes
han expresado su intención de contribuir a la respuesta a través del Fondo.
 OIM lanzó un llamamiento por 98 millones de dólares para asistir a 850.000 personas y 140
entidades los próximos seis meses. La OPS/OMS lanzó un llamamiento de emergencia por casi
24 millones de dólares para apoyar, durante los próximos seis meses, la respuesta en salud y la
recuperación temprana y asignó US$1,5 millones del Fondo de Contingencia para Emergencias. El
PMA realizó un llamamiento inicial de 50 millones de dólares para ampliar la asistencia alimentaria
y apoyar actividades logísticas y de comunicación en emergencia. ACNUR indicó que requiere 14,8
millones de dólares para apoyar a hasta 30.000 personas afectadas durante los próximos seis
meses.
 La Unión Europea asignó 5 millones de euros para apoyar la respuesta a la emergencia, lo que se
suma a los 52 millones de euros ya asignados este año para las operaciones humanitarias en el
país.
 Australia informó de una contribución de 2 millones de dólares para la provisión de alimentos,
alojamiento, atención de salud y acceso a agua segura a través de IFRC y el PMA.
 Suiza anunció una contribución de 2,5 millones de francos suizos para apoyar la respuesta.
 Suecia asignó 25 millones de coronas suecas para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en el país,
mediante programas de asistencia alimentaria, agua, alojamiento temporal, protección y
reunificación familiar implementados por el PMA, ACNUR y Save the Children.
 Dinamarca anunció una contribución adicional de 11 millones de coronas danesas para apoyar la
respuesta humanitaria, incluyendo 10 millones de coronas danesas a través de ACNUR y 1 millón
de coronas danesas a través de DanChurchAid y la Cruz Roja Danesa.
 El Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) anunció una asignación inicial de 7,5 millones de libras
esterlinas para la respuesta al terremoto en Venezuela, incluyendo 2 millones de libras esterlinas
aportados por el Gobierno del Reino Unido mediante UK Aid Match. Los recursos serán
implementados por organizaciones miembros del DEC y sus socios locales para apoyar la respuesta
humanitaria.
 OCHA continúa coordinando con donantes y socios para asegurar una asignación rápida,
estratégica y basada en necesidades.
Apoya la respuesta humanitaria para atender el terremoto en Venezuela

Para mayor información, por favor contactar a la Oficina de OCHA Venezuela:

documents.title: Situation Report No.5: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 12 July 2026
documents.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

- On 24 June 2026, two consecutive earthquakes (M7.2 and M7.5) struck north-central Venezuela, affecting at least seven states, with La Guaira the most severely impacted. Authorities have since reported more than 1,202 aftershocks.
- **The health response has transitioned from rapid damage assessments to restoring the continuity of essential health services**. Functional constraints persist across the affected health network, particularly in La Guaira, where reduced hospital capacity continues to limit specialized care and increase pressure on referral pathways.
- Recovery efforts are focused on restoring health system functionality through coordinated assessments, health facility recovery and Emergency Medical Team (EMT) support. **Damage has been identified in 38 health facilities** across the three most affected states, while Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) remains a priority need, particularly in La Guaira and temporary shelters**.**
- PAHO/WHO is actively supporting the Ministry of Health (MPPS) in deployed **seven Regional Response Team specialists** covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information systems and media, epidemiology, risk communication and community engagement, EMT coordination, and rapid health facility assessment. In coordination with MoH, PAHO/WHO is supporting the **virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization: Thirteen EMTs are operational in La Guaira, Caracas and Miranda and Aragua** increasing clinical capacity in affected areas.
- PAHO/WHO has **locally distributed** an initial 6 tons of supplies, delivering Trauma and Emergency Surgery Kits **to 4 high-complexity hospitals** and medication and equipment modules to **5 community health areas (ASIC) and a specialized clinic**. A chartered plane (with ~27.5 metric tons of supplies) is now being coordinated, carrying Interagency Emergency Health Kits, additional surgery kits, and Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) treatment kits to further strengthen referral hospitals and primary care networks.

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.5
Health Cluster Partner Assessments of Health Facilities
Health Cluster partners conducted rapid assessments of health facilities across the affected. 73 health
facilities have been assessed, with 27 reporting earthquake-related damage, including 13 in Distrito
Capital, 9 in La Guaira and 5 in Miranda. In La Guaira, three health facilities remain non-operational or
with severely limited functionality. While assessments remain concentrated in Distrito Capital, Miranda
and La Guaira, important information gaps persist in Carabobo and Yaracuy, where rapid health facility
assessments remain a priority.
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS)
• Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) remain a priority component of the health
response across the earthquake-affected areas.
• Multiple assessments conducted by PAHO/WHO, the Health Cluster, UNDAC and community-
based Rapid Needs Assessments (RNA) consistently identify sustained psychosocial needs,
particularly in La Guaira, where health service disruptions, displacement and reduced hospital
capacity have increased vulnerabilities.
• Community-based assessments indicate that psychological support remains among the most
frequently reported health priorities, especially in temporary shelters and communities
experiencing prolonged disruptions to essential services.
• Rapid Needs Assessments (RNA) identified La Guaira (68%) and Yaracuy (64%) as the two states
whereas the states where key informants most frequently reported MHPSS among the priority
health needs.
PRIORITY NEEDS
• Continuity of Health Services – Restore continuity of essential health services by supporting
damaged hospitals and health facilities, strengthening trauma, surgical, intensive care, diagnostic,
referral and emergency response capacities, and addressing critical shortages of supplies,
equipment and specialized personnel.
• Hospital Resilience – Reinforce hospital resilience and operational readiness through
improvements in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), infection prevention and control (IPC),
medical waste management, backup power, oxygen and medical gases, cold chain,
communications, and dignified management of the deceased.
• Rehabilitation and workforce capacity – Strengthen integrated rehabilitation and health
workforce capacity, ensuring continuity of care for patients with trauma and disabilities, while
addressing shortages of health personnel, occupational safety, psychosocial support and staff
well-being.
• Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) – Strengthen MHPSS, particularly in La
Guaira and temporary shelters, through psychosocial support, expansion of mhGAP-HIG training,
mental health needs assessments, coordination of the MHPSS Technical Working Group, and
improved access to essential psychotropic medicines.
PAHO/WHO RESPONSE
• PAHO/WHO continues supporting the Ministry of Health through technical coordination, health
information management, health facility assessments, epidemiological surveillance, and
operational prioritization in collaboration with the Health Cluster and national authorities.

• PAHO technical support is facilitating the transition from emergency response to early recovery
through hospital assessments, Emergency Medical Team (EMT) coordination and progressive
demobilization, restoration of essential health services, strengthening of referral networks, and
expansion of digital surveillance and assessment tools.
• PAHO continues building national capacities through technical guidance and field support across
priority response areas, including epidemiological surveillance, infection prevention and control
(IPC), vaccination, EMT, and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), while supporting
key MHPSS coordination and planning activities with the Ministry of Health.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
• No large-scale outbreaks have been confirmed; however, enhanced surveillance remains
essential due to persistent WASH deficiencies and increased communicable disease risks in
temporary shelters.
• Vaccination, alert verification, outbreak investigation and epidemiological surveillance continue to
expand across affected areas, supporting early detection and timely public health action.
• PAHO/WHO is supporting the Ministry of Health through strengthened surveillance systems,
digital reporting, laboratory coordination, IPC guidance and vaccination preparedness in
transitional camps.
SITUATION ANALYSIS
Post-earthquake epidemiological surveillance continues to expand across hospitals, Emergency Medical
Teams (EMTs), temporary camps and affected communities, supporting early detection of priority public
health events and informing operational decision-making. Although no large-scale outbreaks have been
confirmed, field assessments continue to identify environmental and operational conditions that increase
the risk of communicable disease transmission, particularly in temporary camps/shelters with deficiencies
in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), overcrowding and inadequate food safety practices.
National health authorities issued guidelines for epidemiological surveillance, establishing a mandatory
reporting mechanism during the emergency for transitional camps, EMTs, and other points of care. The
reporting flow is organized through the ASICs —Community Integrated Health Areas—, territorial
structures that coordinate the local health network and play a key role in consolidating information,
coordinating sample collection and transport, supporting the investigation of priority events, activating
rapid response teams when needed, including sample collection, preservation and transport to the Rafael
Rangel National Institute of Hygiene.

The national list of diseases prioritized for etiological investigation and immediate mandatory notification
after the earthquake includes: acute respiratory infections/ARI-SARI, acute diarrheal diseases,
cholera, hepatitis A, pertussis, diphtheria, measles-rubella, acute flaccid paralysis, leptospirosis,
dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya, Oropouche, Zika, meningitis, tuberculosis, malaria, and post-
traumatic mycoses.
Early warning and alert verification
Epidemiological alerts under the Early Warning and Response System in transitional camps are being
supported by PAHO/WHO through alert verification and outbreak investigation. Alerts under investigation
include fever-rash illness, foodborne disease events, diarrhoeal disease outbreaks, tuberculosis-related
follow-up and scabies cases reported in camp settings. These events are being treated as alerts under
verification and do not imply confirmed outbreaks or confirmed cases unless laboratory or epidemiological
confirmation is completed.
A fever-rash alert remains under investigation, with sample collection completed and laboratory results
pending, to rapidly rule out measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases.

Vaccination activities are ongoing as part of the public health response in affected areas and transitional

PRIORITY NEEDS
• Strengthen early warning, alert verification and outbreak investigation capacity in
transitional camps, EMTs and health facilities, including timely reporting, field investigation,
laboratory sample collection, sample transport and feedback to response teams. Improve logistics,
digital reporting tools, laboratory support, and field connectivity.
• Laboratory Capacity - Reinforce laboratory capacity and sample referral pathways, including

National Institute of Hygiene, and timely confirmation or rule-out of priority epidemiological alerts.
• WASH and environmental health – Improve water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) conditions,

• Surveillance and IPC guidance – Finalize and implement standardized post-earthquake

• Vaccination in transitional camps – Strengthen targeted vaccination and catch-up activities in
transitional camps and affected communities, prioritizing protection against vaccine-preventable

and pentavalent vaccines, according to national guidance, epidemiological risk and vaccine

• Donated IT equipment and auxiliary materials to epidemiological surveillance teams of the ASICs

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.5
According to national authorities, 89 transitional camps have been established, of which 82 are active
and 7 are under renovation, with an installed capacity of 24,383 people and 17,266 people currently
sheltered. Shelter occupancy remains concentrated in Caracas, La Guaira and Miranda, with La Guaira
hosting the largest share of the sheltered population. The Government continues to establish and expand
transitional camps and collective shelters to accommodate displaced populations.
PAHO/WHO field teams have characterized 16 transitional camps and supported surveillance visits to
9 camps in La Guaira, generating direct evidence on priority health and protection risks. Findings
indicate that shelter–primary health care coordination remains uneven, including limited or inactive links
between some camps and their corresponding ASICs, underscoring the need to clarify health
management roles in camps and standardize population characterization.
Earthquake-affected families remain in temporary
shelters in La Guaira, supported by health and
humanitarian partners. Source: ACNUR
Health assessments in temporary shelters show gaps in access to primary health care, referral pathways,
basic medical supplies and continuity of treatment for chronic conditions. Among the 16 camps
characterized by PAHO/WHO, all required spaces for adult psychosocial support, 12 required
medicines for chronic diseases, 4 required vaccination activities for children and adolescents, 3
required nutritional screening, and 3 required consultations for pregnant women. These findings
point to the need for integrated shelter-based health services, including PHC, MHPSS, maternal care,
vaccination, nutrition screening and referral mechanisms.
Mental health and psychosocial support remain a priority across assessed shelters. Field findings show
high levels of emotional distress among affected populations and camp management teams, while
access to structured psychological support remains limited. In response, PAHO/WHO is supporting the
development and validation of mental health protocols, shelter characterization tools and Psychological
First Aid plans for multidisciplinary teams working in temporary shelters.
WASH and environmental health conditions remain critical in several assessed camps. PAHO/WHO
findings indicate that 12 of the 16 assessed camps require improved water storage, with unsafe
storage practices observed; 5 camps lack a waste management plan, and several have limited or no
adequate shower areas. Surveillance visits in La Guaira also identified open defecation, inadequate solid
waste disposal, fly infestation and unsafe food handling, increasing risks related to gastrointestinal,
dermatological and other communicable disease events.

www.paho.org | © PAHO/WHO, 2026

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.5
Protection-related health risks also require attention. Some assessed shelters lack sex-segregated
sanitation facilities, locks, lighting or safe access to toilets and showers, increasing risks for women,
adolescents and children. Gaps in menstrual hygiene and dignity items remain important, while shelter
design and child-safe space standards require reinforcement in coordination with protection partners.
Operational response in shelters is also constrained by limited connectivity, mobile devices and field tools
for technical teams, affecting timely data collection, reporting and follow-up of health risks. Strengthening
standardized health information, population profiling, referral pathways and intersectoral coordination
with WASH, Protection, Nutrition and Shelter actors remains essential to improve service delivery and
reduce preventable health risks in temporary shelters.
The Health Cluster, continues to coordinate health partners working in temporary camps and affected
communities, supporting the harmonization of assessments, identification of priority gaps and alignment
of partner interventions. Cluster partners have participated with the Inter-Cluster Group in field
assessments of 18 temporary camps in Miranda, helping document needs related to primary health
care, MHPSS, sexual and reproductive health, nutrition, WASH, protection and continuity of treatment
for HIV and tuberculosis. The Cluster is also supporting coordination with partners to strengthen mobile
health brigades, emergency care, referral pathways, delivery of medicines and supplies, and rapid
capacity-building in camp health, nutrition, PSEA and MHPSS.
PRIORITY NEEDS
• WASH and environmental health – Strengthen safe water access, storage, sanitation, showers,
handwashing facilities, hygiene supplies, solid waste management and vector control to reduce
contamination and prevent health risks in temporary shelters.
• Health access and continuity of care – Improve shelter-based primary health care, triage,
referral pathways, essential medicines and continuity of treatment for people with chronic
conditions, pregnant women, children, older persons, people with disabilities and other high-risk
groups.
• Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) – Expand Psychological First Aid,
psychosocial support spaces, identification of people with mental health needs, referral pathways
and sustained support for affected families, camp management teams and frontline workers.
• Population profiling and health information – Standardize population registration, vulnerability
profiling and health characterization in shelters to identify at-risk groups and guide planning,
service delivery and monitoring.
• Surveillance, immunization, and outbreak readiness – Integrate early warning, syndromic
surveillance, WASH, immunization, and outbreak response to detect and respond to risks in
overcrowded shelters.
• Protection-sensitive shelter health services – Improve privacy, lighting, locks, gender-
segregated sanitation, menstrual hygiene and dignity supplies, child-safe spaces and referral
pathways to reduce protection, GBV and child safety risks.
• Food safety, nutrition and inclusion – Strengthen safe food handling, proper storage, nutrition
screening, therapeutic diets and accessible services for older persons, persons with disabilities
and people with reduced mobility.

SITUATION ANALYSIS
The Ministry of Health (MPPS) continues to lead the health response, with territorial implementation
through state health authorities, ASICs, hospitals, medical brigades and health teams deployed in
temporary camps. Technical coordination spaces are active with PAHO/WHO to support epidemiological
surveillance, immunization, health actions in camps and follow-up of health facilities.
The Health Cluster, co-coordinated by PAHO/WHO and the International Rescue Committee (IRC),
coordinates 110 organizations linked to the health response, articulating MPPS, United Nations agencies,
humanitarian partners and technical groups to align actions, avoid duplication and prioritize operational
gaps. Partners maintain activities in La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Falcón and Aragua, including
emergency care, mobile health brigades, sexual and reproductive health, MHPSS, continuity of HIV and
tuberculosis treatment, referrals, and delivery of medicines and supplies.
Joint coordination with MPPS, UNICEF, the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group and technical partners has
supported assessments and planning in health facilities and temporary camps, documenting needs in
primary health care, MHPSS, maternal and child health, nutrition, WASH, protection and continuity of
care. These inputs are also informing the health component of the Humanitarian Response Plan
Addendum.
Despite progress, coordination mechanisms require further consolidation, particularly to standardize
information flows, clarify roles, track agreements and strengthen articulation between national, territorial
and humanitarian partners. Strengthening referral pathways between hospitals, ASICs, EMTs and
community-based services remains essential as the response shifts toward early recovery and continuity
of essential health services.

DISTRIBUTION STRATEGY
PAHO/WHO applied a modular allocation strategy to maximize the impact
of the humanitarian cargo received. Trauma and Emergency Surgery Kits
(TESK) were distributed across 4 high-complexity hospitals, while Non-
Communicable Disease Kits (NCDK) were allocated to 5 Comprehensive
Community Health Areas (ASIC) and 1 specialized outpatient clinic —
matching each resource to the needs of its setting.
STRENGTHENING CARE CAPACITY
These supply blocks — equivalent to supporting 50 complex surgical
patients and 3 months of primary outpatient care for 10,000 people —
directly strengthen hospital and community resilience in the face of the
emergency.
LAST-MILE CLINICAL DELIVERY
Deliveries to the hospital network were tailored to each facility's service
profile to prevent critical shortages:
• Maternidad Concepción Palacios: gynecological instrument sets,
reproductive health and debridement kits, and high-complexity obstetric
surgery modules (laparotomy, cesarean, embryotomy).
• Hospital Dr. Miguel Pérez Carreño: surgical drainage material,
advanced anesthesia supplies, laryngoscopes, immobilization splints,
burn dressings, and specialized craniotomy and pediatric surgery sets.
• Hospital Dr. Domingo Luciani: basic trauma medicines, general
surgery instrument sets, skin grafts, casting material, and an
orthopedic/bone-traction surgical kit.
• Hospital Ricardo Baquero González (Periférico de Catia): sutures
and critical IV solutions for immediate prehospital stabilization.
STRENGTHENING THE COMMUNITY NETWORK IN LA GUAIRA
• Chronic Medication Module (NCDK Mod 1): distributed evenly across
the ASIC of La Páez (Catia La Mar), Guaracarumbo, 10 de Marzo,
Maiquetía, and La Guaira.
• Equipment & Renewable Modules (NCDK Mod 3–4): fully allocated
to the Naiguatá Specialized Outpatient Clinic, restoring its diagnostic
and routine care capacity.

documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 18**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**11 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,170 aftershocks.**
- Official toll: **4,333 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.**
- **Tom Fletcher, the United Nations humanitarian chief, concluded his four-day visit to the country and called for sustained international support for the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP).**
- **An additional appeal for US$298 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,171 aftershocks.**

Seventeen days after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **4,333 people dead, 16,740 injured and 6,462 rescued since the onset of the emergency.** Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people remain without housing.** According to official reports, 315 of those who died have yet to be identified, while search operations for possible survivors remain active at priority sites.

The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher concluded his visit to Venezuela this week and called on the international community to sustain support for the humanitarian response. In this context, he **announced a US$298 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan, aimed at addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.**
