documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Terremoto del 24 de junio de 2026 - Campamento Transitorio Mare Abajo (a 7 de julio 2026)
Clúster Salud Venezuela: Terremotos, 24 de junio. - Informe de situación n° 4. 7 de julio de 2026 [EN/ES]
documents.body_text:
Al 7 de julio el gobierno nacional ha reportado 3.685 personas fallecidas, 16.740 heridos, 6.462 personas rescatadas y 25.970 pacientes atendidos tras la contingencia, según el Parte Oficial del Gobierno. Se han registrado 1.076 réplicas desde el evento inicial, con una tendencia decreciente en frecuencia y magnitud.

El Clúster de Salud como canal de articulación con el Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud (MPPS) para centralizar la información y la ayuda internacional, la cual asciende a más de 707 mil toneladas.

Se han desplegado 29.567 efectivos nacionales y 4.338 rescatistas internacionales.

Un total de 87 campamentos transitorios se encuentran asignados a nivel nacional (Caracas 39, La Guaira 26, Miranda 22), con una capacidad instalada de 20.227 y 14.634 personas alojadas, según el balance de la Vicepresidencia Social (7 de julio). De estos, el Clúster de Salud monitorea directamente los centros de la Gran Caracas, Miranda y La Guaira y ha realizado visitas en terreno a algunos de ellos.

Una misión exploratoria conjunta (MPPS, UNICEF, Clúster de Salud y GTT SMAPS) al campamento Parque del Oeste / Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro caracterizó una población de aproximadamente 6.102 personas, incluidos 800–1.000 niños, niñas y adolescentes y 260 mujeres embarazadas, e identificó brechas agudas en agua segura, SMAPS, tamizaje nutricional y equipos de protección personal. Así como, el campamento ubicado en la Escuela Gran Colombia, donde al momento de la visita tenía una población de 1.200 personas albergadas, se encontraba coordinado por el poder popular y Ministerios del estado.

pdfs.text:
VENEZUELA Terremotos, 24 de junio.
Informe de situación n° 4. 7 de julio de 2026
Periodo de notificación: Cuarta actualización, información disponible a las 08:00 (GMT-4) /
12:00 UTC del 07 de julio de 2026.
Elaborado por: Clúster Salud de Venezuela, con el apoyo de Oficina Regional de OPS y
Clúster de Salud Global.
Número Glide: 2026-000093
Cifras del evento (preliminares – sujetas a cambios):
Personas sin
¹ Parte Oficial del Gobierno de la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, 7 de julio de 2026. ² Análisis de exposición al
terremoto de la OPS/OMS, 25 de junio de 2026.
Aspectos destacados
• Balance de Víctimas y Atención: Al 7 de julio el gobierno nacional ha reportado 3.685 personas fallecidas, 16.740
heridos, 6.462 personas rescatadas y 25.970 pacientes atendidos tras la contingencia, según el Parte Oficial del
Gobierno. Se han registrado 1.076 réplicas desde el evento inicial, con una tendencia decreciente en frecuencia y
magnitud.
• Gobernanza y Coordinación: Se ratificó al Clúster de Salud como canal de articulación con el Ministerio del Poder
Popular para la Salud (MPPS) para centralizar la información y la ayuda internacional, la cual asciende a más de 707
mil toneladas.1
• Respuesta en Terreno: Se han desplegado 29.567 efectivos nacionales y 4.338 rescatistas internacionales.
• Infraestructura de Refugio: Un total de 87 campamentos transitorios se encuentran asignados a nivel nacional
(Caracas 39, La Guaira 26, Miranda 22), con una capacidad instalada de 20.227 y 14.634 personas alojadas, según el
balance de la Vicepresidencia Social (7 de julio). De estos, el Clúster de Salud monitorea directamente los centros de
la Gran Caracas, Miranda y La Guaira y ha realizado visitas en terreno a algunos de ellos.
• Evaluación conjunta en terreno: Una misión exploratoria conjunta (MPPS, UNICEF, Clúster de Salud y GTT SMAPS)
al campamento Parque del Oeste / Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro caracterizó una población de aproximadamente 6.102
personas, incluidos 800–1.000 niños, niñas y adolescentes y 260 mujeres embarazadas, e identificó brechas agudas
en agua segura, SMAPS, tamizaje nutricional y equipos de protección personal. Así como, el campamento ubicado en
la Escuela Gran Colombia, donde al momento de la visita tenía una población de 1.200 personas albergadas, se
encontraba coordinado por el poder popular y Ministerios del estado.
• Adenda del HNRP: Como parte de la respuesta humanitaria al terremoto de Venezuela de 2026, la coordinación del
Clúster de Salud participó activamente en el Taller de Análisis Conjunto Inter-agencial de Venezuela, un espacio de
trabajo que reunió a agencias de las Naciones Unidas, coordinadores de clústeres y socios humanitarios con el
propósito de revisar, contrastar y validar la información disponible proveniente de la Evaluación Rápida de Necesidades
(RNA) coordinada por OCHA. Para el caso de Salud se analizaron las evaluaciones de establecimientos de salud, y
otros insumos técnicos relevantes. A partir de este proceso de análisis conjunto, se consolidó una comprensión común
de las necesidades humanitarias en salud derivadas del terremoto, permitiendo estimar una población afectada de 3,2
millones de personas, un PiN de aproximadamente 2 millones de personas y una población objetivo de 1,3 millones
para la respuesta en salud. Asimismo, se acordaron criterios para identificar y priorizar las áreas geográficas más
afectadas, definir las cifras objetivo por estado y municipio, establecer las intervenciones prioritarias de salud y
desarrollar una estimación inicial de los requerimientos financieros, calculados en aproximadamente USD 40.4
millones. Los resultados del taller sirvieron además como base para la elaboración del borrador narrativo del anexo
1 https://mppre.gob.ve/publicacion/7524-ayuda-internacional-a-venezuela-supera-las-707-mil-toneladas-tras-los-fuertes-
sismos

sectorial de salud al Plan de Respuesta Humanitario, asegurando que las decisiones programáticas y financieras
estuvieran sustentadas en evidencia técnica y en un consenso inter agencial sobre las necesidades y prioridades de
la población afectada.
Resumen de la 2W
Al 30 de junio de 2026, la herramienta 2W muestra una presencia activa de socios en centros de salud clave de la región
centro-norte.
• Según lo reportado por los socios un total de 27 centros de salud en el Distrito Capital, Miranda y La Guaira contaban
con presencia operativa de los socios previo a los terremotos. En el monitoreo realizado de estos centros, posterior a
estos eventos se tiene que la mayoría permanece totalmente operativa; sin embargo, se identificaron seis
establecimientos con afectaciones, de los cuales tres se encuentran suspendidos y tres parcialmente operativos,
principalmente asociados a daños en la infraestructura, fallas eléctricas y necesidades de reparación estructural.
• Distribución por Entidad: de los reportes emitido por los socios la mayor concentración se encuentra en Distrito
Capital donde se reportaron actividades de Acción contra el Hambre, Médicos del Mundo, Project Hope y Ven Da
Tú mano. En Miranda se reportaron actividades de Acción Solidaria, CEDESEX, Project Hope, Ven Da Tú Mano,
mientras que en La Guaira los reportes fueron realizados por Humanity & Inclusion y Project Hope. Además, se
reportan intervenciones iniciales en Aragua y Falcón.2
• Tipos de Centros Apoyados: De acuerdo con los reportes, el apoyo de los socios a los Centros de Salud abraca
distintos niveles de atención, que incluyen, Hospitales (12), Consultorios Populares (15) Centros de Diagnóstico
Integral (CDI) (3). Estas organizaciones centran sus acciones en la operatividad de la red hospitalaria y ambulatoria.
Resumen 3W:
Para el 07 de julio de 2025, la respuesta en salud ante la emergencia por los terremotos reportada por los socios del Clúster
de Salud en la herramienta 3W, a contado con la participación de 22 organizaciones humanitarias incluyendo agencias de
Naciones Unidas, ONG nacionales e internacionales. La respuesta cuenta con una alta concentración operativa en el
estado La Guaira, donde se registra aproximadamente dos tercios (66% aprox.) de las intervenciones reportadas,
principalmente en Caraballeda, Catia La Mar, Maiquetía, Carlos Soublette y Naiguatá, coincidiendo con las zonas de mayor
afectación y concentración de población desplazada.
La atención primaria de salud (APS) constituye la principal línea de respuesta, representando cerca del 47% de las
actividades reportadas. Los socios han desplegado jornadas médicas, clínicas móviles y brigadas comunitarias en
campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas, garantizando acceso a consultas médicas, suministro de tratamientos
y referencia de casos. El componente de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS) sería la segunda línea de respuesta,
estas intervenciones. También se observa un importante esfuerzo orientado al fortalecimiento de la capacidad operativa
del sistema de salud con la entrega de medicamentos, equipos médicos, mobiliario, carpas, equipos informáticos, insumos
de protección personal y apoyo logístico a establecimientos de salud y autoridades sanitarias.
La respuesta también evidencia una integración temprana de salud sexual y reproductiva (SSR), con actividades de control
prenatal, acceso a métodos anticonceptivos, planificación familiar, distribución de kits de parto y realización de pruebas
rápidas para VIH y sífilis en espacios de campamentos transitorios. En materia de gestión de víctimas fatales, la respuesta
ha incluido apoyo sustancial a las instituciones responsables mediante la entrega de más de 5.000 bolsas para cadáveres
e insumos especializados.
Entre los socios que han dado respuesta ante la emergencia se encuentran la Organización Panamericana de la Salud
(OPS/OMS), UNICEF, UNFPA, ONU Mujeres, OIM, Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH), International Medical Corps (IMC),
Première Urgence Internationale (PUI), Save The Childrend (SCI), RET, MDM (Médicos del Mundo), WVI (Visión Mundial
Internacional), HIAS, GOAL, Iniciativa Mentor, así como las organizaciones nacionales Proyecto Esperanza, ADRA, Cáritas
de Venezuela, AVESSOC, Fundación Proyecto Maniapure, REDISALUD, CEDESEX, CESAP, PALUZ, ENCILUZ, FUDEP,
Ven Da Tu Mano (VDTM).
Cabe destacar que los resultados arrojados para la 2W y la 3W responden a instrumentos de recolección distintos,
los cuales dependen de los reportes realizados por los socios.
Resumen de las Capacidades de los socios
• Alcance Organizacional: 25 organizaciones socias han puesto a disposición capacidades técnicas bajo el mecanismo
unificado.
• Talento Humano y Suministros: Se cuenta con 733 profesionales de salud listos para respuesta inmediata, un
inventario de 1.175.219 unidades de medicamentos y 4.277 kits de trauma.
• Equipos Médicos de Emergencia (EMT): 12 equipos EMTs ya están desplegados y operativos en terreno, brindando
servicios en La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda y Aragua; 7 equipos adicionales se encuentran en movilización y se espera

que lleguen o inicien operaciones en las próximas horas o días; 1 equipo se encuentra en proceso de desmovilización;
y 3 equipos están listos para desplegarse si son requeridos.
Resumen de las evaluaciones de los establecimientos de Salud
Luego de recibir las evaluaciones realizadas por los socios: ACH, PE, VDTM, AS, OIM, CEDESEX, MENTOR, HI, OPS a
36 establecimientos monitoreados con Evaluaciones rápidas, el panorama es crítico debido a la presión asistencial y daños
estructurales.
• Estado de Funcionalidad: 1 centro de salud está en condición crítica; 8 se encuentran operativos; 24 parcialmente
operativos, mientras que entras que 4 se encuentran no operativos.
• Hallazgos de Evaluaciones Rápidas (ERES): Las evaluaciones en 8 hospitales de Caracas, Miranda y La Guaira
revelan caos en el flujo de pacientes, colapso de servicios forenses/morgues y una acumulación masiva de cirugías de
trauma, ortopedia y neurocirugía.
• Personal Sanitario: Se reporta personal bajo estrés extremo y extensas guardias; además de brechas críticas por
desaparición de personal clave en zonas de impacto como La Guaira
Panorama de Campamentos Transitorios
Necesidad. El desplazamiento por el temor a réplicas y el daño estructural mantiene a una gran parte de la población en
alojamientos transitorios, con concentración crítica en La Guaira, donde la ocupación se aproxima a la saturación. Persisten
necesidades de atención primaria y de trauma, salud mental, agua segura, saneamiento e insumos esenciales en los
centros.
Respuesta (nivel nacional). Según el balance de la Vicepresidencia Social (7 de julio), se encuentran asignados 87
campamentos transitorios a nivel nacional, con una capacidad instalada de 20.227 y 14.634 personas alojadas.
• Caracas: 39 centros; capacidad instalada 11.192; 4.961 personas alojadas.
• La Guaira: 26 centros (8 en proceso de ampliación); 8.613 personas alojadas.
• Miranda: 22 centros; capacidad instalada 2.003; 1.060 personas alojadas.
Respuesta del Clúster de Salud. El reporte central del Clúster (Gran Caracas, Miranda y La Guaira) monitorea
directamente 26 centros, con una capacidad instalada de 9.230 (ocupación del 81,9%) y 1.867 familias registradas. Dos
centros de Caracas reportan sobrepoblación (U.E.N. Francisco Pimentel: 780 personas frente a 260 de capacidad; C.E.
Miguel Antonio Caro: 1.506 frente a 1.500), y la Universidad Marítima del Caribe (La Guaira) se encuentra en proceso de
desconcentración.
Visitas conjuntas en terreno. La coordinación del Clúster, junto con MPPS, UNICEF y el GTT SMAPS, realizó visitas
exploratorias a dos centros: (1) el complejo Parque del Oeste / Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro (aprox. 6.102 personas, incluidos
800–1.000 niños, niñas y adolescentes y 260 gestantes registradas), con triaje y cobertura 24 horas por la Misión Barrio
Adentro y médicos cubanos, y apoyo de la Cruz Roja Venezolana, Fundasalud y 30 profesionales del Hospital Dr. Domingo
Luciani; y (2) la Escuela Gran Colombia (campamento permanente, aprox. 1.200 personas), con caracterización de
población y hallazgos de salud. Los hallazgos clínicos incluyen deshidratación, vómitos y un clúster de 10 niños con diarrea,
dermatitis aguda y picaduras de insectos, y morbilidad crónica (ENT) en adultos mayores.
El Clúster de Salud, junto con el equipo técnico del Grupo Interclúster, la OPS/OMS y las autoridades municipales, participó
en una misión conjunta de evaluación y coordinación en el municipio Miranda, en articulación con el Estado Mayor de
Gobierno, el Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud (MPPS), la Vicepresidencia Sectorial para el Socialismo Social y
Territorial, y la Mesa Técnica de Género.
Brecha. Se requiere reforzar el suministro de agua segura y saneamiento (agua potable agotada en sitios visitados),
ampliar SMAPS y primeros auxilios psicológicos, cubrir el déficit de equipamiento antropométrico y de tamizaje nutricional,
continuar con las de atención primaria/ambulatoria, provisión de medicamentos esenciales, restituir tarjetas de control
prenatal para las gestantes, y garantizar equipos de protección personal y espacios amigables para la niñez. Cuatro centros
en Caracas siguen en fase de levantamiento de información.

Brechas y Necesidades identificadas
• Suministros críticos y capacidad clínica: Persisten necesidades urgentes de material de osteosíntesis, insumos
quirúrgicos y anestésicos, equipos de quirófano, arcos en C, camas de tracción, equipos de imagen, insumos de
laboratorio, banco de sangre, ventiladores, oxígeno, autoclaves, equipos de cuidados intensivos y medicamentos
esenciales. Estas brechas limitan la capacidad para resolver la deuda quirúrgica, atender trauma, sostener servicios
hospitalarios críticos y garantizar continuidad de atención en establecimientos con funcionalidad reducida.
• Servicios básicos, bioseguridad e infraestructura hospitalaria: Varios establecimientos de salud presentan
interrupciones o limitaciones en agua, electricidad, gases medicinales, saneamiento, manejo de residuos, conectividad
y transporte. Se requiere reforzar agua segura, energía de respaldo, alimentos y condiciones mínimas para el personal
en terreno, así como fortalecer prevención y control de infecciones, gestión de residuos sanitarios, morgues,
contenedores refrigerados y manejo digno y seguro de personas fallecidas.
• Albergues y atención primaria: En alojamientos transitorios persisten brechas en caracterización de población, triaje,
aislamiento, atención primaria, referencia de casos, continuidad de atención para enfermedades crónicas, salud
materno-infantil, salud sexual y reproductiva, protección, seguridad alimentaria, agua segura, saneamiento, higiene,
manejo de residuos, iluminación, privacidad y espacios seguros para niños, niñas y personas en situación de
vulnerabilidad.
• Salud mental, protección y personal de salud: Se mantiene una alta demanda de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial,
incluyendo primeros auxilios psicológicos, identificación y referencia de casos, continuidad de atención para personas
con trastornos mentales severos y acceso a medicamentos psicotrópicos esenciales. También se requiere reforzar
rutas de protección para niños y niñas no acompañados, sobrevivientes de violencia basada en género y otros grupos
vulnerables, así como apoyo psicosocial, descanso, alimentación y condiciones seguras para el personal sanitario
afectado.
• Vigilancia epidemiológica, vacunación y prevención de brotes: Existe necesidad de fortalecer la vigilancia
sindrómica y la alerta temprana en albergues, puntos de atención y establecimientos de salud, priorizando diarrea
aguda acuosa o con sangre, fiebre, fiebre con exantema, infecciones respiratorias, vómitos súbitos, ictericia, síntomas
neurológicos, infecciones de heridas y afecciones de piel. La respuesta debe integrar vacunación, control vectorial,
WASH, toma y transporte de muestras, comunicación de riesgos y continuidad de atención para TB, VIH, enfermedades
crónicas y personas dependientes de medicamentos.
Acciones realizadas en otros estados por clústeres subnacionales.
• Aragua y Carabobo: Se ha iniciado la expansión de la cobertura hacia Aragua y se habilitó un campamento transitorio
en Carabobo para atender a damnificados.
• Yaracuy: Activación de un campamento transitorio y monitoreo del Hospital Dr. Lino Arévalo en Tucacas (Falcón), el
cual se reporta saturado por la emergencia.
• Coordinación Regional: Activación de albergues en Maracay y monitoreo de la red de referencia hacia hospitales
especializados fuera de la zona de desastre inmediata
Acciones realizadas y reportadas por los socios
• PAHO/WHO: En coordinación con el MPPS, la OPS/OMS continúa apoyando la coordinación del CICOM virtual y la
movilización de EMT, la integración de la Red EMT en acciones de vigilancia epidemiológica, fortaleciendo la detección
temprana y el monitoreo de riesgos para la salud en las zonas afectadas. Asimismo, apoyó una evaluación rápida
multisectorial en cuatro albergues temporales del eje Guarenas–Guatire, estado Miranda, identificando brechas
prioritarias en agua, saneamiento e higiene, protección y acceso a servicios de salud. Dotación de mochilas de
emergencia para las unidades ambulancia del SIAMU que continua el traslado de pacientes. En logística, OPS/OMS

ha entregado 6 toneladas de suministros médicos y medicamentos, incluyendo kits de trauma, módulos del IEHK, EPP,
kits para enfermedades no transmisibles, insumos WASH y equipos de terreno. Además, mantiene el apoyo al manejo
digno y seguro de personas fallecidas, con la distribución de 3.000 (de un total de 8.500 bolsas previstas) al
SENAMECF y la coordinación de tres contenedores refrigerados para la gestión de cuerpos. También ha facilitado
compras y donaciones de vacunas y suministros desde Brasil, Chile y Colombia.
• International Medical Corps (IMC) mantiene el despliegue simultáneo de tres Unidades Médicas Móviles (MMU) en
el estado La Guaira, brindando atención en Catia La Mar, Playa Verde, Playa Grande, Puerto Viejo y Las Salinas. Los
equipos están conformados por 3 médicos generales, 3 enfermeras, 2 pediatras, 1 especialista en ginecología y
obstetricia, personal de apoyo y equipos de Salud Mental y Apoyo Psicosocial (SMAPS). Adicionalmente, la
organización continúa apoyando el acceso a agua segura mediante el suministro de agua potable en camiones cisterna
y ha iniciado el despliegue de un Equipo Médico de Emergencia (EMT Tipo 1) en Catia La Mar para reforzar la
capacidad de respuesta sanitaria. Entre el 1 y el 6 de julio de 2026, las unidades médicas móviles realizaron un total
de 698 consultas en comunidades afectadas de La Guaira. Las enfermedades no transmisibles (ENT) representaron
la principal causa de consulta, con 321 atenciones (46%), seguidas por las enfermedades transmisibles (ET) con 236
consultas (33,8%). Asimismo, se registraron 68 consultas de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (9,7%), evidenciando
una importante demanda de estos servicios en la población afectada. Los días con mayor carga asistencial fueron el 3
y 6 de julio, con 172 consultas diarias cada uno.
• Fundación Proyecto Maniapure: Despliegue de 30 profesionales (médicos, psicólogos, voluntarios) en el hospital de
campaña de Tanaguarenas.
• CESAP / AVESSOC / Acción Campesina: Realización de evaluaciones rápidas de daños en infraestructura
residencial y de servicios en Macuto y Caraballeda.
• PUI / HI / ACTED: Levantamiento de necesidades sanitarias y de capacidad de atención en las parroquias más
afectadas de La Guaira
• MEDICOS SIN FRONTERAS: Realizó entrega de insumos y medicamentos esenciales a los principales hospitales de
Caracas.
• Ven Da Tu Mano activó sus equipos móviles de salud dentro de las primeras 24 horas del sismo, desplegándose en
los centros de alojamiento temporal y directamente en las comunidades afectadas de La Guaira. A la fecha, la
organización ha brindado atención médica a más de 2.000 pacientes, con énfasis en consulta de medicina general,
especializada, salud sexual y reproductiva, operando con equipos móviles de salud equipados con personal capacitado
e insumos especializados para la atención en el contexto de emergencia.
• CEDESEX: Donación de equipos de oficina (impresoras y resmas de papel) al laboratorio clínico del Hospital General
Nacional Dr. Miguel Pérez Carreño. Esta acción responde directamente a una solicitud del Viceministerio de Redes de
Atención Ambulatoria de Salud para fortalecer los servicios de hematología y química sanguínea ante las necesidades
crecientes por la emergencia.
• ADRA: Realizó entrega de donaciones de medicamentos e insumos médicos en la red ambulatoria especializada de
los estados afectados.
• UNICEF: Se avanzó en la coordinación de la respuesta sanitaria mediante la definición de estándares para el
despliegue de brigadas móviles integrales, fortaleciendo la articulación entre actores y la estandarización de los
mecanismos de atención y registro. Asimismo, continuó el despliegue de equipos de salud mental y apoyo
psicosocial, incluyendo la coordinación de brigadas especializadas y acciones para ampliar la cobertura de atención.
En salud materna y neonatal, se impulsaron acciones para la reactivación de servicios obstétricos y neonatales en
La Guaira y la planificación de la distribución de kits neonatales. Paralelamente, se coordinó la recepción y gestión
logística de donaciones internacionales de vacunas, así como el fortalecimiento de la cadena de frío y los
mecanismos de almacenamiento y distribución de insumos. Adicionalmente, se mantienen gestiones para asegurar
recursos logísticos, optimizar la coordinación operativa en terreno y facilitar la incorporación y acreditación del personal
de respuesta.
• UNFPA (Polideportivo Vargas, La Guaira, 03 de julio): continuó la prestación de servicios de salud sexual y
reproductiva en espacios de alojamiento temporal y atención a población afectada. En el Polideportivo Vargas, se
realizaron 21 actividades de sensibilización (14 sobre uso de condones, 6 acciones edu-comunicativas y 1 entrega de
kit de higiene), se proporcionaron 8 métodos anticonceptivos inyectables y se efectuó 1 prueba de VIH y 1 prueba de
sífilis. En el Estadio de Béisbol César Nieves, se sensibilizó a 12 personas en temas relacionados con prevención
mediante distribución de condones, se entregaron 8 métodos anticonceptivos modernos (4 inyectables y 4 implantes
subdérmicos) y se realizaron 1 prueba de VIH y 1 prueba de sífilis. Por su parte, en el Estadio de Béisbol Menor se
desarrollaron 93 actividades de sensibilización, incluyendo 71 relacionadas con prevención y uso de condones y 22
acciones edu-comunicativas. En total, UNFPA alcanzó a 126 personas mediante actividades de sensibilización,
distribuyó 16 métodos anticonceptivos modernos y realizó 2 pruebas de VIH y 2 pruebas de sífilis durante la
jornada.
• MPPS / UNICEF / Clúster de Salud / GTT SMAPS (misión exploratoria conjunta): Caracterización conjunta del
campamento transitorio Parque del Oeste / Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro, documentando demografía, cobertura de talento
humano, hallazgos clínicos y brechas multisectoriales (SMAPS, tamizaje nutricional, salud materno-infantil e

inmunización, WASH). UNICEF también está desplegando una herramienta de evaluación de salud y nutrición en KoBo
prevista para su aplicación en 280 establecimientos de salud (EESS).

VENEZUELA Earthquakes, June 24.
Situation Report No. 4. July 7, 2026
Reporting period: Fourth update, information available as of 08:00 (GMT-4) / 12:00 UTC
Prepared by: Venezuela Health Cluster, with the support of PAHO Regional Office and the
Global Health Cluster.
Glide Number: 2026-000093
Event figures (preliminary – subject to change):
¹ Official Report of the Government of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, July 7, 2026. ² PAHO/WHO earthquake
exposure analysis, June 25, 2026.
Highlights
• Casualties and Care Overview: As of July 7, the national government has reported 3,685 people deceased, 16,740
injured, 6,462 people rescued, and 25,970 patients treated following the emergency, according to the Government's
Official Report. A total of 1,076 aftershocks have been recorded since the initial event, with a decreasing trend in
frequency and magnitude.
• Governance and Coordination: The Health Cluster was ratified as the coordination channel with the Ministry of
People's Power for Health (MPPS) to centralize information and international aid, which amounts to more than 707
thousand tons.1
• Field Response: A total of 29,567 national personnel and 4,338 international rescue workers have been deployed.
• Shelter Infrastructure: A total of 87 temporary camps are assigned at the national level (Caracas 39, La Guaira 26,
Miranda 22), with an installed capacity of 20,227 and 14,634 people sheltered, according to the report of the Social
Vice-Presidency (July 7). Of these, the Health Cluster directly monitors the centers in Greater Caracas, Miranda, and
La Guaira, and has carried out field visits to some of them.
• Joint field assessment: A joint exploratory mission (MPPS, UNICEF, Health Cluster, and the MHPSS Technical
Working Group [GTT SMAPS]) to the Parque del Oeste / Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro camp characterized a population
of approximately 6,102 people, including 800–1,000 children and adolescents and 260 pregnant women, and identified
acute gaps in safe water, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), nutritional screening, and personal
protective equipment. Likewise, the camp located at the Gran Colombia School, which at the time of the visit had a
sheltered population of 1,200 people, was coordinated by the people's power and State Ministries.
• HNRP Addendum: As part of the humanitarian response to the 2026 Venezuela earthquake, the Health Cluster
coordination actively participated in the Venezuela Inter-Agency Joint Analysis Workshop, a working space that brought
together United Nations agencies, cluster coordinators, and humanitarian partners with the purpose of reviewing, cross-
checking, and validating the available information from the Rapid Needs Assessment (RNA) coordinated by OCHA. For
the Health sector, health facility assessments and other relevant technical inputs were analyzed. Based on this joint
analysis process, a common understanding of the humanitarian health needs arising from the earthquake was
consolidated, allowing for an estimated affected population of 3.2 million people, a PiN of approximately 2 million people,
and a target population of 1.3 million for the health response. Likewise, criteria were agreed upon to identify and prioritize
the most affected geographic areas, define target figures by state and municipality, establish priority health
interventions, and develop an initial estimate of financial requirements, calculated at approximately USD 40.4 million.
The workshop results also served as the basis for drafting the narrative of the health sector annex to the Humanitarian
Response Plan, ensuring that programmatic and financial decisions were grounded in technical evidence and in an
inter-agency consensus on the needs and priorities of the affected population.

2W Summary
As of June 30, 2026, the 2W tool shows an active presence of partners in key health centers of the north-central region.
• According to partner reports, a total of 27 health centers in the Capital District, Miranda, and La Guaira had operational
partner presence prior to the earthquakes. In the monitoring carried out at these centers following these events, most
remain fully operational; however, six facilities with damage were identified, of which three are suspended and three
partially operational, mainly associated with infrastructure damage, electrical failures, and structural repair needs.
• Distribution by Entity: Based on the reports submitted by partners, the greatest concentration is in the Capital District,
where activities were reported by Acción contra el Hambre, Médicos del Mundo, Project Hope, and Ven Da Tu
Mano. In Miranda, activities were reported by Acción Solidaria, CEDESEX, Project Hope, Ven Da Tu Mano, while in
La Guaira the reports were submitted by Humanity & Inclusion and Project Hope. In addition, initial interventions are
reported in Aragua and Falcón.2
• Types of Centers Supported: According to the reports, partner support to Health Centers spans different levels of
care, including Hospitals (12), Popular Clinics (Consultorios Populares) (15), and Comprehensive Diagnostic
Centers (CDI) (3). These organizations focus their actions on the operability of the hospital and outpatient network.
3W Summary:
As of July 7, 2025, the health response to the earthquake emergency reported by Health Cluster partners in the 3W tool
has involved the participation of 22 humanitarian organizations, including United Nations agencies and national and
international NGOs. The response has a high operational concentration in La Guaira state, where approximately two-thirds
(approx. 66%) of the reported interventions are recorded, mainly in Caraballeda, Catia La Mar, Maiquetía, Carlos Soublette,
and Naiguatá, coinciding with the areas of greatest impact and concentration of displaced population.
Primary health care (PHC) constitutes the main line of response, representing about 47% of the reported activities. Partners
have deployed medical campaigns, mobile clinics, and community brigades in temporary camps and affected communities,
ensuring access to medical consultations, provision of treatments, and case referral. The mental health and psychosocial
support (MHPSS) component would be the second line of response. There is also a significant effort aimed at strengthening
the operational capacity of the health system through the delivery of medicines, medical equipment, furniture, tents, IT
equipment, personal protective equipment, and logistical support to health facilities and health authorities.
The response also shows an early integration of sexual and reproductive health (SRH), with activities in prenatal care,
access to contraceptive methods, family planning, distribution of childbirth kits, and rapid testing for HIV and syphilis in
temporary camp settings. Regarding the management of fatalities, the response has included substantial support to the
responsible institutions through the delivery of more than 5,000 body bags and specialized supplies.
Among the partners that have responded to the emergency are the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO/WHO),
UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women, IOM, Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH), International Medical Corps (IMC), Première Urgence
Internationale (PUI), Save the Children (SCI), RET, MDM (Médicos del Mundo), WVI (World Vision International), HIAS,
GOAL, Mentor Initiative, as well as the national organizations Proyecto Esperanza, ADRA, Cáritas de Venezuela,
AVESSOC, Fundación Proyecto Maniapure, REDISALUD, CEDESEX, CESAP, PALUZ, ENCILUZ, FUDEP, and Ven Da
Tu Mano (VDTM).
It should be noted that the results for the 2W and the 3W come from different collection instruments, which depend
on the reports submitted by partners.
Summary of Partner Capacities
• Organizational Reach: 25 partner organizations have made technical capacities available under the unified
mechanism.
• Human Resources and Supplies: There are 733 health professionals ready for immediate response, an inventory
of 1,175,219 units of medicines and 4,277 trauma kits.
• Emergency Medical Teams (EMT): 12 EMTs are already deployed and operational in the field, providing services in
La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda, and Aragua; 7 additional teams are being mobilized and are expected to arrive or begin
operations in the coming hours or days; 1 team is in the process of demobilization; and 3 teams are ready to deploy if
required.
Summary of Health Facility Assessments
After receiving the assessments carried out by the partners ACH, PE, VDTM, AS, IOM, CEDESEX, MENTOR, HI, and
PAHO of 36 facilities monitored through rapid assessments, the outlook is critical due to the care burden and structural
damage.

• Functionality Status: 1 health center is in critical condition; 8 are operational; 24 are partially operational; while 4 are
non-operational.
• Rapid Assessment Findings (ERES): The assessments in 8 hospitals in Caracas, Miranda, and La Guaira reveal
chaos in patient flow, collapse of forensic services/morgues, and a massive backlog of trauma, orthopedic, and
neurosurgical surgeries.
• Health Personnel: Staff are reported to be under extreme stress and long shifts; in addition, there are critical gaps due
to the disappearance of key personnel in impact areas such as La Guaira
Overview of Temporary Camps
Need. Displacement due to fear of aftershocks and structural damage keeps a large part of the population in temporary
shelters, with critical concentration in La Guaira, where occupancy is approaching saturation. Needs persist for primary and
trauma care, mental health, safe water, sanitation, and essential supplies at the centers.
Response (national level). According to the report of the Social Vice-Presidency (July 7), 87 temporary camps are
assigned at the national level, with an installed capacity of 20,227 and 14,634 people sheltered.
• Caracas: 39 centers; installed capacity 11,192; 4,961 people sheltered.
• La Guaira: 26 centers (8 in the process of expansion); 8,613 people sheltered.
• Miranda: 22 centers; installed capacity 2,003; 1,060 people sheltered.
Health Cluster Response. The Cluster's central report (Greater Caracas, Miranda, and La Guaira) directly monitors 26
centers, with an installed capacity of 9,230 (81.9% occupancy) and 1,867 registered families. Two centers in Caracas report
overcrowding (U.E.N. Francisco Pimentel: 780 people against a capacity of 260; C.E. Miguel Antonio Caro: 1,506 against
1,500), and the Caribbean Maritime University (La Guaira) is in the process of decongestion.
Joint field visits. The Cluster coordination, together with MPPS, UNICEF, and the MHPSS Technical Working Group (GTT
SMAPS), conducted exploratory visits to two centers: (1) the Parque del Oeste / Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro complex (approx.
6,102 people, including 800–1,000 children and adolescents and 260 registered pregnant women), with triage and 24-hour
coverage by the Barrio Adentro Mission and Cuban physicians, and support from the Venezuelan Red Cross, Fundasalud,
and 30 professionals from Hospital Dr. Domingo Luciani; and (2) the Gran Colombia School (permanent camp, approx.
1,200 people), with population characterization and health findings. Clinical findings include dehydration, vomiting, and a
cluster of 10 children with diarrhea, acute dermatitis, and insect bites, and chronic morbidity (NCDs) in older adults.
The Health Cluster, together with the technical team of the Inter-Cluster Group, PAHO/WHO, and municipal authorities,
participated in a joint assessment and coordination mission in Miranda municipality, in coordination with the Government
General Staff, the Ministry of People's Power for Health (MPPS), the Sectoral Vice-Presidency for Social and Territorial
Socialism, and the Gender Technical Roundtable.
Gap. It is necessary to strengthen the supply of safe water and sanitation (potable water depleted at visited sites), expand
MHPSS and psychological first aid, cover the deficit in anthropometric and nutritional screening equipment, continue
primary/outpatient care, provide essential medicines, restore prenatal care cards for pregnant women, and ensure personal
protective equipment and child-friendly spaces. Four centers in Caracas are still in the data-collection phase.

Gaps and Needs Identified
• Critical supplies and clinical capacity: Urgent needs persist for osteosynthesis material, surgical and anesthetic
supplies, operating room equipment, C-arms, traction beds, imaging equipment, laboratory supplies, blood bank,
ventilators, oxygen, autoclaves, intensive care equipment, and essential medicines. These gaps limit the capacity to
resolve the surgical backlog, treat trauma, sustain critical hospital services, and ensure continuity of care in facilities
with reduced functionality.
• Basic services, biosafety, and hospital infrastructure: Several health facilities present interruptions or limitations in
water, electricity, medical gases, sanitation, waste management, connectivity, and transportation. It is necessary to
strengthen safe water, backup power, food, and minimum conditions for field personnel, as well as to strengthen
infection prevention and control, health waste management, morgues, refrigerated containers, and the dignified and
safe management of the deceased.
• Shelters and primary care: In temporary shelters, gaps persist in population characterization, triage, isolation, primary
care, case referral, continuity of care for chronic diseases, maternal and child health, sexual and reproductive health,
protection, food security, safe water, sanitation, hygiene, waste management, lighting, privacy, and safe spaces for
children and people in situations of vulnerability.
• Mental health, protection, and health personnel: There remains a high demand for mental health and psychosocial
support, including psychological first aid, case identification and referral, continuity of care for people with severe mental
disorders, and access to essential psychotropic medicines. It is also necessary to strengthen protection pathways for
unaccompanied children, survivors of gender-based violence, and other vulnerable groups, as well as psychosocial
support, rest, food, and safe conditions for affected health personnel.
• Epidemiological surveillance, vaccination, and outbreak prevention: There is a need to strengthen syndromic
surveillance and early warning in shelters, care points, and health facilities, prioritizing acute watery or bloody diarrhea,
fever, fever with rash, respiratory infections, sudden vomiting, jaundice, neurological symptoms, wound infections, and
skin conditions. The response must integrate vaccination, vector control, WASH, sample collection and transport, risk
communication, and continuity of care for TB, HIV, chronic diseases, and people dependent on medicines.
Actions carried out in other states by subnational clusters.
• Aragua and Carabobo: Coverage expansion toward Aragua has begun, and a temporary camp was set up in Carabobo
to serve those affected.
• Yaracuy: Activation of a temporary camp and monitoring of Hospital Dr. Lino Arévalo in Tucacas (Falcón), which is
reported to be saturated due to the emergency.
• Regional Coordination: Activation of shelters in Maracay and monitoring of the referral network to specialized hospitals
outside the immediate disaster zone
Actions carried out and reported by partners
• PAHO/WHO: In coordination with the MPPS, PAHO/WHO continues to support the coordination of the virtual CICOM
and the mobilization of EMTs, the integration of the EMT Network into epidemiological surveillance actions,
strengthening early detection and monitoring of health risks in the affected areas. It also supported a multisectoral rapid
assessment in four temporary shelters along the Guarenas–Guatire corridor, Miranda state, identifying priority gaps in
water, sanitation and hygiene, protection, and access to health services. Provision of emergency backpacks for the
SIAMU ambulance units that continue to transport patients. In logistics, PAHO/WHO has delivered 6 tons of medical
supplies and medicines, including trauma kits, IEHK modules, PPE, kits for noncommunicable diseases, WASH
supplies, and field equipment. In addition, it maintains support for the dignified and safe management of the deceased,
with the distribution of 3,000 (out of a total of 8,500 planned bags) to SENAMECF and the coordination of three
refrigerated containers for the management of bodies. It has also facilitated purchases and donations of vaccines and
supplies from Brazil, Chile, and Colombia.
• International Medical Corps (IMC) maintains the simultaneous deployment of three Mobile Medical Units (MMU) in La
Guaira state, providing care in Catia La Mar, Playa Verde, Playa Grande, Puerto Viejo, and Las Salinas. The teams are
made up of 3 general physicians, 3 nurses, 2 pediatricians, 1 specialist in gynecology and obstetrics, support staff, and
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) teams. Additionally, the organization continues to support access
to safe water through the supply of potable water by tanker trucks and has begun deploying an Emergency Medical
Team (EMT Type 1) in Catia La Mar to reinforce health response capacity. Between July 1 and 6, 2026, the mobile
medical units carried out a total of 698 consultations in affected communities of La Guaira. Noncommunicable diseases
(NCDs) represented the main reason for consultation, with 321 visits (46%), followed by communicable diseases (CDs)

with 236 consultations (33.8%). Likewise, 68 mental health and psychosocial support consultations were recorded
(9.7%), evidencing a significant demand for these services among the affected population. The days with the highest
care load were July 3 and 6, with 172 consultations each per day.
• Fundación Proyecto Maniapure: Deployment of 30 professionals (physicians, psychologists, volunteers) at the field
hospital in Tanaguarenas.
• CESAP / AVESSOC / Acción Campesina: Carrying out rapid damage assessments of residential and service
infrastructure in Macuto and Caraballeda.
• PUI / HI / ACTED: Assessment of health needs and care capacity in the most affected parishes of La Guaira
• MÉDECINS SANS FRONTIÈRES: Delivered essential supplies and medicines to the main hospitals of Caracas.
• Ven Da Tu Mano activated its mobile health teams within the first 24 hours of the earthquake, deploying to temporary
shelter centers and directly in the affected communities of La Guaira. To date, the organization has provided medical
care to more than 2,000 patients, with an emphasis on general and specialized medical consultations and sexual and
reproductive health, operating with mobile health teams equipped with trained personnel and specialized supplies for
care in the emergency context.
• CEDESEX: Donation of office equipment (printers and reams of paper) to the clinical laboratory of the Hospital General
Nacional Dr. Miguel Pérez Carreño. This action responds directly to a request from the Vice-Ministry of Outpatient
Health Care Networks to strengthen hematology and blood chemistry services in the face of growing needs due to the
emergency.
• ADRA: Delivered donations of medicines and medical supplies to the specialized outpatient network of the affected
states.
• UNICEF: Progress was made in coordinating the health response by defining standards for the deployment of
comprehensive mobile brigades, strengthening coordination among actors and the standardization of care and
registration mechanisms. Likewise, the deployment of mental health and psychosocial support teams continued,
including the coordination of specialized brigades and actions to expand care coverage. In maternal and neonatal
health, actions were promoted for the reactivation of obstetric and neonatal services in La Guaira and the planning
of the distribution of neonatal kits. In parallel, the reception and logistical management of international vaccine
donations was coordinated, as well as the strengthening of the cold chain and the storage and distribution mechanisms
for supplies. Additionally, efforts continue to secure logistical resources, optimize operational coordination in the field,
and facilitate the incorporation and accreditation of response personnel.
• UNFPA (Polideportivo Vargas, La Guaira, July 3): continued the provision of sexual and reproductive health services
in temporary shelter spaces and care for the affected population. At the Polideportivo Vargas, 21 awareness-raising
activities were carried out (14 on condom use, 6 educational-communication actions, and 1 hygiene kit delivery), 8
injectable contraceptive methods were provided, and 1 HIV test and 1 syphilis test were performed. At the César Nieves
Baseball Stadium, 12 people were sensitized on prevention-related topics through condom distribution, 8 modern
contraceptive methods were delivered (4 injectables and 4 subdermal implants), and 1 HIV test and 1 syphilis test were
performed. Meanwhile, at the Minor League Baseball Stadium, 93 awareness-raising activities were carried out,
including 71 related to prevention and condom use and 22 educational-communication actions. In total, UNFPA reached
126 people through awareness-raising activities, distributed 16 modern contraceptive methods, and performed 2
HIV tests and 2 syphilis tests during the day.
• MPPS / UNICEF / Health Cluster / MHPSS Technical Working Group (GTT SMAPS) (joint exploratory mission):
Joint characterization of the Parque del Oeste / Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro temporary camp, documenting
demographics, human-resource coverage, clinical findings, and multisectoral gaps (MHPSS, nutritional screening,
maternal and child health and immunization, WASH). UNICEF is also deploying a health and nutrition assessment tool
in KoBo planned for application in 280 health facilities (EESS).

documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #9 (8 de julio de 2026)
documents.body_text:
El noveno Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela al 8 de julio. También incluye las prioridades del Llamamiento de Fondos de la OIM para ampliar la asistencia urgente.

**Aspectos destacados**

La OIM lanzó un Llamamiento de Fondos de USD 98 millones para asistir a 850.000 personas y 140 entidades entre julio y diciembre de 2026, priorizando alojamiento, recuperación temprana, salud, WASH, protección, datos, DTM y coordinación.

En el Estadio César Nieves, se reanudó el registro, con 20 nuevas familias registradas, alcanzando un total de 482 familias, equivalentes a 1.479 personas. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, el Equipo Médico de Emergencia de la OIM brindó 132 consultas de salud y salud mental.

A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado a 4.011 personas únicas con 6.713 asistencias y servicios de distribución, principalmente en salud, alojamiento y protección.

**Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM continúa apoyando campamentos transitorios priorizados en La Guaira, incluidos el Estadio César Nieves, el Polideportivo José María Vargas y Playa Grande, mediante coordinación de sitio, registro, WASH, protección, salud y coordinación interagencial.

En el Estadio César Nieves, continuaron el registro y la coordinación de la distribución de alimentos, mientras que las mejoras WASH avanzaron con la señalización de baños por sexo y la instalación de duchas. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, se brindaron 132 consultas médicas y de SMAPS.

Las actividades de protección incluyeron seis casos asistidos mediante triaje de protección, sensibilización sobre PEAS, apoyo psicosocial, análisis de riesgo de explotación y abuso sexual, y colocación de materiales informativos sobre PEAS en áreas clave del campamento.

A la fecha, se han movilizado seis vuelos con carga humanitaria, incluidos cinco enviados por DHR del Gobierno de los Estados Unidos en coordinación con la OIM, y un vuelo con suministros de la OIM desde Panamá, con apoyo de DHL.

**Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La OIM continuará enfocándose en la coordinación y gestión de sitios, registro, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, recopilación de datos, DTM y coordinación interagencial en campamentos transitorios priorizados y comunidades afectadas.

El financiamiento adicional a través del Llamamiento de Fondos de USD 98 millones de la OIM permitiría ampliar la asistencia de alojamiento de emergencia, la entrega de artículos esenciales, el apoyo a la recuperación temprana, los servicios de protección, la atención de salud y salud mental, el monitoreo de movilidad y la gestión de información.

VENEZUELA (REPÚBLICA BOLIVARIANA DE) RESPUESTA A TERREMOTO
Reporte de Situación #9 | 8 de julio 2026
LLAMAMIENTO DE FONDOS DE LA OIM: PRIORIDADES DE FINANCIAMIENTO
La OIM solicita USD 98 millones para asistir a 850.000 personas y 140 entidades entre julio y diciembre de 2026. Esto permitirá
a la OIM ampliar una respuesta multisectorial en seis áreas prioritarias, con las siguientes acciones clave propuestas por sector:
ALOJAMIENTO, TIERRA Y ASENTAMIENTOS
• Distribuir materiales de alojamiento de emergencia y artículos de primera necesidad.
• Mejorar campamentos transitorios y sitios colectivos mediante espacios cubiertos, iluminación, drenaje, medidas de seguri-
dad contra incendios, remoción de escombros, adecuaciones de accesibilidad y mejoras básicas del sitio.
• Fortalecer equipos de gestión de sitios, comités comunitarios, puntos de información, mecanismos de quejas y retroali-
mentación, sistemas de derivación y participación inclusiva.
• Integrar estrategias de salida para facilitar retornos, reubicaciones o transiciones hacia la recuperación temprana de manera
segura, voluntaria y digna.
RECUPERACIÓN TEMPRANA Y SOLUCIONES DURADERAS
• Apoyar a los hogares afectados para restaurar medios de vida, acceder a derechos básicos, recuperar documentación, abor-
dar temas de vivienda, tierra y propiedad, y fortalecer la cohesión social.
• Apoyar la elaboración conjunta de planes de recuperación que vinculen las necesidades con soluciones duraderas.
• Apoyar a organizaciones de la sociedad civil y comunitarias mediante asistencia técnica, subvenciones y capacitación
• Rehabilitar infraestructura crítica, incluyendo sistemas de agua, escuelas, establecimientos de salud y mercados.
SALUD Y SALUD MENTAL Y APOYO PSICOSOCIAL — SMAPS
• Desplegar equipos multidisciplinarios adicionales de salud y SMAPS para brindar atención primaria, atención de emergencia,
derivaciones y alcance comunitario en zonas desatendidas.
• Adquirir y preposicionar medicamentos esenciales e insumos médicos para reforzar la capacidad del sistema de salud.
• Apoyar primeros auxilios psicológicos, consejería, telepsicología, derivaciones y actividades comunitarias de SMAPS.
• Fortalecer la vigilancia epidemiológica, la gestión de información en salud, las medidas de prevención y control de infec-
ciones, y la capacidad de respuesta en campamentos transitorios, comunidades afectadas y zonas desatendidas.
AGUA, SANEAMIENTO E HIGIENE (WASH)
• Proveer agua segura mediante distribución, almacenamiento, tratamiento a nivel de hogar y monitoreo de calidad.
• Instalar y/o rehabilitar infraestructura de saneamiento e higiene accesible en campamentos transitorios y comunidades.
• Mejorar el drenaje, la gestión de aguas residuales y residuos sólidos, el desazolve y las jornadas comunitarias de limpieza para
reducir riesgos de salud pública.
• Distribuir suministros de higiene, prevención y control de infecciones, y gestión de higiene menstrual, fortaleciendo al mismo
tiempo las capacidades locales para restaurar y mantener servicios de agua y saneamiento.
PROTECCIÓN
• Ampliar evaluaciones, auditorías de seguridad, derivaciones, orientación legal, gestión de casos y protección comunitaria.
• Fortalecer mecanismos de Rendición de Cuentas a las Poblaciones Afectadas (AAP) y canales seguros, accesibles y confiden-
ciales de reporte, incluidos mecanismos relacionados con la Prevención de la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS).
• Mitigar riesgos de violencia contra la mujer, protección a la niñez, trata, inclusión y acceso a servicios.
• Brindar asistencia a personas con necesidades específicas comopersonas mayores, embarazadas, lactantes, niñas, niños y ad-
olescentes no acompañados, personas con discapacidad, personas indígenas, retornadas y personas sin documentación.
DATOS, DTM Y EVALUACIONES DE NECESIDADES
• Ampliar evaluaciones, registro, seguimiento del desplazamiento y monitoreo de campamentos transitorios
• Producir perfiles de sitios, bases de datos sobre desplazamiento, análisis de tendencias y productos de información para
orientar la priorización y la toma de decisiones.
• Fortalecer conectividad, recopilación de datos, registro, deduplicación, focalización y seguimiento de derivaciones de casos.
• Apoyar la coordinación interagencial mediante intercambio estructurado de información, análisis conjunto, evaluaciones sec-
toriales, orientación técnica y fortalecimiento de capacidades.

documents.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #9 (8 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
The ninth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela as of 8 July. It also includes IOM’s Flash Appeal funding priorities to scale up urgent assistance.

**Highlights**

IOM launched a USD 98 million Appeal to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities between July and December 2026, prioritizing shelter, early recovery, health, WASH, protection, data, DTM and coordination.

At César Nieves Stadium, registration resumed, with 20 new families registered, bringing the total to 482 families, or 1,479 people. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM’s Emergency Medical Team provided 132 health and mental health consultations.

To date, IOM has reached 4,011 unique individuals with 6,713 assistance and distribution services, mainly in health, shelter and protection.

**IOM activities**

IOM continues supporting prioritized transitory camps in La Guaira, including César Nieves Stadium, José María Vargas Sports Complex and Playa Grande, with site coordination, registration, WASH, protection, health and inter-agency coordination.

At César Nieves Stadium, registration and food distribution coordination continued, while WASH improvements advanced through toilet signage by sex and shower installation. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, 132 medical and MHPSS consultations were provided.

Protection activities included six cases assisted through protection triage, PSEA sensitization, psychosocial support, SEA risk analysis and placement of PSEA information materials in key camp areas.

Six humanitarian cargo flights have been mobilized to date, including five sent by DHR of the Government of the United States in coordination with IOM, and one flight with IOM supplies from Panama, supported by DHL.

**IOM planned response**

IOM will continue focusing on site coordination and management, registration, WASH, health and Mental Health, protection, data collection, DTM and inter-agency coordination in prioritized transitory camps and affected communities.

Additional funding through IOM’s USD 98 million Appeal would enable the scale-up of emergency shelter assistance, core relief items, early recovery support, protection services, health and mental health care, mobility monitoring and information management.

VENEZUELA (BOLIVARIAN REPUBLIC OF) EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
Situation Report #9 | 8 July 2026
IOM FLASH APPEAL: FUNDING PRIORITIES
IOM is appealing for USD 98 million to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities between July and December 2026. Additional
funding will enable IOM to scale up a multisectoral response across six priority áreas, key proposed actions per sector are:
SHELTER, LAND AND SITE COORDINATION
• Procure and distribute emergency shelter materials and core relief items, including tarpaulins, tents, solar lamps, kitchen sets,
jerrycans, blankets and other essential household items.
• Improve transitory camps and collective sites through covered spaces, lighting, drainage, fire safety measures, debris removal,
accessibility upgrades and basic site improvements.
• Strengthen site management teams, community committees, information points, complaint and feedback mechanisms, refe-
rral systems and inclusive participation.
• Integrate exit strategies to facilitate safe, voluntary and dignified returns, relocations or transition to early recovery.
EARLY RECOVERY AND SOLUTIONS
• Support affected households to restore livelihoods, access basic rights, recover documentation, address housing, land and
property issues, and strengthen social cohesion.
• Assist authorities and communities to co-create recovery plans that link needs with longer-term durable solutions.
• Support civil society and community-based actors through technical assistance, grants, training and planning.
• Rehabilitate critical infrastructure and essential services, including water systems, schools, health facilities and marketplaces.
HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH AND PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT (MHPSS)
• Deploy additional multidisciplinary health and MHPSS teams to provide primary healthcare, emergency care, referrals and
outreach in underserved areas.
• Procure and pre-position essential medicines, medical supplies and emergency kits to reinforce health system surge capacity.
• Support psychological first aid, counselling, telepsychology, specialized referrals and community-based MHPSS activities.
• Strengthen disease surveillance, health information management, Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) measures and re-
sponse capacity in transitory camps, affected communities and underserved areas.
WATER, SANITATION AND HYGIENE (WASH)
• Conduct assessments and provide safe water through distribution, storage, household treatment and quality monitoring.
• Install, rehabilitate and maintain sex-segregated and accessible sanitation and hygiene infrastructure in transitory camps and
affected communities.
• Improve drainage, wastewater and solid waste management, desludging and community clean-up to reduce health risks.
• Distribute hygiene, infection prevention and control, and menstrual hygiene management supplies, while strengthening local
capacity to restore and maintain WASH services.
PROTECTION
• Expand risk assessments, safety audits, referrals, legal orientation, case management and community-based protection.
• Strengthen Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) mechanisms and safe, accessible and confidential reporting chan-
nels, including mechanisms related to Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA).
• Risk mitigation for violence against women, child protection, trafficking in persons, disability inclusion and access to services.
• Provide assistance to people with specific needs, including older persons, pregnant and lactating women, unaccompanied or
separated children and adolescents, persons with disabilities, Indigenous persons, returnees and people without documentation.
DATA, DISPLACEMENT TRACKING MATRIX (DTM) AND COORDINATION SUPPORT
• Expand assessments, registration, displacement tracking, transitory camp monitoring, mobility analysis and intention surveys.
• Produce site profiles, displacement datasets, trend analyses and products to guide prioritization and decision-making.
• Strengthen connectivity, real-time data , registration, deduplication, vulnerability-based targeting and referral tracking.
• Support inter-agency coordination through structured information-sharing, joint analysis, sectoral assessments, technical gui-
dance and capacity-building.

documents.title: “They’re flinching at the slightest noise” - Children’s mental wellbeing at stake two weeks on from devastating earthquake
documents.body_text:
**Caracas, 9 July 2026 –** Children are showing signs of mental distress in the wake of last month’s devastating earthquakes in Venezuela, with parents and psychologists reporting children flinching at the slightest noise, finding it difficult to sleep, and showing more signs of irritability and aggression.

Children who have undergone such stressful experiences will often show their stress through behaviour changes and need support to recover, said Save the Children.

Save the Children has established safe spaces for children within the earthquake zone where families can bring their children to play and regain a sense of normalcy and strengthen their resilience, while also being assessed for more severe psychosocial distress or other protection concerns.

Counsellors at these spaces have reported some children are showing signs of acute distress including anger, while children as young as seven or eight are saying they are scared of what the future holds. Some parents have told our staff that their children now become anxious when they see the cracks in the ground, while others are struggling to sleep at night and are flinching when they hear loud sounds such as rumbles of thunder.

Some older children told Save the Children staff that they had to protect and rescue younger family members while they escaped from the earthquake, despite feeling deeply scared themselves, and continue to carry this anxiety with them.

Around 1.8 million people including about 680,000 children have been impacted by the earthquakes that struck Venezuela two weeks ago, many of whom witnessed their friends and family members die before their eyes, with mental and health and psychosocial support identified by the UN and NGOs as one of the key needs facing affected people. \[1\]

Children who have experienced extremely distressing events are at risk of long-lasting impacts for months or even years to come unless they receive mental health and psychosocial support at the onset of the distressful event, said Save the Children.

**Two-year-old Daisy\*** was with her parents when the earthquake struck their home in Caracas. When Daisy stopped eating after the earthquake, **her mother Yusmary\*, 24,** brought her to Save the Children’s mobile health clinic, run by local partner Paluz. Yusmary said that Daisy will now only breastfeed for comfort and will only eat a few spoonfuls of solid food if she is extremely hungry.

**Yusmary said:** *“Before the earthquake, \[Daisy\] used to eat normally, just fine. But after the earthquake, she became like this. When she sees cracks on the floor, she starts crying and screaming. Then she calls me and says, "Mom, look at the floor!"*

**Isabel\*,** a psychologist working with Save the Children said: *“In our safe spaces where children come to play and receive support, we are seeing children who are scared about what the future holds. They are telling us things such as ‘my parents worked so hard to have a house, and now we have nothing.’ Children as young as seven or eight are deeply worried about how they're going to rebuild their lives.*

*“Our safe spaces allow children to express themselves in a safe and supportive environment which is vital since some children are telling our teams that they are reluctant to express their fears at home, as they see their parents and caregivers upset and worried”.*

**Fatima Andraca, Save the Children’s Country Director in Venezuela said:**

*“Many children in Venezuela have experienced extremely distressing events that no child should ever have to see. They have witnessed their friends and family members die before their eyes, while others continue to live with the uncertainty of not knowing where their loved ones are. Thousands of children are sheltering in tents in the streets where their daily routines and sense of security have been ripped away.*

*“Protection and psychosocial support are urgent priorities for children. With so many people dead, injured or missing, and so many families uprooted from their homes, children need both immediate and long-term support to ensure that this devastating disaster does not cause long lasting mental harm. With the right help, most children psychologically impacted by the earthquakes will eventually be able to recover.”*

Save the Children is on the ground in Venezuela, working with authorities and local partners and will be providing primary healthcare through mobile clinics, distributing hygiene and shelter kits, clean water and essential supplies. Save the Children is also running safe spaces where children can access mental health support and continue learning while schools remain closed, and where those with more significant needs can be referred for individual support.

Save the Children is an independent, impartial child rights organisation, working in Venezuela since 2019. Since the humanitarian crisis started to rapidly deteriorate a few years ago, Save the Children has been scaling up its response through local partners to support the increasing number of children in need.

\*Names changed for anonymity.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #2 (9th July 2026)
documents.body_text:
Two weeks after the 24 June seismic doublet (magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, 39 seconds apart), Venezuela's emergency has shifted from acute search and rescue into sustained, multi-sector humanitarian operations, even as rescuers occasionally still find survivors and already-weakened buildings continue to collapse.  

The official death toll stands at 3,535, with 16,740 people injured and nearly 18,000 displaced. Authorities now report more than 940 aftershocks. Buildings damaged are reported between 856 (government) and 2,501 (OCHA/ partner tracking), including 190 confirmed collapses.  

More than 55,000 people remain unaccounted for on the national missing-persons platform, of which 123 are children. Authorities report 80 operational transitional camps supporting the displaced population.  

Independent satellite-based analysis (ANOVA Policy Research, with Microsoft AI for Good) suggests population exposure in La Guaira's coastal corridor may be up to three times higher than official figures capture, due to outdated census frameworks and under-counted floating population. Of an estimated 403,784 residents across seven La Guaira parishes, roughly 73,500 lived in structures with observable damage, and 37,600 in structures with severe damage or collapse — the group most likely to need transitional or permanent housing.  

The UNDRR assessment estimates approximately USD 37 billion in direct damage economy-wide, of which roughly USD 24 billion is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools, hospitals, and public facilities, alongside a separate preliminary UNDP estimate of USD 6.7 billion, equivalent to 6% of GDP.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes leave children at greater risk of violence
documents.body_text:
9 July 2026 The earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June have left children increasingly vulnerable to trafficking, sexual exploitation, violence and other forms of abuse, as families struggle to recover from the devastation.

### Trafficking networks target children in emergencies

Yesica Serrano, Regional Child Protection in Humanitarian Action Adviser at Plan International, speaking from Caracas stressed that criminal trafficking networks often seek to take advantage of the chaos that follows emergencies, targeting girls and boys who have been separated from their families, lost their care givers or have missing relatives or who are otherwise left vulnerable by the crisis.

“During emergencies, the protective care environment for children weakens. Caregivers are under immense stress, looking for ways to cope with their situation, may lose a certain level of alertness and vigilance over the care of children. And it is in these lapses that trafficking networks and other perpetrators of abuse take advantage of these moments of vulnerability to target and recruit children,” said Serrano from Caracas.

As an aggravating factor, recruitment of children through social media is common in Latin America, and during emergencies, when children are more connected online and caregivers are focused on rebuilding their lives and other basic needs, attention to the content children consume decreases, which increases the risk of exposure to harmful content.

### Children vulnerable to multiple forms of abuse

Family separation is among the most significant child protection risks following a disaster. When caregivers have died, are hospitalised, or lose contact with children during evacuation children can be left without the care and protection they need. Children who are alone or whose family support networks have been disrupted face heightened risks of trafficking and sexual exploitation.

Adolescent girls and boys are more exposed to child labour, trafficking for the purposes of sexual exploitation, and recruitment by criminal groups, through coercion or false promises, presenting themselves as an alternative solution to meet their needs.

“Emergencies do not affect all children equally. Girls and adolescent girls face increased risks of sexual exploitation, violence and child labour, particularly linked to domestic work, while adolescents in general are more exposed to the possible risk of recruitment by criminal groups.” Said Carmen Elena Alemán, Regional Director for Plan International in Latin America and the Caribbean.

### How Plan works to keep children safe

Plan International works to prevent these risks alongside its partner organisations, providing group-based psychosocial support to caregivers to prevent violence and strengthen protective family environments, and working directly with children to reduce their risk factors for violence, abuse, exploitation, and neglect, and to support their psycho-emotional recovery.

In addition, we are distributing hygiene kits and dignity kits as well as essential household items, providing safe spaces and psychosocial support in communities across 2 affected states, and conducting emergency education and primary health care activities, with a special focus on girls and adolescents.

The organisation calls on various stakeholders to ensure that the humanitarian response in Venezuela incorporates child protection measures from the very beginning: family tracing and reunification processes in coordination with the relevant authorities; strengthened oversight in shelters and collective housing sites; and accessible reporting mechanisms adapted to children’s needs.

documents.title: Situational Report - Response to Venezuela Earthquakes (July 8th, 2026)
documents.body_text:
**Highlights**

• The humanitarian crisis continues to evolve following the twin earthquakes of 24 June. According to OCHA (7 July), 3,685 people have died, 16,740 have been injured, more than 1,000 aftershocks have been recorded and 6,462 people have been rescued, with La Guaira remaining the hardest-hit state. Authorities also report that 17,907 people have been left without housing, increasing humanitarian needs across affected communities.

• The response is progressively shifting from life-saving search and rescue to sustained humanitarian assistance, with temporary camps expanding and growing needs in health, shelter, safe water, sanitation, protection and education.  
Humanitarian actors continue scaling up multisectoral support.

• Child protection concerns continue to intensify. Children remain at heightened risk of family separation, violence, psychosocial distress and disrupted education, reinforcing the need for specialised protection and mental health services.

• Assessments continue to confirm a severe humanitarian crisis, including widespread housing destruction, damaged public infrastructure, overwhelmed health services and critical water and sanitation needs. Authorities report 856 affected buildings, including 190 collapsed structures, while preliminary estimates place direct physical damage at USD 37 billion.

• Preliminary estimates indicate USD 37 billion in direct physical damage, underscoring that humanitarian needs will extend beyond emergency relief into recovery, reconstruction and restoration of essential services.

• Plan International with partners has already reached more than 1,635 people across Distrito Capital and Miranda with psychosocial support, primary health care and emergency relief items, while continuing to scale up operations.

As the response evolves, protecting communities from secondary public health emergencies — including infectious disease outbreaks — is an increasingly important priority.

Project HOPE’s Response

Project HOPE will continue improving access to healthcare in Venezuela, especially
for earthquake-affected communities, by expanding mobile medical services,
strengthening referral pathways between mobile clinics and health facilities, and
scaling up WASH and MHPSS programming to help communities recover and reduce
the risk of secondary public health crises.
Project HOPE is coordinating with other actors to avoid duplication and is working to
deliver response activities at health facilities and within communities, including sites
housing displaced populations. We will continue to work with Ministry of Health,
PAHO, national authorities, and humanitarian partners through established
coordination mechanisms.
Project HOPE is providing primary healthcare and operating mobile medical units
while scaling up additional activities. The team is procuring and coordinating the
delivery of additional humanitarian supplies, including hygiene kits, water filters,
generators, communications equipment, child activity kits, and pharmaceuticals.
Project HOPE has reached more than 5,400 people through all health and
humanitarian response activities, including primary healthcare consultations,
medicine and medical supply deliveries, psychological first aid, WASH activities, and
distributions of essential relief supplies.
Health
• Project HOPE is supporting 13 primary health centers across the affected
area, equipping health workers with what they need to provide care.
• Project HOPE is operating two mobile medical units, with plans to increase
to five mobile medical units later this week and continue expanding our
reach throughout July to improve access in hard-to-reach communities.
Venezuela Earthquakes — July 7, 2026
Page 2 of 3

• Disease surveillance has become an increasing priority and Project HOPE
teams are closely monitoring for potential future outbreaks of cholera,
dengue, typhoid fever, hepatitis A, diarrheal diseases, Zika, Chikungunya,
and malaria — which often emerge when disasters disrupt WASH systems.
• Project HOPE clinical teams are treating patients presenting with
respiratory infections, diarrhea, skin conditions, hypertension, asthma,
and earthquake-related injuries, and one presumptive malaria case has
been referred for testing. Maternal health needs are an increasing concern
as pregnant women face disruptions in care and access barriers.
Mental Health & Psychosocial Support
• With mental health needs continuing to soar, Project HOPE is expanding
psychological first aid and MHPSS services so that survivors, displaced
families, and frontline responders can adequately cope with trauma
• Project HOPE’s psychological first aid services in Venezuela are currently
being offered both in-person during on-site activities and remotely via
telephone.
Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Support
• WASH interventions continue to scale, with Project HOPE distributing more
than 1,000 hygiene kits, delivering safe drinking water to affected
communities, providing water purification tablets, supporting health
facilities with infection prevention and control supplies, and preparing for
future water and sanitation repairs.
• Deliveries of cleaning and disinfection supplies were completed at four
supported health centers in Distrito Capital. These deliveries will benefit an
estimated 300-500 people at each center.
Project HOPE has worked in Venezuela since 2019, strengthening access to health
services, medicines, and health education, while supporting local health workers and
community-based responses to humanitarian needs. Project HOPE has a team of
over 100 in the country, and additional Project HOPE emergency response team
members are mobilizing to support the most urgent health and humanitarian needs.
Project HOPE has responded to multiple earthquakes in recent years, including the
2025 Myanmar earthquake, the 2023 Türkiye-Syria earthquakes, the 2023 Morocco
earthquake, the 2022 West Java earthquake, and the 2021 Haiti earthquake.

documents.title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
documents.body_text:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

On the 24th of June 2026, two earthquakes of 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes affected the centre-north of Venezuela, with particularly severe consequences in the states of La Guaira and Grand Caracas. After 12 days, the emergency continues to evolve in a context marked by internal displacement, temporary shelter arrangements for affected populations in formal or informal collective spaces, persistent disruptions in access to services, and growing demand for humanitarian assistance and protection mechanisms.

The available information shows that protection needs continue to rise among the population affected by the earthquakes. In addition, the effects of the emergency are not strictly limited to the areas directly impacted, as population displacements have been observed toward host communities and other states in the country, including Bolívar, Delta Amacuro, Anzoátegui, Sucre, Zulia, Táchira, and Apure. The loss of homes, displacement, stays in temporary government-managed shelters and informal accommodation sites, as well as the disruption or weakening of family, community, institutional, and protection networks, have increased exposure to protection risks and reduced the coping capacity of affected communities.

Assessments conducted identify significant concerns related to mental health and psychosocial support needs, family separation, inadequate privacy and security in accommodation facilities, and the loss of personal documentation, which may affect access to assistance and essential services. These risks disproportionately affect children and adolescents, women, older persons, persons with disabilities, and other individuals with specific protection needs. In this context, the sector’s priorities continue to focus on strengthening protection mechanisms for the most vulnerable populations, increasing access to specialised services, and helping ensure that affected people can access humanitarian assistance and available services safely and with dignity.
