documents.title: Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela: Transitional Camps (06 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
Following the earthquakes that occurred on 24 June 2026, La Guaira State reported some of the most severe impacts and one of the highest levels of population displacement. In support of the response led by national, state and municipal authorities, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is coordinating the management of three transitory camps — Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Estadio Playa Grande — where, together with other humanitarian actors, it provides assistance services. This coordination facilitates the provision of basic services, identification, case assistance and referrals for people with specific needs.

This document presents information on the occupancy and general characteristics of these three temporary accommodation sites. The figures reflect the situation observed at the time of reporting, are preliminary, and are subject to validation and updates as new information becomes available.

documents.title: República Bolivariana de Venezuela: Campamentos Transitorios (06 de julio de 2026)
documents.body_text:
Tras los terremotos ocurridos el 24 de junio de 2026, el estado La Guaira registró algunas de las afectaciones más severas y uno de los mayores desplazamientos de población reportados. En apoyo a la respuesta liderada por las autoridades nacionales, estadales y municipales, la Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM) coordina la gestión de tres Campamentos Transitorios —Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Estadio Playa Grande— donde, junto con otros actores humanitarios, brinda servicios de asistencia. Esta articulación facilita la provisión de servicios básicos, la identificación, así como la atención de casos y derivación de personas con necesidades específicas.

Este documento presenta información sobre la ocupación y las características generales de estos tres sitios de alojamiento temporal. Las cifras reflejan la situación observada al momento del reporte, son preliminares y están sujetas a validación y actualización conforme se disponga de nueva información.

Venezuela, Caracas.
• Se invita a los socios a continuar registrando las actualizaciones en cuanto a
viabilidad a través de la plataforma LogIE, para mantener informado al público en
general el estado de las vías de acceso a las zonas de contingencia.
1. ACTUALIZACIONES GENERALES DE LA SITUACIÓN
• Balance de víctimas oficial (hasta el 05 de julio de 2026): se reportan 3.342 personas fallecidas, 16.740
heridas y más de 17.345 damnificadas, cifras que continúan en aumento. Asimismo, 6.462 personas han
sido rescatadas.
2. ACTUALIZACIONES LOGÍSTICAS
• Se mantienen desafíos asociados a los procesos de importación y despacho aduanero de la asistencia
humanitaria. El GTL continuará las gestiones con las autoridades nacionales para obtener mayor claridad
sobre los requisitos aplicables al ingreso de carga humanitaria, las definiciones operativas de ayuda
humanitaria y los procedimientos aduaneros que deben seguir las organizaciones humanitarias.
• La Cancillería habilitó un formulario web “https://venezuelanoestasola.com” donde además de recibir
donaciones monetarias, permite solicitar el permiso de llegada de donaciones que lleguen a Venezuela
vía aérea y marítima. Sin embargo, esta web está orientada a donaciones y las organizaciones que
requieren autorización y una comunicación del Coordinador Residente a Cancillería, deben realizar su
solicitud a través de los formularios del GTL.
• El GTL, en coordinación con OCHA, ha extendido el reporte de movilización aérea de carga humanitaria a
todas las organizaciones (nacionales, internacionales y del Sistema de Naciones Unidas), con el fin de
consolidar diariamente esta información, permitiendo que OCHA envíe una Nota Verbal a Cancillería. Las
organizaciones deben mandar la información contenida en el formulario como muy tarde, antes de las
15:00 de la tarde del día anterior a la llegada del vuelo.
3. PRESENTACIÓN DE RESULTADO DE LA ENCUESTA DE BRECHAS Y
NECESIDADES LOGÍSTICAS

van a ser proporcionados a los socios en función de las brechas que se identificaron.

6. ACTUALIZACIONES DE LOS SOCIOS
• Ante la falta de claridad de los procesos de importación para las ONGs, varias ONGs internacionales

proveedores locales. No obstante, la falta de un procedimiento oficial para la importación de ayuda
humanitaria dificulta el acceso a determinados ítems que han visto incrementada su demanda con motivo
de la respuesta y no cuentan con suficiente producción local o para aquellas ONGs internacionales que
dependen de la llegada de insumos importados para la continuidad de sus operaciones.

Minutas de la reunión [06 07 2026]
Venezuela, Caracas.

• Dada la falta de garantías operativas, las organizaciones no han utilizado mecanismos de ingreso terrestre

mantienen a la espera de mayor claridad y oficialización del procedimiento.

Se recordó a los socios los recursos disponibles:
- LogIE para información relativa a infraestructura. Diversos módulos del sistema permiten acceso al
Concepto de Operaciones del GTL, información sobre conectividad en las zonas afectadas, etc.
- La página web dedicada del GTL para la emergencia donde están todos los enlaces y documentos
relevantes. La página web cuenta con un sistema de traducción automática integrado que permite
consultar los documentos del GTL en inglés y otros idiomas.
- En la página web, pueden encontrar los formularios para la movilización terrestre y aérea, así como el
formulario de inscripción para recibir las comunicaciones relativas al GTL.

documents.title: IOM Venezuela Flash Appeal: 2026 Earthquake Response (July - December 2026)
documents.body_text:
**SITUATION OVERVIEW**

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 struck the north-central region of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (henceforth referred to as Venezuela), triggering widespread devastation across several states, including La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, and Falcón. The earthquakes, followed by hundreds of aftershocks, caused significant loss of life, with 3,535 people reported dead and over 16,740 injured, as of 6 July. Damage to more than 2,500 infrastructure assets, including 38 hospitals, has disrupted access to essential services, including healthcare, water supply, and transport systems, placing considerable strain on national response capacities.

The disaster is unfolding in a context of pre-existing structural vulnerabilities, limited access to basic services, weakened public systems, and protracted humanitarian needs. As a result, the earthquakes have triggered an acute-on-chronic emergency, deepening existing vulnerabilities and increasing humanitarian needs across affected areas. Thousands of families have been displaced and are sheltering in collective centres (e.g. schools, sports centres), spontaneous settlements, self-managed sites, and open spaces due to the destruction or structural damage of homes and continued fear of further collapses.

While initial response efforts by national authorities and international actors have focused on search and rescue, emergency medical assistance, and rapid assessments, significant gaps remain across key sectors. These include safe and adequate shelter, core relief items, access to healthcare and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, protection, site-level coordination and management, and reliable data for operational targeting. Needs are particularly acute in overcrowded and informal displacement settings, where limited infrastructure, weak service provision, and the absence of structured site management increase risks of communicable disease outbreaks, violence against women and girls (VAWG) and other vulnerable groups, family separation, and other protection concerns.

To date, a significant share of the humanitarian response has been concentrated in La Guaira, Distrito Capital, and Miranda, where large-scale interventions have been prioritized. However, Falcón, Aragua, and Carabobo have also reported significant impacts. In these areas, infrastructure damage, service disruption, and comparatively lower operational coverage point to unmet needs and emerging gaps in assistance, particularly among populations in dispersed and hard-to-reach locations. Ensuring that these areas are reached will be critical for a coherent, equitable, and needs-based response, while also laying out the foundation for early recovery and longer-term resilience-building efforts.

FUNDING REQUIRED
SHELTER, LAND AND SITE COORDINATION
USD 37,500,000
In order to meet the needs of affected households deprived of their homes, IOM will: TARGET INDIVIDUALS
y Conduct household-level technical shelter assessments to inform the provision
and installation of shelter materials (e.g. tarpaulins, ropes, tents), ensuring safe and
dignified living conditions and integrating mitigation measures for likely hazards,
including heavy rains and heatwaves, in line with the 2026 El Niño outlook.
y Deliver guidance to local authorities, shelter management teams, and affected communities on safer shelter practices, site
planning, fire risk reduction, and accessibility, while verifying quality and implementing corrective measures, in line with minimum
humanitarian standards.
y Establish, upgrade, and adapt safe, covered, communal and emergency shelter spaces; implement light improvements and
small-scale maintenance (e.g. debris removal, drainage, fire safety) to enhance safety, accessibility, and dignified living standards
based on site-level technical assessment results. Interventions integrate protection and disaster risk reduction considerations,
in line with safety audit results.
y Procure, adapt, and distribute core relief items such as blankets, mats, solar lamps, kitchen sets, jerrycans and other household-
level essential items, with tailored logistics to reach prioritized vulnerable and underserved households, including those in
collective sites and hard-to-reach areas, in diverse contexts.
y As needed, establish a mechanism for the distribution of in-kind donations and procured items through sectoral partners, such
as through a common pipeline approach.
y Strengthen governance structures, deploy dedicated site management personnel, and provide technical support through
coaching, training, and accompaniment to ensure consistent, accountable site management, particularly in informal, spontaneous,
and self-managed displacement settings.
y Ensure community involvement through representative committees and engagement activities; establish static and
mobile information desks, complaint and feedback mechanisms, and safe referral systems to ensure accountability
and two-way communication.
y Conduct regular site monitoring and service mapping to identify gaps and inform response planning; coordinate with Shelter,
WASH, Health/MHPSS, and Protection actors to ensure integrated, complementary, and protection-sensitive service delivery
and avoid duplication.
y Promote inclusive engagement adapted to diverse groups; conduct regular site safety, accessibility, and protection risk
assessments implementing mitigation measures such as lighting, fire safety, and safe access.
y Coordinate and facilitate humanitarian movement assistance, evacuation, emergency shelter access, and humanitarian assistance
for people with disabilities, older people and other vulnerable persons.
y Integrate collective center exit strategies from the outset, in coordination with government authorities, linking site management,
household-level assessments, shelter support, referrals, and early recovery planning to enable safe, voluntary, and dignified
return or relocation, support household recovery, and avoid prolonged dependency on collective centers.
4

IOM VENEZUELA FLASH APPEAL | 2026 EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
FUNDING REQUIRED
EARLY RECOVERY AND SOLUTIONS
USD 23,000,000
To promote early recovery, resilience, and durable and inclusive solutions from the TARGET INDIVIDUALS
start for displacement-affected individuals and communities—in alignment with
250,000
the IASC Framework on Durable Solutions and IOM’s Progressive Resolution of
Displacement Situations framework, and furtherance of the UN Secretary-General's TARGET ENTITIES 20
Action Agenda on Internal Displacement—IOM will initiate the following activities:
y Support access to livelihoods, gradually restoring an adequate standard of living, securing basic rights such as housing,
documentation, and safety, and facilitating social cohesion. Combine Push and Pull approaches to strengthen both individual
capacities and broader market systems, ensuring that early recovery efforts lead to lasting economic empowerment and social
inclusion.
y Assist local governments and communities to co-create recovery plans that address immediate needs while contributing to
long-term development and stability.
y Enable the conditions for durable solutions through IOM’s Community-Based Planning approach, which allows communities
to take the lead in prioritization and decision-making in a participative and inclusive manner. By supporting the integration of
community needs into national and local recovery planning, IOM promotes alignment of priorities across all levels of society,
fostering sustainability, resilience and long-term development.
y Strengthen government-led responses to displacement by providing targeted technical support, capacity-building, and reinforcing
coordination mechanisms, thereby enhancing the ability of national and local authorities to lead recovery efforts and deliver
sustainable solutions.
y Foster localization through small grants, training, and skills development for civil society organizations, focused on civil society’s
critical role in supporting communities to transition from early recovery to longer-term durable solutions, resilience, and
sustainable development.
y Foster strategic partnerships with multilateral banks, UN agencies, and the private sector to unlock longer-term financing to
enable the creation of conditions for durable solutions for displaced populations and host communities.
y Support initiatives that promote economic integration of displaced populations by facilitating job placement, skills development, and
private sector engagement, enabling them to contribute to local economies and drive broader regional recovery and prosperity.
y Provide individual direct assistance to the most vulnerable people experiencing housing, land, and property (HLP) issues
through case management, focusing on recovering and/or restoring missing HLP documentation, and safeguarding rights.
y Raise awareness on HLP laws, processes, and rights, all aimed at ascertaining and protecting tenure security.
y Enhance government capacity and deliver training to enhance State ability to address HLP issues and strengthen land dispute
resolution mechanisms.
y Implement initiatives such as entrepreneurship programs and livelihood training to improve affected people’s financial stability
and market-relevant skills, enabling their (re)entry into the labor market and fostering economic self-sufficiency. Support
business recovery, job creation, and community resilience through small grants to small- and medium-sized enterprises, and
investments in critical infrastructure, stimulating local economies and creating sustainable opportunities.
y Support and reinforce local governance mechanisms by fostering collaboration between communities and local authorities,
enhancing accountability, transparency, and the capacity to manage community-driven recovery initiatives.
y Using build-back-better approaches, rebuild and upgrade critical infrastructure and essential services such as water systems,
schools, healthcare facilities, and marketplaces to restore essential services, improve living conditions, enhance safety and
accessibility, and lay the foundation for long-term recovery, resilience, and sustainable development.
5

IOM VENEZUELA FLASH APPEAL | 2026 EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH AND FUNDING REQUIRED
PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT USD 22,500,000
To address the health needs of populations affected by the earthquake, IOM will: TARGET INDIVIDUALS
y Deploy multidisciplinary teams to deliver primary healthcare, emergency care,
referrals, and outreach missions in underserved areas, including fixed service points
in health facilities, shelters, and temporary sites.
y Fast-track procurement, delivery, and prepositioning of essential medicines, medical supplies, and emergency kits (e.g. trauma
surgery kits, blood transfusion kits, trauma backpacks, psychotropic medication) to strengthen emergency care capacity in
trauma units, operating rooms, and blood banks.
y Provide logistical, technical, and operational support to sustain primary healthcare services and reinforce the surge capacity of
the health system.
y Support IPC measures in health facilities and related emergency settings through hygiene and disinfection kits, equipment, and
technical guidance, while strengthening disease surveillance, early warning systems, and outbreak prevention in coordination
with the Ministry of Health, other health authorities, and partners.
y Provide support, systems, and equipment for dignified handling, identification, and registration of injured and deceased
individuals.
y Conduct structural evaluations of health facilities to determine safety and operational capacity and support rapid rehabilitation
and restoration.
y Conduct health facility and service delivery site assessments in coordination with PAHO to identify priority health needs and
service gaps.
y Strengthen health information management through equipment and technical support to improve real-time data collection,
patient tracking, and referral.
y Carry out awareness campaigns about available services, preventive measures, and encourage positive health-seeking behaviors
among affected populations.

An IOM internal medicine physician consults with a displaced person at a temporary shelter in La Guaira, providing medical assessment and care as part of the
emergency earthquake response.

IOM VENEZUELA FLASH APPEAL | 2026 EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
y Deliver MHPSS services through the deployment of mobile teams, psychological first aid, stabilization, community-based
support, and referrals for specialized care, with provision of essential psychotropic medications as needed. This includes
undertaking MHPSS assessments, individual and group counselling, peer support, and low-intensity psychological interventions;
group sessions for adults to strengthen individual, family, and community resilience; and structured psychosocial programming
for children and adolescents.
y Activate and strengthen remote MHPSS mechanisms, including telepsychology helplines, to expand access to affected
populations.
y Strengthen the capacity of community leaders, community health workers, local actors, and authorities through targeted
MHPSS training, focusing on psychological first aid, intercultural and supportive communication, and core psychosocial skills to
ensure sustainable services and foster resilience.
y Support national MHPSS coordination: Co-leadership of the National MHPSS Technical Working Group, including facilitating
inter-agency meetings, contributing to the development of technical guidelines and tools, promoting cross-sectoral integration
with other clusters, and supporting capacity strengthening initiatives across stakeholders.
FUNDING REQUIRED
WATER, SANITATION AND HYGIENE
USD 7,500,000
To increase communities’ access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services, IOM will: TARGET INDIVIDUALS
y Conduct rapid WASH household- and infrastructure-level assessments to identify
underserved populations in need in collective sites and affected areas.
y Provide safe water in the initial phase through water trucking, storage solutions, tap stands, and household water treatment,
while supporting the rehabilitation of water systems in a second phase to strengthen sustainability, recovery, and continuity
of services. When relevant, rehabilitation and repairs will seek to mitigate future risks, such as heavy rains or flood impacts.
y Implement water treatment and quality control measures at community water sources, distribution points, and collective
shelters, including chlorination and regular testing, to ensure safe consumption and reduce public health risks.
y Install and rehabilitate sex-segregated and accessible sanitation and hygiene infrastructure in displacement sites and shelters.
y Provide wastewater management, desludging, drainage solutions, and solid waste management systems in collective sites,
shelters, and affected communities, complemented by community clean-up campaigns to improve safety and living conditions.
y Conduct hygiene promotion and risk communication campaigns to raise awareness on safe practices and strengthen
health-seeking behaviours. Support Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) measures in community settings, including provision
of cleaning and disinfection kits, and installation of handwashing facilities in high-risk areas.
y Distribute hygiene/IPC kits and menstrual hygiene management supplies to vulnerable households, shelters and collective sites
prioritizing informal and hard-to-reach settings.
y Strengthen local authorities, utilities, and site management actors to operate, maintain, and restore WASH services, while
supporting community engagement and local capacity for service management in informal and self-managed displacement
settings.
y Stockpile and distribute hygiene and CRI/NFI kits, factoring in El Niño risks (e.g. flooding, displacement, health vulnerabilities).
7

IOM VENEZUELA FLASH APPEAL | 2026 EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
FUNDING REQUIRED
USD 4,500,000
Affected populations are exposed to compounded protection risks. To address these TARGET INDIVIDUALS
risks, IOM will:
y Conduct regular multisectoral protection risk assessments and safety audits in shelters, displacement sites, and informal settings
to identify risks related to VAWG, child protection, trafficking in persons, and access to services. Use audit findings to inform
site planning, service delivery, and integrated risk mitigation measures across Shelter, Land and Site Coordination, WASH, and
Health sectors.
y Integrate VAWG risk mitigation, disability inclusion, and child protection across all interventions to ensure protection-sensitive
and accessible services.
y Provide individual and household protection assistance, including individualized case management support, emergency in-kind
aid, and referrals. Deliver specialized protection response services, ensuring a survivor-centered approach.
y Strengthen specialized counter-trafficking prevention and protection services by integrating trafficking risk mitigation, screening
for trafficking risk indicators and identification, and referral mechanisms into emergency activities, such as in emergency
shelters, displacement sites, and return locations.
y Conduct trainings for humanitarian actors and frontline staff, and implement awareness campaigns and disseminate anti-
trafficking messages.
y Conduct community-based counter-trafficking outreach and risk awareness activities, through information sessions, protection
messaging, and safe reporting mechanisms to reduce vulnerability to exploitation, abuse and trafficking.
y Enhance referral pathways for survivors of violence, trafficking in persons, unaccompanied/separated children, persons with
disabilities, older persons, and returnees, ensuring safe, timely, and confidential access.
y Establish and strengthen safe spaces in shelters, displacement sites, and communities, including Child-Friendly Spaces and
Women and Girls Safe Spaces, to provide structured psychosocial support and access to specialized services.
y Support State institutions and Child Protection Councils in restoring and strengthening services to address VAWG and child
protection, including case management, family tracing, and reunification.
y Strengthen post-arrival assistance for returnees recently returned and future returnees through transportation, temporary
housing, legal aid, risk mitigation and information sharing, and referrals to national protection and health systems.
y Strengthen safe, accessible, and confidential complaint and feedback mechanisms (including protection from sexual exploitation
and abuse (PSEA) reporting channels, static and mobile protection spaces, and consultations), while disseminating clear,
context-appropriate information on services, rights, referral pathways, and risk awareness messages to affected communities.
y Establish AAP mechanisms in shelters, displacement sites and affected communities to ensure crisis-affected populations are
meaningfully informed, consulted, and able to influence humanitarian assistance.
y Promote community-based protection approaches and inclusive participation to strengthen trust, representation, and
accountability of diverse groups, while systematically collecting and analyzing community feedback to produce accountability
reports.
8

IOM VENEZUELA FLASH APPEAL | 2026 EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
DATA (DTM) AND COORDINATION FUNDING REQUIRED
SUPPORT USD 3,000,000
To support evidence-based targeting, adaptive programming, effective resource TARGET ENTITIES
allocation, improved sustainability and accountability to affected populations, and
coordinated decision-making within the broad response, IOM will:
y Deploy emergency site and needs assessments to generate timely evidence on displacement patterns, population figures, risks,
vulnerabilities, and immediate needs. Deliver data outputs such as site mapping, displaced population counts, and high-level
needs profiles to guide prioritization of assistance.
y Deploy and expand the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) activities to monitor population movements, site conditions, and
multisectoral needs, with systematic rounds of site monitoring to capture evolving living conditions, service gaps, and emerging
risks.
y Monitor intentions and return patterns and conduct targeted, in-depth assessments (e.g. housing damage, infrastructure
functionality, sectoral service gaps) to inform prioritization, guide investments, and support the transition from emergency
response to early recovery.
y Launch the Solutions and Mobility Index to help achieve durable solutions for vulnerable communities by providing data on
stability, development, recovery and reintegration dynamics. Strengthen information systems with equipment, digital tools, and
connectivity to support real-time data collection and processing, while producing and disseminating analytical reports, site
profiles, displacement datasets, and trend analyses to guide operational planning, targeting, and evidence-based decision-making.
y Conduct research or other specialized assessment, as necessary, to ensure evidence-based programming.
y Support the inter-agency coordination mechanism through structured information-sharing, joint analysis, and alignment with
partners and national authorities to enhance coherence and reduce duplication.
y Integrate data collection and analysis across all intervention sectors to ensure a comprehensive, multisectoral understanding
of needs and response gaps.
y Deploy the IOM’s beneficiary management system to conduct registration at displacement sites, ensuring deduplication,
facilitate vulnerability-based targeting, authenticate and track assistance delivery, manage referrals, and support secure data
sharing and interoperability across response actors.
y Continue leading and co-leading inter-agency coordination bodies and mechanisms, including undertaking the activities (i.e.
sectoral partners’ capacity building, sectoral assessments, technical guidelines) and employing the personnel necessary for this
coordination.
9

IOM VENEZUELA FLASH APPEAL | 2026 EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE
COORDINATION AND PARTNERSHIPS
IOM will implement this response through a combination of direct implementation and strategic partnerships with national and
local actors, building on existing collaboration frameworks and operational relationships in Venezuela. The organization will work
with civil society organizations and community-based partners to extend operational reach, facilitate access to hard-to-reach and
underserved populations, and support community engagement and acceptance. Through these partnerships, IOM will be able to
expand its operational reach beyond primary urban centres, such as La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, and Falcón, to other
affected states, ensuring a more geographically balanced and inclusive response.
IOM will coordinate closely with national authorities, UN agencies, humanitarian partners, and relevant sectoral coordination
mechanisms to ensure alignment, complementarity, and adherence to humanitarian standards, avoiding duplication and strengthening
the overall coherence of the response. IOM continues to lead the Infrastructure and Temporary Shelter Working Group and the
Trafficking in Persons Working Group. It also co-leads the Technical Working Group on MHPSS, and actively contributes to
coordination platforms related to Protection, Shelter and NFIs, the PSEA Network, and the Areas of Responsibility for Child
Protection.
ACCOUNTABILITY TO AFFECTED POPULATIONS
Building on community engagement systems, all interventions will strengthen AAP through diversified feedback mechanisms,
improved two-way communication, expanded use of IOM’s Community-Based Planning Manual, and community-based
monitoring where feasible. The focus is on accountable, inclusive, and needs-driven responses, particularly in hard-to-reach
areas. By combining strengthened AAP systems, expanded partnerships, improved monitoring, and enhanced logistics,
IOM ensures predictable, transparent, and equitable assistance delivery to crisis-affected communities.
For more information IOMVenezuelaPSU@iom.int

documents.title: Atrocity Alert No. 490: Sudan, Lebanon and Venezuela
sources: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
documents.body_text:
## Atrocity Alert is a weekly publication by the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect highlighting situations where populations are at risk of, or are enduring, mass atrocity crimes.

### **GROWING RISK OF ATROCITIES AMID ESCALATING CONFLICT IN EL OBEID, SUDAN**

Intensifying clashes in and around El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, are raising serious concerns over the heightened risk of atrocity crimes against civilians. Over the past few weeks, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have reportedly built-up their presence by encircling the city and begun a siege from at least three directions, with a potential offensive appearing imminent. Repeated drone strikes have already led to widespread civilian casualties. Estimates indicate that approximately 500,000 civilians in El Obeid are at risk of large-scale atrocities, including more than 100,000 internally displaced persons.

On 29 June the Yale School of Public Health’s Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL) [reported](https://ysph.yale.edu/download-file/76d1775e-de0c-4861-afae-7aa92c4c0228/) satellite evidence covering the period 25 May to 25 June, indicating widespread and escalating damage to protected civilian infrastructure, including electricity generation facilities, fuel storage sites, multiple gas stations and the main market. Yale HRL concludes that the damage “is consistent with intentional bombardment of civilian infrastructure necessary for the sustainment of life.”

Control over El Obeid and the wider region has remained highly contested, with frontlines [shifting repeatedly](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-487/) between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF. The emerging pattern of encirclement, siege warfare and sustained strikes on civilian infrastructure mirrors RSF tactics previously [documented](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-448/) in El Fasher, North Darfur, where similar methods were used to isolate the city, degrade essential services and intensify pressure on civilian populations through sustained bombardment and encirclement.

During an Enhanced Interactive Dialogue on the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) for the [Sudan’s](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/sudan/) oral update to the UN Human Rights Council (HRC) in June, Norway delivered a statement on behalf of the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention in Sudan and 21 other states, expressing grave alarm at “the urgent risks of atrocities and deliberate killings in Sudan,” and urging all parties “to immediately de-escalate and comply fully with international humanitarian law.” On 20 June the UN Security Council also expressed concern “at the imminent risk of mass atrocities and demanded the RSF immediately halt its assault on El Obeid.”

As atrocities continued to mount, the Global Centre, together with other NGOs, [urged](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/sudan-the-human-rights-council-should-urgently-address-the-situation-in-and-around-el-obeid-north-kordofan-and-take-bold-steps-towards-atrocity-prevention-and-accountability/) the HRC to urgently address the situation in and around El Obeid and take steps towards atrocity prevention and accountability. The HRC convened an urgent debate on 3 July and adopted a resolution on 6 July requesting the FFM to conduct an urgent inquiry.

In light of the rapidly deteriorating situation and the heightened risk of atrocity crimes, all parties must immediately cease attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure and fully comply with their obligations under International Humanitarian Law. The international community should move beyond repeated reactive debates and ensure that investigations and reporting are systematically translated into timely political action. States should base their responses on existing credible findings regarding actors fueling the conflict and ensure that early warning is followed by concrete preventive and accountability measures.

### **NEW FRAMEWORK BETWEEN ISRAEL, US AND LEBANON RAISES JUSTICE CONCERNS**

On 26 June [Lebanon](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/lebanon/), [Israel](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/israel-and-the-occupied-palestinian-territory/) and the United States (US) signed a Trilateral Framework affirming their “shared goal of achieving lasting peace and security.” Brokered by the US after a series of direct talks between Lebanon and Israel, the fourteen-point Framework claims to serve as starting point from which parties will work towards a “full comprehensive peace and security agreement.” However, concerns have been raised over the viability of this Framework and the extent to which its stipulations may undermine justice, accountability and a lasting political resolution. The Framework was signed amid an ongoing ceasefire that has been subject to near-daily violations by Israel, resulting in thousands of casualties.

Despite some of the parties stressing that the Framework does not waive the right of victims to seek justice, clause 13 of the agreement commits Israel and Lebanon to the “cessation of all hostile or adverse actions in international political or legal fora,” which could constrain accountability efforts for Israel’s atrocity crimes in Lebanon, including attempts to revitalize suspended efforts by Lebanon to accept the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court (ICC) following [hostilities](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-412-lebanon-haiti-and-venezuela/) with Israel in 2024. Six human rights and press freedom organizations issued a [statement](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/07/lebanon-israel-framework-agreement-betrays-victims-of-war-crimes-in-lebanon/) warning that the agreement “threatens to betray war crimes victims in Lebanon,” including by appearing to obstruct recourse to justice before international courts and “acquiesce to the prolonged and indefinite forced displacement” of residents from the south.

Since 2 March Israeli forces have progressively moved to occupy an estimated six percent of Lebanese territory, including large swathes of southern Lebanon, and established and expanded a [so-called yellow-line](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-480/). Dozens of villages have been destroyed and over 1 million people have been forcibly displaced by the occupation.

The Framework upholds measures that would delay and prevent the return of tens of thousands of people who remain displaced. Without explicit mention of the withdrawal of Israeli forces, the Framework effectively conditions the “redeployment” of Israeli forces outside of Lebanese territory on the disarmament of Hezbollah – a task assigned to the Lebanese Armed Forces, which continues to present significant challenges for Lebanon despite efforts to do so since 2024. In the days following the signing of the Framework, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz reportedly instructed forces to prepare for a long-term presence in “security zones” in southern Lebanon.

Parties to the Framework must ensure its implementation neither prevents the return of displaced populations nor impedes recourse to justice for victims of atrocity crimes. Lebanon should finalize earlier moves to grant ICC immediate jurisdiction. States must press for the immediate, unconditional withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon, support victims in their pursuit of justice and exert influence on parties to adhere to the ceasefire.

### **CATASTROPHIC EARTHQUAKES DEEPEN VENEZUELA’S MULTIDIMENSIONAL CRISIS**

On 24 June two powerful earthquakes – magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 – struck [Venezuela](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/venezuela/) less than a minute apart, the strongest to hit the country in over a century. Centered in the state of Yaracuy, the quakes also caused widespread destruction across the Capital District and the states of La Guaira, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo and Falcón, among others. The coastal city of La Guaira, north of Caracas, was among the worst hit, with entire neighborhoods reduced to rubble.

At the time of publication, the official death toll released by Venezuelan authorities has climbed above 3,600, but is estimated to be significantly higher as efforts to recover and identify victims remain ongoing and thousands of people remain unaccounted for. More than 16,700 individuals have been reportedly injured and over 17,000 people left homeless, while at least 1,000 buildings, including hospitals, were damaged or destroyed.

Venezuelan authorities have come under intense criticism for a response widely described as grossly inadequate. Rescue efforts were significantly delayed and under-resourced, leaving families to search for and recover victims from the rubble themselves. National humanitarian organizations, international rescue teams, UN agencies and hundreds of civil society volunteers have since carried out the vast majority of the relief effort. Venezuelan human rights NGO Provea also warned of the deployment of security bodies with no legal competence in disaster response – including the military counterintelligence directorate (DGCIM) and the intelligence service (SEBIN) – which could obstruct relief efforts and give rise to human rights abuses.

The catastrophe has struck a country already gripped by a multidimensional protection crisis that has left populations without reliable access to basic services, including clean water and sanitation, nutrition, health care and electricity for over a decade. Venezuelan civil society platform *HumVenezuela* estimates that 18.2 million people were in need as of January 2026, 12.4 million of whom faced critical humanitarian needs. The authorities’ incompetence is the product of more than two decades of large-scale corruption and the erosion of the rule of law. The UN Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela has documented how state actors, including the DGCIM and SEBIN, have been used as instruments of regime survival, responsible for crimes against humanity and silencing dissent. State-led repression has been accompanied by years of systematic attacks against civic space, including criminalization of civil society organizations and independent media, both of which are central to current relief efforts. These dynamics now threaten to place Venezuelans at even greater risk and further exacerbate unprecedented suffering and despair.

Venezuelan authorities must immediately lift restrictions on civic space, allow full and unrestricted access for humanitarian actors and independent media and guarantee prompt and transparent information on relief efforts. Authorities must also urgently ensure the recovery and identification of the dead, provide families with accurate information on those still missing and ensure that affected communities are able to mourn and bury their loved ones with dignity.

documents.title: Au Venezuela, une urgence humanitaire majeure à la suite de séismes dévastateurs
documents.body_text:
## Deux séismes majeurs ont frappé le nord du Venezuela, faisant des milliers de morts et de disparus. La destruction de nombreuses infrastructures aggrave considérablement un système de santé déjà fragile. Pour répondre à cette crise, Médecins du Monde France vient en appui aux équipes de Médecins du Monde Espagne, déjà déployées sur le terrain.

Le 24 juin 2026, les séismes de magnitudes 7,2 et 7,5 ont particulièrement touché la capitale Caracas et l’État de La Guaira. Alors que **plusieurs milliers de personnes sont toujours portées disparues**, le bilan humain continue de s’alourdir. Les opérations de recherche et de secours sont en cours dans un contexte de répliques possibles et de **dégradation des conditions d’accès aux soins**. En conséquence, les besoins en soins d’urgence, traumatologie et santé mentale abondent.

Sur place, les équipes de [**Médecins du Monde Espagne**](https://www.medicosdelmundo.org/) **sont saines et sauves.** Elles se mobilisent pour évaluer et organiser la réponse en lien avec les autorités locales de santé, avec notamment des besoins en matériel et en médicaments.

**Médecins du Monde France** s’est positionnée en appui de Médecins du Monde Espagne pour intervenir rapidement auprès des populations. Nous sommes prêts à mobiliser rapidement depuis la [Colombie](https://www.medecinsdumonde.org/pays/amerique/colombie/) où nous sommes opérationnels, une équipe de médecins, d’infirmiers, de psychologues et de logisticiens, ainsi que des kits médicaux pouvant **permettre la prise en charge d’environ 1 500 personnes.**

Cette intervention contribuera à :

- Assurer des **soins de santé primaires** en première ligne et **distribuer les médicaments** nécessaires,
- **Stabiliser les urgences** en orientant les patientes et patients vers des **structures adaptées,**
- Fournir un **accompagnement en santé mentale**.

documents.title: CADENA mobilises emergency response for earthquake-affected communities in Venezuela
documents.body_text:
[*CADENA International*](https://cadena.ngo/)*, a HelpAge network member with offices across Latin America, has launched an emergency response in Venezuela following the 24 June earthquakes. Its efforts focus on search and rescue, healthcare, relief distributions, psychosocial support and rapid needs assessments.*

*The organisation has deployed international search and rescue specialists, and is delivering emergency supplies including household water filters and solar lamps, working closely with local authorities and humanitarian partners on the ground.*

## **Reaching older people and other at-risk groups**

Among the estimated 1.8 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, around 250,000 older people are expected to require targeted support. Older people represent approximately 14% of the population and are among those facing the greatest risks following the disaster, particularly those living with disabilities, chronic health conditions, mobility limitations, social isolation, or the loss of caregivers.

## **Responding to urgent needs on the ground**

Initial assessments conducted by CADENA found overcrowded shelters, families sleeping outdoors due to fear of aftershocks, limited access to safe drinking water, shortages of basic medical supplies, and growing protection concerns. Teams also reported that many older people had lost essential assistive devices and were struggling to access services and humanitarian assistance.

To address these needs, CADENA is providing emergency relief items, supporting access to safe water, and helping affected households meet their most urgent basic needs. The organisation is prioritising households with older people, particularly those facing additional risks linked to disability, chronic illness, damaged housing, or lack of family support.

## **Providing healthcare and psychosocial support**

Volunteer medical brigades are providing primary healthcare services in affected communities, while additional medical teams and supplies are being mobilised to strengthen the response. Particular attention is being given to ensuring continuity of care for older people and others who rely on regular medication and treatment for chronic conditions.

At the same time, CADENA is delivering mental health and psychosocial support through specialist staff and trained volunteers. Community-based activities and psychological first aid are helping survivors cope with trauma, grief, stress and uncertainty following the earthquakes. Older people, who may be experiencing heightened isolation and distress, are a key focus of these efforts.

A CADENA team member conducts a psychosocial assessment with an earthquake survivor.

## **Scaling up for recovery**

CADENA is preparing to expand its emergency response in the coming weeks. Planned activities include the distribution of water, hygiene and shelter kits, food assistance, protection activities, disaster risk awareness initiatives, healthcare support, and continued mental health and psychosocial services. The aim is to ensure that older people and other at-risk groups are not left behind as affected communities move from emergency response towards recovery.

documents.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #2: Families need safe water and sanitation to reduce health risks | NRC
documents.body_text:
*Media update by Beatriz Ochoa, the Norwegian Refugee Council’s (NRC) Regional Head of Advocacy for Latin America two weeks after earthquakes in Venezuela:*

08. Jul 2026

“Two weeks after the earthquakes struck Venezuela, many families who lost their homes have told me they are concerned about how they will meet their most basic needs. Thousands of people continue to live in temporary shelters, schools, parks and other public spaces. Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services is now becoming increasingly important to prevent health problems and the spread of disease.

“Many families are living in densely populated settings, with limited privacy, exposure to high temperatures and seasonal rains, and sometimes insufficient access to showers, soap and adequate sanitation facilities.

“I have seen families doing everything they can to maintain dignity in extremely difficult conditions. In one temporary shelter, I saw families organising themselves to keep common spaces clean, including through makeshift toilets and basic waste management arrangements. Their determination is remarkable, but families should not have to shoulder this burden alone.

“We urgently need support from international donors so we and other humanitarian organisations can provide access to safe water, toilets, hygiene supplies, and clear public health information to help reduce the risk of diarrhoeal diseases, skin infections and other preventable health problems among displaced families.

“Water is being delivered by tanker trucks to many temporary shelters, but families often lack appropriate containers to store it safely. Access to bottled water, showers and toilets remains limited in some locations. These challenges can be particularly difficult for older people, people with disabilities, pregnant women and families with young children.

"As displacement becomes more protracted, and the days turn into weeks, I have seen families beginning to organise daily life in temporary shelters, including preparing and cooking meals together. In these conditions, access to clean water remains essential to prevent disease and protect people's health.

“Families need basic but essential items, including safe water containers, water purification tablets, soap, chlorine, sanitary pads and tarpaulins.

“NRC has already provided 1,400 displaced people with soap and other hygiene items, water tanks, and jerrycans for safe water storage. We will also be distributing tarpaulins to help protect families protect from exposure to the elements and have supported first responders with personal protective equipment for search and rescue activities.

“As the response evolves, we will work with communities, authorities, and humanitarian actors to establish more suitable solutions, including larger-scale water storage and treatment systems, improved sanitation facilities and community showers that provide greater privacy and dignity.

“The first days of this response were driven by the community. The world should know that this solidarity is not simply a gesture—it is a vital necessity. But it is now time for funding and aid to flow in and support longer-term solutions so people can take the first steps to rebuilding their lives.”

**Notes to editors:**

- Photos and videos from Venezuela are available for use [here](https://visuals.nrc.no?c=15116&k=5b02ed739f).
- At least 3,685 people have been killed and more than 16,740 people injured. The number of dead and injured is likely to rise ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-14-07-july-2026-time-0900-pm)).
- 17,907 people have lost their homes, according to the authorities ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-14-07-july-2026-time-0900-pm)).
- Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-12-05-july-2026-time-0800-pm)).
- 38 hospitals were damaged by the earthquakes ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-no-5-28-june-2026-time-500-pm)).
- In 2026, 7.9 million people in the country are in need of humanitarian assistance, 27.7 per cent of the total population (28.5 million people) ([OCHA](https://www.unocha.org/venezuela)). 5.5 million of them have been targeted for assistance.
- The humanitarian response plan in Venezuela is currently 43.4 per cent funded with 274.4 million of the 632.2 million US dollars required having been delivered ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/overview/2026)).
- The 2025 humanitarian response plan in Venezuela was just 20 per cent funded, while the 2024 plan was 28 per cent funded ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/1517/summary)).
- NRC has been working in Venezuela since 2005 providing education, protection, legal guidance, and water and sanitation support. In 2025 we reached more than 71,000 people across four bordering states. NRC has 70 colleagues in Venezuela, and seven local partners. Our teams are working across areas affected by the earthquakes to provide vital supplies, and will be providing water and sanitation support, emergency education and trauma support for children among other services.
- A full family hygiene kit contains: 8 toilet soaps, 4 toothbrush, toothpaste or dental cream, shampoo, washing powder, bleach, toilet paper and deodorant. The family mobility kit includes mosquito repellent, anti-burn cream, sunscreen, among other essential items.

**For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:**

- NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329

*This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.*

**Summary Points**

- On 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator arrived in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination, support rapid connectivity assessments, and help identify priority communications needs for the humanitarian response.
- Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid connectivity assessment survey across affected areas to map available communications services, identify coverage gaps, and prioritize shared connectivity solutions for humanitarian partners. Organizations operating in affected areas are encouraged to complete the survey to help identify priority connectivity needs and gaps.
- On 06 July, LTC Telecoms assessed three displacement shelters in La Guaira and identified unreliable power supply and internet connectivity gaps as the main operational constraints. Connectivity support, including Starlink terminals and solar power systems, is being deployed to strengthen communications for responders.

Reporting period: 01 – 07 July 2026

(magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for
the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.

Situation Overview
Venezuela continues to face a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes
(magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) that struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June, just 40 seconds apart. The
worst-affected areas include La Guaira State, Greater Caracas, and parts of Miranda, Carabobo,
Yaracuy, Aragua, and Falcón States. Hundreds of aftershocks have continued to affect impacted
communities, hampering rescue efforts and increasing risks to damaged infrastructure. Response
activities remain focused on life-saving assistance, including shelter, health, protection, infrastructure
restoration, and support to thousands of affected households.
1 The ETC and Logistics Cluster have been merged into the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), following the humanitarian reset in 2025.
Bringing logistics and emergency telecommunications under one coordination structure, the WFP-led LTC is the backbone of the entire humanitarian
response, enabling humanitarian action to move, communicate, coordinate, and deliver lifesaving assistance.
Page 1 of 6
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

The Government of Venezuela has declared the most affected areas, particularly La Guaira, disaster
zones and continues to lead response efforts through the deployment of emergency services, military
assets, and international assistance. As of 05 July, authorities reported that more than 6,400 people
had been rescued since the onset of the emergency. Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams remain
active in affected areas, while authorities continue to expand temporary accommodation for displaced
populations, conduct debris removal operations, and carry out structural safety assessments.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) is coordinating
international emergency assistance and supporting humanitarian response efforts. Priority needs
include emergency shelter, medical care, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food
assistance, child protection, and the restoration of telecommunications and other critical infrastructure.
As of 06 July, response operations are gradually shifting from search-and-rescue activities toward
recovery and humanitarian assistance. However, significant challenges persist, including displacement,
infrastructure damage, recurring aftershocks, and growing humanitarian needs. Relief and recovery
efforts are expected to continue for several months.
Telecommunications Overview
The 24 June earthquakes caused significant damage to telecommunications infrastructure across La
Guaira, Greater Caracas, and parts of Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Aragua, and Falcón States.
Although Venezuela’s core national telecommunications networks remain operational, damage to
power systems, fibre-optic infrastructure, mobile base stations, and transmission facilities has
disrupted connectivity in several affected areas. Ongoing aftershocks, infrastructure damage, and
access constraints continue to affect service reliability and restoration efforts.
Telecommunications disruptions have been driven by both direct infrastructure damage and prolonged
power outages, affecting emergency communications, humanitarian coordination, public information
dissemination, and contact between separated family members. La Guaira, the hardest-hit area,
experienced the most severe connectivity disruptions.
Mobile network operators Compañía Anónima Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar,
and Digitel remain operational across most of the country; however, coverage degradation, service
interruptions, and network capacity constraints have been reported in earthquake-affected areas.
Damage to cellular towers, backhaul links, and power systems has reduced network performance,
particularly in densely populated urban and coastal communities. Emergency responders continue to
rely on temporary communications solutions while network restoration activities are underway.
Localized damage to fibre-optic and fixed telecommunications infrastructure, including transmission
routes and utility corridors, has further affected connectivity. Fixed broadband services remain
particularly impacted in areas where power and transmission networks were damaged. As of 06 July,
operators continue restoration efforts in the most severely affected locations. While most national
networks remain operational outside the disaster zone, service availability and quality in heavily
affected areas remain dependent on infrastructure repairs, power restoration, and improved site
access. Telecommunications recovery is expected to continue for several weeks and will remain
critical to humanitarian operations, public safety, and broader recovery efforts.
Page 2 of 6
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

LTC Telecoms Activities
Coordination
LTC Telecoms began monitoring telecommunications networks immediately following the earthquakes
through established partner coordination channels to identify connectivity gaps and assess potential
support requirements. Global LTC Telecoms provided inputs to the WFP Venezuela Concept of
Operations (CONOPS) and continues to support response efforts.
On 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator arrived in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination and
support rapid telecommunications assessments in priority response areas. The coordinator is leading
efforts to identify telecommunications service availability, connectivity gaps, and operational
requirements to inform targeted connectivity support for humanitarian response operations.
Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid telecommunications and connectivity
survey across affected areas. The assessment is mapping operational locations and available
connectivity services, including Starlink, Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT), Broadband Global Area
Network (BGAN), mobile networks, and fixed fibre broadband services. Findings will support a spatial
analysis of connectivity coverage, helping to identify service gaps and prioritise locations for shared
connectivity solutions that enable life-saving humanitarian operations.
To support government-led and inter-agency efforts to restore critical communications, LTC Telecoms
is establishing a telecommunications coordination mechanism in Caracas in collaboration with OCHA,
the National Telecommunications Commission (CONATEL), CANTV, Movistar, Digitel, and international
partners. Coordination efforts will focus on mapping incoming telecommunications assets, identifying
connectivity gaps, avoiding duplication, and prioritising support to the most affected areas.
Planned support will focus on high-impact locations including Petare, Catia, La Guaira, and other
communities where widespread power outages, network disruptions, and damage to critical
infrastructure are limiting access to essential services. Proposed interventions include the provision of
community connectivity services, public Wi-Fi, satellite communications, and solar-powered charging
facilities at shelters, distribution sites, hospitals, urban search-and-rescue bases, and operational
airports. These services will support humanitarian coordination, needs assessments, beneficiary
communications, family tracing activities, and the continuity of relief assistance.
ICT assessments
On 06 July, LTC Telecoms conducted an ICT assessment of three displacement shelter sites in La
Guaira to identify priority connectivity needs and inform operational planning. The assessment found
that the primary constraint across all sites was the lack of reliable electricity, although repair and
restoration efforts had begun in some locations. Only Polideportivo José María Vargas Stadium had
operational internet connectivity through an existing Starlink service. César Nieves Stadium and Playa
Grande lacked both electricity and internet connectivity at the time of assessment, limiting operational
coordination and access to information for affected populations.
The assessment also confirmed that Digitel and Movistar mobile network services were operational
across all three displacement camps. However, intermittent service disruptions continue to affect
network reliability, highlighting the ongoing need for telecommunications and power restoration
efforts.
Page 3 of 6
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

Internet connectivity
To support emergency response operations, SpaceX has activated its disaster response programme,
offering Starlink connectivity kits with three months of free service. While Starlink and other satellite
connectivity solutions, including VSAT systems, are not fully licensed or commercially available for
routine purchase or residential use in Venezuela, authorities have introduced temporary emergency
measures to facilitate the deployment of connectivity services in earthquake-affected areas.
On 03 July, SpaceX donated an additional 10 Starlink kits to support WFP operations across affected
locations. The equipment will help strengthen emergency communications capacity, support
operational coordination, and provide reliable connectivity in areas where telecommunications services
remain disrupted or limited. SpaceX has also indicated its willingness to extend connectivity support to
other response partners, including UNICEF, International Organization for Migration (IOM), OCHA,
United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), United Nations Department of Safety and
Security (UNDSS), and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
To address immediate connectivity needs, LTC Telecoms is scheduled to deploy Starlink terminals and
solar power systems to César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande on 07 July. Global partner
emergency.lu, deployed through the UNDAC system, is supporting the installation of connectivity
services at prioritized locations. These installations will support humanitarian coordination and provide
temporary connectivity services for earthquake-affected populations sheltering at these sites.
The sustainability of connectivity services may be affected by security risks, including theft and
vandalism of deployed telecommunications equipment. LTC Telecoms and partners continue to
coordinate mitigation measures to support the continuity of services.
Secure communications
Security Communications Systems (SCS), including radio communications networks, were reported to
be fully operational prior to the earthquakes, according to {TESS+} assessments conducted in January
2026. These systems play a critical role in maintaining secure communications, supporting incident
reporting, and enabling the monitoring of field missions, particularly in areas where commercial
telecommunications networks are degraded or unavailable.
LTC Telecoms is coordinating with {TESS+} focal points to confirm the pre-crisis baseline and assess
the current operational status of secure communications systems, including any earthquake-related
damage or service interruptions. Further assessments will evaluate the functionality and coverage of
existing radio networks and identify any requirements for repairs, augmentation, or additional support
to ensure continuity of secure communications for humanitarian responders.
Information Management
The Global LTC Telecoms Information Management (IM) team activated dedicated IM and reporting
processes immediately following the earthquakes to support timely, accurate, and consistent
information sharing with humanitarian partners and other stakeholders throughout the response.
A dedicated LTC Telecoms emergency operations page has been established and is supported by a
designated IM Officer and alternate focal points to ensure continuous information flow, operational
visibility, and coordinated reporting across the response.
On 25 June, LTC Telecoms and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) activated the Disaster
Connectivity Map (DCM) to monitor internet connectivity across affected areas. National connectivity
dropped sharply from more than 90 percent to approximately 59–65 percent immediately following the
Page 4 of 6
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

earthquakes before partially recovering to around 77 percent within the following 24–48 hours. As of
03 July, La Guaira remained the most affected area, with connectivity operating at reduced capacity.
Connectivity in Caracas had largely recovered, although isolated outages persisted, while service
disruptions continued to affect parts of Yaracuy and Carabobo States.
Additional IM support is being provided by MapAction and Kobo Toolbox, which have deployed
personnel to La Guaira to support mapping, data collection, analysis, and information-sharing activities
in support of the humanitarian response.
Funding
Donor engagement remains ongoing, including discussions with key partners and the United States
(US) Embassy, while humanitarian funding requirements are being consolidated under the forthcoming
Flash Appeal.
The US Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA) has committed USD 9 million to support the
response, with a further USD 6 million currently being processed, bringing the expected total
contribution to USD 15 million. Funding is primarily focused on strengthening humanitarian supply chain
operations and the delivery of emergency assistance.
The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) has allocated USD 15 million for the Venezuela
earthquake response. Of this amount, WFP is expected to receive approximately USD 2 million to
support humanitarian response activities.
Meetings
A Global LTC Telecoms Partner Teleconference was held on 29 June at 14:00 UTC to support
information exchange and coordination. Minutes of the meeting are available here.
LTC Logistics Area
For more information on the logistics component of the LTC response, a dedicated Venezuela logistics
webpage is available here with the latest updates on working group meetings, key documents, maps,
and available support.
The latest LTC Logistics Situation Report is available here.
Contacts
Francisco Manuel
LTC Telecoms Coordinator Caracas francisco.castillo@wfp.org
Castillo Garrido
Global LTC Telecoms

Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

Global LTC Telecoms

Officer

documents.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 14**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**7 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de mil réplicas**.
- Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado.
- Balance oficial: **3.685 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.**
- **Tom Fletcher, jefe humanitario de las Naciones Unidas, inició una visita oficial a Venezuela para apoyar los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso.**
- El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y  
     continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas.

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.076 réplicas.**

A más de una semana de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **3.685 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, las autoridades reportan que unas **17.907 personas quedaron sin vivienda**.

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la preparación de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. En este marco de estos esfuerzos, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, inició una visita a Venezuela con el fin de conocer de primera mano el impacto de la emergencia y los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso.
