inició una visita a Venezuela con el fin de conocer de primera mano el impacto de la emergencia y los
esfuerzos de respuesta en curso.
Impacto en infraestructura
 Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.
 Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de
Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas,
comercios, escuelas, hospitales e instalaciones públicas. Entre tanto, estimaciones preliminares de
PNUD indican daños físicos directos por 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 6 % del PIB.
Respuesta nacional
 La respuesta gubernamental se mantiene centrada en las labores de búsqueda y rescate, así como
en la atención de las personas afectadas.
 De acuerdo con las autoridades, la respuesta continúa con 87 campamentos transitorios para la
atención de personas afectadas, con capacidad para 20.227 personas y una ocupación de 14.634
personas (72%). Hasta el 7 de julio, 39 campamentos se encuentran instalados en Caracas, 26 en
La Guaira y 22 en Miranda.
 Se decretaron siete (7) días de luto nacional a partir del 1 de julio.
 Se activó una comisión presidencial para la evaluación de habitabilidad de viviendas e
infraestructuras, así como un Estado Mayor para la instalación y coordinación de campamentos
transitorios.
 El Gobierno venezolano anunció la creación de un fondo inicial de reconstrucción equivalente a 200
millones de dólares.
 Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad
(Conapdis) para coordinar una respuesta oportuna e inclusiva en las zonas afectadas.
 Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas
(www.localizapacientes.com) y el reporte de personas afectadas (0-800-RESCATE).
 Las autoridades reanudaron las actividades administrativas en los estados no afectados y en
aquellos donde la infraestructura educativa no presenta daños visibles. Entretanto, las actividades
escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto Cabello,
Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); Distrito Capital
(Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión, Buroz,
Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).
Situación por estado
Distrito Capital (Caracas) y Miranda
 En el estado Miranda, representantes del grupo Interclúster, OPS, OCHA y autoridades regionales
y sectoriales realizaron visita conjunta a cuatro campamentos transitorios en Guarenas para
intercambiar información sobre la situación de estos espacios y fortalecer la coordinación de la
respuesta.
 Con la Vicepresidencia Social y Territorial, se acordó avanzar en recomendaciones de los protocolos
de atención en los campamentos transitorios, junto al grupo de trabajo de infraestructura y
alojamientos temporales y el clúster de protección, contribuyendo a su fortalecimiento.
Acciones de respuesta: Tres (3) organizaciones del FHV con proyectos financiados en municipios del
estado y en Distrito Capital (Cedesex, Construyendo Futuros y FUNDANA) apoyan la respuesta inicial
con servicios en protección general, de la niñez y de violencia basada en género (VBG). Además,
organizaciones como Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA y World Vision se encuentran brindando apoyo en el área
de protección a familias afectadas, especialmente a nivel psicosocial.
La Guaira
 Continúan las gestiones de coordinación entre autoridades, clústeres y organizaciones humanitarias
para fortalecer la respuesta en los campamentos transitorios de La Guaira, incluyendo el
seguimiento de necesidades, la ampliación de servicios sectoriales y la mejora de las condiciones
de alojamiento, protección y atención a la población afectada.
Acciones de respuesta: Cinco (5) organizaciones socias del Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV)
apoyan la respuesta con servicios de atención primaria en salud y atención psicológica (Fundación
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
Proyecto Maniapure, Paluz, Ven Da Tu Mano, Cruz Roja Venezolana y Tinta Violeta).
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro)
 En Carabobo, las principales afectaciones continúan concentrándose en el municipio Juan José
Mora (parroquia Morón). En Yaracuy, particularmente en el municipio Veroes y otras localidades
cercanas a la zona epicentral, se reportan viviendas destruidas o en condición de alto riesgo.
Evaluaciones recientes identifican necesidades prioritarias en protección, salud mental y apoyo
psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH) y seguridad alimentaria.
Acciones de respuesta: Cinco (5) organizaciones (Cruz Roja Venezolana, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas
Morón y Empodérame) brindan respuesta en salud, alimentación, agua y distribución de ayuda
humanitaria.
Falcón (Tucacas – Municipio Silva)
 En el marco del proyecto Salud+, la Organización Panamericana de la Salud (OPS/OMS) programó
una misión al municipio José Laurencio Silva (Tucacas y Boca de Aroa) para valorar daños
estructurales y operativos de la red hospitalaria y ambulatoria, evidenciar y priorizar las necesidades
de salud inmediatas de la población afectada, y fortalecer la articulación con la Cruz Roja
Venezolana, OCHA, las alcaldías de Silva y Miranda y Protección Civil, para la optimización de la
respuesta.
 OCHA y Protección Civil Falcón continúan coordinando acciones para fortalecer los procesos de
levantamiento de información sobre daños y necesidades en las comunidades afectadas. Asimismo,
avanzan los preparativos para la implementación de herramientas digitales de recolección de datos
sobre estructuras afectadas en el municipio Silva.
Acciones de respuesta: Se mantienen las jornadas, acordadas con las autoridades, casa a casa de la
OIM con entrega de enseres, kits de insumos y agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH); así como de Azul
Positivo con kits de ASH y primeros auxilios psicológicos. Está prevista una jornada adicional de otros
actores del Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC) en apoyo psicosocial, asistencia legal y ASH.
Otros estados
 En el estado Bolívar, las autoridades y el Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC) continuaron
fortaleciendo la preparación y coordinación interinstitucional ante la posible llegada de personas
provenientes de las zonas afectadas por los terremotos. Los actores humanitarios reiteraron su
disposición de proporcionar su apoyo, con una respuesta basada en evidencia y alineada con los
principios humanitarios. Además, las autoridades informaron del acondicionamiento de un espacio
en las instalaciones del VEN 911, en San Félix, para la atención de familias afectadas en caso de
necesitarse.
 En el estado Delta Amacuro, se registró la llegada de aproximadamente 50 personas, para quienes
se mantienen en marcha acciones de preparación y articulación con la comunidad humanitaria,
particularmente en los sectores de asistencia alimentaria y distribución de kits familiares. Asimismo,
se realizó una revisión preliminar de las necesidades prioritarias de la población afectada,
identificándose requerimientos adicionales para complementar los kits de asistencia, incluyendo
artículos de higiene personal, sábanas y agua potable. Se avanzó en la coordinación con las
autoridades de Salud para fortalecer la atención psicosocial de las personas afectadas por los
terremotos, tanto a nivel domiciliario como mediante actividades grupales en establecimientos de
salud.
 En el estado Monagas, las autoridades reportaron la llegada de 347 personas (106 familias)
afectadas por los terremotos provenientes principalmente de La Guaira, las cuales han sido
recibidas por redes familiares y comunitarias. En respuesta, las autoridades, en coordinación con
instituciones sectoriales, organizaciones sociales y actores de salud, han activado mecanismos de
atención que incluyen asistencia médica, apoyo psicosocial, suministro de medicamentos e insumos
básicos, así como el seguimiento de necesidades de protección.
 En el estado Nueva Esparta, de acuerdo con reportes locales, al menos 176 personas afectadas
habían arribado a la isla, siendo recibidas principalmente por familiares, mientras las autoridades
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
municipales y regionales mantenían procesos de registro, caracterización de necesidades y
distribución de asistencia básica para garantizar una atención organizada y evitar duplicaciones. La
Cruz Roja Venezolana activó mecanismos de Restablecimiento del Contacto entre Familiares (RCF)
para apoyar la localización de personas y facilitar la reunificación familiar. Organizaciones locales
como ASOMAYOR ampliaron el acceso a servicios de salud y apoyo diagnóstico para las familias
desplazadas. Adicionalmente, la empresa CONFERRY, en coordinación con autoridades locales,
implementó un puente humanitario para el traslado de personal médico, rescatistas, equipos de
respuesta y grupos familiares desde y hacia las zonas afectadas,
 En el estado Zulia, continúa la llegada y el tránsito de familias desplazadas desde La Guaira,
Caracas y Petare. Según el seguimiento de ASONACOP y ODISEF en el terminal de Maracaibo (al
6 de julio), se identificó y asistió a varias familias con destinos dentro del estado (Machiques, Villa
del Rosario y San Francisco) y en tránsito hacia Colombia (Maicao y Santa Marta), con predominio
de mujeres, niñas, niños y adolescentes y personas mayores. Una de las familias estaba integrada
por 13 personas, en su mayoría niñas, niños y adolescentes. La atención incluyó orientación jurídica
y apoyo psicosocial, referencia médica al ambulatorio del terminal (por cuadros de mareo, náuseas,
dolor abdominal en niñas, dolor articular y cefalea), entrega de alimentos servidos, agua e
hidratación, medicamentos, ropa, actualización de documentos y articulación del transporte hacia
los destinos. Se reportan casos de pérdida total de vivienda y de pérdidas humanas en el núcleo
familiar.
Coordinación humanitaria
 El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del
Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, llegó a Venezuela el 7 de julio para una visita de cuatro días,
durante la cual se reunirá con personas afectadas por los terremotos, personal humanitario,
autoridades y otros actores clave, con el fin de conocer de primera mano el impacto de la
emergencia, los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso y los avances hacia la siguiente fase de la
respuesta. A su llegada, realizó un recorrido por zonas afectadas en La Guaira y posteriormente
sostuvo un encuentro con la presidenta encargada, Delcy Rodríguez, el canciller Yván Gil, y el
presidente de la Asamblea Nacional Jorge Rodríguez. En la reunión también participaron el
Coordinador Humanitario, Gianluca Rampolla del Tindaro, y la Jefa de Oficina de OCHA Venezuela,
Vanessa May.
 OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales,
coordina la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias, priorizando
acciones en salud; alojamiento; alimentación; agua, saneamiento e higiene; logística; y protección.
 La coordinación de las operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano (USAR) fue transferida a
Protección Civil de Venezuela, que asumirá la coordinación de los equipos nacionales e
internacionales desplegados en las zonas afectadas. El proceso incluyó el traspaso de información
operativa y la capacitación sobre las metodologías de coordinación USAR utilizadas durante la
respuesta. Paralelamente, los equipos internacionales han iniciado progresivamente su
desmovilización; no obstante, varios equipos, particularmente de América Latina, permanecen
desplegados en las zonas afectadas.
 El Grupo de Coordinación Interclúster (ICCG) participó en el Taller de Análisis Conjunto
Interagencial convocado por OCHA para consolidar la evidencia generada por las evaluaciones
rápidas de necesidades y construir una comprensión común de las necesidades humanitarias
derivadas de los terremotos, orientando la priorización y planificación de la respuesta.
 Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores
al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del
PNUD. Conforme a la metodología internacionalmente de la PDNA, se avanzará en las
coordinaciones correspondientes con las contrapartes relevantes.
 Las autoridades nacionales han agilizado los procedimientos migratorios y administrativos para
facilitar el ingreso al país de equipos internacionales de búsqueda y rescate, personal de Naciones
Unidas, representantes de medios de comunicación y otros especialistas desplegados para apoyar
las operaciones de respuesta a la emergencia.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria
Seguridad Alimentaria
 Desde el inicio de la respuesta, el PMA ha brindado asistencia alimentaria a 30.983 personas.
Solo el 7 de julio, el PMA distribuyó 5.500 kits de alimentos listos para el consumo en Catia La Mar
y Naiguatá, proporcionando asistencia alimentaria inmediata a las poblaciones afectadas por los
terremotos.
 Paralelamente, el PMA entregó 100 cestas alimentarias familiares para apoyar la preparación de
comidas en cocinas comunitarias que operan en alojamientos temporales, incluidas 40 cestas en
el campamento temporal Chato Candela, en el Distrito Capital (parroquia Caruao), y 70 cestas en
el alojamiento temporal Luis Hurtado Higuera, en El Junquito.
Agua, saneamiento e higiene
 En Playa Grande, la OIM coordinó con CISP (socio implementador de UNICEF) autoridades y
actores presentes la definición y distribución de espacios para duchas diferenciadas para mujeres
y hombres.
 UNICEF apoyó el acceso a servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene en los campamentos
transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande. En Polideportivo Vargas,
1.700 personas mantuvieron acceso a kits de higiene, 60 baños operativos, 16 puntos de lavado
de manos y un suministro diario de 20.000 litros de agua, complementado con la movilización de
15 estaciones de duchas y la disponibilidad de 100 contenedores de residuos movilizados por el
Ministerio de Obras Públicas. En Estadio César Nieves, 1.253 personas contaron con acceso a kits
de higiene, 30 baños operativos, ocho puntos de lavado de manos y 20.000 litros diarios de agua,
con el apoyo del Ministerio de Energía y otras organizaciones; además, se instaló una planta
potabilizadora para establecer un punto permanente de agua segura. En Playa Grande, el
campamento mantuvo operativos 18 baños portátiles y recibió 10.000 litros de agua mediante
camiones cisterna, además de kits de higiene distribuidos por Acción contra el Hambre.
Alojamiento, Energía y Enseres
 La OIM fortaleció la coordinación y administración de los campamentos transitorios Estadio César
Nieves, Polideportivo José María Vargas y Playa Grande. Las acciones incluyeron reuniones
interagenciales de coordinación, seguimiento al funcionamiento de los servicios, actualización de
censos y registros de población, planificación de reubicaciones internas, fortalecimiento de
mecanismos de control de acceso y apoyo a la organización comunitaria y las normas de
convivencia.
 En el Estadio César Nieves, se confirmó la entrega de artículos no alimentarios (baldes, lonas y
sets de cocina) a 500 familias, mientras que en Playa Grande se completó la instalación de una
carpa de gran capacidad y se inició la reubicación ordenada de familias hacia espacios más
adecuados de alojamiento.
Logística y Telecomunicaciones
 El Grupo de Trabajo de Logística (GTL) continúa apoyando la respuesta mediante la provisión de
almacenamiento gratuito en La Guaira y servicios de transporte hacia La Guaira y otros estados
afectados. A la fecha, se han preposicionado 20 m³ de artículos no alimentarios (NFI) y se han
facilitado 18 servicios de transporte para socios humanitarios.
 El equipo de Telecomunicaciones (LTC) avanzó en la implementación de un sistema de
conectividad Starlink, incluyendo un sistema de respaldo energético con baterías y paneles solares,
en el Campamento Transitorio Estadio César Nieves, fortaleciendo las comunicaciones de
emergencia y beneficiando aproximadamente a 1.400 personas.
 Desde el Área Temporal de Preposicionamiento (ATP) de La Guaira, el PMA distribuyó 110
raciones familiares, equivalentes a 5,553 MT de alimentos, para apoyar la operación de los
comedores comunitarios.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Nutrición
 UNICEF apoyó la realización de tamizaje nutricional a 61 niños y niñas de entre 6 y 59 meses en
el campamento transitorio Polideportivo Vargas. Asimismo, 15 mujeres embarazadas y lactantes
recibieron suplementación con micronutrientes y 15 personas cuidadoras participaron en sesiones
de consejería sobre Alimentación del Lactante y del Niño Pequeño (ALNP).
Protección (incluidos Áreas de Responsabilidad de niños, niñas y adolescentes y violencia
basada en género)
 OIM mantiene la coordinación de espacio de protección activo. En el campamento transitorio
“Polideportivo Vargas”, se trabaja con la Defensoría del Pueblo, el Servicio de Atención a Niñas,
Niños y Adolescentes (NNA), el Consejo Municipal de Derechos de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes
(CMDNNA), Consejo de Protección de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes de Caracas (CPNNA). Se
realizó la remisión de 7 casos al sistema de protección del NNA.
 ACNUR brindó servicios de protección a 97 personas en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo
Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Estadio Playa Grande, mediante orientación legal, primeros auxilios
psicológicos, promoción de derechos, gestión documental y mesas de información. Asimismo, al
menos 32 personas fueron remitidas de forma segura a servicios especializados y 21 niños, niñas
y adolescentes en situación de riesgo o indocumentación recibieron asesoría jurídica, de los cuales
18 casos fueron referidos a los sistemas de protección infantil y servicios de salud.
 ACNUR fortaleció las condiciones de protección y seguridad en los campamentos mediante la
instalación de 29 reflectores y lámparas solares en áreas comunes del Polideportivo Vargas y el
Estadio Playa Grande.
 ACNUR impulsó acciones de coordinación y fortalecimiento institucional en los tres campamentos,
incluyendo reuniones técnicas con la Defensoría del Pueblo, el Sistema de Protección Integral de
Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes (SPINNA), agencias de las Naciones Unidas y actores humanitarios,
para abordar temas relacionados con PEAS, identificación de necesidades de protección, normas
de convivencia y mecanismos de atención a la población afectada.
 UNFPA desarrolló actividades de prevención y respuesta a la violencia basada en género (VBG) en
los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas y Estadio César Nieves, alcanzando a 84
personas mediante sensibilizaciones sobre mensajes clave de VBG y difusión de servicios
especializados. Asimismo, brindó gestión de casos, apoyo psicosocial y acceso a servicios
especializados para personas con necesidades de protección.
 OIM impulsó acciones de Protección contra la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS) en los
campamentos Estadio César Nieves y Polideportivo José María Vargas, mediante actividades de
sensibilización comunitaria, difusión de mensajes clave, instalación de material informativo y
coordinación interagencial para armonizar mensajes y mecanismos de prevención.
 UNICEF brindó servicios de protección de la niñez a 147 niños, niñas y adolescentes en los
campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande. Las
actividades incluyeron estimulación temprana, apoyo para la identificación y regulación emocional,
detección de factores de riesgo, fortalecimiento de la autonomía corporal, promoción de relaciones
saludables, entre otros.
Salud
 Un total de 43 Equipos Médicos de Emergencia (EMT) y equipos especializados de atención de 22
países participan en el mecanismo de coordinación de la respuesta. Actualmente, 12 EMT se
encuentran operativos en La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda y Aragua, fortaleciendo la capacidad de
atención sanitaria en las zonas afectadas. Además, siete equipos adicionales se encuentran en
proceso de despliegue y se espera que inicien operaciones próximamente, mientras un equipo
concluyó su misión y se encuentra en fase de desmovilización.
 Entre el Ministerio de Salud, la Célula de Información y Coordinación Médica (CICOM) y los EMT
desplegados, se acordó integrar a la Red EMT en las acciones de vigilancia epidemiológica, con el
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
fin de fortalecer la detección temprana y el monitoreo de riesgos para la salud en las zonas
afectadas.
 Se mantiene la entrega de bolsas para el manejo digno y seguro de personas fallecidas al Servicio
Nacional de Medicina y Ciencias Forenses (SENAMECF). Hasta la fecha, se han distribuido 3.000
con el fin de reforzar la capacidad institucional para la gestión de fallecidos en el contexto de la
emergencia.
 El Clúster de Salud y la co-coordinación sectorial fortalecen la gestión de información, los
mecanismos de recolección y análisis de datos, y las prioridades informativas que contribuyan a la
toma de decisiones y a una mejor coordinación de la respuesta.
 El Grupo Técnico de Trabajo de Salud Mental y Apoyo Psicosocial (GTT SMAPS) continúa
fortaleciendo la articulación y coordinación de las intervenciones de salud mental y apoyo
psicosocial en el marco de la respuesta a la emergencia.
 UNFPA brindó servicios de salud sexual y reproductiva en los campamentos transitorios
Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Estadio Playa Grande, incluyendo actividades de
promoción de servicios, sensibilizaciones sobre el uso de condones y sesiones educomunicativas.
Asimismo, se distribuyeron métodos anticonceptivos, se realizaron pruebas de VIH y sífilis, y se
entregó un kit de higiene menstrual.
 En el Campamento Transitorio Polideportivo José María Vargas, OIM brindó atención en salud a
192 personas durante la jornada.
 En el Campamento Transitorio Playa Grande, Project HOPE realizó 70 consultas médicas y seis
atenciones de apoyo psicosocial para personas afectadas.
 UNICEF apoyó jornadas de inmunización en el campamento transitorio Polideportivo Vargas,
donde se vacunó a nueve personas adultas, con la aplicación de dosis de toxoide y fiebre amarilla.
 IMC desplegó una unidad médica móvil desde el 1 de julio en Catia La Mar con capacidad para
atender hasta 100 pacientes por día y prevé ampliar la respuesta mediante unidades móviles
adicionales, y está por desplegar una EMT-Tipo 1 (Equipo Médico de Emergencia) que incluye la
llegada de 21 profesionales de la salud para reforzar la atención sanitaria en las zonas afectadas
de acuerdo a las prioridades del Ministerio de Salud.
Financiamiento humanitario
 Antes de los terremotos, el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria (PRH) 2026 para Venezuela había
recibido aproximadamente 115 millones de dólares, de los 632 millones de dólares requeridos. Tras
la emergencia, el financiamiento reportado para el plan se ubica en 300 millones de dólares.
 Parte del apoyo brindado por UNDAC incluye una especialista en coordinación con el sector privado
para fortalecer la participación empresarial en la respuesta y recuperación. Se encuentra disponible
un rastreador de contribuciones del sector privado para la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela
(https://ven-eq.connectingbusiness.org) y una nota informativa dirigida al sector privado sobre
oportunidades de apoyo. Punto focal: sanchez21@un.org.
 El Fondo Central de Respuesta a Emergencias (CERF, por sus siglas en inglés) realizó una
asignación de 15 millones de dólares para una respuesta multisectorial, junto con la activación del
Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV). Noruega realizó una contribución para apoyar la respuesta
a través del CERF.
 Estados Unidos anunció una contribución de 100 millones de dólares al FHV, y una asignación
adicional de 100 millones de dólares en contribuciones bilaterales para operaciones de respuesta
de OIM, PMA, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse,
Proyecto Esperanza y la Cruz Roja.
 Alemania y Corea realizaron contribuciones al FHV por 5 millones y 1,25 millones de dólares,
respectivamente, para apoyar la acción humanitaria en el país. Otros Estados Miembros y donantes
han expresado su intención de contribuir a la respuesta a través del Fondo.
 El Grupo Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo (Grupo BID) anunció un paquete de donaciones por
al menos 1 millón de dólares para apoyar la asistencia humanitaria inmediata, que se implementará
en coordinación con Cáritas Venezuela, así como las evaluaciones de daños y pérdidas.
 La OPS/OMS lanzó un llamamiento de emergencia por casi 24 millones de dólares para apoyar,
durante los próximos seis meses, la respuesta en salud y la recuperación temprana y asignó US$1,5
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
millones del Fondo de Contingencia para Emergencias. El PMA realizó un llamamiento inicial de 50
millones de dólares para ampliar la asistencia alimentaria y apoyar actividades logísticas y de
comunicación en emergencia. ACNUR indicó que requiere 14,8 millones de dólares para apoyar a
hasta 30.000 personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses.
 La Unión Europea asignó 5 millones de euros para apoyar la respuesta a la emergencia, lo que se
suma a los 52 millones de euros ya asignados este año para las operaciones humanitarias en el
país.
 Australia informó de una contribución de 2 millones de dólares para la provisión de alimentos,
alojamiento, atención de salud y acceso a agua segura a través de IFRC y el PMA.
 Suiza anunció una contribución de 2,5 millones de francos suizos para apoyar la respuesta.
 Suecia asignó 25 millones de coronas suecas para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria en el país,
mediante programas de asistencia alimentaria, agua, alojamiento temporal, protección y
reunificación familiar implementados por el PMA, ACNUR y Save the Children.
 Dinamarca anunció una contribución adicional de 11 millones de coronas danesas para apoyar la
respuesta humanitaria, incluyendo 10 millones de coronas danesas a través de ACNUR y 1 millón
de coronas danesas a través de DanChurchAid y la Cruz Roja Danesa.
 El Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) anunció una asignación inicial de 7,5 millones de libras
esterlinas para la respuesta al terremoto en Venezuela, incluyendo 2 millones de libras esterlinas
aportados por el Gobierno del Reino Unido mediante UK Aid Match. Los recursos serán
implementados por organizaciones miembros del DEC y sus socios locales para apoyar la respuesta
humanitaria.
 OCHA continúa coordinando con donantes y socios para asegurar una asignación rápida,
estratégica y basada en necesidades.
Apoya la respuesta humanitaria para atender el terremoto en Venezuela
Haz tu donación de forma segura y rápida ahora:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
Información de Contacto
Para mayor información, por favor contactar a la Oficina de OCHA Venezuela:
Vanessa May – Jefa de Oficina a.i. - mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Oficial de Asuntos Humanitarios - alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Oficial de Información Pública – moreno7@un.org
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

documents.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #14 (07 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 14**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**07 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,000 aftershocks.**
- At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state.
- Official toll: **3,685 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.**
- **Tom Fletcher, the United Nations humanitarian chief, began an official visit to Venezuela to support ongoing response efforts.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1.076 aftershocks.**

More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **3,685 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued** since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and the assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. In this context, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher began a visit to Venezuela to gain first-hand insight into the impact of the emergency and the ongoing response efforts.

Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
National response
 The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, as well as assistance
to affected people.
 According to authorities, the response continues with 87 transitional camps supporting affected
populations, with a capacity of 20,227 people and a current occupancy of 14,634 people (72 per
cent). As of 7 July, 39 camps are located in Caracas, 26 in La Guaira, and 22 in Miranda.
 A seven (7)-day national mourning period was declared starting on 1 July.
 A presidential commission was activated to assess the habitability of housing and infrastructure,
alongside a coordination structure for the establishment and management of transitional camps.
 The Government of Venezuela announced the creation of an initial reconstruction fund equivalent to
US$200 million.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com) and to
report affected individuals (0-800-RESCATE).
 Authorities have resumed administrative activities in states not affected by the earthquakes and in
areas where educational infrastructure shows no visible damage. Meanwhile, school activities
remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot,
Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua
and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital District (Libertador);
and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión, Buroz, Páez,
Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 In Miranda State, representatives of the Inter-Cluster Group, PAHO, OCHA, and regional and
sectoral authorities conducted a joint visit to four temporary camps in Guarenas to exchange
information on the situation in these sites and strengthen response coordination.
 With the Social and Territorial Vice Presidency, it was agreed to advance recommendations for
temporary camp management protocols, in coordination with the Infrastructure and Temporary
Shelters Working Group and the Protection Cluster, contributing to their strengthening.
Response actions: Three (3) VHF-funded organizations operating in municipalities across Miranda
state and the Capital District (Cedesex, Construyendo Futuros and FUNDANA) are supporting the initial
response through general protection, child protection and gender-based violence (GBV) services. In
addition, organizations such as Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA and World Vision are providing protection
support to affected families, particularly through psychosocial assistance.
La Guaira
 Coordination efforts among authorities, clusters and humanitarian organizations continue to
strengthen the response in La Guaira’s transitional camps, including needs monitoring, the
expansion of sectoral services, and improvements in shelter conditions, protection services and
assistance for affected populations.
Response actions: Five (5) partners of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF) are supporting the
response through primary health care and psychological support services (Fundación Proyecto
Maniapure, Paluz, Ven Da Tu Mano, Venezuelan Red Cross and Tinta Violeta).
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In Carabobo, the most significant impacts continue to be concentrated in Juan José Mora
municipality (Morón parish). In Yaracuy, particularly in Veroes municipality and other localities near
the epicentral area, homes have been reported as destroyed or at high risk. Recent assessments
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
have identified priority needs in protection, mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter,
water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security.
Response actions: Five organizations (Venezuelan Red Cross, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón
and Empodérame) are providing response in health, food, water and the distribution of humanitarian
assistance.
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
 Under the Salud+ project, PAHO/WHO scheduled a mission to José Laurencio Silva Municipality
(Tucacas and Boca de Aroa) to assess structural and operational damage to the hospital and
outpatient care network, identify and prioritize the immediate health needs of the affected population,
and strengthen coordination with the Venezuelan Red Cross, OCHA, the municipalities of Silva and
Miranda, and Civil Protection to optimize the response.
 OCHA and Falcón Civil Protection continue coordinating actions to strengthen damage and needs
data collection processes in affected communities. Preparations are also underway for the
implementation of digital data collection tools to assess affected structures in Silva municipality.
Response actions: Agreed-upon door-to-door outreach activities continue, with IOM distributing
household items, relief kits, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) assistance, while Azul Positivo
provides WASH kits and psychological first aid. An additional response activity by other members of the
Local Coordination Forum (LCF) is planned, focusing on psychosocial support, legal assistance and
WASH.
Other states
 In Bolívar state, authorities and the Local Coordination Forum (LCF) continued strengthening
preparedness and inter-institutional coordination in anticipation of the possible arrival of people from
earthquake-affected areas. Humanitarian actors reiterated their readiness to provide support through
an evidence-based response aligned with humanitarian principles. Authorities also reported the
preparation of a facility at the VEN 911 premises in San Félix to accommodate affected families
should the need arise.
 In Delta Amacuro state, approximately 50 additional arrivals were reported. Preparedness and
coordination efforts with the humanitarian community remain underway, particularly in food
assistance and the distribution of family kits. A preliminary review of priority needs identified
additional requirements to complement relief kits, including personal hygiene items, bed sheets and
drinking water. Coordination also advanced with health authorities to strengthen psychosocial
support for people affected by the earthquakes, both through home-based assistance and group
activities in health facilities.
 In Monagas state, authorities reported the arrival of 347 people (106 families) affected by the
earthquakes, mainly from La Guaira, who have been received by family and community networks.
In response, authorities, together with sectoral institutions, social organizations and health actors,
activated assistance mechanisms that include medical care, psychosocial support, the provision of
medicines and basic supplies, as well as follow-up on protection needs.
 In Nueva Esparta state, local reports indicated that at least 176 affected people had arrived on the
island, where they were mainly received by relatives. Municipal and regional authorities continued
registration, needs profiling and basic assistance distribution efforts to ensure an organized response
and avoid duplication. The Venezuelan Red Cross activated Restoring Family Links (RFL)
mechanisms to support the tracing of individuals and facilitate family reunification. Local
organizations such as ASOMAYOR expanded access to health services and diagnostic support for
displaced families. In addition, the company CONFERRY, in coordination with local authorities,
established a humanitarian bridge for the transportation of medical personnel, rescue teams,
response equipment and family groups to and from the affected areas.
 In Zulia state, the arrival and transit of displaced families from La Guaira, Caracas and Petare
continued. According to monitoring conducted by ASONACOP and ODISEF at the Maracaibo bus
terminal (as of 6 July), several families were identified and assisted, with destinations within the state
(Machiques, Villa del Rosario and San Francisco) and onward transit to Colombia (Maicao and Santa
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
Marta). Women, children, adolescents and older persons represented the majority of those assisted.
One family consisted of 13 members, most of them children and adolescents. Assistance included
legal counselling, psychosocial support, referrals to the terminal’s outpatient clinic, provision of
cooked meals, water and hydration supplies, medicines, clothing, document updates and
transportation support to final destinations. Cases of total housing loss and deaths within family
members were also reported.
Humanitarian coordination
 United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief
Coordinator Tom Fletcher arrived in Venezuela on 7 July for a four-day visit, during which he will
meet with people affected by the earthquakes, humanitarian personnel, authorities and other key
stakeholders to gain first-hand insight into the impact of the emergency, ongoing response efforts
and progress towards the next phase of the response. Upon his arrival, he visited earthquake-
affected areas in La Guaira and subsequently held a meeting with Acting President Delcy Rodríguez,
Foreign Minister Yván Gil and National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez. The meeting was also
attended by the Humanitarian Coordinator, Gianluca Rampolla del Tindaro, and the Head of Office
of OCHA Venezuela, Vanessa May.
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
coordinates the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner organizations,
prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), logistics
and protection.
 The coordination of Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) operations was formally transferred to
Venezuela’s Civil Protection, which will continue coordinating both national and international teams
deployed in the affected areas. The handover process included the transfer of operational
information and training on the USAR coordination methodologies used throughout the response. At
the same time, international USAR teams have begun a gradual demobilization process; however,
several teams, particularly from Latin America, remain deployed in affected areas.
 The Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) participated in the Inter-Agency Joint Analysis
Workshop convened by OCHA to consolidate evidence generated through rapid needs assessments
and build a shared understanding of the humanitarian needs arising from the earthquakes, informing
response prioritization and planning.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
within the framework of the United Nations system and with the support of UNDP. In line with the
internationally recognized PDNA methodology, the corresponding coordination efforts with relevant
counterparts will be advanced.
 National authorities have expedited migration and administrative procedures to facilitate the entry
into the country of international search and rescue teams, United Nations personnel, media
representatives, and other specialists deployed to support emergency response operations.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 Since the beginning of the response, WFP has reached 30,983 people with food assistance. On
7 July alone, WFP distributed 5,500 ready-to-eat food kits in Catia La Mar and Naiguatá, providing
immediate food assistance to earthquake-affected populations.
 In parallel, WFP provided 100 family food baskets to support meal preparation in community kitchens
operating in temporary shelters, including 40 baskets at the Chato Candela temporary camp in the
Capital District (Caruao parish) and 70 baskets at the Luis Hurtado Higuera temporary shelter in El
Junquito.
Health
 A total of 43 Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) and specialized medical teams from 22 countries
are participating in the response coordination mechanism. Currently, 12 EMTs are operational in La
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
Guaira, Caracas, Miranda and Aragua, strengthening health service delivery in the affected areas.
An additional seven teams are in the deployment process and are expected to begin operations
soon, while one team has completed its mission and is currently demobilizing.
 The Ministry of Health, the Medical Information and Coordination Cell (CICOM) and deployed EMTs
agreed to integrate the EMT Network into epidemiological surveillance activities in order to
strengthen early detection and monitoring of health risks in affected areas.
 The distribution of body bags for the dignified and safe management of deceased persons to the
National Service of Forensic Medicine and Sciences (SENAMECF) continues. To date, 3,000 body
bags have been distributed to strengthen institutional capacity for the management of fatalities in the
context of the emergency.
 The Health Cluster and its co-coordination continue to strengthen information management, data
collection and analysis mechanisms, and information priorities that support decision-making and
improved response coordination.
 The Mental Health and Psychosocial Support Technical Working Group (MHPSS TWG) continues
to strengthen the coordination and articulation of mental health and psychosocial support
interventions as part of the emergency response.
 UNFPA provided sexual and reproductive health services in the Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César
Nieves and Estadio Playa Grande temporary camps, including service promotion activities, condom-
use awareness sessions and educational outreach. Contraceptive methods were also distributed,
HIV and syphilis tests were conducted, and one menstrual hygiene kit was provided.
 At the Polideportivo José María Vargas Temporary Camp, IOM provided health assistance to 192
people during the reporting period.
 At the Playa Grande Temporary Camp, Project HOPE conducted 70 medical consultations and
provided six psychosocial support consultations for affected people.
 UNICEF supported immunization activities at the Polideportivo Vargas Temporary Camp, where nine
adults received vaccinations, including tetanus toxoid and yellow fever doses.
 IMC deployed a mobile medical unit in Catia La Mar on 1 July with the capacity to treat up 100
patients per day and plans to expand the response through additional mobile units. IMC is also
preparing to deploy a Type 1 EMT (Emergency Medical Team), including the arrival of 21 health
professionals to strengthen health services in the affected areas in line with Ministry of Health
priorities.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 The Logistics Working Group (LWG) continues to support the response through the provision of free
storage facilities in La Guaira and transport services to La Guaira and other affected states. To date,
20 m³ of non-food items (NFIs) have been pre-positioned, and 18 transport services have been
facilitated for humanitarian partners.
 The Emergency Telecommunications Team (ETT) advanced the installation of a Starlink connectivity
system, including a backup power system with batteries and solar panels, at the Estadio César
Nieves Temporary Camp, strengthening emergency communications and benefiting approximately
1,400 people.
 From the Temporary Prepositioning Area (TPA) in La Guaira, WFP distributed 110 family food
rations, equivalent to 5.553 MT of food, to support the operation of community kitchens.
Nutrition
 UNICEF supported nutrition screening for 61 children aged 6–59 months at the Polideportivo Vargas
Temporary Camp. In addition, 15 pregnant and breastfeeding women received micronutrient
supplementation, and 15 caregivers participated in Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
counselling sessions..
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 IOM continues to coordinate an active protection space. At the Polideportivo Vargas Temporary
Camp, it is working with the Ombudsperson’s Office, the Child and Adolescent Care Service, the
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Municipal Council for the Rights of Children and Adolescents (CMDNNA), and the Caracas Child
and Adolescent Protection Council (CPNNA). Seven cases were referred to the child protection
system.
 UNHCR provided protection services to 97 people in the Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves
and Estadio Playa Grande temporary camps through legal counselling, psychological first aid, rights
awareness activities, documentation support and information desks. In addition, at least 32 people
were safely referred to specialized services, while 21 children and adolescents at risk or lacking
documentation received legal assistance, of whom 18 cases were referred to child protection and
health services.
 UNHCR strengthened protection and safety conditions in the camps through the installation of 29
floodlights and solar lamps in common areas of the Polideportivo Vargas and Estadio Playa Grande
sites.
 UNHCR supported coordination and institutional strengthening activities across the three camps,
including technical meetings with the Ombudsperson’s Office, the Comprehensive Child and
Adolescent Protection System (SPINNA), United Nations agencies and humanitarian actors to
address issues related to PSEA, identification of protection needs, camp rules and mechanisms for
assisting affected populations.
 UNFPA conducted gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response activities at the
Polideportivo Vargas and Estadio César Nieves temporary camps, reaching 84 people through
awareness sessions on key GBV messages and the dissemination of specialized services. UNFPA
also provided case management, psychosocial support and access to specialized services for
people with protection needs.
 IOM promoted Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) activities at the Estadio César
Nieves and Polideportivo José María Vargas camps through community awareness sessions,
dissemination of key messages, installation of information materials and inter-agency coordination
to harmonize prevention messages and mechanisms.
 UNICEF provided child protection services to 147 children and adolescents in the Polideportivo
Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Playa Grande temporary camps. Activities included early
childhood stimulation, support for emotional identification and regulation, identification of risk factors,
strengthening of bodily autonomy, and the promotion of healthy relationships, among others.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 IOM strengthened coordination and management at the Estadio César Nieves, Polideportivo José
María Vargas and Playa Grande temporary camps. Activities included inter-agency coordination
meetings, monitoring of service delivery, updates to population censuses and registration records,
planning of internal relocations, strengthening of access control mechanisms, and support to
community organization and camp rules and regulations.
 At Estadio César Nieves, the delivery of non-food items (NFIs), including buckets, tarpaulins and
kitchen sets, to 500 families was confirmed. At Playa Grande, the installation of a large-capacity tent
was completed and the organized relocation of families to more suitable shelter spaces was initiated.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 In Playa Grande, IOM coordinated with CISP (UNICEF’s implementing partner), authorities and other
actors present to define and allocate separate shower facilities for women and men.
 UNICEF supported access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services in the Polideportivo
Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Playa Grande temporary camps. At Polideportivo Vargas, 1,700
people maintained access to hygiene kits, 60 operational toilets, 16 handwashing stations and a
daily supply of 20,000 litres of water, complemented by the mobilization of 15 shower stations and
the availability of 100 waste containers provided by the Ministry of Public Infrastructure. At Estadio
César Nieves, 1,253 people had access to hygiene kits, 30 operational toilets, eight handwashing
stations and 20,000 litres of water per day, with support from the Ministry of Energy and other
organizations. In addition, a water treatment plant was installed to establish a permanent source of
safe water. At Playa Grande, the camp maintained 18 operational portable toilets and received
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
10,000 litres of water through water trucks, in addition to hygiene kits distributed by Action Against
Hunger.
Humanitarian financing
 Before the earthquakes, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) for Venezuela had received
approximately US$115 million of the US$632 million required. Following the emergency, reported
funding for the plan reached US$300 million.
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country. Other Member States and donors have
expressed their intention to support the response through the Fund.
 The Inter-American Development Bank Group (IDB Group) announced a donation package of at
least US$1 million to support immediate humanitarian assistance, to be implemented in coordination
with Cáritas Venezuela, as well as damage and loss assessments.
 PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support health response
and early recovery activities over the next six months and released US$1.5 million from the
Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP launched an initial appeal for US$50 million to scale up
food assistance and support emergency logistics and communications activities. UNHCR requires
US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52
million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the
earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom
Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and
their local partners to support the humanitarian response.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:

documents.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
Venezuela is facing a severe humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck the country's central-northern region on 24 June. At least 3,342 people have been killed and 16,470 injured. With tens of thousands of people still unaccounted for, the death toll is expected to increase as search and rescue efforts continue.

An estimated 36,700 pregnant women have been affected by the earthquakes, including approximately 4,000 who are expected to give birth in the next month. The health system is under severe strain, with 38 health facilities damaged, significantly limiting access to essential maternal health services for women and newborns. Maintaining emergency obstetric and newborn care is therefore an urgent humanitarian priority.

The disruption of essential services, overcrowded shelters, family separation, and rising psychosocial distress are exacerbating protection risks, particularly for women, adolescent girls, persons with disabilities, and older persons. In addition, more than 10,000 people are currently residing in temporary shelters, where privacy, lighting and protection measures remain insufficient. Strengthening gender-based violence prevention and ensuring safe access to survivor-centred services is critical.

UNFPA is scaling up its responses to ensure continued access to maternal health services, emergency obstetric care, family planning, clinical management of rape, and gender-based violence prevention and response services. Initial shipments of reproductive health supplies and essential equipment are being mobilized to support affected communities. UNFPA estimates it requires approximately US$10 million to sustain life-saving reproductive health and protection interventions for the first three months of the emergency response.

Earthquakes in Venezuela
Flash Update
26 June - 6 July 2026
Highlights
Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes of
magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 that struck the central-northern region of the country on 24 June.
Nearly 1,000 aftershocks have been recorded, while search and rescue operations and
humanitarian assistance continue across affected areas. Official reports indicate that at least
3,342 people have died and more than 16,470 have been injured.1
The states most affected remain La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy,
Falcón and other neighbouring areas. More than 2,500 infrastructures have sustained
damage, including 38 health facilities, while thousands of people remain displaced or
accommodated in temporary shelters.
The disruption of essential services, overcrowding in shelters, family separation and
increased psychosocial distress are heightening protection risks, particularly for women,
adolescent girls, persons with disabilities and older persons. Strengthening survivor-centred
services and safe access to assistance remains an urgent priority.
UNFPA is scaling up its life-saving sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and protection
response to ensure continued access to maternal health services, emergency obstetric care,
family planning, clinical management of rape, and gender-based violence (GBV) prevention
and response. Initial shipments of reproductive health supplies and equipment are being
mobilized to support affected communities.
789,00 36,700 4,000 850,000 230,000
Women of Estimated preg nant Women expected to give People targeted w/ People targeted w/
reproductive age2 women2 birth in the next month2 SRH services GBV programmes
1 OCHA. Situation Report No. 12 Earthquakes in Venezuela. 5 July 2026.
2 Estimated figures are based on the Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for Sexual and Reproductive Health in Humanitarian Settings
calculator.

UNFPA Flash Update I Venezuela I 26 June - 6 July 2026
Situation Overview
Twelve days after the earthquakes, Venezuela remains in an active emergency response phase.
Authorities report more than 1,000 aftershocks, although their frequency and intensity have gradually
decreased. Search and rescue operations continue alongside damage assessments and the
restoration of essential services.
Official figures indicate 3,342 fatalities and 16,470 injuries, although figures are expected to continue
to rise with tens of thousands of people still missing. More than 26,000 people are directly affected
and over 17,345 have lost their homes. Currently, 10,702 people are currently residing across 79
temporary camps, which have been established across the most affected areas.
The health system remains under considerable pressure. Thirty-eight health facilities have sustained
damage, including major hospitals in Caracas, limiting access to essential care for women and
newborns. Disruptions to electricity, transport and communications continue to affect humanitarian
operations and service delivery.
Protection concerns are increasing as displacement, overcrowding in shelters, family separation, and
economic hardship weaken traditional support networks. Women and girls face heightened risks of
GBV, particularly in collective shelters where privacy, lighting and protection measures remain
insufficient. Psychosocial distress and mental health needs are widespread among affected
populations and first responders alike.
Estimates indicate that 36,700 women are currently pregnant in affected areas, including
approximately 4,000 who are expected to give birth during the coming month. More than 1,800
pregnant women are expected to experience complications requiring specialized care during the next
three months. Sustaining emergency obstetric and newborn services therefore remains a critical
humanitarian priority.

UNFPA Flash Update I Venezuela I 26 June - 6 July 2026
UNFPA Response
Sexual and reproductive health: UNFPA continues to support national authorities, humanitarian
partners and local organizations to ensure access to life-saving SRH and protection services for
women, girls and adolescents affected by the earthquakes. Response efforts have expanded from the
initial deployment of emergency supplies to the delivery of integrated services in temporary shelters,
and strengthened support to health facilities in the affected areas.
In La Guaira, UNFPA and its implementing partner are delivering the Minimum Initial Service Package
(MISP) for Sexual and Reproductive Health in Emergencies at the José María Vargas temporary
shelter. Women and adolescent girls are receiving modern contraceptives, menstrual hygiene kits,
condoms, counselling, and information on sexually transmitted infection prevention, pregnancy danger
signs, sexual violence and available referral services. Pregnant women and survivors of sexual
violence are being identified and safely referred through established pathways in coordination with the
public health system.
UNFPA has also begun distributing emergency reproductive health supplies to support the continuity
of essential services in affected areas. This includes post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) kits for the
clinical management of rape, reproductive health commodities and emergency obstetric supplies
provided to referral hospitals and humanitarian health partners.
Gender-based violence: As lead agency for Gender-Based Violence coordination, UNFPA is
coordinating inter-agency prevention and response interventions, including dignity kit distributions,
psychosocial support, case management and legal assistance for survivors. Initial safety assessments
in collective shelters have identified inadequate lighting in some areas as an important protection
concern for women and girls, informing ongoing GBV risk mitigation measures and the prioritization of
additional dignity kits3 and safety interventions.
Coordination Mechanisms
UNFPA continues to actively participate in national and inter-agency coordination mechanisms led by
the Government of Venezuela and OCHA, contributing to needs assessments, humanitarian analysis,
information management and collective response planning.
UNFPA is working closely with health, protection, shelter and mental health actors to ensure that SRH
and GBV remain recognized as life-saving components of the emergency response. Particular
attention is being given to integrating GBV risk mitigation measures within collective shelters and
temporary camps.
Partnerships with women's organizations, youth networks and community-based actors remain central
to delivering an inclusive, locally-led and accountable humanitarian response.
3 Dignity kits contain essential items to maintain hygiene and health as well as increase safety. They include a torch, sanitary pads, soap,
shampoo, underwear, toothbrushes and toothpaste, toilet paper, comb, and a leaflet with key messages on GBV and available support
services.

UNFPA Flash Update I Venezuela I 26 June - 6 July 2026
Funding Status
UNFPA estimates that approximately US$10 million will be required during the first three months of
the response to sustain life-saving SRH and GBV interventions, including the implementation of the
MISP, support to pregnant women, essential supplies, specialized services, coordination, rapid
assessments, and partnerships with local organizations.
Additional resources remain urgently needed to expand access to maternal health services,
strengthen GBV prevention and response programmes, and protect the rights and dignity of women
and girls affected by the earthquakes.
"Across the affected communities, we are witnessing extraordinary
resilience. Health personnel, midwives, social workers and community
volunteers continue to provide life-saving services under extremely
difficult conditions, often while dealing with the impact of the
earthquakes on their own families. Their dedication is inspiring. At the
same time, the needs of women, girls and adolescents are growing
every day, and sustained support is essential to ensure that no one is
left without access to protection, sexual and reproductive healthcare,
and hope for recovery."

Resumen
Las acciones reportadas durante la jornada se concentraron en la provisión de servicios de salud
sexual y reproductiva, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, atención primaria en salud, distribución
de insumos esenciales, evaluaciones rápidas de necesidades y fortalecimiento de la
coordinación técnica de la respuesta.
En los espacios de alojamiento temporal de La Guaira se desarrollaron actividades de
sensibilización comunitaria sobre salud sexual y reproductiva, prevención de infecciones de
transmisión sexual y uso de métodos anticonceptivos, alcanzando a 126 personas, además de la
distribución de 16 métodos anticonceptivos modernos y la realización de pruebas rápidas de VIH
y sífilis.
Las intervenciones en salud mental y apoyo psicosocial incluyeron atención a población afectada
en campamentos y comunidades, así como apoyo al personal de respuesta. Adicionalmente, se
realizaron 15 consultas de salud mental en Playa Verde y Los Corales y se efectuaron
evaluaciones en establecimientos de salud para identificar necesidades operativas y
oportunidades de apoyo.

Las actividades de coordinación y evaluación permitieron completar el levantamiento de
información en 22 centros de atención para personas mayores ubicados en el Área
Metropolitana de Caracas y La Guaira, así como la distribución de insumos médicos y
suministros para fortalecer la atención en establecimientos y puntos de respuesta.
Asimismo, una jornada de atención primaria en salud realizada en la Urbanización José Antonio
Páez, Catia La Mar, brindó 67 atenciones médicas, identificando como principal preocupación el
acceso limitado a agua potable segura, con requerimientos asociados a abastecimiento,
almacenamiento y tratamiento de agua para reducir riesgos sanitarios en la comunidad.

sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
## DESCRIPTION OF THE EVENT

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 302 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. They were also felt in parts of Colombia, the Caribbean and Brazil, reaching as far as Martinique and the Brazilian Amazon, more than 1,700 km from the epicentres.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency and designated La Guaira a disaster zone, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations is concentrated. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.

According to the initial statistical model developed by the United States Geological Survey (USGS), there was a 50 per cent probability that the number of casualties (deaths and injuries) would range between 1,000 and 10,000, and a 30 per cent probability that it would exceed 10,000. International response teams from at least 17 countries have deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the 2 OCHA Situation Report No. 9 Earthquakes in Venezuela coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG).

According to OCHA, as of 2 July2, 2,595 people had been confirmed dead and 12,400 injured. A further 12,841 people had been displaced after their homes were severely damaged. In total, 2,501 structures were affected, including 38 hospitals, 189 buildings that collapsed completely, and 855 buildings that either partially collapsed or sustained significant damage. La Guaira remains the worst-affected state.

CAPACITIES AND RESPONSE
National Society response capacity
1.1 National Society capacity and ongoing response
The Venezuelan Red Cross National Society has 41 branches across the country, supported by 42 local units, and
has been responding since the onset of the emergency. Nationwide, 326 volunteers are providing direct support
to the response, together with 62 contracted staff members. Operational assets include 10 vehicles (one field
hospital truck, two ambulances, five pickup trucks, and two motorcycles for damage assessment), as well as one
field hospital and two first aid posts.
Key response activities include search and rescue, health care and first aid, damage and needs assessments,
restoring family links (RFL), water, hygiene, and sanitation (WASH), logistics, branch mobilisation, and information
management.
5

In the area of health care and first aid, the Venezuelan Red Cross has delivered over 1,900 medical consultations
via field hospital and mobile units, while strengthening referral systems, epidemiological surveillance and
vaccination coordination. In WASH, these interventions have been scaled up through the operation of the
WATSAN system providing safe water to operational sites and affected communities, alongside installation of
sanitation facilities (showers, latrines and handwashing units) in field hospitals and shelters. In parallel, the
National Society continues managing over 2,500 RFL cases and additional tracing requests through fixed and
mobile connectivity points, while expanding PGI and psychosocial support services for affected people in camps
and host communities.
Additionally, the Venezuelan Red Cross is maintaining a monitoring system of 109 shelters across five states,
deploying digital data collection tools, and supporting operational planning. Logistics operations have included
reception and distribution of relief items, stock management and transport coordination, while field teams
continue to provide hydration, hygiene supplies and operational support to response personnel and affected
communities.
1.2 Capacity and response at the national level
The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency and designated La Guaira as a Disaster
Zone. Response operations are being coordinated by the Emergency Joint Staff and include search and rescue
activities led by Civil Protection teams and the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (FANB), working alongside
international teams deployed in the affected areas.
In addition, the public and private health systems has been activated to provided mass casualty care and
humanitarian assistance through the distribution of essential supplies, food, and water; the deployment of field
hospitals to reinforce the existing hospital network; the establishment of temporary shelters in La Guaira and
Caracas; and the activation of platforms for reporting missing persons and housing damage. An initial fund of
USD 200 million3 has also been allocated for infrastructure reconstruction.
1.3 Legal framework in support of the operation
The operation is guided by the Statutes of the Movement, the Fundamental Principles, the Venezuelan Red Cross
Law (10 March 2026), and the IFRC Legal Status Agreement. Together, these provide a robust legal framework
that facilities the operation, recognises the National Society’s auxiliary role to the public authorities, and enables
principled humanitarian action.
International capacity and response
2.1 Red Cross Red Crescent Movement capacity and response
The Movement’s collective response aims to support people and communities affected by the earthquakes
through life-saving actions, humanitarian assistance, protection, early recovery, and resilience building, while
strengthening the institutional and operational capacities of the Venezuelan Red Cross to respond to this
emergency and future crises.
In accordance with the Seville Agreement 2.0, the Venezuelan Red Cross serves as the Convener of the
Movement’s collective response. The IFRC acts as the Co-Convener, supporting the Venezuelan Red Cross in:
• Defining the objectives, priorities, and strategic direction of the collective response.
• Aligning IFRC membership support.
• Mobilising international resources and capacities.
• Coordinating support for the institutional strengthening of the National Society.

Cross in responding to the population movement crisis, while responding to long-term humanitarian needs and
enhancing VRC’s auxiliary role, it also prioritized the Movement’s coordination mechanisms, working closely with
the ICRC and the Participating National Societies with physical presence in Venezuela, such as the German Red
A Tripartite Movement Agreement was signed between the Venezuelan Red Cross, the ICRC, and the IFRC, which
enabled a smooth coordination at operational level and communication, formalized in a Mini Summit held on 28
June 2026 to ensure a unified approach and strategic projection of response actions, complementing the
Venezuelan Red Cross’s national role and mandate as the country's primary first responder. These mechanisms
provide a common platform for strategic decision-making, operational planning, information sharing, resource
allocation and collective accountability, ensuring that the Movement operates as one network in support of
affected communities.
Among the actions carried out by the Secretariat is the delivery within first 48 hours, of a first charter with 17

Given the impact and scale of the emergency, the IFRC activated the Global Response Framework and requested
an Emergency Response Unit (ERU) Clinical Advance Team within the first 48 hours to assess health needs and

midwifery, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), among other health-related specialties. The

Following the initial needs assessment, an additional request was made for a Logistics ERU, which will be

The ERU initially comprises two logistics specialists who will provide flexible operational support through the

The OSH ERU will work closely with the Venezuelan Red Cross, the IFRC, and other operational partners to

Gaps in the response
Initial assessments and available operational reports show critical gaps in health, temporary shelter, WASH,
protection, RFL, proper handling of human remains, community information, and territorial coordination. The
magnitude of the event, the continuation of aftershocks, and the extent of infrastructure damage have exceeded
local capacities in the most affected areas, especially in La Guaira and the Caracas metropolitan area. The
national and international response continues to expand, but significant gaps remain in access to affected
communities, consolidation of information, sectorisation of assistance, and coverage of basic needs in open
spaces, makeshift shelters, and population concentration points.
In health, the public and private network remains under pressure due to trauma care, patient referrals from La
Guaira to Caracas, and the continuity of essential services for people with chronic illnesses, pregnant women,
girls, boys, older persons, and persons with disabilities. Hospital assessments conducted by VRC and IFRC health
teams identify operational facilities, but with mild to moderate damage in some areas, partial functionality in
certain cases, pressure on emergency rooms, and gaps in diagnostic equipment, osteosynthesis materials,
antibiotics, splints, referral pathways, and the linkage between health services, affected communities, and
shelters. The need is no longer limited to initial trauma care; it also includes sustaining community care, patient
follow-up, mental health and psychosocial support, and the progressive recovery of affected health services.
In shelter, WASH, and basic services, thousands of families are unable to return to their homes due to destruction,
structural damage, fear of further aftershocks, or lack of information on building safety. Many remain in open
spaces, sports courts, plazas, safe points, or temporary shelters, with needs for safe water, sanitation, hygiene,
lighting, privacy, protection, clear information, and psychosocial support. The total or intermittent interruption
of electricity, water, gas, and telecommunications in parts of La Guaira limits people’s ability to communicate,

Protection risks are high. Reports include people searching for relatives, bodies being exposed or handled in

Community coping capacities have been weakened by the scale of the damage, the loss of basic services, fear of
