(Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities
report 1.048 aftershocks.
More than a week after the
earthquakes, authorities report a toll of
3,535 people dead, 16,740 injured,
and 6,462 rescued since the onset of
the emergency. Authorities also
reported that approximately 17,854
people lost their homes.
The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and
expansion of transitional camps and the assistance to affected populations. La Guaira remains the most
affected state. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are
implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
National response
 The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, as well as assistance
to affected people.
 A seven (7)-day national mourning period was declared starting on 1 July.
 A presidential commission was activated to assess the habitability of housing and infrastructure,
alongside a coordination structure for the establishment and management of transitional camps.
 According to authorities, the response continues with 80 transitional camps supporting affected
populations, with a capacity of 17,642 people and a current occupancy of 12,806 people (73 per
cent). As of 6 July, 37 camps are located in Caracas, 22 in Miranda and 21 in La Guaira.
 The Government of Venezuela announced the creation of an initial reconstruction fund equivalent to
US$200 million.
 Authorities activated an air bridge between Caracas and Caraballeda (La Guaira) to strengthen the
delivery of supplies and ensure assistance to affected areas.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com) and to
report affected individuals (0-800-RESCATE).
 Authorities have resumed administrative activities in states not affected by the earthquakes and in
areas where educational infrastructure shows no visible damage. Meanwhile, school activities
remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot,
Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua
and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital District (Libertador);
and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión, Buroz, Páez,
Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 Response and assistance activities for affected populations continue in Chacao municipality
(Miranda State), while damage to critical infrastructure and disruptions to basic services persist,
contributing to ongoing humanitarian needs.
Response actions: Three (3) VHF-funded organizations operating in municipalities across Miranda
state and the Capital District (Cedesex, Construyendo Futuros and FUNDANA) are supporting the initial
response through general protection, child protection and gender-based violence (GBV) services. In
addition, organizations such as Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA and World Vision are providing protection
support to affected families, particularly through psychosocial assistance.
La Guaira
 Coordination efforts among authorities, clusters and humanitarian organizations continue to
strengthen the response in La Guaira’s transitional camps, including needs monitoring, the
expansion of sectoral services, and improvements in shelter conditions, protection services and
assistance for affected populations.
Response actions: Five (5) partners of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF) are supporting the
initial response through primary health care and psychological support services (Fundación Proyecto
Maniapure, Paluz, Ven Da Tu Mano, Venezuelan Red Cross and Tinta Violeta).
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In Carabobo, the most significant impacts continue to be concentrated in Juan José Mora
municipality (Morón parish). In Yaracuy, particularly in Veroes municipality and other localities near
the epicentral area, homes have been reported as destroyed or at high risk, while displaced families
from La Guaira continue to arrive. Recent assessments have identified priority needs in protection,
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and
food security.
Response actions: Five organizations (Venezuelan Red Cross, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón
and Empodérame) are providing response in health, food, water and the distribution of humanitarian
assistance.
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
 On 3 July, the Local Coordination Forum (LCF), in coordination with Action Against Hunger, Azul
Positivo and regional authorities, conducted a humanitarian outreach activity in the community of
Cayumar (Boca de Aroa), providing psychosocial support to 46 people and distributing 62 hygiene
kits to the most affected families.
 The State Government and humanitarian partners agreed to conduct a door-to-door assistance
campaign next week in the communities of Cayumar and Barrio Verde. As part of the initiative, IOM
will distribute household items, while Azul Positivo will provide WASH kits. Other LCF partners may
also contribute psychosocial support and legal assistance services.
 OCHA and Falcón Civil Protection continue coordinating actions to strengthen damage and needs
data collection processes in affected communities. Preparations are also underway for the
implementation of digital data collection tools to assess affected structures in Silva municipality.
Response actions: Psychosocial support and needs assessment activities continue for displaced and
affected people in Silva municipality. Humanitarian organizations are also exploring options to scale up
shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security assistance for the most affected
families.
Other states
 In Anzoátegui state, approximately 700 people have arrived in the state through family reunification
processes. In Simón Rodríguez municipality (El Tigre), around 100 people have been received.
Efforts are underway to strengthen the three reception sites and temporary camps that have been
established. The delivery of assistance continues, with a cumulative volume of 365 metric tons of
relief items mobilized from Lechería municipality.
 In Apure state, the State Contingency Plan reports the relocation of 189 people (77 heads of
household registered and 112 family members), the majority of whom originated from La Guaira
(86%). The main destination municipalities are San Fernando (123), Muñoz (24), Achaguas (20),
and Biruaca (18). Assistance provided includes medical care (62 families), food assistance (30),
legal documentation support (15), household items (14), and temporary shelter (11).
 In Bolívar state, the Governor’s Office reported a cumulative volume of approximately 1,600 metric
tons of humanitarian assistance dispatched from the state. Regional authorities continue to maintain
inter-institutional coordination mechanisms with OCHA and the Coordination Advisory Group (CAG).
 In Delta Amacuro state, a second group of 54 people (39 adults and 15 children and adolescents)
relocated from La Guaira was received during the night of 4–5 July. They were initially
accommodated at the Tucupita Indoor Gymnasium and subsequently reunified with previously
identified host households. Authorities and humanitarian actors are assessing priority needs in food
assistance, family and menstrual hygiene kits, psychosocial support, and essential medicines,
particularly for the symptomatic treatment of respiratory infections among children and for people
with cardiovascular conditions. Coordination mechanisms have been activated.
 In Monagas state, Cáritas Maturín is implementing a comprehensive assistance mechanism for
families displaced from La Guaira, including registration, verification, and needs assessments in
localities such as La Pica, Jusepín, the Paramaconi Housing Complex, and the municipalities of
Cedeño and Ezequiel Zamora, with a focus on health, protection, and psychosocial support. The
need to expand the availability of food, medicines, mattresses, clothing, footwear, and household
items has been identified.
 In Nueva Esparta state, Maneiro municipality continues to implement an active reception,
registration, and assistance protocol. The arrival of at least 176 people has been confirmed. The
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
response strategy prioritizes accommodation through family networks on Margarita Island,
complemented by the direct distribution of non-perishable food kits, hygiene kits, and clothing.
 In Sucre state, the Local Coordination Forum (LCF), in coordination with government institutions
and local actors, supported the reception and assistance of 48 returnees on 5 July (29 to Sucre-
Cumaná municipality, 7 to Benítez-El Pilar, 7 to Bermúdez-Carúpano, and 5 to Arismendi-Río
Caribe), facilitating their safe transportation, orientation on institutional services, and the registration
and follow-up of cases with specific needs. Since the beginning of the operation, 275 returnees—
170 women and 105 men—have received assistance. This includes 44 girls and boys, 19
adolescents, 38 older persons, 3 persons with disabilities, and 39 people with chronic illnesses. Of
the total number of people assisted, 205 originated from La Guaira and 70 from Caracas.
 In Táchira state, the San Cristóbal Bus Terminal continues to serve as a transit and assistance point
in anticipation of population movements toward western Venezuela as a result of the earthquakes.
As of 6 July, IOM had registered 417 people at the San Cristóbal land terminal, characterized as
internally displaced by the disaster. The subnational Health Cluster is advancing mental health
coordination efforts, bringing together the public network of psychologists and psychiatrists to
provide support to affected populations and establishing a focal point for response personnel and
volunteers. These actions are coordinated through the Local Coordination Forum and the
Coordination Support Group (CSG) with the authorities, following the meeting convened by the
Comprehensive Protection System for Children and Adolescents (SPINNA) on the identification and
assistance of populations affected by the earthquake.
 In Zulia State, according to ODISEF data, between 29 June and 5 July, 140 people from the affected
areas (103 from La Guaira, 29 from Caracas, and 8 from El Junquito) received assistance at the
Maracaibo terminal. Their main destinations were Maracaibo (81), San Francisco (15), Mara (12),
and Colombia (20). Assistance is being provided by the Governor’s Office, the Venezuelan Red
Cross, UNHCR, ODISEF, and the Office of the Ombudsperson.
Humanitarian coordination
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
coordinates the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner organizations,
prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), logistics
and protection.
 The coordination of Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) operations was formally transferred to
Venezuela’s Civil Protection, which will continue coordinating both national and international teams
deployed in the affected areas. The handover process included the transfer of operational
information and training on the USAR coordination methodologies used throughout the response. At
the same time, international USAR teams have begun a gradual demobilization process; however,
several teams, particularly from Latin America, remain deployed in affected areas.
 The Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) participated in the Inter-Agency Joint Analysis
Workshop convened by OCHA to consolidate evidence generated through rapid needs assessments
and build a shared understanding of the humanitarian needs arising from the earthquakes, informing
response prioritization and planning.
 Venezuelan authorities requested the activation of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
within the framework of the United Nations system and with the support of UNDP. In line with the
internationally recognized PDNA methodology, the corresponding coordination efforts with relevant
counterparts will be advanced.
 Authorities met with national and international organizations. During the meeting, appreciation was
expressed for the international support provided to the emergency response, and a call was made
for joint action and coordination to ensure an effective, people-centered response.
 National authorities have expedited migration and administrative procedures to facilitate the entry
into the country of international search and rescue teams, United Nations personnel, media
representatives, and other specialists deployed to support emergency response operations.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 WFP assisted 2,380 people with ready-to-eat food kits at the Caraballeda Golf Course temporary
shelter and in the San José Obrero Mamo community. These kits contained bread, tortillas, fruit
purée, crackers, and water. Additionally, WFP supported 4,152 people with family food baskets in
Carlos Soublette and Catia La Mar. These baskets contain dry commodities such as maize meal,
pasta, pulses, vegetable oil, and salt, covering 75 percent of their food requirements for 30 days.
WFP also provided 5 MT of food commodities to two community kitchens located in La Guaira.
These kitchens will be providing meals to approximately 400 people affected by the earthquakes for
one month.
 WFP is working with Tinta Violeta, World Vision International, and AVSI to support the management
of three temporary dining halls, functioning as multi-service centers for hot meal distributions, health,
protection, logistics support to the humanitarian community, and assistance coordination for
displaced populations. Since the beginning of the response to the emergency, 25,014 people have
received food assistance.
Health
 The international Emergency Medical Teams (EMT) network, coordinated by PAHO in support of the
Ministry of Health, continues to deploy 11 international teams (1 Type 3 EMT, 1 Type 2 EMT, 4 fixed
Type 1 EMTs, and 5 mobile Type 1 EMTs) across La Guaira, Miranda, and the Capital District to
expand emergency medical and surgical care capacity in the affected areas.
 The Medical Information and Coordination Cell (CICOM), activated by the Ministry of Health in La
Guaira with support from PAHO, continues to coordinate the operations of deployed EMTs, as well
as the monitoring of needs and coordination with national epidemiological surveillance systems.
 The health response continues to evolve from trauma care and hospital support towards primary
health care, outpatient services, assistance in temporary accommodations, and community-based
interventions, with an increasing role played by Type 1 EMTs.
 Rapid needs assessments in health facilities continue to inform the prioritization of interventions and
the deployment of resources. At the same time, referral pathways and continuity of care mechanisms
are being strengthened for people with traumatic injuries requiring specialized and rehabilitation
services.
 Specialized teams continue to provide Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services
in prioritized temporary accommodation sites, including psychological first aid, emotional support,
and the early identification of cases requiring specialized care.
 UNFPA provided sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services in the José María Vargas, César
Nieves, and Playa Grande temporary camps, including awareness-raising activities, service
promotion, provision of contraceptive methods, and HIV and syphilis screening. In Playa Grande,
activities were implemented through the implementing partner VDTM, reaching displaced
populations through information and service promotion activities.
 IMC deployed a mobile medical unit in Catia La Mar on 1 July with the capacity to attend up to 100
patients per day and plans to expand the response through additional mobile units. IMC is also
preparing to deploy a Type 1 EMT (Emergency Medical Team), including the arrival of 21 health
professionals to strengthen health services in the affected areas in line with Ministry of Health
priorities.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 The Logistics Working Group (LWG) presented the findings of a survey on logistics gaps and needs
completed by 52 organizations. The LWG continues to facilitate common logistics services free of
charge for partners, including storage capacity in La Guaira, of which one organization has already
benefited through the use of 20 m³ of storage space.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
 A technical mission was conducted at Maiquetía International Airport to review procedures for the
reception and movement of international assistance, identifying opportunities to strengthen
coordination and facilitate a timely and efficient humanitarian response.
 During an assessment conducted in three camps in La Guaira, needs were primarily identified in
relation to electricity supply, although restoration works have already begun in some areas. Gaps in
internet connectivity were also identified at the César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande sites;
however, WFP is expected to install Starlink systems powered by solar panels at both locations the
following day. Mobile telephone services provided by private operators were confirmed to be
operational across all three camps.
Nutrition
 Sector partners continue to strengthen nutrition and infant and young child feeding interventions in
emergencies. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, the establishment of a breastfeeding space
is underway, while nutritional screening activities led by the Ministry of Health are being coordinated
alongside the training of health personnel in anthropometric assessment using MUAC tapes. In Playa
Grande, technical support was provided to Early Childhood Development in Emergencies activities.
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 IOM continues to coordinate an active protection space. At the “Polideportivo Vargas” temporary
camp, protection activities are being carried out in coordination with the Ombudsperson’s Office, the
Child and Adolescent Care Service, the Municipal Council for the Rights of Children and Adolescents
(CMDNNA), and the Child and Adolescent Protection Council of Caracas (CPNNA). Seven cases
were referred to the child protection system.
 UNFPA conducted gender-based violence (GBV) awareness-raising activities and disseminated
information on specialized services in the José María Vargas and César Nieves temporary camps,
reaching 155 people (105 women, including two adolescent girls, and 50 men). In addition, 10 people
accessed specialized services, including case management, psychosocial support, and legal
counselling. In Playa Grande, UNFPA is working with IOM and UNHCR to reorganize protection
spaces in order to strengthen service delivery for displaced populations.
 UNICEF, through child protection activities in child-friendly spaces, provided psychosocial support,
life skills promotion, and protection activities to 148 children and adolescents in the Polideportivo
Vargas, César Nieves, and Playa Grande temporary camps.
 UNHCR provided specialized protection services to 88 people in the Polideportivo Vargas, César
Nieves, and Playa Grande temporary camps, including case management, psychosocial support,
documentation counselling, and family reunification/tracing services. In addition, 82 people received
information and guidance on access to rights, documentation, child protection, and the search for
missing persons.
 In Playa Grande, 110 people obtained identity documentation through a SAIME identification
campaign, while 18 children and adolescents were referred to the relevant authorities for birth
registration procedures and legal representation.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 Improvements continue across temporary camps in La Guaira to strengthen shelter conditions and
service delivery. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, upgrades were made to registration and
general service areas, spaces were allocated for the installation of a breastfeeding area, and internal
camp organization progressed for the site hosting 455 families.
 At the César Nieves Stadium temporary camp, living conditions were strengthened through the
installation of 45 lights, one power generator, and 27 electrical outlets. In addition, the distribution of
non-food items advanced, reaching 360 families with buckets, kitchen sets, and tarpaulins.
 In Playa Grande, the installation of two large-capacity tents began to support the reorganization of
accommodation areas and camp improvements. In addition, four tents were installed for service
provision and storage, while Fundación Vivienda Popular (FVP) and UNHCR are advancing the
installation of 10 solar lamps to reinforce lighting and safety at the site.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 Access to water, sanitation and hygiene services continues to improve across temporary camps in
La Guaira. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, 1,700 people have access to 60 operational
toilets, 16 handwashing stations, and a daily supply of 20,000 litres of water, in addition to 100 solid
waste containers. Efforts are also underway to install 15 shower stations.
 At the César Nieves Stadium temporary camp, 1,253 people maintain access to 30 operational
toilets, eight handwashing stations, and hygiene kits. In addition, a water treatment plant was
installed, and 20,000 litres of water are distributed daily with the support of UNICEF, the Ministry of
Energy, and partner organizations.
 At the Playa Grande temporary camp, the displaced population has access to 18 operational portable
toilets and received 10,000 litres of water supplied through water trucks. Humanitarian organizations
also continue the distribution of hygiene kits.
Humanitarian financing
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country. Other Member States and donors have
expressed their intention to support the response through the Fund.
 The Inter-American Development Bank Group (IDB Group) announced a donation package of at
least US$1 million to support immediate humanitarian assistance, to be implemented in coordination
with Cáritas Venezuela, as well as damage and loss assessments.
 PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support health response
and early recovery activities over the next six months and released $1.5 million from the Contingency
Fund for Emergencies. WFP launched an initial appeal for US$50 million to scale up food assistance
and support emergency logistics and communications activities. UNHCR requires US$14.8 million
to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52
million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) Venezuela Earthquakes Appeal raised £7 million in 24
hours, including a £2 million contribution from the United Kingdom government through UK Aid
Match.
 Shell will provide $5 million in humanitarian aid for Venezuela through the WFP and local
humanitarian organizations.
 BBVA raised more than 1 million euros in Spain in humanitarian aid through a campaign developed
in conjunction with the Red Cross, UNHCR, and UNICEF.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:
https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis
Contact information
For more information, please contact the OCHA Venezuela Office:
Vanessa May – Head of Office a.i. – mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Humanitarian Affairs Officer – alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Public Information Officer – moreno7@un.org
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

**Reporte de situación N.º 13**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**6 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 8:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de mil réplicas.**
- Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado.
- Balance oficial: **3.535 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas**.
- **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.**
- Los equipos de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano (USAR) internacionales han iniciado progresivamente su desmovilización; no obstante, varios equipos permanecen desplegados en las zonas afectadas.
- **El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.048 réplicas.**

A más de una semana de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **3.535 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, las autoridades reportan que unas **17.854 personas quedaron sin vivienda**.

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la preparación de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta.

Reporte de situación N.º 13
Terremotos en Venezuela
6 de julio de 2026
Hora: 8:00 pm
Destacados
 Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local),
las autoridades reportan más de mil réplicas. 3.535
 Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el
estado más afectado.
fallecidas
 Balance oficial: 3.535 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.
 6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.
 Los equipos de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano (USAR) internacionales
16.740
han iniciado progresivamente su desmovilización; no obstante, varios
equipos permanecen desplegados en las zonas afectadas. personas
 El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en heridas
coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones
multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas.
Situación general
Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia
nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos
de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos
el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la
región centro-norte, con epicentro
sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare -
Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Las
autoridades reportan 1.048
réplicas.
A más de una semana de los
terremotos, las autoridades reportan
un balance de 3.535 personas
fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas
y 6.462 personas rescatadas desde
el inicio de la emergencia.
Asimismo, las autoridades reportan
que unas 17.854 personas
quedaron sin vivienda.
La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la preparación de los
campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado
más afectado. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan
acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta.
Impacto en infraestructura
 Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.
 Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de
Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil
millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas,
comercios, escuelas, hospitales e instalaciones públicas. Entre tanto, estimaciones preliminares de
PNUD indican daños físicos directos por 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 6 % del PIB.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
Respuesta nacional
 La respuesta gubernamental se mantiene centrada en las labores de búsqueda y rescate, así como
en la atención de las personas afectadas.
 Se decretaron siete (7) días de luto nacional a partir del 1 de julio.
 Se activó una comisión presidencial para la evaluación de habitabilidad de viviendas e
infraestructuras, así como un Estado Mayor para la instalación y coordinación de campamentos
transitorios.
 De acuerdo con las autoridades, la respuesta continúa con 80 campamentos transitorios para la
atención de personas afectadas, con capacidad para 17.642 personas y una ocupación de 12.806
personas (73%). Hasta el 6 de julio, 37 campamentos se encuentran instalados en Caracas, 22 en
Miranda y 21 en La Guaira.
 El Gobierno venezolano anunció la creación de un fondo inicial de reconstrucción equivalente a 200
millones de dólares.
 Las autoridades reportan la activación de un puente aéreo entre Caracas-Caraballeda (La Guaira)
para fortalecer el abastecimiento de suministros y garantizar la atención a las zonas afectadas.
 Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad
(Conapdis) para coordinar una respuesta oportuna e inclusiva en las zonas afectadas.
 Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas
(www.localizapacientes.com) y el reporte de personas afectadas (0-800-RESCATE).
 Las autoridades reanudaron las actividades administrativas en los estados no afectados y en
aquellos donde la infraestructura educativa no presenta daños visibles. Entretanto, las actividades
escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados Aragua (Santiago
Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto Cabello,
Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); Distrito Capital
(Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión, Buroz,
Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).
Situación por estado
Distrito Capital (Caracas) y Miranda
 En el municipio Chacao (estado Miranda) continúan las labores de respuesta y atención a las
personas afectadas, mientras persisten afectaciones en infraestructura crítica y servicios básicos
que inciden en las necesidades humanitarias de la población.
Acciones de respuesta: Tres (3) organizaciones del FHV con proyectos financiados en municipios del
estado y en Distrito Capital (Cedesex, Construyendo Futuros y FUNDANA) apoyan la respuesta inicial
con servicios en protección general, de la niñez y de violencia basada en género (VBG). Además,
organizaciones como Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA y World Vision se encuentran brindando apoyo en el área
de protección a familias afectadas, especialmente a nivel psicosocial.
La Guaira
 Continúan las gestiones de coordinación entre autoridades, clústeres y organizaciones humanitarias
para fortalecer la respuesta en los campamentos transitorios de La Guaira, incluyendo el
seguimiento de necesidades, la ampliación de servicios sectoriales y la mejora de las condiciones
de alojamiento, protección y atención a la población afectada.
Acciones de respuesta: Cinco (5) organizaciones socias del Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV)
apoyan la respuesta inicial con servicios de atención primaria en salud y atención psicológica (Fundación
Proyecto Maniapure, Paluz, Ven Da Tu Mano, Cruz Roja Venezolana y Tinta Violeta).
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro)
 En Carabobo, las principales afectaciones continúan concentrándose en el municipio Juan José
Mora (parroquia Morón). En Yaracuy, particularmente en el municipio Veroes y otras localidades
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
cercanas a la zona epicentral, se reportan viviendas destruidas o en condición de alto riesgo, así
como recepción de familias desplazadas provenientes de La Guaira. Evaluaciones recientes
identifican necesidades prioritarias en protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud,
alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH) y seguridad alimentaria.
Acciones de respuesta: Cinco (5) organizaciones (Cruz Roja Venezolana, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas
Morón y Empodérame) brindan respuesta en salud, alimentación, agua y distribución de ayuda
humanitaria.
Falcón (Tucacas – Municipio Silva)
 El 3 de julio, el Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC), en articulación con Acción Contra el Hambre,
Azul Positivo y autoridades regionales, realizó una jornada de atención en la comunidad de Cayumar
(Boca de Aroa), brindando apoyo psicosocial a 46 personas y distribuyendo 62 kits de higiene a las
familias más afectadas.
 Se acordó con la Gobernación la realización de una jornada casa a casa la próxima semana en los
sectores Cayumar y Barrio Verde, donde la OIM hará entrega de enseres y Azul Positivo participará
con la entrega de kits de ASH, con la posibilidad de brindar apoyo psicosocial y asesoría legal por
parte de otras organizaciones del FLC.
 OCHA y Protección Civil Falcón continúan coordinando acciones para fortalecer los procesos de
levantamiento de información sobre daños y necesidades en las comunidades afectadas. Asimismo,
avanzan los preparativos para la implementación de herramientas digitales de recolección de datos
sobre estructuras afectadas en el municipio Silva.
Acciones de respuesta: Continúan las acciones de apoyo psicosocial y evaluación de necesidades para
las personas desplazadas y afectadas en el municipio Silva. Organizaciones humanitarias mantienen el
análisis de opciones para ampliar la asistencia en alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH) y
seguridad alimentaria para las familias más afectadas.
Otros estados
 En Anzoátegui, aproximadamente 700 personas han ingresado a la entidad en procesos de
reunificación familiar. En el municipio Simón Rodríguez (El Tigre) se reporta la recepción de
alrededor de 100 personas. Se fortalecen los tres espacios de acogida y campamentos transitorios
habilitados. Continúa la movilización de asistencia, con un volumen acumulado de 365 toneladas
de insumos movilizados desde el municipio Lechería.
 En el estado Apure, el Plan de Contingencia estadal reporta 189 personas trasladadas (77 jefes de
familia censados y 112 integrantes de los grupos familiares), en su mayoría procedentes de La
Guaira (86%). Los principales municipios de destino son San Fernando (123), Muñoz (24),
Achaguas (20) y Biruaca (18). La atención brindada incluye atención médica (62 familias), alimentos
(30), documentación legal (15), enseres (14) y refugio temporal (11).
 Desde el estado Bolívar, la Gobernación informó un volumen acumulado de aproximadamente
1.600 toneladas de asistencia humanitaria despachadas desde el estado; las autoridades regionales
mantienen los mecanismos de coordinación interinstitucional con OCHA y el Grupo Asesor de
Coordinación (GAC).
 En el estado Delta Amacuro, se recibió un segundo grupo con 54 personas (39 adultos y 15 niñas,
niños y adolescentes) reubicadas desde La Guaira la noche del 4 al 5 de julio, quienes fueron
inicialmente alojadas en el Gimnasio Cubierto de Tucupita y posteriormente reunificadas con
hogares. Las autoridades y actores humanitarios evalúan necesidades prioritarias en asistencia
alimentaria, kits de higiene familiar y menstrual, apoyo psicosocial y medicamentos esenciales,
particularmente para el tratamiento sintomático de infecciones respiratorias en población infantil y
para personas con enfermedades cardiovasculares. Se activaron mecanismos de coordinación.
 En el estado Monagas, Cáritas Maturín implementa un mecanismo de atención integral para las
familias desplazadas desde La Guaira, con registro, verificación y evaluación de necesidades en
localidades como La Pica, Jusepín, el Complejo Habitacional Paramaconi y los municipios Cedeño
y Ezequiel Zamora, con énfasis en salud, protección y apoyo psicosocial. Se señala la necesidad
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
de ampliar la disponibilidad de alimentos, medicamentos, colchonetas, ropa, calzado y enseres
domésticos.
 En el estado Nueva Esparta, el municipio Maneiro mantiene activo un protocolo de recepción,
registro y atención. Se confirma el ingreso de al menos 176 personas. La estrategia prioriza el
alojamiento con redes familiares en la isla de Margarita, con distribución directa de kits de alimentos
no perecederos, higiene y ropa.
 En el estado Sucre, el Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC), en articulación con instituciones
gubernamentales y actores locales, apoyó la recepción y asistencia de 48 personas retornadas el 5
de julio (29 al municipio Sucre-Cumaná, 7 a Benítez-El Pilar, 7 a Bermúdez-Carúpano y 5 a
Arismendi-Río Caribe), facilitando su traslado seguro, la orientación sobre servicios institucionales,
así como el registro y seguimiento de casos con necesidades específicas. Desde el inicio del
operativo, 275 personas, 170 mujeres y 105 hombres, retornadas han recibido asistencia. Esto
incluye 44 niñas y niños, 19 adolescentes, 38 personas mayores, 3 personas con discapacidad y
39 personas con enfermedades crónicas. Del total de personas asistidas, 205 proceden de La
Guaira y 70 de Caracas.
 En el estado Táchira, el Terminal de San Cristóbal se mantiene como punto de tránsito y atención
ante el previsible desplazamiento de personas hacia el occidente del país como consecuencia de
los terremotos. Al 6 de julio, la OIM registró 417 personas en el terminal terrestre de San Cristóbal,
caracterizadas como desplazamiento interno por el desastre. El clúster subnacional de salud avanza
en la coordinación de salud mental, articulando la red pública de psicólogos y psiquiatras para la
atención de las personas afectadas y un punto focal para el personal de los equipos de respuesta
y voluntariado. Estas acciones se articulan a través del Foro Local de Coordinación y el Grupo de
Apoyo a la Coordinación (GAC) con las autoridades, en continuidad con la reunión convocada por
Sistema de Protección Integral de Niñas, Niños y Adolescentes (SPINNA) sobre la identificación y
atención a la población afectada por el sismo.
 En el estado Zulia, según datos de ODISEF, entre el 29 de junio y el 5 de julio, atendieron 140
personas provenientes de las zonas afectadas (103 de La Guaira, 29 de Caracas y 8 de El Junquito)
en el terminal de Maracaibo, con destinos principales en Maracaibo (81), San Francisco (15), Mara
(12) y Colombia (20). La atención es brindada por la Gobernación, Cruz Roja Venezolana, ACNUR,
ODISEF y la Defensoría del Pueblo.
Coordinación humanitaria
 OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales,
coordina la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias, priorizando
acciones en salud; alojamiento; alimentación; agua, saneamiento e higiene; logística; y protección.
 La coordinación de las operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano (USAR) fue transferida a
Protección Civil de Venezuela, que asumirá la coordinación de los equipos nacionales e
internacionales desplegados en las zonas afectadas. El proceso incluyó el traspaso de información
operativa y la capacitación sobre las metodologías de coordinación USAR utilizadas durante la
respuesta. Paralelamente, los equipos internacionales han iniciado progresivamente su
desmovilización; no obstante, varios equipos, particularmente de América Latina, permanecen
desplegados en las zonas afectadas.
 El Grupo de Coordinación Interclúster (ICCG) participó en el Taller de Análisis Conjunto
Interagencial convocado por OCHA para consolidar la evidencia generada por las evaluaciones
rápidas de necesidades y construir una comprensión común de las necesidades humanitarias
derivadas de los terremotos, orientando la priorización y planificación de la respuesta.
 Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores
al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del
PNUD. Conforme a la metodología internacionalmente de la PDNA, se avanzará en las
coordinaciones correspondientes con las contrapartes relevantes.
 Las autoridades se reunieron con organizaciones nacionales e internacionales. En este espacio, se
agradeció el apoyo internacional a la emergencia y se hizo un llamado al trabajo en conjunto y a la
coordinación para asegurar una respuesta efectiva y centrada en las personas.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
 Las autoridades nacionales han agilizado los procedimientos migratorios y administrativos para
facilitar el ingreso al país de equipos internacionales de búsqueda y rescate, personal de Naciones
Unidas, representantes de medios de comunicación y otros especialistas desplegados para apoyar
las operaciones de respuesta a la emergencia.
Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria
Seguridad Alimentaria
 El PMA asistió a 2.380 personas con kits de alimentos listos para el consumo en el albergue
temporal del Campo de Golf de Caraballeda y en la comunidad San José Obrero de Mamo. Estos
kits contenían pan, tortillas, puré de frutas, galletas saladas y agua. Además, apoyó a 4.152
personas con cestas alimentarias familiares en Carlos Soublette y Catia La Mar. Estas cestas
contienen productos secos como harina de maíz, pasta, leguminosas, aceite vegetal y sal,
cubriendo el 75 % de los requerimientos alimentarios durante 30 días. Así mismo, entregó 5
toneladas métricas de alimentos a dos comedores comunitarios ubicados en La Guaira. Estos
comedores proporcionarán comidas a aproximadamente 400 personas afectadas por los
terremotos durante un mes.
 El PMA trabaja con Tinta Violeta, World Vision International y AVSI para apoyar la gestión de tres
comedores temporales que funcionan como centros multiservicios para la distribución de comidas
calientes, servicios de salud, protección, apoyo logístico a la comunidad humanitaria y coordinación
de la asistencia para la población desplazada. Hasta la fecha, 25.014 personas han recibido
asistencia alimentaria como parte de la respuesta a la emergencia.
Agua, saneamiento e higiene
 Las condiciones de acceso a agua, saneamiento e higiene continúan fortaleciéndose en los
campamentos transitorios de La Guaira. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, 1.700 personas
cuentan con acceso a 60 baños operativos, 16 puntos de lavado de manos y un suministro diario
de 20.000 litros de agua, además de 100 contenedores para residuos sólidos. Asimismo, avanzan
las acciones para la instalación de 15 estaciones de duchas.
 En el campamento transitorio Estadio César Nieves, 1.253 personas mantienen acceso a 30 baños
operativos, ocho puntos de lavado de manos y kits de higiene. Asimismo, se instaló una planta
potabilizadora y se distribuyen diariamente 20.000 litros de agua con el apoyo de UNICEF, el
Ministerio de Energía y organizaciones socias.
 En el campamento transitorio Playa Grande, la población albergada cuenta con 18 baños portátiles
operativos y recibió abastecimiento de 10.000 litros de agua mediante camiones cisterna.
Adicionalmente, continúan las distribuciones de kits de higiene por parte de organizaciones
humanitarias.
Alojamiento, Energía y Enseres
 Continúan las mejoras en los campamentos transitorios de La Guaira para fortalecer las
condiciones de alojamiento y la prestación de servicios. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se
realizaron adecuaciones en las áreas de registro y servicios generales, se asignaron espacios para
la instalación de un área de lactancia materna y avanzó la organización interna del campamento
que alberga a 455 familias.
 En el campamento transitorio Estadio César Nieves se fortalecieron las condiciones de
habitabilidad mediante la instalación de 45 luminarias, un generador eléctrico y 27 tomacorrientes.
Asimismo, avanzó la distribución de artículos no alimentarios, alcanzando 360 familias con baldes,
juegos de cocina y lonas.
 En Playa Grande se inició la instalación de dos carpas de gran capacidad para la reorganización
de los espacios de alojamiento y la adecuación del campamento. Adicionalmente, se instalaron
cuatro carpas para servicios y almacenamiento, mientras que la Fundación Vivienda Popular (FVP)
y ACNUR avanzan en la instalación de 10 lámparas solares para reforzar la iluminación y la
seguridad del sitio.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Logística y Telecomunicaciones
 El Grupo de Trabajo de Logística (GTL) presentó los resultados de una encuesta sobre brechas y
necesidades logísticas completada por 52 organizaciones. Asimismo, continúa facilitando servicios
logísticos comunes sin costo para los socios, incluido almacenamiento en La Guaira, del cual una
organización ya se ha beneficiado mediante el uso de 20 m³ de capacidad.
 Se realizó una misión técnica al Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía para revisar los
procedimientos de recepción y movilización de asistencia internacional, identificando
oportunidades para fortalecer la coordinación y facilitar una respuesta humanitaria oportuna y
eficiente.
 Durante la evaluación realizada en tres campamentos de La Guaira, se identificaron necesidades
principalmente relacionadas con el suministro de energía eléctrica, aunque ya se han iniciado
trabajos de restauración en algunas áreas. Asimismo, se detectaron brechas en los servicios de
internet en el Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande, pero se prevé que PMA instale
sistemas Starlink con paneles solares en ambas locaciones al día siguiente. Finalmente, se
constató la operatividad de los servicios de telefonía móvil de los proveedores privados en los tres
campamentos.
Nutrición
 Los socios del sector continúan fortaleciendo las acciones de nutrición y alimentación infantil en
emergencias. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas avanza la habilitación de un espacio de
lactancia materna y se coordinan actividades de tamizaje nutricional lideradas por el Ministerio de
Salud, junto con la capacitación del personal sanitario en diagnóstico antropométrico mediante el
uso de cinta MUAC. En Playa Grande se brindó acompañamiento técnico a actividades de Cuidado
para el Desarrollo Infantil en Emergencias.
Protección (incluidos Áreas de Responsabilidad de niños, niñas y adolescentes y violencia
basada en género)
 OIM mantiene la coordinación de espacio de protección activo. En el campamento transitorio
“Polideportivo Vargas”, se trabaja con la Defensoría del Pueblo, el Servicio de Atención al Niñas,
Niños y Adolescentes (NNA), el Consejo Municipal de Derechos de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes
(CMDNNA), Consejo de Protección de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes de Caracas (CPNNA). Se
realizó la remisión de 7 casos al sistema de protección del NNA.
 UNFPA realizó actividades de sensibilización sobre violencia basada en género (VBG) y difusión de
servicios especializados en los campamentos transitorios José María Vargas y César Nieves,
alcanzando a 155 personas (105 mujeres, incluidas dos adolescentes, y 50 hombres). Asimismo,
10 personas accedieron a servicios especializados, incluidos gestión de casos, apoyo psicosocial y
orientación legal. En Playa Grande, UNFPA trabaja junto con OIM y ACNUR en la reorganización
de los espacios de protección para fortalecer la prestación de servicios a la población desplazada.
 UNICEF, a través de actividades de protección infantil en espacios amigables, brindó apoyo
psicosocial, promoción de habilidades para la vida y actividades de protección a 148 niños, niñas y
adolescentes en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, César Nieves y Playa Grande.
 ACNUR proporcionó servicios especializados de protección a 88 personas en los campamentos
transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, César Nieves y Playa Grande, incluyendo gestión de casos, apoyo
psicosocial, orientación en documentación y reunificación/localización familiar. Además, 82
personas recibieron información y orientación sobre acceso a derechos, documentación, protección
infantil y búsqueda de personas desaparecidas.
 En Playa Grande, 110 personas accedieron a documentación de identidad mediante el operativo de
cedulación del SAIME, mientras que 18 niños, niñas y adolescentes fueron remitidos a las
autoridades competentes para trámites de registro de nacimiento y representación legal.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
Salud
 La red internacional de Equipos Médicos de Emergencia (EMT), coordinada por la OPS en apoyo
al Ministerio de Salud, mantiene desplegados 11 equipos internacionales (1 EMT Tipo 3, 1 EMT
Tipo 2, 4 EMT Tipo 1 fijos y 5 EMT Tipo 1 móviles) en La Guaira, Miranda y el Distrito Capital para
ampliar la capacidad de atención médica y quirúrgica de emergencia en las zonas afectadas.
 La Célula de Información y Coordinación Médica (CICOM), activada por el Ministerio de Salud en
La Guaira con apoyo de la OPS, continúa coordinando las operaciones de los EMT desplegados,
así como el monitoreo de necesidades y la articulación con los sistemas nacionales de vigilancia
epidemiológica.
 La respuesta sanitaria continúa evolucionando desde la atención de trauma y el apoyo a hospitales
hacia la atención primaria de salud, los servicios ambulatorios, la atención en alojamientos
temporales y las intervenciones comunitarias, con un papel creciente de los EMT Tipo 1.
 Las evaluaciones rápidas de necesidades en establecimientos de salud continúan orientando la
priorización de intervenciones y el despliegue de recursos. Asimismo, se fortalecen los
mecanismos de referencia y continuidad de la atención para personas con lesiones traumáticas
que requieren servicios especializados y de rehabilitación.
 Equipos especializados continúan brindando servicios de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial
(SMAPS) en alojamientos temporales priorizados, incluyendo primeros auxilios psicológicos, apoyo

 UNFPA brindó servicios de salud sexual y reproductiva (SSR) en los campamentos transitorios

desplazada mediante acciones de información y promoción de servicios.
 IMC desplegó una unidad médica móvil desde el 1 de julio en Catia La Mar con capacidad para

de acuerdo a las prioridades del Ministerio de Salud.

terremotos en Venezuela (https://ven-eq.connectingbusiness.org) y una nota informativa dirigida al
sector privado sobre oportunidades de apoyo. Punto focal: sanchez21@un.org.
 El Fondo Central de Respuesta a Emergencias (CERF, por sus siglas en inglés) realizó una
asignación de 15 millones de dólares para una respuesta multisectorial, junto con la activación del
Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV). Noruega realizó una contribución para apoyar la respuesta
a través del CERF.
 Estados Unidos anunció una contribución de 100 millones de dólares al FHV, y una asignación
adicional de 100 millones de dólares en contribuciones bilaterales para operaciones de respuesta

Proyecto Esperanza y la Cruz Roja.
 Alemania y Corea realizaron contribuciones al FHV por 5 millones y 1,25 millones de dólares,

millones de dólares para ampliar la asistencia alimentaria y apoyar actividades logísticas y de

documents.title: Venezuela - Food Security Outlook (June 2026 - January 2027): Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes emerge following high-magnitude earthquakes
documents.body_text:
## Key Messages

- **Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected in La Guaira, Distrito Capital (Caracas), Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua** following back-to-back earthquakes of [**7.2**](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us6000t7zc/pager) and [**7.5**](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us6000t7zp/pager) magnitude on June 24. Although post-disaster assessments are still ongoing, direct physical damage is expected to be billions of USD, while overall economic losses are likely to be higher. Among worst-affected poor households, disrupted livelihoods, asset and income losses, the deaths of working family members, and increased medical expenses amid sustained high inflation are driving food consumption gaps and the use of negative coping strategies. **Across the rest of Venezuela, Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected with pockets of households in Crisis (IPC Phase 3),** as extremely low purchasing power continues amid persistent local currency volatility and high general and food inflation rates.
- **In the immediate aftermath of the earthquakes, FEWS NET estimates that between 3.0-3.49 million people are in need of humanitarian food assistance.** The population in need is expected to gradually decline through January 2027 as the clearing of rubble and debris, rebuilding, and restoration of basic services – alongside improving macroeconomic conditions – support the recovery of household livelihoods.
- **Macroeconomic conditions are likely to improve progressively, even though inflation will remain high.** Government revenues are expected to increase due to higher oil production and exports and competitive international prices, supporting continued intervention to contain local currency depreciation and sustain social safety net benefits. Monthly inflation is expected to remain below 15 percent, while annual inflation is anticipated to remain close to 550 percent, similar to 2025 levels. In addition, the gap between the official and parallel exchange rate is expected to remain near 45 percent, eroding the real value of social safety net bonuses and household purchasing power even as the value of most benefits are expected to increase according to indexation. The government has announced an emergency response bonus, but details are limited.

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
Food security context
Venezuela has been experiencing a macroeconomic crisis for over a decade, characterized by the accelerated
loss of purchasing power due to local currency depreciation, high inflation rates, and productive and
industrial capacity decline. Macroeconomic deterioration is strongly influenced by the country’s dependence on oil
revenues: oil accounts for almost all export earnings and serves as the government´s primary revenue source,
determining the government´s capacity to stabilize the exchange rate and finance public spending, including a robust
social safety net. In this context, the volatility of the local currency drove the progressive, informal dollarization of the
economy as a strategy to preserve purchasing power and facilitate commercial transactions. However, amid a
substantial reduction in both income-generating activities and purchasing power, the economic crisis resulted in a
significant flow of millions of Venezuelan migrants to other countries, mainly in South America.
Between 2021 and 2024, the country experienced gradual economic stabilization, supported by the partial recovery
of productive agricultural infrastructure as well as oil exports, with the granting of a restricted license to Chevron to
operate joint ventures in oil production with Venezuela’s state-owned oil and gas company, Petróleos de Venezuela,
S.A. (PDVSA), in 2022. During this period, monthly and annual inflation rates slowed considerably and remained
below 5 and 100 percent, respectively. However, renewed deterioration occurred in 2025, particularly
during Q4. Inflation increased again, spiking to over 600 percent year-on-year, driven by the depreciation of the local
currency, reduced foreign currency supply, and sociopolitical tensions. In early 2026, an easing of international
sanctions began supporting increased government revenues, allowing for more regular government intervention in
the foreign exchange market and gradually reducing macroeconomic volatility.
Nearly 90 percent of the population lives in urban areas (Figure Figure 1
1), and most households rely on multiple income
Population density, 2024
streams (wages, remittances, and social safety net programs),
including from multiple jobs, to cope with inflationary
pressures. Most formal or informal private
sector employees receive salaries in a combination of VED and USD,
while the public sector pays in VED, creating disparities between
private and public incomes. Venezuela utilizes multiple exchange
rates, with an official rate set by the Central Bank of Venezuela
(BCV), a parallel market rate established through informal
transactions, and, more recently, a third rate set by BCV between
the official and parallel rates used in the mechanism for introducing
USD into the wider economy. The official exchange rate serves as a
reference for taxes, salaries, and official transactions, while most
households and businesses rely on the parallel exchange
rate. Households receiving salaries in VED are therefore more
vulnerable to experiencing losses in their purchasing power due to Source: FEWS NET visualization based on
LANDSCAN data
VED fluctuations and the conversion to USD at parallel market
rates for daily transactions. Informal economic activities, such as
informal wage labor, self-employment and petty trade, are an important income source for very poor households in
urban areas, while agricultural activities support incomes in rural areas. However, incomes in the informal sector
remain irregular and are more frequently paid in VED. Remittances also support receiving households, although their
amount and frequency vary considerably. Nearly 60 percent of the population earned less than the equivalent of
100 USD per month in 2025, with poor households earning far less. Between May 2025 and May 2026, the VED has
lost over 450 percent its value. Although incomes have risen in response to inflationary pressures across the private
formal and informal sectors, they have not kept pace with actual inflation rates.
The social safety net system in Venezuela constitutes a key source of income, assisting in covering food
needs, with a variety of government-paid incomes, such as the Ingreso Contra la Guerra Económica (ICGE), (monthly
payments indexed in USD at the official exchange rate and paid in VED), subsidized food
boxes called Comités Locales de Abastecimiento y Producción (CLAP), and the Cestaticket (an electronic food
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 2

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
voucher). Public workers and pensioners, who receive their income in VED, are the main beneficiaries of most
bonuses; however, a significant percentage of the population has historically received the Cestaticket, ICGE, and/or
CLAP deliveries. For private sector workers and those employed in the informal sector, there is a wide range of
smaller cash transfers available, and reports indicate that overall coverage from these benefits is high; however, the
total value of cash transfers that a poor household receives can vary greatly; households must subscribe to receive
each type and may not be aware of, or able to apply to, all for which they are eligible. As benefits are indexed in USD
at the official exchange rate but paid in VED, the parallel market value of the benefits fluctuates, with recipients losing
purchasing power when the gap between the two rates widens.
Due to macroeconomic conditions, the prices of staple products in VED often vary significantly over short
periods. A staple diet for most households includes rice, flour, bread, pasta, oil or margarine, and substitutes such as
plantain, pumpkin, and cassava, while chicken and eggs are the main sources of animal protein. However,
households adjust their purchasing preferences depending on prices and seasonal availability.
National production is supported by irrigation systems and is organized into two annual harvest cycles:
summer (February-May) and winter (August-November). Key crops include maize, rice, beans, cassava,
plantain, and vegetables. Since 2021, agricultural production has stabilized, although it remains below levels
reported prior to the macroeconomic crisis (reference year 2013). Despite improvements, Venezuela requires cereal
imports to meet domestic food needs; imports typically account for 60 percent of the domestic supply. Food
availability has improved since the peak of the macroeconomic crisis, and markets are typically supplied with both
national and imported products.
Learn more
Follow these links for additional information:
Latest Venezuela Food Security Outlook: February to September 2026
Latest Food Security Outlook Update for Venezuela: April to September 2026
Latest Venezuela Key Message Update: May 2026
Overview of FEWS NET’s scenario development methodology
FEWS NET’s approach to estimating the population in need
Overview of the IPC and IPC-compatible analysis
FEWS NET’s approach to humanitarian food assistance analysis
Current anomalies in food security conditions as of June 2026
On June 24, back-to-back earthquakes of 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude struck north-central Venezuela,
affecting more than 3.9 million people and prompting a state of emergency. Although the epicenters were
in Yaracuy and Carabobo states, the earthquake moved east along fault lines, according to the U.S. Geological
Survey (USGS), significantly affecting La Guaira, Distrito Capital (Caracas), and Aragua, while Miranda, Falcón,
Lara, and Guárico were also negatively impacted (Figure 2). Over 600 aftershocks have since been registered,
hampering rescue efforts and initial damage assessments. As of June 29, more than 15,800 people had been
displaced, 1,700 killed, and 5,000 injured, but figures are expected to rise. Multiple temporary sites have been
set up in La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda and many households are sheltering in open spaces, parks, and
plazas due to loss of homes or concern about staying in homes with potential structural damage. Infrastructure
damage, including collapsed buildings, damaged roads, and disruptions to basic services is widespread in
affected areas, with thousands of buildings reportedly damaged, particularly in La Guaira. Preliminary
assessments suggest direct physical damage to be between 4.7 and 8.7 billion USD.
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 3

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
Foreign currency inflows continued to improve in May with Figure 2
an estimated 1.35 billion USD injected into the Venezuelan
Earthquake impact areas, June 24, 2026
economy by BCV. Crude oil exports rose slightly to 1.25
million bpd in May, reflecting a sustained upward trend with
three consecutive months of export increases supported by
increased external demand and competitive international
prices. According to OPEC, crude oil production remained
above 1 million bpd in May, for a second consecutive month,
reflecting gradual improvements in production despite
ongoing structural constraints including limited access to key
inputs and deteriorated infrastructure. Between June 1 and 22,
WTI and Brent international oil prices decreased, averaging
89.97 and 90.31 USD/barrel, respectively.
Exchange rate dynamics and BCV interventions are
reducing macroeconomic volatility. In May 2026, the official
and parallel exchange rates both increased by approximately 8
percent compared to April, reaching 519.15 VED/USD and
702.01 VED/USD, respectively. The gap between rates
remained similar to April, at nearly 36 percent. However,
higher government spending, especially on social safety net
bonus payments, puts more pressure on the national
currency, causing depreciation despite higher foreign currency
inflows. The recently introduced BCV intervention rate – a third
exchange rate set between the official and parallel rates – has remained stable, increasing slightly to 615.52
VED/USD in June, reflecting ongoing BCV efforts to contain volatility. While macroeconomic improvements are
visible, partners report reduced availability of USD in cash for everyday transactions, with most conducted using
digital channels, as banks and other businesses are reinvesting their hard currency.
Inflation rates show gradual, relative improvement. Monthly inflation declined from 10.6 to 6.3 percent,
between April and May 2026, the lowest in 19 months. Annual inflation also decreased, falling from 611.9
percent to 524.5 percent. Similarly, monthly food inflation decreased to 6.3 percent from 11.5 percent, while the
annual food inflation rate dropped to 564.2 percent, decreasing from 671.8 percent registered in April.
However, price increases in VED for key staples remain higher than overall food inflation and price increases
have also been registered in USD for the second consecutive month. Food prices continue to rise due to
speculation, high import costs, and stronger domestic demand associated with improved economic conditions,
the resumption of industrial processing activities for local consumption (such as cassava flour), and the export
of certain processed foods.
The government has announced the Bono de Contingencia 2026 for earthquake-affected households ,
with amounts ranging from approximately 149 to 747 USD at the official exchange rate, equivalent to an
estimated 110.17 to 552.35 USD at the parallel exchange rate; however, details on targeting, coverage, timing,
and duration are not publicly available. Regular bonuses have also seen minor changes in June: the ICGE has
been renamed as Ingreso Integral de los Trabajadores (IIT) and remained indexed at 200 USD, but is now split
into two monthly payments, while the newly renamed Minimum Integrated Income (IMI) (which includes both
the IIT and the CestaTicket) remained indexed at 240 USD but is currently worth approximately 177.46 USD at
the parallel exchange rate. Meanwhile, the monthly “Responsibility and Training” bonus for Ministry of
Education staff increased by nearly 13 percent compared to May. In-kind CLAP distributions remain limited,
with recent reports indicating they were free but with substantially reduced coverage, and only available for
elderly citizens in Caracas and Aragua.
In June, rainfall distribution remained erratic. Soil moisture deficits have expanded in northwestern
Venezuela, where below-average rainfall and above-normal temperatures have been observed since the
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 4

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
onset of the rainy season. In Eastern Venezuela, precipitation has declined during June, partially offsetting early
improvements. These combined effects have contributed to a decline in overall vegetation health; however,
partners in the field reported favorable conditions throughout planting and early crop development – largely
due to irrigation access – with a slightly delayed start of maize and rice planting for small producers in Los
Llanos.
Humanitarian food assistance
Following the June 24 earthquakes, humanitarian food assistance is in the early stages of delivery to affected areas.
General License No. 60 allows for transactions related to earthquake relief efforts, and the UN’s Central Emergency
Response Fund has allocated 15 million USD to the response, while multiple countries have offered bilateral
assistance, likely to be channeled through the newly activated Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). WFP reportedly
has approximately 3,000 MT of food already in country and is expected to target beneficiaries in La Guaira, Distrito
Capital, Carabobo, Falcón, Yaracuy, Aragua, and Miranda. OCHA reported over 22,000 food parcels have been
distributed so far. However, detailed information on food assistance deliveries is not yet publicly available.
Throughout the rest of Venezuela, food assistance remains limited in scale and distribution. As of May 2026, WFP
reached approximately 5,086 people in selected communities of Carabobo, Delta Amacuro, and Bolivar with general
food distributions, according to the Food Security Cluster. This assistance remains insufficient relative to the scale
of need to mitigate outcomes at the area-level.
Current acute food insecurity outcomes as of June 2026
Following the June 24 earthquakes, acute food insecurity
outcomes have worsened quickly in north-central
Venezuela. Since the earthquakes occurred in the final week of the
month, affected areas are still assessed as Stressed (IPC Phase 2) for
the month of June overall, as a majority of the population in north-
central areas could still meet their minimum food needs, though only
maginally, until the earthquakes hit. However, many poor households
are likely already facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes in the aftermath
of the earthquakes in La Guaira, Distrito Capital (Caracas), Yaracuy,
Carabobo, and Aragua. Especially those who have been displaced, lost
assets, cannot work, face new medical costs, or have limited access to
government support, remittances, or USD income. Although damage
assessments are ongoing, poor households in densely populated
areas hit with the most destructive seismic activity are experiencing a
substantial shock including asset losses, building collapse, widespread
livelihood disruptions, and reduced incomes as typical informal labor
opportunities decline. Middle and better-off households and small
and medium businesses are focused on emergency concerns and
recovery. Income shortfalls are expected to be felt most acutely by
households who have lost working family members. However,
livelihoods tied to oil production and refinery have not been
negatively impacted, as these facilities reported no damage. Non-
food expenditures have also increased in the immediate aftermath of
the earthquakes as poor households cope with medical emergencies
and assess the damage to houses and other assets.
Prior to the earthquakes, most poor households were experiencing Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes, with just
enough resources to secure a minimum, poor-quality diet; these new shocks are likely resulting in food consumption
gaps or the use of negative coping strategies across many poor households. Partners in the field report that the
situation in rural areas is not as severe as in the main cities; however, livelihood disruptions remain widespread,
especially for those relying on informal economic activity. Reports indicate that some supermarkets in Caracas have
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 5

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
already resumed normal activity and many smaller markets remain well-supplied with domestic production and
imports. While the Bono de Contingencia 2026 is likely to improve access to food for recipients, details on exact
amounts, targeting, and duration are insufficient to adequately assess its impact. Households with limited to no
access to the Bono de Contingencia 2026, other benefits, or income in USD are of greatest concern. Outside of the
worst-affected states, additional poor households whose livelihoods and assets have been negatively impacted by
the earthquakes are also likely experiencing Crisis (IPC Phase 3), especially in urban and peri-urban areas such as Los
Teques in Miranda, Coro in Falcón, Barquisimeto in Lara, and San Juan de Los Morros in Guárico.
Across the rest of the country, Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes persist, driven by poor macroeconomic
conditions, particularly currency instability and high inflation, limiting households’ ability to meet their essential non-
food needs without the use of coping strategies. Extremely high prices in VED, tied to ongoing depreciation, strong
demand linked to improved economic conditions, speculation and resumption of industrial activities to produce
processed food, as well as more recent price increases in USD, continue to limit access to food, particularly for
households whose sources of income are in local currency. A portion of poor households in densely populated areas,
especially those with irregular sources of income from informal economic activities (where approximately half of
wages are paid in local currency), and little to no access to social safety net programs or remittances are likely facing
Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes, as their wages cannot keep pace with persistently high food prices.
In rural, sparsely populated areas, households are partially offsetting food access constraints through own
production (of both staples and substitutes), fishing, hunting, and wild foods gathering. However, recent rainfall and
temperature anomalies and soil moisture conditions caused delays to the start of season for small farmers without
access to irrigation. Medium and large producers have already started planting for maize, rice, and vegetables in the
major states’ producers: Portuguesa, Guárico, Cojedes and Barinas, resulting in average income for most poor rural
households in these areas. The country’s second largest petrochemical complex, which shut down briefly due to
damage from the earthquakes, has already restarted typical operations, limiting disruption to the agriculture sector.
Nonetheless, pockets of households are likely experiencing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes, especially in remote,
sparsely populated areas where limited access to income in USD and constraints on online banking services restrict
incomes and access to social safety net programs.
Key assumptions about atypical food security conditions underpinning the most likely scenario through
January 2027
Post-earthquake assessments are still ongoing, but negative impacts to livelihoods, housing and other
assets, and reduced coping capacity are expected to persist in north-central Venezuela, particularly in
high-density populated areas of La Guaira, Distrito Capital (Caracas), Yaracuy, Carabobo and Aragua,
through January 2027. Income-generating opportunities in affected areas, especially in the informal sector, are
expected to remain below average amid the extensive damage. Physical and economic recovery is likely to be
gradual, and some households will likely remain displaced. However, remittances are likely to increase to above-
average levels in the immediate aftermath.
Extractive economies and associated government revenues are expected to progressively
increase. Crude oil production is anticipated to remain above 1 million bpd, reaching as high as 1.35 million
bpd by the end of the year, while export volumes are likely to continue increasing and remain above
average. Brent crude and WTI oil prices – which serve as benchmarks for Venezuelan prices - are anticipated to
moderate, declining to 85 and 80 USD/barrel, respectively, by January 2027 (Figure 3). Merey prices, specific to
heavy Venezuelan crude, are not publicly available, but key informants indicate prices are likely to average 80
USD/barrel through 2026. Higher export volumes combined with competitive international oil prices, are
expected to continue increasing government revenues to close to 30 billion USD, according to a local source,
almost double from 2024 (17.5 billion USD) and 2025 (18.2 billion USD), strengthening government intervention
capacity in foreign exchange markets and sustaining public spending on social safety net programs. Formal and
informal income-earning opportunities linked to oil-related activities are expected to increase gradually,
particularly in production areas. Gold exports are also projected to see moderate growth, supported by new
international agreements with Mercuria and Heeney capital, easing international restrictions on gold trade,
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 6

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
and new security conditions in mining areas, though production will remain constrained by aging extraction
infrastructure.
Currency volatility and inflation are expected to ease Figure 3
compared to 2025. Depreciation is likely to slow, supported

expected to remain at historically high levels against the
USD, with the official exchange rate between 650 and 1280
VED/USD and the parallel exchange rate between 850 and
1840 VED/USD. The gap between the two rates is expected to
remain below 45 percent. Monthly inflation is likely to remain
