percent, driven by improved purchasing power and
competitive wheat product prices leading to higher demand
from the milling industry, as the government continues to restrict imported wheat flour and finished products
to encourage domestic milling.
Despite adequate supply, food prices in VED, and to a lesser extent in USD, are projected to remain
above average, driven by continued currency depreciation, strong demand tied to a perception of improved
economic conditions, limited USD availability, and speculation.
Social safety net programs are expected to continue playing a central role in supporting household
income, with government expenditure likely to increase post-disaster and in line with improved oil
revenues. CLAP distributions are likely to remain limited and existing cash transfer programs are likely to
remain in place and continue to be revised upwards according to their indexation to USD; however, their real
value will remain affected by exchange rate differences.
In urban areas with relatively little to no impact from the recent earthquakes, labor demand and
income are likely to be above average among poor households, driven by continued expansion of informal
economic activities such as petty trade, street vendors, and daily service labor as macroeconomic conditions
gradually improve. Income is expected to remain slightly above average and paid in USD or a combination of
VED and USD. In border regions, cross-border trade is expected to continue at typical levels, primarily
conducted in COP and less frequently in USD. In oil-producing areas, particularly in Maracaibo, Zulia, and gold-
producing areas, such as Bolívar, both formal and informal economic activities are expected to improve.
Anticipated below-average erratic rainfall and above-average temperatures are likely to reduce soil
moisture and increase the risk of pests and diseases, as well as reduce water levels in the Simón Bolívar
Hydroelectric Plant, increasing the risk of disrupted electricity generation. Smallholder farmers, particularly
those with limited access to inputs and irrigation, are likely to see below-average yields in some areas. Poultry
are vulnerable to heat stress, and small livestock owners anticipate increased disease and illness among their
flocks. In line with historical El Niño conditions, the Atlantic hurricane season is expected to be below average.
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 7

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
Humanitarian food assistance
Information for planned, funded, and likely humanitarian food assistance is not currently available; however,
deliveries are likely to increase compared to 2025 levels throughout the projection period in response to the
June 24 earthquake emergency. However, as of June 30, uncertainty about the mechanism, coverage, and
duration of assistance persists.
Projected acute food insecurity outcomes through January 2027
Between June and September, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected in La Guaira, Distrito Capital
(Caracas), Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as substantial disruptions to livelihoods, asset losses, and reductions in
labor demand and income from the June 24 earthquakes continue to constrain coping capacity and financial access
to food. Elevated numbers of households facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) are also likely in Falcón, Lara, Miranda, and
Guárico, although the impacts of the earthquakes are relatively fewer, maintaining area-level Stressed (IPC Phase 2)
outcomes. Households that have lost working members of the household and most or all physical assets, who rely on
informal work, and do not receive social safety net benefits or any international remittances are likely to be worst
affected. Markets are likely to remain functioning and supplied with a combination of formal and informal imports
and domestic production, with localized market disruptions expected to dissipate. However, the continuation of poor
macroeconomic conditions, even as inflation rates moderate, are likely to sustain extremely high food prices in VED.
With limited opportunities to earn in the more stable USD, purchasing power is expected to remain extremely low,
and small to moderate food consumption gaps are likely to persist among poor households. In addition, a portion of
poor households are expected to engage in additional, unsustainable coping strategies, such as reducing spending
on health and other non-food essentials.
From October 2026 to January 2027, the number of households in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) in earthquake-affected
areas is expected to decline as livelihoods gradually recover, basic services are restored, and seasonal
income improves from end-of-year double salaries and bonuses and increased economic activity and
remittances around the Christmas holidays. Although these improvements are likely to result in Stressed (IPC
Phase 2) outcomes at the state level, elevated numbers of households in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) are expected to persist
through the end of the outlook period as labor demand remains below average and households continue to rebuild
assets and adjust livelihoods. Those with substantial asset or family losses, and who receive little to no social safety
net benefits or income in USD, remain of highest concern.
Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected throughout the rest of the country through January, driven by
persistently high food prices, volatile local currency, and continued erosion of purchasing
power. Macroeconomic conditions are likely to remain poor, but show relative stabilization supported by
improvements in oil production and exports and increasing foreign currency inflows. Although monthly and annual
inflation are likely to remain below 15 and 550 percent, respectively, the gap between official and parallel exchange
rates is expected to be close to 45 percent, eroding the value of benefits and food prices are expected to remain high
in local currency and to a lesser extent in USD, weakening purchasing power. Income earned in VED or indexed at the
official exchange rate is expected to continue losing value, albeit at a slower pace than in 2025. As a result, most poor
households will rely on multiple income sources and a variety of sustainable coping strategies to maintain food
consumption, such as reducing dietary quality, purchasing on credit or borrowing, and reducing non-essential
expenditures. A portion of households with little to no access to international remittances, income in USD, or social
safety net programs is still expected to be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) as food prices remain out of reach to households
earning only in VED. Nonetheless, progressive macroeconomic recovery and seasonal improvements tied to end-of-
the year bonuses and double salaries and increased remittances and economic activity around the Christmas holiday
are expected to reduce the number of households experiencing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes between October and
January. While in sparsely populated rural areas, households are likely to engage in sustainable coping strategies,
increasing reliance on market purchases during the lean season and supplementing with fishing, hunting, gathering,
and own production. Above-average temperatures and below-average rainfall are not expected to have substantial
impacts on national food production and market supply, and labor demand for key crops such as coffee, sugarcane,
maize, and rice is expected to remain near average. Food stocks for small producers are likely to last through at least
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 8

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
July, despite recent yield reductions and atypically low income from crop sales for those producers with limited to no
access to irrigation. From August, worst-affected small producers are likely to increase their dependence on market
purchase and coping strategies such as purchasing food on credit, consuming less preferred foods, and spending
savings and, from October, national seasonal trends are expected to also improve household food access in rural
areas.

Annex 2: FEWS NET’s analytical approach explained
Early warning of acute food insecurity outcomes requires forecasting months in advance to provide decision makers
with sufficient time to budget, plan, and respond to expected humanitarian crises. However, due to the complex and
variable factors that influence acute food insecurity, definitive predictions are impossible. Scenario Development is
a methodology that allows FEWS NET to meet decision makers’ needs by developing a “most likely” scenario of the
future.
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 9

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
FEWS NET’s scenario development process applies the Disaster Risk Reduction framework and a livelihoods-based
lens to assess acute food insecurity outcomes. A household’s risk of acute food insecurity depends not only on
hazards (such as drought) but also the household’s vulnerability to these hazards (e.g., the level of dependence on
rainfed crop production for food and income) and coping capacity (which considers both the household’s ability to
cope with a given hazard and the use of negative coping strategies that harm future capacity). To evaluate these
factors, FEWS NET bases this analysis on a strong foundational understanding of local livelihoods. FEWS NET’s
scenario development process also accounts for the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework; the Four Dimensions of
Food Security; and UNICEF’s Nutrition Conceptual Framework, and is closely aligned with the Integrated Food
Security Phase Classification (IPC) analytical framework.
How does FEWS NET analyze current acute food insecurity outcomes? FEWS NET assesses the extent to
which households can meet their minimum caloric needs. This analysis converges evidence of current food
security conditions with available direct evidence of household-level food consumption and livelihood change.
FEWS NET also considers available area-level evidence of nutritional status and mortality, focusing on whether
these reflect the physiological impacts of acute food insecurity. FEWS NET uses the globally recognized five-
phase Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) scale to classify current acute food insecurity
outcomes, and the analysis is IPC-compatible. In addition, FEWS NET applies the “!” symbol to designate areas
where the mapped IPC Phase would likely be at least one IPC Phase worse without the effects of ongoing
humanitarian food assistance.
How does FEWS NET develop key assumptions underpinning the most likely scenario? A key step in FEWS
NET’s scenario development process is the development of evidence-based assumptions about factors that
affect food security. These include hazards and anomalies in food security conditions that will impact the
evolution of household food and income during the projection period, as well as factors that may affect
nutritional status. FEWS NET also develops assumptions about factors expected to behave normally. Together,
these assumptions form the foundation of the “most likely” scenario.
How does FEWS NET analyze projected acute food insecurity outcomes? Using the key assumptions that
underpin the “most likely” scenario, FEWS NET projects acute food insecurity outcomes by assessing the
evolution of households’ ability to meet their minimum caloric needs over time. FEWS NET converges
expectations of the likely trajectory of household-level food consumption and livelihood change with area-level
nutritional status and mortality. FEWS NET then classifies acute food insecurity outcomes using the IPC scale.
Lastly, FEWS NET applies the “!” symbol to designate any areas where the mapped IPC Phase would likely be at
least one IPC Phase worse without the effects of planned – and likely to be funded and delivered – food
assistance.
How does FEWS NET analyze humanitarian food assistance? Humanitarian food assistance – defined as
emergency food assistance (in-kind, cash, or voucher) – may play a key role in mitigating the severity of acute
food insecurity outcomes. FEWS NET analysts always incorporate available information on food assistance, with
the caveat that such information can vary significantly across geographies and over time. In line with IPC
protocols, FEWS NET uses the best available information to assess where food assistance is “significant” (defined
by at least 25 percent of households in a given area receiving at least 25 percent of their caloric requirements
through food assistance). In addition, FEWS NET conducts deeper analysis of the likely impacts of food
assistance on the severity of outcomes, as detailed in FEWS NET’s guidance on Integrating Humanitarian Food
Assistance into Scenario Development.
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 10

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
Annex 3: Seasonal calendar
Seasonal calendar
Annex 4: Events that would likely change projected acute food insecurity outcomes
While FEWS NET’s projections are considered the “most likely” scenario, there is always a degree of uncertainty in the
assumptions that underpin the scenario. This means food security conditions and their impacts on acute food security may
evolve differently than projected. FEWS NET issues monthly updates to its projections, but decision makers need advance
information about this uncertainty and an explanation of why things may turn out differently than projected. As such, the
final step in FEWS NET’s scenario development process is to briefly identify key events that would result in a credible
alternative scenario and significantly change the projected outcomes. FEWS NET only considers scenarios that have a
reasonable chance of occurrence.
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 11

Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027
Earthquake affected states, including La Guaira, Distrito Capital (Caracas), Yaracuy, and Carabobo
Substantial delivery of humanitarian food assistance through Sistema la Patria bonuses or international
organizations
Likely impact on acute food insecurity outcomes: Available information on emergency relief in the wake of the
June 24 earthquakes does not currently indicate that food security outcomes are yet being mitigated. However,
should support be scaled up or extended, with sufficient details available for analysis, it is likely that some or most
households facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) would be able to access minimum kilocalorie needs to support improvement to
Stressed! (IPC Phase 2!).
Recommended citation: FEWS NET. Venezuela Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027: Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes
emerge following high-magnitude earthquakes, 2026.
* FEWS NET classification is IPC-compatible with limited exceptions. IPC-compatible analysis follows key IPC protocols but does not necessarily reflect the consensus of national food security
partners. As of IPC 3.0, the IPC no longer assesses the impact of food assistance on classification and thus no longer maps the (!). However, FEWS NET continues to produce food security
maps inclusive of the (!) as well as maps compatible with IPC 3.0/3.1, which include the mapping of food security assistance bags. In rare cases, FEWS NET classification is IPC-aligned but
not IPC-compatible. IPC-aligned analysis is evidence-based but some types of evidence required for IPC-compatibility were not available.
Food Security Outlook
To project food security outcomes, FEWS NET develops a set of assumptions about likely events, their effects, and the probable responses of various actors. FEWS NET analyzes these
assumptions in the context of current conditions and local livelihoods to arrive at a most likely scenario for the coming eight months. Learn more here.
Famine Early Warning Systems Network 12

documents.title: Terremotos en Venezuela: la IFRC envía un hospital de campaña de emergencia y colabora con la Cruz Roja Venezolana en la distribución de kits de ayuda humanitaria
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas / Ciudad de Panamá / Ginebra 06 de julio de 2026** – La Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC) continúa escalando su respuesta a los recientes terremotos en Venezuela y apoyando a la Cruz Roja Venezolana en la entrega de ayuda humanitaria a las personas afectadas por esta catástrofe sin precedentes.

La IFRC envió un hospital de campaña de emergencia a La Guaira durante el fin de semana (5 de julio), en colaboración con la Cruz Roja Española, que también aportó personal médico y sanitario. El hospital de campaña de emergencia puede prestar atención primaria en salud a 30.000 personas y estará plenamente operativo en los próximos días. También puede ofrecer atención materno-infantil, vacunas, vigilancia epidemiológica y nutricional, así como apoyo mental y psicosocial, y tiene capacidad para alojar hasta 20 pacientes en observación nocturna. Asimismo, comenzarán a funcionar clínicas móviles para llegar a las personas afectadas y ayudar a garantizar el acceso a la asistencia sanitaria de las comunidades a las que prestamos servicio.

Este hospital de campaña de emergencia complementará al hospital de campaña ya existente de la Cruz Roja Venezolana, que lleva en funcionamiento desde que comenzó la crisis. Este hospital de campaña ya ha atendido cientos de casos de traumatismos en los días posteriores a los dos terremotos y, actualmente, presta cada vez más atención primaria y apoyo psicosocial a las personas afectadas.

Además de estos servicios de salud, la Cruz Roja Venezolana, con el apoyo de la IFRC, está distribuyendo artículos de socorro en las zonas afectadas, como la parroquia de San Martín en Caracas, en una escuela donde se han refugiado familias tras sufrir daños en sus viviendas a causa de los terremotos. Entre los artículos de emergencia se incluyen kits de higiene, de limpieza y para dormir, así como filtros de agua y bidones. Todo ello forma parte de las 36 toneladas de ayuda humanitaria enviadas a Venezuela desde los centros humanitarios de la IFRC en Panamá y Argentina.

La ampliación de los servicios sanitarios y la distribución de ayuda se produce a medida que las actividades de búsqueda y rescate van disminuyendo. Conforme evoluciona la crisis, también lo hacen las necesidades sanitarias de las comunidades afectadas. En los primeros días tras los terremotos, la atención se centró en la asistencia de emergencia. La evaluación actual identifica el apoyo mental y psicosocial, la salud primaria y materna, la prevención y el agua potable y el saneamiento como elementos clave en esta fase de transición de la respuesta humanitaria.

La IFRC hace un llamado a la comunidad internacional, a los donantes y a los socios para que apoyen el [llamamiento de emergencia](https://www.ifrc.org/es/emergency/venezuela-terremotos-2026), de modo que las comunidades afectadas en Venezuela puedan recibir toda la asistencia vital que necesitan con urgencia.

Portavoces de la IFRC están disponibles para entrevistas desde Caracas y pueden facilitar la cobertura mediática de la respuesta en Caracas y La Guaira, incluyendo la situación humanitaria, las labores de socorro, las necesidades humanitarias y la necesidad de un apoyo internacional continuo en las próximas semanas.

## **Para más información o para concertar una entrevista:** [**\[email protected\]**](https://www.ifrc.org/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#ddb0b8b9b4bc9db4bbafbef3b2afba)

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquakes - Emergency Update #2, 30 June - 4 July
documents.body_text:
## HIGHLIGHTS

• As of the latest official update on 4 July, authorities reported 2,954 fatalities, 16,592 people injured and more than 16,000 people without shelter.  
• Authorities also reported that 6,462 people had been rescued, while search-and-rescue efforts continued in affected areas.  
• The response is gradually moving from search-and-rescue operations towards recovery, as several international search-and-rescue teams have completed their missions and started leaving the country.  
• Government-led multi-service centres, referred to by authorities as transitional spaces, are being established to support people unable to return home. Authorities have reported 79 collective accommodation sites are operational across La Guaira. Capital District and Miranda, hosting 10,702 persans affected by the earthquakes.  
• UNHCR is supporting the response through protection services, technical assistance, shelter support and core relief items. A 20-metric-ton shipment of essential relief items from UNHCR's pre-positioned stocks in Panama has arrived in Venezuela, including solar lamps, jerry cans, mosquito nets, blankets and family tents. This humanitarian flight is a contribution of LAT AM airlines, as part of the contributions received from the private sector.  
• To date, UNHCR has supported local authorities with tools and equipment for the safe collection and management of information on 2,058 affected people accommodated in government-managed multi­service centres across 31 sites in Caracas and La Guaira, helping identify specific needs and facilitate referrals to appropriate services.

documents.title: Direct Relief Supports Venezuela Earthquake Recovery with On-The-Ground Initiatives to Strengthen Medical Logistics, Recovery Efforts
documents.body_text:
## Acción Solidaria and Grupo de Rescate Metropolitano de Caracas, or GREMCA, received emergency funds to support health efforts as earthquake response continues.

Direct Relief recently issued support to two local Venezuelan groups working to distribute medical aid within the country and support health needs in response to last month’s major earthquakes.

Direct Relief is issuing grants to two local Venezuelan organizations, [Acción Solidaria](https://accionsolidaria.info/) and [Grupo de Rescate Metropolitano de Caracas](https://www.rescatecaracas.org.ve/), or GREMCA. Thursday’s financial support builds on funds issued in June for search-and-rescue and medical support efforts.

## **Funding Local Earthquake Recovery Efforts in Venezuela**

Acción Solidaria has been a key partner for Direct Relief in Venezuela, and has over a decade of emergency response experience through their Humanitarian Health Response Unit.

To strengthen the group’s ability to safely store and distribute medical aid locally, Acción Solidaria will use support from Direct Relief to secure a logistics warehouse for earthquake response medical donations. Through a strong local network, Acción Solidaria can support other local emergency response groups and health organizations, and the grant will bolster their ability to safely store aid, including cold chain medications, and allow their logistics operations to operate on a larger scale.

In addition to emergency funds, Acción Solidaria has requested medical aid from Direct Relief, including medicines, medical supplies, field medic packs, medical-grade tents, and more, which are expected to ship in the coming days.

## **Strengthening Medical Stations and Medical Logistics** 

 Direct Relief will also provide financial support to GREMCA, or Grupo de Rescate Metropolitano de Caracas, a local Venezuelan search and rescue and medical response organization focusing its support in the most affected areas by the earthquake, including in La Guaira and Caracas. GREMCA is transitioning from the search-and-rescue phase of the response to the second phase, which involves cleaning and sanitation support.

GREMCA medical personnel have set up medical stations throughout affected areas offering needed healthcare, and Direct Relief’s grant will support the local purchase of medicines and medical supplies to use at these medical stations and to distribute to regional healthcare facilities.

The funds will also support:  
• Supplies for search-and-rescue personnel and medical staff  
• Fuel and transportation costs  
• Operational logistics  
• Communication infrastructure, including portable radios

Direct Relief funded the deployment of Bomberos Unidos Sin Fronteras, or BUSF, a Spain-based search-and-rescue organization, that supported operations in earthquake-impacted areas. Direct Relief also supported the deployment of Medical Impact, a multidisciplinary medical team from Mexico and Colombia that includes emergency physicians to support mobile medical services and health response activities.

In addition to immediate financial support, Direct Relief also continues to pulse requested medical aid into the region to support immediate health needs, as well as supporting medium- and long-term support of the health system.

documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #6 (3 al 5 de julio de 2026)
documents.body_text:
El sexto Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre el impacto de los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela y resume la respuesta en curso y planificada de la OIM en apoyo a las poblaciones afectadas y a los esfuerzos nacionales al 5 de julio.

**Aspectos destacados**

Las cifras oficiales reportan al menos 3.342 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas, 6.462 personas rescatadas y 17.345 personas sin vivienda tras los terremotos del 24 de junio. Las cifras oficiales e interagenciales también reportan 856 edificaciones afectadas y 190 colapsos totales.

Se han reportado 79 campamentos transitorios, con capacidad instalada para 14.599 personas y 10.702 personas actualmente alojadas. La OIM continúa apoyando actividades de alojamiento, coordinación y gestión de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, registro, gestión de información y coordinación interagencial.

Se requiere apoyo adicional urgente para mejorar las condiciones en los campamentos transitorios, ampliar el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento, fortalecer el registro y las derivaciones, y abordar riesgos de protección y salud pública.

**Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM continuó apoyando actividades de alojamiento, coordinación y servicios esenciales en La Guaira, particularmente en el Polideportivo José María Vargas. El apoyo incluyó la recepción de personas recientemente desplazadas, la coordinación con autoridades y socios, la instalación de carpas para áreas clave de servicio y la provisión de 464 literas, equivalentes a 928 camas. La OIM también coordinó con las autoridades pertinentes para mejorar los puntos eléctricos y la iluminación de los campamentos transitorios, mientras continúa realizando evaluaciones y consultas comunitarias en Playa Grande.

En salud y SMAPS, los equipos apoyados por la OIM brindaron 186 consultas médicas y psicosociales en el Polideportivo José María Vargas, incluyendo psiquiatría, psicología, medicina general, pediatría, medicina interna, ginecología y obstetricia. Se realizaron seis traslados médicos relacionados con traumatismos al Hospital Militar de Campaña, todos resueltos de manera oportuna. Las principales necesidades identificadas incluyen síntomas asociados a traumatismos, estrés agudo, enfermedades crónicas, afecciones respiratorias, salud maternoinfantil y servicios de salud sexual y reproductiva.

La OIM también entregó una planta portátil de tratamiento de agua, que será instalada próximamente, apoyó el registro de más de 400 familias en el Estadio César Nieves y continuó con el triaje de protección, la orientación legal y las derivaciones. La OIM facilitó la coordinación interagencial en La Guaira y coordinó con OCHA y ACNUR las estimaciones de población desplazada, población meta y actividades del Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales.

**Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La OIM continuará priorizando alojamiento temporal seguro, coordinación y gestión de sitios, salud y SMAPS, WASH, protección, registro y gestión de información. En los sitios temporales, la OIM apoyará la planificación de sitios, el registro, la coordinación de servicios, la instalación de carpas, iluminación, conectividad, participación comunitaria, provisión de información, AAP, PSEA, mitigación de riesgos de VBG y derivaciones de protección.

La OIM también buscará ampliar los equipos médicos y de SMAPS, las derivaciones, la atención de enfermedades crónicas, los servicios de salud sexual y reproductiva, los primeros auxilios psicológicos y el apoyo especializado en salud mental. Se requiere apoyo adicional urgente para mejorar las condiciones en los campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas, fortalecer servicios seguros y responsables, reducir riesgos de protección y salud pública, y generar datos oportunos que informen una respuesta focalizada, segura y digna que no deje a nadie atrás.

Reporte de Situación #6 | 3 al 5 de julio 2026
PRIORIDADES DE FINANCIAMIENTO: QUÉ PERMITIRÍA EL APOYO ADICIONAL
Se requiere apoyo adicional de manera urgente para sostener y ampliar la asistencia vital, fortalecer una prestación de servicios
segura, digna y con rendición de cuentas en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas, atender necesidades, reducir
riesgos de protección y salud pública, mejorar las condiciones a nivel de campamentos transitorios y generar datos oportunos
para una planificación focalizada y basada en evidencia. Las necesidades urgentes incluyen:
ALOJAMIENTO, TIERRA Y ASENTAMIENTOS
• Adquirir y distribuir materiales de alojamiento de emergencia y artículos básicos de asistencia.
• Mejorar los alojamientos mediante carpas, tarpaulins, iluminación, drenaje, seguridad contra incendios, remoción de escombros y mejoras.
• Fortalecer la gestión de campamentos transitorios, comités comunitarios, puntos de información, mecanismos de retroalimentación, siste-
mas de derivación de casos y participación inclusiva.
• Integrar estrategias de salida desde las etapas iniciales facilitando retornos o reubicaciones seguras, voluntarias y dignas.
SALUD Y SALUD MENTAL Y APOYO PSICOSOCIAL — SMAPS
• Desplegar equipos multidisciplinarios adicionales de salud y SMAPS.
• Reforzar la atención primaria y de emergencia, las derivaciones y las misiones de alcance comunitario.
• Adquirir medicamentos esenciales, insumos médicos y kits de emergencia.
• Brindar primeros auxilios psicológicos, consejería, telepsicología, derivaciones especializadas en salud mental y actividades de SMAPS.
• Fortalecer la vigilancia epidemiológica, gestión de información en salud y capacidad de respuesta en campamentos y comunidades.
AGUA, SANEAMIENTO E HIGIENE (WASH)
• Apoyar evaluaciones rápidas, provisión y distribución de agua, almacenamiento, tratamiento domiciliario y control de calidad del agua.
• Mejorar infraestructura de saneamiento, drenaje, gestión de residuos sólidos y promoción de higiene.
• Distribuir insumos de higiene, prevención y control de infecciones, y gestión de higiene menstrual.
• Fortalecer capacidades locales para restaurar y mantener servicios WASH en comunidades afectadas y campamentos transitorios.
PROTECCIÓN
• Ampliar evaluaciones de riesgos, auditorías de seguridad, derivación de casos, orientación legal, gestión de casos y protección comunitaria.
• Fortalecer mecanismos de rendición de cuentas y canales seguros de reporte, incluidos mecanismos de retroalimentación.
• Apoyar la mitigación de riesgos de violencia basada en género, protección de la niñez, prevención de trata e inclusión.
• Brindar asistencia a personas con necesidades específicas, incluidas personas mayores, embarazadas y lactantes, niñas, niños y adolescentes
no acompañados o separados, personas con discapacidad, personas indígenas, personas retornadas y otros grupos vulnerables.
DATOS, DTM Y EVALUACIONES DE NECESIDADES
• Ampliar evaluaciones de campamentos transitorios y necesidades, registro, seguimiento del desplazamiento, monitoreo de campamentos
transitorios y análisis de movilidad.
• Producir productos de información para orientar la priorización operativa.
• Fortalecer herramientas digitales, conectividad, recolección de datos en tiempo real y registro seguro.
• Apoyar la deduplicación, fortalecer la focalización basada en vulnerabilidades, darseguimiento de derivaciones y toma de decisiones basada
en evidencia en toda la respuesta.

documents.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #6 (3 to 5 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
The sixth Situation Report provides an update on the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and summarizes IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts by July 05.

**Highlights**

Official figures report at least 3,342 fatalities, 16,740 injuries, 6,462 people rescued and 17,345 people without housing following the 24 June earthquakes. Official and inter-agency figures also report 856 buildings affected and 190 total collapses.

A total of 79 transitory camps have been reported, with installed capacity for 14,599 people and 10,702 people currently accommodated. IOM continues supporting shelter, site coordination, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, information management and inter-agency coordination.

Urgent additional support is required to improve conditions in transitory camps, expand access to safe water and sanitation, strengthen registration and referrals, and address protection and public health risks.

**IOM activities**

IOM continued supporting shelter, site coordination and essential services in La Guaira, particularly at Polideportivo José María Vargas. Support included reception of newly displaced individuals, coordination with authorities and partners, installation of tents for key service areas, and provision of 464 bunk beds, equivalent to 928 beds. IOM also coordinated with relevant authorities to improve electricity points and site lighting, while continuing site assessments and community consultations in Playa Grande.

In health and MHPSS, IOM-supported teams provided 186 medical and psychosocial consultations at Polideportivo José María Vargas, including psychiatry, psychology, general medicine, pediatrics, internal medicine, and gynecology and obstetrics. Six trauma-related medical transfers were made to the Military Field Hospital and resolved in a timely manner. Main identified needs include trauma-related symptoms, acute stress, chronic diseases, respiratory conditions, maternal and child health, and sexual and reproductive health services.

IOM also delivered a portable water treatment plant to be installed shortly, supported registration of more than 400 families at Estadio César Nieves, and continued protection triage, legal orientation and referrals. IOM facilitated site-level inter-agency coordination in La Guaira and coordinated with OCHA and UNHCR on displaced population estimates, target populations and activities for the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group.

**IOM planned response**

IOM will continue prioritizing safe temporary accommodation, site coordination and management, health and MHPSS, WASH, protection, registration and information management. In temporary sites, IOM will support site planning, registration, service coordination, tent installation, lighting, connectivity, community engagement, information provision, AAP, PSEA, GBV risk mitigation and protection referrals.

IOM will also seek to expand medical and MHPSS teams, referrals, chronic disease care, sexual and reproductive health services, psychological first aid and specialized mental health support. Additional support remains urgently needed to improve conditions in transitory camps and affected communities, strengthen safe and accountable services, reduce protection and public health risks, and generate timely data to inform a targeted, safe and dignified response who leaves no one behind.

FUNDING PRIORITIES: WHAT SUPPORT CAN ENABLE
Additional support is urgently needed to sustain and scale up life-saving assistance, strengthen safe, dignified and accountable
service delivery in temporary sites and affected communities, address needs, reduce protection and public health risks, improve
site-level conditions, and generate timely data for targeted and evidence-based response planning. Urgent needs are:
SHELTER, LAND AND SITE COORDINATION
• Procure and distribute emergency shelter materials and core relief items.
• Improve accommodation through tents, tarpaulins, lighting, drainage, fire safety measures, debris removal and basic site improvements.
• Strengthen site management community committees, information desks, feedback mechanisms, referral systems and inclusive participation.
• Integrate exit strategies from collective centres from the outset to enable safe, voluntary and dignified return or relocation where feasible.
HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH AND PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT (MHPSS)
• Deploy additional multidisciplinary health and MHPSS teams.
• Reinforce primary and emergency care, referrals and outreach missions.
• Procure essential medicines, medical supplies and emergency kits.
• Provide psychological first aid, counselling, telepsychology, specialized mental health referrals and community-based MHPSS activities.
• Strengthen disease surveillance, health information management and capacity in temporary sites, communities and underserved areas.
WATER, SANITATION AND HYGIENE (WASH)
• Support rapid WASH assessments, safe water provision, water trucking, storage, household water treatment and water quality control.
• Improve sanitation infrastructure, drainage, solid waste management and hygiene promotion.
• Distribute hygiene, infection prevention and control, and menstrual hygiene management supplies.
• Strengthen local capacity to restore and maintain WASH services in affected communities and temporary sites.
PROTECTION
• Expand protection risk assessments, safety audits, case referrals, legal orientation, case management and community-based protection.
• Strengthen AAP mechanisms and safe reporting channels, including PSEA-related feedback mechanisms.
• Support GBV risk mitigation, child protection, trafficking prevention and disability inclusion.
• Provide assistance for people with specific needs, including older persons, pregnant and lactating women, unaccompanied or separated
children, persons with disabilities, indigenous persons, returnees, persons without documentation and others.
DATA, DISPLACEMENT TRACKING MATRIX (DTM) AND NEEDS ASSESSMENTS
• Expand emergency site and needs assessments, registration, displacement tracking, site monitoring and mobility analysis.
• Produce data products to guide operational prioritization.
• Strengthen digital tools, connectivity, real-time data collection and secure registration.
• Support deduplication, vulnerability-based targeting, referral tracking and evidence-based decision-making across the response.

documents.title: Venezuela earthquakes: IFRC dispatches emergency field hospital; supports Venezuelan Red Cross distribution of humanitarian relief kits
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas / Panama City / Geneva 06 July 2026** – The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is continuing to scale up its response to the recent earthquakes in Venezuela and its support to the Venezuelan Red Cross in delivering humanitarian assistance to people affected by the unprecedented disaster.

The IFRC dispatched an emergency field hospital to La Guaira over the weekend (July 5), in partnership with the Spanish Red Cross, which also provided doctors and other health professionals. The emergency field hospital can provide primary health care to 30,000 people and will be fully operational in the coming days. It can also support maternal and infant care, vaccinations, epidemiological and nutritional surveillance, and mental and psychosocial support, and can accommodate up to 20 patients for overnight observation. Mobile health clinics will also begin operating to reach affected people and help ensure healthcare access for the communities we serve.

This emergency field hospital will support the Venezuelan Red Cross's existing field hospital, which has been operating since the crisis began. This field hospital has already treated hundreds of trauma cases in the days following the twin earthquakes and is now increasingly providing primary care and psychosocial support to affected people.

In addition to these health services, the Venezuelan Red Cross, supported by the IFRC, is distributing relief items in affected areas, such as the San Martín Parish in Caracas in a school where families are sheltered after their homes were damaged by the earthquakes. Relief items included hygiene kits, cleaning kits, sleeping kits, water filters and jerrycans. This is part of the 36 tons of humanitarian aid dispatched to Venezuela from IFRC humanitarian hubs in Panama and Argentina.

The scaling up of health services and aid distribution comes as search-and-rescue activities slow down. As the crisis evolves, so do the health needs of affected communities. In the first days after the earthquakes, the focus was on emergency care. Current assessment identifies mental and psychosocial support, primary and maternal health, prevention, and safe water and sanitation as key to this transition phase of the humanitarian response.

The IFRC calls on the international community, donors and partners to support the [**emergency appeal**](https://www.ifrc.org/emergency/venezuela-earthquake-2026?__cf_chl_f_tk=d51eCsBfHWMcOkaKB2F_8ylerGTHEFPoJTkT9jloji0-1783289994-1.0.1.1-OOiRNCGr_RGRrzofbl7uheGpl35Tr.h_G0cVa4kU_5w) so affected communities in Venezuela can receive the full scope of life-saving assistance they urgently need.

IFRC spokespeople are available for interviews from Caracas and can facilitate media reporting on the response in Caracas and La Guaira, including the humanitarian situation, relief efforts, humanitarian needs and the need for continued international support in the weeks ahead.

documents.title: Situational Report - Response to Venezuela Earthquakes (July 3rd, 2026)
documents.body_text:
**Highlights**

- The humanitarian crisis continues to evolve following the earthquakes of 24 June. According to OCHA (1 July), 2,595 people have died, +12,400 have been injured, +26,400 people have been affected and +800 aftershocks have been recorded, with La Guaira remaining the hardest-hit state. Humanitarian operations are increasingly focused on supporting displaced families through temporary shelters and essential services.
- The response is progressively shifting from life-saving search and rescue to sustained humanitarian assistance, as temporary camps expand and pressure on health, water and sanitation services continues to grow.
- Child protection concerns continue to increase. 123 children reported missing or unaccounted for in the first days of the crisis, and clear risks linked to family separation, weak tracing systems, unsafe information sharing and psychosocial distress (CECODAP), highlighting the need for specialised protection services.
- Rapid assessments continue to confirm a severe humanitarian crisis, including the collapse of water and sanitation systems, widespread shelter destruction, overwhelmed health services and acute protection risks. Families continue sleeping outdoors, while more than 55,000 people remain reported without contact through the national missing persons platform. Increasing internal displacement to other Venezuelan states is also being reported, creating growing psychosocial support needs.
- Preliminary estimates indicate USD 37 billion in direct physical damage, underscoring that humanitarian needs will extend beyond emergency relief into recovery, reconstruction and restoration of essential services.
- Plan International has expanded its emergency response with partners, delivering non-food items, shelter kits, psychosocial support and primary health-care. The organisation is also scaling up programming while mobilising additional humanitarian funding

documents.title: Rescue Response International: Venezuela Earthquake Response Update 001 - Response Highlights as of July 5, 2026
sources: Haiti Air Ambulance - Rescue Response International
documents.body_text:
**Response Highlights as of July 5, 2026**

On June 24, two consecutive earthquakes (magnitude 7.2 followed by 7.5 mainshock) struck north-central Venezuela. On Sunday, July 28, Rescue Response International (RRI) mobilized former members of world-renowned UN INSARAG classified search and rescue teams to Venezuela. Thanks to the support of Airlink, who coordinated flights for team members on United Airlines and Avianca, the team was able to get in-country quickly. As always, partnership and coordination are critical in making our work possible.   
  
RRI landed with 13 Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) team members, 3 search dogs, and 4 support staff. RRI-1’s Incident Commander and subject matter experts possess over 25 years of experience. Uniting 3 separate USAR teams under the “RRI-1” umbrella, search dogs, drones, search cameras and Delsar (acoustic listening devices used to find trapped survivors) were used to conduct 17 Assessments, Search, and Rescues (ASR). The sites were tasked by the Local Emergency Management Authority (LEMA) coordination cell, which assigned initial tasks of Wide Area Reconnaissance. As RRI-1 was a light, mobile, and well-trained team, it was able to conduct fast reconnaissance and turn sites over to larger teams for extraction.   
  
While working in the impacted areas, RRI-1 was able to find two “positive hits” - signs of life beneath the rubble confirmed by search dogs and Delsar. The team worked to closely pinpoint the location of trapped victims and then called in teams with heavy equipment to work to extricate any possible survivors. RRI-1’s thorough assessments provided hope to families affected by the earthquake by finding those that might be saved and giving closure to families still searching for loved ones beneath the collapsed buildings.

documents.title: « Nous puisons dans notre force intérieure pour continuer à apporter notre soutien. »
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Antonio Ferreira**, chirurgien orthopédiste bénévole à la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne depuis 21 ans, passe ses journées à prendre en charge un flot ininterrompu de blessés depuis le séisme. Pour lui, ce **ne sont pas les blessures physiques qui pèsent le plus lourd, mais ce que les patients portent en eux.**

*« Le plus difficile, c’est l’impact psychologique. Quand on écoute les patients et qu’on voit tout ce qu’ils ont perdu, il n’existe pas de mots qui puissent les aider à comprendre ce qui s’est passé. »*

La plupart de ses patients sont des enfants et des personnes âgées, les plus vulnérables, qui n’ont pas pu se mettre à l’abri à temps.

```
**Le pompier qui n’a pas pu sauver les siens**

```

Parmi tout ce qu’Antonio a vu, une histoire l’a particulièrement marqué.

Un pompier a été admis pour être soigné après s’être blessé en extrayant des personnes des décombres. Tandis qu’Antonio soignait sa cheville, le pompier a commencé à raconter les vies qu’il avait réussi à sauver… et celle qu’il n’avait pas pu sauver.

*« Même s’il est secouriste, qu’il sait comment intervenir et comment évacuer les victimes, il n’a pas pu mettre ce savoir au service des siens. **Il n’a pas réussi à sauver un membre de sa propre famille. »***

*« C’est difficile à concevoir, parce que cela pourrait arriver à n’importe lequel d’entre nous. En tant que professionnels de santé, nous avons les connaissances, les compétences et les moyens pour aider les autres… **mais malgré tout, il arrive que nous ne puissions rien faire. »***

Situation Update and Response Actors — As of 04 July 2026 | 1700 ET / 2100Z

The response is transitioning from live rescue to recovery. Live rescues are now rare exceptions. Missing-persons estimates range from tens of
thousands (unverified crowd-sourced registries cite 43,000 to 46,000), against no confirmed official figure. The UN is planning against a scenario of up
to 10,000 deaths.
Key Focus Areas
Remains recovery and mortuary affairs
2,954 confirmed dead (GoV, 4 Jul); UN ERC Fletcher states 50,000+ remain missing; tracking registries list ~38,500 unaccounted (4 Jul); GoV says missing number
in the thousands without a figure; USGS PAGER assigns 44% probability final toll exceeds 10,000. GoV acknowledged casualty-registry errors (5 registered dead
Critical found alive); field reporting documents first-72-hour registration collapse (no materials to record names of the dead). 10,000 body bags being procured; La
Guaira provisional morgue reportedly processing ~400 bodies/day with refrigeration exhausted (CNN-sourced morgue staff); wrong-body handovers reported.
GoV formally keeps SAR open at active points (Israeli specialist team assessing) while functional transition proceeds: Netherlands ended rescue ops 1 Jul, UN
frames post-Day-7 extractions as exceptional.
Debris removal and site clearance
855 buildings severely damaged, 189 total collapses (GoV, 29-30 Jun) vs satellite damage analysis (Oregon State researchers) estimating ~58,900 buildings likely
Critical damaged or destroyed, a divergence residents echo; ~2,500 destroyed per DEC; 1,600+ bridges/roads damaged (GoV, 29 Jun). GoV inspection committee applying
red/yellow/green habitability tagging (commission announced 28 Jun). Heavy machinery shortages reported by affected communities (30 Jun); no national debris
volume estimate or disposal plan; demolition-before-remains-recovery sequencing undefined.
Health system restoration
38 hospitals damaged (GoV, 29 Jun); 3 of 21 PAHO-assessed facilities critical, 6 partially functional; 91 hospitals in MMI VI+ zones. Trauma caseload of 12,841
injured (GoV, 4 Jul); three UN field hospitals in La Guaira; Team Rubicon advance medical team arrived Caracas. PAHO US$24M appeal launched 1 Jul (6-month
health recovery, ~700,000 people); funding status not yet reported. La Guaira maternal care coordination gap confirmed.
Shelter and housing (transitional / permanent)
28,380 in temporary camps (30 Jun); damnificados series volatile without published methodology (12,721 on 28 Jun; 15,866 on 30 Jun; 12,841 on 1 Jul). 39% of
Critical housing-displaced remain in streets/public spaces (UNHCR). 14–15 state shelters in La Guaira plus 55 nationwide; UN standing up 3 assistance centres in La
Guaira (medical, food, WASH, protection, MHPSS). GoV end-of-2026 rehousing pledge lacks financing and required soil surveys; storm on 30 Jun exposed tented
populations.
WASH infrastructure repair
National water system severely compromised; 400+ schools and water systems damaged (combined UN figure). GoV claim of restored La Guaira water service
Severe uncorroborated and conflicts with field reporting of acute scarcity. Outbreak risk (dengue, measles, diarrheal disease) rising in crowded shelters; trucking
coverage of 69+ shelters unquantified.
Psychosocial support and mental health
Severe OCHA assesses emotional support as essential as food/water; PAHO expanding MHPSS for families of missing, health workers, responders. No dedicated
program for 15,400+ registered volunteers or forensic staff; MHPSS presence at provisional morgue unconfirmed.
Critical infrastructure (power, comms, transport)
General-aviation PPR (private/executive/non-regular intl flights) EXTENDED to 9 Jul; Maiquetía remains humanitarian/cargo only on single rehabilitated runway,
commercial reopening timeline unpublished; expert estimate ~3 months for full airport infrastructure rehab, compounded by workforce losses among La Guaira-
Severe resident staff. Commercial flow diversified across Valencia PLUS Barcelona and Maracaibo to relieve Valencia capacity limits; American 3 Jul resumption target
overtaken. Ramp 4 humanitarian/military hub active; USMC KC-130 on ramp; Dutch navy ship to Puerto La Guaira. GoV claims 90% power restored La Guaira
(uncorroborated). Starlink MOU 1,600 units. Caracas Metro restored 30 Jun; Metro Los Teques 2 Jul.
Sources: GoV/Asamblea Nacional; OCHA SitReps 1–6; PAHO and ERES assessments; UNICEF SitRep No.2; UNHCR; UNDP; US GOV incl. OFAC GL 60; IFRC; DEC; IRC; Plan International; CORE; NASA Sentinel damage proxies. · 1

Most Affected: Yaracuy and Carabobo | M7.2 + M7.5 Twin Earthquakes Recovery Phase · Day 10
Key Focus Areas
Protection and vulnerable populations
680,000 children among 1.8M in need (UNICEF). Mixed-sex shelters without separated sanitation; elevated GBV and child abuse risk (Plan Intl field reporting).
100+ deported migrants believed dead at Hotel Santuario (AP); cohort requires distinct tracing. 4 CICPC officers detained for looting rubble valuables; unverified
Severe activist reports allege abduction of minors by predators posing as rescuers, with communities requesting expanded security presence; 40 NGOs protest
militarized QR-code access in La Guaira, where GoV reports 19,000+ civilian/military personnel deployed; Amnesty Intl calls for rights-based response. No
published shelter safety standard or GBV referral pathway.
Coordination and information management
Official-channel figures diverge: rescued 6,461 (OCHA SitRep 8, 1 Jul) vs 19,861 (GoV, 30 Jun); affected definitions split within GoV reporting itself (26,403 housing-
impacted) while IOM projects up to 6.8M could be affected (exposure estimate); damnificados series volatile; building counts 855 (GoV) vs
Severe ~58,900 (satellite analysis). GoV admission of casualty-registry errors validates the reconciliation gap; GoV publicly rejecting slow-response criticism amid
documented 72-hour gaps. UN Crisis Relief public donation appeal live (routes to VHF); consolidated inter-agency appeal in preparation, not launched. Channels:
CERF $15M, US $300M ($200M IHA awards + $100M pooled fund), EU €5M + air bridge, China $14.7M, PAHO $24M, UNICEF $52M, GoV portal via CAF. 78 intl
teams (67 USAR, ~2,500 personnel); partial demobilization underway (Dutch, Ecuador, German, Swiss, Canada teams departed); worksite handover data at risk.
Livelihoods and economic recovery
Small business and informal income losses layered on pre-quake crisis (7.9M already in need; HRP only ~23% funded when the quakes struck, vs $606.5M
High requirement). GoV announced initial US$200M reconstruction fund from IMF-held resources after talks with State Dept and IMF; World Bank and IDB offering
non-reimbursable credit lines (2 Jul). UNDP satellite-based damage estimate: US$6.7B in housing/economic assets, ~6% of GDP. OFAC GL 60 (25 Jun) enables
relief transactions; confirm bank/insurer uptake. No market functionality or cash feasibility assessment published; UNDP early recovery design must start now.
Education restoration
400+ schools and water systems damaged (combined UN figure; no school-only inventory); classes suspended nationally through 6 Jul – reopening decision falls
High inside window. Undamaged schools occupied as shelters with no exit strategy. UNICEF $52M earthquake requirement inside a wider appeal only 35% funded
pre-quake. School structural triage within 96 hrs paces shelter decongestion.
Analytic Note: Priority classifications are based on life-safety immediacy, affected population scale, and operational window. The confirmed-dead versus missing-persons divergence is
the dominant analytic uncertainty; all mortuary, shelter, and rehousing projections are sensitive to its resolution.

documents.title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report #03, 5 July 2026
documents.body_text:
Funding Needed  
 FOR THE 1st MONTH OF EMERGENCY: USD 50 Million are required.  
 FOR REGULAR PROGRAMMES, INCLUDING SCHOOL MEALS: USD 20 million are required.  
 Resources and stock from regular programmes are being redirected to the emergency, making donor support critical on both fronts.

Emergency Situation  
 • On 24 June, two major earthquakes (magnitude 7.2 and 7.5) struck north-central Venezuela near Morón (Yaracuy), causing widespread destruction across Caracas and coastal areas, particularly affecting La Guaira.

- The Government declared La Guaira a disaster zone, enabling the deployment of national and international rescue teams. More than 800 international specialists are supporting search-and-rescue operations, debris removal, and providing medical assistance.  
     • As of 5 July, official figures report 2,954 deaths, 16,592 people injured, and more than 16,309 displaced. Over 856 buildings have been damaged, including critical infrastructures such as hospitals, limiting basic service access to affected populations.

Venezuela Earthquake Response: Expected Needs, Next 96 Hours
Situation Update and Response Actors — As of 03 July 2026 | 1700 ET / 2100Z
Most Affected: Yaracuy and Carabobo | M7.2 + M7.5 Twin Earthquakes Recovery Phase · Day 9
2,595 12,400 15,866 28,380 80,870
| | | |
Dead Injured Registered Displaced In Temporary Camps Total Affected
The response is transitioning from live rescue to recovery. Live rescues are now rare exceptions. Missing-persons estimates range from tens of
thousands (unverified crowd-sourced registries cite 43,000 to 46,000), against no confirmed official figure. The UN is planning against a scenario of up
to 10,000 deaths.
Key Focus Areas
Remains recovery and mortuary affairs
2,595 confirmed dead (GoV, 2 Jul); UN ERC Fletcher states 50,000+ remain missing; tracking registries list ~38,500 unaccounted (2 Jul); GoV says missing number
in the thousands without a figure; USGS PAGER assigns 44% probability final toll exceeds 10,000. GoV acknowledged casualty-registry errors (5 registered dead
Critical found alive); field reporting documents first-72-hour registration collapse (no materials to record names of the dead). 10,000 body bags being procured; La
Guaira provisional morgue reportedly processing ~400 bodies/day with refrigeration exhausted (CNN-sourced morgue staff); wrong-body handovers reported.
GoV formally keeps SAR open at active points (Israeli specialist team assessing) while functional transition proceeds: Netherlands ended rescue ops 1 Jul, UN
frames post-Day-7 extractions as exceptional.
Debris removal and site clearance
855 buildings severely damaged, 189 total collapses (GoV, 29-30 Jun) vs satellite damage analysis (Oregon State researchers) estimating ~58,900 buildings likely
Critical damaged or destroyed, a divergence residents echo; ~2,500 destroyed per DEC; 1,600+ bridges/roads damaged (GoV, 29 Jun). GoV inspection committee applying
red/yellow/green habitability tagging (commission announced 28 Jun). Heavy machinery shortages reported by affected communities (30 Jun); no national debris
volume estimate or disposal plan; demolition-before-remains-recovery sequencing undefined.
Health system restoration
38 hospitals damaged (GoV, 29 Jun); 3 of 21 PAHO-assessed facilities critical, 6 partially functional; 91 hospitals in MMI VI+ zones. Trauma caseload of 12,400
injured (GoV, 2 Jul); three UN field hospitals in La Guaira; Team Rubicon advance medical team arrived Caracas. PAHO US$24M appeal launched 1 Jul (6-month
health recovery, ~700,000 people); funding status not yet reported. La Guaira maternal care coordination gap confirmed.
Shelter and housing (transitional / permanent)
28,380 in temporary camps (30 Jun); damnificados series volatile without published methodology (12,721 on 28 Jun; 15,866 on 30 Jun; 12,841 on 1 Jul). 39% of
Critical housing-displaced remain in streets/public spaces (UNHCR). 14–15 state shelters in La Guaira plus 55 nationwide; UN standing up 3 assistance centres in La
Guaira (medical, food, WASH, protection, MHPSS). GoV end-of-2026 rehousing pledge lacks financing and required soil surveys; storm on 30 Jun exposed tented
populations.
WASH infrastructure repair
National water system severely compromised; 400+ schools and water systems damaged (combined UN figure). GoV claim of restored La Guaira water service
uncorroborated and conflicts with field reporting of acute scarcity. Outbreak risk (dengue, measles, diarrheal disease) rising in crowded shelters; trucking
coverage of 69+ shelters unquantified.
Psychosocial support and mental health
Severe OCHA assesses emotional support as essential as food/water; PAHO expanding MHPSS for families of missing, health workers, responders. No dedicated
program for 15,400+ registered volunteers or forensic staff; MHPSS presence at provisional morgue unconfirmed.
Critical infrastructure (power, comms, transport)
General-aviation PPR (private/executive/non-regular intl flights) EXTENDED to 9 Jul; Maiquetía remains humanitarian/cargo only on single rehabilitated runway,
commercial reopening timeline unpublished; expert estimate ~3 months for full airport infrastructure rehab, compounded by workforce losses among La Guaira-
resident staff. Commercial flow diversified across Valencia PLUS Barcelona and Maracaibo to relieve Valencia capacity limits; American 3 Jul resumption target
overtaken. Ramp 4 humanitarian/military hub active; USMC KC-130 on ramp; Dutch navy ship to Puerto La Guaira. GoV claims 90% power restored La Guaira
(uncorroborated). Starlink MOU 1,600 units. Caracas Metro restored 30 Jun; Metro Los Teques 2 Jul.
Sources: GoV/Asamblea Nacional; OCHA SitReps 1–6; PAHO and ERES assessments; UNICEF SitRep No.2; UNHCR; UNDP; US GOV incl. OFAC GL 60; IFRC; DEC; IRC; Plan International; CORE; NASA Sentinel damage proxies. · 1

Venezuela Earthquake Response: Expected Needs, Next 96 Hours
Situation Update and Response Actors — As of 03 July 2026 | 1700 ET / 2100Z
Most Affected: Yaracuy and Carabobo | M7.2 + M7.5 Twin Earthquakes Recovery Phase · Day 9
Key Focus Areas
Protection and vulnerable populations
680,000 children among 1.8M in need (UNICEF). Mixed-sex shelters without separated sanitation; elevated GBV and child abuse risk (Plan Intl field reporting).
100+ deported migrants believed dead at Hotel Santuario (AP); cohort requires distinct tracing. 4 CICPC officers detained for looting rubble valuables; unverified
activist reports allege abduction of minors by predators posing as rescuers, with communities requesting expanded security presence; 40 NGOs protest
militarized QR-code access in La Guaira, where GoV reports 19,000+ civilian/military personnel deployed; Amnesty Intl calls for rights-based response. No
published shelter safety standard or GBV referral pathway.
Coordination and information management
Official-channel figures diverge: rescued 6,461 (OCHA SitRep 8, 1 Jul) vs 19,861 (GoV, 30 Jun); affected definitions split within GoV reporting itself (26,403 housing-
impacted vs 80,870 total affected) while IOM projects up to 6.8M could be affected (exposure estimate); damnificados series volatile; building counts 855 (GoV) vs
Severe ~58,900 (satellite analysis). GoV admission of casualty-registry errors validates the reconciliation gap; GoV publicly rejecting slow-response criticism amid
documented 72-hour gaps. UN Crisis Relief public donation appeal live (routes to VHF); consolidated inter-agency appeal in preparation, not launched. Channels:
CERF $15M, US $300M ($200M IHA awards + $100M pooled fund), EU €5M + air bridge, China $14.7M, PAHO $24M, UNICEF $52M, GoV portal via CAF. 78 intl
teams (65 USAR, ~2,500 personnel); partial demobilization underway (Dutch, Spanish teams departed); worksite handover data at risk.
Livelihoods and economic recovery
Small business and informal income losses layered on pre-quake crisis (7.9M already in need; HRP only ~23% funded when the quakes struck, vs $606.5M
High requirement). GoV announced initial US$200M reconstruction fund from IMF-held resources after talks with State Dept and IMF; World Bank and IDB offering
non-reimbursable credit lines (2 Jul). UNDP satellite-based damage estimate: US$6.7B in housing/economic assets, ~6% of GDP. OFAC GL 60 (25 Jun) enables
relief transactions; confirm bank/insurer uptake. No market functionality or cash feasibility assessment published; UNDP early recovery design must start now.
Education restoration
400+ schools and water systems damaged (combined UN figure; no school-only inventory); classes suspended nationally through 6 Jul – reopening decision falls
inside window. Undamaged schools occupied as shelters with no exit strategy. UNICEF $52M earthquake requirement inside a wider appeal only 35% funded
pre-quake. School structural triage within 96 hrs paces shelter decongestion.
Analytic Note: Priority classifications are based on life-safety immediacy, affected population scale, and operational window. The confirmed-dead versus missing-persons divergence is
the dominant analytic uncertainty; all mortuary, shelter, and rehousing projections are sensitive to its resolution.
Sources: GoV/Asamblea Nacional; OCHA SitReps 1–6; PAHO and ERES assessments; UNICEF SitRep No.2; UNHCR; UNDP; US GOV incl. OFAC GL 60; IFRC; DEC; IRC; Plan International; CORE; Sentinel damage proxies. · 2

documents.title: QRCS contributes to Qatari relief airlift for victims of Venezuela earthquakes [EN/AR]
documents.body_text:
**July 3rd, 2026 ― Doha, Qatar:** As part of the State of Qatar’s efforts to provide relief for those affected by the recent double devastating earthquake in Venezuela, Qatar Red Crescent Society (QRCS) has launched an emergency humanitarian response to the disaster, in cooperation with Qatari government authorities and in coordination with Movement partners.

Shortly after the magnitude 7.2 and magnitude 7.5 earthquakes struck northwestern and central Venezuela respectively, QRCS activated its Disaster Information Management Center (DIMC) to receive humanitarian situation updates and keep in touch with the Venezuelan Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

On board a relief aircraft of the Qatari airlift ordered by His Highness Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Emir of Qatar, QRCS deployed a medical and relief aid shipment containing 24 tons of medications, medical supplies, and hygiene kits, as an immediate response to the emergency appeal issued by IFRC and UN agencies.

In addition to the Qatari International Search and Rescue Group of the Internal Security Force (Lekhwiya), the aircraft transported a medical and relief delegation from Hamad Medical Corporation (HMC) and QRCS, to take part in field relief efforts.

HMC sent anesthesiology, plastic surgery, and orthopedics specialists/consultants, while QRCS sent emergency medicine, general surgery, and orthopedics doctors, along with development projects, disaster response, and psychosocial support professionals.

Given the difficult conditions and large-scale destruction in the affected parts of Venezuela, QRCS launched a fundraising campaign to expand relief operations.

“Inspired by Qatar’s tradition of helping affected people in times of crisis, this charitable drive has been launched to intensify vital humanitarian aid, address the limited local resources in Venezuela, avoid growth of the death toll, and bring back hope and reassurance to the affected families and communities,” said Mohamed Bader Al-Sada, Assistant Secretary-General for Relief and International Development at QRCS.

He called upon benevolent donors to support this noble endeavor, by donating via the website ([https://qrcs.qa/R-Venezuela](https://qrcs.qa/R-Venezuela)), mobile app (QRCS), donor service (66666364), home donation collection service (33998898), or donation agents/desks at malls and shopping centers.

“Thanks to the generosity of the people of Qatar, we will be able to provide the people of Venezuela with shelter, medical care, and relief supplies, saving the lives and alleviating the suffering of affected people. Together, let’s cherish the call of duty and humanity. With your contributions, we can extend a helping hand to those most in need,” Mr. Al-Sada concluded.

International government and media reports reveal a serious impact of the Venezuela earthquakes. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), there are more than 1,430 casualties, thousands missing, and tens of thousands affected.

The severe tremors destroyed 1,500 buildings, main roads, and transportation networks. The basic public services were also disrupted in the affected areas. Direct economic losses are estimated at around $6.7 billion, approximately 6% of the country’s GDP.

In the initial assessments, the key current needs include medical/ambulance care, makeshift shelter, food aid, drinking water, nonfood aid (e.g., blankets, clothing, and hygiene items), electric generators, and rehabilitation of damaged infrastructure (e.g., roads, bridges, power and water supply, and sewage system).

\##End of Text##

**About Qatar Red Crescent Society (QRCS)**

Established in 1978, Qatar Red Crescent Society (QRCS) is Qatar’s first humanitarian and volunteering organization that aims to assist and empower vulnerable individuals and communities without partiality or discrimination.

QRCS is a member of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, which consists of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and 191 National Societies. It is also a member of several GCC, Arab, and Islamic organizations, such as the Islamic Committee of International Crescent (ICIC) and the Arab Red Crescent and Red Cross Organization (ARCO). In this legally recognized capacity, QRCS has access to disaster and conflict zones, thus serving as an auxiliary to the State of Qatar in its humanitarian and social efforts — a role that distinguishes it from other local charities and NGOs.

Both locally and internationally, QRCS has relief and development operations in numerous countries throughout the Middle East, Asia, Africa, Europe, and Central and South America. Its humanitarian mandates include disaster preparedness, response, recovery, and risk reduction. To mitigate the impact of disasters and improve the livelihoods of affected populations, QRCS provides medical services, food, water, shelter, and other needs of local communities. It is also active at the humanitarian diplomacy and advocacy front.

With the help of a vast network of trained, committed staff and volunteers, QRCS aspires to improve the lives of vulnerable people by mobilizing the power of humanity, inspired by the seven Fundamental Principles of humanitarian action: humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, unity, and universality.

documents.title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.3 (Earthquake), 02 July 2026
documents.body_text:
**Highlights**

- Eight days after two powerful earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the humanitarian situation continues to deteriorate. As of 02 July, official figures indicate that at least 2,295 people have died, 11,267 have been injured and 12,841 have been left homeless. In total so far, approximately 26,403 people have been affected. Search and rescue operations remain ongoing, and the number of casualties is expected to increase as access improves and assessments continue in affected areas. Authorities have declared a State of Emergency to strengthen coordination and scale up response efforts, including the mobilisation of international search and rescue and humanitarian assistance.
- According to official figures, at least 855 buildings have been affected, including 189 that collapsed entirely and 666 with partial collapse or severe structural damage, further disrupting access to essential services.3 Preliminary information also indicates that 432 schools in the Capital District have been affected, representing approximately 34 per cent of all schools in the district.
- Through its response, UNICEF aims to reach approximately 650,000 people, including 234,000 children, with critical interventions across health, nutrition, WASH, child protection and education.
- UNICEF has scaled up its emergency response, mobilising life-saving supplies and surge capacity to support children and families affected by the earthquakes. A first air shipment carrying 20 metric tons of medical supplies and WASH items arrived in Venezuela on 27 June. A second shipment from UNICEF's global supply hub in Copenhagen, containing an additional 48 metric tons of relief items, arrived on 30 June, and distribution of the first wave of supplies is already under way.
- UNICEF estimates that US$52 million is required to deliver its planned humanitarian response and address the urgent needs of the affected population.

mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). It is updating the
mapping of critical protection services to enable referrals, delivering
psychological first aid and individual support sessions, and
disseminating family-separation-prevention and UASC key
messages through partners and community networks. Protection-risk
mitigation is under way through rapid risk analyses and safety audits
in shelters, collective centres, distribution points and health facilities.
Venezuela Humanitarian Fund partners are delivering protection,
child protection and GBV services in Miranda and the Capital
District; authorities have deployed judges across Greater Caracas to
support affected children and adolescents; and the three La Guaira
sites (Polideportivo José María Vargas, César Nieves Stadium and
Playa Grande Stadium) will provide multisectoral services, including
protection. As of the most recent figures, 34 protection services were
operational and at least 11 organisations had staff available to
support the response.
HUMAN INTEREST STORIES AND
EXTERNAL MEDIA

Rodríguez, 01 July 2026. Figures for injured (11,267), displaced (12,841) and persons assisted (22,619): National Assembly, report by
Deputy Jorge Rodríguez, 01 July 2026.

requirements are subject to revision as damage and needs assessments continue and more information becomes available on the situation
and needs of children and families affected by the earthquakes.

documents.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #12 (05 July 2026, Time: 08:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 12**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**05 July 2026**  
**Time: 8:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report nearly 1,000 aftershocks.**
- At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state.
- Official toll: **3,342 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.**
- Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams remain deployed in the affected areas, in coordination with OCHA, more than one week after the earthquakes.
- **The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 995 aftershocks.**

More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **3,342 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued** since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately **17,345** people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and the assistance to affected populations. La Guaira remains the most affected state. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.
