Situation overview
Venezuela is facing a national
emergency following two consecutive
high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and
7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local
time) in the north-central region, with
the epicentre located along the San
Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis
(Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities
report 995 aftershocks.
More than a week after the
earthquakes, authorities report a toll of
3,342 people dead, 16,740 injured,
and 6,462 rescued since the onset of
the emergency. Authorities also
reported that approximately 17,345
people lost their homes.
The Government response remains
focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and the
assistance to affected populations. La Guaira remains the most affected state. The United Nations and its
partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response
activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.
Impact on infrastructure
 Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.
 An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates
that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. Most of
the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools,
hospitals, and public facilities. Meanwhile, preliminary estimates by UNDP indicate direct physical
damage of US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
National response
 The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, as well as assistance
to affected people.
 A seven (7)-day national mourning period was declared starting on 1 July.
 A presidential commission was activated to assess the habitability of housing and infrastructure,
alongside a coordination structure for the establishment and management of transitional camps.
 According to authorities, the response continues with 79 operational transitional camps, with a
capacity of 14,599 people and a current occupancy of 10,702 people (73 per cent). As of 5 July, 37
camps are located in Caracas, 22 in Miranda and 20 in La Guaira.
 The Government of Venezuela announced the creation of an initial reconstruction fund equivalent to
US$200 million.
 Authorities activated an air bridge between Caracas and Caraballeda (La Guaira) to strengthen the
delivery of supplies and ensure assistance to affected areas.
 A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.
 A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS)
to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons (www.localizapacientes.com) and to
report affected individuals (0-800-RESCATE).
 Authorities reported that administrative activities will resume on 6 July in states not affected by the
earthquakes and in areas where educational infrastructure shows no visible damage.
 Meanwhile, school activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua
(Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora,
Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the
Capital District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora,
Acevedo, Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual).
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda
 Response and assistance activities for affected populations continue in Chacao municipality
(Miranda State), while damage to critical infrastructure and disruptions to basic services persist,
contributing to ongoing humanitarian needs.
Response actions: Three (3) VHF-funded organizations operating in municipalities across Miranda
state and the Capital District (Cedesex, Construyendo Futuros and FUNDANA) are supporting the initial
response through general protection, child protection and gender-based violence (GBV) services. In
addition, organizations such as Tinta Violeta, FUNDANA and World Vision are providing protection
support to affected families, particularly through psychosocial assistance.
La Guaira
 Coordination efforts among authorities, clusters and humanitarian organizations continue to
strengthen the response in La Guaira’s transitional camps, including needs monitoring, the
expansion of sectoral services, and improvements in shelter conditions, protection services and
assistance for affected populations.
Response actions: Five (5) partners of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF) are supporting the
initial response through primary health care and psychological support services (Fundación Proyecto
Maniapure, Paluz, Ven Da Tu Mano, Venezuelan Red Cross and Tinta Violeta).
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In Carabobo, the most significant impacts continue to be concentrated in Juan José Mora
municipality (Morón parish). In Yaracuy, particularly in Veroes municipality and other localities near
the epicentral area, homes have been reported as destroyed or at high risk, while displaced families
from La Guaira continue to arrive. Recent assessments have identified priority needs in protection,
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and
food security.
Response actions: Five organizations (Venezuelan Red Cross, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón
and Empodérame) are providing response in health, food, water and the distribution of humanitarian
assistance.
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
 OCHA and Falcón Civil Protection continue coordinating actions to strengthen damage and needs
data collection processes in affected communities. Preparations are also underway for the
implementation of digital data collection tools to assess affected structures in Silva municipality.
 The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) has expressed its willingness to support the response in Falcón
through psychosocial assistance, with the possibility of expanding its activities based on needs
assessments and agreements with the authorities. The Local Coordination Forum (LCF) is
coordinating a meeting with authorities to define complementary support in other affected sectors.
Response actions: Psychosocial support and needs assessment activities continue for displaced and
affected people in Silva municipality. Humanitarian organizations are also exploring options to scale up
shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security assistance for the most affected
families.
Other states
 In Anzoátegui State, approximately 700 people have arrived through family reunification processes;
around 100 people have been received in Simón Rodríguez municipality (El Tigre). Efforts continue
to strengthen the three reception sites and transitional camps currently in operation, while the
activation of additional facilities is being assessed. Humanitarian assistance continues to be
mobilized, including a new 40-ton shipment from Lechería, bringing the total volume of relief supplies
dispatched from the municipality to 365 tons.
 In Bolívar State, the State Government reported the departure of a fifth humanitarian assistance
shipment totaling 140 tons, bringing the overall volume of supplies dispatched from the state to
approximately 1,600 tons. This effort has been supported by more than 30 active collection centres
across the state's 11 municipalities. Regional authorities continue to maintain inter-institutional
coordination mechanisms and are planning a follow-up meeting with humanitarian actors, including
OCHA and the Coordination Advisory Group (CAG).
 In Delta Amacuro State, planning continues for the relocation of people from La Guaira, with
projections of up to 400 people to be transported in groups of 50 to 80. The expected arrival of a
group of 40 people has been confirmed. Upon arrival, people are initially received at the Tucupita
Indoor Gymnasium before being referred to four temporary accommodation sites. Immediate actions
include the provision of a water storage tank by MSF, the installation of water filtration systems in
coordination with UNICEF, coordination between UNFPA and UNICEF under the Protection Cluster,
and training in Psychological First Aid (PFA) for 120 volunteers delivered by Cáritas and CESAP.
 In Táchira State, the Local Coordination Forum (LCF) is strengthening assistance mechanisms at
the San Cristóbal Bus Terminal in anticipation of population movements to different states as people
seek support and protection networks following the earthquakes. On 3 July, a joint visit was
conducted with the State First Lady and the Mayor of San Cristóbal municipality to review services
coordinated between the LCF, the Comprehensive System for the Protection of Children and
Adolescents (SIPINNA) and terminal authorities.
 During a meeting convened by local authorities, participants discussed operational guidelines for the
earthquake response, institutional coordination mechanisms, referral pathways, and procedures for
the identification and assistance of affected populations. The Autonomous Institute for the Rights of
Children and Adolescents (IDENNA) reported the identification of people who arrived in local
communities as a result of the earthquakes and who subsequently received psychosocial support.
The LCF and the Coordination Support Group (CSG) continue working with authorities to facilitate
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
the participation of United Nations agencies and international, national and local non-governmental
organizations in response coordination and assistance efforts.
 In Sucre State, the reception of people affected by the earthquakes from La Guaira continues
through two assistance points located in Sucre municipality (Cumaná) and Bermúdez municipality
(Carúpano), from where onward transportation to other municipalities is coordinated. In most cases,
affected people are temporarily accommodated with relatives. The LCF provides support through
case management, psychosocial assistance and accompaniment during household visits, with the
participation of Cáritas, Médecins du Monde (MdM), the Danish Refugee Council (DRC), Tinta
Violeta and CEDISUC. Authorities have arranged free transportation from Caracas for affected
people relocating to the state.
 In Monagas State, Cáritas Maturín is implementing a comprehensive assistance mechanism for
families displaced from La Guaira, including registration, verification and needs assessments in
localities such as La Pica, Jusepín, the Paramaconi Housing Complex, and the municipalities of
Cedeño and Ezequiel Zamora, with a focus on health, protection and psychosocial support. Identified
priority needs include food, medicines, mattresses, clothing, footwear and household items.
 In Nueva Esparta State, a reception, registration and assistance protocol was activated in Maneiro
municipality, where the arrival of at least 176 affected people has been confirmed. The response
strategy prioritizes accommodation through family networks on Margarita Island, complemented by
direct distribution of non-perishable food, hygiene and clothing kits.
 In Zulia State, the State Government reports the arrival of approximately 126 displaced people from
La Guaira and Caracas, with concentrations in Maracaibo, Villa del Rosario and Tres Bocas (Mara),
as well as individual cases in San Francisco and Rosario de Perijá. Assistance is being provided by
the State Government, the Venezuelan Red Cross, UNHCR, ODISEF and the Ombudsman’s Office.
Humanitarian coordination
 OCHA, together with the Humanitarian Coordinator and in coordination with national authorities,
coordinates the humanitarian response with the United Nations and partner organizations,
prioritizing actions in health, shelter, food security, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), logistics
and protection.
 More than one week after the earthquakes, coordination of Urban Search and Rescue (USAR)
operations was formally transferred to Venezuela’s Civil Protection, which will continue coordinating
both national and international teams deployed in the affected areas. The handover process included
the transfer of operational information and training on the USAR coordination methodologies used
throughout the response. At the same time, international USAR teams have begun a gradual
demobilization process; however, several teams, particularly from Latin America, remain deployed
in affected areas. Operations continue to focus on sites where reports of possible survivors persist,
while in other locations international teams are supporting national authorities and local responders
in the recovery of bodies.
 Humanitarian actors continue strengthening coordination for the management of transitional camps
in La Guaira, including the harmonization of population registration and assistance tracking systems,
the reinforcement of site planning and design standards to mitigate protection and security risks, and
the planning of additional temporary accommodation sites based on evolving needs.
 Under IOM’s coordination, the registration process of the population accommodated at the César
Nieves Stadium transitional camp continues, reaching 420 registered families and supporting the
planning and delivery of humanitarian assistance.
 Humanitarian organizations providing services at the César Nieves Stadium transitional camp (IOM,
UNHCR, UNFPA, WFP and FUNDAINIL) continue coordinating assistance delivery arrangements
within the site.
 The Social Protection Directorate of the La Guaira State Government will establish a situation room
at the Playa Grande transitional camp to strengthen operational coordination and response
monitoring.
 OCHA/UNDAC and the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) continue advancing the Rapid
Needs Assessment (RNA), including the finalization of tools and trainings, while infrastructure
assessments and information products are being developed to support needs analysis, response
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
monitoring and operational planning. Efforts also continue to consolidate data and strengthen
intersectoral monitoring and coordination mechanisms.
 National authorities have streamlined immigration and administrative procedures to facilitate the
entry of international search and rescue teams, United Nations personnel, media representatives
and other specialists deployed to support emergency response operations.
Initial humanitarian response
Food Security
 WFP assisted 4,000 people affected by the earthquakes through the distribution of ready-to-eat
individual food rations in the parishes of Naiguatá (2,500 people), Urimare and Carlos Soublette
(1,500 people). Each ration is designed to meet urgent food needs for 72 hours. In addition, the
collective kitchens established at the José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium
and Playa Grande remained operational throughout the day. Since the beginning of the response, a
total of 18,082 people have received food assistance.
Health
 Health partners continue providing primary health care, mental health and psychosocial support
(MHPSS), sexual and reproductive health services, and specialized care in transitional camps and
affected communities. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM delivered 186 medical and
psychosocial consultations, including general medicine, paediatrics, internal medicine, gynaecology
and obstetrics, psychology, and psychiatry. Assessments also identified significant mental health
needs, with acute trauma-related symptoms observed in approximately 90 per cent of the people
assessed. Project HOPE, SAMU and UNFPA continue providing complementary health and
psychosocial support services.
 At the César Nieves Stadium transitional camp, IOM continues to lead primary health care and
screening activities, including 18 referrals to specialized health, protection and gender-based
violence (GBV) services. Ven Da Tu Mano, a UNFPA partner, has initiated the provision of sexual
and reproductive health services.
 A Type 1 field hospital provided by the Dominican Republic was installed at the César Nieves
Stadium transitional camp in coordination with the Ministry of Health and PAHO through the Medical
Information and Coordination Cell (CICOM). The facility is staffed by a multidisciplinary team of
health professionals.
 International Medical Corps (IMC) conducted rapid assessments in five communities and five health
facilities in La Guaira, identifying critical gaps in the availability of health services, medicines and
medical supplies for affected populations.
 Since 1 July, IMC has deployed a mobile medical unit in Catia La Mar with the capacity to assist up
to 100 patients per day. IMC also plans to expand its response through additional mobile medical
units and the deployment of a Type 1 Emergency Medical Team (EMT), including 21 health
professionals, to strengthen health care services in priority areas identified by the Ministry of Health.
Logistics and Telecommunications
 The CANTV strengthened connectivity in the transitional camps through the installation of internet
services at the José María Vargas Sports Complex and the deployment of fiber-optic connectivity in
Playa Grande to support humanitarian operations and response coordination.
 The Logistics Working Group is consolidating a gaps and needs analysis to identify key operational
challenges and guide logistics support activities over the coming weeks.
 International humanitarian cargo continues to arrive at Simón Bolívar International Airport. In
coordination with WFP, logistics services in La Guaira are being strengthened to facilitate the
transport, temporary storage and distribution of humanitarian assistance.
 Through a joint initiative involving UN Women, DVC, Telefónica, Hyundai and companies from the
WEPs community, direct assistance was provided to 459 affected families (1,836 people) across La
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 6
Guaira, Miranda and Caracas through the collection and distribution of food, water, medicines,
hygiene items, mattresses, clothing and other essential supplies. In addition, with support from
Telefónica, two Starlink antennas were installed at the José María Vargas Sports Complex and
César Nieves Stadium to strengthen connectivity for inter-agency humanitarian teams operating in
the transitional camps.
Nutrition
 Efforts continue to strengthen nutritional support in the transitional camps. The installation of
breastfeeding spaces is planned at the José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves Stadium
and Playa Grande, through coordinated action between humanitarian actors and authorities.
Protection (including Children and Gender-Based Violence)
 Protection partners continue to expand service delivery in transitional camps. UNHCR provided
information and counselling to 68 people through information desks, delivered specialized protection
services to 28 people, and supported documentation processes for 60 people in Playa Grande.
Together with IOM, UNHCR also strengthened protection mechanisms, legal counselling, access to
rights, protection screening and referrals to specialized services.
 In the areas of child protection and gender-based violence (GBV), UNHCR conducted awareness-
raising sessions with community leaders and officials on protection risks, child protection, GBV,
Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), and accountability mechanisms. UNFPA
provided psychosocial support, GBV case management and prevention and awareness-raising
activities, reaching 52 people. In Playa Grande, coordination among partners was strengthened to
expand psychosocial support services, Child-Friendly Spaces, family reunification activities, sexual
and reproductive health services, and support for GBV survivors.
 Protection partners continued child protection and psychosocial support activities in transitional
camps, reaching 143 children and adolescents (56 at the José María Vargas Sports Complex, 47 at
César Nieves Stadium and 40 at Playa Grande). Activities included early childhood stimulation,
emotional management, art therapy, recreational activities and hygiene promotion.
 UN Women continues to provide remote psychosocial support to people affected by the earthquakes,
reaching 64 cases (59 women, 4 men and 1 non-binary person). Thirty-four per cent of requests
originated from people directly affected by the emergency, 20 per cent from humanitarian personnel
and 8 per cent from individuals with high public exposure.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
 Improvements continue across La Guaira’s transitional camps through the expansion of
infrastructure for coordination, protection and assistance services for affected populations. At the
José María Vargas Sports Complex, five tents were installed for service delivery and coordination
purposes, 164 additional bunk beds were received, and site improvements are underway to
strengthen lighting, electricity supply and shower facilities.
 At Playa Grande, IOM, authorities and community leaders continue site improvement activities,
including the planned installation of two tents to reorganize family accommodation units. Efforts are
also ongoing to strengthen protection conditions, habitability standards and participatory camp
management.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
 Access to safe water and sanitation services continues to be strengthened in transitional camps. At
the César Nieves Stadium camp, a water supply point and mobile sanitation facilities were installed,
while Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) chlorinated water storage tanks to ensure a safe water
supply. Distributions of hygiene kits and the expansion of sanitation infrastructure in temporary
accommodation sites also continue.
 At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, authorities delivered a water treatment unit, which will
be installed in coordination with UNICEF to strengthen access to safe water for the sheltered
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 7
population. In addition, an extra handwashing station was installed, and the Ministry of Water and
Electric Energy conducted inspections for the installation of 20 showers.
 Over the next 24 hours, the distribution of 700 family hygiene kits (500 for César Nieves Stadium
and 200 for Playa Grande Stadium) is planned, together with 80 water containers (100 litres each)
and general cleaning supplies.
 At the José María Vargas Sports Complex transitional camp, 1,700 people maintained access to
water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services through 30 operational toilets and 12 handwashing
stations. Efforts are also underway to install 20 shower units.
 At the César Nieves Stadium transitional camp, 1,253 people were reached through the distribution
of 561 family hygiene kits and 80 water containers of 100 litres each. The sheltered population also
has access to 30 operational toilets and three handwashing stations.
 At the Playa Grande transitional camp, 283 people maintain access to essential sanitation services
through 10 operational portable toilets installed in coordination with the State Government.
Humanitarian financing
 As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist
to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. A private sector contributions
tracker for the Venezuela earthquake response is available at https://ven-
eq.connectingbusiness.org, together with a briefing note for the private sector outlining opportunities
for engagement. Focal point: sanchez21@un.org.
 The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral
response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed
to support the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further
US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF,
International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and
the Red Cross.
 Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to
the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country. Other Member States and donors have
expressed their intention to support the response through the Fund.
 The Inter-American Development Bank Group (IDB Group) announced a donation package of at
least US$1 million to support immediate humanitarian assistance, to be implemented in coordination
with Cáritas Venezuela, as well as damage and loss assessments.
 PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support health response
and early recovery activities over the next six months and released $1.5 million from the Contingency
Fund for Emergencies. WFP launched an initial appeal for US$50 million to scale up food assistance
and support emergency logistics and communications activities. UNHCR requires US$14.8 million
to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.
 The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52
million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.
 Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare
and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.
 Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.
 Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance,
water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP,
UNHCR and Save the Children.
 Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian
response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and
the Danish Red Cross.
 The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) Venezuela Earthquakes Appeal raised £7 million in 24
hours, including a £2 million contribution from the United Kingdom government through UK Aid
Match.
 Shell will provide $5 million in humanitarian aid for Venezuela through the WFP and local
humanitarian organizations.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 8
 BBVA raised more than 1 million euros in Spain in humanitarian aid through a campaign developed
in conjunction with the Red Cross, UNHCR, and UNICEF.
 OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based
allocation of resources.

documents.title: Situation Report No.4: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), July 5, 2026
documents.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

- On 24 June 2026, two consecutive earthquakes (M7.2 and M7.5) struck north-central Venezuela, affecting at least seven states, with La Guaira the most severely impacted. Authorities have since reported more than 995 aftershocks.
- **Assessments of 11 priority health facilities identified persistent operational constraints** across the referral network. Two hospitals (Vargas-IVSS and Rafael Medina Jiménez) continue to operate with major functional restrictions, while at least two facilities reported infection prevention and control gaps and three reported compromised morgue capacity. Patient referral remains largely ad hoc due to the absence of real-time bed visibility, contributing to a persistent surgical backlog and continued reliance on contingency measures for essential support services.
- At least **two specialized mental health services in La Guaira sustained infrastructure damage and reduced capacity**; critical shortages persist in medications for crisis management and the care of patients with acute mental health conditions.
- PAHO/WHO is actively supporting the Ministry of Health in deployed **six Regional Response Team specialists** covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information systems and media, risk communication and community engagement, EMT coordination, and rapid health facility assessment. In coordination with MoH, PAHO/WHO is supporting the **virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization: Nine EMTs are operational in La Guaira, Caracas and Miranda** increasing clinical capacity in affected areas.
- PAHO/WHO **delivered 6 metric tons of medical supplies**, including trauma kits, Interagency Emergency Health Kit (IEHK) modules, personal protective equipment (PPE), Non-Communicable Disease (NCD) kits, WASH supplies, and field equipment. Also provided technical support to facilitate vaccine donations from the Ministries of Health of Chile and Brazil.

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.4
HEALTH SITUATION (2-5)
Between 1 and 3 July 2026, the Ministry of Health, local health authorities, and PAHO/WHO conducted
rapid visits to 10 health facilities across La Guaira and the Capital District/Greater Caracas to assess
post-earthquake hospital response capacity and identify priority needs. The facilities visited included
Hospital Dr. Miguel Pérez Carreño, Hospital Dr. Domingo Luciani, Hospital Dr. Jesús Yerena (Lídice),
Hospital Dr. Ricardo Baquero González (Periférico de Catia), Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández
(Magallanes de Catia), Hospital de las Grandes Misiones Hugo Chávez, Clínica Popular Especializada
Dr. Alfredo Machado, Hospital Dr. Rafael Medina Jiménez (Periférico de Pariata), Hospital Dr. José María
Vargas-IVSS, and Hospital Materno-Infantil Ana Teresa de Jesús Ponce (Maternidad de Macuto). The
visits focused on hospital functionality, available beds, emergency and surgical capacity, ICU and trauma
shock areas, diagnostic services, blood bank capacity, patient flow, referral mechanisms, infrastructure
limitations, lifelines, infection prevention and control, waste management, and critical operational gaps
requiring immediate support.
Separately, the Hospital Militar de la India, deployed as an EMT Type II, was also assessed to document
its installed capacity and integration into the response. The team reported 50 beds, one operating room
with two surgical tables, emergency capacity for adults and pediatrics, trauma shock capacity, laboratory,
radiology and telemedicine services.
The assessed hospital network across the Capital District, La Guaira, and Miranda includes 55 facilities,
with Type II hospitals representing the largest group, followed by Type IV and Type I facilities.

CROSS-CUTTING OPERATIONAL FINDINGS
The Expanded Technical Report — a consolidated assessment of 11
facilities across Gran Caracas — identifies operational patterns that affect
the network as a whole, beyond any single facility:
Hospital functionality
• Reported bed counts understate real occupancy pressure:
Vargas-IVSS is hospitalizing 96 patients against a formal 8-bed
capacity, while Pérez Carreño and Domingo Luciani are both
operating at close to half their architectural bed capacity.
• Some facilities (Pariata, Vargas-IVSS) have been functionally
reduced to single-service emergency units, with hospitalization
floors and main operating theatres taken out of service.
Referral and patient regulation
• First clinical contact often falls to security or non-clinical staff
before formal triage, and patient records remain largely paper- or
spreadsheet-based, with no real-time, network-wide view of bed
availability.
• Inter-hospital referral is happening ad hoc — including
WhatsApp-coordinated transfers between hospital directors —

Surgical capacity
• A recurring “hidden surgical debt”: available surgical specialists do not translate into resolving capacity
when supporting equipment fails (inoperative C-arms, no traction beds), masking true backlog in bed-
occupancy indicators.
• Confirmed post-earthquake surgical backlogs include at least 13 patients awaiting surgery at Pérez Carreño
(likely undercounted) and 25 at Domingo Luciani, despite 130 procedures already completed there.
Infection prevention and control (IPC)
• At least 2 of the 11 assessed facilities have no active infection-control committee, with inadequate
biohazard waste handling and compromised morgue capacity at 3 or more facilities — a network-wide
biosafety risk compounded by high trauma patient volumes.
Health workforce
• Pre-existing shortages are compounding direct earthquake impact on staff: Pérez Carreño reports only 679
of the 1,500 nursing staff required, while Magallanes de Catia reports one death and multiple staff with
housing loss — unevenly across the network, requiring explicit psychosocial support planning.
Essential support services
• Water and power continuity depend heavily on backup generators and manual water hauling where these
fail (e.g., Vargas-IVSS, three times daily); saturated waste collection points at multiple facilities further
compound infection-control risk.

Health Cluster partner assessments of health facilities
• The Health Cluster dashboard currently consolidates information on 73 assessed health facilities,
of which 25 report damages, 20 report severe shortages, with 1,038 active doctors and an
estimated 1,772,260 people in the facilities’ areas of influence.
• Health Cluster partners are consolidating rapid health facility assessments from multiple sources,
including KoBo partner reports, PAHO/ERES assessments and UNICEF inputs, covering
operational status, damage, basic services, shortages, human resources and priority needs.
• UNICEF reported having assessed 108 health facilities where it maintains a permanent presence
through implementing partners, initially conducting a rapid operational assessment during the first
72 hours of the response.
• Available data indicate that several facilities remain operational or partially operational, but with
significant constraints related to infrastructure damage, severe shortages, interrupted basic
services, limited referral capacity, and reduced ability to manage trauma and specialized care
needs.
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS):
• Damage to infrastructure and reduced operational capacity has been reported in at least two
specialized mental health services in La Guaira, underscoring the need to reinforce mental health
service provision in Caracas to maintain continuity of care.
• Critical shortages persist in medications for crisis management and the care of patients with acute
mental health conditions. Additional supplies provided by UN agencies remain pending delivery.
• Mental health needs assessment and monitoring activities have not yet been fully consolidated,
representing a key gap for response planning and prioritization.
• The Ministry of Health established a toll-free (0800) hotline for mental health and psychosocial
support.
Immediate priorities in Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) include:
• Strengthening coordination of the MHPSS Technical Working Group (TGG) and toll-free helplines.
• Collaborative implementation of the Mental Health Damage and Needs Assessment and the
MHPSS 4W matrix.
• Strengthening the response in shelters and distribution of mental health kits.
• Assessment of additional needs for essential psychotropic medications.
• Mobilization and supervision of specialized volunteers.
• Mass rollout of the virtual mhGAP-Humanitarian Intervention Guide (mhGAP-HIG) training, at the
request of health authorities, to strengthen identification and management of mental health
conditions in primary health care (PHC), to be followed by small-scale practical workshops.
• Ensuring psychosocial support for health workers and strengthening of the mental health team.
• Development of an operational workplan for MHPSS coordination.

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.4
SHELTERS (1)
According to the Official Report of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (5 July 2026), 17,345 people
were reported to have lost their homes following the earthquakes. Authorities have established 79
transitional camps with a total capacity of 14,599 people, currently accommodating 10,702 displaced
persons. Official assessments also report 856 affected buildings, including 190 collapsed structures,
highlighting the substantial shelter needs resulting from the disaster.
Priority gaps remain in:
• Lack of population characterization and profiling to promptly identify vulnerable groups that
require monitoring to prevent morbidity, mortality, and preventable disability.
• Insufficient capacity for medical care, triage, and isolation in shelters, which increases the risk of
disease transmission due to overcrowding.
• Safe food handling is necessary, including supervision of kitchens, proper storage, equipment,
and strict hygiene controls.
• Optimal access to safe drinking water, functional sanitation, hygiene supplies, and proper solid
waste management in shelters must be strengthened.
• Absence or inadequacy of protective measures to ensure safe shelter design, adequate lighting,
privacy, child protection, and mitigation of the risk of gender-based violence (GBV).
• Barriers to access to primary health care (PHC) and continuity of care, affecting general medical
consultations, maternal and child health, injury prevention, and the treatment of people with
chronic diseases or comorbidities.
• Gaps in the coverage of mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, given the
lack of psychological first aid (PFA), identification of disorders, referral pathways, and ongoing
support for vulnerable families and groups.
• Limitations in the provision of sexual and reproductive health services, including a lack of obstetric
and neonatal care emergency care, STI prevention, prevention of sexual violence, and
specialized clinical care for survivors of sexual violence.
• There is a need for greater integration between early warning systems, syndromic surveillance
for the timely detection of risks, outbreak response, and the water, sanitation, and hygiene
(WASH) program.

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.4
Response
• The United Nations system and humanitarian partners are providing a multisectoral response,
including: Primary health care, Nutrition, Maternal, newborn and child health, Mental Health and
Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), Protection, including child protection and gender-based violence
(GBV) prevention and response, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), Shelter and other
essential services.
• PAHO will support syndromic surveillance in shelters and transitional camps, given the
increased risk of communicable diseases in crowded settings, especially acute
respiratory infections, influenza-like illness, acute watery diarrhoea, skin infections, fever-
rash illness, and other vaccine-preventable diseases. This is particularly important given
the regional measles outbreak in the Americas.
Recommended priority actions:
PRIORITY HEALTH NEEDS (1-5)
1. Health response coordination
• Continue strengthening operational coordination among the Ministry of Health, PAHO/WHO, the
Health Cluster, Civil Protection, EMTs, UN agencies and health partners to maintain a single
information flow for prioritization, gap analysis, resource allocation and duplication avoidance.
• Consolidate Health Cluster processes for harmonizing partner assessments, updating operational
presence matrices, and mapping which actors are supporting each health facility and transitional
camp, so reported gaps are translated into prioritized operational actions.
• For EMTs, the priority is no longer the arrival of additional international teams, as health services
are no longer overwhelmed as in the initial phase. The current need is to coordinate the
integration, retasking, specialization or phased demobilization of EMT capacities according to
specific remaining gaps.
2. Health system, hospitals and health facilities
• Ensure continuity of operations in affected hospitals and health facilities, particularly those with
structural damage, reduced bed capacity, restricted service areas, intermittent basic services,
severe shortages, or limitations in trauma care, surgery, ICU, laboratory, imaging, blood bank,
PAHO/WHO Regional Situation Report No. 4 - Earthquakes in Venezuela. Washington, D.C.: PAHO/WHO; 2026.
www.paho.org | © PAHO/WHO, 2026

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.4
morgue and ambulance capacity.
• Address the surgical and trauma care backlog through surgical and anesthetic supplies,
osteosynthesis materials, operating room equipment, C-arms, traction beds, imaging equipment,
and specialized staffing for anesthesia, surgical nursing, intensive care and trauma surgery.
• Strengthen hospital diagnostic capacity, including portable X-ray, ultrasound/FAST, clinical
laboratory capacity, reagents, blood bank supplies, connectivity, referral systems, patient tracking
and transfer traceability.
• Address cross-cutting gaps in biosafety, infection prevention and control, health care waste
management, water and sanitation, backup power, medical gases, oxygen, ventilators,
autoclaves, incinerators, morgues, refrigerated containers and dignified management of the dead.
• Integrate early rehabilitation and disability-inclusive care, including physiotherapy, prosthetics,
wheelchairs, crutches, canes, assistive devices and continuity of care for people with
amputations, fractures, crush injuries or major trauma.
• Address the impact on the health workforce, including nursing shortages, transport constraints,
damaged or destroyed homes, injuries or deaths among health workers, psychosocial support,
safe working conditions, food, rest areas and operational continuity.
• For Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), strengthen coordination of the MHPSS
Technical Working Group and toll-free helplines; implement the mental health damage and needs
assessment and the MHPSS 4W matrix; reinforce the shelter response and distribution of mental
health kits; assess additional needs for essential psychotropic medicines; and mobilize and
supervise specialized volunteers.
3. Epidemiological surveillance, vaccination and public health
• Establish and strengthen syndromic surveillance and early warning in shelters, transitional camps,
points of care and health facilities, prioritizing acute watery or bloody diarrhoea, fever, fever with
rash, respiratory infections, sudden vomiting, jaundice, neurological symptoms, wound infections
and skin conditions.
• Reinforce surveillance and response in shelters and collective settings, where overcrowding,
limited ventilation, disruption of safe water, sanitation and hygiene, and limited capacity to
separate symptomatic individuals increase the risk of respiratory, gastrointestinal, skin and
hygiene-related infections.
• Ensure preparedness for gastroenteritis, norovirus and hepatitis A. Priority actions include safe
water, sanitation, hand hygiene, safe food handling, surveillance of acute watery diarrhoea and
laboratoy diagnostic capacity to confirm if a signal is detected.
• Maintain prevention of tetanus and wound-associated infections, especially among people injured
by debris, metal, glass, crush injuries or delayed surgical care, including wound cleaning, clinical
assessment, tetanus prophylaxis according to vaccination history and immunoglobulin when
indicated.
• Integrate vaccination as an operational component of the response, prioritizing tetanus, routine
catch-up vaccination in children, measles-rubella, DTP, polio, hepatitis B, and influenza/COVID-
19 vaccination for risk groups, as well as specific vaccines according to risk and exposure.
• Maintain a locally adapted approach for Caracas and La Guaira. Dengue and other urban Aedes-
borne arboviruses require surveillance and vector control, particularly where water storage, debris
and disruption of vector control activities increase risk. Malaria and yellow fever remain relevant
nationally but do not appear to be immediate priority risks in the main affected areas.
• Ensure continuity of care for TB, HIV, chronic diseases and people dependent on medicines,
preventing interruptions in diagnosis, treatment or follow-up that could increase individual
vulnerability and reduce early detection of clusters.
4. Shelters and transitional camps
• Strengthen population profiling in shelters and transitional camps to identify people at higher risk,
including children, pregnant women, older adults, persons with disabilities, people with chronic
diseases, people with injuries, survivors with protection needs, and people requiring clinical or
psychosocial follow-up.

www.paho.org | © PAHO/WHO, 2026

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.4
• Ensure minimum capacity for primary health care, triage, isolation, referral and continuity of care
in shelters, including maternal and child health, sexual and reproductive health, chronic disease
care, injury care, mental health, and prevention and response to gender-based violence.
• Improve access to safe water, sanitation, hygiene, waste management, food safety, lighting,
privacy, child protection and security measures to reduce communicable disease and protection
risks.
• Integrate syndromic surveillance in shelters with WASH, sample collection and transport for public
health events, health promotion, risk communication, vaccination, vector control and referral
pathways to the health service network.
EMERGENCY RESPONSE
PAHO/WHO RESPONSE ACTIONS:
PAHO/WHO supports national authorities and the health sector response through technical cooperation,
coordination, information management and readiness for additional surge support. Priority support
actions include:
COORDINATION:
• PAHO/WHO continues to coordinate with the Ministry of Health, Civil Protection, the Health
Cluster, and health partners to align response priorities, consolidate information, conduct health
facility assessments, support the MoH response plan, and address priority health needs and gaps.
• PAHO/WHO continues to strengthen health response coordination in support of the Ministry of
Health, with particular emphasis on: (a) intra-ministerial coordination for effective decision-
making; (b) Emergency Medical Team coordination; (c) coordination with UN agencies and the
broader humanitarian architecture, including active participation in UNDAC and OSSOC; and (d)
Health Cluster coordination, which has seen a substantial increase in engaged agencies and
partners — from 46 to 114 — making structured coordination critical to ensuring the effective and
targeted delivery of assistance.
• Health Cluster partners are updating operational matrices to map which actors are supporting
each health facility and transitional camp, helping avoid duplication and improve coordination of
the health response.
• Health Cluster monitoring tools are being updated to capture specialized care gaps, particularly
trauma care, physiotherapy and rehabilitation, to better identify needs linked to injury
management and early recovery.
• PAHO has deployed six specialists as part of the Regional Response Team to support in health
emergency coordination, logistics, information systems and media, risk communication and
community engagement, and EMT coordination.
CLINICAL CARE:
• Geospatial analysis, based on Copernicus Emergency Management Service satellite imagery, to
classify apparent structural damage, identify priority facilities for field verification, and inform
service-impact analysis and response planning. Available from: Venezuela Hospitals (Earthquake
2026)
• PAHO is supporting the Ministry of Health through rapid health facility assessments and needs
analysis. To date, assessments have been completed at 11 health facilities covering structural
damage, emergency care flows (laboratory and imaging), prehospital coordination, and supply
inventory.
• Supported the Ministry of Health on site visits to assess operational capacities at health facilities
in Caracas and La Guaira, and carried out a separate site visit to La Victoria Hospital (Aragua
state), where a Type 2 Emergency Medical Team (EMT) from Barbados will be installed.

Earthquake in Venezuela
Situation Report N.4
• Mental Health and Psychosocial Support:
o Co-led by PAHO/WHO and IOM, alongside the Ministry of Health, the MHPSS Technical
Working Group is coordinating the response.
o PAHO/WHO, in support of the Ministry of Health, is conducting psychosocial support
interventions in affected areas, including Psychological First Aid (PFA), individual crisis
care, and group emotional regulation activities. Given identified coordination challenges
and protection risks, the shelter response continues to be prioritized.
o Developed and disseminated risk communication and psychosocial support materials,
including mental health guidance messages and information on available helplines.
o Continued strengthening capacities through the promotion of virtual courses offered by
the Virtual Public Health Campus on Psychological First Aid (PFA), mhGAP-HIG, and
additionally self-care and MHPSS. In collaboration with universities and the Federation of
Psychologists, PFA refresher trainings delivered to 217 psychologists to support the
response.
o Maintained, in support of the Ministry of Health, efforts to ensure continuity of care for
people with severe mental disorders and access to essential psychotropic medications.
o The Ministry of Health, alongside PAHO, UNICEF, the Health Cluster, and the Mental
Health and Psychosocial Support Technical Working Group conducted an exploratory visit
to temporary shelters located at Parque del Oeste, Liceo Miguel Antonio Caro, and
Escuela Gran Colombia, in the Capital District. The Health Cluster will continue supporting
coordination efforts with national authorities and humanitarian partners to strengthen the
health response and ensure timely access to essential services for the affected population.
• Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs):
o On 26 June, the Virtual CICOM (Coordination Cell) was established in La Guaira under
the leadership of the Ministry of Health, with technical support from PAHO, to process
international Emergency Medical Team (EMT) offers, and coordinate their acceptance and
deployment.
o Nine Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) are currently providing services in La Guaira,
Caracas, Miranda, and Aragua representing an increase in deployed clinical capacity. An
additional nine teams continue mobilizing toward their assigned locations and are
expected to become operative within the next few hours to days.
o Rehabilitation care has been integrated into the earthquake EMT response. The deployed
Type 3 EMT, Type 2 EMTs and several Type 1 Fixed EMTs have been providing
rehabilitation care as part of their routine clinical services. To further strengthen this
capacity, a dedicated Rehabilitation Specialized Care Team (SCT) is now mobilizing,
reinforcing specialized rehabilitation services and supporting continuity of care for injured
patients.
o The response is progressively transitioning from trauma and hospital surge support
towards primary health care, outpatient services, shelter health and community-based
care, with Type 1 EMTs assuming an increasingly prominent role.
o Nineteen teams remain in standby or monitoring status: 5 on standby and 14 under
monitoring.

COLLABORATIVE SURVEILLANCE:
PAHO/WHO is preparing to scale up laboratory support capacity, should it be requested.
• Reagents and materials for molecular diagnosis and detection of priority pathogens
(arboviruses, hemorrhagic fever viruses, respiratory viruses, and Leptospira) are being readied
for dispatch to the Rafael Rangel National Institute of Hygiene, to support surveillance efforts
if and when needed.
• Anticipating potential needs for identification of human remains through genetic methodologies
and building on previously implemented sequencing platforms in the country, PAHO/WHO is
arranging the procurement of specific supplies for forensic characterization via genetic
markers, including DNA extraction materials and dedicated sequencing kits, for use should the
need arise.
COUNTERMEASURES/ LOGISTICS:
• PAHO/WHO is supporting the response with a delivery of 6 tons of key medical supplies and
medicines:
o On 26 June 2026 delivered 2.18 tons of medical supplies and medicines to the La Guaira
Regional Health Directorate to support care of earthquake-affected patients. Supplies
included a Trauma Kit module (surgical medicines, oral and IV medications, dextrose,
infusion sets, medical consumables), a supplementary Inter-Agency Health Kit module
(injectable medicines), and PPE (gowns, gloves, surgical masks), along with IV catheters,
syringes, and suture materials.
o On 1 July 2026 delivered of 4 tons of supplies from PAHO's Strategic Reserve in Panama
comprising essential medical trauma kits, medicines and supplies, as well as field
equipment—including rapid deployment backpacks, personal protective gear, shelter
items, lighting, water purification supplies, and basic medical and survival tools—designed
to enable immediate response in crisis conditions
▪ TESK Kit: 50 surgical patients / up to 100 emergency surgical interventions
▪ NCD Kit: 10,000 people for 3 months
o In parallel, 320 body bags were dispatched, and coordination was completed for the
placement of 3 refrigerated containers for body management, located at La Guaira port
and the crematoria of Paracoto and Bonanza.

Emergency supply shipment dispatched to Venezuela to support response
operations Source: PAHO/WHO
• In coordination with the Ministry of Health, PAHO is channeling offers from neighboring countries
to facilitate the Ministry's receipt of supplies and ensure adherence to the necessary quality
standards.
• PAHO/WHO, through its Colombia Office and Regional EOC, coordinated with Colombia's
Ministry of Health and Social Protection to mobilize 646 kg of medical supplies to Venezuela,
comprising 3 medicine kits (384 kg) and 2 medical supply kits (262 kg), with logistics supported
by UNGRD and the Colombian Red Cross.
• PAHO worked jointly with the National Health Supplies Corporation (CONSALUD) of the Ministry
of Health, conducting site visits to the Autonomous Service for Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
(SEFAR) warehouse in Las Adjuntas and the CONSALUD Jipana Main Warehouse, to carry out
a preliminary assessment of immediate operational needs. Operations at these facilities have
already been affected by prolonged resource constraints, a situation further compounded by the
high volume of medicines and medical supplies currently being managed in support of the health
system.
• The Ministry of Health of Brazil, with technical and logistical support from PAHO/WHO — including
the procurement of cold boxes for shipment — is donating vaccines to support the population
affected by the earthquake in Venezuela. The donation includes 1.5 million doses, as follows:
o Pentavalent vaccine (DPT-HepB-Hib): 1,000,000 doses
o MMR vaccine (Measles, Mumps, Rubella): 102,000 doses
o BCG vaccine (Tuberculosis): 48,000 doses
o Yellow fever: 100,000 doses
o Canine Rabies Vaccine: 250,000 doses
• The Ministry of Health of Chile, with technical support from PAHO/WHO, has donated
immunization-related supplies to support the response in Venezuela. The donation includes a
total of 76,000 units of vaccines and complementary supplies, as follows:
o Tetanus vaccine (dT): 30,000 doses
o MMR vaccine (Measles, Mumps, Rubella): 5,000 doses
o MMR diluent: 5,000 units
o 1 ml syringes with 23G x 1" needle: 36,000 units

**Destacados**

- Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan casi mil réplicas.**
- Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado.
- Balance oficial: **3.342 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.**
- Los equipos de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano (USAR) continúan desplegados en las zonas afectadas, en coordinación con OCHA, a más de una semana de los terremotos.
- **El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 995 réplicas**.

A más de una semana de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **3.342 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, las autoridades reportan que unas 17.345 personas han quedado damnificadas.

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la preparación de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta.
