documents.title: Venezuela – Operación de respuesta a terremotos, Reporte Situacional #1, 2 Julio 2026
documents.body_text:
**Período de reporte 26 Junio – 2 Julio**

El 24 de junio de 2026 se registraron dos terremotos consecutivos de magnitud 7.2 y 7.5 en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo), afectando a los estados La Guaira (declarado como zona de desastre), Distrito Capital, Miranda, Falcón, Aragua, Carabobo y Yaracuy. Desde el evento hasta la fecha, las autoridades han reportado más de 609 réplicas, 1.719 personas fallecidas, 5.034 personas heridas, 15.866 personas damnificadas y 2.501 edificaciones afectadas. Inicialmente, las prioridades identificadas por el Gobierno Nacional para dar la respuesta humanitaria son los sectores de Salud, Alimentación (ready to eat), Refugio y Agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH).

pdfs.text:
Reporte Situacional #1, 2 Julio 2026
Venezuela – Operación de respuesta a terremotos
Período de reporte 26 Junio – 2 Julio
El 24 de junio de 2026 se registraron dos terremotos consecutivos de magnitud 7.2 y 7.5 en la región centro-
norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo), afectando a los estados
La Guaira (declarado como zona de desastre), Distrito Capital, Miranda, Falcón, Aragua, Carabobo y Yaracuy.
Desde el evento hasta la fecha, las autoridades han reportado más de 609 réplicas, 1.719 personas fallecidas,
5.034 personas heridas, 15.866 personas damnificadas y 2.501 edificaciones afectadas. Inicialmente, las
prioridades identificadas por el Gobierno Nacional para dar la respuesta humanitaria son los sectores de Salud,
Alimentación (ready to eat), Refugio y Agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH).
Tras la desactivación del Clúster de Logística en Venezuela (inicialmente activado en 2019) se realizó una
transición estratégica hacia un Grupo de Trabajo de Logística (GTL) en mayo de 2025. Esta evolución mantiene
el liderazgo del Programa Mundial de Alimentos (WFP) y reafirma el compromiso de continuar trabajando junto
con los actores humanitarios para fortalecer la coordinación logística y mejorar la eficiencia de las respuestas
humanitarias, especialmente en apoyo a las 50 organizaciones miembros del GTL.
Venezuela – Terremoto 2026 sitio web

Reporte Situacional #1, 2 Julio 2026
Venezuela – Operación de respuesta a terremotos
Período de reporte 26 Junio – 2 Julio
1. Actualizaciones logísticas
Generales
En atención a la zona de desastres en La Guaira, se habilitaron tres refugios multiservicios:
o
Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves (Catia La Mar) y el Estadio Playa Grande, este último de
manera provisional.
Aeropuertos
El 26 de junio de 2026, el Gobierno Nacional informó que el Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía
o
(CCS), ubicado en La Guaira, sería destinado exclusivamente para la recepción de carga vinculada a la
operación de respuesta. A la fecha ha sido utilizado para el envío de carga humanitaria de gobierno a
gobierno y del Sistema de Naciones Unidas, pero aún resta conocer los procesos que se establecerán
para que el resto de las organizaciones humanitarias interesadas en apoyar la respuesta.
Las cargas deben ser procesadas con agentes aduanales y ser recomienda incluir todos los servicios de
o
movilización de carga.
Puentes aéreos:
o
 UNICEF, OIM, OPS, ACNUR y el Movimiento Internacional de la Cruz Roja han estado enviando
carga humanitaria a Venezuela durante el período de reporte.
 DG-ECHO y el Departamento de Estado de Estados Unidos están explorando opciones de puentes
aéreos desde Miami, Ciudad de Panamá y otras ubicaciones clave.
 Airlink está listo para mover la carga de socios desde Estados Unidos.
 UNHRD listo para mover la carga de sus socios desde Panamá.
 Socios del sector privado evaluando posibilidades de apoyo según sean las necesidades de las
organizaciones de respuesta (DHL, United Airlines y otros).
El Aeropuerto Internacional Arturo Michelena (VLN) en Valencia, está operativo y funciona con
o
normalidad para vuelos comerciales tras ciertas disrupciones en los primeros días tras los terremotos.
Puertos
El 01 de julio de 2026, las autoridades informaron que el Puerto de La Guaira se habilitaría para recibir
o
únicamente carga humanitaria. Información recopilada por los socios, destaca que los muelles del
norte, del 2 al 4, se observan mayormente sin daños significativos. Se aprecian marcas o impactos
aproximadamente cada 20 metros. En el extremo occidental del muelle 2 se observa una grieta. Los
muelles del norte, del 6 al 8, están siendo utilizados para la identificación de víctimas Los muelles del
sur, del 15 al 20, son antiguos y cuentan con barreras de protección en mal estado. Sin embargo, la
estructura parece estar prácticamente intacta. Se utilizan llantas viejas como defensas. Ese recomienda
Venezuela – Terremoto 2026 sitio web

Reporte Situacional #1, 2 Julio 2026
Venezuela – Operación de respuesta a terremotos
Período de reporte 26 Junio – 2 Julio
contar con barreras de protección propias. La profundidad medida coincide con la profundidad
indicada en la carta náutica. La profundidad junto al muelle 19 es de al menos 9 metros.
De las operaciones en Puerto Cabello, el complejo portuario más importante de Venezuela, no se
o
cuenta con información oficial o verificada acerca de su estado o funcionamiento.
Transporte Terrestre
El acceso a través de la principal vía terrestre hacia La Guaira (Autopista Caracas – La Guaira) está
o
siendo regulado por el Estado Venezolano, quien solicita un permiso obligatorio a todos los vehículos,
con excepción de aquellos pertenecientes a las Naciones Unidas, la Cruz Roja Venezolana y el Comité
Internacional de la Cruz Roja (CICR). Sin embargo, reportes proporcionados por organizaciones socias
confirman que esta situación ha experimentado variaciones diarias.
La vía desde Valencia hasta Caracas se encuentra en condiciones normales. A la fecha no se ha
o
reportado ninguna afectación, en su mayor parte es una vía de doble carril en ambas direcciones.
Repecto al cruce fronterizo terrestre entre Colombia y Venezuela a través del Puente Internacional
o
Simón Bolívar, el Foro Local de Coordinación en Táchira sostuvo una reunión con las autoridades
estatales, quienes indicaron que se prevé autorizar la movilización de vehículos con asistencia
humanitaria desde este punto fronterizo hasta La Guaira. Sin embargo, hasta el momento no se
dispone de información detallada sobre los procedimientos o autorizaciones requeridos para el ingreso
de esta carga al territorio venezolano.
Aduanas y procesos de importación
A la fecha, no se cuenta con un proceso definido para la importación de artículos humanitarios
o
vinculados a la emergencia. Se espera pronunciamiento de las autoridades al respecto.
El Grupo de Trabajo “IMPortation and Customs Clearance Together” (IMPACCT) se ha reunido con los
o
socios de su red RHIC (Regional Humanitarian Importation and Customs) para discutir los principales
desafíos en esta respuesta y abogar por la claridad del proceso con las autoridades, mientras brinda
orientación a los socios. El Grupo IMPACCT puede contactarse a través de impacct.2021@gmail.com.
El día 28 Junio, IMPACCT publicó el primer boletín de Procedimientos de Aduanas (Link) donde se
destacan los siguientes puntos:
 La importación de equipos de telecomunicaciones se encuentra suspendida por CONATEL. Sin
embargo, estos equipos pueden ingresar si cuentan con una autorización expresa emitida por
la Cancillería. Aun así, no se han definido los procedimientos específicos.
 El sistema SIDUNEAWorld se encuentra operativo. Asimismo, se mantienen las
recomendaciones de utilizar la modalidad de “envíos urgentes” para carga humanitaria,
gestionada a través de un agende aduanero autorizado en Venezuela.

Período de reporte 26 Junio – 2 Julio
El boletín incorpora las directrices del Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud (MPPS) sobre los
o
requisitos básicos para recibir donaciones de medicamentos, material médico-quirúrgico y equipos
médicos que sean consignados a este Ente.
Telecomunicaciones
Desde el inicio del desastre hasta la fecha, las telecomunicaciones en La Guaira se mantienen
o
mayormente con señal satelital, con pérdidas de conectividad de hasta el 90%.
Existe cierta conectividad móvil en algunas zonas urbanas, aunque se degrada rápidamente fuera
o
de los centros poblados.
El 26 de junio de 2026, CONATEL otorgó una autorización temporal de uso de espectro a la empresa
o
telefónica Movistar Venezuela para activar un servicio satelital Direct-to-Device (D2D) en el estado
de La Guaira, como medida temporal de emergencia para restablecer la comunicación en la zona
afectada.
Información adicional sobre la conectividad puede encontrarse en LogIE, seleccionando la capa de
o
Mapa de Conectividad (connectivity mapping)
Más información puede encontrarse en el SitRep del Área de Telecomunicaciones de Clúster de
o
Logística y Telecomunicaciones
2. Actividades del Grupo de Trabajo de Logística
Coordinación
• Se han llevado a cabo dos reuniones extraordinarias del Grupo de Trabajo Nacional de Logística como
parte de la operación de respuesta a los terremotos, los días 26 y 29 de junio de 2026 (Minutas 26
Junio y 29 Junio). Más de 40 organizaciones humanitarias asistieron a las reuniones. Los desafíos y
preguntas más comunes de los socios principalmente destacados por los socios principalmente
preguntaron sobre restricciones de acceso físico y sobre los procedimientos de ingreso de carga
humanitaria al país (envío, aduanas e importación y liberación de carga). La próxima reunión está
planeada para el día 2 de Julio a las 17:00.
• A nivel global el Clúster de Logística y Telecomunicaciones también organizó una reunión con los
puntos focales globales de agencias socias y con puntos focales del Grupo de Trabajo Regional de
Logística (LAC) el domingo 28 de junio, con la finalidad de discutir y compartir información acerca de
los vuelos internacionales planeados para el Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar (CCS).
• El GTL, en coordinación con OCHA, ha compartido con los socios dos encuestas para mapear la carga
aérea entrante (pipeline) y el transporte terrestre a La Guaira (movimientos de carga en el país) de las
Agencias, Fondos y Programas de Naciones Unidas. Ambos formularios se difundieron con los socios
Venezuela – Terremoto 2026 sitio web

Reporte Situacional #1, 2 Julio 2026
Venezuela – Operación de respuesta a terremotos
Período de reporte 26 Junio – 2 Julio
afectados y esta información está siendo compartida con el Gobierno para facilitar la preparación y
mejorar la coordinación.
• EL GTL estará llevando a cabo un análisis de brechas y necesidades para identificar y prevenir
impedimentos o cuellos de botella que puedan enfrentan los socios para atender la emergencia. Este
ejercicio, llevado a cabo a través de una encuesta será crítico para definir las prioridades de trabajo del
GTL.
Gestión de la información
• El Grupo de Trabajo de Logística está apoyando a las organizaciones humanitarias en identificar las
rutas posibles y más efectivas para sus suministros. Este esfuerzo se orienta a identificar el estado y
operatividad de los puertos y aeropuertos, accesibilidad de los puntos fronterizos (particularmente con
Colombia) y el estado físico de las carreteras y puentes.
• Con el propósito de facilitar el acceso a esta información, la plataforma LogIE proporciona una visión
dinámica de las principales actualizaciones de mapeo de restricciones físicas de acceso, incluyendo el
estado de los aeropuertos, puertos, infraestructura dañada y puntos de entrada transfronterizos. La
plataforma aloja información adicional en la plataforma sobre gestión de residuos e instalaciones de
reciclaje, mapeo de stocks y conectividad.
• La página web creada para la emergencia contiene toda la información relevante para los socios,
incluyendo los documentos disponibles (minutas, guías de aduanas, etc), información de contacto y el
formulario de suscripción para recibir las comunicaciones del Grupo de Trabajo de Logística.
Provisión de servicios logísticos
El Programa Mundial de Alimentos, a través del Grupo de Trabajo de Logística, está poniendo a disposición de
los socios humanitarios servicios logísticos sin coste para los usuarios. Por el momento, se pone a disposición
de las organizaciones 500 m2 de almacenamiento a corto plazo (máximo 24 horas) en La Guaira para apoyar
las labores de consolidación de carga previa a su distribución. En los próximos días más detalles serán
proporcionados a través de los Procedimientos Operativos Standard (SOPs)

documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #4 (1 de julio de 2026)
documents.body_text:
El cuarto Informe de Situación presenta una actualización sobre el impacto de los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela y resume la respuesta en curso y planificada de la OIM en apoyo a las poblaciones afectadas y a los esfuerzos nacionales.

## Aspectos destacados

Las cifras oficiales reportan al menos 2.295 personas fallecidas, 11.267 heridas, 12.841 personas severamente afectadas y 26.403 personas afectadas tras los terremotos del 24 de junio. Las cifras pendientes de nueva actualización incluyen 855 edificaciones afectadas, 189 colapsos totales y 6.461 personas rescatadas.

Los daños a viviendas e infraestructura urbana continúan generando desplazamiento y necesidades de alojamiento temporal, incluidas familias en campamentos transitorios y personas que duermen fuera de viviendas dañadas por preocupaciones de seguridad o para proteger sus pertenencias.

La OIM continúa apoyando actividades de alojamiento temporal, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección y gestión de información, incluido el apoyo a sitios temporales en La Guaira y la provisión de 809 servicios de asistencia en salud a personas afectadas.

## Actividades de la OIM

La OIM ha continuado apoyando alojamiento, coordinación de sitios y servicios esenciales en campamentos transitorios. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, se organizaron literas con apoyo de líderes comunitarios, se reorganizaron insumos para distribuciones y se reforzaron los procesos de registro e ingreso/salida. La OIM también instaló la primera de siete carpas previstas para proporcionar espacio de descanso para 100 personas. En el Estadio César Nieves, la OIM inició la instalación de espacios con sombra para apoyar la prestación de servicios y a las poblaciones afectadas.

En salud, SMAPS, WASH, protección y datos, la OIM y sus socios han proporcionado 809 servicios de asistencia en salud mediante apoyo directo y brigadas médicas. El 1 de julio, la asistencia incluyó pediatría, ginecología y obstetricia, medicina general e interna, consultas individuales de SMAPS, primeros auxilios psicológicos y cuatro referencias médicas. La OIM también apoyó la llegada de una planta portátil de tratamiento de agua a Maiquetía, continuó brindando orientación en protección y apoyo a referencias de casos, actualizó el mapeo de alojamientos temporales, confirmó el uso de la herramienta IMS de registro de beneficiarios y participó con OCHA en el proceso de Evaluación Rápida de Necesidades.

## Respuesta planificada de la OIM

La respuesta planificada de la OIM continuará priorizando alojamiento temporal seguro, coordinación y gestión de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, datos y evaluaciones de necesidades.

En los campamentos transitorios, la OIM continuará apoyando la planificación de sitios, el registro, la gestión de almacenes y la instalación de carpas y arreglos básicos para mejorar la seguridad, la dignidad y la protección. Esto se complementará con apoyo a la organización comunitaria, normas de convivencia, provisión de información y mecanismos de rendición de cuentas, incluidos AAP, mitigación de riesgos de VBG y medidas de PEAS.

En WASH y salud, la OIM se enfocará en ampliar el acceso a agua segura, promoción de higiene, saneamiento básico y servicios móviles de salud en comunidades afectadas y sitios temporales. El apoyo en salud priorizará equipos médicos, referencias, atención de enfermedades crónicas, salud sexual y reproductiva, primeros auxilios psicológicos y SMAPS, junto con la provisión de medicamentos esenciales, insumos y dispositivos de asistencia para personas con necesidades específicas.

En protección y gestión de información, la OIM continuará el monitoreo de riesgos, las referencias seguras y el apoyo a personas con necesidades específicas, incluidos niños, niñas y adolescentes, personas mayores, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes, y personas afectadas por la pérdida o daño de documentos de identidad. La OIM también apoyará Evaluaciones Rápidas de Necesidades, mientras produce perfiles de sitios, actualizaciones de movilidad, mapas y análisis de necesidades para orientar la priorización multisectorial.

documents.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #4 (1 July 2026)
documents.body_text:
This fourth Situation Report provides an updated overview of the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and outlines IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts.

## Highlights

Official figures report at least 2,295 fatalities, 11,267 injuries, 12,841 people severely affected and 26,403 people affected following the 24 June earthquakes. Figures pending further update include 855 buildings affected, 189 total collapses and 6,461 people rescued.

Damage to housing and urban infrastructure continues to drive displacement and temporary accommodation needs, including among families in temporary sites and people sleeping outside damaged homes due to safety concerns or to protect their belongings.

IOM continues supporting temporary accommodation, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection and information management activities, including support to temporary sites in La Guaira and the provision of 809 health assistance services to affected people.

## IOM activities

IOM has continued supporting shelter, site coordination and essential services in temporary accommodation sites. At Polideportivo José María Vargas, bunk beds were arranged with support from community leaders, supplies were reorganized for distributions, and registration and entry/exit processes were reinforced. IOM also installed the first of seven tents planned to provide sleeping space for 100 people. At Estadio César Nieves, IOM began installing shaded spaces to support service provision and affected populations.

In health, MHPSS, WASH, protection and data, IOM and partners have provided 809 health assistance services through direct support and medical brigades. On 1 July, assistance included paediatrics, gynaecology and obstetrics, general and internal medicine, individual MHPSS consultations, psychological first aid and four medical referrals. IOM also supported the arrival of one portable water treatment plant in Maiquetía, continued protection orientation and referral support, updated temporary accommodation mapping, confirmed the use of an IMS registration tool and participated with OCHA in the Rapid Needs Assessment process.

## IOM planned response

IOM’s planned response will continue prioritizing safe temporary accommodation, site coordination and management, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, and data and needs assessments.

In temporary accommodation sites, IOM will continue supporting site planning, registration, warehouse management and the installation of tents and basic site arrangements to improve safety, dignity and protection. This will be complemented by support to community organization, coexistence rules, information provision and accountability mechanisms, including AAP, GBV risk mitigation and PSEA measures.

In WASH and health, IOM will focus on expanding access to safe water, hygiene promotion, basic sanitation and mobile health services in affected communities and temporary sites. Health support will prioritize medical teams, referrals, chronic disease care, sexual and reproductive health, psychological first aid and MHPSS, alongside the provision of essential medicines, supplies and assistive devices for people with specific needs.

In protection and information management, IOM will continue risk monitoring, safe referrals and support to people with specific needs, including children and adolescents, older persons, pregnant and lactating women, and people affected by the loss or damage of identity documents. IOM will also support Rapid Needs Assessments, while producing site profiles, mobility updates, maps and needs analyses to inform multisectoral prioritization.

## Summary

Guidelines from the Ministry of People's Power for Health on the Donation of Medical Supplies

## Content

  
**GUIDELINES FOR DONATING MEDICAL**  
**SUPPLIES** Donations of medical supplies (medications, surgical supplies, medical equipment) sent to the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) must comply with these guidelines to ensure their effective and efficient distribution and use.  
**General Acceptance Criteria:**  
Donations must comply with the provisions set forth in the List published by the MPPS.  
They must be classified and identified according to  
:- Type of supply: medication, surgical supplies, medical equipment  
\- Name of the supply: catheters, Jelco tubes, IV lines, syringes, gauze, gloves, ETC.  
\- Medical supplies not included on the official list or that require a cold chain must be approved by the Ministry of Popular Power for Health prior to donation, via email to: donacionesmpps2026@gmail.com  
Supplies must have a remaining shelf life of at least 12 months at the time of donation  
.  
All supplies must be clearly labeled in Spanish, English, or Portuguese, indicating the expiration date, manufacturer, country of origin, and lot number.  
Additionally, medication labels must include the following information:  
 Name of the active ingredient(s),  
 Concentration or potency.  
 Dosage form.  
Lists of controlled medications, psychotropic drugs, or narcotic substances must be submitted so that the lists can be signed and stamped by the Autonomous Services of the State Health Oversight Agencies.  
**UNACCEPTED SUPPLIES:**  
\- Expired or past-date products  
\- Any opened or damaged medical supplies  
\- Supplies in individual-dose units from private sources (boxes, ampoules, blister packs, vials, among others)  
\- Mixed medical supplies.  
Donating institutions or organizations must send the supplies to:  
Collection Center, CONSALUD Warehouse (Former SEFAR), Las Adjuntas, Kilometer 0,  
Los Teques Highway.

documents.title: UNAIDS supports efforts to protect the continuity of the HIV response during the emergency in Venezuela
documents.body_text:
**CARACAS/PANAMA CITY, 1 July 2026**—UNAIDS mourns the tragic loss of life and expresses solidarity with the people and communities affected by the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June. UNAIDS reaffirms its commitment to supporting efforts to ensure the continuity of HIV-related services during the emergency.

“The disruption of health services and population displacement caused by the disaster have created significant challenges for people living with HIV and other vulnerable populations,” said Luisa Cabal, UNAIDS Regional Director for Latin America and the Caribbean. “UNAIDS is working alongside national authorities, United Nations agencies, community organizations and development partners to help ensure support and continued access to HIV treatment, care and information.”

According to the latest update from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), at least 2,295 people have lost their lives, more than 11,200 have been injured and over 26,000 have been directly affected. At least 38 hospitals have sustained damage, posing significant challenges to the continuity of health services.

As part of these efforts, the UNAIDS office in Venezuela activated an Emergency Registry to identify and support people living with HIV affected by the crisis. As of 30 June, 69% of registered individuals reported having interrupted their antiretroviral treatment and 28% reported needing psychological support as a result of the emergency, highlighting the urgent need to adopt measures to ensure continuity of care and access to essential medicines.

The United Nations system, in coordination with national authorities, is providing a multisectoral response in three strategic locations across La Guaira state, the area hardest hit by the earthquakes, to address the population’s most urgent needs.

UNAIDS is working with multiple partners to protect the continuity of HIV-related services, in coordination with the United Nations Development Programme. In addition, in collaboration with the Venezuelan Network of Positive People (Red Venezolana de Gente Positiva), UNAIDS is strengthening community-based mechanisms to facilitate access to antiretroviral treatment and provide timely information to people affected.

During the first week of the humanitarian response, UNAIDS adapted existing guidance for HIV in emergencies to be applied in the specific context of Venezuela for the support to people living with HIV during emergencies and disasters. The guidance is intended for the Health Cluster and partner organizations within the Humanitarian Country Team that lead interventions in the initial shelters and reception sites established, to support continuity of care and protect the rights of affected people.

**UNAIDS**

The Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) leads and inspires the world to achieve its shared vision of zero new HIV infections, zero discrimination and zero AIDS-related deaths. UNAIDS unites the efforts of 11 UN organizations—UNHCR, UNICEF, WFP, UNDP, UNFPA, UNODC, UN Women, ILO, UNESCO, WHO and the World Bank—and works closely with global and national partners towards ending the AIDS epidemic by 2030 as part of the Sustainable Development Goals. Learn more at [unaids.org](https://www.unaids.org/en) and connect with us on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/UNAIDS), [Twitter](https://twitter.com/#!/UNAIDS), [Instagram](https://instagram.com/unaidsglobal) and [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/user/UNAIDS).

Venezuela Earthquake Response: Expected Needs, Next 96 Hours
Situation Update and Response Actors — As of 01 July 2026 | 1700 ET / 2100Z
Most Affected: Yaracuy and Carabobo | M7.2 + M7.5 Twin Earthquakes Recovery Phase · Day 7

Dead Injured Registered Displaced In Temporary Camps Total Affected

The response is transitioning from live rescue to recovery. Live rescues are now rare exceptions. Missing-persons estimates range from tens of
thousands (unverified crowd-sourced registries cite 43,000 to 46,000), against no confirmed official figure. The UN is planning against a scenario of up
to 10,000 deaths.
Key Focus Areas
Remains recovery and mortuary affairs
10,000 body bags being procured (UN/GoV agreement); provisional morgue reported at Bolipuerto, La Guaira. Forensic and morgue services overwhelmed
(PAHO ERES); 2,295 confirmed dead vs 43,000–50,000 missing across unofficial registries and UN-cited estimates; no reconciled official figure. USAR-to-recovery
transition expected within 24–72 hrs.
Debris removal and site clearance
855 buildings severely damaged; 189 total collapses (158 in La Guaira); ~2,500 destroyed per DEC estimate. GoV inspection committee applying red/yellow/green
habitability tagging since 29 Jun. Heavy machinery shortages reported by affected communities (30 Jun); no national debris volume estimate or disposal plan;
demolition-before-remains-recovery sequencing undefined.
Health system restoration
Critical 3 of 21 assessed facilities critical, 6 partially functional; 91 hospitals in MMI VI+ zones. Trauma caseload of 10,571 injured; three UN field hospitals in La Guaira.
PAHO US$24M appeal launched 1 Jul (6-month health recovery, ~700,000 people) – currently unfunded. La Guaira maternal care coordination gap confirmed.
Shelter and housing (transitional / permanent)
Critical 28,380 in temporary camps; 15,866 registered victims; 39% of housing-displaced remain in streets/public spaces (UNHCR). 14–15 state shelters in La Guaira plus
55 nationwide. GoV end-of-2026 rehousing pledge lacks financing and required soil surveys; storm on 30 Jun exposed tented populations.
WASH infrastructure repair
National water system severely compromised; 400+ schools and water systems damaged (combined UN figure). GoV claim of restored La Guaira water service
uncorroborated and conflicts with field reporting of acute scarcity. Outbreak risk (dengue, measles, diarrheal disease) rising in crowded shelters; trucking
coverage of 69+ shelters unconfirmed.
Psychosocial support and mental health
Severe OCHA assesses emotional support as essential as food/water; PAHO expanding MHPSS for families of missing, health workers, responders. No dedicated
program for 15,400+ registered volunteers or forensic staff; MHPSS presence at provisional morgue unconfirmed.
Critical infrastructure (power, comms, transport)
Caracas Metro and Metrobús fully restored 30 Jun. Maiquetía partially reopened 27 Jun on runway 10R only (10L unserviceable); military/humanitarian flights
Severe under prior-authorization NOTAM expiring 2 Jul – decision point inside window. Commercial traffic diverted to Valencia (Arturo Michelena), which IATA warns is
near saturation. Grid damage in epicentral Yaracuy/Carabobo unassessed.
Protection and vulnerable populations
680,000 children among 1.8M in need (UNICEF). Mixed-sex shelters without separated sanitation; elevated gender-based violence and child abuse risk (Plan Intl
Severe field reporting). Deported-migrant cohort (Hotel Santuario dead) requires distinct tracing. Looting reported in EQ zone; 40 NGOs protest militarized QR-code
access controls in La Guaira. No published shelter safety standard or gender-based violence referral pathway.

Following the devastating earthquakes that struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, thousands of families
have been affected by loss of life, injuries, displacement, damage to homes and disruption of essential services.
UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, is scaling up its response and seeks USD 14.85 million in flexible funding to

The response will focus on protection, emergency relief items and temporary shelter support for displaced and
vulnerable populations, including refugees, asylum-seekers, returnees and affected host communities.
UNHCR is working with local authorities to assess needs and identify how UNHCR can further support response efforts.

UNHCR Preparedness and Response | Venezuela Earthquake Emergency 2026
OVERVIEW AND HUMANITARIAN IMPACT
The boundaries and names shown and the designations used on this map do not imply official endorsement or acceptance by the United Nations. Creation date: As of 27 June (8:00 GMT-4)
Sources: OCHA Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) Team Snapshot
On 24 June 2026, two major earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela, causing
extensive loss of life, injuries, displacement and damage in densely populated areas. As of 29 June, at least 1,719
people had been reported dead, more than 5,034 remained in hospitals and 15,866 people were reported affected,
with figures expected to evolve as search-and-rescue operations continue.
The most severe impact has been reported in La Guaira and the Greater Caracas area, with damage also recorded
in Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and Aragua. Multiple aftershocks continue to endanger affected
communities and weaken already damaged structures. Updated reports indicate 2,501 damaged infrastructure
sites, including 774 housing units and 38 hospitals, while 189 housing units have completely collapsed.
Damage to electricity, water, telecommunications, roads, bridges, health facilities and the Simón Bolívar
International Airport in Maiquetía has disrupted essential services and constrained access.
Many families are staying with relatives or neighbours, sleeping in streets and public spaces, or sheltering in
churches, schools, stadiums and other improvised sites. In La Guaira, food shortages, lack of connectivity and
disruptions to basic services are increasing pressure on communities.
The impact is unfolding in a context of pre-existing vulnerabilities, limited household coping capacity and already
strained basic services. The emergency has a strong protection dimension. Families displaced from unsafe homes
face heightened risks, particularly where shelters lack privacy, lighting, water and sanitation, and referral
mechanisms. Refugees, asylum-seekers, returnees, older persons, persons with disabilities, children and people
without documentation may face additional barriers to information, assistance and services. Immediate priorities
include protection services, identification and referral of people with specific needs, mental health and psychosocial
support, child protection, gender-based violence prevention and response, core relief items and temporary shelter
assistance.
3

UNHCR Preparedness and Response | Venezuela Earthquake Emergency 2026
RESPONSE STRATEGY
Why UNHCR is responding
The earthquakes have displaced families, damaged homes and public infrastructure, and increased protection risks
across affected areas. Many people are sheltering in collective centres or improvised sites where access to
information, services, privacy and referral mechanisms remains limited. Refugees, asylum-seekers, returnees and
vulnerable host communities may face additional barriers to assistance and recovery.
UNHCR is scaling up its response to support up to 30,000 earthquake-affected people over six months, focusing
on protection, emergency relief items and temporary shelter

WHAT THE FUNDING WILL DELIVER
Objective 1 | Protect people at heightened risk
UNHCR will help earthquake-affected people access protection, information and essential services, with priority
given to those facing the greatest risks.
Funding will enable UNHCR to:
identify and support people with specific protection needs, including children at risk, older persons, persons
with disabilities and people requiring urgent referrals;
provide legal orientation and support to people who have lost civil or identity documents;
support local authorities with tools and equipment for the safe collection and management of information on
affected people
strengthen referral pathways for protection, health, psychosocial support and other critical services;
expand community-based protection and information-sharing in affected communities and shelter sites;
provide mental health and psychosocial support and specialized protection services, including for survivors of
gender-based violence and children at risk.
Objective 2 | Meet immediate household needs and promote safe and dignified temporary
accommodation
UNHCR will help displaced families meet urgent basic needs after losing access to homes, belongings and
services.
Funding will enable UNHCR to:
Distribute emergency relief items to displaced families.
Support vulnerable households living in temporary, collective shelters public spaces and improvised sites.
prioritize assistance for families with specific needs and limited coping capacity;
provide essential household items such as blankets, sleeping mats, hygiene items, kitchen sets, solar lamps
and water containers.
promote protection-sensitive shelter standards, including safe access, lighting, privacy, and referral
mechanisms;
support authorities and partners to reduce risks in shelter settings and improve access to services.
Provide tents, housing units and other shelter solutions to support functional spaces for protection services,
case management, safe referrals and assistance, including support related to gender-based violence, in
multi-service centres and formal collective centres.
COORDINATION
The earthquake response is led by national authorities through Venezuela’s established emergency coordination
structure. UNHCR will align its activities with the Government-led response, the Resident and Humanitarian
Coordinator, OCHA and inter-agency coordination mechanisms to ensure complementarity with search-and-rescue
operations and sectoral response efforts.
UNHCR brings a clear coordination role and operational capacity to the response. As Protection Cluster lead in
Venezuela, UNHCR is supporting rapid analysis of protection risks, mapping of critical services and coordination
among protection partners. The Protection Cluster has activated coordination with its Strategic Advisory Group and
Areas of Responsibility, including Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence, to identify immediate priorities,
strengthen referral pathways and support safe access to services. Partners are updating service mapping for mental
health and psychosocial support, child protection, gender-based violence prevention and response, legal
orientation, family tracing and assistance for people with specific needs.
UNHCR is also supporting coordination on emergency shelter, core relief items and temporary shelter standards
through the Infrastructure and Temporary Shelter Working Group. This includes mapping available stocks,
identifying gaps, providing technical guidance on temporary site arrangements and helping ensure that shelter
interventions integrate protection standards, including safety, privacy, accessibility, lighting, and referral
mechanisms.
UNHCR will continue working closely with OCHA, Civil Protection, the Venezuelan Red Cross, national and local
authorities, operational partners and community networks. The response will be guided by rapid assessments,
protection monitoring, partner reporting and inter-agency prioritization. This coordination approach will help avoid
duplication, target available resources and ensure that assistance reaches the most at-risk earthquake-affected
families.
5

UNHCR Preparedness and Response | Venezuela Earthquake Emergency 2026
FINANCIAL REQUIREMENTS
This appeal seeks US$ 14.85 million for the period July to December 2026 to support UNHCR’s immediate
earthquake response in Venezuela. Funding will enable UNHCR to reach up to 30,000 people, prioritizing
displaced families, refugees, asylum-seekers, returnees and affected host communities facing heightened
protection risks. The response will focus on life-saving protection services, core relief items and temporary shelter
support in the most affected areas, particularly La Guaira, Caracas and Miranda, and other locations where needs
are confirmed through rapid assessments and inter-agency coordination.

Core Relief Items & Shelter $10.850.000
Existing resources are insufficient to meet the scale and urgency of earthquake-related needs in Venezuela. Before
the earthquakes, UNHCR’s Venezuela operation was only 11 per cent funded, with an indicative funding gap of US$
39.9 million against 2026 requirements. The emergency has created additional protection, relief item and
temporary shelter needs that cannot be absorbed without affecting ongoing activities for refugees, asylum-seekers,
returnees and host communities. Timely and flexible funding is therefore essential to enable UNHCR to scale up
life-saving protection services, deliver emergency relief items and support safe temporary shelter for the most at-
risk affected families.

Flexible funding will also help UNHCR respond

target assistance where it is most needed and
adjust the response as the situation develops.
Timely and flexible donor support is essential to
enable UNHCR to protect and assist earthquake-

seekers, returnees and vulnerable host
communities, as the humanitarian situation
continues to evolve.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake Emergency Update 24-29 June 2026
documents.body_text:
• Two major earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June, with the strongest impact reported in La Guaira and the Greater Caracas area.

• As of 29 June, at least 1,719 people had been reported dead, more than 5,034 people injured and 15,866 were reported affected. Figures are expected to evolve as search-and-rescue operations and assessments continue.

• Updated reports indicate 2,501 damaged infrastructure sites, including 774 housing units and 38 hospitals. Among housing units, 189 have completely collapsed, while others have sustained damage or partial collapse.

• Families displaced from damaged or unsafe homes are staying with relatives, in streets and public spaces, and in churches, schools, stadiums and other improvised shelters. Many temporary sites do not yet meet minimum protection standards.

• UNHCR is supporting local authorities in set-up of government-led multi-service centres, while providing tools and equipment for the safe collection and management of information to identify protection needs, deliver protection services, and facilitate referrals to appropriate specialized services.

• UNHCR is scaling up support in two priority areas: protection and core relief items and shelter, and requires $14.8 million to support up to 30,000 earthquake-affected people over six months.

• Initial reports also indicate that a temporary accommodation site used for the reception of returnees in La Guaira was severely affected, underscoring the specific risks faced by people who were already in vulnerable situations prior to the earthquake.

and requires $14.8 million to support up to 30,000 earthquake-affected people over six months.

www.unhcr.org 1

EMERGENCY UPDATE > Venezuela Earthquake
Operational context
On 24 June 2026, two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela,
severely affecting densely populated urban and coastal areas. La Guaira and the Greater Caracas area
have reported the most significant impact, with damage also recorded in Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy,
Falcón and Aragua. Multiple aftershocks continue to create risks for affected communities, further
weaken damaged structures and complicate humanitarian operations.
The earthquakes have caused extensive loss of life, injuries, displacement and disruption of essential
services. Damage to electricity, water, telecommunications, roads, bridges, health facilities and the
Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía has affected mobility, access to services and the
operating environment for the response. In La Guaira, damage to key infrastructure has further
constrained access to severely affected areas.
Thousands of people are unable or unwilling to return to damaged homes because of structural risks
and fear of aftershocks. Affected families are staying with relatives and neighbours, sleeping in streets
and public spaces, or seeking shelter in churches, educational facilities, stadiums, sports facilities and
other improvised sites. Rapid protection monitoring indicates that many temporary shelters and
improvised sites do not yet meet minimum standards for safety, privacy, lighting, water and sanitation,
and referral mechanisms.
The emergency is unfolding in a context of pre-existing vulnerabilities, limited household coping
strategies and strained basic services. Refugees, asylum-seekers, returnees and affected host
communities may face additional barriers to information, assistance and services, including
documentation challenges, reduced support networks and difficulties navigating referral pathways.
Humanitarian response
UNHCR is supporting the Government-led emergency response in coordination with the Resident
and Humanitarian Coordinator, OCHA, national and local authorities, the Venezuelan Red Cross,
partners and community networks. UNHCR’s response focuses on protection and core relief items
and shelter, drawing on its established presence in Venezuela, partner network, Protection Cluster
leadership and shelter and relief expertise.
Protection
• UNHCR conducted a rapid needs assessment in La Guaira, the Capital District, Miranda, Aragua
and Carabobo to identify protection risks and priority needs among affected communities. The
assessment found major concerns related to mental health, displacement, family separation, lack
of private spaces in shelters and risks affecting older persons, persons with disabilities and
children.
• UNHCR is supporting the set-up of government-led multi-service centres in La Guaira to help
local authorities safely collect and manage information on affected people, identify specific
protection needs, deliver protection services, provide on-site support where possible and
facilitate referrals to appropriate specialized services. To support this work, UNHCR donated IT
equipment and provided technical training to help authorities systematize information on
earthquake affected people and strengthen referrals to appropriate services.
www.unhcr.org 2

EMERGENCY UPDATE > Venezuela Earthquake
• UNHCR is working through the Protection Cluster and partners to support coordinated referrals,
including through the Interagency Help Line, which is operating in close coordination with the
Protection Cluster to share information on available services and facilitate referrals.
• UNHCR, together with the Protection Cluster, engaged with the Social Sector Vice Presidency to
discuss three mechanisms proposed by the authorities to expand protection outreach, with a
particular focus on child protection: (i) deployment of territorial brigades for the registration of
children, adolescents and families; (ii) establishment of government-led multi-service centres
under a “one-stop shop” approach; and (iii) setting up temporary accommodation spaces where
protection services are expected to be delivered.
Core Relief items & Shelter
UNHCR is mobilizing and pre-positioning core relief items to support affected people and
complement the response led by authorities and partners.
• UNHCR is moving non-food items from its warehouse in Táchira to La Guaira and is
increasing the availability of items for distribution through multi-service centres, based on
identified needs.
• LATAM is supporting the transport of UNHCR core relief items from Panama and Colombia,
including more than 20 tons of items from Panama.
• Civil Defence teams across the country are distributing relief items previously donated by
UNHCR as they move to the most affected areas.
• In Táchira, the UNHCR-supported multi-service centre is being used by local Civil Defence
authorities and community members as a collection point for community-donated supplies
for people affected by the earthquakes.
• UNHCR partner Cáritas installed UNHCR tents and a rub hall at the Episcopal Conference
premises to help safeguard medicines, clothing, food and other relief items, supporting the
reception and management of donations.
• FUNDELEC, a government-affiliated foundation, reported that it will install 182 solar-
powered outdoor lights previously donated by UNHCR in affected areas of La Guaira, helping
improve safety and visibility in areas affected by service disruptions.
• UNHCR is supporting authorities in La Guaira to set-up three government-led multi-sectoral
centres that are currently functioning as temporary shelters and hosting more than 3,000
people. These centres aim to provide immediate multi-sectoral assistance to affected people
and support referrals to accommodation facilities being identified by authorities.
• Cáritas Venezuela is supporting the establishment of shelters for affected people in Caracas
and La Guaira, using 400 tents previously donated by UNHCR.
• In Los Corales, La Guaira, at least 10 family groups are sheltering in a community centre
previously built by UNHCR. The community is also using the centre to prepare meals for
around 300 people per day.
Coordination
• The earthquake response is led by national authorities through Venezuela’s established
emergency coordination structure. UNHCR is aligning its activities with the Government-led
response, the Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, OCHA and inter-agency coordination

mechanisms to ensure complementarity with search-and-rescue operations and sectoral
response efforts.
• As Protection Cluster lead in Venezuela, UNHCR is supporting rapid analysis of protection
risks, mapping of critical services and coordination among protection partners. The Protection
Cluster has activated coordination with its Strategic Advisory Group and Areas of
Responsibility, including Child Protection and Violence Against Women and Childre, to
identify immediate priorities, strengthen referral pathways and support safe access to
services.
• Through the Infrastructure and Temporary Shelter Working Group, UNHCR is also supporting
coordination on emergency shelter, core relief items and temporary shelter standards. This
includes mapping available stocks, identifying gaps, supporting technical guidance for
temporary site arrangements and helping ensure that shelter interventions integrate
protection standards.
• The Shelter and Infrastructure Working Group finalized the operational plan for the
government-led multi-service centres approach. The centres will bring protection services,
information, counselling, and referrals closer to affected populations through community

imminently, with humanitarian partners already mobilized for implementation.

documents.title: Venezuela earthquake: ICRC mobilizes rapid response in support of the Venezuelan Red Cross
sources: International Committee of the Red Cross
documents.body_text:
**In the days following the 24 June earthquakes, the Venezuelan Red Cross (VRC) has moved quickly to support affected communities and national authorities. The ICRC supported their efforts, with emergency assistance spanning water, health, forensic management and detainee welfare.**

## Water supply

So far, the ICRC has donated **18,400 water purification tablets** to Venezuela's Ministry of Water (MPPAA), enabling the treatment of up to **755,000 litres of water** for use in hospitals. According to Sphere standards, this quantity can cover the daily water needs of approximately 50,000 people at 15 litres per person per day.

**21 water cisterns** were also delivered to four hospitals and two shelters in La Guaira, the most affected area, providing more than **297,000 litres of water**. Additionally, **300 twenty-litre water bottles** were donated to the Ministry of Water, and **9,000 plastic bags** and **24 protective goggles** were donated to the Caracas fire service.

ICRC water and habitat engineers also provided technical support to the Venezuelan Red Cross WASH team, contributing to the design of shower facilities and the electrical systems for the field hospital in La Guaira, and procured and installed eight showers and a generator for the field hospital, as well as **14 waste containers** for use at the facility.

## Health

The ICRC has provided **technical support and medical supplies** to the Venezuelan Red Cross, including assistance in setting up a field hospital in La Guaira. On 26 June, the ICRC supported the transportation of a VRC water purification unit from Barquisimeto to La Guaira Stadium, where the field hospital is operating, so that it can provide clean water for both patients and the surrounding population.

## Forensic support

The ICRC donated a total of **540 body bags** over 25 and 26 June to the National Forensic Medicine and Forensic Sciences Service (SENAMECF) at Bello Monte.

On 27 June, a further **650 body bags** were distributed across three locations in La Guaira and an additional 150 body bags were donated to the Caracas fire service. The ICRC also provided technical guidance to the VRC field hospital team on setting up a temporary morgue tent.

## Economic security and essential items

**100 mattresses and sheets** were donated to the Venezuelan Red Cross headquarters. The ICRC also provided technical support to the VRC Disaster Risk Management Directorate for a rapid basic needs assessment and information management.

## Detainees and people deprived of liberty

The ICRC intervened with prison authorities to facilitate Restoring Family Links (RFL) activities for people deprived of liberty. Information was shared to help them notify their families and re-establish contact with relatives from whom they had been separated. In addition, **300 individual hygiene kits** – 150 for men and 150 for women – were donated to the Ministry of Prison Services (MPPSP).

## Restoring family links (RFL) and connectivity

The ICRC has provided **10 mobile phones** to the Venezuelan Red Cross to support connectivity and family links activities and helped the VRC activate communication systems previously donated. Nine VRC volunteers received basic training on connectivity services and family links needs assessment. The ICRC also accompanied VRC teams conducting RFL needs assessments at four hospitals in Caracas and at two shelters, and supported the VRC hotline, providing direct assistance to people calling for information.

In addition, **two laptops** were made available to the VRC, and communications systems previously donated by the ICRC were deployed to La Guaira to support connectivity for the response. A family links assessment was conducted in La Guaira to map shelters, identify people with family contact needs, and assess the response capacity of local authorities and other organizations.

### Continuing support for communities

The ICRC has been present in Venezuela since 1966, working alongside national authorities, the Venezuelan Red Cross, and civil society to address the humanitarian consequences of violence, detention, and displacement. In the wake of the earthquake on 24 June, we have drawn on our established presence and partnerships across the country to scale up support rapidly. We will continue to assess needs and adjust our response in the coming days.

documents.title: Health risks for children skyrocket one week after Venezuela earthquakes – Save the Children
documents.body_text:
Aid agencies are racing to deliver hygiene kits and other essential supplies to Caracas and La Guaira, as families sheltering outside face high temperatures in the day and heavy downpours at night, putting them at risk of dehydration, diarrhoea and respiratory illnesses.

**CARACAS, 2 July 2026 —** Children affected by last week’s earthquakes in Venezuela are facing increasing health risks as many families in shelters and temporary settlements lack access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services, Save the Children said.

Aid agencies are racing to deliver hygiene kits and other essential supplies to Caracas and La Guaira – two areas hardest hit by the earthquakes – as families sheltering outside face high temperatures in the day and heavy downpours at night, putting them at risk of dehydration, diarrhoea and respiratory illnesses. The disaster comes at a time when Venezuela’s healthcare system is already under pressure to meet urgent medical needs.

Powerful storms, rain and thunder – which frequently occur during the peak months of the rainy season - are also adding to the anxiety children are facing. Parents of children sheltering outside in tents have told our teams on the ground how powerful storms, rain and thunder, have left children already distressed from the devastating earthquakes terrified.

**Paolina\*, a Save the Children staff member in Venezuela, said:**

*“Many people have lost their homes. Many have lost family members. This is undoubtedly overwhelming... facing this situation and seeing all these children affected.*

*"The experience has been traumatic for many adults and especially for children, many of whom still do not understand what happened in Venezuela.”*

More than [600 aftershocks](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/terremotos-en-venezuela-reporte-de-situacion-6-29-de-junio-de-2026-hora-0600-pm) have been recorded since the initial earthquakes, according to the UN, with many children too scared to sleep indoors one week on.

About 680,000 children have been impacted by the earthquakes, according to the UN.

Save the Children has launched a humanitarian response to help people in the affected regions, as survivors desperately need assistance such as health and psychosocial support and mobile safe spaces where children are protected and can get emergency items, such as shelter kits, tents and hygiene kits, and learning activities while schools remain closed.

**Fatima Andraca, Save the Children’s Country Director in Venezuela, said:**

*“The earthquakes have already taken a devastating toll on children. Now a lack of adequate shelter, clean water and exposure to the elements including heavy downpours are creating a second emergency, exposing families sleeping outdoors or in informal settlements to new health risks. Hospitals have been damaged and are strained with the thousands of injuries they are trying to treat. If illnesses or other health risks intensify, the pressure on the health system will only worsen. Families urgently need access to clean and safe drinking water, adequate shelter, and mobile health care if they do get sick.”*

Save the Children is on the ground in Venezuela, working with authorities and local partners and will be providing primary healthcare through mobile clinics, distributing hygiene kits, clean water and essential supplies, and setting up safe spaces where children can access mental health support and continue learning while schools remain closed. The organisation will also be providing coordinated child protection services with key stakeholders.

Save the Children is an independent, impartial child rights organisation with our focus on the urgent humanitarian needs of children and families in Venezuela.

Save the Children has been working in Venezuela since 2019. Since the humanitarian crisis started to rapidly deteriorate a few years ago, Save the Children has been scaling its response through local partners to support the increasing number of children in need. Save the Children is delivering health, nutrition, education, child protection, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene and food security and livelihoods support.

Nearly five days after the twin earthquakes struck, frequent aftershocks on the ground are being felt by Save the Children teams in Venezuela, causing further terror for children.

People walk past a collapsed building following an earthquake in Caracas on June 25, 2026. Manaure Quintero / AFP via Getty Images

Save the Children’s teams and local partners on the ground have reported child deaths and injuries and children have been confirmed separated from their families during evacuations in the capital Caracas and La Guaira – a major port city.

Buildings damaged by earthquakes in Caracas, Venezuela on 24 June 2026. Save the Children

Save the Children is assessing the situation on the ground and working with our staff and local partners to understand urgent needs and support affected families as quickly as possible.

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Acute and Compounding Risks to Children – Flash Update #1
documents.body_text:
1. Situation at a Glance

On 24 June 2026, two successive earthquakes of 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude struck north-central Venezuela — the strongest seismic event in Venezuela in over 100 years.  
Five days into the response, the scale of destruction continues to grow, and only now are we beginning to understand the true magnitude of the devastation.

At least 1,430 people have been killed, more than 3,238 injured, and over 68,900 reported missing. According to the President of the National Assembly, Jorge Rodriguez, 774 buildings collapsed (189 were completely destroyed) and 2,501 buildings were damaged, including hospitals, shopping centers, bridges and roads. In La Guaira alone, more than 1,400 buildings were destroyed and more than 11,200 people are missing. A magnitude 4.7 aftershock on 26 June caused additional building damage in Caracas and collapsed the bridge connecting Caraballeda to the rest of La Guaira, further disrupting relief efforts. A damaged runway at Simon Bolivar International Airport delayed the arrival of rescue teams; however, as of June 28, 30 international search and rescue teams with more than 1,600 personnel and over 100 dogs are on the ground. More than 400 aftershocks have been recorded in total.)

The UNDP estimated direct physical damage of between USD 4.7 and 8.7 billion — approximately 6% of Venezuela's GDP — not including infrastructure loss, longterm economic disruption or reconstruction costs.

This emergency is compounding an already fragile humanitarian situation: prior to the earthquakes, nearly 8 million people in Venezuela were already in need of humanitarian assistance.

documents.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #01 (Reporting period: 24–30 June 2026)
documents.body_text:
*This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.*

**Summary Points**

• Two high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) caused widespread damage across north-central Venezuela, disrupting telecommunications infrastructure and services in several of the country's most densely populated areas.

• Internet and mobile connectivity remain significantly affected in La Guaira and other impacted locations, with restoration efforts supported by emergency measures including temporary satellite-based communications services.

• LTC Telecoms is coordinating with partners to assess connectivity gaps, support response planning, and mobilize emergency telecommunications and information management support for humanitarian responders.

Venezuela: Earthquakes
LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #01
Reporting period: 24–30 June 2026
This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026
(magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for
the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.
Summary Points
• Two high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5)
caused widespread damage across north-central
Venezuela, disrupting telecommunications
infrastructure and services in several of the
country's most densely populated areas.
• Internet and mobile connectivity remain significantly
affected in La Guaira and other impacted locations,
with restoration efforts supported by emergency
measures including temporary satellite-based
communications services.
• LTC Telecoms is coordinating with partners to
assess connectivity gaps, support response
planning, and mobilize emergency
telecommunications and information management
A destroyed residential building in Catia La
support for humanitarian responders.
Mar, a coastal community in La Guaira state
near Caracas, located close to the epicentral
area of the earthquakes. Photo: Ronald Pena
R/EPA.
Situation Overview
On 24 June 2026, two high‑magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) struck north‑central Venezuela in
rapid succession, with epicentres located near Morón in the Yaracuy–Carabobo region, approximately
150 kilometres west of Caracas.
The earthquakes generated widespread strong ground shaking across north‑central Venezuela. Areas
along the Yaracuy–Carabobo–Caracas corridor experienced Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) VII (very
strong) to MMI VIII (severe) shaking. Preliminary estimates indicate that approximately 6.1 million
people were exposed to MMI ≥ VII and 644,000 to MMI ≥ VIII, with the highest concentrations of
damage expected in urban centres including the Capital District, La Guaira and Carabobo states. The
intensity distribution suggests significant structural damage and disruption to critical infrastructure,
particularly in densely populated areas.
The Government of Venezuela has declared a state of emergency and activated national response
mechanisms, prioritizing search and rescue, emergency medical care, and rapid damage assessments.
1 The ETC and Logistics Cluster have been merged into the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), following the humanitarian reset in 2025.
Bringing logistics and emergency telecommunications under one coordination structure, the WFP-led LTC is the backbone of the entire humanitarian
response, enabling humanitarian action to move, communicate, coordinate, and deliver lifesaving assistance.
Page 1 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

The response is being led by national authorities, including the National Directorate of Civil Protection
and Disaster Management (Protección Civil).
At the international level, the UN and humanitarian partners are supporting government-led efforts.
OCHA is coordinating international assistance, including the deployment of Urban Search and Rescue
(USAR) teams and surge support through the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination
(UNDAC) mechanism. Multiple humanitarian organizations, including IOM, UNICEF and the Red Cross
Movement, are mobilizing emergency shelter, health, WASH and protection assistance while
supporting the restoration of critical services and infrastructure.
Telecommunications Overview
Telecommunications infrastructure sustained significant damage and remains substantially disrupted
across key affected areas, including Caracas, La Guaira, Petare and Catia. According to network
monitoring data, including analysis from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Disaster
Connectivity Map (DCM), national internet connectivity dropped sharply from over 90 percent to
approximately 59–65 percent immediately following the earthquakes on 24 June before partially
recovering to around 77 percent within the first 24–48 hours. Connectivity remains below normal levels
in many locations.
The severity of disruptions varies considerably by region. La Guaira remains the most affected area,
with connectivity losses reaching up to 90 percent immediately after the event and services continuing
to operate at reduced capacity. In contrast, connectivity in Caracas has largely recovered, although
isolated outages persist, while disruptions continue across parts of Yaracuy and Carabobo states.
Mobile and fixed networks continue to experience outages, congestion, and intermittent service,
driven in part by persistent power disruptions affecting telecommunications infrastructure. Users have
reported service interruptions across Caracas, Miranda and La Guaira, particularly on Movistar
networks, while other operators, including Digitel, appear to have been less affected in some locations.
High call congestion continues to hinder communications, including efforts by affected populations to
contact relatives. Field teams in La Guaira report that connectivity remains extremely limited outside
areas supported by satellite communications, with only isolated Starlink connectivity available near key
response locations.
Venezuela's three main telecommunications providers (Movistar, Digitel and CANTV) have introduced
emergency measures to support affected communities, including temporary free calls and SMS
services. CANTV also provided free internet, fixed telephone and television services for 48 hours.
Additional emergency connectivity support is being provided through satellite-based solutions. Despite
these efforts, outages and service instability persist.
Telecommunications disruptions continue to constrain communication between affected populations
and responders, limiting situational awareness and the coordination of response activities. Recovery
remains closely linked to the restoration of power and other critical infrastructure. Despite recent
emergency authorizations, regulatory uncertainty surrounding the longer-term use and importation of
satellite communications equipment continues to complicate efforts to expand emergency
connectivity.
Page 2 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

LTC Telecoms Activities
Coordination
LTC Telecoms began monitoring communications networks immediately after the event through
established partner coordination channels to identify connectivity gaps and assess support needs. No
formal surge request or cluster activation has been received. Coordination is being managed remotely
by national, regional, and global teams. Telecommunications coordination is taking place through the
WFP-led ICT Working Group, alongside broader humanitarian coordination efforts led by OCHA and the
UNDAC mission deployed on 25 June.
Based on needs identified to date, planned telecommunications support includes establishing
coordination mechanisms in Caracas with national authorities and service providers, and supporting
government-led efforts to ensure equitable connectivity access in high-impact areas, including Petare,
Catia, and La Guaira. Priority is being given to locations where telecommunications disruptions are
compounded by limited access to shelter, healthcare, and response capacity.
Additional planned support includes the provision of common connectivity services at key operational
sites, such as distribution points, hospitals, USAR bases, airports, temporary shelters and humanitarian
coordination hubs, as well as the establishment of community access points to enable affected
populations to restore communication.
LTC Telecoms partners are mobilizing telecommunications support capabilities for the response.
Emergency.lu has deployed telecommunications specialists and equipment to La Guaira, MapAction
has deployed mapping and information management capacity, and Disaster Tech Lab has pre-
positioned Starlink terminals and solar power systems for deployment pending authorization to enter
the country. ITU continues to provide connectivity monitoring and analysis products to support
response planning.
Internet connectivity
SpaceX has activated its disaster response offer, providing Starlink connectivity kits with three months
of free service to support response operations. While Starlink and other satellite communications
solutions, including VSAT systems, are not fully licensed or commercially available for local purchase or
standard residential use in Venezuela, authorities have introduced temporary emergency measures to
facilitate connectivity restoration in earthquake-affected areas.
On 26 June, the National Telecommunications Commission (CONATEL) granted temporary spectrum
authorization to Movistar Venezuela to activate a satellite-based Direct-to-Device (D2D) service in La
Guaira, the state most severely affected by the earthquakes. Using Starlink satellites, the service
enables SMS messaging directly to compatible LTE smartphones within a geofenced area and is
available free of charge. The authorization reportedly applies for up to three months and is intended to
restore basic communications where terrestrial networks have been severely damaged. Movistar is
also required to make the service available to customers of other operators, including Digitel and
Movilnet.
Despite these measures, field teams in La Guaira report that connectivity remains extremely limited
outside areas supported by satellite communications. Only one Starlink terminal was reported
operational near the airport and reception centre, while broader internet access in affected areas
continues to rely heavily on satellite-based solutions. Mobile connectivity remains available in some
urban areas but deteriorates rapidly outside population centres. Humanitarian teams entering the
country by air and across land borders have reportedly been able to import Starlink and VSAT
Page 3 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

equipment without significant difficulties, with authorities facilitating the importation of
communications equipment for disaster response purposes.
LTC Telecoms is engaging with Starlink to transition existing WFP terminals, currently operating under
a Marlink subscription, to the disaster response package, enabling the use of the three-month free
service period. Discussions are ongoing with WFP Venezuela regarding the required transfer process.
Global LTC Telecoms is also engaging with Starlink on the availability of in-country equipment and
potential support arrangements for humanitarian responders.
Secure communications
Security Communications Systems (SCS), including radio communications, were reported to be fully
operational in-country prior to the earthquake, in line with {TESS+} scorecard assessments as of
January 2026. These systems are critical for secure communication, incident reporting, and monitoring
field missions, particularly where other networks are degraded or unavailable.
LTC Telecoms is engaging with {TESS+} to confirm the pre-crisis baseline and assess the current
status of the network, including any earthquake-related damage or service disruption. Further
assessments will determine the functionality and coverage of existing radio networks and identify any
required repairs, augmentation, or support to ensure continuity of secure communications for
responders.
Information Management
The Global LTC Telecoms Information Management (IM) team has activated an IM and reporting
process to ensure timely, accurate, and consistent information sharing with partners and relevant
stakeholders throughout the response.
An emergency operations page for the LTC Telecoms earthquake response has been established and
is supported by a designated IM Officer and alternates to maintain continuous information flow and
ensure coordinated reporting across the operation.
The ITU DCM has been activated for Venezuela, and data collection is underway. Initial analysis from
the DCM confirms significant geographic variation in connectivity impacts, with the most severe
disruptions concentrated in La Guaira while connectivity in Caracas has largely recovered.
Additional information management support is being provided by MapAction, which has deployed a
team to La Guaira to support mapping, analysis and information sharing activities for the response.
Funding
Donor engagement is ongoing, including discussions with key partners and the US Embassy, alongside
consolidation of contributions under a Flash Appeal.
The US Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA) has committed USD 9 million, with an additional
USD 6 million in process, bringing the total contribution to USD 15 million, primarily focused on
strengthening the humanitarian supply chain.
The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) has allocated USD 15 million to Venezuela; however,
WFP is expected to receive approximately USD 2 million.
Page 4 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

Meetings
A Global LTC Telecoms Partner Teleconference was held on 29 June at 14:00 UTC to support
information exchange and coordination. Minutes of the meeting will become available here.
LTC Logistics Area
For more information on the logistics component of the LTC response, a dedicated Venezuela logistics
webpage is available here with the latest updates on working group meetings, key documents, maps,
and available support.
Contacts
Global LTC Telecoms
Phyza Jameel Remote Phyza.Jameel@wfp.org
Deputy Coordinator
Global LTC Telecoms
Elizabeth
Information Management Remote Elizabeth.Millership@wfp.org
Millership
Officer
More information: www.etcluster.org/emergency/venezuela-earthquakes
Contact: Venezuela.LTCTelecoms@wfp.org
Page 5 of 5
Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org | www.LOGcluster.org

documents.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 8**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**01 July 2026**  
**Time: 7:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), authorities report more than 700 aftershocks.
- At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state.
- Official toll: 2,295 people dead and 11,267 injured.
- More than 26,000 people have been affected.
- A total of 6,461 people have been rescued.
- One week after the earthquakes, Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams continue operations in coordination with OCHA.
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

**Situation overview**  
 Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 782 aftershocks. Although their frequency and intensity have decreased, risk conditions persist.

One week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 2,295 people dead, 11,267 injured, and 6,461 rescued since the onset of the emergency. In addition, approximately 13,000 people have been discharged from health facilities following their recovery.

Authorities report a total of 26,403 affected people, including 12,841 displaced and severely affected individuals, as well as people whose homes have been damaged or who have experienced physical or psychological impacts as a result of the earthquakes.

The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations and on the preparation and expansion of transitional camps to assist affected populations. La Guaira remains the most affected state. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.
