Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

Agenda
1. Situation update
2. Global LTC Telecoms update
3. Global LTC Logistics update
4. Partner updates
5. AOB
Minutes
1. Situation Update
Overview
• On 24 June, Venezuela was struck by two major earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and
7.5, occurring 40 seconds apart, with the epicentre located 23 kilometres southeast
of Yumare, west of Caracas. Several aftershocks have continued to affect the
country.
• The earthquakes caused significant damage to homes, public buildings, and critical
infrastructure, including power and telecommunications networks. Maiquetía
International Airport remains closed due to damage, with commercial flights
suspended until at least 02 July, while all other airports remain operational.
• Following the declaration of a state of emergency, the Government continues to
prioritize search and rescue efforts and is coordinating the deployment of
international rescue teams and emergency equipment from at least 27 countries.
• Humanitarian responders are supporting search and rescue operations on the
ground. While authorities have permitted the entry of search and rescue teams and
selected emergency responders, broader humanitarian access remains limited and
uncertain.
Telecommunications status
• Telecommunications services remain significantly disrupted nationwide following the
24 June twin earthquakes. Damage to telecommunications infrastructure and
interdependent power systems caused a sharp decline in internet connectivity
across the country, including in Caracas.
• Available data indicates national connectivity dropped from approximately 90
percent to between 20 and 30 percent immediately after the earthquakes on 24
June, before partially recovering to an average of around 70 percent by 25 June.
Connectivity levels continue to vary by location.
Page 2 of 8
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

• Widespread communications outages have left many people unreachable, affecting
emergency communications and family tracing efforts.
• Telecommunications disruptions continue to hamper coordination among search and
rescue teams and humanitarian responders.
• Power and connectivity systems remain highly interdependent and unstable,
resulting in intermittent service restoration across affected areas. Connectivity at
Maiquetía International Airport has reportedly been partially restored, although the
reliability and coverage of services remain under assessment.
• Venezuela's three national mobile network operators (Movistar, Digitel and Cantv)
have implemented measures to support affected populations. Cantv has reportedly
partnered with SpaceX to provide temporary internet connectivity in La Guaira
through Starlink devices, while Movistar and Digitel offered complimentary calls and
SMS services for 48 hours following the earthquakes. However, these measures
have not fully mitigated ongoing outages, network congestion and service instability.
2. Global LTC Telecoms Update
Cluster status
• As of 29 June, the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) had not been
formally activated, and no formal request for LTC support had been received despite
emerging funding appeals and offers of assistance.
• Telecommunications and logistics coordination are working through existing national
and humanitarian working groups, allowing operational information-sharing and
response coordination without formal cluster activation.
Coordination
• Coordination efforts are being supported by established humanitarian mechanisms,
including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC)
mission, which arrived on 25 June.
• At the OCHA level, an assessment and analysis cell is operational and working to
identify priority response gaps and coordination needs.
• It remains unclear whether formal LTC activation is under consideration. Any decision
is expected to be informed by ongoing assessments and the findings of the UNDAC
mission, with authorities and humanitarian partners evaluating whether identified
gaps can be addressed through existing coordination structures or require formal
activation.
Telecoms equipment importation
• Starlink terminals have previously been authorized only for limited use in Venezuela,
particularly devices registered outside the country. While authorities have reportedly
accepted offers involving SpaceX, no new official regulatory guidance has been
Page 3 of 8
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

issued. Humanitarian organizations have reportedly imported Starlink equipment
without encountering major entry restrictions.
• One NGO reported successfully transporting telecommunications equipment across
the Colombia–Venezuela border without difficulty. However, humanitarian partners
continue to seek formal guidance from the national telecommunications regulator
before recommending the importation of additional equipment.
• According to IFRC, discussions with Starlink's crisis response team indicated that
terminals could be supplied through local resellers in Venezuela, with equipment
available to support humanitarian operations. Clarification is still required on whether
government approvals have been secured and how equipment distribution would be
managed.
• Global LTC Telecoms remains engaged with Starlink and understands that
equipment is available and operational. However, confirmation from the national
telecommunications regulator remains a priority to ensure partners operate within
the country's regulatory framework.
3. LTC Logistics update
• LTC Logistics is gathering initial information on route accessibility and logistics
constraints, which will be published through a dedicated response information
platform.
• Although the Cluster has not been formally activated, a Logistics Working Group is
operational in-country, supported by a logistics coordinator and Information
Management Officer (IMO). Coordination meetings are being held every three days.
• During a Global LTC Logistics coordination meeting on 28 June, partners reported
that humanitarian flights were continuing to arrive in Caracas. Early responders
included UNICEF, Samaritan’s Purse and other humanitarian organizations. However,
in the absence of established customs procedures for the response, entry and
clearance processes remain largely ad hoc and are being managed on a case-by-
case basis.
• Ground handling services at Maiquetía International Airport are reported to be
operational, with cargo-handling equipment available to support incoming relief
flights. While initial operations have been described as functioning smoothly, further
assessment is ongoing as flight volumes increase.
• The logistics team is also mapping incoming cargo movements to Caracas and
Valencia, currently the two operational entry points identified for humanitarian cargo.
Partners have been encouraged to join the logistics WhatsApp coordination group to
facilitate real-time information sharing and operational coordination.
Page 4 of 8
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

4. Partners update
Government of Luxembourg
• Emergency.lu reported that European Union (EU) support operations were expanding
in Venezuela and appeared to be welcomed by the Government. EU personnel and
telecommunications equipment had entered the country without significant customs
or access challenges, with additional equipment expected to arrive on 30 June.
• Philippe Hein (emergency.lu), who deployed on 28 June, reported limited
connectivity in La Guaira. Only one Starlink terminal was operational near the airport
and reception centre, with no reliable internet connectivity elsewhere in the airport
area. Along the coast, limited mobile connectivity was available, but service quality
deteriorated rapidly outside urban areas. WhatsApp remained functional, while
broader internet access largely depended on satellite-based connectivity.
• Telecommunications requirements at the response base remained difficult to assess
due to the mixed availability of connectivity solutions among responders. While some
teams were deploying with their own satellite communications equipment, many local
volunteers continued to face limited internet access.
World Food Programme (WFP)
• WFP is leading both the logistics and ICT working groups in Venezuela. While
discussions on a possible LTC activation are ongoing, no formal decision has been
taken by the Humanitarian Coordinator (HC) or Humanitarian Country Team (HCT).
• WFP reported that the primary operational constraint remains access to reliable
power. Although communications equipment is available, electricity shortages are
limiting its effective use. Regulatory restrictions also continue to hinder the activation
of existing Starlink equipment.
• On 27 June, the UN established an operational base camp in La Guaira to support
response coordination. Telecommunications capacity at the site remains limited, with
most ICT assets already deployed elsewhere. Access restrictions to the UN tower in
Caracas have further constrained access to communications equipment stored
there.
• WFP's Regional Bureau for Latin America and the Caribbean (LACRO) and Global LTC
Telecoms remain on standby to provide support if requested.
International Telecommunications Union (ITU)
• ITU activated its Disaster Connectivity Maps (DCM) platform to monitor connectivity
trends in affected areas. Initial analysis identified connectivity disruptions in Yaracuy
and Carabobo states, although the current assessment area does not yet include La
Guaira or Caracas.
• ITU analysis using Internet Outage Detection and Analysis (IODA) data indicated a
national connectivity decline of approximately 30 percent immediately following the
earthquakes, with most services subsequently recovering and a residual national
connectivity loss of around five percent.
Page 5 of 8
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

• Connectivity impacts varied significantly by location. Caracas experienced an initial
30 percent reduction in connectivity but has largely recovered. Yaracuy and
Carabobo recorded peak losses of approximately 70 percent and 60 percent
respectively, with Carabobo showing near-full recovery. La Guaira remains the most
severely affected area, with connectivity dropping by approximately 90 percent
immediately after the earthquakes and an estimated 30 percent loss persisting
several days later.
Disaster Tech Lab
• Disaster Tech Lab reported that a deployment team has remained on standby in San
Antonio, Texas, since 24 June, with ten Starlink terminals and supporting solar power
equipment ready for deployment. Despite pursuing multiple channels, the
organization had not yet secured authorization to enter Venezuela and was seeking
support to facilitate the approval process.
• The organization reported ongoing engagement with Starlink's crisis response team,
which was reportedly working directly with the Venezuelan authorities to support the
use of Starlink services for humanitarian responders and organizations already
operating equipment in-country.
• Disaster Tech Lab also expressed its readiness to provide Starlink connectivity
equipment to humanitarian organizations that have been granted access to
Venezuela.
Page 6 of 8
Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area www.ETCluster.org

MapAction
• MapAction has deployed a two-person team to Venezuela to provide mapping and
information management support to the response. The team is currently based in La
Guaira and is equipped with a Starlink terminal to support connectivity and
information sharing.
• Humanitarian organizations requiring mapping products or information management
support are encouraged to contact MapAction directly at gfricz@mapaction.org.
5. Key Constraints
• The LTC has not been formally activated, with response coordination continuing
through logistics and ICT working groups.
• Power outages in La Guaira and parts of Caracas remain a major operational
challenge, limiting the use of available telecommunications equipment and
connectivity solutions.
• Communications services remain unstable in several affected areas, particularly
around La Guaira and Maiquetía International Airport, constraining information
sharing and operational coordination.
• Regulatory requirements for the importation and operation of Starlink terminals and
other telecommunications equipment remain unclear, creating uncertainty for
humanitarian partners seeking to deploy connectivity solutions.
• Access to some pre-positioned communications equipment remains restricted,
including assets located in the UN tower in Caracas.
• Ongoing aftershocks continue to pose safety risks and have disrupted operational
planning, including the establishment of response facilities.
• Humanitarian access remains constrained, with search and rescue teams reportedly
receiving priority entry while permissions for other response actors continue to be
processed on a case-by-case basis.
• Customs procedures for humanitarian relief items have not yet been formally
established. While initial cargo movements have been cleared through ad hoc
arrangements, the absence of standard operating procedures continues to create
uncertainty for incoming humanitarian shipments.
6. AOB
• N/a

documents.title: ACNUR refuerza su respuesta en Venezuela ante las crecientes vulnerabilidades provocadas por los terremotos
documents.body_text:
GINEBRA – La evaluación inicial de necesidades realizada sobre el terreno en Venezuela ha revelado un aumento drástico de las necesidades humanitarias y de protección en los últimos días, mientras los equipos valoran el impacto total de los devastadores terremotos de la semana pasada. En La Guaira, el estado más afectado, escasean los alimentos, los servicios básicos han colapsado y la conectividad se ha visto interrumpida en gran medida. Las tensiones en la comunidad están aumentando, ya que el acceso a la asistencia sigue siendo limitado.

ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, se ha movilizado de inmediato para apoyar a las comunidades afectadas y, durante los días 26 y 27 de junio, llevó a cabo una evaluación rápida de necesidades con participantes de La Guaira, el Distrito Capital, Miranda, Aragua y Carabobo. Las conclusiones iniciales arrojan que:

- El 75 por ciento de los encuestados informó de heridos en sus comunidades; el 56 por ciento reportó muertes.
- Las personas de edad avanzada y personas con discapacidad se enfrentan a riesgos agravados debido a la movilidad reducida y el acceso limitado a información digital.
- La mitad de los evaluados se aloja con vecinos o familiares; el 39 por ciento está viviendo en calles y espacios públicos, y otros en iglesias, escuelas o instalaciones improvisadas.
- Los refugios improvisados no cumplen los estándares mínimos de protección, por ejemplo, en privacidad, espacios seguros e higiene y comodidad básicas.
- El 17 por ciento de los encuestados informó de la presencia de niños no acompañados o separados en sus comunidades.

El Clúster de Protección liderado por ACNUR ha lanzado una campaña para abordar los riesgos de protección de la infancia, en particular la separación familiar. Los esfuerzos se centran en concienciación, identificación, búsqueda de familiares y garantizar la seguridad de las niñas y niños.

ACNUR está intensificando la asistencia de emergencia y los servicios de protección en múltiples frentes. Estamos apoyando a las autoridades locales con herramientas y equipos para la recopilar y gestionar de forma segura la información sobre las personas afectadas, facilitando la identificación de necesidades específicas y la derivación a servicios apropiados.

Al mismo tiempo, se están trasladando suministros de emergencia desde el almacén local de ACNUR en Táchira a La Guaira, y hay capacidad adicional para movilizar más de 20 toneladas de artículos de ayuda humanitaria desde las reservas globales de ACNUR en Panamá, con el fin de reforzar aún más la asistencia. Cáritas, socio de ACNUR, ha establecido un centro de recepción y almacenamiento de donaciones en las instalaciones de la Conferencia Episcopal, que cuenta con tiendas de y una carpa de ACNUR, para apoyar la distribución de ayuda.

Las autoridades han confirmado 1.719 víctimas mortales, al menos 5.034 heridos y 15.866 personas afectadas a 29 de junio. El daño en infraestructuras es enorme: un total de 189 estructuras se han derrumbado, mientras que 666 han sufrido daños o colapso parcial.

Conforme la situación evoluciona y los riesgos de protección aumentan, ACNUR reitera la importancia de proporcionar apoyo temprano y adaptado a las necesidades de las personas en situación crítica, en todas las comunidades afectadas. ACNUR requiere una cantidad estimada de 14,85 millones de dólares (USD) para aumentar los servicios de protección, la provisión de artículos de primera necesidad y de alojamiento temporal para 30.000 personas afectadas por el terremoto durante seis meses.

## **Para más información, por favor, contacta:**

- En Ginebra, Carlotta Wolf, wolf@unhcr.org, +41 79 546 67 07
- En Ciudad de Panamá, Stefano Zanfardino, zanfardi@unhcr.org, +507 6979-6818

documents.title: UNHCR scales up response in Venezuela amid growing post-earthquake vulnerabilities
documents.body_text:
*This is a summary of what was said by UNHCR spokesperson Carlotta Wolf – to whom quoted text may be attributed – at today's press briefing at the Palais des Nations in Geneva.*

GENEVA – Initial, on-the-ground needs assessments from Venezuela have revealed a dramatic surge in humanitarian and protection needs in recent days as teams evaluate the full impact of last week’s devastating earthquakes. In La Guaira – the hardest-hit state – food shortages are widespread, basic services have broken down, and connectivity has been largely severed. Community tensions are rising as access to assistance remains constrained.

UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, has immediately mobilized to support affected communities, and conducted a rapid needs assessment on 26-27 June with participants across La Guaira, the Capital District, Miranda, Aragua, and Carabobo states. The initial findings showed that:

- 75 per cent of respondents had reported injuries in their communities; 56 per cent reported fatalities.
- Older people and those with disabilities face compounded risks, due to limited mobility and reduced access to digital information.
- Half of those assessed are staying with neighbours or relatives, 39 per cent are living in streets and public spaces, and others in churches, schools, or improvised facilities.
- Improvised shelters do not meet minimum protection standards, for example for privacy, safe spaces and basic levels of hygiene and comfort.
- 17 per cent of those surveyed reported the presence of unaccompanied or separated children in their communities.

The UNHCR-led Protection Cluster has launched a campaign to address child protection risks, particularly family separation. Efforts focus on awareness-raising, identification, family tracing, and ensuring children’s safety.

UNHCR is scaling up life-saving assistance and protection services across multiple fronts. We are supporting local authorities with tools and equipment for the safe collection and management of information on affected people, helping identify specific needs and facilitate referrals to appropriate services.

At the same time, emergency supplies are being transported from UNHCR’s local warehouse in Táchira to La Guaira, with additional capacity to mobilize more than 20 tonnes of relief items from UNHCR’s global stockpiles in Panama to further bolster assistance. UNHCR partner CARITAS has established a donation collection and storage centre at the Episcopal Conference premises, including with UNHCR tents and a rub hall, to support aid distributions.

Authorities have confirmed 1,719 fatalities, at least 5,034 people injured, and 15,866 people affected as of 29 June. Infrastructure damage is extensive: a total of 189 structures have collapsed, while 666 have sustained damage or partial collapse.

As the situation evolves and protection risks grow, UNHCR reiterates the importance of timely, flexible support for people in dire need, across all the affected communities. UNHCR requires an estimated $14.85 million to scale up protection, core relief items, and temporary shelter support for 30,000 earthquake-affected people over six months.

## **For more information, please contact:**

- In Panama City, Stefano Zanfardino, zanfardi@unhcr.org, +507 6979-6818

documents.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #3 (30 de junio de 2026)
documents.body_text:
Este tercer Informe de Situación presenta una actualización sobre el impacto de los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela y resume las actividades en curso y la respuesta planificada de la OIM en apoyo a las poblaciones afectadas y a los esfuerzos nacionales.

**Aspectos destacados**

Las cifras oficiales reportan al menos 1.943 personas fallecidas, 10.571 personas heridas, 15.866 personas severamente afectadas y 6.461 personas rescatadas tras los terremotos del 24 de junio.

Al menos 855 edificaciones se mantienen reportadas como afectadas, incluyendo 189 colapsos totales, mientras que los daños a viviendas continúan generando necesidades de alojamiento temporal y desplazamiento.

La OIM continúa apoyando actividades de alojamiento temporal, agua, saneamiento e higiene, salud, salud mental, protección y gestión de datos, incluida la verificación de 15 de los 39 campamentos transitorios identificados, el apoyo a la coordinación de sitios y el monitoreo de movimientos de población hacia otros estados.

**Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM ha continuado apoyando acciones de alojamiento, gestión de sitios y servicios esenciales en campamentos transitorios. En coordinación con socios y autoridades, se ha avanzado en el mapeo de 39 campamentos transitorios, de los cuales 15 han sido verificados por la OIM junto con el Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, la OIM y las autoridades establecieron espacios de gestión del sitio, recepción, derivación, almacenamiento, triaje médico y protección; además, se entregaron 180 literas y se están activando servicios de protección. También se han identificado necesidades prioritarias en sitios mapeados, incluyendo agua, artículos de higiene, materiales de limpieza, medicamentos, baños, duchas, ropa, artículos para niñas y niños, apoyo eléctrico y capacidad adicional de alojamiento.

En Salud, Salud Mental, WASH, protección y datos, la OIM ha mantenido el apoyo a servicios de salud de emergencia y monitoreo de necesidades en sitios prioritarios. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, en La Guaira, se brindó asistencia médica a 62 personas mediante servicios de pediatría, medicina general y ginecología, incluidas dos derivaciones a establecimientos de salud. A través de la organización socia Ven Da Tu Mano, se apoyó una jornada médica en el campamento transitorio instalado en el Estadio de Béisbol Menor de Maiquetía, donde aproximadamente 150 familias desplazadas se encuentran alojadas. La OIM también desplegó personal de protección, participó en espacios de coordinación del Clúster de Protección, desarrolló herramientas de registro, elaboró mapas de campamentos transitorios y mantuvo el monitoreo remoto de movilidad y de flujos en zonas fronterizas.

**Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La respuesta planificada de la OIM continuará priorizando el alojamiento de emergencia y artículos de primera necesidad, la gestión de sitios, salud y SMAPS, WASH, protección, y datos y evaluaciones de necesidades. En alojamiento y gestión de sitios, la OIM continuará el monitoreo de campamentos transitorios, el mapeo de servicios, la planificación de sitios, el registro de población y la digitalización de herramientas de registro. También fortalecerá la organización comunitaria, las normas de convivencia, la provisión de información y las medidas de AAP, VBG y PEAS, además de apoyar mejoras en los sitios y la entrega de carpas, toldos y arreglos básicos para mejorar la seguridad, dignidad y protección de las personas afectadas.

En salud, WASH, protección y datos, la OIM continuará brindando servicios móviles de salud en campamentos transitorios, incluyendo medicina general, pediatría, ginecología y obstetricia, primeros auxilios psicológicos y derivaciones. También priorizará la adquisición y distribución de medicamentos e insumos médicos, el fortalecimiento de rutas de derivación para casos severos y personas con movilidad reducida, y el apoyo de SMAPS mediante mensajes de autocuidado, líneas de contacto gratuitas y asistencia psicológica voluntaria organizada. En WASH, se prevé apoyar el acceso de emergencia al agua, almacenamiento y distribución, instalación de baños, kits de higiene, puntos de lavado de manos, saneamiento, gestión de residuos y promoción de higiene. Las actividades de protección se enfocarán en el monitoreo de riesgos, rutas de derivación seguras, asistencia a personas con necesidades específicas, participación comunitaria y capacitaciones en AAP, PEAS, prevención de VBG y trata de personas. La OIM también continuará desarrollando productos DTM, perfiles de sitios, mapas, análisis de necesidades y monitoreo de movilidad para informar la coordinación, focalización y priorización multisectorial.

documents.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #3 (30 June 2026)
documents.body_text:
This third Situation Report provides an updated overview of the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and outlines IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts.

**Highlights**

Official figures report at least 1,943 fatalities, 10,571 injuries, 15,866 people severely affected and 6,461 people rescued following the 24 June earthquakes.

At least 855 buildings remain reported as affected, including 189 total collapses, while damage to housing and urban infrastructure continues to drive displacement and temporary accommodation needs.

IOM continues supporting temporary accommodation, WASH, health, mental health, protection and data activities, including the verification of 15 of 39 mapped temporary accommodation sites, site coordination support and monitoring of population movements towards other states.

**IOM activities**

IOM has continued supporting shelter, site coordination and essential services in temporary accommodation sites. IOM and partners have mapped 39 temporary accommodation sites, of which 15 have been verified together with the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group. Newly mapped sites in La Guaira include schools and institutional facilities hosting affected families, with reported needs including water, hygiene items, cleaning materials, medicines, toilets, showers, child-focused items, clothing and additional sleeping capacity. At Polideportivo José María Vargas, IOM and authorities have supported the establishment of site management, reception, referral, warehouse, medical triage and protection spaces, with 180 bunk beds delivered and key protection services being activated.

In health, MHPSS, WASH, protection and data, IOM has provided health assistance at Polideportivo José María Vargas, reaching 62 people with paediatrics, general medicine and gynaecology services, including two referrals to health facilities. Through partner organization Ven Da Tu Mano, IOM also supported a medical brigade at the temporary site installed in the Minor Baseball Stadium of Maiquetía, where approximately 150 displaced families are sheltering. IOM has also deployed protection staff, supported coordination with site management teams, participated in Protection Cluster discussions, maintained DTM-based mapping and mobility monitoring, and reported movements of internally displaced families from La Guaira towards municipalities in Zulia, including Maracaibo, San Francisco, Rosario de Perijá and Cabimas.

**IOM planned response**

IOM’s planned response will continue to prioritize emergency accommodation and core relief items, site coordination and management, health and MHPSS, WASH, protection, and data and needs assessments. In site coordination, IOM will continue monitoring, service mapping and verification of temporary accommodation sites, support site planning, population registration and digitalization of registration, and strengthen community organization, coexistence rules, information provision, AAP, GBV and PSEA measures. IOM will also support site improvements and the delivery of tents, tarpaulins and basic arrangements to improve safety, dignity and protection.

Across health, WASH, protection and data, IOM will continue mobile health activities in temporary accommodation sites, including general medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology and obstetrics, psychological first aid and referrals. IOM will prioritize medicines, supplies, referral pathways for severe medical cases and persons with reduced mobility, while maintaining MHPSS support, WASH interventions, hygiene kits, water storage, handwashing spaces, sanitation, waste management and infection prevention and control. Protection activities will focus on risk monitoring, safe referrals, community engagement, information provision and training for response actors, while DTM products, site profiles, mobility updates, maps and needs analyses will continue informing multisectoral prioritization.

documents.title: Un cargamento de ayuda de UNICEF llega a Venezuela tras los catastróficos terremotos
documents.body_text:
## Un cargamento de 47 toneladas métricas de suministros de salud, agua y educación fue movilizado desde el depósito de la EU en Copenhague; se espera que llegue más ayuda en los próximos días.

**CARACAS/COPENHAGUE/NUEVA YORK, 30 de junio de 2026 –** En respuesta a los catastróficos terremotos que afectaron a Venezuela el 24 de junio, un cargamento de 47 toneladas métricas de suministros humanitarios de UNICEF ha llegado hoy al país para apoyar a los niños, niñas y las familias afectadas.

El cargamento —movilizado desde el depósito de la Unión Europea alojado en el centro mundial de suministros y logística de UNICEF en Copenhague— incluye kits de salud de emergencia para atención médica urgente, incluyendo suministros para partos seguros, cuidado del recién nacido, prevención y tratamiento de enfermedades; suministros de purificación y almacenamiento de agua para contribuir a proporcionar agua potable segura; carpas para establecer espacios amigables para la infancia y puntos de servicios; ayudas para la movilidad, incluyendo sillas de ruedas; y materiales de recreación y desarrollo infantil temprano para ayudar a los niños y niñas a recuperar la sensación de normalidad y continuar aprendiendo.

"Este cargamento no podría llegar en un momento más crítico para los niños de Venezuela," afirmó Roberto Benes, Director Regional de UNICEF para América Latina y el Caribe. "Las familias de los estados afectados necesitan urgentemente agua segura, así como acceso a atención de salud. Muchas están durmiendo al aire libre, con miedo a nuevas réplicas. Estos suministros nos ayudarán a llegar a los niños y familias con lo que más necesitan en este momento —atención médica, agua limpia, espacios seguros. Pero las necesidades sobre el terreno son mucho mayores que lo que ha llegado hoy, y necesitamos apoyo sostenido para seguir ampliando nuestra respuesta."

Se estima que aproximadamente 680,000 niños necesitan asistencia humanitaria en los seis estados afectados por los terremotos —que fueron el evento sísmico más significativo que ha afectado a Venezuela en más de un siglo. Las comunidades continúan en riesgo por las réplicas persistentes, que han superado las 600 desde los terremotos iniciales.

Este cargamento, junto con uno regional que llegó desde Panamá el 28 de junio, apoyará a más de 100,000 niños y familias durante un período de tres meses.

UNICEF continúa coordinando con las autoridades nacionales, el Equipo de País de las Naciones Unidas y socios humanitarios para evaluar necesidades y ampliar la respuesta en protección de la infancia, salud, nutrición y WASH.

UNICEF estima que se requieren 52 millones de dólares estadounidenses para responder a la emergencia por el terremoto, como parte de su más amplio llamamiento de Acción Humanitaria para la Infancia 2026 para Venezuela, que asciende a 137,6 millones de dólares estadounidenses y que, antes de los terremotos, contaba solo con un 35 por ciento de financiación. UNICEF ha movilizado aproximadamente 3,5 millones de dólares estadounidenses de sus propios fondos de emergencia interna para permitir el despliegue inicial rápido de suministros y personal.

documents.title: WFP amplía la asistencia a las familias afectadas por los terremotos de Venezuela
documents.body_text:
**CARACAS, Venezuela –** El Programa Mundial de las Naciones Unidas (WFP) está ampliando rápidamente sus operaciones en Venezuela y aumentando la asistencia alimentaria con el objetivo de llegar a hasta medio millón de personas en las zonas más afectadas por los terremotos de la semana pasada.

Miles de personas se han visto desplazadas tras los dos potentes terremotos que sacudieron el país el 24 de junio, destruyendo viviendas, infraestructuras y medios de subsistencia en al menos siete estados. Muchas familias se encuentran ahora refugiadas en centros de evacuación abarrotados, donde las necesidades de alimentos, agua potable, refugio y servicios básicos aumentan día a día.

WFP ha puesto en marcha distribuciones de alimentos en La Guaira, el estado más afectado, proporcionando hasta ahora paquetes que contienen raciones alimentarias para un mes (cereales, legumbres y aceite vegetal) a 1 200 personas, y ha establecido centros de alimentación temporales en el estado. Estos centros agrupan los servicios humanitarios en un único lugar, lo que permite a las comunidades afectadas acceder a la asistencia alimentaria y recibir apoyo de la OIM y UNICEF para otras necesidades esenciales.

«En La Guaira, las viviendas, los mercados y las reservas de alimentos han quedado devastados, lo que ha dejado a las familias con poco o nada que comer», afirmó Stephanie Hochstetter, directora nacional de WFP en Venezuela. «En estos momentos, además de los servicios médicos de emergencia, el acceso a alimentos, agua y refugio son las prioridades más urgentes. Los equipos de WFP trabajan sin descanso para hacer llegar a los supervivientes la ayuda que necesitan desesperadamente».

A medida que se va conociendo mejor la magnitud de la emergencia, WFP también está ampliando sus operaciones más allá de La Guaira a otras zonas afectadas del país. Se están desplegando equipos de WFP para evaluar las condiciones sobre el terreno y planificar una posible asistencia alimentaria adicional allí donde se considere necesario.

WFP también está apoyando la respuesta humanitaria en general a través de su capacidad logística, ayudando a transportar suministros, proporcionando capacidad de almacenamiento y mejorando la conectividad en zonas donde las carreteras, los servicios y las infraestructuras han resultado dañadas.

WFP lleva cinco años prestando apoyo humanitario esencial en Venezuela, y en 2025 ha atendido a más de 760 000 personas en 12 estados. WFP ya cuenta con más de 3 000 toneladas métricas de alimentos en el país —suficientes para abastecer a más de 10 000 familias durante dos meses— y está trayendo suministros adicionales. Además, más de 1 400 toneladas métricas de artículos de socorro procedentes de socios humanitarios se encuentran preposicionadas en el Depósito de Respuesta Humanitaria de las Naciones Unidas gestionado por WFP en Panamá y listas para su envío.

WFP hace un llamamiento urgente por un monto inicial de 50 millones de dólares para brindar asistencia alimentaria de emergencia a hasta 500.000 personas durante los próximos tres meses. La respuesta también cubrirá los gastos de logística y comunicaciones de emergencia. WFP tiene capacidad para ampliar sus operaciones hasta satisfacer las necesidades alimentarias de un millón de personas, si se consigue la financiación suficiente.

El acceso a los alimentos ya era una de las principales preocupaciones de los venezolanos incluso antes de que se produjeran los terremotos. Los precios de los alimentos siguen estando muy por encima del alcance de muchos hogares, ya que la cesta de la compra mensual media cuesta a las familias más de 600 dólares, una cifra varias veces superior a los ingresos medios de los hogares.

documents.title: Earthquake leaves Venezuela in ruins as approximately 50,000 remain missing and survivors go without water
documents.body_text:
## In Caracas and La Guaira families are sleeping in the streets and parks, searching rubble with bare hands, and competing for clean water as the survival window closes

- Almost 50,0000 people, including children remain missing under rubble, with rescue workers racing against a closing survival window, IRC teams most concerned about elevated risks to children.
- Authorities report 12,721 people have been displaced and 774 buildings have collapsed.
- The national water system has failed across seven states, putting survivors, the injured, and rescue workers at risk.
- Families fled with nothing; Women and children in shelters have no documents, no medication, nowhere to return.
- Some collapsed buildings may contain survivors but the critical window has closed; international crews continue extracting survivors from the rubble as late as Monday.

**Caracas, Venezuela, June 30, 2026** — Almost a week after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela, and roughly 48 hours after the critical 72-hour survival window closed, search and rescue operations continue. IRC teams and partners on the ground in Caracas and La Guaira report tens of thousands of people still missing beneath collapsed buildings, and survivors across multiple states struggle to find safe drinking water. IRC is concerned about elevated child protection risks given the scale of missing persons, and is prioritizing family tracing and reunification support.

The scale of the response does not meet the scale of humanitarian need. Medical services at health centers and mobile units are overwhelmed, shelters are at full capacity, and water and electricity services remain disrupted across the affected areas. A massive but uncoordinated influx of aid has led to significant food spoilage, with distribution points turning away donations due to oversupply. As search and rescue teams begin to withdraw in the coming days, aid organizations are warning that food needs are expected to resurface and intensify even as the rescue phase winds down. The IRC is scaling its response as field teams report the full scale of destruction becoming clearer with each passing hour.

*"What we are seeing in the shelters is heartbreaking; women alone with young children, no documents, no medicine, no idea where their partners or relatives are,"* **said Nicole Kast, IRC Venezuela Country Director.** *"Children are not sleeping. Every aftershock sends collective panic through the shelters, and the psychological toll of that will last long after the rubble is cleared."*

The states of Caracas, La Guaira and Miranda have been declared a disaster zone, where teams are witnessing families lined up under the sun for water and food. IRC partners are also observing a massive flow of people moving toward Caracas, both to assist relief efforts and to search for missing family members. Families are sheltering outdoors rather than risk returning to structurally compromised buildings - a fear made more acute by hundreds of aftershocks since the quake struck, which seismologists warn could continue for three to six months. Schools in affected neighborhoods have been converted into shelters housing entire families who left their homes in seconds with only the clothes on their backs.

A near-total collapse of the national water system across multiple states simultaneously is leaving survivors in shelters, injured people in hospitals, and rescue workers in the field without guaranteed access to safe drinking water. IRC local partners are responding to the emergency through health, protection, water and sanitation services and distributing essential supplies in La Guaira, but report that demand far outstrips what is available. Communications remain cut in several sectors. Families have now gone more than five days without knowing whether their loved ones are alive.

The earthquake struck on a national holiday, when many families were home together. IRC teams in the Altamira and San Bernardino neighborhoods report witnessing families searching for loved ones in the rubble with their bare hands.

IRC teams also report an extraordinary display of solidarity emerging across the city. Delivery motorcyclists who normally carry food orders have organized themselves to transport water and supplies into areas trucks cannot reach. Spontaneous community collection points have appeared across Caracas, with neighbors gathering water, clothing, and medicine to send to the hardest-hit areas.

IRC has been operational in Venezuela since 2021, providing health care, food security, nutrition, clean water, protection services, education, and economic support to some of the country's most vulnerable people. The organization is urgently scaling its earthquake response and calling on donors and the international community to act immediately to ensure life-saving resources reach those who need them.

**Situation Report No. 6**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**29 June 2026**  
**Time: 6:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), authorities report 609 aftershocks.
- At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira continues to record the highest level of impact.
- Official toll: 1,719 people dead and 5,034 injured; the figure continues to rise.
- More than 15,800 people have been affected.
- At least 855 buildings were affected.
- Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams remain deployed in affected areas, in coordination with OCHA.
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are already responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people

**Situation overview**  
 Venezuela is facing a national emergency following the two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) of 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 609 aftershocks. A magnitude 4.2 earthquake was recorded off the central coast on the morning of 29 June; no additional damage was reported.  
 The official toll stands at 1,719 people dead and 5,034 injured. Authorities also reported that 15,866 people have been displaced. In addition, at least 855 buildings were affected. As of 28 June, a total of 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some level of damage, including 38 hospitals. Figures remain under review as operations advance.  
 The Government response has focused on search and rescue, emergency medical care and damage assessments. Up to seven (7) states were affected, including La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Falcón, Carabobo, and Yaracuy. The United Nations and its partners, in coordination with the authorities, will deliver a multisectoral response to affected people in three strategic locations across La Guaira.

United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
Impact on infrastructure
 At least 855 buildings were affected. As of Sunday 28 June, a total of 2,501 infrastructure
assets had sustained some level of damage.
 Up to 38 hospitals have been affected, including the J.M. de los Ríos Children’s Hospital
(Caracas) and Hospital de Coche.
 The Caracas Metro system temporarily suspended services on Monday to conduct inspections
following aftershocks.
 Maiquetía International Airport remains closed to commercial operations. Authorities and
national and international experts conducted an initial inspection.
 Authorities and United States personnel conducted an inspection at the Port of La Guaira.
 Preliminary estimates indicate direct physical damages amounting to USD 6.7 billion,
equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP, according to UNDP data.
 Internet and telecommunications connectivity remains unstable in some areas, affecting
communication.
National and international response
 The Venezuelan Government maintains contingency plans to safeguard the lives of affected
people.
 A large-scale deployment of Civil Protection and security forces, and the public and private
health system have been mobilized.
 A presidential commission has been established to assess the habitability of housing and
infrastructure, comprising relevant ministries, professional associations and academia, as well
as a coordination structure to establish transitional camps for affected people.
International support:
 Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) operations continue. A total of 49 teams from 28 countries,
comprising 2,358 personnel and 189 search dogs, are deployed in the most affected areas to
support rescue efforts and provide medical assistance.
 OCHA is providing logistical support to search and rescue teams on the ground.
 International support continues: China is providing assistance valued at 100 million yuan;
Brazil has dispatched a fourth humanitarian flight; Cuba has deployed a second contingent of
rescuers; Colombia has sent an additional flight with 3,200 relief items, as well as fortified
food supplements and medicines; Lithuania has deployed medical and rescue teams; and
Germany is deploying medical teams in coordination with national authorities and PAHO.
 The Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF) announced the creation of
the Venezuela Recovery and Reconstruction Fund with an initial capital of USD 1 million.
 The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has launched
an Emergency Appeal for 50 million Swiss francs.
Measures adopted
 Judges have been deployed, in coordination with relevant entities, to medical facilities, parks
and other designated sites across the Greater Caracas area to support affected children and
adolescents.
 A psychosocial support hotline is available for affected people (0800-AYUDA-01).
 A digital form has been created by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities
(CONAPDIS) to coordinate a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.
 A website has been launched (http://localizapacientes.com) to help locate missing persons.
 A hotline has been activated to directly report missing persons: 0-800-RESCATE (7372283),
as well as the VenApp platform for reporting affected individuals.
 A total of 10,834 volunteers have been registered and deployed to support rescue operations,
logistics and food assistance, among other activities.
 PDVSA has deployed an emergency plan and preventive monitoring to detect and control gas
leaks.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
 A total of 7,2 kg of food and 22,478 food parcels have been distributed across affected states.
 Some 75,238 families have received support, including hydration, food assistance, transport,
and medical and psychosocial care.
 Classes have been suspended for an additional week, from 29 June to 5 July.
 Transitional camps have been established in affected states.
Situation by state
Capital District (Caracas)
 A total of 50 transitional camps have been established across the Greater Caracas area
(including affected municipalities in Miranda state) to support affected people.
 Two major collection centres have been established: one at La Carlota and another at
Almacenadora Caracas (Catia).
 The Caracas Metro system temporarily suspended services to conduct inspections following
aftershocks.
La Guaira
 The Government has restricted access and maintains an increased security presence in the
state to ensure safety and support response operations in affected areas.
 A total of 15 shelters have been established to assist affected people in the state.
 Electricity supply has been restored to 90 per cent. As of Sunday 28 June, water supply stood
at 68 per cent and road access at 90 per cent.
 Health services are under significant pressure due to the high number of injured people,
including those in critical condition.
 The Social Security morgue is facing capacity constraints in light of current and projected
caseloads.
 United Nations agencies are providing essential services to affected populations in
coordination with national authorities.
 Five partners of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF) present in the state are supporting
the initial response through primary health care and psychosocial support services.
Miranda
 Damage to infrastructure has been reported, with up to 33 housing units and 7 buildings
collapsed, mainly in the municipalities of Chacao, Eulalia Buroz and Plaza.
 The highest concentrations of affected people are reported in the municipalities of Chacao,
Independencia, Brión, Zamora and Eulalia Buroz.
 Damage to critical infrastructure has been reported, including health facilities, educational
centres and public institutions, as well as commercial establishments, religious and sports
facilities across several municipalities.
 Four (4) partners of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF), with projects in the state and in
the Capital District, are supporting the initial response through general protection, child
protection and gender-based violence (GBV) services.
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
 In both states, some material damage has been reported, including impacts on housing and
buildings, as well as road infrastructure, with cracked roads (e.g. the Morón roundabout).
 Material damage has been reported in both states, including impacts on housing, buildings
and road infrastructure; including cracked roads (e.g. the Morón roundabout).
 In Carabobo, the main impacts are concentrated in Juan José Mora municipality, particularly
in Morón parish, where 9 of the affected sectors are located.
 Overall, 1,091 people have been affected and 10 fatalities have been reported.
 A total of 170 houses have been affected (42 with structural damage, 12 partially collapsed
and 11 totally collapsed).
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
 A total of 12 buildings have been affected, of which 9 have been declared uninhabitable and
3 totally affected, including the Tucacas Hotel (Falcón).
 Five organizations (Venezuelan Red Cross, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón and
Empodérame) are providing response in health, food, water and the distribution of
humanitarian assistance during this initial phase.
 Preliminary needs include search and rescue, structural assessments, temporary shelter,
health care, water, food, hygiene and psychosocial support.
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
 A localized emergency in Silva municipality is being addressed by regional authorities, which
announced the cessation of search and rescue operations in Tucacas parish (official toll of 12
people deceased).
 The regional government is advancing a comprehensive response plan for 87 affected families
(252 people) in Boca de Aroa parish.
 The arrival of affected people from La Guaira to the municipalities of Miranda and Falcón has
been reported.
 The Venezuelan Red Cross supported search and rescue operations, logistics and
psychosocial assistance, while Caritas established a collection centre in Coro and supported
the transport of relief supplies.
 OCHA maintains coordination with regional authorities to identify opportunities for
collaboration and facilitate the timely provision of complementary support by the humanitarian
community.
 The Local Coordination Forum (LCF), with support from the Zulia state forum, has completed
a mapping of available capacities and resources and remains ready for a potential deployment.
Other states
 In Apure state, the return of local populations from affected states has been reported; the state
government has arranged ground transport through various institutions. The Local
Coordination Forum (LCF) is providing complementary support to the response.
 In Delta Amacuro state, humanitarian organizations have coordinated with authorities to
provide psychosocial support to affected people arriving from Caracas.
 In Táchira state, humanitarian organizations and authorities held coordination meetings and
were informed of the flexibilization of protocols to facilitate assistance to the emergency in
Caracas and La Guaira.
 In Trujillo and Lara states, humanitarian coordination mechanisms are being prepared should
they be required.
 In Sucre state, authorities have deployed more than 200 personnel for search and rescue, pre-
hospital care and logistical support to the most affected areas.
Humanitarian coordination
 The United Nations and its partners, in coordination with the authorities, are focusing their
efforts on health; shelter; food assistance; water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); logistical
support; and protection.
 Three strategic locations have been identified in La Guaira state to provide multisectoral
services to affected people: Polideportivo Vargas, César Nieves Stadium (Catia La Mar) and
Playa Grande Stadium.
 WFP has initiated food distributions in Catia La Mar (La Guaira), reaching more than 1,200
people with a one-month food ration.
 Rapid assessments have been initiated to identify priority needs and guide the scale-up of
general food distributions.
 IOM has supported site establishment and management, including the provision of relief items,
the set-up of spaces for health and protection activities, storage, as well as coordination and
reception mechanisms for affected people. UNHCR is supporting authorities with data
management. Additional UN agencies are expected to activate services in the coming hours,
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
including food assistance; water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); protection (including GBV);
and sexual and reproductive health.
 Local Coordination Forums and Groups (LCF/LCG) have been activated; clusters and working
groups are maintaining inter-agency coordination mechanisms to ensure a coherent and
relevant response.
Humanitarian financing
 Resource mobilization includes a US$ 15 million allocation from the Central Emergency
Response Fund (CERF) to support a multisectoral response, alongside the activation of the
Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF) to channel funding to operational partners in affected
areas.
 Norway announced a contribution to the response through CERF.
 The United States announced a US$ 100 million contribution to the VHF, as well as an
additional allocation bringing bilateral contributions to a further US$ 100 million to support
response operations by IOM, WFP, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief
Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Porject HOPE and the Red Cross.
 The Republic of Korea announced a US$ 1.25 million contribution to the humanitarian
response through the VHF. Other Member States and donors have expressed their intention
to support this mechanism and increase available funding.
 The European Union has allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition
to the €52 million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.
 OCHA will continue coordinating with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and
needs-based allocation.
Support the humanitarian response to address the earthquake in Venezuela
Make your donation safely and quickly now:

For more information, please contact the OCHA Venezuela Office:
Vanessa May – Head of Office a.i. – mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Humanitarian Affairs Officer – alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Public Information Officer – moreno7@un.org

documents.title: Emergency Assistance in Response to the Earthquake Damage in Venezuela
documents.body_text:
On June 30, upon the request of the Government of Venezuela, the Government of Japan has decided to provide emergency relief goods (plastic sheet (Tarpaulin), portable jerry can, and water purifier) through the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) to Venezuela in response to the earthquake damages.

1. In addition, a JICA survey team has been dispatched to the site since June 26 to assess local medical, recovery, and reconstruction needs.
2. The Government of Japan will continue to stand by the people of Venezuela and stands ready to study further necessary assistance, bearing in mid the human security needs.

## (Reference)

In Venezuela, a magnitude 7+ earthquake that occurred on Thursday, June 25, caused numerous casualties, including deaths and injuries, and property damage. According to the Venezuelan government's announcement, the damage includes 1,719 deaths, over 5,034 injuries, and over 885 damaged houses, and the full extent of the damage is still unknown (as of June 30).

**Destacados**

- Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), las autoridades reportan 609 réplicas.
- Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado con las mayores afectaciones.

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Las autoridades reportan 609 réplicas. En la mañana del lunes 29 de junio se registró un sismo de magnitud 4,2 con epicentro frente a la costa central; no generó daños adicionales.  
 El balance oficial asciende a 1.719 personas fallecidas y 5.034 heridas. Autoridades también reportaron 15.866 personas damnificadas. Asimismo, al menos hasta 855 edificios se vieron afectados. Hasta el domingo 28 de junio, se reportaron 2.501 infraestructuras con algún tipo de daño, entre ellos 38 hospitales. Las cifras se mantienen en revisión a medida que avanzan las operaciones.  
 La respuesta gubernamental se ha centrado en búsqueda y rescate, atención médica de emergencia y evaluación de daños. Hasta siete (7) estados se vieron afectados, entre ellos La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Falcón, Carabobo y Yaracuy. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, ofrecerán una respuesta multisectorial a las personas afectadas en tres ubicaciones estratégicas en La Guaira.

 Instalación de dos (2) grandes centros de acopio: uno en la carpa de La Carlota y otro en la
Almacenadora Caracas (Catia).
 Sistema de Metro de Caracas suspendió el servicio temporalmente para realizar inspección
por réplica.
La Guaira
 Gobierno mantiene restringido el acceso y militarizó el estado para garantizar la seguridad y
respuesta en las zonas afectadas.
 Instalados 15 refugios para la atención de las personas afectadas en el estado.
 Ya se recuperó el 90% del servicio eléctrico del estado. Hasta el domingo 28 de junio, el
servicio de agua se encontraba a un 68% y la vialidad en un 90%.
 Los servicios de salud enfrentan una fuerte presión debido al elevado número de personas
heridas.
 La morgue del Seguro Social presenta limitaciones de capacidad frente al volumen actual y
proyectado.
 Agencias de la ONU se encuentran brindando servicios esenciales de forma articulada a la
población afectada.
 Cinco (5) organizaciones socias del Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV) con presencia
en el estado apoyan la respuesta inicial con servicios de atención primaria en salud y atención
psicológica.
 El Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía sufrió daños y se mantienen suspendidas
operaciones comerciales.
Miranda
 Se reportan daños en infraestructura, con hasta 33 viviendas y 7 edificios colapsados, en su
mayoría en los municipios Chacao, Eulalia Buroz y Plaza.
 Las mayores concentraciones de personas damnificadas se registran en los municipios
Chacao, Independencia, Brión, Zamora y Eulalia Buroz.
 Se reportan afectaciones en infraestructura crítica, incluyendo centros de salud, centros
educativos y entes públicos; así como daños en establecimientos comerciales, centros
religiosos y deportivos en distintos municipios del estado.
 Cuatro (4) organizaciones del FHV con proyectos financiados en municipios del estado y en
Distrito Capital apoyan la respuesta inicial con servicios en protección general, de la niñez y
de violencia basada en género (VBG).
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro)
 Se reportan daños materiales en ambos estados, con afectaciones en viviendas, edificaciones
e infraestructura vial; incluyendo carreteras agrietadas (por ejemplo, la redoma de Morón).
 En Carabobo, las principales afectaciones se concentran en el municipio Juan José Mora,
especialmente en la parroquia Morón, donde se ubican 9 de los sectores afectados.
 A nivel general, se reportan 1.091 personas afectadas y 10 personas fallecidas.
 Se contabilizan 170 viviendas afectadas (42 con daños estructurales, 12 con colapso parcial
y 11 con colapso total).
 Se reportan 12 edificios afectados, de los cuales 9 fueron declarados no habitables y 3
totalmente afectados, incluido el Hotel Tucacas (Falcón).
 Cinco organizaciones (Cruz Roja Venezolana, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón y
Empodérame) brindan respuesta en salud, alimentación, agua y distribución de ayuda
humanitaria durante esta fase inicial.
 Las necesidades preliminares incluyen búsqueda y rescate, evaluación estructural,
alojamiento temporal, atención en salud, agua, alimentación, higiene y apoyo psicosocial.
Falcón (Tucacas – Municipio Silva)
 Emergencia focalizada en el municipio Silva, atendida por el gobierno regional, que anunció
el cese formal de las operaciones de búsqueda y rescate en la parroquia Tucacas (balance
oficial de 12 personas fallecidas).
 El gobierno regional adelanta un plan integral de atención para 87 familias afectadas (252
personas) en la parroquia Boca de Aroa.
 Se reporta la llegada de personas desplazadas desde La Guaira hacia los municipios Miranda
y Falcón.
 La Cruz Roja Venezolana acompañó las operaciones de búsqueda y rescate, la logística y la
atención psicosocial, y Cáritas habilitó un centro de acopio en Coro y apoyó el traslado de
insumos.
 OCHA mantiene coordinación con las autoridades regionales para identificar oportunidades
de colaboración y facilitar oportunamente el apoyo complementario de la comunidad
humanitaria.
 El Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC), con el apoyo del Foro del estado Zulia, completó un
mapeo de capacidades y recursos disponibles y se mantiene preparado para un eventual
despliegue.
Otros estados
 En el estado Apure, se reporta el retorno de población local que se encontraba en los estados
afectados; la Gobernación dispuso traslado terrestre a través de diversas instituciones. El
Foro Local de Coordinación (FLC) apoya de forma complementaria.
 En el estado Delta Amacuro, se articuló con las autoridades la atención psicológica por parte
de las organizaciones humanitarias de un grupo de personas afectadas provenientes de
Caracas.
 En el estado Táchira, las organizaciones humanitarias y las autoridades se reunieron para
coordinar acciones e informar sobre la flexibilización de protocolos para la asistencia a la
emergencia en Caracas y La Guaira.
 En los estados Trujillo y Lara, los espacios para la coordinación humanitaria se preparan en
caso de ser requerido.
 En el estado Sucre, autoridades desplegaron más de 200 funcionarios de búsqueda y rescate,
atención prehospitalaria y logística en apoyo a las zonas más afectadas.
Coordinación humanitaria
 Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, centran sus
esfuerzos en: servicios de salud; alojamiento; alimentación; agua, saneamiento e higiene;
apoyo logístico y protección.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 5
 Se identificaron tres ubicaciones estratégicas en el estado La Guaira para ofrecer servicios
multisectoriales a las personas afectadas: Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves
(Catia La Mar) y el Estadio Playa Grande.
 El campamento del Polideportivo José María Vargas cumple doble función de centro de acopio
y alojamiento temporal, albergando a más de 1.200 personas.
 El PMA inició distribuciones de alimentos en Catia La Mar (La Guaira), alcanzando a más de
1.200 personas con una ración para un mes. Se iniciaron evaluaciones rápidas para identificar
necesidades prioritarias y orientar la ampliación de las distribuciones generales de alimentos.
 OIM ha apoyado la instalación y gestión del sitio, incluyendo la provisión de insumos, la
habilitación de espacios para atención de salud, actividades de protección y almacenamiento,
así como mecanismos de coordinación y recepción de personas afectadas. ACNUR apoya a
las autoridades en la gestión de datos. En las próximas horas, se espera que otras agencias
de Naciones Unidas activen servicios de alimentación; agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH);
protección (incluida la VBG); y salud sexual y reproductiva.
 Activados los Foros Locales y Grupos de Coordinación (FLC/GLC); los clústeres y grupos de
trabajo mantienen los mecanismos de coordinación interinstitucional para asegurar la
articulación y pertinencia de la respuesta.
Financiamiento humanitario
 La movilización de recursos incluye una asignación de US$15 millones del Fondo Central de
Respuesta a Emergencias (CERF, por sus siglas en inglés) para una respuesta multisectorial,
junto con la activación del Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela (FHV) para canalizar recursos a
socios con capacidad operativa en las zonas afectadas.
 Noruega anunció una contribución para apoyar la respuesta a través del CERF.
 Estados Unidos anunció una contribución de US$100 millones al FHV, y una asignación
adicional para llegar a otros US$100 millones en contribuciones bilaterales para operaciones
de respuesta de OIM, PMA, UNICEF, International Medical Corp, Catholic Relief Services,
Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza y la Cruz Roja.
 Corea anunció una contribución US$ 1,25 millones a la respuesta humanitaria a través de
FHV. Otros Estados Miembros y donantes han expresado su intención de apoyar a través de
este mecanismo y ampliar el financiamiento disponible.
 La Unión Europea asignó 5 millones de euros para apoyar la respuesta a la emergencia, lo
que se suma a los 52 millones de euros ya asignados este año para las operaciones
humanitarias en el país.
 OCHA continuará coordinando con donantes y socios para asegurar una asignación rápida,
estratégica y basada en necesidades.

documents.title: WFP scales up assistance for families hit by Venezuela earthquakes
documents.body_text:
**CARACAS, Venezuela –** The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) is rapidly scaling its operations in Venezuela and expanding food assistance aimed at reaching up to half a million people in the areas hardest hit by last week’s earthquakes.

Thousands of people have been displaced after two powerful earthquakes struck on 24 June, destroying homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods across at least seven states. Many families are now sheltering in crowded evacuation centers with needs growing for food, clean water, shelter and basic services by the day.

WFP has launched food distributions in La Guaira, the worst-affected state, providing parcels that contain one-month’s worth of food rations (cereals, pulses and vegetable oil) for 1,200 people so far and setting up temporary feeding centers in the state. These centers bring humanitarian services together in one location, enabling impacted communities to access food assistance and receive IOM and UNICEF support for other essential needs.

“In La Guaira, homes, markets, and food supplies have been devastated, leaving families with little or nothing to eat,” said Stephanie Hochstetter, WFP Country Director in Venezuela. “Right now, in addition to emergency medical services, access to food, water and shelter are the most urgent priorities. WFP teams are working around the clock to reach survivors with the assistance they desperately need.”

As the scale of the emergency becomes clearer, WFP is also expanding operations beyond La Guaira into other impacted areas of the country. WFP teams are deploying to assess conditions on the ground and plan for possible further food assistance where it is considered necessary.

WFP is also supporting the wider humanitarian response through its logistics capacity, helping to transport supplies, provide storage capacity and improve connectivity in areas where roads, services and infrastructure have been damaged.

WFP has been providing essential humanitarian support in Venezuela for five years, reaching more than 760,000 people in 12 states in 2025. WFP already has more than 3,000 metric tons of food in the country — enough to support more than 10,000 families for two months — and is bringing in additional supplies. In addition, more than 1,400 metric tons of relief items from humanitarian partners are pre-positioned at the WFP-managed United Nations Humanitarian Response Depot in Panama and ready for dispatch.

WFP is urgently appealing for an initial USD50 million to provide emergency food assistance to up to 500,000 people over the next three months. The response will also support logistics and emergency communications. WFP has the capacity to scale up to meet the food needs of one million people, if sufficient funding is secured.

Access to food was already of top concern for Venezuelans even before the earthquakes hit. Food prices remain far beyond the reach of many households, with the average monthly food basket costing families more than US$600, several times higher than the average household income.

documents.title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response: Situation Report #01 (29 June 2026)
documents.body_text:
**IN NUMBERS**

+5,000 People injured

+1,700 Reported deaths

+15,000 People displaced

+2,501 Infrastructures affected

189 Total collapsed buildings

**KEY HIGHLIGHTS**

• Twin earthquakes have caused widespread destruction and escalating humanitarian needs in north-central Venezuela, particularly in La Guaira state.

• Critical infrastructure damage is constraining access and disrupting essential services, including food supply chains.

• Food security conditions, already fragile, are expected to deteriorate further due to loss of livelihoods and market disruptions.

• The humanitarian situation remains highly dynamic, with needs continuing to evolve.

• WFP aims to reach up to 500,000 people in shelters in the first three months and has the capacity to scale up to one million.

**Funding Needed**  
FOR THE 1st MONTH OF EMERGENCY: USD 50 Million are required.  
FOR REGULAR PROGRAMMES, INCLUDING SCHOOL MEALS: USD 20 Million are required.  
Resources and stock from regular programmes are being redirected to the emergency, making donor support critical on both fronts.

**Situation Update**

• On 24 June 2026, two major earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela near Morón (Yaracuy), causing widespread destruction across Caracas and coastal areas, particularly affecting La Guaira.

• A state of emergency was declared on 24 June. National authorities and the international community deployed emergency teams for search and rescue, damage assessments, and response operations.

• As of 28 June, official figures report 1,700 deaths, over 22,000 people are in hospitals, 15,000 displaced, with numbers expected to rise.

• Critical infrastructure, including housing, transport, electricity networks and telecommunications, has been severely damaged, limiting access to affected populations and essential services.
