documents.title: Thousands of children at risk after powerful earthquakes strike Venezuela [EN/AR/ZH]
documents.body_text:
**CARACAS/NEW YORK, 25 June 2026 –** An estimated 3.9 million children live in the areas affected by the powerful 7.5 and 7.2 magnitude earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June, putting thousands of children and families at risk.

The earthquakes affected communities in Caracas and the states of Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, La Guaira, Miranda and surrounding areas. The most affected regions have seen dozens of buildings collapse, with children reportedly among the casualties. As authorities continue to assess the extent of the damage, reports indicate impacts on homes, public infrastructure and essential services, while communities remain at risk from possible aftershocks.

“The images we are seeing from Venezuela and the stories we hear from colleagues on the ground are heartbreaking," said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. "Our thoughts are with the children and families who have lost loved ones and all of those whose lives have been upended. As the scale of the damage becomes clearer, children's safety, protection and well-being must remain at the center of the response.”

Children are among the most vulnerable when disasters strike. In the hours and days ahead, affected children can face injury, family separation, displacement, distress, and disruptions to services including healthcare, safe water, education and protection.

Thousands of families will require urgent assistance as damage assessments continue. Homes, schools, health facilities, water systems and other critical infrastructure that may have been damaged, disrupting access to essential services and increasing risks for children and their caregivers.

UNICEF is coordinating with national authorities and partners to assess the needs of affected populations and support response efforts to help ensure that children and families have access to medical care, protection services, psychosocial support, safe water, and safe spaces.

UNICEF is on the ground and remains committed to supporting national efforts to address the needs of affected children and their families, particularly the most vulnerable. Prior to the earthquakes, UNICEF's 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children appeal for Venezuela stood at US$137.6 million with only 35 per cent funded.

documents.title: Good Neighbors Statement on the Venezuela Earthquake
documents.body_text:
Good Neighbors expresses its deepest sympathy to the communities affected by the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026. The earthquakes caused widespread destruction to homes, public infrastructure, and essential services, leaving thousands of families in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. Families have lost loved ones, their homes, and their sense of safety. Children, in particular, are facing fear, uncertainty, and significant disruption to their daily lives.

As aftershocks continue, many families remain displaced, taking shelter in cars, makeshift tents, and other temporary accommodations without reliable access to electricity, safe drinking water, food, or protection services.

In response to this crisis, Good Neighbors is preparing an emergency response to protect the safety, well-being, and dignity of children and their families. Initial support is expected to include emergency shelter and other essential relief items, while additional assistance will be determined based on ongoing needs assessments and operational feasibility. We are closely monitoring the evolving situation through our humanitarian networks and local partners and coordinating with relevant authorities and humanitarian organizations to identify priority needs and provide timely, needs-based assistance in accordance with humanitarian principles.

We stand ready to work alongside affected communities, national authorities, and humanitarian partners to support communities affected. We call upon the international community to stand in solidarity with the people of Venezuela by supporting timely, coordinated, and needs-based humanitarian assistance. Together, we can help children, families, and communities recover, rebuild, and look toward the future with hope.

documents.title: Trump Administration Leads a Robust Life-Saving Response to the Venezuelan Earthquakes
documents.body_text:
The United States is mobilizing an unprecedented, large-scale response to the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on June 24, 2026. The Trump Administration has deployed a Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART) with more than 250 people, including three specialized Urban Search-and-Rescue (USAR) teams, which will conduct crucial life-saving operations.

## Life-Saving Support

The Department activated three Urban Search-and-Rescue teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, Los Angeles County, California, and Miami-Dade County, Florida.

The Fairfax County Fire and Rescue Department (USA-1), which deployed with 79 members and six canines, and the Los Angeles County Fire Department (USA-2), which will land soon, deployed with 74 members and six canines, after transportation from U.S. Air Force C-17 Globemaster aircraft. The Miami-Dade Fire Rescue (FLTF-1) is en route with 80 members and six canines and expected to arrive late Friday, June 26. These USAR teams will conduct systematic search operations across collapsed structures, working to locate and extract survivors, and coordinate with local emergency responders and the Venezuelan interim government to prioritize the most heavily impacted areas.

Together, they bring more than 200,000 pounds of specialized equipment. Each team is a multidisciplinary unit comprising firefighters trained in structural-collapse rescue, physicians and paramedics providing on-site emergency medical care, structural engineers assessing building integrity and collapse risk, and canine search specialists capable of locating survivors in rubble and debris fields.

All teams have prior international deployment experience. The Los Angeles and Fairfax teams have trained and deployed with the State Department and were activated in response to Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, where they surveyed affected areas in Jamaica, cleared debris to facilitate access, and assisted with the transportation of relief commodities to communities in need.

## SOUTHCOM Logistical Support

The Department of State has requested the uniquely specialized capabilities of the U.S. military to support State-led disaster response and humanitarian assistance operations in Venezuela. The Department of War (DoW) is playing a crucial role in securing logistics for the response, including by leveraging military assets already positioned in the region and forward deploying personnel to accelerate the delivery of life-saving assistance. The DART and elements from U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) are working together to implement life-saving activities in close coordination with partners on the ground, drawing on SOUTHCOM’s regional presence to ensure rapid and sustained operational support.

This includes:

- U.S. Air Force C-17s transporting Urban Search and Rescue teams and load-movement equipment to Caracas;
- U.S. Marine Corps MV-22 Ospreys conducting airfield assessments near the earthquake epicenter;
- U.S. Navy vessels USS Fort Lauderdale and USS Billings providing naval support in waters near Venezuela;
- U.S. Army CH-47 Chinooks deploying from Honduras to transport personnel and supplies;
- U.S. Space Force satellite imagery supporting damage assessment and prioritization of aid efforts.

SOUTHCOM’s involvement reflects the deepening civil-military partnership with the Department’s Bureau of Disaster and Humanitarian Response (DHR), including the recent establishment of a U.S. humanitarian assistance hub in South Florida and the embedding of DHR disaster and humanitarian advisors at SOUTHCOM to strengthen coordination and technical expertise across the region.

## Restoring Connectivity: The U.S.-Starlink Partnership

When disaster strikes, restoring connectivity is critical to saving lives. The U.S. Government is working with Starlink to provide free satellite internet service to those affected by the Venezuelan earthquakes, rapidly deploying Starlink terminals to restore connectivity in the hardest-hit areas.

This partnership is made possible by a two-year Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed between the U.S. Department of State and Starlink on June 11, 2026. The MOU leverages Starlink’s low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite technology, an American innovation, to restore critical communications when crises and natural disasters damage infrastructure. Under the agreement, DHR coordinates with Starlink to provide rapid connectivity to emergency responders, humanitarian organizations, and people in acute need.

This response marks one of the first major activations of this partnership, demonstrating the real-world impact of the Trump Administration’s commitment to harnessing American innovation in service of humanitarian response.

## Humanitarian Assistance

The Trump Administration is mobilizing $150 million in assistance to Venezuela, including:

- $50 million in new bilateral awards to partners including World Vision, Samaritan’s Purse, Catholic Relief Services, the International Organization for Migration, UNICEF, and the World Food Program; and
- $100 million contribution to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) Venezuela pooled fund.

## Assisting Americans

The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans. The Department of State is working tirelessly to provide consular assistance to U.S. citizens and their families in the affected areas. We are also monitoring conditions in [**Venezuela**](https://ve.usembassy.gov/) as recovery work proceeds. Americans in Venezuela can reach us 24/7 at +1-202-501-4444 for assistance. Family and friends in the United States who are concerned about Americans in Venezuela can call toll free +1-888-407-4747. Enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) at [**STEP.state.gov**](http://step.state.gov/) to receive safety and security updates from the U.S. Embassy, review the [**Department’s Travel Advisory for Venezuela**](https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/travel-advisories/venezuela.html), and follow @TravelGov and @USEmbassyVE on social media and WhatsApp “U.S. Department of State – Security Updates for U.S. Citizens” for the latest information.

Those who wish to donate or find other ways to help may [**visit the response webpage**](https://www.state.gov/responding-to-venezuela-earthquakes/).

documents.body_text: Devastating 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes have caused widespread damage, building collapses, and impacted healthcare in Venezuela. Critical infrastructure is damaged, access to power and clean water is disrupted, and Simón Bolívar International Airport is closed. Health workers and first responders continue to work to save lives, but aftershocks, severe damage, and chronic shortages of medical supplies are straining an already weakened health system and limiting access to care. Project HOPEsupported health facilities are responding and providing emergency and trauma care. Project HOPE has deployed three rapid assessment teams to La Guaira, Distrito Capital, and Miranda to scale up our response.

documents.title: After Venezuela Earthquakes, Direct Relief Supports Medical Deployment in Critical Response Window
documents.body_text:
***Emergency grants to a search and rescue organization and medical brigade bolster immediate response, while Direct Relief advances wraparound medical support strategy.***

As an elite medical team deploys to Venezuela, Direct Relief is mobilizing an emergency grant to support their swift, effective response to Wednesday’s cataclysmic double earthquakes.

The several days following a disaster are the most critical for medical intervention. Often working amid the rubble or in makeshift displacement centers, medical teams are able to save the lives of severely injured patients and keep emergent needs from spiraling into secondary crises.

Medical Impact, a Mexico- and Colombia-based emergency response group with a storied history of responding in the immediate aftermath of natural disasters, sends mobile medical teams to global emergency settings from Guatemala to Gaza.

Equipped with field medic packs and emergency medicine caches – often provided by Direct Relief – they move through devastated terrain, treat physical trauma, prevent infection, help people purify water for drinking, and prevent people with conditions like asthma, diabetes, and HIV/AIDS from spiraling into medical crisis.

An emergency grant “enables us to jump-start the response so we can start right away,” Dr. Giorgio Franyuti, Medical Impact’s executive director, told Direct Relief during a response to severe flooding in Mexico last October.

Direct Relief also funded the deployment of a Spain-based search-and-rescue organization, [Bomberos Unidos Sin Fronteras](https://busf.org/), with extensive [experience responding to this kind of devastation](https://www.directrelief.org/2024/11/direct-relief-supports-first-responders-in-spain-after-devastating-floods/?_gl=1*mqggxp*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTEyOTYyMTE3My4xNzgyNTAwOTM5*_ga_WYKLEGJW76*czE3ODI1MDA5MzgkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODI1MDExMjIkajU1JGwwJGgyMTIyNjc2NzU.).

The next day’s activity will be critical in Northern Venezuela, where the earthquake toppled about 250 buildings, trapping survivors beneath. The death toll, already in the hundreds, is expected to drastically rise. Finding survivors and providing medical care in the field are the best ways to prevent unnecessary deaths.

Medical Impact’s physician team generally deploys as soon as they receive clearance to do so. Logistical issues are generally resolved ad hoc, in the field, because damaged roads and communication blackouts make it difficult to assess medical needs and high-level strategy from afar.

“We do not know where we’re going to stay, but we have to deploy anyway. It is so time-sensitive, and so critical. We usually resolve \[issues like shelter\] on the spot,” Dr. Franyuti explained last year.

People trapped under rubble are at severe risk of developing crush syndrome, which can damage muscle tissue and then, once the person is free, release life-threatening toxins into the bloodstream. Wounds will be vulnerable to infection and long-term complications; many chronic conditions will have gone unmanaged since Wednesday.

In Venezuela, where the health system was already severely compromised before this disaster, these concerns take on even greater urgency. Providers working on the ground have noted that medical centers are overwhelmed by the emergent need.

Medical needs in earthquake-affected areas are likely to shift over time, from trauma care and emergency surgery to care for complex medical crises, severe mental health impacts, and interruptions to sanitation, healthcare access, and livelihoods. However, the widespread demand for urgent medical care is likely to remain overwhelmingly high for the foreseeable future. The U.N. estimates that nearly seven million people in Venezuela have been affected. The need for longer-term humanitarian intervention is almost guaranteed.

Direct Relief is currently assessing medical needs and strategic priorities in collaboration with healthcare partners on the ground in Venezuela. The organization’s goal will be to outfit under-resourced hospitals and healthcare workers responding on the ground, filling vital medical supply gaps and supporting the local and regional response.

documents.title: Korean Government Provides Humanitarian Assistance to Venezuela Following Earthquake
sources: Government of the Republic of Korea
documents.body_text:
The government of the Republic of Korea has decided to provide Venezuela with USD5 million in humanitarian assistance through international organizations operating on the ground, in order to support the rapid response to and facilitate an early recovery from the recent devastating earthquake in the country that caused a loss of lives and damage to properties.

\- According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)'s 2026 Global Humanitarian Overview, even prior to the earthquake, Venezuela already had 7.9 million people — more than 25% of its total population — in need of humanitarian assistance, owing to frequent natural disasters such as heavy rains and floodings, as well as political and economic instability including extreme inflation.

The government of the Republic of Korea hopes that this assistance will contribute to a swift recovery of the affected areas and to an early restoration of normalcy to daily lives of affected communities.

documents.title: Message on the Venezuela earthquakes: Attributable to Jorge Moreira da Silva, UN Under-Secretary-General and UNOPS Executive Director
documents.body_text:
Devastating news from Venezuela.

Reports indicate last night’s powerful earthquakes have caused significant loss of life, widespread injuries, and severe damage to homes and vital infrastructure in Caracas and elsewhere.

My deepest condolences to those who have lost loved ones and our thoughts are with all affected by this tragedy.

UNOPS stands with the people of Venezuela. We are ready to support rapid response efforts wherever needed.

documents.title: Declaración de UNICEF sobre los terremotos de magnitud 7,5 y 7,2 en Venezuela
documents.body_text:
**CARACAS / PANAMA, 25 de junio de 2026** – UNICEF se solidariza con los niños, niñas, adolescentes y familias afectados por los terremotos de magnitud 7,5 y 7,2 que sacudieron Venezuela el 24 de junio de 2026.

Los terremotos han afectado a comunidades de Caracas y de los estados Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, La Guaira, Miranda y zonas cercanas. A medida que las evaluaciones oficiales de la situación evolucionan, se insta a las comunidades a mantenerse alerta ante posibles réplicas y a seguir las orientaciones de las autoridades.

UNICEF está monitoreando de cerca la situación y enfatiza la importancia de garantizar la protección de los niños y las niñas afectados, asegurando que sus derechos permanezcan en el centro de la respuesta.

En las próximas horas y días, los niños y niñas necesitarán protección, apoyo psicosocial, agua segura, atención sanitaria y espacios seguros a medida que las comunidades se recuperan de la conmoción y la destrucción. UNICEF reafirma su compromiso de apoyar los esfuerzos nacionales para atender las necesidades de los niños afectados y sus familias, especialmente las de los más vulnerables.

**Acerca de UNICEF**

UNICEF es el organismo de las Naciones Unidas dedicado a la infancia, y su misión es proteger los derechos de todos los niños y niñas en todas partes, en especial los de los más desfavorecidos y de aquellos a los que resulta más difícil llegar. Trabajamos en más de 190 países y territorios, y hacemos lo que sea necesario para ayudarlos a sobrevivir, prosperar y desarrollar todo su potencial.

 Para obtener más información sobre UNICEF y su labor, visite [www.unicef.org/](http://www.unicef.org/es)lac

documents.title: Venezuela Health Cluster: Earthquakes Situation Report #1 (25 June 2026) [EN/ES]
documents.body_text:
*English version follows*

**Aspectos destacados y panorama del impacto**

El 24 de junio de 2026, un "doblete sísmico" de alta intensidad, compuesto por dos grandes terremotos poco profundos (M7,2 y M7,5), sacudió el centro-norte de Venezuela en rápida sucesión, con epicentro cerca de Morón, en el eje Carabobo/Yaracuy. El Sistema Global de Alerta y Coordinación en Casos de Desastre (GDACS) emitió una Alerta Roja para el evento. La presidenta encargada, Delcy Rodríguez, declaró el estado de emergencia nacional, confirmando oficialmente 164 muertes y 971 heridos a nivel nacional, mientras que las autoridades del estado Miranda reportan, por separado, 20 muertes y 209 heridos adicionales en sus municipios.

**Activación del sector salud y estado de los establecimientos críticos**

La infraestructura de salud pública y privada ha sido plenamente activada en todo el país. Según el modelo preliminar de exposición de la OPS/OMS, hasta 91 hospitales de emergencia se encuentran en zonas de sacudida severa, incluidos 20 hospitales directamente expuestos a una intensidad de Mercalli VII o superior. Se ha registrado una fuerte presión operativa, evacuaciones parciales y daños estructurales confirmados en múltiples establecimientos:

- **Hospital Domingo Luciani (El Llanito):** Evacuado por completo como medida preventiva; las evaluaciones técnicas de funcionalidad continúan en curso.
- **Hospital Dr. Francisco A. Rísquez (Cotiza):** Sufrió el colapso del ala del piso inferior, lo que provocó su evacuación y solicitudes urgentes de evaluación estructural.
- **Hospital Magallanes de Catia:** Varios pisos evacuados debido a roturas de tuberías y daños en la mampostería; se mantienen activas las solicitudes de carpas de emergencia y suministros de campo.
- **Hospital Victorino Santaella Ruiz (Los Teques):** Evacuado por las autoridades tras confirmarse daños estructurales en paredes internas y externas.
- **Otros establecimientos clave desbordados:** Se han reportado colapsos funcionales de las áreas de triaje de emergencia debido a la afluencia masiva de pacientes en el Hospital José María Vargas, el Hospital Pérez de León I y II, y el Hospital Vargas de La Guaira.

**Logística, entrada humanitaria y redes ciudadanas**

Los servicios públicos críticos (electricidad, agua, gas médico y telecomunicaciones) están sufriendo interrupciones severas, lo que amenaza la continuidad de la atención hospitalaria. Si bien el Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar (Maiquetía) sufrió daños en su infraestructura, ha sido reabierto exclusivamente para operaciones humanitarias y de respuesta. La Base Aérea Generalísimo Francisco de Miranda (La Carlota), en Caracas, funciona como el principal Punto de Entrada internacional. Venezuela solicitó formalmente la activación de la red INSARAG, autorizando el despliegue inmediato de los equipos internacionales de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano (USAR). Este informe institucional oficial reconoce además un amplio ecosistema de redes ciudadanas digitales activas y registros de personas desaparecidas (como la red Todos Con Venezuela), que aportan recopilación descentralizada de datos y mapeo de recursos sobre el terreno.

\------------------------

*English version:*

**Highlights & Impact Overview**

On 24 June 2026, a high-intensity 'seismic doublet' consisting of two shallow, major earthquakes ($M7.2$ and $M7.5$) struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with the epicentre located near Morón along the Carabobo/Yaracuy axis. The Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS) has issued a **Red Alert** for the event. Acting President Delcy Rodríguez declared a national state of emergency, officially confirming **164 deaths and 971 injuries** nationwide , while Miranda State authorities separately report an additional **20 deaths and 209 injuries** across its municipalities.

**Health Sector Activation & Critical Facility Status**

The public and private healthcare infrastructure has been fully activated across the country. According to preliminary PAHO/WHO exposure modelling, up to 91 emergency hospitals are located in severe shaking areas, including 20 hospitals directly exposed to Mercalli intensity VII or higher. Severe operational strain, partial evacuations, and confirmed structural damages have been registered across multiple facilities:

- **Hospital Domingo Luciani (El Llanito):** Fully evacuated as a preventative measure; technical functionality evaluations remain ongoing.
- **Hospital Dr. Francisco A. Rísquez (Cotiza):** Suffered a lower floor wing collapse, leading to an evacuation and urgent requests for structural assessments.
- **Hospital Magallanes de Catia:** Multiple floors evacuated due to ruptured pipelines and masonry damage; requests for emergency tents and field supplies are active.
- **Hospital Victorino Santaella Ruiz (Los Teques):** Evacuated by authorities following confirmed structural damage to internal and external walls.
- **Other Key Overwhelmed Facilities:** Functional collapses of emergency triage areas due to massive patient influxes have been reported at *Hospital José María Vargas*, *Hospital Pérez de León I and II*, and *Hospital Vargas de La Guaira*.

**Logistics, Humanitarian Entry & Citizen Networks**

Critical utility lifelines (electricity, water, medical gas, and telecommunications) are experiencing severe disruptions, threatening the continuity of hospital care. While Simón Bolívar International Airport (Maiquetía) sustained infrastructure damage, it has been reopened strictly for humanitarian and response operations. Generalísimo Francisco de Miranda Air Base (La Carlota) in Caracas is serving as the primary international Point of Entry. Venezuela has formally requested INSARAG network activation, authorizing international Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams to deploy immediately. This official institutional report also acknowledges a broad ecosystem of active digital citizen-led networks and missing-persons registries (such as the *Todos Con Venezuela* network) providing decentralized data collection and resource mapping on the ground.

1. Situation Overview
On 24 June 2026, at 18:04 local time, two major
earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid
succession. According to the United States Geological
Survey (USGS), the first event registered magnitude
7.1–7.2 with its epicentre west of Morón (Caribbean
coast), at approximately 13 km depth. About one
minute later, a second earthquake of magnitude 7.5
occurred southwest of Morón, at approximately 10 km
depth. Both events are considered among the most
powerful to have affected Venezuela in over a century.
Described as a 'seismic doublet', both earthquakes
were shallow, increasing their destructive intensity.
They were felt across much of Venezuela and in
neighbouring countries. The most affected areas
reported to date are La Guaira, the Capital
District/Caracas, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón,
Zulia, Yaracuy and Lara.
Acting President Delcy Rodríguez declared a national
state of emergency. A Unified Command Post has
been established with the Resident Coordinator and
OCHA present. Venezuelan authorities deployed
security forces nationwide and authorized the
preventive shut-off of domestic gas supply in buildings
at risk. School activities and non-essential work have
been suspended in affected areas, and some hotels
have been converted into temporary shelters. A
tsunami advisory for parts of the Caribbean was
subsequently cancelled. At least 30 aftershocks have
been registered; further aftershocks remain possible
and may worsen damage in already weakened
structures.
Access and Logistics
Simón Bolívar International Airport (Maiquetía) sustained severe infrastructure damage, was initially closed and
commercial flights diverted to Aruba and Curaçao. The Unified Command Post has confirmed that the airport is
operational for humanitarian and response flights. La Carlota Air Base (ICAO: SVFM), located in Caracas with Runway 09
available, is operating as the primary point of entry for international assistance. Charter flights have operational priority.
Acting President Rodríguez activated the VenApp mobile application to allow citizens to report missing persons and
housing situations.
International Response
Venezuela formally requested the activation of the INSARAG framework through Verbal Note No. 0987 of its Permanent
Mission in Geneva, 25 June 2026. All international USAR teams have been authorized to deploy. Confirmed arrivals in the
coming hours include teams from the United States, Dominican Republic and El Salvador; Qatar is preparing for
deployment the following day. Mexico, China, Brazil and Caribbean countries have offered assistance. An UNDAC team is
being mobilized (contact: jaggi@un.org). More than 30 search and rescue organizations from Latin America, Europe, Asia
and the Middle East are reporting active monitoring or mobilization in the Virtual OSOCC.

2. Health Situation and Preliminary Impact
Casualties and Impact
National authorities have officially reported 164 deaths, 971 injured and 30 aftershocks following the two main seismic
events (Ministry of Health, 25 June 2026). These figures continue to evolve as search and rescue operations and damage
assessments progress.
Miranda state reports, separately, 20 deaths and 209 injured across its municipalities, as detailed below:
TOTAL – Miranda State 209 20
increase significantly.
Population and Hospital Exposure
PAHO/WHO preliminary exposure analysis estimates that 91 emergency hospitals are in areas exposed to Mercalli
intensity VI or above, including 20 hospitals exposed to intensity VII or higher — mainly in Carabobo and Yaracuy —
prioritized for rapid functionality and damage assessment. An estimated 712,223 people are potentially exposed in 9
municipalities with Mercalli intensity VI–VII.5. These figures are for planning purposes and do not represent confirmed
damage or confirmed affected population. (Source: PAHO/WHO SitRep #1, 25 June 2026.)
Health System Activation
The public and private health system has been activated nationwide, with special emphasis on the Capital District and the
states of La Guaira, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo and Falcón. Eight public hospitals and 12 private facilities in Gran
Caracas have been made available for triage, evaluation, treatment and hospitalization of the affected population.
Health Facility Status by Area
Capital District / Gran Caracas
• Hospital Domingo Luciani (El Llanito) — evacuated as a precaution; patients receiving treatment in the car park.
Subsequently listed by the Ministry of Health among hospitals available for care, pending ongoing technical
assessment.
• Hospital Militar Dr. Carlos Arvelo — receiving a high volume of trauma and neurosurgical patients.
• Hospital Dr. Francisco A. Rísquez (Cotiza) — lower floor wing collapse; evacuated and requires structural
assessment. Experiencing difficulties for patient referrals.
• Hospital Oncológico Luis Razzeti — infrastructure damage reported.
• Hospital Magallanes de Catia — several floors evacuated due to masonry damage and pipe ruptures; requests tents
and emergency supplies. Damage assessment planned with specialist staff.
• Hospital Pérez de León I and II (Petare) — high influx of emergencies; stretchers in the facility courtyard.
• Hospital José María Vargas — functional collapse of the emergency area due to massive patient influx, no
expansion capacity available.

• Maternidad Concepción Palacios — patients evacuated to the metro area; less critical patients discharged due to
capacity constraints. Ambulance transfer difficulties reported.
• Maternidad del Valle HRCF — minor masonry damage, electrical system failure; backup generator connected in
alternate mode covering critical areas only.
• Clínica Ávila (private) — severe structural damage reported, pending official confirmation and urgent functionality
verification.
• CLP Gramoven — masonry and glass damage; influx of patients with mild trauma and hypertensive crises; additional
care areas activated.
La Guaira
La Guaira is reported as one of the most severely affected areas, with multiple collapsed buildings, ongoing search and
rescue operations, and a disaster-area declaration. Health services are under extreme pressure.
• Hospital Vargas de La Guaira — receiving a high influx of patients and operating beyond capacity.
• Hospital Pariata — overwhelmed by patient demand. Official assessment of functionality and capacity is urgently
needed.
Zulia / Maracaibo
At least three hospitals report some level of structural damage. No total hospital collapse has been reported. Detailed
functionality and capacity assessments are ongoing.
Carabobo / Valencia
Unofficial reports suggest the main hospital in Valencia may have been affected; assessment is ongoing.
Miranda State
• Hospital Victorino Santaella Ruiz (Los Teques) — evacuated by authorities; structural damage to internal and
external walls confirmed.
Other Areas
Structural damage and health service disruptions have been reported across multiple states. Additional reports are
expected as local assessments progress.
Essential Service Disruptions
Electricity outages, water interruptions, domestic gas failures, telecommunications disruptions and transport restrictions
are reported in several affected areas. These disruptions affect health service continuity, referral pathways, hospital
operations, ambulance dispatch and coordination.
3. Health Cluster Coordination
The Venezuela Health Cluster, with PAHO/WHO support and coordination with the Global Health Cluster, is monitoring
the situation and maintaining contact with health authorities, partners, Civil Protection and regional response structures.
The Cluster is prioritizing: (i) verification of health sector information — facility functionality and structural status, trauma
and emergency care capacity, referral pathways, ambulance services and continuity of essential services; (ii) mapping
partner presence and capacity in affected states; (iii) identification of gaps; and (iv) support to a coordinated response
aligned with national priorities.
The Situation Monitoring and Mapping Technical Working Group (GTT SMAPS) has been activated. Neighbouring
countries, regional response teams and PAHO/WHO strategic stockpiles are on standby and ready to provide support if
required.
Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs)
PAHO/WHO reports the identification of 21 EMTs from 15 countries as of 25 June 2026:
Samaritan's Purse (USA); Dominican Republic MoH T1F; BHSR
Ready to deploy 3
Colombia T1F

EMT; Johanniter; CMAT; Massachusetts General Hospital; ISAR
Germany; TMAT Japan; Korea Disaster Relief Team; Lithuanian
EMT; EMERCOM Russia; EMT2 Toscana
TOTAL 21 15 countries
4. Priority Health Risks and Needs
Pre-existing Health Risks (Aggravated by the Earthquake)
Venezuela's protracted humanitarian crisis had severely weakened the health system prior to the earthquake, including a
37% shortage index for hospital emergency supplies (September 2024), critical staffing gaps, limited access to diagnostic
and imaging services, and the inability of most hospitals to sustain essential services — water, electricity and medical
gases — for more than 72 hours during outages. From an epidemiological perspective, Venezuela faces re-emergence of
vaccine-preventable diseases (measles, diphtheria, pertussis) and persistent vector-borne disease burden (dengue,
chikungunya, Zika, Oropouche, malaria, yellow fever). The earthquake is likely to generate additional demands for
emergency medical supplies, trauma care, health facility assessment capacity and operational coordination.
Immediate Health Priorities
• Mass casualty management and trauma care: Strengthen triage, emergency care, surgical capacity, referral
pathways and management of injured people, particularly in areas with collapsed buildings and ongoing search
and rescue operations.
• Health facility functionality and structural safety: Rapid assessment of hospitals and priority health facilities in
affected states — structural safety, emergency department capacity, operating theatres, inpatient beds, blood
supply, oxygen, water, electricity, fuel, telecommunications and availability of essential medicines.
• Continuity of essential health services: Maintain critical services including emergency care, maternal and
newborn care, dialysis, chronic disease treatment, emergency surgery, mental health and psychosocial support,
and disease surveillance.
• Ambulance services and referral routes: Verify ambulance capacity, road access, referral pathways and
transport constraints, particularly in areas with debris, damaged buildings or disrupted infrastructure.
• Medical supplies and logistics: Identify urgent needs for trauma supplies, surgical materials, emergency health
kits, medicines, PPE, oxygen, fuel and other critical supplies, and coordinate replenishment and transport.
• Public health risks in shelters and evacuation sites: Monitor WASH conditions, overcrowding, access to basic
health care, continuity of treatment for chronic patients, and risk communication needs in temporary shelters and
gathering points.
• Risk communication and community guidance: Support clear messaging on aftershocks, safe evacuation,
avoiding damaged structures, when and where to seek emergency care, and how to report missing persons.
5. Immediate Next Steps
The Health Cluster will prioritize the following actions over the next 24–48 hours:
• The Health Cluster partner meeting is called for Friday June the 26th — duty of care for partner organizations'
staff and initial mapping of health response capacity in affected states.
• Establish a consolidated health sector information cell to compile and verify updates from PAHO/WHO, health
authorities, partners and Civil Protection.

• Update 3W/4W partner presence mapping and identify partners with operational capacity in affected areas,
immediate health needs and gaps.
• Launch a rapid health facility functionality and damage assessment covering priority affected states.
• Support the identification of urgent needs related to triage, mass casualty management, trauma care, surgical
and neurosurgical capacity, referral pathways, ambulance services and patient distribution across the public
and private network.
• Identify urgent needs for medicines, trauma supplies, surgical materials, oxygen, emergency health kits, fuel
and other critical inputs.
6. Citizen Initiatives and Digital Support Networks
Alongside the institutional response, a broad network of citizen-led initiatives and digital humanitarian support platforms
has emerged, which the Health Cluster recognizes as part of the response ecosystem:
• desaparecidosterremotovenezuela.com — Citizen-led missing persons registration and tracking platform.
Managing over 10,000 records, focusing on verifying the safety status of individuals temporarily unreachable due to
telecommunications and power failures.
• venezuelatebusca.com — Crowd-sourced family tracing and missing persons mapping database across affected
states.
• hazlohoy.org/terremoto-caracas/ — Centralized mutual aid and donation platform for digital fundraising, volunteer
recruitment and coordination of localized relief inside Venezuela.
• juntossepuede.co — Portal of the 'Juntos Se Puede' organization: physical logistics support, verified collection
centres in Bogotá and transparent financial management channels for aid delivery.
• ayuda.cruzrojacolombiana.org/emergencia-terremoto-en-venezuela — Official Colombian Red Cross corridor for
donations and cross-border relief operations into Venezuela.
• donate.caritas.org/venezuelaSP/ — Cáritas international donation portal for deploying medical supplies, emergency
food and triage aid within affected parishes.
• donorbox.org/emergency-relief-for-venezuela-s-earthquake-survivors — International crowdfunding campaign
coordinated with UCV Volunteer Firefighters (Bomberos UCV) deployed in La Guaira to source rescue tools, field
medicine and equipment.
• venezuelajuntos.online/ — Emergency response platform cross-referencing crowd-sourced damage reports,
volunteer deployment registries and international resource pipelines.
• bokitas.org — Humanitarian foundation portal specializing in resource distribution for vulnerable demographics,
targeting pregnant women, lactating mothers and malnourished children in low-income sectors.
The 'Todos Con Venezuela' network, comprising over 151 active members including technology specialists, health
professionals and logistics coordinators, is collaborating directly with UCV Volunteer Firefighters, Cruz Roja, Cáritas and
other local organizations to map field needs. This network is auditing and segmenting collection centres and logistics
routes — supported by technology infrastructure and cross-border partnerships — to ensure aid reaches affected
populations transparently and directly. The Health Cluster notes the importance of linking these citizen initiatives with
formal humanitarian coordination mechanisms to maximize impact and minimize duplication.
7. Venezuela Health Cluster Baseline
Prior to the earthquake, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan identified 7.9 million people in need, while the Health
Cluster estimated 10.5 million people in need of health assistance and targeted 5.2 million people for health interventions.
The Cluster coordination architecture includes over 46 partners and 8 sub-national teams. Initial earthquake exposure
modelling indicates that up to 13.3 million people and 289 hospitals may be in areas exposed to shaking intensity V or
above; these figures are for planning purposes only and do not represent confirmed damage.

1. Panorama general de la situación
El 24 de junio de 2026, a las 18:04 hora local, dos
grandes terremotos sacudieron el centro-norte de
Venezuela en rápida sucesión. Según el Servicio
Geológico de los Estados Unidos (USGS), el primer
evento registró una magnitud de 7,1–7,2 con epicentro
al oeste de Morón (costa caribeña), a una profundidad
aproximada de 13 km. Aproximadamente un minuto
después, ocurrió un segundo terremoto de magnitud
7,5 al suroeste de Morón, a una profundidad
aproximada de 10 km. Ambos eventos se consideran
entre los más poderosos que han afectado a
Venezuela en más de un siglo.
Descritos como un ‘doblete sísmico’, ambos
terremotos fueron poco profundos, lo que aumentó su
intensidad destructiva. Se sintieron en gran parte de
Venezuela y en países vecinos. Las zonas más
afectadas reportadas hasta la fecha son La Guaira, el
Distrito Capital/Caracas, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo,
Falcón, Zulia, Yaracuy y Lara.
La presidenta encargada Delcy Rodríguez declaró el
estado de emergencia nacional. Se estableció un
Puesto de Comando Unificado con la presencia del
Coordinador Residente y OCHA. Las autoridades
venezolanas desplegaron fuerzas de seguridad a nivel
nacional y autorizaron el corte preventivo del
suministro de gas doméstico en edificios en riesgo.
Las actividades escolares y el trabajo no esencial han
sido suspendidos en las zonas afectadas, y algunos
hoteles han sido convertidos en refugios temporales.
Posteriormente se canceló un aviso de tsunami para
partes del Caribe. Se han registrado al menos 30
réplicas; es posible que ocurran más réplicas, lo que
podría agravar los daños en estructuras ya debilitadas.
Acceso y logística
El Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar (Maiquetía) sufrió graves daños en su infraestructura, fue cerrado inicialmente
y los vuelos comerciales fueron desviados a Aruba y Curazao. El Puesto de Comando Unificado confirmó que el
aeropuerto está operativo para vuelos humanitarios y de respuesta. La Base Aérea La Carlota (OACI: SVFM), ubicada en
Caracas con la pista 09 disponible, funciona como el principal punto de entrada para la asistencia internacional. Los
vuelos chárter tienen prioridad operativa. La presidenta encargada Rodríguez activó la aplicación móvil VenApp para
permitir que los ciudadanos reporten personas desaparecidas y situaciones de vivienda.

Respuesta internacional
Venezuela solicitó formalmente la activación del marco INSARAG mediante la Nota Verbal n.º 0987 de su Misión
Permanente en Ginebra, 25 de junio de 2026. Se ha autorizado el despliegue de todos los equipos internacionales
USAR. Entre las llegadas confirmadas para las próximas horas se incluyen equipos de Estados Unidos, República
Dominicana y El Salvador; Catar se prepara para desplegarse al día siguiente. México, China, Brasil y países del Caribe
han ofrecido asistencia. Se está movilizando un equipo UNDAC (contacto: jaggi@un.org). Más de 30 organizaciones de
búsqueda y rescate de América Latina, Europa, Asia y Oriente Medio reportan monitoreo activo o movilización en el
OSOCC Virtual.

avanzan las operaciones de búsqueda y rescate y las evaluaciones de daños.

Exposición de población y hospitales
El análisis preliminar de exposición de la OPS/OMS estima que 91 hospitales de emergencia se encuentran en zonas

4. Riesgos y necesidades de salud prioritarios
Riesgos de salud preexistentes (agravados por el terremoto)
La prolongada crisis humanitaria de Venezuela había debilitado gravemente el sistema de salud antes del terremoto,
incluyendo un índice de desabastecimiento del 37 % en insumos de emergencia hospitalaria (septiembre de 2024),
brechas críticas de personal, acceso limitado a servicios de diagnóstico e imagenología, y la incapacidad de la mayoría
de los hospitales para sostener servicios esenciales — agua, electricidad y gases médicos — durante más de 72 horas
en caso de interrupciones. Desde una perspectiva epidemiológica, Venezuela enfrenta la reaparición de enfermedades
prevenibles por vacunación (sarampión, difteria, tos ferina) y una carga persistente de enfermedades transmitidas por
vectores (dengue, chikunguña, zika, Oropouche, malaria, fiebre amarilla). Es probable que el terremoto genere
demandas adicionales de insumos médicos de emergencia, atención de trauma, capacidad de evaluación de
establecimientos de salud y coordinación operativa.
Prioridades de salud inmediatas
• Manejo de víctimas en masa y atención de trauma: Fortalecer el triaje, la atención de emergencias, la
capacidad quirúrgica, las rutas de referencia y el manejo de personas heridas, particularmente en zonas con
edificios colapsados y operaciones de búsqueda y rescate en curso.
• Funcionalidad de los establecimientos de salud y seguridad estructural: Evaluación rápida de hospitales y
establecimientos de salud prioritarios en los estados afectados — seguridad estructural, capacidad del
departamento de emergencias, quirófanos, camas de hospitalización, suministro de sangre, oxígeno, agua,
electricidad, combustible, telecomunicaciones y disponibilidad de medicamentos esenciales.

• Continuidad de los servicios de salud esenciales: Mantener servicios críticos, incluyendo atención de
emergencias, atención materna y neonatal, diálisis, tratamiento de enfermedades crónicas, cirugía de
emergencia, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, y vigilancia de enfermedades.
• Servicios de ambulancia y rutas de referencia: Verificar la capacidad de ambulancias, el acceso vial, las rutas
de referencia y las limitaciones de transporte, particularmente en zonas con escombros, edificios dañados o
infraestructura interrumpida.
• Insumos médicos y logística: Identificar necesidades urgentes de insumos para trauma, materiales quirúrgicos,
kits de salud de emergencia, medicamentos, EPP, oxígeno, combustible y otros suministros críticos, y coordinar
su reabastecimiento y transporte.
• Riesgos de salud pública en refugios y sitios de evacuación: Monitorear las condiciones de agua,
saneamiento e higiene (WASH), el hacinamiento, el acceso a la atención básica de salud, la continuidad del
tratamiento de pacientes crónicos y las necesidades de comunicación de riesgos en refugios temporales y puntos
de concentración.
• Comunicación de riesgos y orientación comunitaria: Apoyar mensajes claros sobre réplicas, evacuación
segura, evitar estructuras dañadas, cuándo y dónde buscar atención de emergencia, y cómo reportar personas
desaparecidas.
5. Próximos pasos inmediatos
El Clúster de Salud priorizará las siguientes acciones en las próximas 24–48 horas:
• Se convoca a la reunión de socios del Clúster de Salud para el viernes 26 de junio — deber de cuidado del
personal de las organizaciones socias y mapeo inicial de la capacidad de respuesta en salud en los estados
afectados.
• Establecer una célula de información consolidada del sector salud para compilar y verificar actualizaciones
de la OPS/OMS, las autoridades de salud, los socios y Protección Civil.
• Actualizar el mapeo de presencia de socios 3W/4W e identificar socios con capacidad operativa en las zonas
afectadas, necesidades de salud inmediatas y brechas.
• Lanzar una evaluación rápida de funcionalidad y daños de los establecimientos de salud que abarque los
estados afectados prioritarios.
• Apoyar la identificación de necesidades urgentes relacionadas con el triaje, el manejo de víctimas en masa,
la atención de trauma, la capacidad quirúrgica y neuroquirúrgica, las rutas de referencia, los servicios de
ambulancia y la distribución de pacientes en la red pública y privada.
• Identificar necesidades urgentes de medicamentos, insumos para trauma, materiales quirúrgicos, oxígeno,
kits de salud de emergencia, combustible y otros insumos críticos.
6. Iniciativas ciudadanas y redes de apoyo digital
Junto con la respuesta institucional, ha surgido una amplia red de iniciativas lideradas por ciudadanos y plataformas
digitales de apoyo humanitario, que el Clúster de Salud reconoce como parte del ecosistema de respuesta:
• desaparecidosterremotovenezuela.com — Plataforma ciudadana de registro y seguimiento de personas
desaparecidas. Gestiona más de 10.000 registros, enfocada en verificar el estado de seguridad de personas
temporalmente inubicables debido a fallas de telecomunicaciones y electricidad.
• venezuelatebusca.com — Base de datos colaborativa de localización familiar y mapeo de personas desaparecidas
en los estados afectados.
• hazlohoy.org/terremoto-caracas/ — Plataforma centralizada de ayuda mutua y donaciones para recaudación digital
de fondos, reclutamiento de voluntarios y coordinación de ayuda local dentro de Venezuela.
• juntossepuede.co — Portal de la organización ‘Juntos Se Puede’: apoyo logístico físico, centros de acopio
verificados en Bogotá y canales transparentes de manejo financiero para la entrega de ayuda.
• ayuda.cruzrojacolombiana.org/emergencia-terremoto-en-venezuela — Corredor oficial de la Cruz Roja
Colombiana para donaciones y operaciones de ayuda transfronteriza hacia Venezuela.
• donate.caritas.org/venezuelaSP/ — Portal internacional de donaciones de Cáritas para el despliegue de insumos
médicos, alimentos de emergencia y ayuda de triaje dentro de las parroquias afectadas.
• donorbox.org/emergency-relief-for-venezuela-s-earthquake-survivors — Campaña internacional de recaudación
de fondos coordinada con los Bomberos Voluntarios de la UCV desplegados en La Guaira para obtener herramientas
de rescate, medicina de campo y equipos.

• venezuelajuntos.online/ — Plataforma de respuesta de emergencia que cruza reportes colaborativos de daños,
registros de despliegue de voluntarios y canales internacionales de recursos.
• bokitas.org — Portal de fundación humanitaria especializada en la distribución de recursos para poblaciones
vulnerables, dirigido a mujeres embarazadas, madres lactantes y niños con desnutrición en sectores de bajos
ingresos.
La red ‘Todos Con Venezuela’, integrada por más de 151 miembros activos, entre ellos especialistas en tecnología,
profesionales de la salud y coordinadores logísticos, está colaborando directamente con los Bomberos Voluntarios de la
UCV, la Cruz Roja, Cáritas y otras organizaciones locales para mapear las necesidades en el terreno. Esta red está
auditando y segmentando los centros de acopio y las rutas logísticas — con el apoyo de infraestructura tecnológica y
alianzas transfronterizas — para garantizar que la ayuda llegue a las poblaciones afectadas de forma transparente y
directa. El Clúster de Salud señala la importancia de vincular estas iniciativas ciudadanas con los mecanismos formales
de coordinación humanitaria para maximizar el impacto y minimizar la duplicación.
7. Línea base del Clúster de Salud de Venezuela
Antes del terremoto, el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026 identificó a 7,9 millones de personas con necesidades,
mientras que el Clúster de Salud estimó 10,5 millones de personas con necesidad de asistencia en salud y fijó como
meta 5,2 millones de personas para intervenciones de salud. La arquitectura de coordinación del Clúster incluye más de
46 socios y 8 equipos subnacionales. La modelación inicial de exposición al terremoto indica que hasta 13,3 millones de
personas y 289 hospitales podrían estar en zonas expuestas a una intensidad de sacudida V o superior; estas cifras
tienen fines exclusivamente de planificación y no representan daños confirmados.

**CARACAS / PANAMA 25 June 2026 –** UNICEF stands in solidarity with the children and families affected by the 7.5 and 7.2 magnitude earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026.

The earthquakes have affected communities in Caracas and the states of Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, La Guaira, Miranda and nearby areas. As official situation assessments evolve, communities are urged to remain alert for possible aftershocks and follow official guidance.

UNICEF is monitoring the situation closely and emphasizes the importance of ensuring that affected children are protected and that their rights remain at the centre of the response.

In the hours and days ahead, children will need protection, psychosocial support, safe water, healthcare and safe spaces as communities recover from the shock and destruction. UNICEF is committed to supporting national efforts to address the needs of affected children and their families, particularly the most vulnerable.

**About UNICEF**

UNICEF, the United Nations agency for children, works to protect the rights of every child, everywhere, especially the most disadvantaged children and in the toughest places to reach. Across more than 190 countries and territories, we do whatever it takes to help children survive, thrive, and fulfil their potential.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Reporte de situación #2**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**25 de junio de 2026**  
**Hora: 3:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- Dos sismos consecutivos de magnitud 7.2 y 7.5 registrados alrededor de las 18:00 del miércoles 24 de julio. Al momento de reporte, se han reportado más de 130.
- 211 personas fallecidas y 1261 heridas, según autoridades a la tarde del jueves 25 de junio.
- 250 edificios se vieron afectados o sufrieron perdida total, particularmente en La Guaira, según información oficial.
- Estado La Guaira identificado como el más afectado, con múltiples edificaciones colapsadas.
- Daños estructurales significativos en Caracas, incluyendo colapsos parciales y evacuaciones masivas.
- Activación del Estado de Emergencia y del Estado Mayor de respuesta.
- Equipos internacionales de rescate en camino.

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras la ocurrencia de dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud en la región centro-norte del país el 24 de junio alrededor de las 18:00 (hora local). El primer evento (M7.2) fue seguido por un segundo de mayor intensidad (hasta M7.5), lo que amplificó significativamente el impacto en superficie. La ocurrencia de múltiples réplicas (más de 130 según datos oficiales) mantiene condiciones de riesgo elevado.

Los dos eventos principales ocurrieron con apenas 39–40 segundos de diferencia, con epicentro frente a la costa centro-norte, a unos 28–30 km al noroeste de Montalbán (estado Carabobo).

La respuesta gubernamental está centrada en operaciones de búsqueda y rescate, atención médica de emergencia y evaluación de daños. El impacto ha sido severo y generalizado, afectando infraestructura crítica, servicios públicos y viviendas en varios estados, con mayor concentración en Distrito Capital, La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo y Yaracuy.

Caracas registró sacudidas prolongadas (60 segundos), resultando en pánico generalizado, evacuaciones y daños estructurales significativos en edificaciones. El estado La Guaira ha sido identificado como el epicentro del impacto más severo, con reportes de múltiples colapsos y condiciones calificadas como zona de desastre, donde continúan operaciones intensivas de rescate.

El balance oficial hasta el momento reporta 211 personas fallecidas y 1261 heridas. Estas cifras están sujetas a actualización conforme avanzan las labores de búsqueda y rescate.

• Vaticano confirmó una donación de $100.000 para asistencia humanitaria.

• Búsqueda y rescate de personas atrapadas en estructuras colapsadas
• Atención médica de emergencia para los heridos
• Evaluación estructural de edificaciones
• Alojamiento temporal para población afectada
Medidas adoptadas
• Suspensión de clases y actividades no esenciales.
• Habilitación de refugios temporales.
• Plataformas activas para reporte de personas desaparecidas y daños en viviendas.
• Llamado a la calma, unidad nacional y evacuación de estructuras inseguras.

www.unocha.org

Distrito Capital (Caracas)

• Colapso o daños críticos en infraestructuras específicas, incluyendo edificaciones residenciales y

• Afectaciones relevantes en Los Palos Grandes (municipio Chacao), donde se reportan estructuras

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Situation Report #2**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**25 June 2026**  
**Time: 3:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Two consecutive earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 recorded at around 18:00 on Wednesday 24 June, with more than 130 aftershocks.
- 211 people dead and 1261 injured (provisional figure), according to authorities as of the afternoon of Thursday, June 25.
- 250 buildings were affected or suffered total loss, particularly in La Guaira, according to official information.
- La Guaira state identified as the most affected, with multiple collapsed buildings.
- Significant structural damage in Caracas, including partial collapses and mass evacuations.
- Activation of the State of Emergency and the response General Staff.
- International rescue teams on the way.

**General situation**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes in the north-central region of the country on 24 June at around 18:00 (local time). The first event (M7.2) was followed by a second of greater intensity (up to M7.5), which significantly amplified the surface impact. The occurrence of multiple aftershocks (more than 130 aftershocks, according to official information.) maintains elevated risk conditions.

The two main events occurred just 39–40 seconds apart, with an epicenter off the central-northern coast, about 28–30 km northwest of Montalbán (Carabobo state).

The governmental response is focused on search-and-rescue operations, emergency medical care and damage assessment. The impact has been severe and widespread, affecting critical infrastructure, public services and housing in several states, with the greatest concentration in the Capital District, La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo and Yaracuy.

Caracas experienced prolonged shaking (60 seconds), resulting in widespread panic, evacuations and significant structural damage to buildings. La Guaira state has been identified as the epicentre of the most severe impact, with reports of multiple collapses and conditions classified as a disaster zone, where intensive rescue operations continue.

The provisional official toll reports 211 people dead and 1261 injured. These figures subject to revision as work continues in collapsed structures.

information at the time of the report.
• Disruptions to electricity, water and telecommunications in multiple states.
• Power outages reported in Caracas, Mérida, San Cristóbal, Barquisimeto, Coro, Maracay, Valencia

• Transport system disrupted: Caracas Metro and railways out of operation.
• Maiquetía International Airport closed due to infrastructure damage.

cancelled flights and are applying flexibility policies.
National and international response
• Activation of the National Emergency System and Civil Protection.
• Deployment of search-and-rescue teams in affected areas.
• Establishment of the coordination General Staff and declaration of a national state of emergency.
• Activation of the public and private health network for mass treatment of the injured.
International support:
• Response mechanisms are being mobilized, with the UN Disaster Assessment and Coordination
Team (UNDAC) activated at an initial level. Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams, under
INSARAG coordination, are also being deployed.

United States, Spain, France, Italy, Jordan, the Netherlands, the Czech Republic, the Dominican
Republic, Switzerland, and Qatar.Offers of assistance from China, Brazil, Caribbean countries and
multilateral bodies.

organizations.
• France: dispatch of 85 specialists in urban search and rescue.
• Ecuador: immediate dispatch of humanitarian aid, on the instruction of President Daniel Noboa.

in new bilateral allocations to partners on the ground and a $100 million contribution to the OCHA
pooled fund in Venezuela.
• Deployment of a medical assessment team (AECID).
• CAF announced a donation of $300,000 to support the emergency response.
• The Vatican confirmed a donation of $100,000 for humanitarian assistance.
Immediate needs and priorities
• Search and rescue of people trapped in collapsed structures
• Emergency medical care for the injured
• Structural assessment of buildings
• Temporary shelter for the affected population
Measures adopted
• Suspension of classes and non-essential activities.
• Opening of temporary shelters.
• Active platforms to report missing persons and housing damage.
• Call for calm, national unity and evacuation of unsafe structures.
United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3

Capital District (Caracas)
• Intense shaking (>60 seconds) with widespread panic and mass evacuations.
• Collapse or critical damage to specific infrastructure, including residential and commercial
buildings.
• Significant impacts in Los Palos Grandes (Chacao municipality), where collapsed structures and
an active emergency response are reported.
• Five (5) shelters were set up in Caracas with a capacity for 375 families, 75 families each. They
are located in Quinta Crespo, Pinto Salinas, El Valle, Caricuao, and La Vega.
• Suspension of the Metro and railway system.
• The Venezuelan Red Cross described the situation in Greater Caracas as “the worst they have
witnessed”; some of its facilities were rendered unusable, although its hospital network remains
operational.
•
La Guaira
• Declared a disaster zone.
• Multiple collapsed buildings, including homes, commercial facilities and public infrastructure.
• Severe damage to Maiquetía International Airport, with full closure and suspension of operations.
• Intensive rescue operations under way.
• Set-up of a temporary shelter in Macuto (baseball stadium).
• Confirmed as the most affected state.
Miranda
• Injured people, especially in Guatire.
Carabobo and Yaracuy (epicentral zone)
• Severe damage to homes, infrastructure and roads.
• Visible structural damage to critical infrastructure.
• Disruptions to basic services.
Falcón (Tucacas – Silva municipality)
• Approximally 15 people missing and 35 injured (under search and treatment).
• Of the 35 people injured, 32 are hospitalized and 2 in critical condition were referred to a higher-
complexity facility, according to official information.
• Saturation of local services and an urgent request for medical, logistical and transport support.

affected to a lesser extent.

Government restricted heavy-cargo traffic on the Morón–Coro highway.

of Tucacas) and a school in Boca de Aroa were affected.
• The Felipe Estévez School will be set up as a shelter and response-management point for the

documents.title: Situation Report No.1: Earthquakes in Venezuela (M7.2 and M7.5), June 25, 2026
documents.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

• On 24 June 2026, two consecutive earthquakes (M7.2 and M7.5) struck Yaracuy state in north-central Venezuela with ~3.9 million people exposed to severe shaking.

• The earthquake was felt across several states, including Miranda, Aragua, Yaracuy, Lara, Mérida, Falcón, Carabobo, La Guaira and the Capital District. La Guaira may be among the worst affected –with multiple collapsed buildings, ongoing search and rescue, and a disaster-area declaration – while collapsed buildings and damaged infrastructure are also reported in parts of Caracas and Miranda. Assessments are still ongoing

• Venezuela's Acting President, Delcy Rodríguez, has declared a state of emergency and reported on Thursday that 164 deaths and 971 injuries had been registered following the two major earthquakes.

• The public and private health networks have reportedly been mobilized to provide immediate care to injured people (including 20 public and private health facilities in Gran Caracas). Reported disruptions to electricity, water, domestic gas, transport systems and telecommunications in affected areas may further affect health service continuity, emergency referrals, hospital operations, ambulance dispatch, referral pathways and coordination.

• The Simon Bolivar International Airport was reportedly seriously affected and is currently closed.

• Authorities have reportedly suspended school activities and non-essential work in affected areas to facilitate response, some hotels have been turned into shelters available for those displaced or with structurally unsafe homes, and activated a national crisis management mechanism.

• The main risks at this stage remain structural collapse, aftershocks, trauma injuries, disruption of health services, damage to health facilities, interruptions to power, water and connectivity, access constraints.

• PAHO/WHO staff are reported safe, and the PAHO office withstood the earthquake.

 • PAHO/WHO is supporting health sector coordination with the Ministry of Health, Civil Protection and the Health Cluster—convening partners, supporting evaluations, mapping partner presence and capacity, and engaging regional counterparts on potential donations. It is supporting rapid health facility functionality and damage assessments and identification of urgent needs for medicines, supplies, oxygen, fuel and other critical response needs. The PAHO Regional Response Team is on standby, with specialists identified for potential deployment across coordination, hospital safety, mass casualty care, logistics and other key areas.

• Domingo Luciani Hospital was evacuated as a precaution and is under technical assessment but

• The Military Hospital Dr. Carlos Arvelo is reportedly receiving a high number of trauma and

• Media reports suggest possible damage to Hospital Dr. Francisco Antonio Rísquez (Cotiza) and
severe structural damage to Clínica Ávila, a private facility—both requiring official confirmation and
urgent verification of functionality.
La Guaira
• La Guaira is reported as one of the most affected areas, with collapsed buildings, ongoing search
and rescue operations, and high pressure on health services.
• Vargas Hospital in La Guaira is reportedly receiving a high influx of patients and operating beyond
capacity, while Pariata Hospital is reportedly overwhelmed by patient demand. Official assessment
of hospital functionality and capacity is needed.
Zulia / Maracaibo
• At least three hospitals have reported some level of structural damage. No total hospital collapse
has been reported so far.
• Detailed functionality and capacity assessments are ongoing.
Carabobo / Valencia
• Unofficial reports suggest the main hospital in Valencia may have been affected, though
assessment is ongoing.
Other affected states
The earthquake was felt across several states, including Miranda, Aragua, Yaracuy, Lara, Mérida, Falcón,
Carabobo, La Guaira and the Capital District. Additional reports of structural damage and health service
disruption may emerge as local assessments progress.
3. Health Cluster coordination
4

Earthquake in Venezuela: Sitrep #1
• Venezuela’s Health Cluster, with PAHO/WHO support and coordination with the Global Health
Cluster, is monitoring the situation and maintaining contact with health authorities, partners, Civil
Protection and regional response structures.
• The Health Cluster is prioritizing the verification of health sector information—facility functionality
and structural status, trauma and emergency care capacity, referral pathways, ambulance services,
and continuity of essential services—alongside mapping partner presence and capacity in affected
states, identifying gaps, and supporting a coordinated response aligned with national priorities.
• Neighboring countries, regional response teams and PAHO’s Strategic Reserve stockpiles are on
standby and ready to support if required.
4. Priority health risks and needs
Health risks:
• Venezuela’s protracted humanitarian crisis has severely weakened the health system, driving
widespread medicine shortages – reflected in a 37% shortage index for hospital emergency
supplies as of September 2024 – alongside deteriorating service quality, critical staffing gaps
and limited access to diagnostic and imaging services.
• Many hospitals cannot sustain essential services—water, power, and medical gas—for 72 hours
during outages, and no contingency plans have been reported.
• From an epidemiological perspective, Venezuela faces substantial public health threats, including
the re-emergence of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, diphtheria, and pertussis,
driven by insufficient immunization coverage. In addition, vector-borne diseases—including dengue,
chikungunya, Zika, Oropouche, malaria, and yellow fever—remain significant and persistent health
challenges.
• Given the pre-existing fragility of the health system and the protracted humanitarian emergency in
Venezuela, the earthquake is likely to drive additional requests for support, including emergency
medical supplies, trauma care, health facility assessments, and operational coordination.
Immediate health priorities:
• Mass casualty management and trauma care: Strengthen triage, emergency care, surgical
capacity, referral pathways and management of injured people, particularly in areas with collapsed
buildings and ongoing search and rescue operations.
• Health facility functionality and structural safety: Rapidly assess hospitals and priority health
facilities in affected states, including structural safety, emergency department capacity, operating
theatres, inpatient beds, blood supply, oxygen, water, electricity, fuel, telecommunications and
availability of essential medicines.
• Continuity of essential health services: Maintain critical services, including emergency care,
maternal and newborn care, dialysis, chronic disease treatment, emergency surgery, mental health
and psychosocial support, and disease surveillance.
• Ambulance services and referral routes: Verify ambulance capacity, road access, referral
pathways and transport constraints, particularly in areas with debris, damaged buildings or disrupted
transport infrastructure.
5

Earthquake in Venezuela: Sitrep #1
• Medical supplies and logistics: Identify urgent needs for trauma supplies, surgical materials,
emergency health kits, medicines, PPE, oxygen, fuel and other critical supplies, and coordinate
potential replenishment and transport.1
• Public health risks in shelters and evacuation sites: Monitor WASH conditions, overcrowding,
access to basic health care, continuity of treatment for chronic patients, and risk communication
needs in temporary shelters and gathering points.
• Risk communication and community guidance: Support clear messaging on aftershocks, safe
evacuation, avoiding damaged structures, when and where to seek emergency care, and how to
report missing persons or urgent health needs.
Emergency response:
PAHO/WHO response actions:
PAHO/WHO is supporting national authorities and the health sector response through technical
cooperation, coordination, information management and readiness for additional surge support. Priority
support actions include:
• Health sector coordination: Support coordination with the Ministry of Health, Civil Protection, the
Health Cluster and health partners to align response priorities, consolidate information and avoid
duplication. PAHO/WHO is also engaging with neighboring countries and regional counterparts to
explore potential health-related donations and support, according to identified needs and national
requests.
• Health Cluster coordination: Convene a Health Cluster partner meeting to review the evolving
situation, address duty of care for partner organizations’ staff, establish a consolidated health sector
information cell, compile and verify updates from PAHO/WHO, the Ministry of Health, Civil
Protection and partners, update the 3W/4W partner presence and operational capacity mapping,
identify immediate health needs and gaps in affected areas, and launch a rapid health facility
functionality and damage assessment covering priority affected states.
• Partner capacity mapping: Update partner presence, operational capacity and available stocks in
affected areas to support a coordinated health response.
• Emergency, trauma and specialized care: Support the identification of urgent needs related to
triage, mass casualty management, trauma care, surgical and neurosurgical capacity, referral
pathways, ambulance services and patient distribution across the public and private network.
• Medical supplies and logistics: Help identify urgent needs for medicines, trauma supplies,
surgical materials, oxygen, emergency health kits, fuel and other critical inputs, and coordinate with
logistics actors and strategic stockpiles if additional support is requested.
• Regional surge readiness: PAHO Regional Response Team is on standby and specialists have
been identified and could be made available for deployment if requested, including experts in health
emergency coordination, hospital functionality and structural safety assessment, mass casualty
management, trauma and emergency care, logistics and medical supplies, information
management, risk communication, mental health and psychosocial support, WASH in health
facilities, and continuity of essential health services.
• Emergency Medical Teams readiness: PAHO/WHO is monitoring the availability of regional and
international Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) to support the response, in coordination with
national authorities and subject to formal request. As of 25 June 2026, 21 EMTs from 15 countries
have been identified, including 3 teams ready to deploy, 5 teams on stand-by and 13 teams under
monitoring. Available capacities include Type 1 fixed and mobile teams, Type 2 teams, one Type 3
team and one specialized rehabilitation/specialized care team.

documents.title: Terremotos en Venezuela: Reporte de situación #1 (25 de junio de 2026, Hora: 03:00 am)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**25 de junio de 2026**  
**Hora: 03:00 am**

**Destacados**

- Dos sismos consecutivos de magnitud 7.2 y 7.5 registrados alrededor de las 18:00 H, con más de 20 réplicas.
- 32 personas fallecidas (preliminar) y más de 700 heridos, según autoridades.
- Estado La Guaira identificado como el más afectado, con múltiples edificaciones colapsadas.
- Daños estructurales significativos en Caracas, incluyendo colapsos parciales y evacuaciones masivas.
- Aeropuerto de Maiquetía cerrado, Metro y ferrocarril suspendidos.
- Activación del Estado de Emergencia y del Estado Mayor de respuesta.
- Equipos internacionales de rescate en camino.

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras la ocurrencia de dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud en la región centro-norte del país el 24 de junio alrededor de las 18:00 (hora local). El primer evento (M7.2) fue seguido por un segundo de mayor intensidad (hasta M7.5), lo que amplificó significativamente el impacto en superficie. La ocurrencia de múltiples réplicas (más de 20) mantiene condiciones de riesgo elevado.

La respuesta gubernamental está centrada en operaciones de búsqueda y rescate, atención médica de emergencia y evaluación de daños. El impacto ha sido severo y generalizado, afectando infraestructura crítica, servicios públicos y viviendas en varios estados, con mayor concentración en Distrito Capital, La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo y Yaracuy.

Caracas registró sacudidas prolongadas (60 segundos), resultando en pánico generalizado, evacuaciones y daños estructurales significativos en edificaciones. El estado La Guaira ha sido identificado como el epicentro del impacto más severo, con reportes de colapsos múltiples y condiciones calificadas como zona de desastre, donde continúan operaciones intensivas de rescate.

El balance preliminar reporta 32 personas fallecidas y más de 700 heridas, con cifras sujetas a actualización conforme avanzan las labores en estructuras colapsadas.
