identificado como el epicentro del impacto más severo, con reportes de colapsos múltiples y
condiciones calificadas como zona de desastre, donde continúan operaciones intensivas de rescate.
El balance preliminar reporta 32 personas fallecidas y más de 700 heridas, con cifras sujetas a
actualización conforme avanzan las labores en estructuras colapsadas.
Impacto en infraestructura
• Daños severos en viviendas y edificaciones, incluyendo colapsos parciales y totales.
• Afectaciones en electricidad, agua y telecomunicaciones en múltiples estados.
• Suspensión preventiva del gas doméstico en áreas críticas.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 2
• Sistema de transporte interrumpido: Metro de Caracas y ferrocarriles fuera de operación.
• Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía cerrado por daños en infraestructura.
Respuesta nacional e internacional
• Activación del Sistema Nacional de Emergencias y Protección Civil.
• Despliegue de equipos de búsqueda y rescate en zonas afectadas.
• Instalación del Estado Mayor de coordinación y declaración de estado de emergencia nacional.
• Activación de la red de salud pública y privada para atención masiva de heridos.
Apoyo internacional:
• Equipos de rescate en despliegue desde: Estados Unidos, República Dominicana, El Salvador y
Qatar.
• Coordinación adicional con México.
• Ofrecimientos de asistencia de China, Brasil, países del Caribe y organismos multilaterales.
Necesidades y prioridades inmediatas
• Búsqueda y rescate de personas atrapadas en estructuras colapsadas
• Atención médica de emergencia para los heridos
• Evaluación estructural de edificaciones
• Restablecimiento de servicios básicos esenciales
• Alojamiento temporal para población afectada
Medidas adoptadas
• Suspensión de clases y actividades no esenciales.
• Habilitación de refugios temporales.
• Plataformas activas para reporte de personas desaparecidas y daños en viviendas.
• Llamado a la calma, unidad nacional y evacuación de estructuras inseguras.
• Recomendación de seguir únicamente información oficial.
Situación por estado
Distrito Capital (Caracas)
• Sacudidas intensas (>60 segundos) con pánico generalizado y evacuaciones masivas.
• Daños estructurales significativos, incluyendo colapso parcial de edificaciones y caída de
fachadas.
• Reportes de colapso de al menos cuatro edificios, con operaciones de rescate enfocadas en
personas atrapadas.
• Afectaciones relevantes en Los Palos Grandes (municipio Chacao), donde se reportan estructuras
colapsadas y respuesta activa de emergencia.
• Colapso o daños críticos en infraestructuras específicas, incluyendo edificaciones residenciales y
comerciales.
• Suspensión del Metro y sistema ferroviario.
•
La Guaira
• Declarada zona de desastre.
• Múltiples edificaciones colapsadas, incluyendo viviendas, instalaciones comerciales e
infraestructura pública.
• Daños severos en el Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía, con cierre total y suspensión de
operaciones.
• Operaciones intensivas de rescate en curso.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 3
• Instalación de albergue temporal en Macuto (estadio de béisbol).
Miranda
• Personas lesionadas, especialmente en Guatire.
• Evacuaciones masivas y población a la intemperie.
• Alta congestión vial en principales corredores.
Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona epicentral)
• Daños severos en viviendas, infraestructura y vías.
• Afectaciones estructurales visibles en infraestructura crítica.
• Interrupciones en servicios básicos.
Falcón (Tucacas – Municipio Silva)
• Emergencia crítica: colapso total de estructura residencial.
• 15 personas desaparecidas y 35 lesionadas (en búsqueda y atención).
• Saturación de servicios locales y solicitud urgente de apoyo médico, logístico y de transporte.
Aragua
• Daños en zonas costeras, incluyendo áreas turísticas.
Lara
• Interrupciones severas del servicio eléctrico, incrementando vulnerabilidades preexistentes.
Táchira
• Sin daños estructurales reportados.
• Activación preventiva de protocolos de evaluación.
• Infraestructura aeroportuaria operativa.
Sucre
• Sin afectaciones reportadas.
• Autoridades descartan alerta de tsunami en la región oriental.
Otros estados (Apure, Zulia, Amazonas, Mérida, Trujillo)
• Sin novedades relevantes reportadas al momento.
Coordinación humanitaria
• Las organizaciones humanitarias se mantienen en monitoreo constante de la situación a nivel
nacional.
• OCHA sostiene comunicación continua con Protección Civil y autoridades competentes, facilitando
el intercambio de información y seguimiento de necesidades.
• Activados los mecanismos de coordinación a través de los Foros Locales y Grupos de
Coordinación (FLC/GLC).
• Socios humanitarios avanzan en la evaluación de posibles intervenciones, incluyendo apoyo en
salud, protección y atención a población afectada.
• Se promueve la articulación de acciones en salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS), primeros
auxilios psicológicos (PAP) y servicios de atención primaria (APS).
• Equipos técnicos (incluyendo ingenieros) en coordinación para evaluaciones rápidas de
infraestructura crítica, particularmente en centros de salud.
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

OCHA | 4
• Se encuentra en proceso la activación del mecanismo UNDAC (UN Disaster Assessment and
Coordination) para un posible despliegue de equipo de apoyo en el país.
• Equipos USAR bajo el marco INSARAG están en fase inicial de organización y alistamiento para
despliegue, con detalles operativos aún en definición.
• OCHA mantiene comunicación permanente con Protección Civil y autoridades nacionales,
apoyando el monitoreo de la situación y la consolidación de información.
Informacion de Contacto
Para mayor información, por favor contactar a la Oficina de OCHA Venezuela:
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
Vanessa May – Oficial de Asuntos Humanitarios - mayv@un.org
Alfonso Zabaleta – Oficial de Asuntos Humanitarios - alfonso.zabaleta@un.org
Jennifer Moreno – Oficial de Información Pública – moreno7@un.org
Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)
www.unocha.org

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake Situation Overview (25 June, 2026)
documents.body_text:
On 24 June 2026, northern Venezuela was struck by two powerful earthquakes approximately 40 seconds apart - a magnitude 7.2 foreshock followed by a magnitude 7.5 mainshock, making it the country's strongest recorded earthquake in more than 125 years. The shallow earthquakes generated violent ground shaking across northern Venezuela, causing widespread damage to homes, health facilities, schools, transport infrastructure, and essential services. As of 25 June, at least 164 people have been confirmed dead and 971 injured, although casualty figures are expected to rise as search and rescue operations continue and assessments reach previously inaccessible areas.

This report provides a consolidated overview of the evolving humanitarian situation, including the geographic extent of the earthquake and an assessment of the most affected states, municipalities, and parishes. It also analyses the humanitarian impacts in the context of Venezuela's pre-existing vulnerabilities, which are likely to compound the effects of the disaster and increase humanitarian needs. Drawing on available information, the report identifies priority humanitarian needs across key sectors, highlights the populations and locations facing the greatest risks, and outlines key response considerations and likely operational priorities to support emergency response, humanitarian coordination, and the transition towards early recovery.

The methodology utilized in this report has been jointly developed with GiveDirectly.

Earthquake overview
On the evening of 24 June 2026, two major earthquakes struck northern Venezuela about 40 seconds
apart: a magnitude 7.2 foreshock and a magnitude 7.5 mainshock. The USGS records it as the strongest
earthquake in Venezuela in more than 125 years (USGS 24/06/2026, Al Jazeera 25/06/2026.
Both shocks were shallow on the Boconó-Morón-El Pilar fault system, at the Caribbean and South
American plate boundary; the mainshockʼs depth of about 10 km amplified surface shaking, with peak
intensity approaching MMI 9 (violent). Shaking was felt across northern Venezuela and into Colombia
(USGS 24/06/2026, Al Jazeera 25/06/2026.

The PAGER red alert indicates that high casualties and extensive damage are probable. At least 20
aftershocks followed within roughly two hours, six of them felt in Caracas, and the USGS puts the
chance of a magnitude 6 or greater aftershock in the first week at about 40 percent. A brief Caribbean
tsunami advisory was cancelled within about an hour (USGS 24/06/2026, CNN 25/06/2026, NPR
25/06/2026.
2

Casualties and exposure
At least 164 people are confirmed dead and 971 injured nationally, in an update from Acting President
Delcy Rodríguez early on 25 June, revised up from an initial 32 dead and around 700 injured. These are
confirmed minimums and are expected to rise; the toll does not yet include La Guaira, which Rodríguez
described as a disaster zone, so the national figure is already higher. Local authorities reported three
dead in Baruta and one in Chacao, 15 people being searched for in Falcón alongside 35 injured, and
several collapse sites still being worked in Caracas (NPR 25/06/2026, CNN 25/06/2026.
Modelled estimates run far above the confirmed count, as is normal this early. The USGS PAGER model
gives a probable range of 10,000 to 100,000 deaths under a red alert, and a DFS run of the same
method returns a central estimate of about 9,600, roughly 60 times the confirmed count so far (USGS

are probabilistic model outputs, not counts, and carry very wide uncertainty. They are for early planning only; the
confirmed figures issued by the Venezuelan authorities take precedence as verification proceeds.
3

About 6.6 million people felt the earthquake. Roughly 4.33 million were within the MMI VI band where
damage begins, about 690,000 at MMI VII or above, and about 124,000 in the severe MMI VIII band, with
none at MMI IX. This aligns with USGS exposure estimates of more than 500,000 in the severe zone and
about 117,000 in the most intense. Around 279 km² of built-up surface, about three quarters of the
analysed total, lies inside the damage zone, which contains 848 health facilities and 880 schools
needing structural assessment (USGS 24/06/2026.2
Geographic distribution
The epicentre lies in sparsely populated Veroes, in Yaracuy, but the heaviest burden falls east and
south-east along the fault toward the Caracas, La Guaira, Valencia and Maracay corridor, home to 6 to 7
million people. The states below are ordered by modelled severity rather than by media attention, which
over-represents Caracas and La Guaira and under-represents the epicentral states of Carabobo and
Yaracuy. Available information remains qualitative, so this order reflects modelled intensity and fatalities,
not measured impact (USGS 24/06/2026, Al Jazeera 25/06/2026.

Carabobo carries about two thirds of the modelled deaths, followed by La Guaira and Yaracuy; together
the three account for roughly 96 percent of the total. Distrito Capital and Miranda hold the largest
exposed populations but show few modelled deaths, because peak shaking there reached only MMI 6.8
to 7.4 against the near-MMI 9 of the epicentral corridor. Aragua and Falcón record lighter impact; Trujillo
and Zulia, named in early accounts, fall outside the damaging-shaking footprint (CNN 25/06/2026, Al
Jazeera 25/06/2026.
2Modelled figures (exposure, fatalities and the relevance score) are produced by the DFS disaster-analytics pipeline
from open data; Annex 2 sets out the sources and method.

most of the modelled deaths, while high-population states such as Miranda and Distrito Capital sit
almost entirely in the lower MMI VI band. Health and school counts are highest in Caracas and Miranda
and sparse in the epicentral states, which reflects OpenStreetMap coverage as much as the real
distribution of facilities.
Priority parishes for assessment
Below the state level the model resolves to 164 parishes. The table shows two different measures side
by side, and they answer different questions. The relevance score, a 0 to 100 measure in the dataset,
estimates how many likely-deprived people felt damaging shaking: the population exposed at MMI VI or
above, weighted by deprivation. It counts exposure above the VI threshold and does not scale with how
intense the shaking was. Estimated fatalities come from a separate model USGS PAGER driven by
shaking intensity, which for Venezuela rises steeply, so deaths concentrate in the highest-intensity
parishes near the epicentre. The two diverge by design: relevance shows where many vulnerable
people were exposed, PAGER shows where deaths are most likely. The parishes below are ordered by
relevance; the full list by state is in Annex 1.
The two maps below show this divergence geographically. Estimated casualties cluster in the epicentral
corridor and along the La Guaira coast, while relevance spreads across the populous, deprived belt
around Caracas, Valencia and the Miranda highlands, much of it well away from the strongest shaking.
The same contrast drives the parish ranking that follows.
5

vulnerable population exposed at MMI VI or above, spread across the Caracas, Valencia and Miranda
belt. The single black parish on the coast in both is Carayaca, which scores high on each. The two
panels use different colour scales and are not directly comparable colour for colour; they are shown
together only to illustrate that casualty risk and vulnerability-weighted exposure point to different
parishes. Sources: USGS PAGER and ShakeMap; WorldPop; deprivation from NASA SEDAC GRDI and

The list is dominated by large, deprived suburbs in the Caracas, Miranda and Valencia belt. Several of
the highest scores are not near the epicentre: after Carayaca, the top parishes lie 100 to 170 km from the
rupture, where peak shaking reached only MMI 6 to 7. Because the relevance score counts vulnerable
population exposed above the MMI VI threshold without scaling for intensity, a large, poor parish that
felt moderate shaking can outrank a smaller one closer to the epicentre that was shaken far harder. This
ranking is therefore indicative: a way to flag where many vulnerable people were likely affected and to
direct rapid assessment, not a measurement of damage or casualties. It should be validated against
field reports, official assessments and other partners' prioritisations before resources are committed,
particularly for high-scoring parishes far from the epicentre.
Pre-Crisis Context
The earthquake has struck a country already hosting one of the most severe humanitarian crises in the
Western Hemisphere, and one in the midst of a fragile political transition following the removal of
President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026. Before the disaster, an estimated 7.98.0 million people, over
a quarter of the population were in humanitarian need, against a 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan
which is currently only around 23.2% funded (ECHO assessed 25/06/2026, HumVenezuela 31/03/2026,
OCHA HNRP assessed 25/06/2026.
7

Pre-earthquake indicator (national) Figure
People in humanitarian need 7.9–8.0 million
Population living in extreme poverty 56%
Limited access to reliable health-system 70%

Moderate-to-severe food insecurity 40%
Children not attending class regularly 30%
Housing needing rehabilitation (national) 53.8%
Measles, diphtheria,

National sectoral People in Need PiN estimates highlight that Venezuela was already facing significant
humanitarian challenges before any earthquake-related impacts occurred, leaving limited capacity to
absorb a large-scale shock. Prior to the seismic event, an estimated 3.4 million people 12.0% of the
population) required food security assistance, reflecting persistent challenges related to food access
and livelihoods. The health sector recorded 5.5 million people 19.3% in need due to constraints on
healthcare access, service availability, and essential medicines. Needs were particularly acute in the
WASH sector, where 11.6 million people required support to access safe water, sanitation, and hygiene
services. Severe food insecurity continues to increase, going from 2.9 to 3.4 million people affected
between 2024 and 2025, which indicates a critical situation of lack of livelihoods and a more
pronounced multidimensional poverty, which would not improve with income increases. In addition, 2.1
million children and adolescents remained out of school - half are between 0 to 5 years old, highlighting
longstanding barriers to safe and continuous learning. Collectively, these figures illustrate that the
earthquake struck a population with substantial pre-existing humanitarian needs, increasing the
likelihood that disruptions to infrastructure and essential services will translate into disproportionately
severe impacts and place additional strain on already overstretched response capacities (ECHO
assessed 25/06/2026, HumVenezuela 31/03/2026, OCHA HNRP assessed 25/06/2026.
Impact on Population and Services
This is a rapidly evolving emergency less than 24 hours old. All figures should be used with attribution
to the originating source and date. No government or UN agency has published a total displaced
persons count as of this report.
Displacement
The twin earthquakes triggered large-scale displacement across multiple states in northern and central
Venezuela. Residents moved into the streets as buildings shook and remained outdoors well after
nightfall, with power cuts, toppled electric poles, and debris blocking streets across affected areas (CBS
News 25/06/2026. Preventative evacuations were carried out in several cities, with children and
families moving into open areas as aftershocks continue. The earthquakes struck during the evening
when many people were returning home, increasing concerns that individuals may be trapped beneath
collapsed structures (Save the Children 25/06/2026.
8

Displacement by Location
Spontaneous displacement was confirmed across several locations:
● La Guaira: the coastal state north of Caracas was the worst-affected area and was declared a
disaster zone, with extensive building collapse reported in Macuto and Catia La Mar (CNN,
25/06/2026. No formal shelter count has been published for the state.
● Falcón state: Governor Víctor Clark confirmed 32 people hospitalized and 15 still trapped hours
after the quake (NBC Miami, 25/06/2026.
● Caracas: more than 500 emergency workers were deployed to collapsed and damaged
buildings in Chacao municipality alone, gas supply was cut, and large areas lost power (CNN,
25/06/2026.
● Brazil (cross-border): Buildings were also evacuated in Brazilʼs Amazon cities of Manaus, Belém,
and Macapá as tremors were felt, though no damage or injuries were reported there (NBC
Miami, 25/06/2026.
Damage to Shelter
● National authorities activated search-and-rescue operations and set up reception centres for
people affected, while hospitals received the injured (IFRC 25/06/2026.
● Venezuelaʼs Ministry of Education announced late Wednesday that some schools would be used
as shelters and donation centres, though this sits in tension with the governmentʼs simultaneous
multi-day school closure order, indicating shelter capacity planning is still being established
(CBS News 25/06/2026.
● The Red Cross confirmed its nationwide hospital and clinic network was operational and that
volunteers were supporting relief efforts, with priorities centered on survivor rescue, emergency
shelter, healthcare, and safe water and sanitation access (CNN 25/06/2026. However, the Red
Cross's own national headquarters sustained critical damage in the earthquake, compounding
coordination capacity (CNN 25/06/2026.
Infrastructure and Services
Transport
● Simón Bolívar International Airport CCS in Maiquetía, La Guaira sustained severe structural
damage and was closed indefinitely. Footage reviewed by aviation publication Airways
Magazine showed fallen ceiling panels, debris across the terminal floor, dust filling the hall, and
people evacuating (Airways Magazine 24/06/2026.
● Acting President Rodríguez confirmed the closure due to “severe damage to its infrastructureˮ.
The U.S. Department of Defense committed to deploying assets there, and Germany offered six
military transport aircraft to move personnel and equipment into the country and facilitate
internal flights. (CNN 25/06/2026.
● No verified reporting has yet confirmed the status of secondary airports, including those in
Maracaibo, Valencia, or Barquisimeto, or of Venezuela's main seaport at La Guaira, which sits in
the same disaster zone as the airport.
● Subway and rail services in Caracas were suspended (CNN 25/06/2026. Collapsed buildings,
toppled electric poles, and debris blocked streets across the capital, further impeding
emergency vehicle movement (CBS News 25/06/2026.
● In the epicentral area west of Caracas, landslides are anticipated to have further blocked roads
and cut off rural communities. Geoscientist Dave Petley warned that silence from rural western
9

areas should be read as a danger signal, not an absence of impact (AGU Landslide Blog,
25/06/2026.
Power Supply and Gas Infrastructure
● Power outages were reported across multiple states, affecting Caracas and the northwestern
states of Aragua, Carabobo, and Falcón (CNN, 25/06/2026. As a preventative measure against
gas leaks and explosions, the government cut gas supply to buildings and areas across Caracas
(ABC7/AP, 25/06/2026.
● Chevron, which has the largest U.S. oil company presence in Venezuela, confirmed all
employees were accounted for and that it remained operational despite power outages along
the northern coast, though one source noted extended power loss could affect crude output
until service is restored (CNN, 25/06/2026, Khaleej Times/Reuters 25/06/2026.
● The broader impact on oil exports remains unclear at a sensitive moment, with Venezuela
ramping up production and the global energy market still recovering from the closure of the
Strait of Hormuz (CNN, 25/06/2026.
Telecommunications
● Internet connectivity dropped to a low of 59% of normal levels immediately after the
earthquakes, partially recovering to 77% in the hours following, according to watchdog
NetBlocks (CNN 25/06/2026.
● The IFRC confirmed that power and telecommunications disruptions left public services
intermittently available across affected areas (IFRC, 25/06/2026.
● Cellphone signal was lost in parts of the capital entirely (CBS News 25/06/2026.
● The U.S. government committed to providing overhead satellite imagery to compensate for
degraded ground-level access and communications in coastal areas.
● The EU also activated its Copernicus satellite imagery system to provide support on the ground
(CNN 25/06/2026
Health infrastructure
● At Hospital de Clínicas in Caracas, staff were asked to double night shifts to manage the influx
of injured. Video from the hospital showed structural interior damage, ceiling panels hanging by
cables and plaster on the floor, raising concerns about the safety of the facility while it received
patients (CNBC/Reuters 25/06/2026.
● The IFRC confirmed critical damage to essential health infrastructure across the affected area,
with public health services left intermittently available (IFRC 25/06/2026.
● World Vision reported damaged hospitals among the initial impacts (World Vision 25/06/2026.
● Acting President Rodríguez called on all healthcare professionals nationwide to report to
hospitals immediately (CBS News 25/06/2026.
10

Priority Needs
The following is based on confirmed reporting and statements from humanitarian actors active on the
ground as of 25 June 2026, and is not an exhaustive needs assessment. Several priorities identified
below are inferred from fragmented early reporting, pre-existing vulnerability data, and established
patterns from comparable earthquake responses.
Every need identified below lands on a population and a system already under severe stress: nearly 8
million people in Venezuela were in need of humanitarian support before the earthquake struck, against
a response plan only 23.2% funded (OCHA 25/06/2026, NRC, 25/06/2026.
Search and Rescue (immediate, life-saving)
● Active rescue operations are ongoing at multiple confirmed collapse sites across Caracas,
including San Bernardino, El Paraíso, Altamira, and Chacao, as well as in La Guaira and Falcón
state. The mayor of Chacao confirmed that rescue teams could still hear people alive under the
rubble overnight (CNN 25/06/2026.
● OCHA is coordinating the international deployment of urban search and rescue teams through
the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group and has surged a rapid response team to
reinforce its in-country presence (OCHA 25/06/2026.
Debris removal
● Acting President Rodríguez made a direct public appeal to the private sector for heavy
machinery to assist with rescue and debris removal, signaling that the governmentʼs own
equipment capacity is insufficient for the scale of collapse across multiple states (Yahoo
News/AP 25/06/2026. Debris removal is not only a recovery task, but an active life-saving
priority while people remain confirmed trapped under rubble in Caracas and La Guaira (CNN
25/06/2026.
Health
● With hospitals confirmed to be damaged and operating under strain, the immediate medical gap
centres on trauma surgery, crush injury care, wound treatment, and blood supply.
● Direct Relief and International Medical Corps are mobilizing surgical supplies, antibiotics, and
wound care kits in response to requests from local health partners (Direct Relief 25/06/2026,
International Medical Corps 25/06/2026.
● The IFRC additionally flags psychosocial support as an immediate priority (IFRC 25/06/2026.
This falls on a health system where approximately 70% of the population already had lacked
reliable access to care before the earthquake (European Commission ECHO 2026.
● The domestic market for essential items, including medical supplies, is likely insufficient to meet
needs at the current scale, making international imports critical (Al Jazeera 25/06/2026.
Shelter and Non-Food Items
● With families unable to return to collapsed or structurally unsafe homes, and ongoing aftershock
risk preventing structural assessments of standing buildings (see Displacement & Shelter), the
operational gap is emergency shelter materials and essential household items for displaced
families. The IOM confirmed it is preparing to provide both (IOM 25/06/2026.
● Structural assessment of standing but damaged buildings is also an urgent need: several
neighbourhoods in Caracas have been partially restricted due to the risk of further collapse, and
residents cannot safely return until buildings are inspected (CNN 25/06/2026.
11

● The capacity of schools and reception centres activated as shelters relative to actual need
remains unknown.
Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene WASH
● With power outages disrupting pumping infrastructure and water access already severely
limited before the earthquake (see Water & Sanitation), the immediate operational need is
emergency water supply, trucking and purification, alongside sanitation provision for displaced
populations and hygiene kits. Both the IFRC and IOM have flagged this as a priority need in the
hours and days ahead (IFRC 25/06/2026, IOM 25/06/2026.
Protection
● Protection monitoring for displaced populations, particularly women and children in makeshift
and collective shelter settings, is an immediate need that has not yet been addressed in
published response plans.
● Reflecting the scale of family separation caused by the disaster, Red Cross Societies in six
countries, Ecuador, Colombia, Mexico, Costa Rica, Honduras, and Argentina, have activated
restoring family links services to help Venezuelan diaspora communities locate relatives (IFRC
25/06/2026.
● No confirmed reporting on broader protection risks, including gender-based violence,
exploitation, or abuse in displacement settings, has been published as of this report. These risks
should be monitored closely as displaced populations move into collective shelter settings.
Access and Logistics
● As documented in the Transport section, the airport closure and unconfirmed status of the La
Guaira seaport represent the primary bottleneck for incoming international relief. The
operational priority is the rapid assessment of alternative entry points, secondary airports and
land crossings from Colombia, and the clearance of debris blocking internal routes.
● The U.S. Department of Defense and Germany have both committed assets to support access
(CNN 25/06/2026.
Education
● Classes have been suspended nationwide for at least one week, and some school buildings
have been repurposed as shelters and donation centres (CBS News 25/06/2026 The
immediate need is the rapid assessment of school buildings for structural safety, both to
determine which can reopen and which cannot safely serve as shelters, and the establishment
of temporary or alternative learning spaces for affected children.
● School closures caused by the earthquake therefore risk deepening an already acute learning
crisis, particularly for children who were already attending irregularly or not at all.
12

Outlook
The following outlook is a forward-looking scenario based on lessons from previous earthquake
responses, established humanitarian response patterns, and pre-crisis vulnerability data for Venezuela.
It is not a prediction of confirmed events. Actual impacts, priorities, and response timelines will depend
on the scale of damage, evolving assessments, government actions, and the availability of humanitarian
assistance.
Immediate phase 072 hours)
Search and rescue dominates along with debris removal; the ~72-hour crush-survival window makes
airport reopening or alternative entry decisive for incoming teams. Casualty figures will climb sharply
as teams reach unassessed areas, above all La Guaira and the epicentral states of Carabobo and
Yaracuy and aftershocks will complicate and endanger operations. Emergency medical demand
peaks; displaced populations need immediate shelter, water and food; and power and
telecommunications restoration is critical for coordination.
Days 47 (assessment and scale-up)
As rescue transitions to recovery, the full scale of casualties, displacement and damage clarifies.
Coordination mechanisms OCHA, cluster system) should be fully operational; shelter and NFI
distribution should reach scale; WASH interventions become critical as stored water runs out; damaged
health facilities need rehabilitation and resupply; and food distributions should be operational. Mw 6
aftershocks remain possible and could generate secondary casualties.
Days 814 (sustained emergency and early transition)
Disease surveillance and outbreak response should intensify given extreme baseline vulnerability.
Temporary learning spaces and sustained protection monitoring GBV, unaccompanied children,
trafficking) are needed. Debris removal and structural-safety assessment will determine continued
displacement. Funding mobilisation - likely a flash appeal - will be decisive against the pre-existing 24%
funded plan, and Venezuela's political transition and oil-revenue capacity will shape the speed and
scale of international engagement.
13

Annex 1. Parishes by state, ranked by modelled impact
For each focus state in severity order, the parishes ranked highest by the model, ordered by estimated
fatalities and then by relevance. Estimated fatalities USGS PAGER reflect shaking intensity; the
relevance score 0 to 100 reflects the vulnerable population exposed at MMI VI or above. Peak MMI is
the highest intensity recorded in the parish. Parish names are as recorded in the dataset. All figures are
modelled estimates, indicative only and superseded by confirmed official counts.

Annex 2. Estimation method and data sources
The modelled figures in this report come from a hazard-analytics pipeline that overlays the USGS
ShakeMap for the event on population and infrastructure layers and outputs a ranking of parishes
(admin-3 units) by humanitarian priority. It uses only open data and holds one row for each parish inside
the damaging-shaking footprint.
Shaking and population exposure. The USGS ShakeMap provides the modelled intensity MMI surface.
WorldPop population is summed within each intensity band to give the population that felt the
earthquake MMI II and above) and the populations exposed at the damage threshold MMI VI, very
strong VII, severe VIII and violent IX shaking. A population-weighted mean MMI summarises the
intensity people actually experienced.
Fatalities and economic loss. Estimated fatalities apply the USGS PAGER model, a lognormal loss
function with country-specific parameters, to the exposed population; PAGER also produces the
probabilistic fatality and economic-loss ranges and the alert level. These are statistical estimates for
planning, not counts.
Built-up surface and facilities. Built-up area exposed to MMI VI and above is taken from the GHSL
built-up layer. Health and education facilities in the shaking zone are counted from OpenStreetMap,
accessed through HDX; these counts depend on mapping completeness and should be read as a floor
rather than a full census.
Relevance score. The relevance score answers a specific question: how many likely-deprived people
felt damaging shaking. It takes the population exposed to MMI VI or above, a fixed threshold, so it
counts exposure above VI rather than scaling with how intense the shaking was, and weights it by a
deprivation score blending NASA SEDAC's Gridded Relative Deprivation Index with OPHI's
Multidimensional Poverty Index. The vulnerability-weighted population, the affected population
multiplied by one plus that deprivation score, is rescaled to a 0 to 100 score within the event. It is
distinct from the PAGER fatality estimate above, which is driven by shaking intensity and, for Venezuela,
by a steep loss function that concentrates deaths in the highest-intensity parishes. The relevance score
is an initial version that the modelling team intends to refine, including treating intensity continuously
rather than at a fixed VI threshold; it is indicative and should be validated against field and official
sources.
Aggregation and uncertainty. National and state totals are sums of the per-parish values, not figures
taken from a single cell. All values are modelled estimates at parish level and carry wide uncertainty;
confirmed official figures are the authoritative record and take precedence over any modelled estimate
as verification proceeds.
The methodology utilized in this report has been jointly developed with GiveDirectly.

documents.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #1 (June 25, 2026, Time: 3:00 am)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**June 25, 2026**  
**Time: 3:00 am**

**Highlights**

- Two consecutive earthquakes of approximately M7.2 and M7.5 occurred around 18:00 local time, followed by more than 20 aftershocks.
- 32 fatalities (preliminary) and over 700 injured, according to authorities.
- La Guaira State identified as the most affected, with multiple buildings collapsed.
- Significant structural damage in Caracas, including partial collapses and mass evacuations.
- Maiquetía International Airport closed; Metro and rail services suspended.
- State of Emergency declared and Emergency Operations Command activated.
- International rescue teams are being deployed.

**Situation Overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes in the central-northern region of the country on June 24 at approximately 18:00 local time. The first event (M7.2) was followed by a stronger second earthquake (up to M7.5), significantly amplifying surface impacts. The occurrence of multiple aftershocks (more than 20) continues to pose a high level of risk.

The Government response is focused on search and rescue operations, emergency medical care, and damage assessment. The impact has been severe and widespread, affecting critical infrastructure, public services, and housing across several states, with the highest concentration in the Capital District, La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo, and Yaracuy.

Caracas experienced prolonged shaking (>60 seconds), resulting in widespread panic, evacuations, and significant structural damage to buildings. La Guaira State has been identified as the area with the most severe impact, with multiple building collapses and conditions classified as a disaster zone, where intensive search and rescue operations are ongoing.

Preliminary figures report 32 fatalities and more than 700 injured, with numbers expected to rise as rescue efforts continue in collapsed structures.

documents.title: Venezuela: IRC launches emergency response in wake of devastating twin earthquakes
documents.body_text:
**Thousands of people face urgent humanitarian needs following powerful twin earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 on the Richter scale**

Caracas, Venezuela, June 25, 2026 — Two powerful earthquakes have killed at least 164 people and injured nearly 1,000 across Venezuela, leaving thousands more in urgent need of emergency assistance. The International Rescue Committee (IRC) is mobilizing an initial emergency response to reach those in need, including the distribution of essential relief items and emergency medical supplies to frontline workers in the most affected areas. As the situation develops, the IRC will assess further needs across affected communities.

The earthquakes have compounded an already severe humanitarian situation in Venezuela, where years of economic collapse and displacement have left communities with little capacity to absorb a disaster of this scale. Many families impacted by the earthquakes were already struggling to meet their most basic needs. With national services under significant strain, essential rescue and recovery efforts may take weeks if not months.

*"What we are seeing is catastrophic,"* **said Nicole Kast, IRC Venezuela Country Director.** *"People have lost everything in a matter of seconds, and the need for immediate support is overwhelming. In some of the hardest-hit areas, damaged infrastructure and limited civil response capacity mean people may be trapped and unable to reach safety or be reached by those trying to help. We are working to get supplies to frontline workers as fast as possible so that lives can be saved."*

Venezuela was already facing a protracted humanitarian crisis before these earthquakes struck with nearly 8 million people in need of urgent humanitarian assistance and millions of people living in poverty with limited access to basic services.

The IRC has been working in Venezuela since 2021, providing health, protection, and emergency support to vulnerable populations. Our teams work with local partners to address urgent health, nutrition, protection, education, food security, and livelihood needs for Venezuelans inside Venezuela and across the border in Colombia.

documents.title: Declaración del portavoz de la OIM sobre los terremotos en Venezuela
documents.body_text:
**Ginebra, 25 de junio de 2026** – La Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM) expresa su profunda consternación ante los devastadores terremotos que han afectado a Venezuela, causando destrucción, numerosas víctimas mortales y heridos, y afectando a numerosas familias y comunidades.

Nuestros pensamientos están con quienes han perdido a sus seres queridos, han resultado heridos o han perdido sus hogares y medios de vida. En este difícil momento, expresamos nuestra solidaridad con el pueblo de Venezuela y con los equipos de primera respuesta que trabajan incansablemente para salvar vidas y asistir a las personas afectadas.

Muchas personas se encuentran desplazadas o requieren asistencia urgente. Los equipos de la OIM están evaluando la situación y en coordinación estrecha estrechamente con las autoridades nacionales y locales, los asociados de las Naciones Unidas y las organizaciones humanitarias para determinar las necesidades más urgentes y apoyar una respuesta rápida.

Como parte de sus esfuerzos de preparación, la OIM se está movilizando para brindar asistencia vital, incluidos servicios de alojamiento de emergencia, agua, saneamiento e higiene, así como atención de salud y artículos no alimentarios esenciales para las familias afectadas, al tiempo que apoya los esfuerzos para garantizar que las familias desplazadas reciban la protección y la asistencia que necesitan.

La magnitud de esta crisis exige una acción rápida y colectiva. Cada hora cuenta para llegar a quienes lo han perdido todo y ayudar a las comunidades a emprender el camino hacia la recuperación.

La OIM hace un llamamiento a la comunidad internacional para que apoye los esfuerzos humanitarios y se solidarice con el pueblo de Venezuela en este momento en que enfrenta las consecuencias devastadoras de este desastre.

La OIM reafirma su compromiso de trabajar junto a sus socios para brindar asistencia que salva vidas y apoyar los esfuerzos de recuperación en los días y semanas venideros.

*Visite la página de donaciones de la OIM* [***Emergencia Terremotos Venezuela***](https://www.iom.int/venezuela-earthquake-response?form=venezuela-earthquake&utm_source=press-release&utm_medium=referral) *para hacer una contribución.*

*Para más información, visite el* [***Centro de Medios de la OIM***](https://www.iom.int/media-inquiries)*.*

documents.title: M 7.5 - 28 km SE of Yumare, Venezuela | Shake MMI Impact Zones
documents.body_text:
Two major earthquakes struck near Yumare, Venezuela on 24 June — an M 7.2 followed one minute later by an M 7.5, both triggering red USGS alerts.

iMMAP's rapid impact analysis, combining USGS ShakeMap intensity data with WorldPop 2026 population figures, shows the scale of potential exposure:

→ ~590,000 people in severe to violent shaking zones (MMI VII+) across both events  
→ 4.8 million exposed to strong shaking (VI) from the M 7.5 alone  
→ Over 16 million people within the total earthquake footprint

The shaking footprint of the stronger, shallower M 7.5 event extends toward the Valencia–Caracas urban corridor — one of Venezuela's most densely populated areas — placing significant urban populations within high-intensity zones.

The sequential nature of these events compounds the challenge: cumulative structural damage, disrupted access routes, and overlapping needs will shape what an effective response looks like in the hours and days ahead.

The European Union conveys its condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims of the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela. At this difficult moment, the European Union expresses its solidarity with the people of Venezuela and with all those engaged in rescue and relief operations.   
  
These earthquakes come at a time when millions of Venezuelans continue to face significant humanitarian needs. The European Union is in contact with the authorities and stands ready to support emergency response efforts while already working with partners to assess urgent humanitarian needs as more information becomes available.   
  
The EU stands ready to mobilise assistance through the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism, should we receive a request. In the meantime, to support the response, the Copernicus satellite system has been activated in emergency mapping mode.   
  
We remain in close communication with our humanitarian partners and stand ready to provide all necessary operational support.

documents.title: Venezuela: Deadly earthquake will deepen suffering
documents.body_text:
## Venezuela: Deadly earthquake will deepen suffering

Statement by Jan Egeland, the Norwegian Refugee Council’s (NRC) Secretary General following the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes in Venezuela:


“What NRC aid workers witness on the ground in and around Caracas is devastation beyond belief in the wake of the major earthquakes that had their epicentre West of Venezuela’s capital. The deadly earthquake struck in the evening of a national holiday, when many families were at home. The NRC office building in Caracas sustained damage, but thankfully all our staff are safe and accounted for.

“This earthquake will deepen the suffering for millions already in dire need. More than a quarter of the country’s population needed urgent aid even before the earthquakes.

“NRC has been working in Venezuela for more than two decades and will provide emergency relief to the countless families that have lost their homes and property and have seen loved one perish in the rubble. We are currently assessing the most urgent needs and will seek funding from donor nations and the private sector to scale up our support for those most severely stricken.

“The deep suffering of the crisis-engulfed people in Venezuela has been neglected for too long. For the last three years aid workers on the ground have received less than a third of the funding needed for providing even the minimum of humanitarian relief needed. Donors must urgently step up support as this earthquake has become a catastrophe on top of a crisis. There can be no delay in this support. National authorities and the international community must step up their cooperation immediately to provide relief and enable a viable plan for much needed reconstruction.”

**Notes to editors:**

- On the evening of 24 June, Venezuela was hit by two back-to-back earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 on the Richter scale. The epicentre of the earthquakes is close to the capital Caracas, which was seen significant damage including to NRC’s office. Significant damage has also been witnessed in areas across the north of the country with the earthquake felt as far away as Bogota, Colombia.
- In 2026, 7.9 million people in the country are in need of humanitarian assistance, 27.7 per cent of the total population (28.5 million people) ([OCHA](https://www.unocha.org/venezuela)). 5.5 million of them have been targeted for assistance.
- The humanitarian response plan in Venezuela is currently 23.2 per cent funded with 146.9 million of the 632.2 million US dollars required having been delivered ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/overview/2026)).
- The 2025 humanitarian response plan in Venezuela was just 20 per cent funded, while the 2024 plan was 28 per cent funded ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/1517/summary)).
- NRC has been working in Venezuela since 2005 providing education, protection, legal guidance, and water and sanitation support. In 2025 we reached more than 65,000 people across four states.

**For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:**

- NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329

documents.title: Declaración sobre Venezuela del Secretario General Adjunto de Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia Tom Fletcher, 25 de junio de 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
Estamos plenamente movilizados para apoyar al pueblo de Venezuela tras los mortíferos devastadores terremotos que azotaron el país ayer.

Estoy en contacto constante con nuestro equipo en Caracas, dirigido por el Coordinador Humanitario Gianluca Rampolla, para garantizar una respuesta rápida y eficaz. Esta mañana ha hablado con la Presidenta interina y estamos evaluando con carácter de urgencia cuáles son las necesidades. Nuestro equipo en Venezuela está colaborando con las autoridades para identificar las prioridades.

OCHA está coordinando el despliegue rápido de equipos de búsqueda y rescate urbano, procedentes de toda la comunidad internacional, a través del Grupo Asesor Internacional de Operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate. Estoy enviando un equipo de respuesta rápida para reforzar al equipo de OCHA en el país.

La solidaridad y las ofertas concretas originarias de la región y de otros lugares han sido magníficas. Los próximos días requerirán un esfuerzo colectivo masivo para apoyar la respuesta liderada por el Gobierno y para ayudar a las comunidades.

Incluso antes de estos terremotos, casi 8 millones de personas en Venezuela necesitaban ayuda humanitaria. Este desastre corre el riesgo de agravar las vulnerabilidades existentes.

Es esencial y urgente contar con un apoyo internacional sostenido para las organizaciones humanitarias que están respondiendo sobre el terreno.

documents.title: Statement on Venezuela by Tom Fletcher, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, 25 June 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
documents.body_text:
*Geneva, 25 June 2026*

We are fully mobilised to support the people of [Venezuela](https://www.unocha.org/venezuela) following the deadly and devastating earthquakes that hit the country yesterday.

I’m in constant contact with our team in Caracas, led by Humanitarian Coordinator Gianluca Rampolla, to ensure a swift and effective response. He has spoken this morning to the interim President and we are assessing urgently what is needed. Our team in Venezuela is working with the authorities to identify priorities.

OCHA is coordinating the rapid deployment of Urban Search and Rescue Teams from across the international community through the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group. I am surging a rapid response team to reinforce the OCHA team in country.

The solidarity and practical offers from the region and beyond are superb. The coming days will require a massive collective effort to support the Government-led response and help communities.

Even before these earthquakes, nearly 8 million people in Venezuela were in need of humanitarian support. This disaster risks deepening existing vulnerabilities.

Sustained international support for humanitarian organizations responding on the ground is essential and urgent.

documents.title: La Croix-Rouge intervient au Venezuela alors que les besoins augmentent à la suite de deux puissants séismes successifs
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas/Panama/Genève, le 25 juin 2026** — Deux puissants séismes ont frappé le centre-nord du Venezuela dans la soirée du 24 juin, à moins d'une minute d'intervalle : une première secousse de magnitude 7,2 s'est produite vers 18 h 04 (heure locale), suivie 39 secondes plus tard d'un séisme principal de magnitude 7,5. Les épicentres étaient situés dans la région de Yaracuy, selon l'Institut d'études géologiques des États-Unis (USGS).

Les séismes ont provoqué l'effondrement de bâtiments et endommagé des habitations ainsi que des commerces à Caracas et dans plusieurs États du pays. Les dégâts les plus importants ont été signalés à La Guaira et dans le Grand Caracas. Les autorités nationales ont déclaré l'état d'urgence, suspendu les cours et les activités non essentielles, ordonné des évacuations préventives, lancé des opérations de recherche et de sauvetage et mis en place des centres d'accueil pour les personnes sinistrées, tandis que les hôpitaux prennent en charge les blessés.

Les réseaux d'électricité, de télécommunications et de transport ont été perturbés. D'importants dommages ont également été signalés sur des infrastructures essentielles de santé et de transport, entraînant des interruptions ou un fonctionnement limité de certains services publics.

Les évaluations des dégâts restent préliminaires et l'ampleur réelle de l'impact humain n'est pas encore connue. De fortes répliques continuent de représenter un risque supplémentaire pour les communautés touchées ainsi que pour les équipes d'intervention.

La Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne est pleinement mobilisée. Son réseau national d'hôpitaux et de polycliniques reste opérationnel et continue de fournir des soins. La Société nationale a déployé des équipes de secours pour soutenir les opérations d'évacuation et de recherche et a envoyé, durant la nuit, quatre équipes d'évaluation rapide dans les zones les plus touchées, tout en mobilisant les stocks de secours prépositionnés.

Bien que son siège national ait subi d'importants dégâts, la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne s'assure de la sécurité de son personnel et de ses volontaires, active ses protocoles de sécurité et diffuse des conseils de prévention face aux séismes auprès des communautés, alors même que nombre de ses volontaires interviennent tout en étant eux-mêmes touchés dans leurs quartiers.

Alors que les évaluations se poursuivent, les besoins les plus urgents devraient concerner les opérations de recherche et de sauvetage, les abris d'urgence pour les familles dont les habitations ont été endommagées ou détruites, ainsi que les soins de santé d'urgence, notamment la prise en charge des traumatismes et le soutien psychosocial.

L'accès à l'eau potable, aux services d'assainissement et aux articles ménagers essentiels devrait également constituer une priorité dans les prochaines heures et les prochains jours.

Les communications étant perturbées et de nombreuses familles ayant été séparées, les Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge d'Équateur, de Colombie, du Mexique, du Costa Rica, du Honduras et d'Argentine — des pays qui accueillent d'importantes communautés vénézuéliennes — ont déjà activé leurs services de rétablissement des liens familiaux afin d'aider les personnes à retrouver des nouvelles de leurs proches.

La Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) active ses mécanismes d'intervention, notamment son Fonds d'urgence pour les secours en cas de catastrophe (IFRC-DREF), à mesure que de nouvelles informations deviennent disponibles.

documents.title: IOM Spokesperson Statement on Venezuela Earthquakes
documents.body_text:
**Geneva, 25 June 2026** – The International Organization for Migration (IOM) is deeply saddened by the devastating earthquakes that have struck Venezuela, causing widespread destruction, numerous fatalities and injuries, and affecting countless families and communities.

Our thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones, been injured, or seen their homes and livelihoods destroyed. At this difficult moment, we stand in solidarity with the people of Venezuela as well as the first responders working tirelessly to save lives and assist those affected.

Many people are displaced or in urgent need of assistance. IOM teams are assessing the situation and coordinating closely with national and local authorities, UN partners, and humanitarian organizations to determine the most pressing needs and support a rapid response.

As part of its preparedness efforts, IOM is gearing up to provide emergency shelter assistance, water, sanitation, hygiene, and health services as well as essential non-food items to affected families, while supporting efforts to ensure that displaced populations receive the protection and assistance they need.

The scale of this disaster demands swift and collective action. Every hour counts in reaching those who have lost everything and helping communities begin the path to recovery. IOM calls on the international community to support humanitarian efforts and stand with the people of Venezuela as they confront the devastating consequences of this earthquake.

IOM remains committed to working alongside partners to deliver life-saving assistance and support recovery efforts in the days and weeks ahead.

*For more information, please visit [IOM’s Media Centre](https://www.iom.int/media-inquiries).*

documents.title: Déclaration du porte-parole de l’OIM sur les séismes au Venezuela
documents.body_text:
**Genève, 25 juin 2026** – L'Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM) est profondément attristée par les séismes dévastateurs qui ont frappé le Venezuela, causant des destructions massives, de nombreux décès et blessés, et affectant d'innombrables familles et communautés.

Nos pensées vont à toutes les personnes qui ont perdu des proches, ont été blessées ou ont vu leurs foyers et leurs moyens de subsistance anéantis. En ce moment difficile, nous nous tenons aux côtés du peuple vénézuélien ainsi que des premiers intervenants qui œuvrent sans relâche pour sauver des vies et porter assistance aux personnes affectées.

De nombreuses personnes ont été déplacées ou ont un besoin urgent d’assistance. Les équipes de l’OIM évaluent la situation et coordonnent étroitement leurs actions avec les autorités nationales et locales, les partenaires des Nations Unies et les organisations humanitaires, afin de déterminer les besoins les plus pressants et d’appuyer une réponse rapide et coordonnée.

Dans le cadre de ses efforts de préparation, l’OIM se prépare à fournir une assistance d’urgence en matière d’abris, d’eau, d’assainissement et d’hygiène, de services de santé, ainsi que des articles essentiels non alimentaires aux familles touchées, tout en veillant à ce que les populations déplacées bénéficient de protection et d’assistance.

L’ampleur de cette catastrophe exige une action rapide et collective. Chaque heure compte pour atteindre ceux qui ont tout perdu et aider les communautés à s’engager sur la voie du relèvement. L’OIM appelle la communauté internationale à soutenir les efforts humanitaires et à se tenir aux côtés du peuple vénézuélien alors qu’il fait face aux conséquences dévastatrices de ces séismes.

L’OIM reste déterminée à travailler aux côtés de ses partenaires pour apporter une assistance vitale et soutenir les efforts de relèvement dans les jours et les semaines à venir.

*Pour de plus amples informations, veuillez consulter le [Centre médias de l’OIM](https://www.iom.int/media-inquiries).*

documents.title: Venezuela: Cruz Roja responde a las necesidades que emergen tras dos devastadores terremotos consecutivos
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas/Panamá/Ginebra, 25 de junio de 2026** — Dos potentes terremotos sacudieron el centro-norte de Venezuela la noche del 24 de junio, con menos de un minuto de diferencia: un sismo precursor de magnitud 7.2 a eso de las 6:04 p. m., hora local, seguido 39 segundos después por un sismo principal de magnitud 7.5, con epicentros en la región de Yaracuy, según el Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos (USGS).

Los terremotos provocaron colapsos estructurales y daños en viviendas y comercios en Caracas y en varios estados, con afectaciones particularmente graves en La Guaira y la Gran Caracas. Las autoridades nacionales declararon estado de emergencia, suspendieron las clases y las actividades no esenciales, ordenaron evacuaciones preventivas, activaron operaciones de búsqueda y rescate y habilitaron centros de recepción para las personas afectadas, mientras los hospitales atienden a quienes resultaron heridas.

El suministro eléctrico, las telecomunicaciones y el transporte se han visto interrumpidos, y se han reportado daños críticos en infraestructura esencial de salud y transporte, lo que deja los servicios públicos intermitentes o interrumpidos en algunas zonas. Las evaluaciones de daños siguen siendo preliminares y aún no se conoce el impacto humano total, mientras fuertes réplicas suponen riesgos adicionales para las comunidades afectadas y para los equipos que responden.

La Cruz Roja Venezolana está operativa y respondiendo. Su red nacional de hospitales y centros de salud se mantiene activa y continúa prestando atención. La Sociedad Nacional activó equipos de rescate para apoyar las labores de evacuación y búsqueda, y desplegó durante la noche cuatro equipos de evaluación para realizar valoraciones rápidas en las zonas más afectadas, al tiempo que moviliza suministros de socorro preposicionados.

Aunque ha reportado daños críticos en su propia Sede Nacional, la Cruz Roja Venezolana verifica la seguridad de su personal y su voluntariado, activa protocolos de seguridad y difunde recomendaciones de seguridad ante sismos entre las comunidades, incluso mientras muchas de sus personas voluntarias responden enfrentando esta emergencia en sus propios barrios.

Mientras continúan las evaluaciones, las necesidades más urgentes que se anticipan son la búsqueda y el rescate, el albergue de emergencia para las familias cuyas viviendas resultaron dañadas o destruidas, y la atención médica de urgencia, incluida la atención de trauma y el apoyo psicosocial. También se prevé que el agua segura y el saneamiento, así como los artículos esenciales para el hogar, sean prioridades en las próximas horas y días.

Con las comunicaciones interrumpidas y muchas familias separadas, las Sociedades de la Cruz Roja de Ecuador, Colombia, México, Costa Rica y Argentina —países que albergan a numerosas comunidades venezolanas— ya activaron sus servicios de restablecimiento del contacto entre familiares, para ayudar a las personas a buscar noticias de sus seres queridos.

La Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y la Media Luna Roja está activando sus mecanismos de respuesta, incluido su Fondo de Emergencia para la Respuesta a Desastres (IFRC-DREF) a medida que se dispone de más información.

documents.title: Venezuela: Red Cross responds as needs emerge in the aftermath of powerful back-to-back earthquakes
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
**Caracas/Panama City/Geneva, 25 June 2026** — Two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on the evening of 24 June, less than a minute apart: a 7.2 magnitude foreshock at around 6:04 p.m. local time, followed 39 seconds later by a 7.5 magnitude mainshock, with epicentres in the Yaracuy region, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS).

The earthquakes caused structural collapses and damage to homes and businesses in Caracas and across several states, with particularly serious impact reported in La Guaira and Greater Caracas. National authorities have declared a state of emergency, suspended classes and non-essential activities, ordered preventive evacuations, activated search-and-rescue operations and set up reception centres for people affected, while hospitals receive the injured.

Power, telecommunications and transport have been disrupted, and critical damage has been reported to essential health and transport infrastructure, leaving public services intermittent or interrupted in some areas. Damage assessments remain preliminary, and the full human impact is not yet known while strong aftershocks are posing additional risks to affected communities and to the teams responding.

The Venezuelan Red Cross is operational and responding. Its nationwide network of hospitals and polyclinics remains active and continues to deliver care. The National Society has activated rescue teams to support evacuation and search efforts and deployed four assessment teams overnight to carry out rapid evaluations in the worst-affected areas, while mobilising prepositioned relief supplies.

Although it has reported critical damage to its own National Headquarters, the Venezuelan Red Cross is accounting for the safety of its staff and volunteers, activating security protocols and sharing earthquake safety guidance with communities — even as many of its volunteers respond while facing this emergency in their own neighbourhoods.

While assessments continue, the most urgent anticipated needs are search and rescue, emergency shelter for families whose homes have been damaged or destroyed, and emergency health care, including trauma care and psychosocial support. Safe water and sanitation and essential household items are also expected to be priorities in the hours and days ahead.

With communications disrupted and many families separated, Red Cross Societies in Ecuador, Colombia, Mexico, Costa Rica, Honduras and Argentina — countries home to large Venezuelan communities — have already activated their restoring family links services, helping people search for news of their loved ones.

The International Federation of the Red Cross and the Red Crescent Societies is activating its response mechanisms, including its Disaster Response Emergency Fund (IFRC-DREF), as more information becomes available.

[https://x.com/CruzRojaVe/status/2070015232089420141](https://x.com/CruzRojaVe/status/2070015232089420141?s=20)

documents.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Rescuers race to free people trapped in rubble as children forced from their homes by massive quakes
documents.body_text:
## **Save the Children is assessing the situation on the ground and working with our staff and local partners to understand urgent needs and support affected families as quickly as possible.**

**CARACAS, 25 June 2026** – Rescuers are racing to find people trapped in the rubble of collapsed buildings after two massive earthquakes struck west of the capital Caracas, forcing children and their families from their homes, Save the Children said.

The double earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude have cut off communications and power in some areas so the extent of the destruction and casualties will take time to become clear.

The earthquakes struck during the evening when many people were returning home, increasing concerns that individuals may be trapped beneath collapsed structures.

Save the Children works with partners in the affected areas and is working to assess urgent needs. Preventative evacuations have been carried out in several cities, with some children and families moving into open areas as aftershocks continue.

**Fatima Andraca, Country Director, Save the Children in Venezuela said:**

“Children are among the most vulnerable after these earthquakes. Some will have lost their homes and aftershocks are continuing, causing further terror for children and heightening the risk of further damage and casualties.

“While the extent of the destruction will take time to become clear, we know from past experience that children will need urgent support to access shelter, food, water and healthcare now. They may have been separated from their families in the chaos and could be at risk of exploitation and abuse.

“Save the Children is assessing the situation on the ground and working with our staff and local partners to understand urgent needs and support affected families as quickly as possible."

documents.title: VEN: Earthquake - 06-2026 - Earthquake ( 2026-06-25)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
documents.body_text:
## **Description**

On 24 June 2026, two strong earthquakes, preliminarily measured at magnitudes 7.1 and 7.5, struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with epicentres near Morón, Carabobo State. The earthquakes were felt across much of the country, including Caracas, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo and neighbouring states. Therefore, the national goverment of Venezuela declared the state of emergency.

Preliminary information indicates damage to residential and commercial buildings, with reports of structural collapses in parts of Caracas and damage to infrastructure in several affected areas. Search and rescue operations have been activated while authorities continue rapid damage assessments. Power and telecommunications interruptions have been reported in some locations, and hospitals are receiving injured people.

The full humanitarian impact is still being assessed. Official information on casualties, displaced people and infrastructure damage remains limited. Significant aftershocks are expected, posing additional risks to affected communities and emergency responders. In addition, the National Headquarters of the Venezuelan Red Cross reported critical damage in the infrastructure.

Critical damage has also been reported to essential social infrastructure, including the airport and hospitals, while public services are intermittent or completely disrupted

## **Request For Assistance**

Government Requests International Assistance: **No**

NS Requests International Assistance: **No**

## **Information Bulletin Published**

No

## **Actions taken by National Society**

### **General**

Damage/Needs assessment

Search & Rescue

Camp management

RFL

Evacuation

**Summary**

The National Society and IFRC are participating in a coordination meeting held by the Ministry of Disaster Risk Management, alongside other relief agencies present in the area to begin coordinating the response. Additionally, at the national headquarters level, the Emergency Operations Center has been activated, ambulances have been deployed in the Capital District, rescue teams have been mobilized to assist those affected by the collapse of infrastructure, and shelter facilities are being prepared for people in need of refuge. The overall situation of the emergency remains uncertain, and a preliminary assessment of the impact is expected shortly to coordinate actions following the search and rescue operations.

## **Actions taken by Federation**

**Summary**

The IFRC through its delegaton is providing technical support to the Venezuelan Red Cross regarding emergency, to assess the appropriate response mechanism. A coordination call with the Americas Regional office took place at 2100 local time.

## **Actions taken by RCRC**

**Summary**

The Colombian Red Cross has begun mobilizing its search and rescue teams and stands ready for international deployment should the Venezuelan Red Cross request it. Coordination efforts are underway to assess the scale of the situation, and crisis centers are being established in the countries that make up the closest response ring for Venezuela. Similarly, the German Red Cross is actively considering the implementation of its crisis response plan should the National Health Service require it.

## **Actions taken by others**

Deployment of search and rescue teams and medical assistance by civil protection, the police, public agencies, and other emergency response organizations.

DESCRIPTION
On 24 June 2026, two strong earthquakes, preliminarily measured at magnitudes 7.1 and 7.5, struck
north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with epicentres near Morón, Carabobo State. The
earthquakes were felt across much of the country, including Caracas, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo
and neighbouring states. Therefore, the national goverment of Venezuela declared the state of
emergency.
Preliminary information indicates damage to residential and commercial buildings, with reports of
structural collapses in parts of Caracas and damage to infrastructure in several affected areas.
Search and rescue operations have been activated while authorities continue rapid damage
assessments. Power and telecommunications interruptions have been reported in some locations,
and hospitals are receiving injured people.
The full humanitarian impact is still being assessed. Official information on casualties, displaced
people and infrastructure damage remains limited. Significant aftershocks are expected, posing
additional risks to affected communities and emergency responders. In addition, the National
Headquarters of the Venezuelan Red Cross reported critical damage in the infrastructure.
Critical damage has also been reported to essential social infrastructure, including the airport and
hospitals, while public services are intermittent or completely disrupted

Summary:
The National Society and IFRC are participating in a coordination meeting held by the Ministry of
Disaster Risk Management, alongside other relief agencies present in the area to begin coordinating
the response. Additionally, at the national headquarters level, the Emergency Operations Center has
been activated, ambulances have been deployed in the Capital District, rescue teams have been
mobilized to assist those affected by the collapse of infrastructure, and shelter facilities are being
prepared for people in need of refuge. The overall situation of the emergency remains uncertain, and a
preliminary assessment of the impact is expected shortly to coordinate actions following the search
and rescue operations.
ACTIONS TAKEN BY FEDERATION
Summary:
The IFRC through its delegaton is providing technical support to the Venezuelan Red Cross regarding
emergency, to assess the appropriate response mechanism. A coordination call with the Americas
Regional office took place at 2100 local time.
ACTIONS TAKEN BY RCRC
Summary:
The Colombian Red Cross has begun mobilizing its search and rescue teams and stands ready for
international deployment should the Venezuelan Red Cross request it. Coordination efforts are
underway to assess the scale of the situation, and crisis centers are being established in the countries
that make up the closest response ring for Venezuela. Similarly, the German Red Cross is actively
considering the implementation of its crisis response plan should the National Health Service require
it.
ACTIONS TAKEN BY OTHERS
Deployment of search and rescue teams and medical assistance by civil protection, the police, public
agencies, and other emergency response organizations.
